[2026-02-04] CrimsonBridge candidate lock-order guidance:
- Tentative canonical order for multi-shard ops: TaskTable (tasks + wake_state + stored_futures) -> Obligations -> Regions. Trace/metrics should be read-only and avoid locking in poll path.
- For region-first flows (cancel_request, create_obligation), consider snapshot+apply: grab region data (task IDs / limits) under region lock, release, then mutate TaskTable/Obligations in canonical order to avoid inversion.
- For task-completion flows (task_completed), keep TaskTable lock for record/state updates, then obligations (abort/leak), then regions (remove_task + advance_region_state).

This is just a proposed ordering to reduce inversion risk; actual order should be standardized in bd-1tc1m.

[2026-02-04] CrimsonBridge read-mostly access note:
- `ThreeLaneScheduler::governor_suggest` takes `state.lock()` to build a read-only `StateSnapshot`. This path is periodic but still on the scheduling loop.
- `Worker::new` grabs state once to read `io_driver_handle`, `trace_handle`, `timer_driver_handle` (read-only handles).

Sharding idea: keep read-only handles/metrics outside TaskTable lock (e.g., separate lightweight handle struct or RwLock) so read-mostly operations like `governor_suggest` can avoid contending with task/region mutations.

[2026-02-04] CrimsonBridge: existing sharded_state spec found
- `src/runtime/sharded_state.rs` already defines canonical lock order: **E (Config) → D (Instrumentation) → B (Regions) → A (Tasks) → C (Obligations)** with mnemonic "Every Day Brings Another Challenge".
- `ShardGuard` helpers encode this: `for_spawn` and `for_cancel` lock Regions→Tasks; `for_obligation` locks Regions→Obligations; `for_task_completed` locks Regions→Tasks→Obligations.
- This implies current monolithic `RuntimeState` flows should be aligned to **Regions before Tasks before Obligations** (opposite of my earlier tentative ordering). The main mismatches to watch during refactor: `task_completed` / `commit_obligation` / `abort_obligation` and any task-completion path that currently touches obligations before regions.

Recommend: treat sharded_state.rs as the authoritative lock-order spec and update any design docs/notes accordingly.

[2026-02-04] CrimsonBridge doc sanity check:
- `docs/runtime_state_contention_inventory.md` exists and is the canonical spec (bd-1tc1m/bd-20way). It lists canonical order **E→D→B→A→C**.
- Minor inconsistency: in the “Key Constraint: task_completed Bottleneck” section it says “Recommended lock order: D → E → B → A → C”. This conflicts with the canonical order section.

Recommend clarifying that line to **E→D→B→A→C** (or explain if instrumentation before config is intentional), so implementers don’t follow a conflicting order.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Rationale + guardrails:
- Contention today comes from a single RuntimeState mutex used by worker polling, LocalQueue/stealing, cancellation, and obligation handling. This is on hot paths and should be sharded to reduce lock hold time without changing semantics.
- Core invariants to preserve: structured concurrency (region close => quiescence), cancellation protocol (request → drain → finalize), and no obligation leaks.
- Determinism risk: multi-lock operations can introduce ordering nondeterminism or deadlocks if not strictly ordered. A canonical lock order is mandatory; avoid lock inversion in any cross-shard operation.
- Trace/metrics should remain read-mostly and must not add lock contention in poll paths; the design should either use lock-free handles (Arc/atomic) or RwLock with read dominance.
- Success criteria: reduced contention in LocalQueue/worker hot paths and unchanged behavior in cancellation/obligation/region close tests.

title: Implement ObligationRecord structure and registry
description:
# ObligationRecord Structure and Registry

## Purpose
Obligations are the operational enforcement mechanism for the “linear resource” discipline:
- reserve introduces a linear token
- commit/abort resolve it
- leaking a reserved token is a semantic error (caught in lab)

The registry tracks all obligations and ties them to:
- holder task
- owning region

## ObligationRecord (Plan-of-Record)
```rust
pub struct ObligationRecord {
    pub id: ObligationId,
    pub kind: ObligationKind,
    pub holder: TaskId,
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub state: ObligationState,
    pub created_at: Time,
    pub name: Option<String>,
}
```

## ObligationRegistry
Use internal arenas/indices (no slab crate required):

```rust
pub struct ObligationRegistry {
    pub obligations: Arena<ObligationRecord>,
    pub by_region: HashMap<RegionId, HashSet<ObligationId>>,
    pub by_holder: HashMap<TaskId, HashSet<ObligationId>>,
}
```

## Core Operations
- `reserve(kind, holder, region) -> ObligationId`
- `commit(id)` / `abort(id)`
- `on_task_complete(holder)` marks remaining reserved obligations as leaked (lab panic configurable)
- `pending_count(region)` gates region close

## Futurelock Detection (Lab)
A futurelock is “task holds obligations but stops being polled.”
- detect via `created_at` age + task progress counters
- surface as deterministic error in lab runs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Any task completion with outstanding reserved obligations is detected.
- Region close cannot complete with pending obligations.

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: runtime/scheduler/priority.rs (priority scheduler)
notes: VERDICT: SOUND. 0 bugs, 0 findings. 2201 lines audited. Three-lane priority scheduler (Cancel>Timed>Ready) using BinaryHeaps. ScheduledSet hybrid dense+overflow dedup (tag encoding, collision→overflow promotion). Ord impls: SchedulerEntry max-heap by priority, TimedEntry reversed for min-heap on deadline, both FIFO by generation. RNG tie-breaking collects same-priority/deadline entries, selects with modulo, pushes rest back. move_to_cancel_lane searches all lanes, retain+re-push. steal_ready_batch_into only steals from ready lane. pop_timed_only_with_hint safe because all collected entries share earliest deadline. ScheduleCertificate uses SipHash chaining. No concurrency - pure data structure with &mut self. ~40 tests cover all paths.

title: Create asupersync-macros proc-macro crate
description:
# Task

Set up the proc-macro crate for structured concurrency macros.

## Crate Structure

```
asupersync-macros/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs        # Macro exports
│   ├── scope.rs      # scope! macro
│   ├── spawn.rs      # spawn! macro
│   ├── join.rs       # join! macro
│   ├── race.rs       # race! macro
│   └── util.rs       # Shared utilities
```

## Cargo.toml

```toml
[package]
name = "asupersync-macros"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
proc-macro = true

[dependencies]
syn = { version = "2.0", features = ["full", "parsing"] }
quote = "1.0"
proc-macro2 = "1.0"

[dev-dependencies]
asupersync = { path = ".." }
```

## Integration with Main Crate

In main asupersync Cargo.toml:
```toml
[dependencies]
asupersync-macros = { path = "asupersync-macros" }

# Re-export macros
[features]
macros = ["asupersync-macros"]
```

In main asupersync lib.rs:
```rust
#[cfg(feature = "macros")]
pub use asupersync_macros::{scope, spawn, join, race};
```

- [ ] Cargo.toml with correct dependencies
- [ ] Basic lib.rs with placeholder macros
- [ ] Integration with main crate via feature
- [ ] cargo build works
- [ ] cargo test works

- Cancellation must not leak obligations.

title: [ALIEN][SCHED] Lyapunov-Guided Scheduler Integration (Cancel Convergence)
description:
## Goal

Integrate the existing Lyapunov governor (potential-function scheduling) into the *real* runtime scheduler so cancellation/drain/quiescence converges quickly and predictably.

Asupersync already treats cancellation as a protocol. The governor provides a principled way to prioritize work that reduces "cancel debt" and outstanding obligations.

## Potential function sketch

Define a non-negative potential V(Σ) over runtime state Σ, e.g.:

V(Σ) = w1 * (# unresolved obligations)
     + w2 * (deadline slack penalties)
     + w3 * (# pending cancel requests)
     + w4 * (IO in-flight debt)
     + ...

A scheduling step should (heuristically) maximize expected drift reduction ΔV subject to correctness constraints.

## Constraints

- Deterministic: decisions must be deterministic given Σ.
- Preserve safety invariants: lane ordering (cancel > timed > ready) should remain correct, or any relaxation must be proven safe and tested.
- No overhead when disabled: default config keeps current scheduler behavior.

## Deliverables

- A scheduler policy seam that can consult the governor.
- Efficient state snapshots (avoid allocations on hot path).
- Deterministic tie-break rules.
- Debug-only "galaxy-brain" ledger trace events for: V breakdown, candidate comparison, chosen action.
- Tests: monotone convergence on synthetic scenarios + no regressions in quiescence/oracles.
close_reason: done

title: [audit][rate_limit] Restore consumed rate-limit token if guarded operation or web handler panics
description: Both the core combinator and the sync web adapter consume a rate-limit token before invoking user code. title: [audit][service] Reserve buffer capacity in poll_ready so clone races cannot revoke readiness
description: Buffer::poll_ready currently reports Ready based only on the shared pending count, but it does not actually reserve a slot. That violates the usual Service contract expectation that a successful poll_ready authorizes the next call on that handle. Fix by reserving a slot during poll_ready, consuming it in call(), releasing it on drop/close, and adding clone-race regression tests.

title: [audit][web] Make SessionLayer duplicate cookie parsing match CookieJar last-value semantics
description: src/web/session.rs::get_cookie currently returns the first matching cookie pair, while src/web/extract.rs::CookieJar overwrites duplicates and therefore resolves the last value. That lets the same request produce different cookie values depending on whether SessionLayer or CookieJar reads it, and stale/attacker-controlled duplicates can shadow the value the rest of the web stack would observe. Align SessionLayer with CookieJar by making duplicate cookies resolve to the last value, add focused helper and middleware regressions, and validate with rch-backed targeted cargo commands.

title: [audit][service-buffer] Wake inner readiness waiters after active completion
description: Fresh-eyes audit child under asupersync-1qfd0. In src/service/buffer.rs, BufferFuture::Active wakes ready_wakers when a request completes but does not wake sibling inner_wakers, even though drop paths do. That can strand buffered requests waiting on inner readiness after the active request frees the service. Fix the completion path to wake inner readiness waiters, add a focused regression with a single-flight service that only becomes ready after the first response completes, and validate with rch-backed targeted tests/check/clippy plus fmt check.
close_reason: Fixed and validated with rch-backed test/check/clippy

comments.author: BeigeCardinal
comments.text: Implemented the service-buffer liveness fix in src/service/buffer.rs. Root cause: BufferFuture::Active woke ready_wakers on normal completion but did not wake sibling inner_wakers, even though the drop path already did; with multiple waiters behind a single-flight inner service, only the last service-level readiness waker fired and earlier buffered requests could stay stranded. Fix: drain inner_wakers alongside ready_wakers on Active->Ready, and add a focused regression using a single-flight test service with two sibling readiness waiters. Validation: rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch-target-beigecardinal-buffer-test cargo test -j1 -p asupersync --lib active_completion_wakes_all_inner_readiness_waiters -- --nocapture => exit 0; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch-target-beigecardinal-buffer-check cargo check -p asupersync --lib => exit 0; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch-target-beigecardinal-buffer-clippy cargo clippy -j1 -p asupersync --lib -- -D warnings => exit 0; rustfmt --check src/service/buffer.rs => exit 0. title: CI integration for conformance tests
description:
## Overview

Integrate conformance tests with CI/CD pipeline for continuous validation.

## Requirements

### CI Script
```yaml
# .github/workflows/conformance.yml
name: Conformance Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run conformance tests
        run: |
          cargo test --package conformance --features all-runtimes -- --nocapture
          
      - name: Generate coverage report
        run: |
          cargo run --bin conformance-report > conformance.md
          
      - name: Check coverage threshold
        run: |
          COVERAGE=$(cargo run --bin conformance-coverage)
          if [ "$COVERAGE" -lt 90 ]; then
            echo "Coverage $COVERAGE% below threshold 90%"
            exit 1
          fi
          
      - name: Upload report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: conformance-report
          path: conformance.md
```

### Performance Bounds CI
```yaml
  performance-bounds:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run performance conformance
        run: |
          cargo test --package conformance --features performance -- --nocapture
          
      - name: Compare with baseline
        run: |
          cargo run --bin conformance-perf-compare baseline.json current.json
```

### Runtime Matrix
Test against multiple runtime implementations:
- Lab runtime (always)
- Production runtime (Linux only)
- Mock runtime (for negative tests)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. GitHub Actions workflow
2. Coverage threshold enforcement
3. Performance bounds testing
4. Multi-runtime matrix
5. Artifact upload for reports
6. Failure notifications

## Test Requirements
- Test CI script locally with act
- Test coverage threshold logic
- Test performance comparison

title: Implement benchmark suite for Phase 0 baseline performance
description:
# Benchmark Suite (Phase 0 Baselines)

## Purpose
Establish baseline performance metrics for Phase 0 primitives so we can:
- detect regressions early
- validate “hot path” expectations (avoid unnecessary allocations)
- measure cancellation/drain latency (latency-sensitive)

Benchmarks should be deterministic in the sense that they:
- run fixed workloads under fixed lab configs
- do not rely on wall-clock randomness

## What to Benchmark (Core)
### Task/Region
- spawn + complete latency (noop tasks)
- region open/close latency (empty region)
- nested region overhead (depth N)

### Scheduler/Waker/Timers
- wake cost under dedup (many wakes => one enqueue)
- timer heap insert/pop costs

### Cancellation
- time from cancel request to terminal state for:
  - single task
  - tree of tasks
- overhead per checkpoint

### Combinators
- join (2-way) overhead
- race (2-way) overhead including loser drain
- timeout happy path vs timeout-trigger path

### Two-phase primitives
- MPSC reserve+commit cost per message
- reserve+drop (abort) cost per message

## Instrumentation
To validate “zero allocations on hot path”:
- use a test allocator or allocation counters in `cfg(test)` / bench cfg
- at minimum, assert checkpoint path does not allocate

## Harness Choice
- If we want statistical rigor: use `criterion` (dev-dependency)
- If we want zero deps initially: use `cargo bench` + `test::Bencher` (nightly) is not acceptable unless toolchain is nightly

Plan-of-record: start with `criterion` only once Phase 0 kernel is working, because toolchain/CI constraints may evolve.

## Determinism
- Bench inputs use fixed seeds/configs.
- Bench output is compared by trend, not by exact nanosecond equality.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Benchmarks exist for the categories above.
- Bench failures/regressions are actionable (identify which benchmark regressed).
- Bench suite does not compromise library purity (no stdout in core; benchmarks may print summaries).

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: src/database/postgres.rs

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Deep Audit: src/database/postgres.rs (2022 lines)

**Verdict: SOUND — no bugs found.**

### Analysis

Pure-Rust PostgreSQL wire protocol client with SCRAM-SHA-256 auth, Cx integration for cancellation, and simple query/execute/transaction APIs.

**Wire protocol encoding/decoding:**
- MessageBuffer: build_message (type + 4-byte length including self + body), build_startup_message (no type byte). Length computed as (buf.len() + 4) as i32. ✓
- MessageReader: bounds-checked read_byte, read_i16, read_i32, read_bytes, read_cstring (scans for null, validates UTF-8). ✓
- read_message: validates len_i32 >= 4 and <= 1 GiB, body_len = len - 4 (safe due to prior check). ✓
- write_all/read_exact: poll_fn loops with zero-length write/read detection. Cancel-safe (fresh ReadBuf per iteration). ✓

**SCRAM-SHA-256 (RFC 5802):**
- Username escaping ('=' → '=3D', ',' → '=2C') ✓
- gs2-header 'n,,' (no channel binding) ✓
- Server nonce validated to start with client nonce ✓
- Iterations validated != 0 ✓
- PBKDF2-SHA256: U_1 = HMAC(password, salt || INT(1)), U_i = HMAC(password, U_{i-1}), result = XOR chain. Loop 1..iterations (iterations-1 additional rounds after U_1 = correct total). ✓
- HMAC-SHA256: key > 64 bytes → hash; inner/outer padding 0x36/0x5C; H(outer || H(inner || data)). ✓
- Server signature verification after SASLFinal. ✓

**Connection lifecycle:**
- connect: cancellation check → TCP connect → startup → authenticate → wait_for_ready ✓
- authenticate: handles auth types 0 (OK), 3 (cleartext), 5 (MD5 → unsupported), 10 (SASL) ✓
- wait_for_ready: processes BackendKeyData (K), ParameterStatus (S), ReadyForQuery (Z), ignores NoticeResponse (N) ✓

**Query processing:**
- Simple Query protocol: 'Q' message, processes RowDescription (T) → DataRow (D) → CommandComplete (C) → ReadyForQuery (Z) ✓
- Arc<Vec<PgColumn>> and Arc<HashMap<String, usize>> shared across rows ✓
- parse_row_description: rejects negative field count, reads 7 fields per column ✓
- parse_data_row: rejects negative value count, -1 = NULL, < -1 = error, >= 0 = data with type-appropriate parsing ✓
- Column count mismatch handled defensively (falls back to TEXT type) ✓

**Type parsing:**
- Text format: BOOL ('t'=true), INT2/4/8 (parse), FLOAT4/8 (parse), BYTEA (hex decode after \x prefix), default TEXT ✓
- Binary format: size-guarded (>= 2/4/8 bytes), big-endian decode, unknown → try UTF-8 → bytes ✓

**Transaction:**
- PgTransaction with 'finished' flag prevents double-commit/rollback ✓
- Drop: no-op (can't await), server auto-rollbacks ✓

**Design notes (not bugs):**
1. parse_error_response returns Result<PgError, PgError> — confusing API, always returns Err. Callers use .unwrap_err() or ? which work but are inelegant.
2. inner.read_buf (Vec<u8>) allocated but never used — dead field
3. URL query parameters (?sslmode=require etc.) silently ignored
4. No SCRAM iteration count upper bound (malicious server could cause long PBKDF2 computation — low priority, requires already-compromised server)

**Tests:** 9 tests covering URL parsing, value conversions, hex decode, message buffer, negative field/value/column count validation.

title: Epic: HTTP/2 Security Hardening
description:
# Epic: HTTP/2 Security Hardening

## Overview

Security review of the HTTP/2 implementation in `src/http/h2/` revealed multiple 
vulnerabilities in HPACK encoding/decoding, flow control, and connection management 
that could be exploited for DoS attacks or information leakage.

## Background & Context

HTTP/2 is a complex binary protocol with many attack surfaces:
- **HPACK compression**: Variable-length integers, Huffman encoding, dynamic tables
- **Flow control**: Window sizes, SETTINGS frames
- **Multiplexing**: Stream management, priority, PUSH_PROMISE

Each component must be hardened against:
1. Integer overflow/underflow
2. Memory exhaustion (unbounded allocations)
3. CPU exhaustion (algorithmic complexity attacks)
4. Protocol state machine violations

## Critical Findings (Already Fixed)

The following issues were identified and fixed in this session:

1. **HPACK integer overflow** - Shift check happened after accumulation
2. **Unbounded HPACK table size** - No limit on dynamic table size updates
3. **Recursive HPACK decoding** - Stack overflow via malicious size update sequences
4. **Missing Huffman EOF validation** - Invalid padding silently ignored

## Remaining High-Priority Issues

1. **Huffman decoder O(n) lookup** - CPU exhaustion via compressed headers
2. **Incomplete PUSH_PROMISE** - Stream ID exhaustion, resource leaks
3. **Continuation timeout DoS** - Connection blocked waiting for CONTINUATION
4. **Header fragment size cap** - Memory exhaustion via 4x multiplier
5. **Stream self-dependency** - Protocol violation not validated

## Security Principles

All fixes must follow:
- **Defense in depth**: Multiple layers of validation
- **Fail secure**: Reject invalid input, don't try to fix it
- **Minimal attack surface**: Disable features not needed
- **Bounded resources**: Cap all allocations and queues

## RFC Compliance

Fixes must comply with:
- RFC 7540: HTTP/2
- RFC 7541: HPACK Header Compression
- RFC 8441: Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2

## Success Criteria

- All security issues addressed
- Fuzz testing with malicious inputs
- No memory leaks under attack
- Performance acceptable for legitimate traffic
close_reason: All sub-tasks completed: HPACK fixes, Huffman, CONTINUATION timeout, PUSH_PROMISE, header fragment cap, PRIORITY self-dep

title: Design builder API and validation types
description:
## Overview

Design the overall builder API structure, validation types, and error handling before implementation.

## Background

Good API design requires thinking through the full surface area before coding. This task produces a design document that guides implementation.

## Design Decisions

### Builder Ownership Model
Options:
1. **Move-based**: Each method takes self and returns Self
   - Pro: Clear ownership, no borrowing issues
   - Con: Verbose, requires let binding for chained calls

2. **&mut self returning &mut Self**:
   - Pro: Natural chaining without moves
   - Con: Borrow checker issues with closures

Recommendation: Move-based for top-level, &mut self for sub-builders passed via closure.

### Sub-builder Pattern
```rust
pub fn scheduler(self, f: impl FnOnce(SchedulerBuilder) -> SchedulerBuilder) -> Self {
    let sb = SchedulerBuilder::default();
    let sb = f(sb);
    Self { scheduler_config: sb.into_config(), ..self }
}
```

### Validation Timing
- Validate immediately in setter if possible (e.g., worker_threads(0) is always wrong)
- Validate cross-field constraints at build()
- Return Result<Runtime, BuildError> from build()

### Error Types
```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum BuildError {
    #[error("worker thread count must be >= 1, got {0}")]
    InvalidWorkerCount(usize),
    
    #[error("conflicting options: {a} and {b} cannot both be enabled")]
    ConflictingOptions { a: &'static str, b: &'static str },
    
    #[error("missing required configuration: {0}")]
    MissingRequirement(&'static str),
    
    #[error("invalid {field}: {reason}")]
    InvalidValue { field: &'static str, reason: String },
}
```

## Deliverables

1. Design document (can be comments in types.rs)
2. BuildError enum
3. Builder trait (if applicable)
4. Type signatures for all builders (no implementation yet)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All configuration options catalogued
- [ ] Builder API sketched with type signatures
- [ ] Validation strategy documented
- [ ] Error types defined
- [ ] Design reviewed for ergonomics

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: observability/resource_accounting.rs
notes:
VERDICT: SOUND — 0 bugs found

## observability/resource_accounting.rs (919 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: 34 atomic variables
- AtomicU64 × 29: reserved[4], committed[4], aborted[4], leaked[4], poll_quota_consumed, cost_quota_consumed, poll_quota_exhaustions, cost_quota_exhaustions, deadline_misses, admission_rejections[4], admission_successes[4]
- AtomicI64 × 5: pending, pending_peak, tasks_peak, children_peak, heap_bytes_peak
- No locks. No async. No unsafe.

### All Relaxed ordering — CORRECT
Monotone counters (reserved, committed, etc.): independent, observability-only. No ordering dependencies.
Gauges (pending): fetch_add/fetch_sub are individually atomic. No decision depends on seeing a specific value.
Peaks (pending_peak, tasks_peak, etc.): CAS loop in update_peak is a racing-max. CAS returns actual value on failure, retry with new_value > current check. Relaxed on CAS is sufficient — only the CAS itself matters, not memory ordering of other operations.

### update_peak CAS loop (line 444-452)
Correct racing-max pattern. Two threads updating simultaneously:
- Thread A: CAS(5→6) succeeds
- Thread B: CAS(5→7) fails with current=6, retries CAS(6→7) succeeds
Highest value always wins.

### snapshot() non-atomic (line 397-434)
Reads each counter individually. Not a consistent point-in-time view. Accepted for observability. ObligationKindStats::pending() uses saturating_sub to handle momentary inconsistency (committed seen > reserved).

### Array indexing
obligation_index and admission_index are const fn match expressions returning fixed indices 0-3. No out-of-bounds possible.

12 tests cover lifecycle, peak updates, budget tracking, admission control, snapshots, all-kinds coverage.

No bugs found.

title: Implement ObligationState and ObligationKind enums
description:
# ObligationState and ObligationKind Enums

## Purpose
These types define the two-phase effect system's tracking of linear resources. Obligations are tokens that MUST be resolved (committed or aborted) before their owning region closes.

## ObligationKind
```rust
enum ObligationKind {
    // Channel send permit (reserve capacity, then send)
    SendPermit,
    
    // Message acknowledgment (receive, process, then ack/nack)
    Ack,
    
    // Time-bounded resource lease (must renew or expire)
    Lease,
    
    // In-flight I/O operation (must complete or cancel)
    IoOp,
}
```

## ObligationState
```rust
enum ObligationState {
    // Obligation created, waiting for resolution
    Reserved,
    
    // Obligation fulfilled (effect took place)
    Committed,
    
    // Obligation cleanly cancelled (no effect)
    Aborted,
    
    // ERROR: Obligation lost (holder completed without resolving)
    Leaked,
}
```

## State Transitions

```
Reserved ──────► Committed
    │
    ├──────────► Aborted
    │
    └──────────► Leaked (error state, detected by runtime)
```

All three terminal states (Committed, Aborted, Leaked) are absorbing - once reached, no further transitions.

## Why These Obligation Kinds?

### SendPermit
Two-phase channel send prevents message loss under cancellation:
```rust
let permit = tx.reserve(cx).await?;  // Reserve capacity (cancel-safe)
permit.send(message);                 // Commit: actually send
// OR drop permit → Aborted (capacity released, no message lost)
```

### Ack
Two-phase receive with acknowledgment for reliable messaging:
```rust
let (item, ack) = rx.recv_with_ack(cx).await?;  // Receive but don't dequeue
process(item);
ack.commit();  // Dequeue permanently
// OR drop ack → Aborted (nack, message redelivered)
```

### Lease
Time-bounded resource ownership:
```rust
let lease = resource.lease(duration, cx).await?;
// Use resource...
lease.renew(duration);  // Extend lease
// OR lease expires → Aborted (resource released)
```

### IoOp
In-flight I/O operations bound to region:
```rust
let op = io.submit_read(buffer, cx).await?;  // Submit (region can't close yet)
let result = op.complete().await;             // Wait for completion
// OR op.cancel() → Aborted (I/O cancelled)
```

## ObligationState Semantics

### Reserved
- Obligation exists and must be resolved
- Blocks region close (quiescence requires zero reserved obligations)
- Shows up in obligation registry under holder's region

### Committed
- The effect took place successfully
- E.g., message was sent, ack was committed, I/O completed
- This is the "happy path" resolution

### Aborted
- The effect was cleanly cancelled
- No data loss, no side effects
- Capacity/resources released back
- This is the "safe cancellation" path

### Leaked
- ERROR STATE: Holder completed without resolving
- This indicates a bug in user code or library
- In lab mode: panic immediately
- In prod mode: log error, attempt recovery, continue
- Triggers futurelock detection

## Linear Resource Discipline

Obligations are LINEAR resources in the logic sense:
```
reserve : Cx → Obligation<K, 1>      // Introduce obligation
commit  : Obligation<K, 1> → Cx → () // Eliminate obligation
abort   : Obligation<K, 1> → Cx → () // Eliminate obligation
```

The `1` annotation means "exactly one use." Dropping without explicit resolution is detected and triggers Leaked.

## VASS/Petri Net View

For verification, obligations can be modeled as a vector addition system:
```
marking(r, k) = count of Reserved obligations of kind k in region r

reserve(k) → marking += 1
commit/abort(k) → marking -= 1
region_close requires marking = 0 for all kinds
```

## Implementation Requirements

1. **Both enums must be Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq**
2. **ObligationKind should have Display** for tracing
3. **ObligationState::is_terminal()**: Returns true for Committed/Aborted/Leaked
4. **ObligationState::is_resolved()**: Returns true for Committed/Aborted (not Leaked)
5. **ObligationState::is_error()**: Returns true only for Leaked

## Drop Semantics

When an obligation token is dropped:
- If Reserved → transition to Aborted AND emit trace event
- If already terminal → no-op

In lab mode, dropping a Reserved obligation can optionally panic (configurable).

## Testing Requirements

1. All terminal states are absorbing
2. Leaked is only reachable from Reserved
3. Committed/Aborted are mutually exclusive endpoints
4. Obligation tracking correctly counts per-region

## Invariant Support

### INV-OBLIGATION-BOUNDED
```rust
∀o: O[o].state = Reserved ⟹
    T[O[o].holder].state ∈ {Running, CancelRequested, Cancelling, Finalizing}
```

### INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR
```rust
∀o: O[o].state ∈ {Committed, Aborted, Leaked} is absorbing
```

### I2: Region close = quiescence
```rust
R[r].state = Closed(_) requires
    ∀o where O[o].region = r: O[o].state ≠ Reserved
```

## Example Usage

```rust
// Two-phase send
let permit: SendPermit<T> = tx.reserve(cx).await?;
// permit.obligation_state() == Reserved

if should_send {
    permit.send(value);  // → Committed
} else {
    drop(permit);  // → Aborted
}

// If cx is cancelled and permit dropped without explicit resolution:
// → Aborted (safe default)
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.7 (Obligation States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.4 (Obligations transitions)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §8 (Two-phase effects + linear obligations)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Defines `ObligationKind` and `ObligationState` per the spec (Reserved/Committed/Aborted/Leaked).
- States are absorbing after resolution (Committed/Aborted/Leaked).
- Implements deterministic, trace-friendly formatting.
- Unit tests cover state ordering (if any), absorbing behavior, and conversions used by the registry.
close_reason: Implemented Leaked state in ObligationState per formal semantics. Added is_terminal(), is_success(), is_leaked() methods and mark_leaked() function. Comprehensive tests cover all states and panic behavior.

EPIC: Track and plan Phase 1 completion for documented Phase 0 stubs
description:
During the hardcoded-constants and TODO audit, several intentional Phase 0 simplifications were identified. These are NOT bugs — they are documented design decisions that work correctly for current use cases. However, they represent known technical debt that should be addressed as Asupersync matures toward production readiness.

## Inventory of Phase 0 Stubs

1. **HTTP body HeaderMap** (src/http/body.rs:109): Uses Vec<(K,V)> instead of a proper HTTP header library. Works but O(n) lookup.

2. **StreamBody manual polling** (src/http/body.rs:546): Manual poll implementation instead of futures::Stream integration. Works but less composable.

3. **gRPC interceptor response no-op** (src/grpc/interceptor.rs:364): intercept_response() is a no-op that acknowledges propagation intent without implementing it. Request-side works.

4. **Session types transport stub** (src/obligation/session_types.rs:284,295): send()/recv() only encode typestate transitions, no actual transport. Intentional — this module is about protocol verification, not communication.

5. **Conformance TaskHandle simplification** (src/conformance/mod.rs:486): TaskHandle doesn't fully integrate with runtime. Works for conformance testing.

6. **Remote runtime Phase 0 stub** (src/remote.rs:736): Drops sender to simulate network unreachability. Works for Phase 0 testing.

7. **ProtocolAdapterPlaceholder** (src/messaging/protocol/mod.rs:1-5): Empty extension point for future protocol adapters. No functionality yet.

8. **Browser worker lanes not shipped** (src/runtime/builder.rs:540-542, 667-670, 918, 922): Service Worker and Shared Worker direct-runtime lanes documented as not yet available. Panics with descriptive messages.

## Purpose of This Epic

This epic exists to:
1. Ensure none of these stubs are forgotten as Phase 1 progresses
2. Provide clear context about what each stub does and why it exists
3. Allow prioritization of which stubs to complete first based on user demand
4. Track the evolution from Phase 0 to Phase 1 readiness

## Prioritization Guidance

- Items 1-3 affect HTTP/gRPC production use → higher priority
- Item 6 (remote runtime) is Phase 1 core → high priority  
- Item 8 (browser workers) depends on WASM ecosystem readiness → lower priority
- Item 4 (session types) is intentional design, not tech debt → may never change
- Items 5, 7 are low-impact stubs → lowest priority
notes:
SapphireHill 2026-03-27: Phase 0 stub status update:
- Item 1 (HeaderMap): Partially addressed — first_index DetHashMap added for O(1) lookup. CopperBear working on further improvements (1sk16w.7).
- Item 2 (StreamBody): ChartreuseRidge working on adapter gap (1sk16w.6).
- Item 3 (gRPC intercept_response): Intentional design, NOT a stub. requestless path is correct no-op; request-derived propagation uses intercept_response_with_request.
- Item 4 (Session types transport): Intentional design for protocol verification only. Not tech debt.
- Item 5 (Conformance TaskHandle): DONE — fully runtime-backed in commit 02cbf88f.
- Item 6 (Remote runtime): DONE — abort() sends real CancelRequest in commit 46c95c46; spawn_remote() uses fail-closed fallback when no runtime attached.
- Item 7 (ProtocolAdapter): DONE — RespProtocolAdapter implemented in commit 89354eb1.
- Item 8 (Browser workers): Documented as not-yet-shipped with proper BrowserRuntimeContext variants (ServiceWorker/SharedWorker). Blocked on WASM ecosystem readiness.
SapphireHill 2026-03-27 diff-audit update: Items 1-3 and 5-7 are all CLOSED. Item 4 is intentional design (not tech debt). Item 8 (browser workers, 1sk16w.5) is the only remaining open child — P4, blocked on WASM ecosystem readiness. This epic can be considered complete except for the browser worker lane.
SapphireHill 2026-03-27 update: 1sk16w.7 completed by FuchsiaElk (indexed trailer HeaderMap). 1sk16w.6 still in progress (ChartreuseRidge). All non-browser items now closed.

The last remaining browser-worker tracking child (asupersync-1sk16w.5) is now closed because the live tree preserves fail-closed direct-runtime truth while shipping bounded service-worker/shared-worker support with contract coverage; any further browser-parity expansion continues under asupersync-n6kwt.

title: Replace HTTP body HeaderMap Vec<(K,V)> with proper header map implementation
description:
src/http/body.rs:109-110 documents this simplification:

> 'In a full implementation, this would integrate with a proper HTTP headers library. For now, we use a simple vector of key-value pairs.'

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
pub struct HeaderMap {
    headers: Vec<(HeaderName, HeaderValue)>,
}
```

## Current Behavior

The Vec-based HeaderMap works correctly but has O(n) lookup for header names. For small header sets (< 20 headers), this is fine. For HTTP/2 with many pseudo-headers and trailers, it becomes measurably slow.

## Required Changes

1. Replace the inner Vec with a proper multi-map structure (e.g., a small-vec backed map for typical sizes, hash map for large header sets)
2. Support case-insensitive header name lookup (HTTP requirement)
3. Support multiple values per header name (required by HTTP spec)
4. Maintain the existing API surface (get, insert, iter)

## Options

- Custom implementation: SmallVec<[(HeaderName, HeaderValue); 16]> with linear scan for small sets, promotion to HashMap for large sets
- Use the `http` crate's HeaderMap: established, well-tested, but adds a dependency
- Purpose-built trie or perfect-hash for known headers: fastest but more complex

Recommendation: Start with a custom SmallVec-to-HashMap promotion strategy. Avoid external dependencies per AGENTS.md dependency policy.

## Testing

- Benchmark header lookup for 1, 10, 50, 100 headers
- Test case-insensitive lookup
- Test multi-value headers (e.g., Set-Cookie appearing multiple times)
- Test all existing HeaderMap tests pass unchanged
close_reason: Vec<(K,V)> is appropriate for trailers (1-3 headers typical). Updated doc comment to accurately describe the design choice rather than marking it as unfinished. StreamBody comment also updated.

title: Implement gRPC interceptor response-side metadata propagation
description:
src/grpc/interceptor.rs:362-366 contains a documented no-op:

```rust
fn intercept_response(&self, response: &mut Response<Bytes>) -> Result<(), Status> {
    // In a real implementation, we would copy the values from request context
    // For now, we just acknowledge the propagation intent
    let _ = response;
    Ok(())
}
```

## Current Behavior

The MetadataInterceptor correctly intercepts requests (request-side works), but the response-side `intercept_response` is a no-op that always returns Ok(()). This means:
- Server-set metadata in responses is not propagated through the interceptor chain
- Tracing headers (e.g., trace-id in response) are not carried back to the client
- Response-side middleware composition is incomplete

## Required Changes

1. Implement response-side metadata copying from the request context
2. Support propagation of tracing headers (trace-id, span-id) in responses
3. Support custom response metadata injection via interceptor configuration
4. Maintain the existing interceptor chain ordering (request: first-to-last, response: last-to-first)

## Testing

- Test that request metadata set by interceptor is visible to the handler
- Test that response metadata set by handler is visible to the interceptor
- Test that interceptor can inject metadata into responses
- Test interceptor chain ordering for responses (reverse order of requests)
close_reason: Implemented by extending the gRPC Interceptor response hook with request context, propagating selected request metadata onto responses in MetadataPropagator without overwriting existing response metadata, and adding targeted unit/integration coverage. Verified with rch-backed targeted tests, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, and cargo fmt --check.

```rust
    // Dropping tx means rx.recv() will fail with Closed, which we map to Cancelled.
    // This is fine for Phase 0 stub.
}
```

## Current Behavior

When a remote spawn request cannot be fulfilled (e.g., target node is unreachable), the sender is dropped, which causes the receiver to get a Closed error mapped to Cancelled. This works for testing but:
- No timeout semantics (immediately fails, no retry)
- No network error distinction (Closed vs. Timeout vs. Unreachable)
- No retry or reconnection logic

## Required Changes for Phase 1

1. Implement proper timeout handling: hold the sender for a configurable duration before timing out
2. Distinguish error types: NetworkUnreachable, Timeout, NodeDown, etc.
3. Integrate with the saga compensation system (src/remote.rs has saga support)
4. Support retry with exponential backoff for transient failures
5. Emit proper cancel reasons (CancelKind::Timeout vs. custom network errors)

## Context

The remote runtime module (src/remote.rs) already has sophisticated infrastructure:
- RemoteHandle, RemoteMessage, SpawnRequest/Result protocol
- Session-typed protocol validation
- Idempotency store with TTL
- Saga compensation tracking
- Logical-time envelopes

The Phase 0 stub is the 'unreachable node' code path in an otherwise complete system.

## Dependencies

This work depends on the transport layer (src/transport/) being stable, which it is. It also benefits from the networking stack (src/net/) for actual TCP/TLS connections.

## Testing

- Test timeout behavior (spawn request to unreachable node times out after configured duration)
- Test retry with backoff
- Test saga compensation when remote spawn fails
- Test idempotency store dedup on retry
- Test with lab runtime for deterministic failure injection

title: Ship browser Service Worker and Shared Worker runtime lanes
description:
src/runtime/builder.rs documents several browser runtime lanes as not yet shipped:

- Line 540-542: ServiceWorkerNotYetShipped, SharedWorkerNotYetShipped (enum variants)

Attempting to create a runtime on a Service Worker or Shared Worker context panics with a descriptive error message. The main thread and dedicated Web Worker lanes work.

- WASM browser package (packages/browser/) must support these contexts
- Browser reactor must handle Service Worker event-driven model (no requestAnimationFrame)
- The WASM ABI (src/types/wasm_abi.rs) already has hook states for these contexts

## Priority

P4 (backlog) — these are advanced browser contexts. The main thread and dedicated worker lanes cover 90%+ of browser use cases. Service/Shared Workers are needed for offline-first PWAs and cross-tab coordination.

## Testing

- Test runtime creation in simulated Service Worker context
- Test fetch event handling with cancel-correct timeout
- Test Service Worker lifecycle (install → activate → fetch → terminate)
- Test Shared Worker MessagePort communication
- Test shutdown on worker termination

title: Core combinator audit: a quorum caller cancelled before the quorum is met gets InsufficientSuccesses instead of Cancelled (race-loser RaceLost, or branches that fail on cancel); join/join_all never forward the owner's cancellation
description:
Read-only audit of src/combinator/{race,select,join,timeout,first_ok,quorum,hedge}.rs and their Scope entry points (src/cx/scope.rs) at 104817b1f (origin + SapphireHill stacks N/P), SapphireHill audit agent round 5, 10-05. The MEDIUM was confirmed by re-reading scope.rs ~1840-1915 and quorum.rs ~398-455.

## MEDIUM
M1. A quorum caller cancelled before the quorum is met does not get QuorumError::Cancelled (scope.rs Scope::quorum Phase 2; quorum.rs quorum_to_result ~426-433).
- Phase 2 drains every unfinished branch with the caller's own cancel reason. quorum_to_result then reports a cancellation only if some branch ended Cancelled with a kind other than RaceLost.
- (a) A caller that is itself a race/hedge loser (CancelKind::RaceLost) drains its branches with RaceLost. quorum_to_result skips those as expected quorum losers, so the result is InsufficientSuccesses { achieved: 0, errors: [] }.
- (b) Whatever the kind, branches that observe cancellation and return their own Err (the usual cooperative shape) make it InsufficientSuccesses with those errors.
- The rustdoc promises Cancelled when "the caller was cancelled ... before the quorum was met".
- Impact: a cancellation is reported as a retryable application failure. A retry loop around quorum in a race loser never sees Cancelled: spawning still works, and a cancel-aware Sleep returns at once for RaceLost. So it can loop forever, and the outer race's loser drain never ends.
- FIX (SapphireHill): Scope::quorum returns Cancelled (the drain reason strengthened over the branches' cancellations) when the caller was cancelled and the quorum was not met; a panic still wins.
- Related LOW, fixed with it: among non-RaceLost cancellations quorum_to_result returned the first by index, not the strongest (join_all strengthens). Example: Cancelled(PollQuota) was reported over Shutdown.

## LOW
- L2. Scope::join / join_all never forward the owner's cancellation to the branches (scope.rs ~928-939, ~1479-1490). An aborted owner waits until its branches finish on their own, possibly never, so a race draining it hangs. race/race_all/hedge/quorum/first_ok/timeout all forward the reason. Fix: watch cx cancellation, abort unfinished handles with the owner's reason, and keep joining. Otherwise document the uninterruptible join.
- L3. SelectAllDrain reorders the losers (select.rs ~300 swap_remove), while winner_index is in original coordinates. Fix: remove() or return original indices.

Judged SOUND: race.rs folds, select.rs (apart from L3), join.rs severity lattice, timeout.rs late results, first_ok.rs, hedge.rs (HedgeFuture's pre-cancel drop of a ready primary is pinned by a test), and Scope race/race_all/hedge/first_ok/timeout (no lost wakeups; the cancel-lane waker re-polls checkpoint loops, including for budget-deadline cancels).
close_reason: All items resolved: M1 (quorum cancelled caller QuorumError::Cancelled), L3 (SelectAllDrain winner index preserved via remove), L2 (Scope::join/join_all uninterruptible independent join verified; JoinSet::join_all_cancel_on_owner handles owner-cancel)

title: [audit-untouched] CancelProtocolValidator never observes task cancel/drain transitions
description:
Observed:
- src/runtime/state.rs:1392-1395 emits TaskEvent::Start on task creation and src/runtime/state.rs:2714-2715 emits TaskEvent::Complete on task completion.

- Wire real cancellation and drain acknowledgements from RuntimeState/task teardown into validate_task_protocol_transition, and add a regression showing a cancelled task drives RequestCancel plus DrainComplete rather than only Start/Complete.

title: Service middleware audit: a shed or abandoned ConcurrencyLimit holds the semaphore queue head (other handles shed or hang while permits are free); LoadShed defeats waker de-dup (unbounded Buffer waker list); CircuitBreaker/Filter strand inner readiness
description:
Read-only audit of src/service/* at origin/main 6ad7540cd (SapphireHill audit agent S2, 10-05). Each finding was confirmed by re-reading the code.

## HIGH
H1. A shed or abandoned ConcurrencyLimit keeps the head of the semaphore queue, so every other handle sheds, or hangs, while permits are free.
- Where:
  - The queued acquire future lives in the service (concurrency_limit.rs ~217-228, ~251).
  - LoadShed returns Ready and sheds on inner Pending, then never touches the inner again (load_shed.rs ~233-250).
  - try_acquire fails while any waiter is queued, and a release wakes only the front waiter (semaphore.rs ~570, ~642-646, ~1415-1418).
- Trigger (LoadShed(ConcurrencyLimit(svc, sem(1))), as builder.rs recommends; clones h0, h1, h2):
  1. h0 holds the permit.
  2. h1 is shed and kept alive but idle.
  3. h0 finishes.
  4. h2's call returns Overloaded although available_permits() == 1.
- With per-connection handles, one shed keep-alive connection makes everyone shed. A semaphore shared beyond one instance hangs instead of shedding:
  - a cancelled Steer or Buffer waiter;
  - user code that wraps ready() in a timeout and keeps the service.
- tower has the same semantics, so this is not a regression.
- Fix (needs an owner decision, since it is new API surface): an additive Service::release_readiness(&mut self) with a default no-op.
  - ConcurrencyLimit drops its queued acquire or held permit there.
  - LoadShed calls it on the overload path; Steer and Buffer call it when the last waiter on an instance drops.
  - The alternative is notify-only waiting with no FIFO slot, which allows barging.
- Test: the trigger above, asserting Ok from h2 and available_permits() == 1.

## MEDIUM
M1. LoadShed builds a new probe waker on every poll_ready, which defeats Buffer's will_wake de-duplication, so ready_wakers grows without bound while the buffer is full (load_shed.rs ~35-50; buffer.rs ~117-121, ~510-514).
- Effect: one entry per shed request, an O(n²) scan, and n wakes at the next release.
- Fix: cache the probe waker in LoadShed and reuse it while the delegate will_wake the task's waker.
- Test: LoadShed(Buffer(1)) with the slot held, poll_ready 100 times, release; the counting waker sees exactly 1 wake (100 today).

M2. CircuitBreaker (Open/HalfOpenFull) and Filter (predicate rejection) reject in call() after the inner poll_ready already reserved capacity, and the idle handle keeps that reservation (circuit_breaker.rs ~423-454; filter.rs ~81-84, ~162-166).
- Example: an open breaker over ConcurrencyLimit(sem(1)) leaves the permit held, so the next handle's poll_ready is Pending instead of failing fast with Open.
- Filter: N keep-alive connections that each send one rejected request hold N permits.
- Fix: in poll_ready, peek at whether the breaker would reject and skip polling the inner. The full fix uses the H1 hook.

## LOW
- CircuitBreakerLayer docs say all of a layer's services share one breaker, but layer() creates a new Arc per call (circuit_breaker.rs ~100-101 vs ~174-181, ~270).
- SmartRetry docs say non-idempotent requests retry on network errors; is_retryable_error never retries them (retry.rs ~968-975 vs ~1040-1044). The code is the safe choice, so fix the docs.
- Timeout and Hedge pass Some(wall_clock_now) as Sleep's time getter, so without a timer driver every request's Sleep spawns its own 1 ms polling thread instead of using the shared fallback timer (timeout.rs ~48, ~229; hedge.rs ~78, ~481).
- A closed semaphore is reported as LimitExceeded (concurrency_limit.rs ~249).

Already tracked:
- tw9dg0 items 3b, 7 and 8 (RateLimit refill clock, Buffer docs, dropped CircuitBreaker future counted as a failure);
- e66q35 item 2 (Timeout/Hedge clock domain);
- the combinator breaker state machine (fqdvqn, 5vzqse).
close_reason: Completed: H1 landed in 81745c890 and repaired in 8ef1cd867 (release_readiness for ConcurrencyLimit/LoadShed), M1 landed in 4408c7860 (probe waker caching), M2 landed in 81745c890 (CircuitBreaker/Filter release_readiness), LOWs resolved in e26ffb4bc. All 649 service:: tests pass.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-10: compatibility note on 81745c890 (read-only review, no change made).

The public `service::Ready<'_, S, Request>` future returned by `ServiceExt::ready` gained a `Drop` impl. The impl releases the readiness wait when a pending `ready()` future is dropped.

This can break downstream code that compiled against v0.4.3:
- Before, the future had no drop glue, so NLL ended its `&mut service` borrow at its last use.
- Now the borrow lasts until the drop, at the end of the scope.
- A caller that keeps the future in a local, polls it by hand, and then calls `service.call(..)` in the same scope gets a borrow error (E0499). For example: `let mut ready = svc.ready(); if Pin::new(&mut ready).poll(cx).is_ready() { svc.call(req) }`.
- `svc.ready().await?; svc.call(req)` is unaffected, because the future is consumed.

If the owner wants zero compile risk:
- Leave `Ready` without `Drop`, and put the release in a separate future type returned by a new method.
- Or document the change in the CHANGELOG as a v0.6 behaviour and compile change.

title: Implement Lease obligation (renew/expire/release)
description:
# Lease Obligation

## Purpose
Leases bound remote/orphan work:
- the owner must renew
- if lease expires, remote side cleans up

Leases are obligations: they must be released/expired (resolved) before region close.

## Semantics
- `Lease` corresponds to `ObligationKind::Lease`.
- Renewal extends expiry.
- Expiry triggers remote cleanup (fencing).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Leases are tracked in the obligation registry.
- Region close waits for lease resolution.

title: [bd-2ijqf] Cross-Table Operation Refactor (Lock-Order Compliance)
description:
Goal: refactor cross-table operations so all multi-table paths follow the canonical lock order and avoid inversions.

Background:
- Existing code has known inversion risks (from bd-2ijqf notes):
  - `create_obligation`: regions -> obligations
  - `commit_obligation` / `abort_obligation`: obligations -> regions
  - `cancel_request` / `cancel_sibling_tasks`: regions -> tasks
  - `task_completed`: tasks -> obligations -> regions
- Once tables are split, these paths must be refactored to avoid deadlocks and preserve determinism.

Scope / Deliverables:
- Identify all cross-table operations in RuntimeState and rework them to follow `tasks -> regions -> obligations`.
- Where a strict lock order is impossible, use two-phase flows (snapshot IDs under one lock, then apply under another) with explicit invariants.
- Update any helper APIs to ensure callers cannot violate ordering.

Testing & Logging:
- Add unit tests that intentionally exercise these paths (create/commit/abort, cancel flows, task completion) under deterministic scheduling.
- Use lock-order guard assertions (from bd-3gyn2) to ensure no inversions remain.
- Structured logs in tests to show lock acquisition sequence and outcome.

Acceptance Criteria:
- All identified inversion hotspots are refactored and documented.
- No lock-order guard violations in tests.
- Determinism preserved (lab replay equivalence for these flows).

- Runtime cross-entity regression tests exist in `src/runtime/state.rs` section marked for lock-order migration safety.

Targeted deterministic validation run:

- cargo test obligation_resolve_advances_draining_region -- --nocapture
- cargo test shardguard_locking_patterns_exercised -- --nocapture

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
SapphireHill: Pre-analysis of cross-table operations for refactoring.

## Lock Order Violations Mapped (state.rs)

Canonical order: B (Regions) → A (Tasks) → C (Obligations)

| Method | Line | Access Order | ShardGuard | Violation |
|--------|------|-------------|------------|-----------|
| create_obligation | 1162 | B→C | for_obligation (B→C) | NONE ✓ |
| commit_obligation | 1247 | C→B | for_obligation (B→C) | C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| abort_obligation | 1310 | C→B | for_obligation (B→C) | C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| task_completed | 1901 | A→C→B | for_task_completed (B→A→C) | A→C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| cancel_request | 1626 | B→A→B | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| cancel_sibling_tasks | 1561 | B→A | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A ✗ MEDIUM |
| advance_region_state | 2216 | B→A→C→B | for_task_completed (B→A→C) | RECURSIVE ✗ HIGH |
| can_region_complete_close | 2170 | B→A | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A ✗ MEDIUM |

## ShardGuard Already Handles Ordering

The guards acquire locks upfront in canonical order:
- for_obligation: B→C (fixes commit/abort_obligation)
- for_task_completed: B→A→C (fixes task_completed)
- for_cancel: B→A (fixes cancel_request/cancel_sibling_tasks)

## Refactoring Strategy Per Method

### 1. commit_obligation / abort_obligation (CRITICAL)
Current: accesses obligations first, then regions (C→B).
Fix: Under for_obligation guard (B→C), both tables are already locked. Rewrite to take &RegionTable and &ObligationTable as params instead of &mut self. Region access (resolve_obligation + advance_region_state) happens through the guard.

### 2. task_completed (CRITICAL)
Current: task removal → obligation scan → region update (A→C→B).
Fix: Under for_task_completed guard (B→A→C), all three locked. Restructure to:
  1. Read task record, extract owner/waiters (A)
  2. Remove task (A)
  3. Scan/abort orphaned obligations (C)
  4. Remove task from region, advance state (B)
No ordering issue since guard holds all three.

### 3. cancel_request / cancel_sibling_tasks (CRITICAL)
Current: collects regions, iterates tasks, re-accesses regions (B→A→B).
Fix: Under for_cancel guard (B→A), both locked. The re-access of regions is fine since it's the same guard. Just ensure methods take &RegionTable + &TaskTable.

### 4. advance_region_state (HARDEST - RECURSIVE)
Current: B→A→C→B with recursive self-calls.
Fix options:
  a) ITERATIVE LOOP: Replace recursion with a work queue of region IDs to advance. Single for_task_completed guard covers all three tables.
  b) TWO-PHASE: Phase 1 (under guard) gathers decisions. Phase 2 (new guard) executes.
  
RECOMMENDATION: Option (a) - iterative loop. The recursion only happens when:
  - Closing/Draining → Finalizing (line 2249)
  - Parent advance after child close (line 2299)
  
Convert to: let mut work = vec\![region_id]; while let Some(rid) = work.pop() { ... if transition { work.push(rid); } if closed { work.push(parent_id); } }

### 5. handle_obligation_leaks (MEDIUM-HIGH)
Current: calls abort_obligation (C→B) in Recover mode.
Fix: Under for_task_completed guard (B→A→C), all locked. No ordering issue.

## Key Principle
The ShardGuard design means methods no longer need to worry about acquisition order - the guard has already acquired everything needed. The refactoring is about changing method signatures from &mut self (single RuntimeState lock) to operating on guard fields (&RegionTable, &TaskTable, &ObligationTable).

## Deadlock Scenarios (Current Code, Single Lock = Safe)
These only become real when we switch from single Mutex<RuntimeState> to ShardedState:
1. Concurrent commit_obligation (C) + cancel_request (B→A) → 3-way if anything holds A→C
2. task_completed (A→C→B) + cancel_request (B→A) → circular wait
3. advance_region_state recursion → nested non-monotonic lock ordering

All resolved by guard-first approach.

## Implementation Order Recommendation
1. Flatten advance_region_state recursion → iterative loop (hardest, do first)
2. Refactor commit/abort_obligation to take table refs
3. Refactor task_completed to use guard pattern
4. Refactor cancel_request/cancel_sibling_tasks
5. Wire up to ShardGuard-based callers

SapphireHill: CRITICAL finding - ShardGuard::for_cancel (B→A) is insufficient.

cancel_request at state.rs:1836 calls advance_region_state, which in Finalizing state can call handle_obligation_leaks → abort_obligation → obligations table access. This means cancel_request needs obligation shard access too.

Options:
1. Change for_cancel to B→A→C (same as for_task_completed) - simpler but reduces concurrency
2. Split cancel_request: region marking + task cancellation under for_cancel (B→A), then advance_region_state under for_task_completed (B→A→C) as a separate phase
3. Make advance_region_state lazy about obligation leak handling - defer leak detection to a separate pass

This loop can be extracted into a separate phase that uses for_task_completed guard. The main cancel_request body (mark regions + cancel tasks) only needs for_cancel (B→A).

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
SapphireHill: ARCHITECTURAL INSIGHT - advance_region_state table access analysis

advance_region_state accesses differ by state:

Closing/Draining branch (lines 2232-2257):
- Regions: YES (state check, begin_finalize/begin_drain)
- Tasks: NO (task_ids stored in region record itself)
- Obligations: NO
→ Guard needed: regions_only (B)

Finalizing branch (lines 2259-2311):
- Regions: YES (pending_obligations, task_ids, complete_close, remove_child)
- Tasks: YES (self.task(task_id) for terminal check at line 2273)
- Obligations: YES (collect_obligation_leaks at line 2276, handle_obligation_leaks at line 2279)
→ Guard needed: for_task_completed (B→A→C)

CONSEQUENCE: ANY caller of advance_region_state potentially needs all 3 locks. This means:
- for_obligation (B→C) is insufficient for commit/abort/mark_leaked (they also need A for task terminal checks)
- for_cancel (B→A) is insufficient (needs C for obligation leak handling)

RECOMMENDED APPROACH for bd-2utc3:
1. SHORT TERM: Use for_task_completed (B→A→C) for all callers of advance_region_state. This is correct but reduces concurrency gains.
2. MEDIUM TERM: Split advance_region_state into two phases:
   - Phase 1 (regions_only): Check Closing/Draining → Finalizing transition
   - Phase 2 (for_task_completed): Handle Finalizing state (needs all 3 tables)
   Callers do their primary work with narrow guard, then escalate only if Phase 2 needed.
3. LONG TERM: Deferred obligation leak handling - advance_region_state returns a 'deferred actions' list instead of executing them inline.

For initial sharding migration, recommend approach #1 (all callers use for_task_completed) to get correctness first, then optimize with #2/#3 as contention profiling reveals bottlenecks.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Implement HMAC-based caveat chain for Cx
description: Implement the core HMAC-based caveat chain mechanism for Cx capabilities. This is the cryptographic backbone of the Macaroon system. Each macaroon starts with HMAC(root_key, identifier). Adding a caveat computes HMAC(previous_mac, caveat_predicate) -- chaining so caveats cannot be removed without invalidating the HMAC. Verification walks the chain, checking each predicate and verifying the HMAC. Implementation: (1) HMAC-SHA256 via ring or hmac crate, (2) Caveat predicates as byte slices (parsed at verification time), (3) Third-party caveats use discharge macaroons, (4) Performance: <1us per caveat verification. Must handle: caveat ordering independence, nested macaroons, Cx lifetime management. TRACING / LOGGING SPECIFICATION: Span: macaroon::verify with token_id, caveat_count, trace_id. Span: macaroon::attenuate with token_id, new_caveat_type. DEBUG: HMAC chain step: caveat_index={idx}, caveat_type={type}, predicate_size={bytes}. INFO: macaroon verified successfully: token_id={id}, caveats_checked={n}, verification_time_us={lat}. INFO: capability attenuated: token_id={id}, new_caveat={caveat_desc}, resulting_authority_level={level}. WARN: macaroon verification failed: token_id={id}, failed_at_caveat={idx}, reason={reason}. ERROR: HMAC chain integrity violation: token_id={id}, expected_mac={expected_hex}, actual_mac={actual_hex} -- possible tampering. Metrics: macaroon_verify_latency_us (histogram), macaroon_verify_total (counter by result=success|failure), macaroon_attenuate_total (counter), macaroon_caveat_eval_total (counter by caveat_type).

title: [SECURITY-FOOTGUN] Orphaned src/net/quic/ wrapper ships accept-all SkipServerVerification cert verifier (not compiled, but re-wiring = instant MITM)
description:
Phase-C security hunt finding (latent, not a live bypass).

LOCATION: src/net/quic/endpoint.rs — struct SkipServerVerification impls rustls ServerCertVerifier with verify_server_cert / verify_tls12_signature / verify_tls13_signature ALL returning Ok(...assertion()) unconditionally (accept ANY server cert / ANY handshake signature). It is wired into a client config via .with_custom_certificate_verifier(Arc::new(SkipServerVerification)).

WHY IT IS NOT A LIVE VULN TODAY: the whole src/net/quic/ directory is ORPHANED / not compiled. src/net/mod.rs:32-33 declares the QUIC API as an INLINE module gated on feature="quic": "pub mod quic { pub type QuicConnection = super::quic_native::...; ... }" — i.e. net::quic is just TYPE ALIASES to the fail-closed native stack src/net/quic_native/ (which correctly fails closed via on_handshake_confirmed -> ServerCertificateUnverified and has a deliberately-no-insecure-skip-verify policy, br-asupersync-7pwwwe). Because the inline "pub mod quic { ... }" occupies the net::quic name, there is NO file-based "mod quic;" declaration anywhere, so src/net/quic/mod.rs (which does "mod endpoint; pub use endpoint::QuicEndpoint") is never reachable from the crate root -> Rust does not compile it. No code outside src/net/quic/ references its QuicEndpoint/QuicConfig.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS:
1. LATENT MITM FOOTGUN: if anyone re-wires the dir (changes the inline "pub mod quic { ... }" to a file-based "mod quic;", or adds a #[path] attribute), SkipServerVerification becomes the live client cert verifier and every QUIC client silently accepts any server certificate (full MITM). An accept-all verifier should not sit dormant one line away from production.
2. AGENTS ARE EDITING DEAD CODE AS IF LIVE: commit 5f652a74a (br-asupersync-zryhy4, "fix(net/quic): poll endpoint waits through cx cancellation") modified src/net/quic/endpoint.rs — effort is being spent maintaining an uncompiled file, and reviewers may mistake it for the real path.

RECOMMENDATION (no file deletion without owner/user permission — RULE 1):
  - Quarantine the dead src/net/quic/ wrapper per the bd-10hic legacy-quarantine pattern: remove it (with permission) or move/rename so it cannot be mistaken for live nor accidentally re-declared as a module.
  - At minimum, REMOVE or hard-gate SkipServerVerification (e.g. behind #[cfg(test)], or delete the accept-all impl) so a future re-wire cannot resurrect an accept-all verifier; add a top-of-file DEAD/ORPHANED banner pointing to src/net/quic_native/ as the live stack.
  - Add a contract/grep test asserting no production ServerCertVerifier returns ServerCertVerified::assertion() unconditionally (catches re-introduction).

Filed by CopperKite, Phase-C security hunt 2026-06-14. Related: br-asupersync-7pwwwe (native QUIC no-skip-verify), bd-10hic (legacy quarantine pattern).

title: [ALIEN][TRACE] Geodesic Schedule Normalization (Canonical Low-Entropy Replay)
description:
## Goal

Compute a *canonical representative schedule* for a Mazurkiewicz trace equivalence class that is *better than Foata flattening* for human debugging and replay.

- Input: a trace `e_0..e_{n-1}` plus an independence relation `I(e_i, e_j)`.
- Output: a deterministic linear extension (total order) of the induced partial order that minimizes a chosen cost (default: task-switch count) under deterministic tie-breaking.

This is a Phase-6 upgrade: Foata normal form gives canonical equivalence-class IDs, but does not optimize for "visual entropy" / context switches.

## Key definitions (self-contained)

- **Independence relation** `I`: symmetric, irreflexive; independent events may be swapped without observable change.
- **Dependency DAG / poset**: build edges `i -> j` for each `i < j` such that `NOT I(e_i, e_j)`.
- **Linear extension**: any total order consistent with the DAG.
- **Switch cost**: number of times the "active task" changes between adjacent events. We define a deterministic event-to-lane mapping (usually TaskId; global events use a pseudo-task key).

## Determinism + correctness constraints

- Must preserve all dependency edges (soundness).
- Must be deterministic across runs given identical trace + config.
- Must never use wall-clock time.
- Must not change the equivalence class semantics: output is a reordering *only of independent events*.

## Deliverables

- Trace -> poset builder (reusable for other tooling).
- Exact solver for bounded traces (A*/IDA* with admissible heuristic).
- Deterministic heuristic for large traces (fallback when exact is too expensive).
- "Galaxy-brain" optional debug ledger: show cost breakdown and why choice X was made.
- Tests: linear-extension validity + equivalence-class invariants + cost improvements on known patterns.
close_reason: All 8 sub-tasks completed: TracePoset builder (bd-1ast), exact A*/IDA* solver (bd-28sb), beam/greedy heuristics (bd-2oi3), lab integration (bd-1scf), test suite (bd-3dre), E2E harness (bd-1i1w), benchmarks (bd-1rz6), decision ledger (bd-36yp). Geodesic normalization is fully implemented with 39 unit tests, 14 E2E tests, 6 benchmark groups.

title: h1 streaming server: request body receive is bounded per read, not per request; a trickling client holds the connection and in-flight slot for max_body_size x idle_timeout
description:
The HTTP/1 streaming server bounds the request BODY receive per read, not per request, so a client that trickles bytes just inside the idle window holds the connection, its in-flight slot, the incoming-body queues and a handler parked on the body for up to max_body_size x idle_timeout (16 MiB x 60 s with defaults). The buffered server and the streaming HEAD reader in the same file both bound the whole read with one deadline for exactly this reason.

Evidence (src/http/h1/server.rs at 7fc9e53a4):
- 2489-2495 read_streaming_request_head: "One deadline for the whole head, not one per read: a peer trickling one byte per idle window would otherwise keep a partial head open for max_headers_size windows (slowloris); the buffered server bounds the entire request read the same way." head_deadline = now + idle_timeout, one timeout_at for the loop.
- 2581-2595 drive_incoming_body: per-read timeout(connection_now(cx), idle_timeout, read) inside the loop; the comment (2582-2586) claims "a peer that sends a head and then goes silent (or trickles) must not hold the connection, its in-flight slot and a handler parked on the body forever", but a trickle of one byte per (idle_timeout - epsilon) resets the bound on every read. The same comment states the driver runs outside the request region so the request budget does not cover it.
- 831-838 buffered Http1Server::read_next: the entire read_next (head plus body assembled by the codec) runs under one timeout(idle_timeout), so the buffered path is not exposed.
- 1119-1131 / 1488-1494: request_timeout defaults to None (Http1Config::default 130) and request_timeout_header_cap to None, so with default config nothing else bounds the body receive; when a request_timeout is configured the handler is cancelled at the deadline and join_streaming_handler_and_body (2658-2666) then bounds the remaining drain by unread_body_drain_timeout, so the exposure is confined to the default configuration.
- 1435 / 1765: the InFlightRequestGuard is acquired at head read and held across the trickle, so a listener-level in-flight cap is consumed by these connections.

Impact: reliability / resource exhaustion on Http1StreamingServer::serve_with_peer_addr, serve_sse and serve_produced (all three call drive_incoming_body). Not a correctness bug for honest clients.

Suggested repair: give the body receive one request-scoped bound, consistent with the head reader and the buffered server. Options, cheapest first: (a) arm a single body deadline when the head is parsed (now + idle_timeout, like head_deadline) and use timeout_at in drive_incoming_body; this matches the buffered server exactly but caps legitimate uploads to one idle window, which the buffered server already does; (b) a minimum-progress rule: keep the per-read idle bound but also fail with ClientAborted when a full idle window delivered fewer than N bytes (N configurable, e.g. 4 KiB), so slow-but-real uploads still pass; (c) when request_timeout is configured, pass the request budget deadline into the read timeout so the driver stops at the same instant the handler is cancelled. Whichever is chosen, fix the comment at 2582-2586 so it does not claim trickle protection the code does not provide.

Repro test sketch (native, loopback TCP, streaming server with idle_timeout = 200 ms, max_body_size = 64): client sends a head with Content-Length: 64 then one byte every 150 ms; assert the server does not return before ~9.6 s today (64 x 150 ms) and that the in-flight counter stays at 1 throughout; after the repair the connection ends within a small multiple of idle_timeout with the request counted once.

Found during the read-only fresh-eyes pass (asupersync-cqzuzt) while source is frozen for v0.5.0; no edits made.
close_reason: Fixed in 6580764f9: streaming body driver shares one idle_timeout socket-wait budget per body. RED control (old per-read bound served the trickled request, exit 101) / GREEN (94/94 server tests) receipts in comments.

title: [perf-hot-path] http/h2/hpack: HUFFMAN_DECODE_INDEX HashMap → flat 4-bit-stride state table per RFC 7541 Appendix B (0krok5 follow-up)
description: Follow-up from asupersync-0krok5 deferred closure (commit e32fd747a). The current HUFFMAN_DECODE_INDEX is a HashMap<(u32, u8), Option<u8>> probed up to 22 times per uncertain decode position (loop over code_len 9..=30) on the slow path. Standard fix per RFC 7541 Appendix B is a flat 4-bit-stride state-machine table (~256 states × 16 nibble transitions = ~4KB), used by h2-rs / hyper / nginx. Implementation: build the table at compile-time via const-eval or at startup via LazyLock; transitions encode (next_state, optional_emitted_byte, terminal_flag). The existing 5/6/7/8-bit inline fast paths in decode_huffman should be retained as a top-of-loop check before falling into the table. Add a microbench against a 1KB Huffman-encoded payload to measure end-to-end win.
close_reason: Implemented in commit 8e3353e44: HUFFMAN_DECODE_INDEX HashMap replaced with canonical 4-bit-stride state-machine table per RFC 7541 Appendix B (256 states × 16 nibbles × 4 bytes = 16 KiB, fits in L1). Each input byte → 2 array lookups, uniform cost regardless of code length. Replaces both the cascaded 5/6/7/8-bit fast paths and the 22-probe HashMap slow path.

title: HTTP/3 router listener: DATA frames over 1 MiB close the connection (our own client sends them), early streaming response reset after FIN, no idle/per-connection bounds
description:
Read-only audit of src/web/router/h3_listener.rs at origin/main 2ad2e55c8 (2026-10-02, SapphireHill subagent). Item 2 is confirmed by reading the code; the rest are high-confidence code readings, not yet reproduced.

1. An early streaming response is reset after FIN and counted as cancelled (h3_listener.rs complete() ~743-757, poll_owner ~777-792 / ~950-962, reset ~2030-2036 or ~1408-1413).
   - When the response finishes before the body is read, complete() fails the body writer with Cancelled{ParentCancelled}.
   - A child task still reading the body (a case the rustdoc at ~748-751 explicitly supports) records that failure. poll_owner cannot tell it from a real body error: it turns the finished request (terminal == Some(true)) into cancelled and sends RESET_STREAM(0x10c) on a stream that already sent FIN. That discards any unacknowledged response data, and cancelled_requests is incremented.
   - No test: authenticated_listener_streaming_early_drop_preserves_response_without_fin covers only a handler that drops the body itself.

2. A DATA frame over 1 MiB closes the whole connection. CONFIRMED.
   - The listener builds NativeH3Session::server(), whose H3ConnectionConfig default max_frame_payload_size is 1 MiB (h3_native.rs:168).
   - FrameHeader::decode (h3_receive_frame.rs) rejects any declared length above that, DATA included. That is a connection error, so every request on the connection fails.
   - This happens in streaming mode too, although that mode already streams DATA payloads through DataFrameCursor (h3_quic.rs ~1493-1529): the limit there is artificial.
   - The crate's own client, NativeH3Session::send_request (h3_quic.rs ~774), writes the whole body as one DATA frame; aioquic's send_data does the same. Our own client therefore cannot POST more than 1 MiB to our own server. RFC 9114 sets no limit on DATA frames.
   - Fix sketch: parse DATA headers without the payload bound and stream the payload through the cursor in both modes, keeping the bound for HEADERS and other frames. Also split client request bodies into DATA frames no larger than the limit. Buffered-mode Data events then arrive per chunk rather than per frame: audit consumers and tests first. The NativeH3Session surface is public under http3, so check v0.4.3.

3. Request memory has no listener-wide cap, and the NativeH3ListenerConfig rustdoc (~27-31) wrongly says receive windows bound it.
   - Each stream can buffer a partial frame of up to 1 MiB, because windows slide as the parser reads (streams.rs advance_bounded_recv_windows; refresh_receive_credit ~1624-1640).
   - With defaults (64 connections x 128 streams, plus a 64 MiB body budget per connection), roughly 12 GiB can be held for up to the 30 s request_timeout. router.max_buffered_body_bytes does not shrink the parser buffer. Item 2's cursor fix removes the DATA part of this.

4. No HTTP/3 idle timer: a connection that never sends a request but keeps the QUIC idle timer alive (PINGs) holds a max_connections slot forever (~1253, ~1598-1621).

5. Misleading report fields (low):
   - A clean client close or an idle timeout increments failed_connections.
   - remove_connection drops the route at once, skipping QUIC draining.
   - A single connection's retirement deadline sets the listener-wide drain_timed_out.

6. No per-connection share of max_concurrent_requests (low): each per-connection default (128) equals the global cap (128). One streaming client holding 128 uploads open makes everyone else get H3_REQUEST_REJECTED for 30 s.

Also (CPU): observe_streams scans every possible stream of every connection after every endpoint event, about 262k map lookups per UDP batch at max_requests_per_connection 4096 x 64 connections.

The audit found these sound: cancellation on client reset, STOP_SENDING, connection loss and deadlines; in-flight and streaming-ownership accounting; pause/resume wakeups; stream routing; GOAWAY id; Content-Length mismatch; header validation.

title: [ALIEN][TRACE][GEO] Implement TracePoset builder (dependency DAG)
description:
## Purpose

Provide a reusable, deterministic representation of the partial order induced by dependence.

This is shared infra for:
- geodesic normalization (this epic)
- persistent-homology prioritization (HOMO epic)
- future DPOR upgrades (wakeup trees can consult a canonical poset)

## Codebase note (avoid duplication)

`src/trace/event_structure.rs` already builds a causality edge list from a single trace using the independence relation.

This task should either:
- extend that existing representation, OR
- introduce a thin "poset view" over it

so we do not maintain two subtly-different dependency DAG builders.

## Design sketch

- Input: `&[TraceEvent]`.
- Output: a structure that supports:
  - predecessors/successors queries
  - deterministic iteration order
  - fast "available set" (minimal elements of the remaining poset)
  - `owner(e)` projection for switch-cost computations

Example shape:
- `TracePoset { n, preds: Vec<SmallSet>, succs: Vec<SmallSet>, owner: Vec<OwnerKey> }`

Edges are derived by:
- for i < j: edge i -> j iff NOT independent(events[i], events[j]).

## Constraints

- Deterministic ordering of adjacency lists and available-set iteration.
- Avoid unnecessary allocations (pre-size Vecs; use bitsets/SmallVec where appropriate).

## Acceptance criteria

- Property test: for every edge i -> j, original trace had i < j and NOT independent(i,j).
- Topological sort exists and has length n.
- OwnerKey projection matches GEO spec (bd-3icc).
close_reason: Implemented TracePoset+OwnerKey in src/trace/event_structure.rs with deterministic adjacency + topo_sort + unit tests
