title: [RAPTORQ-RFC6330] Full Conformance, Correctness Closure, and Optimization Program
description:
Comprehensive execution program to make Asupersync's RaptorQ implementation RFC 6330-accurate, algorithmically correct under adversarial erasure patterns, deterministically testable, and dramatically faster on real workloads.

Background and rationale:
- Current implementation passes internal tests but diverges from RFC 6330 mechanics in key areas (parameter derivation, tuple/degree usage, equation construction, and tolerated failure surfaces).
- Internal consistency is not enough for interoperability or formal correctness claims.
- Profiling shows large optimization headroom, especially in GF(256) arithmetic and decoder linear algebra.

Program intent:
1) Correctness first: strict RFC behavior and deterministic decode guarantees for in-scope conditions.
2) Performance second: optimization only inside proven-safe envelopes.
3) Operational durability: CI gates and artifacts that keep the implementation correct and fast over time.

This epic is self-contained so future contributors can execute the full plan directly from beads without consulting separate design docs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. RFC 6330 conformance matrix is complete for implemented feature scope and each requirement has code/tests linked.
2. Encoder/decoder pathways use RFC-aligned parameter derivation and tuple/equation generation semantics for supported object sizes.
3. Test suite includes deterministic golden vectors, differential checks, and metamorphic/property checks with no tolerated silent decode corruption.
4. Comprehensive unit-test matrix and deterministic E2E script suite are both complete for all in-scope scenario families.
5. Structured logging schema is applied across unit/E2E/bench flows with stable scenario IDs, seeds, and artifact pointers.
6. Every failure path includes a direct repro command and stable fixture/seed reference.
7. Performance program demonstrates substantial wins on representative workloads while preserving determinism and correctness.
8. CI gates enforce formatting, compiler/lint quality, correctness suites, and performance regression budgets.
9. Final sign-off package includes residual-risk register, unsupported RFC surface explicitly declared, and maintenance procedures.
10. Program closure requires explicit evidence that comprehensive unit tests and deterministic E2E suites both pass with schema-validated structured logs and replayable artifacts for each critical scenario family.
notes:
Execution principles:
- Never trade correctness for speed; optimization tracks are downstream of correctness gates.
- Preserve deterministic behavior in lab-style testing environments.
- Keep all results reproducible with concrete commands and artifacts.

Known anchor findings this program addresses:
- Heuristic parameter derivation instead of strict systematic-index-table lookup.
- Non-RFC equation construction in source/LT/repair rows.
- Decoder reconstruction symmetry gaps and solver robustness risks.
- Tests that currently tolerate decode failures in some fuzz/property scenarios.
- Measured hotspots concentrated in GF(256) multiply-add and elimination logic.

Over-arching project alignment:
- Supports Asupersync goals: cancel-correctness culture, deterministic testing, no hidden ambient behavior, and high-assurance primitives.
- Produces auditable evidence for future optimization and conformance claims.

Validation rigor guardrail:
- This epic is not complete until unit coverage and deterministic E2E coverage are both implemented with structured forensic logging and reproducible replay commands.

title: [RaptorQ] Make Symbol::new_for_test source-by-default and add explicit repair helper
description:
# Summary
`Symbol::new_for_test(object, sbn, esi, data)` currently infers `SymbolKind` as `Source` only for `esi == 0` and `Repair` otherwise. That is not a valid RaptorQ rule because source-vs-repair depends on block K, not on whether ESI equals zero.

# Why this is a bug
Many tests use `new_for_test` as a generic symbol constructor for ordered source-like sequences (`esi = 0,1,2,...`). The current helper silently misclassifies every nonzero ESI as repair, which can distort `SymbolSet` accounting and any other test logic that inspects symbol kind.

# Plan
- make the default helper construct a source symbol
- add an explicit repair-specific test helper
- update only the call sites that truly need repair-kind semantics
- validate affected surfaces with `rch exec -- ...` cargo commands

title: [FOUNDATION] franken_decision crate — Decision Contract Schema and Runtime
description: Implement the franken_decision crate that defines the canonical Decision Contract infrastructure used across ALL FrankenSuite projects. This crate is the third leg of the foundation tripod (franken_kernel types, franken_evidence ledger, franken_decision contracts). MOTIVATION: Currently, Decision Contracts exist only in the methodology bead (bd-1e2if.6) and are scheduler-specific. But Decision Contracts are a cross-cutting concern -- every FrankenSuite project that makes runtime decisions must use the same contract schema. SCOPE: (1) DecisionContract trait: state_space(), action_set(), loss_matrix(), update_posterior(), choose_action(), fallback_action(). (2) LossMatrix<S,A> struct: indexed by (state, action) pairs, non-negative values, serializable to/from TOML. (3) Posterior struct: probability distribution over states, must sum to 1.0. (4) FallbackPolicy: calibration drift threshold, e-process breach, confidence interval width triggers. (5) DecisionAuditEntry: links to EvidenceLedger for structured audit records. DEPENDENCIES: Depends on franken_kernel (TraceId, DecisionId, Cx) and franken_evidence (EvidenceLedger). TRACING SPEC: Span: decision::evaluate with decision_id, contract_name. INFO log: decision made (action, expected_loss, calibration, fallback). WARN log: calibration drift detected. ERROR log: e-process breach. DEBUG log: posterior update details. Metrics: decision_latency_us (histogram), fallback_active_total (counter), calibration_score (gauge). ACCEPTANCE: DecisionContract implementable in <50 lines, LossMatrix supports TOML reconfig, posterior update O(|S|) no alloc, decision latency <5us, all decisions auditable via EvidenceLedger.

title: Implement algebraic law property tests for combinators
description:
## Purpose
Implement property-based tests that verify the algebraic laws from asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §7. These laws enable optimizations, compositional reasoning, and are core semantic guarantees.

## The Laws

### LAW-JOIN-ASSOC
```
join(join(a, b), c) ≃ join(a, join(b, c))
```

### LAW-JOIN-COMM (when policy allows)
```
join(a, b) ≃ join(b, a)   // Outcomes may be reordered
```

### LAW-RACE-COMM
```
race(a, b) ≃ race(b, a)   // Winner depends on schedule
```

### LAW-TIMEOUT-MIN
```
timeout(d1, timeout(d2, f)) ≃ timeout(min(d1, d2), f)
```

### LAW-RACE-NEVER
```
race(f, never) ≃ f
```

### LAW-RACE-JOIN-DIST (speculative execution)
```
race(join(a, b), join(a, c)) ≃ join(a, race(b, c))
// Don't run 'a' twice
```

## What ≃ Means (from §7.0)
Observational equivalence up to:
1. Eliding silent steps (τ)
2. Quotienting traces by swaps of independent actions
3. Renaming fresh ids consistently

## Implementation Strategy

Use `proptest` to generate:
- Random task durations
- Random success/failure outcomes
- Random cancellation timing

For each law, verify that the LHS and RHS produce equivalent results.

### Equivalence Checking
```rust
fn outcomes_equivalent(a: Outcome, b: Outcome) -> bool {
    // Same variant and value (up to permutation for join)
}

fn traces_equivalent(a: &Trace, b: &Trace) -> bool {
    // Normalize both traces, compare
}
```

## Test Categories

### 1) Lattice Laws (Outcome)
- Associativity of combine
- Commutativity of combine
- Idempotence of combine
- Identity element (Ok is identity for combine)

### 2) Semiring Laws (Budget)
- Associativity of meet
- Commutativity of meet
- Idempotence of meet (min is idempotent)

### 3) Strengthen Laws (CancelReason)
- Idempotence
- Associativity
- Monotonicity

### 4) Combinator Laws
- All laws listed above

## Acceptance Criteria
- Property tests run deterministically with fixed seeds
- Coverage of all listed laws
- Failures include counterexample and trace

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §7: Algebraic Laws
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.2: Near-semiring structure
notes: Added race law property tests in tests/algebraic_laws.rs (race comm/never/join-dist severity). Ran cargo fmt --check, cargo check, cargo clippy; full cargo test hung on doc test (limit.rs); ran cargo test --test algebraic_laws OK.

The design calls out admission control and backpressure as core scheduling features:

title: [security-audit][HIGH] grpc/interceptor.rs: BearerAuthValidator validator closure typically uses non-constant-time string comparison — timing oracle on the bearer token
description: src/grpc/interceptor.rs:309-344. BearerAuthValidator::intercept_request extracts the bearer token from the Authorization header and calls (self.validator)(token). The validator is user-supplied F: Fn(&str) -> bool. The canonical user implementation is "|t| t == EXPECTED_TOKEN" or similar, which uses Rust string equality — byte-by-byte short-circuit comparison. An attacker can iterate the token byte-by-byte and observe response timing (Status::unauthenticated returns slightly faster on early-byte mismatch than on late-byte mismatch). For ASCII tokens of length N, the attack reduces token recovery from O(256^N) to O(256*N). Library cannot fix the user-supplied closure, but MUST document the constant-time-comparison requirement and ideally provide a SafeBearerAuthValidator built on subtle::ConstantTimeEq that takes the expected token directly rather than a closure. Severity HIGH P1 because the failure mode is silent — code that "looks right" leaks the secret. The same gap exists in any auth_validator(closure) call path.
close_reason: Implemented constant-time bearer-token comparison in grpc/interceptor.rs. Added private constant_time_eq() with XOR accumulator + std::hint::black_box barrier (functionally equivalent to subtle::ConstantTimeEq, no new dependency). Added BearerAuthValidator::with_token / auth_validator_with_token safe-by-default constructors that compare presented token to expected via constant_time_eq. Documented BearerAuthValidator::new (closure path) as caller-responsibility with explicit warning. Three tests: constant_time_eq_correctness (covers identical / first-byte / last-byte / mismatched-length / empty / black-box-wrapped runtime cases), bearer_auth_validator_with_token_accepts_correct_token, bearer_auth_validator_with_token_rejects_wrong_token_at_any_position (iterates first-byte-differ / last-byte-differ / shorter / longer / unrelated / empty). Length mismatch returns fast — length is not secret. Commit 4e33aff88.

title: [memory-ordering] observability/otel.rs: sample_counter Relaxed fetch_add — non-deterministic sampling decisions across threads
description:
src/observability/otel.rs:989 — should_sample() does:

  let count = self.sample_counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
  let threshold = (sampling.sample_rate * 100.0) as u64;
  (count % 100) < threshold

With Relaxed ordering, two threads racing fetch_add on the same counter can observe DIFFERENT counter values for what should be sequential decisions. On weakly-ordered targets, the sampling decision is therefore non-deterministic across threads — same span, two threads, different "should_sample" verdicts depending on which fetch_add the CPU sees as first.

Threat model: lab replay should produce identical sampled-event streams for identical input. With Relaxed, two replays on different host architectures (or even the same host under different scheduler decisions) can produce different sampled sets.

Fix direction:
  - fetch_add(1, Ordering::Release) on the writer (paired with Acquire on any reader that loads the counter for stats).
  - OR, since the counter is only read inside the same fetch_add, switching to AcqRel preserves single-CAS semantics and gives the visibility property.
  - Alternative: avoid the counter entirely and use a per-thread counter + deterministic seed; but that requires plumbing a Cx-rooted thread id which is a larger refactor.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting deepest 8th-pass on src/observability/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: AcqRel ordering on sample_counter.fetch_add in OtelMetrics::should_sample landed in commit f844f5555. Comments document why AcqRel preserves the deterministic-sampling property the lab-replay contract depends on, while Relaxed allowed weakly-ordered targets to observe stale counter values across threads (same input, different replays, different sampled-event sets).

title: [RAPTORQ-RFC6330-CONFORMANCE] RFC 6330 Specification Clause Matrix and Test Enumeration
description:
## Overview

Systematically enumerate and categorize every testable requirement from RFC 6330 to create the foundational conformance matrix for RaptorQ implementation validation.

## Background

Current RaptorQ testing focuses on implementation correctness and performance but lacks systematic RFC 6330 conformance verification. This bead establishes the specification-driven test foundation required for claiming standards compliance.

## Scope

**IDENTIFY Phase (Conformance Loop Step 1)**
- RFC 6330: RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery
- Version: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6330.html (final version)
- Focus: All implementable sections for asupersync's use case

**EXTRACT Phase (Conformance Loop Step 2)**  
- Enumerate every MUST/SHOULD/MAY clause by section
- Categorize requirements by: Parameter Derivation, Encoding, Decoding, Systematic Index, Tuple Generation, Matrix Construction
- Priority: MUST clauses (conformance critical) > SHOULD clauses > MAY clauses
- Tag each requirement with: section number, requirement level, testability category

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **Complete RFC 6330 clause inventory** produced as structured data (JSON/YAML)
2. **Requirement categorization** with these dimensions:
   - Section: 4.1 (Objects), 4.2 (Encoding), 4.3 (Decoding), 5.1-5.5 (Parameters/Tuples), etc.
   - Level: MUST, SHOULD, MAY  
   - Category: Unit testable, Integration testable, Edge case, Performance constraint
   - Implementation status: Implemented, Not implemented, Partially implemented
3. **Testability assessment** for each requirement:
   - Direct test: Can write isolated test
   - Differential test: Need reference implementation comparison  
   - Property test: Need metamorphic/invariant testing
   - Manual verification: Requires human inspection
4. **Coverage baseline** establishing current test gaps
5. **Priority matrix** for conformance test creation order

## Deliverables



## Validation

- Matrix completeness: Every RFC section 4-5 requirement enumerated
- Testability classification: Each requirement has test strategy
- Priority scoring: MUST clause coverage plan exists
- Implementation mapping: Each requirement linked to current code (if exists)

## Dependencies

None (foundational bead)

## Time Estimate

4 hours (systematic RFC review + structured data creation)

title: TLS: CRL config refuses every chain not covered by a CRL (contradicts docs); handshake may report done before its final flight is sent; read after an error reports clean EOF
description:
Read-only audit of src/tls (stream, connector, acceptor, types) at origin/main 731a0f5b1 (2026-10-03, SapphireHill subagent), checked against the rustls 0.23.45 / webpki 0.103.15 sources. It found no buffer, waker or data-loss bug in normal read/write/flush/shutdown use. Excluded as already filed: 0n1dvh (0-RTT), kjyh84 (certificate expiry).

1. (medium) With CRLs configured, any chain not fully covered by the CRLs is refused (connector.rs ~1156-1159).
   - WebPkiServerVerifier::builder(..).with_crls(..) keeps the rustls defaults: check the whole chain, and treat a missing CRL as UnknownRevocationStatus.
   - The rustdoc (~994-1004) says each CRL applies only to its issuer and is otherwise silently inert.
   - Effect: with_webpki_roots().with_crl_pem(corp_ca_crl) fails every handshake to public hosts. Expired CRLs are accepted without warning.
   - No test proves enforcement.
2. (medium-low) Strict validation, which is on by default, rejects chain certificates with an empty subject (no CN, OU or O; acceptor.rs ~543-552). RFC 5280 allows SAN-only certificates. The only workaround also disables the expiry checks.
3. (low-medium) The handshake can report done while its final flight is unsent (stream.rs ~323-336).
   - When the last write returned Pending, `!is_handshaking()` still returns Ready, and connect()/accept() never flush.
   - A TLS 1.2 server's final ChangeCipherSpec+Finished, or a TLS 1.3 client before a server-speaks-first protocol, can then deadlock both sides until a timeout. This is reachable over bounded or tunnelled transports.
4. (low) After a read error (truncation without close_notify, or a fatal record), the state becomes Closed and the next poll_read returns a clean EOF (stream.rs ~489-491, 534, 544). A caller that polls again treats a truncated stream as complete.
5. (low) The require_sni, alpn_required and sni_alpn_allow_list rejections happen after a completed handshake, by a bare close with no alert (acceptor.rs ~250-318). The client has already received the certificate. The docs claim this prevents exposing the default certificate.
6. (low) An invalid max_fragment_size passes build(), then every accept() fails (rustls accepts 32-16389).
7. (low) An empty enforcing pin set validates any certificate (types.rs ~668-670), yet its Default doc says "secure-by-default".
8. (low; third-party IO only) The flush loops treat Ok(0) from the transport as done; the full-buffer write path can spin; poll_write can return Err after rustls already accepted bytes.
9. (low) Version bounds: max_protocol_version(TLSv1_1) maps to no cap; min_protocol_version(TLSv1_0) is a build error.
10. (low, API) Every handshake error becomes TlsError::Handshake(String). The Certificate* and ChainValidation variants are never produced by connect or accept.

The auditor found these sound: read and write buffering across Pending; close_notify; UnexpectedEof on the first truncated read; shutdown sequencing; wakers in both directions; fatal alerts flushed; handshake timeout and cancellation; root stores add rather than replace; SNI for IP literals and trailing dots; ALPN preference; the mTLS matrix.

Multiple lock ordering patterns (reason→listeners, children→cancelled_at) create cognitive burden. Consider simplifying the cancellation protocol or adding formal verification of the lock orderings.
close_reason:
won't-fix: Complexity necessary for correctness in distributed cancellation protocol.

The 5747-line symbol_cancel.rs implements race-free cancellation with sophisticated lock ordering (reason→listeners, children→cancelled_at) and Release/Acquire semantics. This complexity is justified because:

1. Distributed cancellation requires complex coordination to avoid race conditions
2. Lock ordering prevents deadlocks in concurrent symbol broadcast scenarios  
3. The code is working correctly in production with no reported race bugs
4. Simplification would likely introduce subtle concurrency bugs
5. Formal verification (suggested alternative) would be more expensive than maintenance

The cognitive burden is acceptable given the critical nature of cancellation correctness. Any simplification should be deferred until we have evidence of actual maintenance issues or bugs caused by the complexity.

title: Create InjectionReport with actionable failure information
description:
# Task

Design and implement the `InjectionReport` that provides actionable information
about cancellation testing results.

## Report Requirements

1. **Summary Statistics**
   - Total await points discovered
   - Points tested (depends on strategy)
   - Points passed / failed
   - Overall pass/fail verdict

2. **Failure Details** (for each failed point)
   - Await point identifier (ideally source location)
   - Which oracles failed
   - What invariant was violated
   - Relevant context (task IDs, region IDs, etc.)

3. **Debugging Aids**
   - Seed for reproduction
   - Execution trace (if tracing enabled)
   - Minimal reproduction command

4. **Machine-Readable Output**
   - JSON format for CI integration
   - JUnit XML format for test frameworks

## Report Format

```
Cancellation Injection Test Report
==================================

Summary:
  Await points discovered: 47
  Points tested: 47 (strategy: AllPoints)
  Passed: 45
  Failed: 2

Failures:

  [1] Await point at src/http/client.rs:142
      Seed: 12345
      Failed oracles:
        - ObligationLeakOracle: SendPermit(id=55) leaked by Task(100)
          Obligation was Reserved when task completed with Cancelled(Timeout)
      
      To reproduce:
        Lab::new()
            .with_seed(12345)
            .with_injection_point("src/http/client.rs:142")
            .run(test_fn);

  [2] Await point at src/http/client.rs:198
      Seed: 12345
      Failed oracles:
        - TaskLeakOracle: Task(101) not completed when Region(5) closed
          Task was in state Running, parent region closed with Cancelled
      
      To reproduce:
        Lab::new()
            .with_seed(12345)
            .with_injection_point("src/http/client.rs:198")
            .run(test_fn);
```

## Implementation

```rust
impl InjectionReport {
    pub fn display(&self) -> impl Display;
    pub fn to_json(&self) -> serde_json::Value;
    pub fn to_junit_xml(&self) -> String;
    pub fn is_success(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn failed_points(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &InjectionFailure>;
}

impl InjectionFailure {
    pub fn reproduction_code(&self) -> String;
    pub fn source_location(&self) -> Option<&str>;
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Human-readable summary with counts
- [ ] Detailed failure information
- [ ] Source location for await points (when available)
- [ ] Reproduction instructions for each failure
- [ ] JSON output for CI
- [ ] JUnit XML output for test frameworks
- [ ] Clear pass/fail verdict

title: E2E integration test suite with scenario-based testing
description:
# E2E Integration Test Suite (Scenario-Based)

## Purpose
Verify that Phase 0 components work together correctly through realistic scenarios, using the lab runtime for determinism and the trace system for rich diagnostics.

E2E tests should answer:
- “Do the invariants hold in realistic compositions?”
- “Are failures reproducible and explainable?”

## Diagnostics / Logging Strategy
- Do **not** rely on global logging crates.
- Use the runtime’s `TraceBuffer` and dump formatted traces on failure.
- For determinism tests, run the scenario twice and compare traces.

## Canonical Scenarios (Phase 0)
Each scenario must end with invariant checks:
- no task leaks
- no obligation leaks
- losers drained
- quiescence on close
- all finalizers ran
- no ambient authority
- determinism (where applicable)

### 1) Basic lifecycle
- spawn task → complete

### 2) Nested region quiescence
- inner region closes before outer continues

### 3) Cancellation protocol end-to-end
- request cancel → checkpoint acknowledge → drain → finalize → terminal

### 4) Race with loser draining
- loser holds a resource; ensure drain releases it

### 5) Two-phase channels
- reserve/commit send; cancel mid-reserve; ensure no leaks

### 6) Obligation abort on cancellation
- hold permit then cancel; permit aborts (no leak)

### 7) Budget exhaustion behavior
- intentionally non-terminating task; verify budget-driven cancellation/termination semantics (must match the “budget exhaustion” decision bead)

### 8) Finalizer LIFO + masking
- multiple finalizers run in reverse order, even under cancellation

### 9) Deterministic replay
- same seed/config yields identical trace

### 10) Stress (many tasks)
- spawn many tasks; ensure completion and no leaks

## Acceptance Criteria
- Suite runs deterministically under lab runtime.
- Failures include:
  - formatted trace
  - invariant violation evidence
  - determinism divergence report when applicable

## Dependencies
- Lab runtime
- Trace infrastructure
- Unit-test fixtures/utilities

title: QUIC native TLS audit (r8): pub server-identity confirmation without proof of key possession; no CONNECTION_CLOSE with CRYPTO_ERROR; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of src/net/quic_native/tls.rs and its call sites (handshake_driver.rs, connection.rs, quic_core, transport_quic/native_link.rs) at origin/main 0023804e6 (SapphireHill audit agent round 8, 10-05). Report: /data/tmp/rc_20260923/audit_r8_quic_tls.md. H1 (ATP accept stash unbounded and source-blind before the peer is known) is fixed under 8vrx8q. M1 (one stray long-header datagram aborts accept) was already fixed in stack N (5f1fcj).

Re-checked at origin 3d43b3fe9 (10-06): M2, M3, L1 and L2 hold (no CRYPTO_ERROR close anywhere in quic_native or quic_core; the standalone server still spends HANDSHAKE_MAX_FLIGHTS = 64 loop turns whatever arrives; a full early-1-RTT queue still fails the handshake). 5f1fcj (872e7c4e0, 82b3e34b3) has changed handshake_driver.rs since, so line numbers here are 0023804e6's.

## MEDIUM
M2. QuicConnection::verify_server_identity_and_confirm_handshake (tls.rs ~320-341, connection.rs ~767-812) clears the client identity gate on WebPKI chain + hostname checks alone; nothing proves the server holds the key or binds the chain to the session keys. The docs and threat model §5.2 present it as the production path; tests/quic_native_x509_verification.rs ~44-63 reaches Established with no TLS exchange. A man in the middle could relay the server's public certificate. The in-tree rustls paths do not call it, but it is pub. Fix options: derive the receipt only from a completed client QuicHandshakeDriver (record_verified_server_identity pub(crate) behind a sealed proof type), or move the method behind test-internals and correct the docs. Either changes a pub API: owner decision.
M3. handshake_driver.rs ~1358-1367 drops the TLS alert, and nothing sends CONNECTION_CLOSE with CRYPTO_ERROR (0x0100 + alert, RFC 9001 §4.8); ~1147-1150 also ignores a peer's CONNECTION_CLOSE in Initial/Handshake packets. On ALPN or certificate failure the peer retransmits for up to ~96 s (64 flights) and the reason (e.g. 0x178 no_application_protocol) never surfaces. Fix: send CONNECTION_CLOSE with the alert in the highest long-header space with keys; treat a received close as terminal at least in Handshake space.

## LOW
L1 standalone server loop spends its 64-iteration budget on stray datagrams (handshake_driver.rs ~1901; sibling of 5f1fcj). L2 a full early-1-RTT queue aborts the handshake instead of dropping (~1730, ~1944). L3 transport-parameter decode accepts server-only parameters from a client, does not validate active_connection_id_limit or the reset token, quadratic duplicate check (quic_core/mod.rs ~571-650). L4 0-RTT modelled without real keys; the model allows application sends at the wrong levels (tls.rs ~1794). L5 transcript never recorded (key_id/transcript_hash identical across connections). L6 discarding keys only sets a flag (see 3whs3i/18hhdp). L7 no encryption-level check on CRYPTO data, no coalesced-DCID check, 1-RTT CRYPTO silently dropped. L8 stale "no certificate verification" docs (tls.rs ~97-103, connection.rs ~714-720, handshake_driver.rs ~30-32). L9 tests that cannot fail; a conformance harness compares the code with a copy of itself; no update_key or full-packet RFC 9001 vector tests.
SUSPECTED (not traced): retained 1-RTT packets possibly resent under older keys after a key update (RFC 9001 §6.4); whether webpki accepts a self-signed leaf present in the root store.

Already tracked elsewhere: ncbhg3 / 18hhdp F3, 3whs3i / 18hhdp, o7stss, y1jsbw / 80q0ob.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill e0155ea8, 2026-10-07: claiming M3.

Re-read at S4 tip 4c43e1787 (not landed yet; it changes handshake_driver.rs). M3 still holds:
- read_handshake maps a TLS alert to handshake_failure("read_hs_fatal_alert"), and nothing sends it. client_handshake_over_udp, server_handshake_over_udp_with_early_data and the managed endpoint's admission all return or fail without a CONNECTION_CLOSE.
- process_long_header_packet ignores every non-CRYPTO frame, so a peer's CONNECTION_CLOSE in Initial or Handshake space is skipped. The client then retransmits until its 64-flight budget runs out (64 x 1.5 s = 96 s).

Plan (one stack after S4):
- A local TLS alert sends CONNECTION_CLOSE (0x1c) with CRYPTO_ERROR = 0x0100 + alert (RFC 9001 section 4.8), in the long-header spaces RFC 9000 section 10.2.3 names: Handshake once its keys exist, and Initial as well while the peer may lack Handshake keys. The server's close stays inside its anti-amplification budget.
- A CONNECTION_CLOSE received in Initial or Handshake space ends the handshake at once with a stable code ("peer_closed_crypto_error" for 0x0100..=0x01ff, "peer_closed" otherwise). The driver keeps the peer's error code for callers that hold it.
- QuicTlsError is a public, exhaustive enum from v0.4.3, so no new variant is added.

Not in this claim: M2 (a pub API change, owner decision) and the LOWs.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill e0155ea8, 2026-10-07: M3, L1 and L2 LANDED (main = master a4742ee5e).

M3 (889b4af5b): a TLS refusal during the handshake is reported to the peer, and a peer's close ends the handshake at once.
- Before: a client that offered an ALPN the server refuses retransmitted for its whole flight budget (64 x 1.5 s = 96 s) and failed with client_handshake_recv_timeout. A server whose certificate the client rejected retransmitted until its own budget ran out.
- Sending: QuicHandshakeDriver::assemble_crypto_error_close builds CONNECTION_CLOSE (0x1c) with CRYPTO_ERROR = 0x0100 + the TLS alert (RFC 9001 4.8).
  - It uses the spaces RFC 9000 10.2.3 names: a client uses its highest space; a server whose client may lack Handshake keys uses Initial and Handshake.
  - Only a client's Initial is padded.
  - A TLS failure pins the failing packet's source CID, so the close reaches the peer even on its first packet.
  - Sent by client_handshake_over_udp, the standalone server loop (inside its anti-amplification budget), the managed endpoint's admissions (within 3x authenticated bytes, sharing the Retry's bounded queue slack) and ATP's accept loop.
- Receiving: a CONNECTION_CLOSE in an Initial or Handshake packet fails the handshake with "peer_closed_crypto_error" (0x0100..=0x01ff) or "peer_closed". The new QuicHandshakeDriver::peer_close_error_code (additive) has the exact code. QuicTlsError is a public exhaustive enum from v0.4.3, so it gains no variant.
- Tests: an_alpn_refusal_reaches_the_client_as_a_crypto_error_close (code 0x0178), a_rejected_certificate_reaches_the_server_as_a_handshake_space_close, a_refused_alpn_ends_both_udp_handshakes_promptly (both UDP loops end within 10 s) and managed_alpn_refusal_closes_the_client_handshake.

L1 (ace9b23c5): the standalone server loop no longer spends its 64-flight budget on stray datagrams.
- A flight now counts only for a PTO or for a batch with an accepted packet.
- The receive deadline is absolute, so a trickle of strays cannot keep the loop alive either.
- Test: stray_datagrams_do_not_spend_the_server_flight_budget (140 rounds of 8 strays before the client's Initial).

L2 (ace9b23c5): both standalone loops keep an early short-header packet only when it is addressed to their own connection ID. A full early queue drops the packet instead of ending the handshake (early_one_rtt_queue_exhausted is gone).
- Test: a_full_early_one_rtt_queue_drops_packets_instead_of_ending_the_handshake (48 packets for another CID, then 2000 for the client).

Controls: the combined control fails each of these six tests at its guard. Receipts are in the commit messages.
Still open: M2 (pub API, owner decision) and L3-L9.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Implement coordination-free execution for monotone saga steps
description:
For saga operations classified as monotone (per the CALM theorem analysis in bd-2wrsc.1), implement a coordination-free execution path that bypasses synchronization barriers. Instead of waiting for confirmation at each step, monotone steps execute speculatively and merge results via lattice join.

BACKGROUND (CALM Theorem, Graveyard section 13.3): The CALM theorem (Hellerstein and Alvaro, Keeping CALM: When Distributed Consistency is Easy, 2020) proves that monotone programs -- those whose outputs grow monotonically with inputs -- can execute without coordination while preserving consistency. Non-monotone operations (deletes, threshold checks, negation) require coordination because new input can invalidate previous conclusions.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Define a Lattice<T> trait with join, bottom, laws: associativity, commutativity, idempotency. Use lattices or crdts crate as reference. (2) Implement MonotoneSagaExecutor that groups consecutive monotone steps into coordination-free batches, executes concurrently via tokio::JoinSet, merges outputs via Lattice::join, inserts coordination barriers only before non-monotone steps. (3) Data structures: SagaPlan with Vec<SagaStep> where SagaStep has monotonicity field. SagaExecutionPlan with batches that are either CoordinationFree(Vec<SagaStep>) or Coordinated(SagaStep). (4) Conflict detection at boundaries: before executing a non-monotone step, verify all preceding monotone outputs have merged to fixed point. (5) Fallback: if monotonicity annotation is incorrect (post-hoc verification), abort coordination-free execution and fall back to fully-coordinated. Log fallback reason to EvidenceLedger.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Sagas with 100% monotone steps execute with zero coordination barriers. (2) Mixed sagas use coordination only at non-monotone boundaries. (3) Lattice merge produces identical final state regardless of execution order (1000 random orderings via FrankenLab). (4) Fallback triggers correctly when monotonicity is violated. (5) Latency improvement >= 1.5x for sagas with >50% monotone steps (criterion.rs, 95% CI excludes 1.0).

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Structured JSON via tracing with fields: saga_id, batch_index, batch_type, step_count, merge_count, merge_latency_us, final_state_hash. EvidenceLedger entry per saga execution: component=saga_executor, action=calm_optimized|fully_coordinated, top_features includes monotone_step_ratio. On fallback: WARN log with saga_id, failed_step_id, violation_reason. Trace span saga::batch with otel attributes.

TESTING APPROACH: Unit tests verify Lattice trait laws (proptest 10000 cases). Integration tests run mixed sagas under FrankenLab deterministic scheduler. Benchmark with criterion.rs for CALM-optimized vs baseline.

title: Implement determinism oracle: identical seed/config => identical trace
description:
# Determinism Oracle (Seed/Config => Identical Trace)

## Purpose
One of the non-negotiable invariants is **Determinism is first-class**. In Phase 0, this means:

> Given the same lab configuration (including seed) and the same user program, the runtime produces the same observable trace.

This oracle makes that guarantee executable.

## What This Oracle Checks
For a chosen scenario/program `P` and lab config `C`:
1. Run `P` under `C` and capture trace `T1`.
2. Run `P` again under the *same* `C` and capture trace `T2`.
3. Assert `T1 == T2` (byte-for-byte or structurally equal).

If not equal, report:
- first divergence index
- expected event vs actual event
- surrounding context window
- relevant runtime snapshot (optional)

## Design Notes
- Determinism must include:
  - task selection decisions
  - timer wake ordering
  - cancellation propagation ordering
  - obligation IDs (or stable renaming normalization)

### ID renaming normalization (important)
If IDs are allocated in a deterministic order, raw equality is fine.
If not, we must canonicalize traces by renaming “fresh IDs” consistently before comparison.

Phase 0 goal: **make ID allocation deterministic** so canonicalization is minimal.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The oracle exists as a helper (e.g., `LabRuntime::assert_deterministic(program)` or standalone function).
- At least 3 E2E scenarios use it:
  - nested regions
  - race + loser draining
  - two-phase channel under cancellation

## Testing
- Intentionally break determinism (e.g., by using wall-clock time) in a test-only “bad runtime” to ensure oracle detects divergence.

title: Epic: Sync Primitives Security & Correctness Audit
description:
# Epic: Sync Primitives Security & Correctness Audit

## Overview

Deep code review of the sync primitives (mutex, semaphore, barrier, rwlock, notify, once_cell) 
revealed several concurrency bugs, race conditions, and correctness issues that could cause 
deadlocks, starvation, or incorrect behavior under load.

## Background & Context

The sync primitives in `src/sync/` are foundational to the async runtime. Any bugs here 
propagate to all higher-level abstractions. Issues were discovered through systematic 
first-principles analysis of:

1. **Lock ordering** - Are locks acquired in consistent order to prevent deadlocks?
2. **Memory ordering** - Are Acquire/Release/SeqCst semantics used correctly?
3. **Spurious wakeups** - Are waiters re-checked after waking?
4. **Queue management** - Can waiter queues grow unbounded?
5. **Cancellation paths** - Are resources properly cleaned up on cancel?

## Severity Assessment

- **HIGH**: Mutex wake-while-holding-lock (can cause deadlock)
- **MEDIUM**: Semaphore fairness violation (queue jumping)
- **MEDIUM**: Barrier cancellation race (missed notifications)
- **LOW**: RwLock writer starvation characteristics (by design, but undocumented)

## Architectural Considerations

These fixes must preserve:
- Cancel-correctness (cancellation is a protocol, not instant)
- No ambient authority (effects flow through Cx)
- Structured concurrency (region close = quiescence)

## Success Criteria

- All sync primitive tests pass
- No clippy warnings in sync module
- Deadlock-free under stress testing
- Documented fairness/starvation characteristics

title: Phase 0: Cancellation Protocol & Finalization
description:
# Phase 0: Cancellation Protocol & Finalization

## Purpose
Cancellation is a **protocol** (request → drain → finalize), not a boolean flag. This feature ensures:
- cancellation is explicit, enumerable, and schedulable
- cleanup is bounded (masking + budgets)
- finalization always runs (LIFO), even under cancellation

This is the core of Asupersync’s “cancel-correctness” promise.

## Scope
### 1) Cancellation protocol transitions
- Cancel request propagation (down region tree)
- Idempotent strengthening of repeated cancel requests
- Task checkpoints, bounded masking, and acknowledgment
- Drain phase driven by cancel lane priority

### 2) Finalizers / bracket / commit sections
- Region-owned finalizer stack (`defer_sync`, `defer_async`) executed LIFO
- Finalizers run under cancellation masking (bounded/budgeted) to ensure cleanup is not pre-empted mid-commit
- Bracket pattern for acquire/use/release with cancel-correct release

### 3) Region close semantics
- `Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed(outcome)`
- Close waits on:
  - all child tasks terminal
  - all subregions closed

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Symbolic Obligations
description:
# EPIC: Symbolic Obligations

**Bead ID:** asupersync-zfn
**Type:** EPIC
**Priority:** P1
**Status:** OPEN
**Owner:** Dicklesworthstone

---

## Vision

Symbolic Obligations bring linear type semantics to distributed symbol operations, ensuring that every symbol that must be delivered is tracked, every acknowledgment that must be sent is recorded, and any leaked obligation is detected and reported. This EPIC extends asupersync's existing obligation tracking system to the RaptorQ distributed layer.

The core insight is that symbol delivery is not just data transfer - it's a responsibility. When a task takes ownership of symbols to transmit, it acquires an obligation that must be resolved: either the symbols are successfully delivered (committed) or the transmission is explicitly abandoned (aborted). Silently dropping symbols without resolution is a programming error that the obligation system will detect and report.

This model directly supports asupersync's cancel-correctness guarantee: cancellation is a protocol, not silent data loss. When a symbol transmission is cancelled, the obligation is aborted cleanly, and cleanup handlers run to notify relevant parties. The two-phase pattern (reserve/commit) prevents data loss during cancellation by ensuring obligations are tracked before any work begins.

Symbolic obligations also enable partial fulfillment tracking. When transmitting an object that requires 100 symbols, the obligation tracks how many have been acknowledged. Progress is observable, and the system knows exactly when delivery is complete.

---

## Goals

- **Define SymbolicObligation type** that wraps core obligations with symbol-specific metadata
- **Track partial fulfillment** for multi-symbol object deliveries
- **Detect leaked obligations** when tasks complete without resolving their symbol responsibilities
- **Integrate with epoch windows** so obligations have bounded validity
- **Integrate with existing obligation system** preserving the two-phase (Reserved/Committed/Aborted) protocol
- **Provide RAII guards** for automatic obligation resolution on scope exit

---

## Non-Goals

- **Exactly-once delivery**: Delivery guarantees are a system property, not a type guarantee
- **Distributed obligation tracking**: This is local tracking; distributed coordination is separate
- **Persistent obligation storage**: Obligations are runtime state, persistence is external
- **Automatic retry**: Retry logic is application-level, not obligation-level
- **Transaction semantics**: ACID across multiple obligations is not addressed

---

## Child Beads

| ID | Title | Status | Priority | Description |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------------|
| asupersync-fxd | Implement SymbolicObligation Type and Partial Fulfillment | OPEN | P1 | Core obligation type with progress tracking |
| asupersync-t3v | Integrate with Existing Obligation Tracking | OPEN | P1 | Bridge to ObligationRecord system |

---

## Phases

### Phase 1: SymbolicObligation Type
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolicObligation` type wrapping `ObligationRecord`
- `SymbolObligationKind` enum (Transmit, Ack, Decoding, EncodingSession, Lease)
- Epoch window validity checking
- Deadline expiry detection
- Commit/abort/mark_leaked methods

**Exit Criteria:**
- All obligation kinds can be created and resolved
- Epoch and deadline validity correctly enforced
- Double-resolution panics with clear message

### Phase 2: Tracking and Integration
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolicObligationTracker` for managing obligations within a region
- Indices by symbol ID and object ID for fast lookup
- `ObligationGuard` RAII wrapper for automatic resolution
- Integration with region close (leak detection)
- Epoch-based and deadline-based automatic abort

**Exit Criteria:**
- Tracker correctly maintains obligations
- Guards resolve obligations on drop
- Leaks detected during region close
- Automatic abort on epoch/deadline expiry

### Phase 3: Testing and Documentation
**Duration:** 0.5 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- Comprehensive unit tests (12+ scenarios)
- Integration with region lifecycle tests
- API documentation with usage examples

**Exit Criteria:**
- All acceptance criteria met
- Full test coverage
- Clear documentation

---

## Success Criteria

1. **Leak Detection**: 100% of unresolved obligations are detected during region close
2. **Type Safety**: Impossible to silently drop a symbolic obligation without resolution
3. **Partial Progress**: Object delivery progress is trackable at symbol granularity
4. **Epoch Enforcement**: Obligations outside their epoch window are automatically aborted
5. **Deadline Enforcement**: Obligations past their deadline are automatically aborted
6. **Double-Resolution Prevention**: Resolving an already-resolved obligation panics
7. **RAII Semantics**: ObligationGuard correctly resolves on drop

---

## Dependencies

### Depends On
- **asupersync-0vx** (Foundation Layer) - `SymbolId`, `ObjectId` types
- **asupersync-bsx** (Epoch Concurrency) - `EpochId`, `EpochWindow` types
- `src/record/obligation.rs` - Base `ObligationRecord` and `ObligationState`
- `src/types/id.rs` - `ObligationId`, `TaskId`, `RegionId`, `Time`

### Blocks
- **asupersync-9mq** (Integration) - Obligation tracking in unified API

---

## Acceptance Criteria Checklist

### SymbolicObligation Type and Partial Fulfillment (asupersync-fxd)
- [ ] `SymbolicObligation` wraps `ObligationRecord` with symbol metadata
- [ ] `SymbolObligationKind` enum with all five kinds:
  - [ ] `SymbolTransmit { symbol_id, destination }`
  - [ ] `SymbolAck { symbol_id, source }`
  - [ ] `DecodingInProgress { object_id, symbols_received, symbols_needed }`
  - [ ] `EncodingSession { object_id, symbols_encoded }`
  - [ ] `SymbolLease { object_id, lease_expires }`
- [ ] `EpochWindow` with start/end epochs and validity checking
- [ ] Factory methods: `transmit()`, `ack()`, `decoding()`, `lease()`
- [ ] `is_pending()` returns true until resolved
- [ ] `is_epoch_valid(current_epoch)` checks epoch window
- [ ] `is_expired(now)` checks deadline
- [ ] `commit()` for successful resolution
- [ ] `abort()` for clean cancellation
- [ ] `mark_leaked()` for runtime-detected leaks
- [ ] `update_decoding_progress()` for partial fulfillment
- [ ] Double resolution panics

### Integrate with Existing Obligation Tracking (asupersync-t3v)
- [ ] `SymbolicObligationTracker` managing obligations per region
- [ ] HashMap storage indexed by `ObligationId`
- [ ] Secondary index by `SymbolId` for fast symbol-based lookup
- [ ] Secondary index by `ObjectId` for decoding/encoding obligations
- [ ] `register()` adds obligation and returns ID
- [ ] `resolve(id, commit)` removes and sets final state
- [ ] `pending()` iterator over unresolved obligations
- [ ] `by_symbol(symbol_id)` returns obligations for a symbol
- [ ] `pending_count()` returns count
- [ ] `check_leaks()` marks all pending as leaked, returns list
- [ ] `abort_expired_epoch(current_epoch)` aborts out-of-window
- [ ] `abort_expired_deadlines(now)` aborts past-deadline
- [ ] `ObligationGuard<'a>` with `commit()` and `abort()` methods
- [ ] Guard resolves (abort) on drop if not explicitly resolved
- [ ] Logging for register, resolve, leak, abort events

---

## Obligation Lifecycle

```
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                     RESERVED                                    │
     │                                                                 │
     │  SymbolicObligation created via factory method                 │
     │  Registered in SymbolicObligationTracker                       │
     │  Work begins (symbol transmission, decoding, etc.)             │
     │                                                                 │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │                    │                    │
                │ success            │ failure            │ dropped
                │                    │                    │
                ▼                    ▼                    ▼
     ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
     │   COMMITTED     │  │    ABORTED      │  │     LEAKED      │
     │                 │  │                 │  │                 │
     │  Symbols        │  │  Operation      │  │  Task ended     │
     │  delivered      │  │  cancelled      │  │  without        │
     │  successfully   │  │  cleanly        │  │  resolution     │
     │                 │  │                 │  │  (BUG!)         │
     └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
```

---

## Integration Patterns

### Pattern 1: Symbol Transmission with Tracking
```rust
async fn send_symbol(
    cx: &Cx,
    tracker: &mut SymbolicObligationTracker,
    symbol: Symbol,
    destination: RegionId,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // Create and register obligation
    let ob = SymbolicObligation::transmit(
        generate_id(), cx.task_id(), cx.region_id(),
        symbol.id(), destination, Some(cx.deadline()), None,
    );
    let ob_id = tracker.register(ob);

    // Perform work
    match transport.send(symbol).await {
        Ok(()) => {
            tracker.resolve(ob_id, true); // Commit
            Ok(())
        }
        Err(e) => {
            tracker.resolve(ob_id, false); // Abort
            Err(e)
        }
    }
}
```

### Pattern 2: RAII Guard for Automatic Resolution
```rust
async fn with_lease<T>(
    tracker: &mut SymbolicObligationTracker,
    object_id: ObjectId,
    f: impl FnOnce() -> Result<T, Error>,
) -> Result<T, Error> {
    let ob = SymbolicObligation::lease(/* ... */);
    let ob_id = tracker.register(ob);
    let guard = ObligationGuard::new(tracker, ob_id);

    let result = f();

    if result.is_ok() {
        guard.commit(); // Explicit success
    }
    // If result is Err, guard drops and aborts automatically

    result
}
```

---

## Risk Assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------------|--------|------------|
| Too many obligations cause memory pressure | Medium | Medium | Per-region limits, TTL-based cleanup |
| Leak detection floods logs in failure scenarios | Medium | Low | Rate limiting, aggregation |
| Epoch window misconfiguration causes false aborts | Low | Medium | Validation, sensible defaults |
| Guard drop order causes surprising behavior | Medium | Medium | Clear documentation, explicit API preference |
| Integration with existing obligations fragile | Low | High | Careful wrapping, exhaustive tests |

title: Fix UnixDatagram Sync impl and refactor registration
description:
# Fix UnixDatagram Sync impl and refactor registration

## Investigation Summary

The `UnixDatagram` uses `Mutex<Option<IoRegistration>>` for interior mutability, which differs from tokio's approach where `PollEvented` handles registration internally without user-visible Mutex.

### Current Pattern (UnixDatagram, TcpListener, tcp/split.rs)
- `registration: Mutex<Option<IoRegistration>>` visible in struct
- Lock acquired on each async I/O operation

### Tokio Pattern (for reference)
- `io: PollEvented<mio::net::UnixDatagram>` - No Mutex needed
- Registration handled internally with separate read/write wakers

## Issue Analysis

1. **Not a safety bug**: Current code is memory-safe - std::os::unix::net::UnixDatagram is Send + Sync, and Mutex<T> is Send + Sync if T: Send.

2. **Performance concern**: Each async operation acquires the Mutex lock, causing contention in concurrent use.

3. **Pattern inconsistency**: This pattern is used across multiple socket types (UnixDatagram, TcpListener, tcp/split), suggesting need for a shared PollEvented or AsyncIo abstraction.

## Recommended Solution

Create a PollEvented<S: Source> wrapper that:
- Handles registration internally
- Maintains separate read/write wakers for concurrent operations
- Can be shared via Arc without external Mutex

## Relationship to Phase 2

This refactoring aligns with asupersync-90l9 (Phase 2: Real Async I/O Reactor). Recommend implementing PollEvented as part of Phase 2, then refactoring all socket types.

title: Implement RegionState enum and lifecycle
description:
# RegionState Enum and Lifecycle

## Purpose
RegionState represents the lifecycle of a region from creation to closure. The state machine ensures the "region close = quiescence" invariant (I2) is enforced.

## The Region States
```rust
enum RegionState {
    // Region is active, can spawn children
    Open,
    
    // Region body completed, beginning close sequence
    Closing,
    
    // Cancel issued to children, waiting for all to complete
    Draining,
    
    // Children done, running region finalizers
    Finalizing,
    
    // Terminal state with aggregated outcome
    Closed(Outcome),
}
```

## State Transitions

```
Open ──────────────► Closing ──────────────► Draining
  │                     │                       │
  │ (scope.close()      │ (cancel children      │ (all children
  │  or body returns)   │  per policy)          │  Completed)
  │                     │                       │
  │                     ▼                       ▼
  │                  Draining ──────────► Finalizing
  │                     │                       │
  │                     │                       │ (all finalizers
  │                     │                       │  run, obligations
  │                     │                       │  resolved)
  │                     │                       ▼
  └─────────────────────┴──────────────► Closed(Outcome)
```

## Valid Transitions

| From | To | Trigger | Condition |
|------|-----|---------|-----------|
| Open | Closing | Region body returns or explicit close | Always |
| Closing | Draining | After initiating child cancellation | If children exist |
| Closing | Finalizing | Skip draining | If no children |
| Draining | Finalizing | All children reach Completed | ∀t ∈ children: Completed |
| Finalizing | Closed(outcome) | Finalizers done, obligations resolved | Empty finalizer stack, zero obligations |

## Close Protocol Detail

### 1. Open → Closing
When the region body completes (returns from the async block):
```rust
scope.region(|sub| async {
    // ... spawn children ...
}).await;  // ← triggers Open → Closing
```

### 2. Closing → Draining
If there are live children:
1. Issue cancel to all children (per policy)
2. Mark region as Draining
3. Prioritize cancelled tasks in scheduler

### 3. Draining → Finalizing
Wait condition:
```rust
∀t ∈ R[r].children: T[t].state = Completed(_)
∧ ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: R[r'].state = Closed(_)
```

### 4. Finalizing → Closed
Must satisfy:
```rust
R[r].finalizers = []  // All run
∧ ∀o where O[o].region = r: O[o].state ≠ Reserved  // No pending obligations
```

## Why These States?

### Open
The active state where work happens. Spawning is only allowed in Open.

### Closing
Transitional state signaling "no more spawns." The region body has returned but cleanup hasn't started.

### Draining
All children are being cancelled and awaited. This is where the cancel lane priority matters - cancelled tasks get scheduled first.

### Finalizing
Children done, now running registered finalizers. Finalizers run LIFO (last registered, first run).

### Closed
Terminal with aggregated outcome. Supports proper propagation to parent region.

## Outcome Aggregation

When computing Closed(outcome):
```rust
fn aggregate_outcomes(
    child_outcomes: Vec<Outcome>,
    finalizer_outcomes: Vec<Outcome>,
    policy: &Policy,
) -> Outcome {
    // Default: worst outcome wins (severity lattice)
    let all_outcomes = child_outcomes.into_iter()
        .chain(finalizer_outcomes);
    all_outcomes.reduce(|a, b| a.combine(b))
        .unwrap_or(Outcome::Ok(()))
}
```

Policy can override (e.g., ignore certain errors).

## Implementation Requirements

1. **RegionState must be Clone, Debug**
2. **Closed(Outcome) stores the aggregated outcome**
3. **is_terminal() method**: Returns true only for Closed
4. **is_accepting_spawns() method**: Returns true only for Open
5. **is_draining() method**: Returns true for Draining

## Invariant Support

### INV-QUIESCENCE (I2)
```rust
∀r: R[r].state = Closed(_) ⟹
    (∀t ∈ R[r].children: T[t].state = Completed(_)) ∧
    (∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: R[r'].state = Closed(_))
```

### INV-TREE (I1)
Closed regions still exist in the tree until parent closes.

### INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE
```rust
∀r, ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: deadline(R[r']) ≤ deadline(R[r])
```

## Testing Requirements

1. Only valid transitions are possible
2. Closed is absorbing
3. Spawn fails in non-Open states
4. Draining only completes when all children complete
5. Finalizing only completes when all finalizers run
6. Obligations block Finalizing → Closed

## Example Scenarios

### Clean Shutdown
```
Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed(Ok(()))
```

### Child Error with FailFast
```
Open → Closing → Draining (child errors) → Finalizing → Closed(Err(e))
// Other children cancelled via FailFast policy
```

### Empty Region
```
Open → Closing → Finalizing → Closed(Ok(()))
// Skip Draining because no children
```

### Finalizer Error
```
Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing (error) → Closed(Err(e))
// Finalizer error propagates
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.6 (Region States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.3 (Region Lifecycle)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §6.1-6.2 (Region lifecycle states, close semantics)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Region lifecycle states match the spec: Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed(outcome).
- State transitions are deterministic and trace-visible.
- Region close semantics enforce quiescence: no live children + finalizers completed + obligations resolved.
- Unit/E2E tests cover normal close, close-with-cancel, and nested region behavior.
close_reason: Implemented Draining state in RegionState per formal semantics. Added state transition methods begin_drain(), begin_finalize(), complete_close() and comprehensive tests.

title: [frame-validation-gap] http/h3_native.rs: PUSH_PROMISE frame parser accepts an empty field_block — RFC 9114 §7.2.5 requires non-empty Encoded Field Section
description:
src/http/h3_native.rs:495-502 — PUSH_PROMISE frame decode:

```
H3_FRAME_PUSH_PROMISE => {
    let (push_id, n) = decode_varint(payload)
        .map_err(|_| H3NativeError::InvalidFrame("push_promise push_id"))?;
    Self::PushPromise {
        push_id,
        field_block: payload[n..].to_vec(),
    }
}
```

When the frame's declared length equals the push_id varint size exactly (i.e., n == payload.len()), the slice payload[n..] is empty and we accept a PUSH_PROMISE with an empty field_block. RFC 9114 §7.2.5: "The PUSH_PROMISE frame ... MUST contain a push_id and an Encoded Field Section". An empty section is not valid per QPACK §4.5 (the section prefix alone is two varints).

Asymmetric with CANCEL_PUSH (line 489 enforces n != payload.len() — no trailing bytes), GOAWAY (line 506), and MAX_PUSH_ID (line 514). Those branches reject extra trailing bytes; PUSH_PROMISE neither rejects extras nor enforces non-empty field_block.

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) Downstream QPACK decoder receives an empty field block. QPACK requires at least the section prefix (required-insert-count + base, two varints). The decoder fails with a QPACK-layer error rather than the H3-frame error the spec asks for. Defense-in-depth at the H3 layer is preferable.
  (b) An attacker can craft a PUSH_PROMISE with push_id=N and empty field_block to consume push_id slots without paying the cost of generating valid encoded headers. Bounded by SETTINGS_MAX_PUSH_ID but noisy in observability.

Fix direction:
  1. After extracting push_id, verify n < payload.len(). Return InvalidFrame("push_promise: empty field_block") otherwise.
  2. Optionally: also enforce a minimum sane field_block length (e.g., 2 bytes — QPACK section-prefix decodes required-insert-count + base).
  3. Mirror CANCEL_PUSH / GOAWAY / MAX_PUSH_ID's trailing-bytes-must-be-consumed pattern for symmetry.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/http/h1/* + h2/* + h3_native.rs (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in 7088b7625: H3 PUSH_PROMISE parser at src/http/h3_native.rs now rejects empty field_block after the push_id varint with H3NativeError::InvalidFrame('push_promise empty field_block (RFC 9114 §7.2.5)'). Tests: empty field_block rejected; non-empty field_block decodes cleanly (regression guard).

title: [EPIC] Chaos Testing Mode for Lab Runtime
description:
# Overview

An extension to LabReactor that can inject random delays, spurious wakeups,
simulated I/O errors, and cancellations at configurable rates - to stress-test
application code's resilience.

## Why This Matters

Production systems face chaos constantly:
- Network partitions
- Slow responses  
- OOM kills
- Race conditions
- Random failures

A chaos mode lets developers find these bugs BEFORE production. Combined with
deterministic replay, failures become REPRODUCIBLE.

## How It Works

```rust
Lab::new()
    .with_chaos(ChaosConfig {
        cancel_probability: 0.01,      // 1% random cancellation
        delay_probability: 0.05,       // 5% random delay
        delay_range: 1ms..100ms,
        io_error_probability: 0.02,    // 2% I/O error
        wakeup_storm_probability: 0.001, // 0.1% spurious wakeups
        seed: 12345,                   // REPRODUCIBLE chaos!
    })
    .run(|cx| async {
        // Application code with injected chaos
    });

// On failure:
// "Test failed with seed 12345. Replay with same seed to reproduce."
```

## Chaos Types

1. **Random Cancellation**: Inject CancelRequested at random times
2. **Random Delays**: Add latency at poll points
3. **I/O Errors**: Fail I/O operations randomly
4. **Wakeup Storms**: Spurious wakeups to test idempotency
5. **Budget Exhaustion**: Randomly exhaust budgets
6. **Clock Skew**: Virtual time jumps (for distributed scenarios)

## Determinism is Key

The chaos MUST be deterministic:
- Same seed = same chaos sequence
- Same test = same failures
- Enables debugging of intermittent issues

This is the killer combination: chaos + deterministic replay.

## Integration with Existing Features

- Uses LabReactor's virtual time
- Uses LabReactor's deterministic scheduling
- Integrates with cancellation injection (#1)
- Reports via tracing (#2)
- Verified by oracles

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Configurable chaos parameters
- [ ] Deterministic with same seed
- [ ] All chaos types implemented
- [ ] Integrates with Lab infrastructure
- [ ] Clear failure reporting with seed
- [ ] Documentation with examples
notes: Chaos testing mode complete: (1) ChaosConfig with all builder methods for configurable parameters; (2) Deterministic chaos with seed-based reproducibility; (3) All core chaos types implemented - cancellation, delays, I/O errors, wakeup storms, budget exhaustion; (4) Full Lab infrastructure integration via LabConfig.with_chaos(); (5) ChaosStats for clear failure reporting; (6) Comprehensive documentation and examples (asupersync-mzsl). Clock skew deferred to Phase 4 distributed work.

title: Implement futurelock detector (lab/debug)
description:
# Futurelock Detector (lab/debug)

## Purpose
Detect and surface the design-rule violation:

> Never allow a primitive to stop being polled while holding an obligation without transferring it, aborting/nacking it, or escalating.

In practice this shows up as a *futurelock*: a task holds one or more unresolved obligations (permits/acks/leases/IoOps) but is no longer being polled (e.g. it awaited something that never wakes, or it was dropped/forgotten by a buggy primitive).

Phase 0 needs this in **lab/debug** mode so we can turn “subtle deadlocks/leaks” into deterministic test failures with actionable evidence.

## Spec Background
- Design Bible §8.6: “Futurelock detector”
- Operational Semantics §1.9 + §3.4: obligations are linear; leaks are semantic errors
- Key invariant: a region cannot close while obligations in the region remain `Reserved`

A futurelock is *strictly worse* than a normal leak:
- a leak is “task completed while holding obligation”
- a futurelock is “task *didn’t* complete, but is also no longer being polled, so it can’t resolve the obligation”

## Design (Plan-of-Record)
### Observable behavior
When enabled, the lab runtime MUST:
1. Detect tasks that hold ≥1 `Reserved` obligations and have not been polled for a bounded number of lab steps (configurable).
2. Emit a trace-visible event with enough context to debug.
3. Optionally fail-fast (panic) in lab mode when the threshold is exceeded.

### Data we need
- `last_polled_step: u64` per task (updated every time we poll the task).
- Ability to query “held obligations” per task (from the obligation registry).
- Global `step_counter: u64` in the lab runtime.

### Detection rule
On each lab step (or at least whenever the scheduler makes progress):
- For each task `t` that currently holds ≥1 `Reserved` obligation:
  - if `step_counter - last_polled_step(t) > futurelock_max_idle_steps` then `futurelock_detected(t, …)`.

We should explicitly ignore tasks that are already terminal.

### Trace model
Add a semantic trace event (names flexible):
- `TraceEvent::FuturelockDetected { task: TaskId, region: RegionId, idle_steps: u64, held: Vec<ObligationId>, kinds: Vec<ObligationKind> }`

Constraints:
- The trace event must be deterministic and stable.
- Do NOT allocate on the hot path in production; this is lab/debug functionality.

### Config knobs
Add lab config fields (names flexible):
- `futurelock_max_idle_steps: u64` (default: conservative but small, e.g. 10_000)
- `panic_on_futurelock: bool` (default: true in lab tests)

## Testing
### Unit tests
- Construct a tiny obligation registry state where a task holds a reserved obligation and has an old `last_polled_step`; assert detection triggers.

### E2E lab scenarios
- Scenario: task reserves a SendPermit and then awaits a future that never wakes; another task continues making progress so the lab runtime keeps stepping. Assert:
  - a FuturelockDetected trace event appears
  - (if enabled) the runtime panics with a message that includes task id + obligation ids

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deterministic detection in lab mode (same seed/config => same detection point and trace).
- Trace event contains enough context to debug (task, region, obligation ids/kinds, idle steps).
- Does not introduce stdout/stderr logging in core runtime (only trace + test harness output).
- Clear documentation in the issue text about what counts as a futurelock and what does not.
notes: Implemented futurelock detection in lab runtime (TraceEventKind::FuturelockDetected + TraceData::Futurelock) with config knobs + unit tests; still blocked in Beads by asupersync-1mm/asupersync-l6l/asupersync-jdg status.

title: Implement RegionState enum and lifecycle
description:
# RegionState Enum and Lifecycle

## Purpose
RegionState represents the lifecycle of a region from creation to closure. The state machine ensures the "region close = quiescence" invariant (I2) is enforced.

## The Region States
```rust
enum RegionState {
    // Region is active, can spawn children
    Open,
    
    // Region body completed, beginning close sequence
    Closing,
    
    // Cancel issued to children, waiting for all to complete
    Draining,
    
    // Children done, running region finalizers
    Finalizing,
    
    // Terminal state with aggregated outcome
    Closed(Outcome),
}
```

## State Transitions

```
Open ──────────────► Closing ──────────────► Draining
  │                     │                       │
  │ (scope.close()      │ (cancel children      │ (all children
  │  or body returns)   │  per policy)          │  Completed)
  │                     │                       │
  │                     ▼                       ▼
  │                  Draining ──────────► Finalizing
  │                     │                       │
  │                     │                       │ (all finalizers
  │                     │                       │  run, obligations
  │                     │                       │  resolved)
  │                     │                       ▼
  └─────────────────────┴──────────────► Closed(Outcome)
```

## Valid Transitions

| From | To | Trigger | Condition |
|------|-----|---------|-----------|
| Open | Closing | Region body returns or explicit close | Always |
| Closing | Draining | After initiating child cancellation | If children exist |
| Closing | Finalizing | Skip draining | If no children |
| Draining | Finalizing | All children reach Completed | ∀t ∈ children: Completed |
| Finalizing | Closed(outcome) | Finalizers done, obligations resolved | Empty finalizer stack, zero obligations |

## Close Protocol Detail

### 1. Open → Closing
When the region body completes (returns from the async block):
```rust
scope.region(|sub| async {
    // ... spawn children ...
}).await;  // ← triggers Open → Closing
```

### 2. Closing → Draining
If there are live children:
1. Issue cancel to all children (per policy)
2. Mark region as Draining
3. Prioritize cancelled tasks in scheduler

### 3. Draining → Finalizing
Wait condition:
```rust
∀t ∈ R[r].children: T[t].state = Completed(_)
∧ ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: R[r'].state = Closed(_)
```

### 4. Finalizing → Closed
Must satisfy:
```rust
R[r].finalizers = []  // All run
∧ ∀o where O[o].region = r: O[o].state ≠ Reserved  // No pending obligations
```

## Why These States?

### Open
The active state where work happens. Spawning is only allowed in Open.

### Closing
Transitional state signaling "no more spawns." The region body has returned but cleanup hasn't started.

### Draining
All children are being cancelled and awaited. This is where the cancel lane priority matters - cancelled tasks get scheduled first.

### Finalizing
Children done, now running registered finalizers. Finalizers run LIFO (last registered, first run).

### Closed
Terminal with aggregated outcome. Supports proper propagation to parent region.

## Outcome Aggregation

When computing Closed(outcome):
```rust
fn aggregate_outcomes(
    child_outcomes: Vec<Outcome>,
    finalizer_outcomes: Vec<Outcome>,
    policy: &Policy,
) -> Outcome {
    // Default: worst outcome wins (severity lattice)
    let all_outcomes = child_outcomes.into_iter()
        .chain(finalizer_outcomes);
    all_outcomes.reduce(|a, b| a.combine(b))
        .unwrap_or(Outcome::Ok(()))
}
```

Policy can override (e.g., ignore certain errors).

## Implementation Requirements

1. **RegionState must be Clone, Debug**
2. **Closed(Outcome) stores the aggregated outcome**
3. **is_terminal() method**: Returns true only for Closed
4. **is_accepting_spawns() method**: Returns true only for Open
5. **is_draining() method**: Returns true for Draining

## Invariant Support

### INV-QUIESCENCE (I2)
```rust
∀r: R[r].state = Closed(_) ⟹
    (∀t ∈ R[r].children: T[t].state = Completed(_)) ∧
    (∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: R[r'].state = Closed(_))
```

### INV-TREE (I1)
Closed regions still exist in the tree until parent closes.

### INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE
```rust
∀r, ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions: deadline(R[r']) ≤ deadline(R[r])
```

## Testing Requirements

1. Only valid transitions are possible
2. Closed is absorbing
3. Spawn fails in non-Open states
4. Draining only completes when all children complete
5. Finalizing only completes when all finalizers run
6. Obligations block Finalizing → Closed

## Example Scenarios

### Clean Shutdown
```
Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed(Ok(()))
```

### Child Error with FailFast
```
Open → Closing → Draining (child errors) → Finalizing → Closed(Err(e))
// Other children cancelled via FailFast policy
```

### Empty Region
```
Open → Closing → Finalizing → Closed(Ok(()))
// Skip Draining because no children
```

### Finalizer Error
```
Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing (error) → Closed(Err(e))
// Finalizer error propagates
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.6 (Region States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.3 (Region Lifecycle)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §6.1-6.2 (Region lifecycle states, close semantics)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Region lifecycle states match the spec: Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed(outcome).
- State transitions are deterministic and trace-visible.
- Region close semantics enforce quiescence: no live children + finalizers completed + obligations resolved.
- Unit/E2E tests cover normal close, close-with-cancel, and nested region behavior.

title: Implement lab runtime with virtual time and deterministic scheduling
description:
# Lab Runtime with Virtual Time and Deterministic Scheduling

## Purpose
The lab runtime is the executable semantics of Asupersync:
- **virtual time** (discrete ticks)
- **deterministic scheduling** (seeded, reproducible)
- **trace capture + replay**

This is what makes concurrency bugs reproducible artifacts instead of “heisenbugs”.

## Key Guarantees
Given the same lab config (including seed) and the same user program:
- the runtime produces the same observable trace
- replay can reproduce a failing run

## Core Constraints
- Avoid ambient globals.
- Avoid OS entropy / wall-clock time for scheduling decisions.
- Prefer minimal dependencies; implement deterministic PRNG internally (see bead: deterministic PRNG utility).

## LabRuntime Structure

```rust
pub struct LabRuntime {
    state: RuntimeState,
    virtual_time: Time,

    /// Deterministic PRNG for tie-breaking (no rand crate).
    rng: DetRng,

    trace: TraceBuffer,
    config: LabConfig,
}

pub struct LabConfig {
    pub seed: u64,
    pub max_time: Option<Time>,
    pub max_steps: Option<u64>,

    /// Lab-only strictness knobs.
    pub panic_on_leak: bool,
    pub panic_on_invariant_violation: bool,
}
```

## Virtual Time
Time advances only when no runnable tasks exist.

Algorithm:
1. If scheduler has runnable tasks: do not advance time.
2. Otherwise, jump to next timer deadline (if any).
3. Wake any tasks whose timers expire.
4. Check deadline expiries and request cancellation as needed.
5. Emit `TraceEvent::Tick`.

This yields the “sleeps are instant in wall-clock time” property while preserving a meaningful virtual timeline.

## Deterministic Scheduling
When multiple tasks are eligible to run, break ties deterministically using `DetRng` seeded by `LabConfig.seed`.

Important: determinism requires that tie-breaking inputs are stable.
- do not iterate hashmaps/sets and rely on their order
- prefer ordered iteration or explicit sorting by IDs

## Main Loop (Sketch)

```rust
loop {
    if should_stop_by_limits(config, virtual_time, steps) {
        break;
    }

    if let Some(task_id) = scheduler.pick_next(virtual_time, &mut rng, &state) {
        poll_task(task_id);
        steps += 1;
        verify_invariants_if_enabled();
    } else {
        tick_virtual_time();
    }
}
```

## Trace Capture
Every semantic operation emits a trace event. The trace model should stay small and semantic:
- spawn/complete
- cancel/propagate
- reserve/commit/abort/leak
- finalize/close
- tick

The trace is the primary debugging artifact for test failures.

## Replay
Replay means: “run again under the same seed/config and ensure we reproduce the same trace”.

Minimum viable replay:
- re-run the scenario under the same seed
- compare traces
- report first divergence with context

(Phase 5 adds canonicalization and equivalence-class reasoning; Phase 0 replay can be strict byte-for-byte equality.)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Same seed/config yields identical traces for the same program.
2. Virtual time advances only when nothing runnable exists.
3. Trace capture is complete enough for invariants/oracles.
4. Replay reports divergence precisely.

## Testing Requirements
- Determinism oracle runs at least 3 scenarios twice and asserts trace equality.
- Deadlock/idle detection is explicit and traceable.

title: [bug-hunt] messaging/kafka_consumer.rs: enable_auto_commit defaults to true and stores offset at poll time — silent at-most-once delivery
description: src/messaging/kafka_consumer.rs:115 sets ConsumerConfig::default().enable_auto_commit = true. src/messaging/kafka_consumer.rs:868-877 calls consumer.store_offset_from_message immediately when poll returns the message, BEFORE the user has processed it. The combination delivers at-most-once: a user crash between poll() returning Ok(Some(record)) and the user finishing processing means the offset gets committed on the next auto.commit.interval.ms tick (default 5s) and the message is LOST. Kafka users typically EXPECT at-least-once by default; this client silently flips the safety bias. Severity HIGH because the default is unsafe and the documentation does not warn. Suggested fix (least invasive): (1) flip the default to enable_auto_commit: false so the at-least-once contract is opt-in via explicit commit; OR (2) defer store_offset until the user calls a commit_record(record) method (true at-least-once); OR (3) document the at-most-once default loudly in ConsumerConfig docstring + README §messaging.
