title: Compositional Latency Algebra — (min,+) Network Calculus for Combinator DAGs
description:
# Compositional Latency Algebra

## File: src/plan/latency_algebra.rs (2,675 lines, 48 tests)

## What It Does

Provides provable worst-case end-to-end latency bounds for any composition of asupersync concurrency combinators (join, race, timeout, pipeline, etc.). Users annotate leaf nodes of a PlanDag with arrival/service curves, then the analyzer walks the DAG bottom-up computing delay and backlog bounds with full provenance.

## Mathematical Foundation — Network Calculus (Le Boudec & Thiran, 2001)

Uses the (min,+) dioid (tropical semiring):
- Arrival curve alpha(t): upper bound on cumulative arrivals in interval [0,t]
- Service curve beta(t): lower bound on cumulative service in interval [0,t]  
- Delay bound d* = horizontal deviation = sup_t { inf { d >= 0 : alpha(t) <= beta(t+d) } }
- Backlog bound b* = vertical deviation = sup_t { alpha(t) - beta(t) }

Combinator composition rules:
- Join:     d_join = max(d_children) — waits for all children
- Race:     d_race = min(d_children) — first finisher wins
- Timeout:  d_timeout = min(d_child, tau) — deadline caps delay
- Pipeline: beta_total = beta_1 (x) beta_2 — (min,+) convolution of service curves

Closed-form for token-bucket arrival + rate-latency service:
  d* = T + sigma/R  (latency T, burst sigma, rate R)
  b* = sigma + rho*T (arrival rate rho)

## Why This Is Smart for Asupersync

The project already uses tropical semiring semantics for budgets (deadline = min, quota = min). The plan DAG infrastructure exists (src/plan/mod.rs) with a rewrite engine and law sheet. But there was no way to answer: "what is the worst-case latency of join(race(a,b), timeout(pipeline(c,d), 500ms))?" This module answers that with a mathematical proof, not a guess.

No other Rust async runtime provides compile-time latency certificates for combinator compositions.

## Architecture

### Core Types

- Segment: { start: f64, rate: f64, burst: f64 } — single piecewise-linear segment
- PiecewiseLinearCurve: ordered Vec<Segment> with O(log n) eval via binary search
- ArrivalCurve(PiecewiseLinearCurve): typed wrapper with token_bucket(), constant_rate()
- ServiceCurve(PiecewiseLinearCurve): typed wrapper with rate_latency(), scale(), sequential()
- LatencyBound: { delay, backlog, utilization, provenance: Vec<BoundContribution> }
- BoundContribution: { node_id: PlanId, delay: f64, description: String }
- NodeCurves: { arrival: ArrivalCurve, service: ServiceCurve } — leaf annotation
- LatencyAnalyzer: walks PlanDag bottom-up with memoization
- LatencyAnalysis: full report with per-node maps, root bound, DAG reference

### Key Operations

- min_plus_convolution(f, g): the (min,+) semiring operation, O(n*m) on segment counts
- min_plus_deconvolution(f, g): for output arrival curve computation
- horizontal_deviation(alpha, beta): worst-case delay
- vertical_deviation(alpha, beta): worst-case backlog

### Integration Points

- PlanDag/PlanNode/PlanId from src/plan/mod.rs (direct integration)
- Complements PlanAnalyzer from src/plan/analysis.rs (obligation/cancel safety)
- Registered as pub mod latency_algebra in src/plan/mod.rs

## Test Coverage (48 tests)

Curve basics (8): zero, affine, rate-latency eval, segment validation, negative time
Delay bounds (4): closed-form verification, equal rates, unstable, zero-burst
Backlog bounds (3): closed-form, unstable systems
Tropical semiring (5): commutativity, associativity, isotonicity, identity, rate-latency sum
Service curves (2): scaling, sequential composition
DAG integration (5): join max, race min, timeout cap, empty join/race
Algebraic laws (2): nested timeout collapsing (TIMEOUT-MIN), race-join distributivity
Complex DAGs (2): multi-level composition, wide fan-in (20 children)
Monotonicity (2): delay increases with burst and latency
Provenance (3): unannotated leaves, bottleneck ID, missing annotations
Display (1): formatting coverage

## Status: COMPLETED — SapphireHill, 2026-02-24

description: Implement the core Segment and PiecewiseLinearCurve types for piecewise-linear function representation. Segments are (start, rate, burst) triples defining f(t) = burst + rate*(t-start). The curve maintains segments sorted by start time with validation: sorted, non-negative rates, continuity at segment boundaries. Evaluation uses binary search for O(log n) lookup. Includes constructors: zero(), affine(rate, burst), rate_latency(rate, latency), staircase(step_size, period, num_steps), from_segments(). File: src/plan/latency_algebra.rs.

Core tropical semiring operations:
- min_plus_convolution(f, g): (f (x) g)(t) = inf_{0<=s<=t} { f(s) + g(t-s) }. O(n*m) on segment counts. Used for sequential pipeline composition.
- min_plus_deconvolution(f, g): (f (/) g)(t) = sup_{s>=0} { f(t+s) - g(s) }. Used for output arrival curve computation.
- horizontal_deviation(alpha, beta): d* = sup_t { inf { d >= 0 : alpha(t) <= beta(t+d) } }. Worst-case delay bound.
- vertical_deviation(alpha, beta): b* = sup_t { alpha(t) - beta(t) }. Worst-case backlog bound.

title: Spectral Runtime Health Monitor — Graph Laplacian Eigenvalue Analysis
description:
# Spectral Runtime Health Monitor

## File: src/observability/spectral_health.rs (1,959 lines, 53 tests)

## What It Does

Provides real-time health diagnostics by computing the spectral gap of the task/region dependency graph. The Fiedler value (second-smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian) is a powerful indicator of system health:
- Fiedler -> 0: system approaching deadlock (graph about to disconnect)
- Fiedler large: healthy, well-connected task graph
- Oscillatory eigenvalues: potential livelock (periodic behavior)
- The Fiedler vector identifies exactly which tasks form the bottleneck

## Mathematical Foundation — Spectral Graph Theory

For a task dependency graph G = (V, E):
- Degree matrix D: diagonal, D[i,i] = degree of node i
- Adjacency matrix A: A[i,j] = 1 if edge (i,j) exists
- Laplacian L = D - A (positive semidefinite)
- Eigenvalues 0 = lambda_1 <= lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n
- Fiedler value lambda_2: algebraic connectivity (= 0 iff disconnected, i.e., deadlock)

Key theorems leveraged:
- Cheeger inequality: h(G)/2 <= lambda_2 <= 2h(G) where h(G) = edge expansion
  (links spectral gap to how "bottlenecked" the graph is)
- Fiedler vector: eigenvector of lambda_2 identifies the minimum cut
  (the tasks that separate the graph into weakly-connected halves)
- Spectral radius lambda_n: bounds worst-case cascade propagation speed
- Effective resistance: R_eff(u,v) = sum (phi_i(u) - phi_i(v))^2 / lambda_i
  (measures "distance" between tasks through the dependency web)

## Why This Is Smart for Asupersync

The existing diagnostics (src/observability/diagnostics.rs) explain AFTER THE FACT why a region won't close. Spectral analysis PREDICTS BEFORE IT HAPPENS that the system is approaching deadlock. The difference:
- diagnostics.rs: "region 5 won't close because task 7 is blocked"
- spectral_health.rs: "lambda_2 = 0.003 and falling at -0.001/step; deadlock in ~3 steps; bottleneck is tasks {7, 12} forming a bridge between obligation clusters"

The bifurcation early-warning integrates with the Lyapunov governor's StateSnapshot, providing an additional signal dimension for the Bayesian decision contract.

## Architecture

### Core Types

- SpectralThresholds: configurable health classification thresholds (deadlock_epsilon, degraded_threshold, critical_threshold, bottleneck_threshold, convergence settings)
- DependencyLaplacian: implicit representation (adjacency list + degree vector), avoids O(n^2) matrix materialization. Supports laplacian_multiply(x) in O(|V|+|E|), union-find component detection with path compression + union-by-rank
- SpectralDecomposition: { eigenvalues, fiedler_value, fiedler_vector, spectral_gap, spectral_radius }
- HealthClassification: Healthy{margin} | Degraded{fiedler, bottleneck_nodes} | Critical{fiedler, approaching_disconnect} | Deadlocked{components}
- BottleneckNode: { index, fiedler_component, is_bridge_candidate }
- SpectralHistory: ring buffer of Fiedler values for trend analysis
- SpectralTrend: Improving | Stable | Deteriorating | Oscillating (with slope, r_squared, sign_changes)
- BifurcationWarning: { trend, time_to_critical, confidence }
- SpectralHealthReport: combines classification + decomposition + bifurcation + bottlenecks
- SpectralHealthMonitor: stateful facade maintaining history across calls

### Eigenvalue Computation

Uses power iteration (no external deps):
- Largest eigenvalue: standard power iteration on L
- Fiedler value: shifted power iteration on (sigma*I - L) with constant-vector deflation
- Handles degenerate cases: 0 nodes, 1 node, disconnected graphs
- Convergence tolerance configurable via SpectralThresholds

### Bifurcation Detection

Detects approach to critical transitions using:
- Linear regression slope of Fiedler history (deteriorating = slope < -epsilon)
- Sign-change analysis for oscillation detection (livelock signature)
- Time-to-critical extrapolation: current_fiedler / |slope|
- R-squared confidence scoring for prediction quality

### Integration Points

- Registered as pub mod spectral_health in src/observability/mod.rs
- Designed to accept (node_count, edges) from RuntimeState task/region dependency data
- Health classification feeds into existing Bayesian decision contract framework
- BifurcationWarning compatible with Lyapunov StateSnapshot extension

## Test Coverage (53 tests)

Laplacian construction (4): empty, single node, dedup/self-loops, out-of-bounds
Connected components (3): single component, multi-component, isolated nodes
Known spectra (7): K4 (fiedler=4), P4 (fiedler=2-sqrt(2)), C4 (fiedler=2), S5 (fiedler=1), K2, empty, disconnected
Fiedler vector (2): orthogonality to constant vector, unit norm
Health classification (3): healthy/degraded/deadlocked thresholds
Bottleneck analysis (4): barbell bridge detection, threshold, empty, complete graph
Effective resistance (3): adjacent nodes, disconnected (=infinity), out-of-bounds
History/trend (5): ring buffer, min capacity, deteriorating/improving/oscillating
Linear regression (4): perfect line, constant, negative slope, edge cases
Monitor integration (4): healthy, deadlocked, history tracking, empty
Display/Debug/Clone (8): all public types covered
Scale test (1): P100 convergence

## Status: COMPLETED — SapphireHill, 2026-02-24

title: Martingale Progress Certificates — Supermartingale Convergence Proofs for Cancellation Drain
description:
# Martingale Progress Certificates

## File: src/cancel/progress_certificate.rs (1,895 lines, 52 tests)

## What It Does

Provides cryptographic-strength statistical guarantees that cancellation drain is converging toward quiescence. Tracks the Lyapunov potential V(Sigma_t) as a stochastic process and applies three classical probability tools to produce auditable certificates with explicit confidence bounds.

Turns "cancellation is probably working" into "with 99% confidence, quiescence will be reached within 347 more steps."

## Mathematical Foundation — Supermartingale Theory

Define the progress process:
  M_t = V(Sigma_t) + sum_{i=1}^{t} c_i
where V is the Lyapunov potential and c_i = max(0, -Delta_i) is progress credit at step i.

Three probabilistic tools:

1. Optional Stopping Theorem: If M_t is a supermartingale and V >= 0, then
   E[tau] <= V(Sigma_0) / mean_credit
   where tau = inf{t : V(Sigma_t) = 0} is hitting time of quiescence.
   Gives EXPECTED time to quiescence.

2. Azuma-Hoeffding Concentration Bound:
   P(V(Sigma_t) > V(Sigma_0) - t*mu + lambda) <= exp(-2*lambda^2 / (t*c^2))
   where mu = mean progress/step, c = max step size.
   Gives PROBABILISTIC guarantee with explicit confidence level.

3. Ville's Maximal Inequality (already used in eprocess.rs):
   P(sup_{t>=0} M_t >= C) <= M_0/C
   Bounds worst-case exceedance of the progress process.

Together these produce a certificate: "with probability >= 1-delta, quiescence is reached within T steps."

## Why This Is Smart for Asupersync

The Lyapunov governor (src/obligation/lyapunov.rs) already computes V(Sigma) and has a ConvergenceVerdict. But the verdict is binary (monotone or not) and says nothing about WHEN quiescence will be reached or HOW CONFIDENT we are. This module adds three powerful guarantees:

- Expected remaining time (Optional Stopping)
- Probabilistic deadline ("99% chance within 347 steps") (Azuma-Hoeffding)
- Worst-case bound on potential excursions (Ville)

The certificates are AUDITABLE — every entry in the evidence trail shows the step, potential, bound, and reason. This is the kind of guarantee financial systems (one of asupersync's target markets) actually need.

Naturally extends the e-process framework (src/lab/oracle/eprocess.rs) which already uses Ville's inequality for anytime-valid invariant monitoring.

## Architecture

### Core Types

- ProgressConfig: { confidence (default 0.99), max_step_bound (100.0), stall_threshold (50), min_observations (10), epsilon (1e-10) }. Three presets: default(), aggressive(), tolerant().

- ProgressObservation: { step, potential, delta (= V_t - V_{t-1}), credit (= max(0, -delta)) }

- ProgressCertificate: the main tracker. Maintains O(1) running totals:
  - total_credit, credit_sum_sq, max_abs_delta (for Azuma bound)
  - increase_count, stall_run (for convergence/stall detection)
  - initial_potential, current potential
  Key methods: observe(), observe_potential_record(), verdict(), martingale_value(), martingale_ratio(), delta_variance(), compact(), reset()

- CertificateVerdict: { converging: bool, estimated_remaining_steps: Option<f64>, confidence_bound: f64, stall_detected: bool, azuma_bound: f64, evidence: Vec<EvidenceEntry> }

- EvidenceEntry: { step, potential, bound, description: String } — auditable proof line

### Convergence Determination

A process is declared "converging" when ALL THREE conditions hold:
1. Mean credit per step is positive (net downward trend)
2. No stall detected (< stall_threshold consecutive non-decreasing steps)
3. Either Azuma bound is tight (< 1-confidence) OR potential decreased by >50% of initial (empirical confirmation)

The dual criterion (Azuma OR empirical) handles the case where step sizes vary widely (e.g., exponential decay has large early steps but tiny late ones, making Azuma loose).

### Integration Points

- Direct integration with crate::obligation::lyapunov::PotentialRecord via observe_potential_record()
- Registered as pub mod progress_certificate in src/cancel/mod.rs
- Re-exports: CertificateVerdict, EvidenceEntry, ProgressCertificate, ProgressConfig, ProgressObservation
- Compatible with existing e-process monitor (src/lab/oracle/eprocess.rs) — uses same Ville inequality

## Test Coverage (52 tests)

Config validation (9): defaults, aggressive, tolerant, boundary values
Basic mechanics (4): empty, single observation, credit accumulation, negative clamping
Stall detection (3): flat sequences, broken by decrease, increases count
Convergence (4): linear decrease, exponential decay, harmonic series, step functions
Non-convergence (3): diverging, constant, oscillating
Azuma-Hoeffding (2): tightness with matched bound, valid probability
Supermartingale (3): conservation under monotone, ratio with increases, bounded walk
Ville's bound (2): exact computation, zero initial
Variance (2): constant deltas (zero), alternating deltas (exact = 25)
Evidence trail (4): quiescence, stall, violations, exceeded bound
Edge cases (3): single step to zero, all zeros, very large/small potentials
Integration (1): observe_potential_record with real PotentialRecord/StateSnapshot
Realistic scenario (1): two-phase drain (rapid + slow tail with jitter)
Optional Stopping (1): exact computation for constant decrease
Display (1): formatting

## Status: COMPLETED — SapphireHill, 2026-02-24

title: Implement ProgressCertificate tracker with O(1) incremental statistics
description:
The main tracker maintains O(1) running totals for incremental updates without storing full history:
- total_credit: cumulative progress credit sum_{i=1}^{t} c_i where c_i = max(0, -Delta_i)
- credit_sum_sq: sum of squared credits for variance computation
- max_abs_delta: maximum absolute step size (needed for Azuma-Hoeffding c parameter)
- increase_count: number of steps where potential increased (supermartingale violations)
- stall_run: consecutive non-decreasing steps (for stall detection)
- initial_potential, current potential

Key methods: observe(potential) for raw values, observe_potential_record(PotentialRecord) for Lyapunov integration, martingale_value() = V(Sigma_t) + total_credit, martingale_ratio() = martingale_value / initial for exceedance checking, delta_variance() for step-size distribution analysis.

Three ProgressConfig presets: default (99% confidence), aggressive (99.9%), tolerant (95%). File: src/cancel/progress_certificate.rs.

title: Implement Azuma-Hoeffding concentration bound and Optional Stopping estimate
description:
Two probabilistic tools for convergence certification:

1. Azuma-Hoeffding bound: P(V(Sigma_t) > V(Sigma_0) - t*mu + lambda) <= exp(-2*lambda^2/(t*c^2))
   where mu = mean_credit, c = max_abs_delta. Computing: set lambda = V(Sigma_0) - t*mu (asking P(not quiescent by step t)), giving bound = exp(-2*(V0 - t*mu)^2 / (t*c^2)). Used for confidence_bound in verdict.

2. Optional Stopping estimate: E[tau] <= V(Sigma_current) / mean_credit
   where tau = hitting time of zero. Gives expected remaining steps.

Convergence declared when ALL THREE conditions hold:
a) Mean credit > 0 (net downward trend)
b) stall_run < stall_threshold (no long flat runs)
c) Azuma bound < 1-confidence OR potential decreased >50% (dual criterion handles variable step sizes)

File: src/cancel/progress_certificate.rs.

title: Implement Ville bound and auditable evidence trail
description:
Ville's maximal inequality: P(sup M_t >= C) <= M_0/C. Used for worst-case exceedance bounding.

Evidence trail: CertificateVerdict contains Vec<EvidenceEntry> where each entry has { step, potential, bound, description }. Evidence entries document:
- Initial potential observation
- Quiescence reached (potential = 0)
- Stall detection (N consecutive non-decreasing steps)
- Supermartingale violations (potential increased)
- Step bound exceeded (more steps than max_step_bound / mean_credit)

title: Obligation tracker: real-time view of held obligations and potential leaks
description:
# Obligation Tracker

## Overview
Real-time dashboard for tracking all obligations (permits, leases, acks) across the
runtime, with leak detection and aging warnings.

## Design

### Obligation Overview
```rust
pub struct ObligationTracker {
    state: Arc<RuntimeState>,
    console: Console,
}

impl ObligationTracker {
    /// List all active obligations.
    pub fn list_obligations(&self) -> Vec<ObligationInfo> {
        self.state.all_obligations()
            .map(|o| ObligationInfo {
                id: o.id(),
                type_name: o.type_name(),
                holder_task: o.holder_task(),
                holder_region: o.holder_region(),
                created_at: o.created_at(),
                age: o.age(),
                state: o.state(),
            })
            .collect()
    }
    
    /// Find potentially leaked obligations.
    pub fn find_potential_leaks(&self, age_threshold: Duration) -> Vec<ObligationInfo> {
        self.list_obligations()
            .into_iter()
            .filter(|o| o.age > age_threshold && o.state.is_active())
            .collect()
    }
    
    /// Get obligations by type.
    pub fn by_type(&self, type_name: &str) -> Vec<ObligationInfo> {
        self.list_obligations()
            .into_iter()
            .filter(|o| o.type_name == type_name)
            .collect()
    }
}
```

### Obligation Types Tracked
- **ConnectionLease**: Database/network connections
- **TransactionLock**: Uncommitted transactions
- **ChannelPermit**: Bounded channel send permits
- **MessageAck**: Unacknowledged queue messages
- **FileLock**: File reservation leases
- **TimerHandle**: Active timer registrations

### Output Format
```

│ Active Obligations: 12  │  Potential Leaks: 2  │  Age > 1m: 5 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Type              Count  Oldest    Holder                   │

│ ConnectionLease     5    2.3s      Region-2 (HttpHandler)   │

│   TransactionLock held by Task-42 for 45.2s                 │
│     -> Created at: src/db/queries.rs:89                     │
│     -> Recommendation: Check for missing commit/rollback    │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Interactive Features (TUI)
- Filter by obligation type
- Sort by age, holder, type
- Click to drill down
- Threshold alerts configuration

title: [EPIC] Structured Concurrency Macro DSL
description:
# Overview

A set of procedural macros (`scope!`, `spawn!`, `race!`, `join!`) that generate
correct structured concurrency patterns with less boilerplate and compile-time guidance.

## Why This Matters

The current API is correct but verbose. Making the correct thing easy to write:
1. Reduces errors (can't forget to await children)
2. Lowers adoption barrier
3. Makes code more readable
4. Provides better compile-time error messages

## The Macros

### scope! - Create a scoped region

```rust
// Current API:
cx.region(|scope| async move {
    // ... spawn tasks
}).await

// With macro:
scope!(cx, {
    // ... spawn tasks
}) // Automatically awaits, ensures all children complete
```

### spawn! - Spawn a task in current scope

```rust
// Current API:
let handle = scope.spawn(async { task1().await });

// With macro:
let handle = spawn!(task1()); // Captures scope from context
```

### join! - Await multiple handles

```rust
// Current API:
let (r1, r2, r3) = cx.join((h1, h2, h3)).await;

// With macro:
let (r1, r2, r3) = join!(h1, h2, h3); // Type inference, proper cancellation
```

### race! - Race with automatic loser cleanup

```rust
// Current API:
let winner = cx.race(vec![
    Box::pin(async { fetch_primary().await }),
    Box::pin(async { fetch_replica().await }),
]).await;

// With macro:
let winner = race!(cx, {
    fetch_primary(),
    fetch_replica(),
}); // Losers automatically cancelled and drained
```

## Design Principles

1. **No hidden behavior**: Macros expand to standard API calls
2. **Better errors**: Macro can provide context-aware error messages
3. **Type inference**: Avoid explicit type annotations where possible
4. **Zero overhead**: Macro expansion is as efficient as hand-written code

## Implementation Approach

1. Create `asupersync-macros` proc-macro crate
2. Parse macro input using syn
3. Generate standard API calls using quote
4. Add compile-time validation for common mistakes

## Relationship to Formal Semantics

The macros enforce patterns from the formal semantics:
- `scope!` ensures region lifecycle (§4.2)
- `spawn!` ensures task ownership (§4.1)
- `join!` implements join semantics (§5.1)
- `race!` implements race with loser drain (§5.2)

## Success Criteria

- [ ] scope! macro with automatic await
- [ ] spawn! macro with scope capture
- [ ] join! macro with tuple/array support
- [ ] race! macro with automatic loser cleanup
- [ ] Compile-time errors for misuse
- [ ] Documentation with examples
- [ ] Zero overhead vs hand-written code

title: Implement race_all combinator (N-way race with loser draining)
description:
# race_all (N-way Race with Loser Draining)

## Purpose
Generalize `race(a,b)` to `race_all(futures)`:
- first terminal outcome wins
- every loser is cancelled and drained to terminal

This is essential for timeouts, hedges, speculative execution, and quorum-style patterns.

## Semantics
1. spawn all participants in a subregion
2. wait for the first terminal completion
3. request cancellation on every loser
4. **drain** every loser by awaiting completion
5. return winner outcome

## Acceptance Criteria
- Winner is returned.
- Every spawned participant reaches a terminal state before `race_all` returns.
- Loser finalizers run.
- Loser obligations are resolved.

## Testing
- E2E: include a loser holding a permit/guard; verify it is released due to drain.

title: HTTP/gRPC Security Audit - Clean Bill of Health
description:
Comprehensive security audit of src/http/** and src/grpc/** modules revealed robust protections against known attack vectors:

**HTTP/1.1 Codec (src/http/h1/codec.rs)**:
- CL/TE request smuggling prevention: AmbiguousBodyLength error for both headers
- Strict Content-Length parsing: rejects signed integers (+5) to prevent parser disagreement
- Strict chunk size parsing: rejects non-hex prefixes 
- Bare CR detection: prevents framing confusion
- Header limits: 64KB max headers, 128 max count, 8KB max request line

**HTTP/2 (src/http/h2/)**:
- HPACK bomb protection: 1MB max table size, 256KB max string length, 16 max consecutive size updates
- CVE-2023-44487 Rapid Reset protection: RST_STREAM rate limiting (100/30s)
- Frame size validation: enforced against SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE (16KB-16MB)
- Proper CONTINUATION frame handling to prevent interleaving attacks

**gRPC (src/grpc/)**:
- Message size limits: 4MB default, configurable per-codec
- Pre-allocation DoS protection: validates compressed frame length before buffer allocation
- Post-compression size validation: prevents compression bombs
- Comprehensive encode/decode size enforcement

All implementations follow RFC specifications and include extensive test coverage for boundary conditions. No security vulnerabilities found requiring immediate attention.

title: Implement Outcome type with severity lattice
description:
# Outcome Type with Severity Lattice

## Purpose
The Outcome type is the fundamental result type for all tasks and regions in Asupersync. Unlike Result<T, E>, it has FOUR variants ordered by severity, enabling monotone aggregation where "worse always wins."

## The Four Outcomes (Severity Order)
```rust
enum Outcome<V, E, R, P> {
    Ok(V),           // Severity 0: Success with value
    Err(E),          // Severity 1: Application error
    Cancelled(R),    // Severity 2: Cancelled with reason
    Panicked(P),     // Severity 3: Panic (unrecoverable)
}
```

## Why Four Values?
Traditional async runtimes conflate cancellation with errors or ignore it entirely. This causes:
- Silent data loss when cancellation drops in-progress work
- No distinction between "I failed" vs "I was stopped"
- Panics and errors treated the same way

Asupersync makes cancellation a first-class citizen because:
1. **Explicit Reasoning**: Code can pattern match on WHY something stopped
2. **Monotone Aggregation**: When combining outcomes, we want consistent behavior
3. **Policy-Aware**: Different outcomes may trigger different policies (restart, propagate, etc.)

## Mathematical Structure: Severity Lattice
The outcomes form a lattice under severity ordering:
```
Panicked
    ↑
Cancelled
    ↑
  Err
    ↑
  Ok
```

The lattice operations:
- **Join (⊔)**: Returns the more severe outcome (used for aggregation)
- **Meet (⊓)**: Returns the less severe outcome (rarely used)

## Key Operations

### severity() -> u8
Returns 0-3 for comparison. Must be implemented as a const fn for performance.

### combine(self, other) -> Self (for same V types)
Implements the join operation: `max_by_severity(self, other)`

This is used when:
- A region aggregates child outcomes
- A join combinator combines results
- Supervision decides on escalation

### is_terminal() -> bool
All variants are terminal (a task/region has finished).

### is_success() -> bool
Only Ok is success.

### into_result() -> Result<V, CombinedError<E, R, P>>
Converts to traditional Result for interop.

## Implementation Requirements

1. **Generic over all four type parameters**: V (value), E (error), R (cancel reason), P (panic payload)

2. **Default type parameters**:
   - E = Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>
   - R = CancelReason
   - P = Box<dyn Any + Send>

3. **Must implement**:
   - Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq (when inner types do)
   - PartialOrd, Ord based on severity
   - From<Result<V, E>> for easy interop

4. **Combinators**:
   - map, map_err, map_cancelled, map_panicked
   - and_then, or_else
   - unwrap_or, unwrap_or_else
   - ok(), err(), cancelled(), panicked() extractors

## Invariant Preservation

This type supports INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR: outcomes are absorbing states. Once a task reaches Completed(outcome), it cannot transition again.

## Testing Requirements

1. Severity ordering is correct: Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked
2. combine() always returns the more severe outcome
3. Lattice laws hold (associativity, commutativity, idempotence)
4. From<Result> conversions are correct

## Performance Considerations

- Outcome should be repr(u8) discriminant for fast severity checks
- No heap allocation for the Outcome enum itself
- Clone should be cheap (inner types may heap-allocate)

## Example Usage
```rust
let child_outcomes = vec![
    Outcome::Ok(42),
    Outcome::Err(MyError),
    Outcome::Ok(17),
];
let region_outcome = child_outcomes.into_iter()
    .reduce(|a, b| a.combine(b))
    .unwrap_or(Outcome::Ok(()));
// Result: Outcome::Err(MyError) - worst wins
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.2 (Outcomes)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.1 (Outcomes form a severity lattice)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Outcome has variants Ok/Err/Cancelled/Panicked with a total severity order (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked).
- Provides `severity()` and ordering/aggregation helpers used by region close + combinators.
- Aggregation is monotone: combining outcomes never yields a "less severe" result.
- Unit tests cover ordering, lattice laws (assoc/comm/idempotent), and conversions.
acceptance_criteria:

- Provides severity() and Ord/PartialOrd consistent with the lattice.

title: Sub-Epic: Runtime Debug Console - Ops-Grade Observability Tooling
description:
# Sub-Epic: Runtime Debug Console

## Overview
Implements a runtime debug console (TUI and/or web) providing ops-grade
observability for Asupersync applications, superior to tokio-console.

## Background & Motivation
Tokio has tokio-console with tracing ecosystem maturity. To win that comparison,
we need a cohesive tooling suite that surfaces:
- Region tree, tasks, cancellation state machine phase
- Obligations held, budgets remaining, stall reasons
- Deterministic trace capture and replay hooks
- 'Explain why' diagnostics

## Raid Plan: rich_rust Parts

### Available Parts
| Module | What to Raid | Target in asupersync |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|
| console.rs | Terminal detection, color downgrade | src/cli/console.rs |
| progress.rs | Progress bars for lab runtime | src/lab/progress.rs |
| table.rs | Table rendering for traces | src/trace/render.rs |
| tree.rs | Tree rendering for regions | src/cx/debug.rs |
| traceback.rs | Stack frame rendering | src/error/display.rs |

## Features

### 1. Runtime TUI
- Real-time region tree view
- Task list with status, state, budget
- Cancellation state machine visualization
- Obligation tracker
- Memory/CPU metrics

### 2. Web Dashboard (Optional)
- Browser-based interface
- WebSocket updates
- Trace timeline view
- Flame graphs

### 3. 'Explain Why' Diagnostics
- Why can't this region close?
- What's blocking this task?
- Why was this task cancelled?
- Which obligation is leaking?

### 4. Trace Capture
- Structured event recording
- Deterministic replay preparation
- Export to various formats

## Tasks in This Sub-Epic
1. Console rendering primitives (raid rich_rust)
2. Region tree visualization
3. Task inspector
4. Obligation tracker
5. Budget monitor
6. 'Explain why' diagnostics engine
7. Debug console E2E tests

## Integration Points
- Hooks into RuntimeState
- Trace buffer access
- Cx inspection
- Lab runtime integration

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] TUI shows live runtime state
- [ ] Region tree visualization works
- [ ] Task details accessible
- [ ] Obligations tracked and displayed
- [ ] 'Explain why' provides useful diagnostics
- [ ] Web dashboard (optional)
- [ ] Beautiful output (raid rich_rust)
- [ ] Low overhead when disabled

comments.author: CopperForest
comments.text: [2026-03-06 CopperForest] Baseline for this backlog: As of 2026-03-06, Asupersync is not yet a usable WASM/JS/TS library. The repo has substantial WASM/browser contracts, docs, and policy/test scaffolding, but not the actual product surface. Key facts this epic encodes so future work does not need the original markdown analysis: (1) Cargo explicitly frames wasm-browser-preview as guarded compilation, not full parity; (2) there is no packages/ tree, no committed package.json manifests, and no pkg/ output directory; (3) there are no concrete #[wasm_bindgen] exports in src/; (4) the browser reactor is still a scaffold/stub; (5) direct runtime execution is only a client-hydrated target, while server/node/edge are bridge-only by design; (6) remote check cargo check -p asupersync --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --no-default-features --features wasm-browser-minimal currently fails due native-surface leakage, including config/http1 imports, reactor/source assumptions, socket2 usage in net/tcp, and libc use in trace/file. Success for this epic means we have real packages, real bindings, real browser host integration, real consumer validation, and release gates backed by actual shipped artifacts rather than doc-only evidence.

comments.author: CopperForest
comments.text:
Current repo-state summary that justifies this epic:

- As of 2026-03-06, asupersync is not yet a usable JS/TS library in the practical sense of `install from npm`, import typed entrypoints, and build a browser app against real shipped artifacts.
- The repo already has substantial design/policy material for Browser Edition, but the implementation is still incomplete in the places that determine whether users can actually consume it.
- The intended direct-runtime target is the hydrated browser client boundary. Node/server/edge are bridge-only by design and should not silently drift into a fake "full runtime everywhere" story.

Concrete evidence captured during recon:

- There is no physical JS package tree today: no `packages/`, no `pkg/`, no `package.json` in the repo root or package subtrees.
- There are currently no concrete `wasm_bindgen` exports in `src/`; searches for `#[wasm_bindgen]`, `use wasm_bindgen`, `serde_wasm_bindgen`, and `tsify` came back empty.
- `src/runtime/reactor/browser.rs` is a scaffold/stub, not a finished host integration.
- `src/io/browser_stream.rs` documents that the wasm32 path "would interface" with JS host streams, which means the bridge is still aspirational instead of implemented.
- Several wasm tests currently validate docs/contracts and release-policy tokens, not installable package artifacts.

Operational goal of this epic:

Ship Browser Edition as something a real consumer can build against: compile-clean wasm profiles, real exported ABI, real package manifests/artifacts, framework adapters, and artifact-backed validation/release gates. The child tracks below decompose that goal so that future work does not need to rediscover either the current blockers or the intended product boundary.

comments.author: CopperForest
comments.text:
Plan-space revision after graph audit: the first version captured the core implementation lanes, but it under-modeled three things that matter to users and to future execution quality.

1. Quality and failure-forensics needed to be explicit first-class work, not implied. A usable WASM/JS/TS library needs comprehensive unit/integration coverage, packaged E2E harnesses, rich logging, and retained artifacts so failures are debuggable.
2. Developer experience needed its own track. Examples, quickstarts, compatibility boundaries, troubleshooting, and reference/versioning guidance are part of product usability, not optional garnish.
3. The priority graph needed rebalancing so `bv` would recommend actionable dependency-clearing work instead of blocked integration milestones.

This revision therefore adds track `.8` for QA/forensics, track `.9` for DX/examples/docs, task `.5.7` for unsupported-runtime diagnostics, task `.6.7` for performance budgets, and lowers blocked integration epics/tasks so the compile-closure blockers surface first.

title: [security-audit] distributed/snapshot: wall-clock timestamp as merge tiebreaker is non-canonical
description:
src/distributed/snapshot.rs:426-435 RegionSnapshot::merge_crdt() uses (sequence, timestamp.as_nanos(), state.as_u8()) as the lexicographic tiebreaker for selecting between two snapshots' cancel_reason fields when sequence numbers tie. The merge IS deterministic from frozen snapshot data (both nodes see the same timestamps embedded in the snapshots, so merge(A,B) and merge(B,A) pick the same winner) — so this is NOT a split-brain in the strict sense. However, wall-clock-derived tiebreakers are a known code smell in CRDT design:

  * Clock skew between nodes (±100ms typical with NTP) means SNAPSHOT-CREATION-TIME order does not match the WALL-CLOCK timestamp order encoded in the snapshot. An attacker who controls one node's clock can artificially advance/retard their snapshot's timestamp to force their cancel_reason to win at any tie.
  * The choice of which cancel_reason 'wins' at a tie is observable — so this can be used to bias diagnostic output, mask a contributing failure mode, or selectively suppress evidence of a competing node's actions.
  * Standard CRDT practice replaces wall-clock with logical/causal clocks (Lamport timestamps, vector clocks, or HLCs) precisely to avoid this attack surface.

Severity LOW — the cancel_reason selection doesn't grant authority (it's an explanatory string for diagnostics), so the worst-case is biased forensic output. Worth filing as a hardening note since the project carries the I7 'no ambient authority' invariant and the wall-clock dependency at this site is one of the few such dependencies in the distributed/ subtree.

Suggested fix: use a vector-clock or HLC-derived field instead of timestamp.as_nanos(). Or, if the cancel_reason tiebreaker is operationally unimportant, just always prefer self's reason (lexicographic on bytes if needed — anything attacker-incontrollable).
close_reason: Fixed in latest commit: tiebreaker now uses (sequence, &cancel_reason, state.as_u8()) — content-derived, clock-skew-immune. 3 new regression tests cover content-precedence, None vs Some, and primary-key precedence.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] OpenTelemetry Metrics Export
description:
## Overview

Implement OpenTelemetry metrics export for runtime observability, enabling integration with standard monitoring systems like Prometheus, Datadog, and Grafana.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Production systems need metrics for monitoring and alerting. Without standard metrics export, operators must build custom solutions.

**Why OpenTelemetry**: OTel is the emerging standard for observability. It supports multiple backends (Prometheus, OTLP, etc.) through a single API.

**Production Requirement**: Any runtime targeting production use needs metrics. This is table stakes for enterprise adoption.

## Metrics Categories

### Runtime Metrics
- `asupersync.tasks.active` - Currently running tasks (gauge)
- `asupersync.tasks.spawned` - Total tasks spawned (counter)
- `asupersync.tasks.completed` - Tasks completed by outcome (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.regions.active` - Currently open regions (gauge)
- `asupersync.regions.created` - Total regions created (counter)

### Timing Metrics
- `asupersync.task.duration` - Task execution time (histogram)
- `asupersync.region.lifetime` - Region open duration (histogram)
- `asupersync.scheduler.poll_time` - Time spent in poll (histogram)

### Cancellation Metrics
- `asupersync.cancellations` - Cancellation count by reason (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.drain_duration` - Time spent in drain phase (histogram)

### Budget Metrics
- `asupersync.deadline.remaining` - Time remaining at task start (histogram)
- `asupersync.poll_quota.usage` - Poll quota utilization (histogram)

### Resource Metrics
- `asupersync.obligations.active` - Undischarged obligations (gauge)
- `asupersync.obligations.undischarged` - Obligations dropped undischarged (counter)

## Integration Design

### Feature Flag
```toml
[features]
metrics = ["opentelemetry", "opentelemetry-prometheus"]
```

### Metrics Provider
```rust
pub trait MetricsProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn task_spawned(&self, region_id: RegionId);
    fn task_completed(&self, task_id: TaskId, outcome: &Outcome<()>, duration: Duration);
    fn region_created(&self, region_id: RegionId, parent: Option<RegionId>);
    fn region_closed(&self, region_id: RegionId, lifetime: Duration);
    fn cancellation(&self, region_id: RegionId, kind: CancelKind);
    // ... etc
}
```

### OpenTelemetry Implementation
```rust
pub struct OtelMetrics {
    tasks_active: ObservableGauge<u64>,
    tasks_spawned: Counter<u64>,
    task_duration: Histogram<f64>,
    // ...
}

impl MetricsProvider for OtelMetrics { ... }
```

### Integration
```rust
RuntimeBuilder::new()
    .metrics(OtelMetrics::new(meter_provider))
    .build()
```

## Prometheus Example

```
# HELP asupersync_tasks_active Currently running tasks
# TYPE asupersync_tasks_active gauge
asupersync_tasks_active 42

# HELP asupersync_tasks_completed_total Tasks completed
# TYPE asupersync_tasks_completed_total counter
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="ok"} 1000
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="err"} 50
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="cancelled"} 10
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="panicked"} 2

# HELP asupersync_task_duration_seconds Task execution duration
# TYPE asupersync_task_duration_seconds histogram
asupersync_task_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.001"} 500
asupersync_task_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.01"} 800
...
```

## Acceptance Criteria

1. MetricsProvider trait defined
2. OtelMetrics implementation
3. All metrics categories implemented
4. Feature-gated (no mandatory OTel dependency)
5. Prometheus exporter example
6. Grafana dashboard template
7. Documentation with setup guide

## Dependencies

- Optional opentelemetry dependency
- Uses runtime hooks for metrics collection

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #15 because while essential for production, metrics are a "nice to have" during development. Users can add metrics later once they move toward production.

title: Epic: Combinator Implementation (join!/race!/select!)
description:
# Epic: Combinator Implementation

## Overview

Implement the structured concurrency combinators that compose concurrent operations: join (wait for all), race (wait for first), select (wait for any with continuation), and related patterns.

## Background

Asupersync's combinators differ from typical async combinator libraries:
1. **Cancel-correct**: Losers in a race are properly cancelled and drained
2. **Two-phase aware**: Combinator results use Outcome, not Result
3. **Region-integrated**: Combinators operate within structured concurrency regions
4. **Obligation-safe**: Obligations are properly resolved across all branches

## Combinators to Implement

### join!
Wait for all futures, return tuple of results:
```rust
let (a, b, c) = join!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await;
```

Semantics:
- All futures run concurrently
- If any fails, others continue (collect all Outcomes)
- If any panics, others continue
- Final Outcome is the 'worst' (highest severity)

### race!
Wait for first to complete, cancel losers:
```rust
let winner: Either3<A, B, C> = race!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await;
```

Semantics:
- All futures run concurrently
- First to complete is the winner
- Losers are cancelled (request → drain → finalize)
- Wait for losers to fully drain before returning

### select!
Pattern-match on first completion with cancellation:
```rust
select! {
    a = future_a => handle_a(a),
    b = future_b => handle_b(b),
    else => handle_none(),
}
```

### timeout!
Race a future against a deadline:
```rust
let result = timeout!(Duration::from_secs(5), operation).await;
```

### try_join!
Like join but short-circuit on first error:
```rust
let (a, b, c) = try_join!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await?;
```

## Implementation Approach

1. **Macro-based**: Procedural macros for ergonomic syntax
2. **Type-safe**: Full type inference for all branches
3. **Cancelable**: All branches respond to cancellation
4. **Budget-aware**: Track poll counts across branches

## Dependencies

- Cancellation system must be complete
- Region tree must support concurrent children
- Obligation tracking for two-phase operations

## Success Criteria

- All combinators work correctly
- Losers properly drained in races
- Obligations resolved across all branches
- Type inference works without annotations
- Lab runtime tests deterministic
- Documentation with examples

## References

- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 3.2: Concurrency Combinators
- Tokio join!/select! macros (for syntax reference)
- futures-rs FutureExt (for trait patterns)

title: Actor mailbox: bounded channel with backpressure
description:
# Actor Mailbox Implementation

## Goal

Implement bounded mailboxes for actors that provide backpressure and integrate with the cancellation protocol.

## Background

Actors receive messages through mailboxes. Unlike unbounded queues (which can cause OOM), bounded mailboxes provide backpressure: when full, senders must wait or get backpressure signals.

## Design

### Mailbox<M>
- Wrapper around bounded mpsc channel
- Capacity specified at actor spawn time
- Integrates with two-phase send (reserve→commit)

### MailboxConfig
- capacity: usize (default: 64)
- overflow_policy: OverflowPolicy (Block, DropOldest, DropNewest, Error)
- priority_levels: Option<u8> (for priority mailboxes)

### MailboxHandle<M>
- Sender half given to ActorRef
- Methods: send(msg), try_send(msg), reserve() -> SendPermit

### MailboxReceiver<M>
- Receiver half held by ActorCell
- Methods: recv() -> Option<M>, try_recv(), is_empty(), len()

## Backpressure Semantics

When mailbox is full:
1. Block (default): Sender awaits until space available
2. DropOldest: Remove oldest message, insert new one
3. DropNewest: Reject new message immediately
4. Error: Return MailboxFull error

## Cancellation Integration

- recv() respects cancellation checkpoints
- Pending sends are aborted cleanly on actor cancellation
- SendPermit is an obligation (must commit or abort)

## Priority Mailbox (Optional)

For actors that need priority message handling:
- Multiple internal queues by priority level
- High-priority messages processed first
- Prevents priority inversion

## Implementation Notes

- Build on existing channel primitives in src/channel/
- MailboxConfig stored in ActorCell
- Metrics: messages_received, messages_dropped, current_depth

## Testing

- Backpressure: verify senders block when full
- Cancellation: verify clean abort of pending sends
- Priority: verify high-priority messages processed first
- Lab runtime: deterministic message ordering

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Mailbox<M> with configurable capacity
- [ ] OverflowPolicy enum with 4 strategies
- [ ] Two-phase send integration (SendPermit)
- [ ] Cancellation-safe recv()
- [ ] Optional priority levels
- [ ] Metrics for observability

title: [SPORK] OTP-Grade Layer for Asupersync (Beats Elixir Naturally)
description:
Goal: build **Spork**, an OTP-grade ergonomics layer on top of asupersync that feels as natural as Elixir/Erlang for building long-lived concurrent systems, but is **strictly stronger** on determinism, cancellation-correctness, and auditable reasoning.

Why this exists:
- OTP is an operational model, not an actor library. The win is the *defaults*: supervision, naming, linking/monitoring, backpressure conventions, and coherent shutdown.
- asupersync already has most of the hard primitives: region ownership + quiescence, two-phase cancel-safe effects, supervision policies, lab determinism + DPOR tooling.
- What is missing is a compiled, opinionated surface that makes the right thing the easy thing.

Non-negotiable invariants (Spork must preserve):
- Region close => quiescence (no live children, finalizers done).
- Cancellation is a protocol: request -> drain -> finalize.
- Losers are drained (no abandoned tasks after races).
- No obligation leaks (permits/acks/leases committed or aborted).
- No ambient authority: Spork features are capabilities hanging off `Cx`/regions.

Alien-artifact bar:
- Explainability: supervisors/registries produce evidence ledgers for decisions.
- Formal hooks: traces are canonicalizable and replayable; failures emit minimal repro artifacts.
- Deterministic testing: lab runs + DPOR exploration are first-class for Spork apps.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Context: "Beat Elixir Naturally" (OTP++)

This epic is the answer to:

- Jose Valim (Elixir author) arguing Elixir is a top-tier language for AI agents because the *operational model* is friendly: immutability, docs, stability, and tooling.
- Darin's pushback: "don't try to replicate OTP" and "there are already 20 actor libs in Rust".

The synthesis here is:

1. **Darin is right** if we interpret the goal as "make yet another Rust actor library".
2. **Jeff is right** if we interpret the goal as "ship an OTP-grade *operational model*".

Spork is explicitly the latter: an OTP-class toolkit compiled onto asupersync's kernel primitives.

# The Core Claim

Spork can be *more natural than OTP* while being strictly stronger, because asupersync already has primitives OTP doesn't:

- **Structured concurrency** (region ownership) rather than unowned processes.
- **Close = quiescence** as an invariant, not a social convention.
- **Cancellation as a protocol** (request -> drain -> finalize), not ad-hoc `exit/2`.
- **Two-phase effects / obligations** so reply-or-abort is enforced (no silent drops).
- **Deterministic lab runtime** so failures are replayable and schedule-explorable.
- **Crash artifacts + trace canonicalization** so bugs become files, not mysteries.
- Optional: **formal semantics hooks** (Lean/TLA scaffolding) so we can state and check real claims.

In other words: OTP gives amazing defaults. Spork aims to give *even better* defaults because our substrate can enforce them.

# What "More Natural Than OTP" Means

"Natural" is not syntax; it's that the correct architecture is the path of least resistance:

- You start a service under a supervisor, and it is *owned*.
- You name it without globals, and names cannot go stale.
- You call/cast it, and cancellation cannot silently drop protocol obligations.
- When something fails, you get:
  - a canonicalized trace fingerprint
  - a seed + minimal divergent prefix
  - a crashpack manifest
  - an evidence ledger
  - a single command to replay

If we deliver that, Spork is better-than-Elixir for AI agents even if the language is Rust.

# Key Architecture Decision: "Compile OTP to Regions"

OTP runtime model:
- process tree + supervisors + links/monitors + name registry

Spork runtime model:
- **region tree** is the source of truth
- supervisors are *compiled* into region ownership + policy application
- links/monitors are explicit cancellation/failure propagation edges with deterministic ordering
- registry is a `Cx` capability: lease obligations prevent stale names

This is why we don't need yet another actor library: the meaning lives in the composition of region + obligation + lab determinism.

# Proposed User-Facing Surface (Sketch)

A minimal high-level surface (not final API):

- `spork::app::{App, AppHandle, AppSpec}`
- `spork::supervisor::{SupervisorSpec, Strategy, ChildSpec}`
- `spork::gen_server::{GenServer, ServerHandle}`
- `spork::registry::{Registry, NameLease}` (capability)
- `spork::monitor::{monitor, link, trap_exit}`

Pseudo-usage:

```rust
cx.region(|root| async move {
  let app = MyApp::spec()
    .with_registry(root.registry())
    .with_supervisor(|sup| {
      sup.one_for_one()
        .child("chat", ChatServer::spec())
        .child("presence", Presence::spec());
    });

  let handle = app.start(root).await?;
  // ...
  handle.stop(root).await?; // closes region => quiescence
}).await;
```

# Acceptance: How We'll Know We Won

- Conformance: an OTP mental-model suite passes for GenServer/Supervisor/Registry/Link-Monitor.
- Determinism: every failing Spork app test emits a crashpack with replay.
- Correctness: no obligation leaks, no task leaks, losers drained.
- Ergonomics: "happy path" app code is smaller than Rust actor libs, because policies are defaults.

# Dependencies: Big Rocks

This epic is intentionally decomposed into sub-epics:

- Spec + ordering contracts (`bd-11z9a`)
- GenServer (`bd-1zok9`)
- Supervisors (`bd-2n7yw`)
- Registry (`bd-3rpp8`)
- Link/Monitor (`bd-pr46z`)
- Lab harness + DPOR (`bd-1vk6c`)
- Crash artifacts (`bd-qbcnu`)
- Observability (`bd-iu07v`)
- Performance kernel (`bd-2u7ns`)
- Formal hooks (`bd-3ccru`)

The new epics added in this pass extend the missing "OTP Application" layer and the explicit AI/agent-first ergonomics layer.

title: [FOUNDATION] Define canonical Cx type for suite-wide use
description: Define the canonical Cx (capability context) type in franken_kernel for suite-wide use. Cx is the core abstraction that threads through all Asupersync operations -- it carries capabilities, budget, deadline, trace context, and evidence ledger reference. The franken_kernel Cx must be: (1) Generic over capability set -- Cx<C: CapabilitySet> so each project defines its own capabilities, (2) Lifetime-bound -- Cx<'a, C> ensures capabilities cannot outlive their scope, (3) Propagation-aware -- child Cx inherits parent capabilities (attenuated via Macaroons), (4) Budget-aware -- carries remaining budget in tropical semiring (min, +), (5) Trace-aware -- carries TraceId for cross-project distributed tracing. Must define the CapabilitySet trait with methods: has<T>(), get<T>(), attenuate<T>(caveat). This is the most critical type in the entire FrankenSuite. TRACING / LOGGING SPECIFICATION: Span: cx::new with parent_trace_id, budget_remaining_ms, capability_count. Span: cx::propagate when creating child Cx from parent. DEBUG: Cx<C> created with trace_id={id}, budget={budget_ms}ms, capabilities=[{cap_names}]. DEBUG: Cx attenuated: capability={cap_name}, caveat={caveat_desc}. INFO: Cx budget exhausted: trace_id={id}, original_budget={orig}ms, elapsed={elapsed}ms -- emitted once per exhaustion event. WARN: Cx capability check failed: trace_id={id}, required={cap_name}, available=[{available_caps}]. Metrics: cx_creation_total (counter), cx_propagation_total (counter), cx_budget_exhaustion_total (counter), cx_capability_check_total (counter by result=granted|denied), cx_budget_remaining_ms (histogram at propagation boundaries).

title: Epic: Scheduler Lost Wakeup & Race Condition Fixes
description:
# Epic: Scheduler Lost Wakeup & Race Condition Fixes

## Overview

Deep review of the scheduler implementation in `src/runtime/scheduler/` revealed 
critical concurrency bugs that can cause workers to permanently park, miss wakeups, 
or execute tasks multiple times.

## Background & Context

The scheduler is the heart of the async runtime. It manages:
- **Workers**: OS threads that execute async tasks
- **Queues**: Local (per-worker) and global task queues
- **Parking**: Workers sleep when no work available
- **Stealing**: Idle workers steal from busy workers

Bugs here cause:
- Tasks never executed (lost wakeups)
- Tasks executed multiple times (duplicate scheduling)
- Workers stuck indefinitely (deadlock-like behavior)
- Performance degradation (unnecessary spinning)

## Critical Findings

### Lost Wakeup Issues

1. **Parker race condition** (`worker.rs:268-294`)
   - Window between lock acquire and condvar wait
   - Unpark notification can be lost

2. **Backoff-to-park race** (`worker.rs:150-168`, `three_lane.rs:228-264`)
   - Work injected between empty check and park
   - Worker parks despite pending work

3. **Wake state race** (`worker.rs:183-196`, `three_lane.rs:418-420`)
   - Task woken while being polled
   - Can cause duplicate scheduling

### Fairness Issues

4. **Cancel lane monopoly** (`three_lane.rs:204-208`)
   - No bound on consecutive cancel executions
   - Ready work can starve

## Root Cause Analysis

The fundamental issue is **non-atomic state transitions**:
- Check if work available (reads queue)
- Decide to park (based on empty)
- Actually park (condvar wait)

Between any two steps, state can change. The classic solution is 
"double-checked locking" but async schedulers need more nuanced approaches.

## Success Criteria

- No lost wakeups under stress testing
- No duplicate task execution
- Workers wake promptly when work available
- Fairness across priority lanes
- Documented concurrency model

## Testing Strategy

1. **Stress tests**: High concurrency with many wake/park cycles
2. **Loom tests**: Systematic exploration of interleavings

title: Unit and integration tests for Methodology framework adoption
description:
Comprehensive test suite verifying that the section 0 Alien-Artifact Implementation Framework is correctly adopted across Asupersync. This tests the methodology infrastructure itself -- the baselines, golden checksums, evidence ledger integration, and CI gates.

BACKGROUND: The methodology framework (bd-1e2if) establishes four pillars: performance baselines, golden output checksums, evidence ledger integration, and CI artifact gates. Each pillar needs its own validation tests to ensure the methodology enforcement is working correctly.

UNIT TESTS:
(1) Baseline infrastructure: verify that criterion.rs benchmarks produce valid JSON output matching the baseline schema ({ operation, p50_ns, p95_ns, p99_ns, ci95_lower_ns, ci95_upper_ns, timestamp, git_sha }). Test with a known-cost operation and verify latency is within expected bounds.
(2) Golden checksum framework: verify the capture/verify workflow. Capture a checksum, verify it passes. Modify the output, verify the check fails with a clear error message. Test GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 regeneration.
(3) EvidenceLedger integration: verify all decision points that should emit EvidenceLedger entries actually do. Mock the ledger sink, trigger each decision type (scheduler, cancellation, budget, capability), verify entries appear with all required fields.
(4) Property-based test infrastructure: verify proptest configuration (case count, shrinking, regression directory) matches the standard defined in bd-1e2if.4.
(5) Decision Contract validation: verify the DecisionContract trait implementations (bd-1e2if.6) satisfy required invariants: loss matrix is non-negative, posterior sums to 1.0, argmin selection is correct.
(6) Opportunity Matrix Gate: verify that only implementations with opportunity score >= 2.0 pass the gate. Test with scores above and below threshold.

INTEGRATION TESTS:
(7) Full methodology pipeline: make a code change to a hot-path module, run the CI pipeline locally (simulated), verify all four gates fire and produce correct artifacts.
(8) Regression detection: artificially degrade a benchmark by 10%, run baseline comparison, verify the gate catches it.
(9) Evidence ledger end-to-end: run a realistic workload, collect all EvidenceLedger entries, verify they form a complete audit trail of all runtime decisions.
(10) Cross-subsystem consistency: verify that baselines, golden checksums, and evidence ledger entries are all tagged with the same git SHA and timestamp.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each test logs: test_name, methodology_pillar (baseline|golden|evidence|ci_gate), assertion_count, pass_fail, execution_time_ms. On failure: log the specific methodology requirement that was violated. CI summary: pillars_tested, tests_passed, tests_failed, coverage_by_pillar.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) All four methodology pillars have dedicated validation tests. (2) Tests detect intentional methodology violations (missing baseline, wrong checksum, missing evidence entry, bypassed gate). (3) Tests complete in under 3 minutes on CI. (4) At least one test per methodology pillar is a property-based test.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Conformance Test Suite
description:
## Overview

Create a comprehensive conformance test suite that verifies runtime implementations adhere to the structured concurrency specification. This serves as both validation and documentation.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Multiple runtime implementations (Lab, production epoll) must provide identical semantics. Without conformance tests, subtle behavioral differences can cause bugs that only appear in production.

**Why Conformance Suite**:
- Single source of truth for expected behavior
- Tests serve as executable specification
- Prevents regression when modifying runtimes
- Enables third-party runtime implementations

**Quality Assurance**: Conformance tests are how we prove correctness. They encode the invariants from the spec document as executable assertions.

## Test Categories

### Category 1: Region Lifecycle
- Region creation and nesting
- Region close waits for all children
- Orphan task prevention
- Region tree structure invariants

### Category 2: Cancellation Protocol
- Cancel request propagation
- Drain phase behavior
- Finalize phase behavior
- Cancel-safety of primitive operations

### Category 3: Outcome Semantics
- Four-valued outcome (Ok, Err, Cancelled, Panicked)
- Outcome joining rules
- Panic capture and propagation

### Category 4: Obligation System
- Obligation creation and discharge
- Undischarged obligation detection
- Obligation transfer rules

### Category 5: Budget Enforcement
- Deadline expiration
- Poll quota exhaustion
- Cost budget tracking

### Category 6: Two-Phase Commit
- Reserve/commit pattern
- Abort on cancel
- No data loss guarantees

## Test Infrastructure

### Conformance Trait
```rust
pub trait ConformanceTarget {
    type Runtime;
    fn create_runtime() -> Self::Runtime;
    fn block_on<F: Future>(runtime: &Self::Runtime, f: F) -> F::Output;
    // ... other required operations
}
```

### Test Macros
```rust
conformance_test!(region_close_waits_for_children, |runtime| {
    // Test implementation
});
```

## Acceptance Criteria

1. At least 50 conformance tests across all categories
2. Both Lab and production runtimes pass all tests
3. Tests are self-documenting (reference spec sections)
4. Test failure messages are diagnostic
5. Tests can run against third-party runtimes

## Dependencies

- Builds on existing Lab runtime
- May use oracles from chaos testing (Epic #5)

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #9 because while extremely valuable for quality assurance, it does not add user-facing features. Its value is in preventing bugs and enabling confident refactoring.

Implementation: Define a choreography DSL for saga protocols. Compile to per-participant Asupersync tasks. Integrate with session types (Epic 1) for type-safe message passing.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Design Macaroon-based Cx capability token format
description: Design the token format for Macaroon-based Cx capabilities. The format must support: (a) Binary serialization for zero-copy passing between tasks, (b) Human-readable debug representation for EvidenceLedger logging, (c) Version field for forward compatibility. Must define the caveat predicate language -- a simple expression DSL for time bounds, scope restrictions, rate limits, and custom predicates. DEBUG: token format example rendered at each detail level (binary hex, debug display, JSONL). WARN: design review found potential issue: {issue_description}. Metrics: (design deliverable -- no runtime metrics, but define the metrics contract that implementations must follow): macaroon_verification_latency_us (histogram), macaroon_caveat_count (histogram), macaroon_token_size_bytes (histogram).

title: [bug-hunt] grpc/reflection: ReflectionService has no opt-in auth callback for production hardening
description:
src/grpc/reflection.rs:147 — list_services_async() and describe_service_async() unconditionally serve responses to any client with TCP access. While unauthenticated reflection is the conventional pattern (clients use it to discover services before auth), production deployments often want the option to gate reflection — e.g., only allow reflection to clients in a private VPC or holding a specific token, while still allowing unauth health checks. Currently there's no API surface for that.

Suggested fix: add an optional reflection_auth: Option<Box<dyn Fn(&Request) -> bool + Send + Sync>> field to ReflectionService::new_with_auth(...). Default behavior unchanged (unauth, matches conventional gRPC reflection). When set, return Status::permission_denied('reflection requires authorization') if the callback returns false. Severity LOW — current behavior is conventional and not exploitable for unauth attackers (reflection only enumerates SERVICE NAMES that the operator chose to register), but the hardening hook is a low-cost defense-in-depth addition that operators with sensitive service surfaces can opt into.
close_reason: Added ReflectionService::with_auth(callback: Fn(&Cx, &str) -> Result<(), Status>). Default = no auth (dev-friendly). check_auth() called from all 4 RPC entry points (list_services, describe_service, *_async). list_services return type changed to Result<Vec<String>, Status>; 2 callers updated. 3 new tests: default-open, callback-rejection, method-name routing.

title: Session types: typed actor communication protocols
description:
# Session Types for Actor Communication ## Goal Implement optional session types that provide compile-time guarantees for actor communication protocols. ## ⚠️ OPTIONAL FEATURE **This task is OPTIONAL and can be deferred.** Session types add value for complex protocols but are not required for basic actor functionality. The core actor system (mailbox, lifecycle, supervision) works without session types. Consider implementing this after: - Core actor system is stable - Real-world protocol needs emerge - Team has bandwidth for advanced type system work ## Background Session types encode communication protocols in the type system. Instead of runtime checks for 'did I send the right message in the right order?', the compiler rejects invalid protocols. This is optional but valuable for: - Complex multi-step protocols (authentication, transactions) - Protocol versioning (types change between versions) - Documentation (types ARE the protocol spec) ## Core Concepts ### Session

A channel endpoint typed by the protocol P it implements. ### Protocol DSL Send: Send message of type T, continue with protocol P Recv: Receive message of type T, continue with protocol P End: Protocol complete Choose: Client picks branch Offer: Server waits for client choice Rec

: Recursive protocol ## Example: Login Protocol Client side: Send> Server side (dual): Recv> ## Testing Test Files: - tests/session_types/unit/: Protocol DSL, duality, linearity - tests/session_types/integration/: Simple protocols, branching, recursion - tests/session_types/compile_fail/: Wrong order, missing branch, dropped session Use trybuild for compile-fail tests to verify protocol violations are compile errors. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] Core session type constructors (Send, Recv, End, Choose, Offer) - [ ] SessionChannel with typed operations - [ ] Protocol duality verification - [ ] Integration with ActorContext - [ ] #[must_use] for linearity warnings - [ ] At least 3 example protocols - [ ] Compile-fail tests for violations - [ ] Documentation explaining when to use session types

title: Instrument task lifecycle with tracing spans
description:
# Task

Add tracing instrumentation to task lifecycle in runtime/scheduler.

## What to Instrument

1. **Task spawn**: When `scope.spawn()` is called
   - Fields: task_id, owning_region, name (if provided), initial_state
   
2. **Task poll**: Each time the task is polled
   - Fields: task_id, poll_number, budget_remaining
   - Keep as trace-level to avoid overhead
   
3. **Task wake**: When waker is invoked
   - Fields: task_id, wake_source (timer, io, explicit)
   
4. **Task state transitions**: Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed
   - Fields: task_id, from_state, to_state, outcome (on completion)

5. **Task completion**: Final outcome
   - Fields: task_id, outcome_kind (Ok/Err/Cancelled/Panicked), duration, poll_count

## Implementation Notes

- Task span should be child of region span
- Use span.in_scope() for poll instrumentation
- Wake events use follows_from to link to waker source
- Completion closes the task span

## Causality Links

```
Region[1] ──creates──> Task[100]
Task[100] ──woken_by──> Timer[5] 
Task[100] ──woken_by──> IoEvent[fd=3]
Task[100] ──cancelled_by──> Region[1].close()
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Spawn creates task span as child of region
- [ ] Poll events recorded at trace level
- [ ] Wake events include source
- [ ] State transitions recorded
- [ ] Completion includes outcome and metrics
- [ ] Causality links correctly established

title: Implement determinism oracle: identical seed/config => identical trace
description:
# Determinism Oracle (Seed/Config => Identical Trace)

## Purpose
One of the non-negotiable invariants is **Determinism is first-class**. In Phase 0, this means:

> Given the same lab configuration (including seed) and the same user program, the runtime produces the same observable trace.

This oracle makes that guarantee executable.

## What This Oracle Checks
For a chosen scenario/program `P` and lab config `C`:
1. Run `P` under `C` and capture trace `T1`.
2. Run `P` again under the *same* `C` and capture trace `T2`.
3. Assert `T1 == T2` (byte-for-byte or structurally equal).

If not equal, report:
- first divergence index
- expected event vs actual event
- surrounding context window
- relevant runtime snapshot (optional)

## Design Notes
- Determinism must include:
  - task selection decisions
  - timer wake ordering
  - cancellation propagation ordering
  - obligation IDs (or stable renaming normalization)

### ID renaming normalization (important)
If IDs are allocated in a deterministic order, raw equality is fine.
If not, we must canonicalize traces by renaming “fresh IDs” consistently before comparison.

Phase 0 goal: **make ID allocation deterministic** so canonicalization is minimal.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The oracle exists as a helper (e.g., `LabRuntime::assert_deterministic(program)` or standalone function).
- At least 3 E2E scenarios use it:
  - nested regions
  - race + loser draining
  - two-phase channel under cancellation

## Testing
- Intentionally break determinism (e.g., by using wall-clock time) in a test-only “bad runtime” to ensure oracle detects divergence.
close_reason: Implemented DeterminismOracle with verify(), compare_traces(), assert_deterministic(), and assert_deterministic_multi(). All tests pass.

title: Region tree visualization: hierarchical display of runtime structure
description:
# Region Tree Visualization

## Overview
Visual representation of the region hierarchy showing parent-child relationships,
task counts, cancellation state, and budget consumption.

## Design

### Tree Rendering (raid from rich_rust/tree.rs)
```rust
pub struct RegionTree {
    console: Console,
    state: Arc<RuntimeState>,
}

impl RegionTree {
    /// Render the current region tree.
    pub fn render(&self) -> String {
        let root = self.state.root_region();
        self.render_region(&root, 0, true)
    }
    
    fn render_region(&self, region: &Region, depth: usize, is_last: bool) -> String {
        let prefix = self.tree_prefix(depth, is_last);
        let status = self.region_status(region);
        let budget = self.budget_bar(region);
        
        format!(
            "{}{} {} [{}] {}",
            prefix,
            self.region_icon(region),
            region.id(),
            status,
            budget
        )
    }
}
```

### Output Format
```
Runtime Region Tree
├─ Root (Region-0) [Running] ████████░░ 80%
│  ├─ HttpServer (Region-1) [Running] ███████░░░ 70%
│  │  ├─ Request-1 (Region-2) [Running] █████░░░░░ 50%
│  │  │  └─ Task: handle_request [Polling]
│  │  └─ Request-2 (Region-3) [Draining] ██░░░░░░░░ 20%
│  │     └─ Task: handle_request [Cancelled]
│  └─ BackgroundJobs (Region-4) [Running] ██████████ 100%
│     ├─ Task: cleanup_expired [Pending]
```
