title: [EPIC] Epoch-Structured Concurrency
description:
# EPIC: Epoch-Structured Concurrency

**Bead ID:** asupersync-bsx
**Type:** EPIC
**Priority:** P1
**Status:** OPEN
**Owner:** Dicklesworthstone

---

## Vision

Epoch-Structured Concurrency introduces time-bounded operation windows into asupersync's distributed coordination model. Epochs are logical time boundaries that define when operations, symbols, and state are valid. This EPIC provides the foundation for coordinating distributed systems where nodes must agree on "what time it is" without relying on synchronized physical clocks.

The core abstraction is the `EpochId` - a monotonically increasing identifier that partitions time into discrete windows. Within an epoch, all operations share a consistent view of validity. When an epoch ends, all operations scoped to that epoch must complete or abort, enabling clean garbage collection of old state and preventing unbounded resource accumulation.

Epochs solve a fundamental problem in distributed systems: how to bound uncertainty. Without epochs, operations might wait indefinitely for responses that will never arrive. With epochs, every operation has a well-defined validity window, and the system can make progress by transitioning to new epochs rather than blocking forever on failed nodes.

This EPIC integrates epochs with asupersync's existing combinator infrastructure (`join`, `select`, `race`, `bulkhead`), making epoch-awareness a natural extension of the structured concurrency model rather than an additional concern.

---

## Goals

- **Define epoch primitives** (`EpochId`, `Epoch`, `EpochConfig`) that serve as logical time boundaries
- **Implement EpochBarrier** for synchronizing epoch transitions across participants
- **Implement EpochClock** for monotonic epoch progression with configurable duration
- **Integrate with combinators** making `join`, `race`, `select`, `bulkhead` epoch-aware
- **Support symbol validity windows** tying symbol lifetime to epoch ranges
- **Enable epoch-scoped operations** where all children in a combinator share epoch context
- **Provide clean epoch transitions** with automatic abort/cleanup when entering new epoch

---

## Non-Goals

- **Physical clock synchronization**: This is logical time, not wall-clock time
- **Distributed consensus on epoch transitions**: Epoch progression is leader-driven or pre-configured
- **Transaction isolation levels**: ACID semantics are a higher-level concern
- **Global epoch coordination**: Each region/cluster manages its own epoch sequence
- **Persistence of epoch state**: Durable epoch tracking is external to this layer

---

## Child Beads

| ID | Title | Status | Priority | Description |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------------|
| asupersync-573 | Implement Epoch Model Types and EpochBarrier | OPEN | P1 | Core epoch types, barrier synchronization, epoch clock |
| asupersync-2vt | Integrate Epochs with Existing Combinators | OPEN | P1 | Epoch-aware join, race, select, bulkhead |
| asupersync-ups | Comprehensive Epoch Tests | OPEN | P2 | Integration tests for epoch behavior |

---

## Phases

### Phase 1: Core Epoch Types
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `EpochId` with monotonic ordering and arithmetic
- `Epoch` with metadata (start time, duration, configuration)
- `EpochConfig` with configurable epoch duration and grace periods
- `EpochClock` for epoch progression with callbacks
- `SymbolValidityWindow` tying symbols to epoch ranges

**Exit Criteria:**
- Epoch IDs can be compared, incremented, and serialized
- EpochClock advances epochs deterministically
- Validity windows correctly identify valid/expired epochs

### Phase 2: EpochBarrier and Synchronization
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `EpochBarrier` for multi-participant synchronization
- Barrier wait with timeout
- Epoch transition callbacks
- Integration with budget/deadline system

**Exit Criteria:**
- All participants must arrive before barrier releases
- Late arrivals after epoch transition are handled correctly
- Barriers integrate with cancellation

### Phase 3: Combinator Integration
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `EpochScope` wrapper for epoch-bounded operations
- `EpochJoin`, `EpochRace`, `EpochSelect` variants
- Automatic epoch propagation through combinator trees
- Graceful cleanup when epoch expires mid-operation

**Exit Criteria:**
- All combinators correctly handle epoch boundaries
- Operations abort cleanly when epoch expires
- Nested combinators inherit epoch context

---

## Success Criteria

1. **Epoch Monotonicity**: EpochId always increases, never goes backward
2. **Barrier Correctness**: All N participants must arrive before any are released
3. **Validity Enforcement**: Operations outside their epoch window fail with clear errors
4. **Combinator Compatibility**: All existing combinator semantics preserved, epoch awareness additive
5. **Clean Transitions**: No resource leaks when operations abort at epoch boundary
6. **Determinism**: Same epoch progression with same seed produces identical behavior
7. **Latency Bounded**: Epoch transition overhead <1ms

---

## Dependencies

### Depends On
- **asupersync-0vx** (Foundation Layer) - Symbol types for validity windows
- `src/combinator/` - Existing join, race, select, bulkhead implementations
- `src/cx/` - Execution context for epoch propagation
- `src/types/id.rs` - Base `Time` type

### Blocks
- **asupersync-y1p** (Distributed Regions) - Uses epochs for state versioning
- **asupersync-zfn** (Symbolic Obligations) - Uses epoch windows for obligation validity
- **asupersync-k0c** (Distributed Trace) - Uses epoch IDs in trace correlation
- **asupersync-9mq** (Integration) - Epoch-aware unified API

---

## Acceptance Criteria Checklist

### Epoch Model Types and EpochBarrier (asupersync-573)
- [ ] `EpochId` with `GENESIS`, `next()`, comparison operators
- [ ] `Epoch` with start time, duration, metadata
- [ ] `EpochConfig` with configurable duration, grace period, max participants
- [ ] `EpochClock` with `current()`, `advance()`, tick-based progression
- [ ] `EpochBarrier` with `wait()`, `try_wait()`, `timeout_wait()`
- [ ] Barrier synchronization: all-or-nothing semantics
- [ ] `SymbolValidityWindow` with start/end epochs and validity checking
- [ ] `EpochTransitionCallback` trait for custom transition logic
- [ ] Metrics for epoch transitions and barrier waits

### Integrate Epochs with Existing Combinators (asupersync-2vt)
- [ ] `EpochScope<F>` wrapper that bounds future to epoch
- [ ] `EpochJoin` that aborts all children when epoch expires
- [ ] `EpochRace` that completes or aborts at epoch boundary
- [ ] `EpochSelect` with epoch-aware branch selection
- [ ] `with_epoch()` extension method for any future
- [ ] Epoch context propagation through combinator trees
- [ ] Automatic cleanup of resources when epoch expires
- [ ] `epoch_deadline()` combining epoch boundary with budget deadline
- [ ] Error types: `EpochExpired`, `EpochMismatch`

### Test Suite (asupersync-ups)
- [ ] Epoch progression tests
- [ ] Barrier synchronization tests with various participant counts
- [ ] Combinator epoch boundary tests
- [ ] Validity window tests
- [ ] Determinism tests
- [ ] Performance benchmarks for epoch overhead

---

## Epoch Lifecycle

```
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                        Epoch N                                  │
     │                                                                 │
     │  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐       │
     │  │   Operation   │  │   Operation   │  │   Operation   │       │
     │  │   (valid)     │  │   (valid)     │  │   (valid)     │       │
     │  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘       │
     │                                                                 │
     │        Symbols valid: EpochId(N-1) to EpochId(N+1)             │
     │                                                                 │
─────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────
                                    │
                                    ▼ EpochBarrier (all participants arrive)
                                    │
─────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────
     │                        Epoch N+1                                │
     │                                                                 │
     │  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐                          │
     │  │   Operation   │  │   Operation   │  Operations from N       │
     │  │   (valid)     │  │   (valid)     │  now ABORTED             │
     │  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘                          │
     │                                                                 │
     │        Symbols valid: EpochId(N) to EpochId(N+2)               │
     │        Symbols from N-1 now EXPIRED                            │
     │                                                                 │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Combinator Integration Pattern

```rust
// Before: Standard join (not epoch-aware)
let (a, b) = cx.join(
    async { do_work_a().await },
    async { do_work_b().await },
).await?;

// After: Epoch-aware join
let (a, b) = cx.epoch_join(
    epoch_id,
    async { do_work_a().await },
    async { do_work_b().await },
).await?;
// If epoch expires before both complete:
// - Both operations are cancelled
// - EpochExpired error returned
// - No partial results

// Extension method style
let result = some_future
    .with_epoch(epoch_id)
    .await?;
```

---

## Risk Assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------------|--------|------------|
| Epoch transition storms during high load | Medium | High | Rate limiting on transitions, grace periods |
| Barrier deadlock from missing participant | Medium | High | Timeout-based barrier with configurable behavior |
| Combinator behavior surprise at epoch boundary | Medium | Medium | Clear documentation, explicit opt-in for epoch awareness |
| Epoch clock drift in distributed scenarios | Low | Medium | Clock synchronization advisory, not enforced |
| Too-short epochs cause constant abortion | Medium | Medium | Configurable minimums, adaptive epoch duration |

title: Browser storage host reads bypass value and cache quotas
description:
BrowserStorageAdapter::get and get_async authorize StorageRequest::get with value_len=0, then sync_entry_cache unconditionally clones and inserts host-returned values. A host backend can therefore return a value above max_value_bytes, populate more than max_entries, and drive used_bytes above max_total_bytes; the calls still return Ok and their telemetry records Allowed. Example: a Get-only cap with max_value=4, max_total=8, max_entries=1 can cache host entries (n,a)=5 bytes and (n,b)=1 byte, ending at 10 tracked bytes and two entries.

Impact is an in-process explicit capability/resource-bound bypass with extra clone amplification. This does not prove host-wide quota across restarts, and practical usize counter corruption is not claimed.

Fix direction: validate Some(host_value) before mutating cache, reuse a checked quota projection for value/entry/total limits, preserve prior cached state on denial, and record the observed value length in denial telemetry. None may remove a cached entry. Add sync and async regressions for oversized value, total-byte and entry-count overflow, boundary-equal acceptance, replacement accounting, unchanged cache on denial, and precise reason/value-length telemetry.

description:
# Fix UnixDatagram Sync impl and refactor registration

## Investigation Summary

The `UnixDatagram` uses `Mutex<Option<IoRegistration>>` for interior mutability, which differs from tokio's approach where `PollEvented` handles registration internally without user-visible Mutex.

### Current Pattern (UnixDatagram, TcpListener, tcp/split.rs)
- `registration: Mutex<Option<IoRegistration>>` visible in struct
- Lock acquired on each async I/O operation

### Tokio Pattern (for reference)
- `io: PollEvented<mio::net::UnixDatagram>` - No Mutex needed
- Registration handled internally with separate read/write wakers

## Issue Analysis

1. **Not a safety bug**: Current code is memory-safe - std::os::unix::net::UnixDatagram is Send + Sync, and Mutex<T> is Send + Sync if T: Send.

2. **Performance concern**: Each async operation acquires the Mutex lock, causing contention in concurrent use.

3. **Pattern inconsistency**: This pattern is used across multiple socket types (UnixDatagram, TcpListener, tcp/split), suggesting need for a shared PollEvented or AsyncIo abstraction.

## Recommended Solution

Create a PollEvented<S: Source> wrapper that:
- Handles registration internally
- Maintains separate read/write wakers for concurrent operations
- Can be shared via Arc without external Mutex

## Relationship to Phase 2

This refactoring aligns with asupersync-90l9 (Phase 2: Real Async I/O Reactor). Recommend implementing PollEvented as part of Phase 2, then refactoring all socket types.

# Codec Framework

## Overview
Bidirectional encoding/decoding with framing support.

## Core Traits

### Decoder
```rust
pub trait Decoder {
    type Item;
    type Error;
    fn decode(&mut self, src: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<Option<Self::Item>, Self::Error>;
}
```

### Encoder
```rust
pub trait Encoder<Item> {
    type Error;
    fn encode(&mut self, item: Item, dst: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
}
```

## Standard Codecs

### 1. LinesCodec
- Newline-delimited text
- Configurable max line length

### 2. LengthDelimitedCodec
- Length-prefixed framing
- Configurable length field (u8, u16, u32, u64)
- Big/little endian

### 3. BytesCodec
- Raw bytes passthrough

### 4. AnyDelimiterCodec
- Custom delimiter support

## Framed Transport

### FramedRead<T, D>
- Combines AsyncRead + Decoder
- Implements Stream

### FramedWrite<T, E>
- Combines AsyncWrite + Encoder
- Implements Sink

### Framed<T, U>
- Full duplex codec transport
- Stream + Sink

## Cancel-Safety
- Decode: partial frame preserved in buffer
- Encode: atomic frame writes
- Framed: tracks partial state

## Bytes Integration
- bytes::Bytes and BytesMut
- Zero-copy where possible

title: Epic: DPOR & Formal Verification Tooling (Phase 5)
description:
# Epic: DPOR & Formal Verification Tooling (Phase 5)

## Overview

This epic implements Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR) for systematic schedule exploration, plus integration with formal verification tools like TLA+. Together, these provide high-assurance testing of concurrent code.

## Background & Context

The Asupersync roadmap defines Phase 5 as 'DPOR + TLA+ tooling'. This is the capstone of the testing story:

- **Phase 0-1**: Lab runtime with deterministic scheduling
- **Phase 2-4**: Oracles, chaos testing, distributed simulation
- **Phase 5**: Systematic exploration to find ALL bugs

## The Problem

Random testing (even with many seeds) can miss bugs:
- Some interleavings are rare
- Bug-triggering schedules may never be sampled
- No coverage guarantees

DPOR solves this: systematically explore distinct schedules, pruning equivalent ones.

## What is DPOR?

Dynamic Partial Order Reduction:
1. **Run program** with one schedule
2. **Identify races**: places where different orders give different results
3. **Backtrack**: try alternative orders at race points
4. **Prune**: skip schedules equivalent to already-explored ones

Result: explore O(races) schedules instead of O(n!) interleavings.

## Key Concepts

### Happens-Before Relation
Events a and b are **independent** if:
- Different threads/tasks
- Don't access same memory
- Commuting operations

Independent events can be reordered without changing outcome.

### Mazurkiewicz Traces
Equivalence classes of executions under independent event reordering.
DPOR explores one representative per equivalence class.

### Backtracking
When a race is found:
1. Save state at the decision point
2. Continue current exploration
3. Later, restore state and try alternative

## Architecture

```
ScheduleExplorer
├── ExecutionTree         # Tree of explored schedules
├── RaceDetector          # Identifies happens-before violations
├── BacktrackSet          # Pending alternative schedules
├── StateCheckpoint       # Snapshot for backtracking
├── CoverageTracker       # What's been explored
└── ReportGenerator       # Bug reports with replay traces
```

## Relationship to Existing Code

The codebase already has scaffolding:
- src/lab/explorer.rs: ScheduleExplorer, CoverageMetrics
- src/lab/oracle.rs: Invariant verification
- src/trace/: Trace capture and replay

Phase 5 completes these into a working DPOR implementation.

## TLA+ Integration

TLA+ is a formal specification language. Integration options:
1. **Export traces**: Convert Asupersync traces to TLA+ format
2. **Check traces**: Verify traces satisfy TLA+ spec
3. **Import specs**: Generate test harnesses from TLA+ specs

## Success Criteria

- DPOR explores schedules systematically
- Provably covers all distinct interleavings (up to equivalence)
- Finds bugs that random testing misses
- Reasonable performance (< 1min for small programs)
- TLA+ traces can be verified against specs
- Clear bug reports with replay instructions

## Dependencies

This epic BLOCKS on:
- bd-1j64: Runtime Core Maturity (stable lab runtime)
- bd-z6qn: Lab/production determinism parity

## References

- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 7.3: Schedule Exploration
- 'Partial-Order Methods for the Verification of Concurrent Systems' (Godefroid)
- 'Dynamic Partial-Order Reduction for Model Checking Software' (Flanagan & Godefroid)
- Loom library for Rust (inspiration, not dependency)

## Non-Goals

- Real-time model checking (too slow)
- Full TLA+ model checker (use existing TLC)
- Verification of arbitrary Rust code (focus on Asupersync programs)

title: QUIC managed endpoint: coalesced 1-RTT after route publish dropped, address_validated from first packet only, bad trailing packet voids datagram; keys never discarded (RFC 9001 4.9)
description:
## Findings (read-only review of 302e1d2da, SapphireHill subagent, 2026-09-28, origin 17f130960). No HIGH/MEDIUM; these are LOW.
The review confirmed: the coalesced request is retained under the existing 1024-packet / 2 MiB budget and dropped on failed or displaced admissions; the final Handshake-space ACK is ACK-only, sent once and within the amplification credit; the route is published only after the socket commits the ACK; the native test fails without the retention.

1. The router drops a coalesced 1-RTT packet once the route is published (src/net/quic_native/connection_manager.rs ~696-737: non-OneRtt routing returns Routed with no outgoing packets). If the single final ACK is lost, the client's Finished retransmission carries 1-RTT data that is discarded. For server admissions final_handshake_flight is empty, so nothing re-ACKs. Recovery comes from HANDSHAKE_DONE and client resends: extra latency, no data loss. Fix: after the handshake-only branch, split at the long packet's Length and route the short-header remainder through the 1-RTT path.
2. address_validated is derived from the datagram's FIRST packet only (managed_endpoint.rs ~431). A client datagram [Initial ACK][Handshake Finished][1-RTT] leaves it false. The 2d7843fdd displacement (evicting automatic, unvalidated admissions) can then evict a handshake whose TLS already completed during the ACK-commit wait. Fix: set it from any authenticated Handshake packet, for example when handshake_recv_packet_numbers[1] is non-empty.
3. One bad later packet voids the whole datagram after TLS consumed an earlier one (handshake_driver.rs ~1077 returns Err; managed_endpoint.rs ~413-420 turns it into Ok(())). [Handshake(Finished)][forged long packet] skips received_packets, the retained request and the final ACK, and the admission then publishes with no ACK. [Initial(ClientHello)][0-RTT] fails with unexpected_long_packet_type on every resend, so the client never connects (unlikely: no session tickets are issued). Fix: after an earlier packet authenticates, skip an unauthenticated or unsupported later packet the way a stale one is skipped.

Outside the diff, not further reviewed: the server never discards its Initial/Handshake keys (discard_keys is called only from tests), contrary to RFC 9001 section 4.9. Initial keys are derivable by anyone who observes the client's first DCID, so accepting Initial packets after the handshake leaves an on-path injection surface (for example a forged Initial CONNECTION_CLOSE). Worth its own check.
close_reason: Resolved in 168379675: routed coalesced 1-RTT, validated address from any authenticated Handshake packet, and protected authenticated datagrams from trailing invalid packets.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Landed in commit 168379675:
1. Coalesced 1-RTT packet extraction in ConnectionRouter (RFC 9000 §12.2): When a coalesced datagram with long-header and short-header (1-RTT) is received on a published route, decode prefix and route remaining short-header bytes through the 1-RTT pipeline rather than dropping them.
2. Address validation on any authenticated handshake packet (RFC 9000 §8.1): PendingAuthenticatedAccept derives address_validated from header.packet_type == LongPacketType::Handshake || self.driver.has_authenticated_handshake_packet().
3. QuicHandshakeDriver::drive_receive: Ignore trailing unauthenticated/invalid follower packets once preceding packets in the datagram have authenticated and advanced TLS state.

title: [replay-determinism + perf] raptorq/offline_tuner.rs: ambient SystemTime::now in benchmark_timestamp + std HashMap with default hasher across hot paths
description:
src/raptorq/offline_tuner.rs has THREE clusters of ambient/non-deterministic patterns that compound into a single fix bead:

  Cluster A — ambient wall-clock leak (line 349):
    benchmark_timestamp: format!("{:?}", std::time::SystemTime::now()),
    The OfflineTuner emits a profile pack manifest with a wall-clock-derived timestamp string. Two replays of the same tuning run produce different manifests (and thus different content hashes) even when the underlying benchmark results are identical — defeating manifest deduplication and forcing CI artifact diffs to scrub the timestamp manually.

  Cluster B — ambient Instant::now (line 769):
    let start = Instant::now();
    Used to time benchmark iterations. The duration ends up in the ProfilePack metadata, again breaking replay-determinism for any caller that hashes the metadata.

  Cluster C — std HashMap / HashSet with default hasher (lines 44, 360, 438, 478, 1069):
    use std::collections::HashMap;
    let mut candidate_scores: HashMap<String, f64> = HashMap::new();
    .collect::<std::collections::HashSet<_>>()
    let op_workloads: std::collections::HashSet<&str> = ...
    let mut candidate_ids = std::collections::HashSet::new();

  The candidate_scores HashMap is iterated to pick the optimal candidate (select_optimal_candidate at line 354). When two candidates score identically, HashMap iteration order — which is randomised per process — picks the winner. Two tuning runs against the same benchmark corpus produce different selected candidates on ties. The op_workloads / candidate_ids HashSets have similar ordering issues when their iteration drives subsequent collect() calls.

Combined effect: the OfflineTuner produces a non-replayable, non-deterministic profile pack. Operators trying to compare 'the same workload on two different commits' see noise that drowns the signal.

Fix direction:
  1. Replace SystemTime/Instant timing with replay-deterministic time sourced from the surrounding LabRuntime / Cx (or take a Time parameter). Where that is impossible (production-side tuner runs without a Cx), document the wall-clock dependency in a separate envelope field that is excluded from the deterministic content hash.
  2. Replace all three HashMap/HashSet sites with util::DetHashMap / DetHashSet (deterministic hasher, used elsewhere in the codebase).
  3. For tied-score selection, add an explicit tiebreaker (e.g., lex-smallest candidate name) so the choice is fully a function of the input.
  4. Audit any downstream consumer of OfflineTuner output that hashes the result — these will silently change after the fix lands (a deliberate consequence of restoring replay-determinism).

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/raptorq/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: OfflineTuner now sources benchmark_timestamp from a per-tuner clock anchor (with_clock_anchor) with wall_now fallback; HashMap/HashSet replaced with BTreeMap (sorted tiebreaker) + BTreeSet (sorted Vec emission) + DetHashSet (consistent hasher). Instant::now in measurement loop preserved (legitimate use). 2 regression tests + cargo check verified.

title: [SUB-EPIC] macOS Reactor (kqueue)
description:
# Sub-Epic: macOS Reactor (kqueue)

## Purpose

Implement a production-quality kqueue-based reactor for macOS and BSD systems. Important for developer experience since many developers use Macs.

## Background

### What is kqueue?

kqueue (kernel event queue) is the BSD/macOS event notification mechanism. Similar to epoll in goals, but different API and semantics.

Key syscalls:
- `kqueue()` - Create kqueue instance
- `kevent()` - Register interest and wait for events (combined operation)

### kqueue vs epoll

| Feature | epoll (Linux) | kqueue (BSD/macOS) |
|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| Level/Edge | Both, flag | Edge by default |
| Add/Wait | Separate calls | Combined in kevent() |
| Multiple events | No | Yes (one call) |
| Timer support | timerfd | Built-in |
| Signal support | signalfd | Built-in |

### Edge-Triggered Behavior

kqueue is edge-triggered by default:
- EV_CLEAR flag re-arms after delivery (like edge-triggered)
- Without EV_CLEAR, event is disabled after delivery (one-shot)

We'll use EV_CLEAR for persistent monitoring.

## Design

```rust
pub struct KqueueReactor {
    /// The kqueue file descriptor
    kq_fd: RawFd,
    /// Token slab and state
    inner: Mutex<KqueueInner>,
}

struct KqueueInner {
    wakers: TokenSlab,
    /// Track registered fds to prevent double-registration
    registrations: HashSet<(RawFd, i16)>, // (fd, filter)
}
```

## Key Differences from Epoll Implementation

1. **Combined register + wait**: kevent() does both
2. **Filters**: EVFILT_READ, EVFILT_WRITE (not flags)
3. **User data**: udata field for token (like epoll_event.data)
4. **Wakeup**: Use pipe or EVFILT_USER (macOS 10.6+)

## Platform Requirements

- macOS 10.6+ (for EVFILT_USER)
- Or FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFlyBSD

## Deliverables

1. KqueueReactor implementing Reactor trait
2. EVFILT_USER wakeup mechanism (or pipe fallback)
3. EV_CLEAR for persistent monitoring
4. Unit tests with real sockets
5. Cross-platform test coverage with Linux

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Feature parity with EpollReactor
- [ ] Works on macOS Ventura+
- [ ] Cross-thread wakeup reliable
- [ ] All epoll tests have kqueue equivalents

title: [security] util/arena.rs: ArenaIndex::new is pub — anyone can forge an ArenaIndex bypassing the capability-token contract on TaskId/RegionId/ObligationId
description:
src/util/arena.rs:24-29 — ArenaIndex::new(index: u32, generation: u32) is fully pub const fn:

  #[inline]
  #[must_use]
  pub const fn new(index: u32, generation: u32) -> Self {
      Self { index, generation }
  }

ArenaIndex is the substrate for capability tokens across the runtime — TaskId, RegionId, ObligationId all wrap an ArenaIndex (see types/typed_symbol.rs and the from_arena constructors on TaskId/RegionId/ObligationId). The whole point of these tokens is that holding one is a capability: only the runtime should mint them, and consumers should be able to assume that a TaskId in their possession came from a successful insert into the corresponding arena.

With pub const fn new, anyone — including a chain of safe transformations starting from completely unrelated u32 inputs — can synthesise an ArenaIndex pointing at any (index, generation) pair. Combined with the public Arena::get / Arena::get_mut, this lets a caller probe the arena for arbitrary slots and obtain references to whichever happens to share that (index, generation) — bypassing the ledger machinery that normally gates access through legitimate task/region creation.

Reachable via: any safe code that has a u32 (e.g., parsed from a wire payload, derived from user input, read from a config file) can call ArenaIndex::new(parsed_u32, parsed_u32) and feed the result into a public RuntimeState API that expects 'a TaskId from our arena'. There is no signing, MAC, or per-runtime nonce baked into ArenaIndex.

Fix direction:
  1. Restrict the constructor: pub(crate) const fn new — only crate-internal code (the arena itself and the typed-token wrappers) can construct one.
  2. Optionally add a runtime-instance fingerprint (e.g., a u64 nonce derived from runtime entropy at startup) to ArenaIndex and check it on every Arena::get/get_mut/remove call. This converts the integrity check from 'index/generation match' to 'index/generation/fingerprint match' and forecloses cross-runtime / forged-from-zero attacks.
  3. Audit every #[cfg(test)] use of ArenaIndex::new to confirm tests still compile after restricting visibility, since several test helpers in obligation_table.rs and region_table.rs construct fake ArenaIndex(99,0) intentionally.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/util/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: DEFERRED — needs sweeping rename. ArenaIndex::new is forge-able but making it pub(crate) breaks ~792 call sites across src/ and tests/. Per-batch scope; filed for separate sweep with sealed-wrapper design.

title: [runtime-state] runtime/timer.rs: TimerHeap has no per-task cancel and no rescheduling dedup — cancelled / rescheduled tasks accumulate stale entries that fire spurious wakeups and consume heap memory
description:
src/runtime/timer.rs — TimerHeap exposes `insert(task, deadline)`, `pop_expired(now)`, `peek_deadline`, and `clear()`. There is NO method to cancel a single (task, deadline) entry. Every other primitive must drain the heap entirely or live with stale entries.

Two failure modes flow from this:

  (a) **Reschedule duplicates accumulate.** When a task extends or shortens its deadline (a routine pattern in cancel-aware futures, especially Sleep::with_time_getter or any Cx::with_deadline change), the call site does:
      timer_heap.insert(task, new_deadline);
      // The OLD entry is still in the heap.
  Each reschedule adds one entry without removing the previous one. Long-lived tasks that reschedule every poll (e.g., a slowly-growing read deadline) accumulate one entry per reschedule. The heap's BinaryHeap implementation is O(N) memory in the number of inserts, NOT in the number of live timers.

  (b) **Cancelled-task wakeups fire spuriously.** When a task is cancelled (region close, Cx cancellation, dropped future), the timer entry stays in the heap until pop_expired drains it at the deadline. The expired wakeup then fires a Waker that targets a task that no longer exists. Wake is normally idempotent so this is harmless, BUT:
    - It consumes one waker.wake() call per stale entry, adding latency to the reactor's dispatch loop.
    - It increments wakers_dispatched stats, polluting telemetry.
    - It triggers a poll on the (zombie) task that immediately returns Ready(Cancelled), wasting scheduler tick budget.

  (c) **Memory leak under sustained reschedule pressure.** A task that reschedules 1000 times before any deadline expires accumulates 1000 entries. With u64 generation counter at line 43, the only bound is the ticking of pop_expired — which only drains entries whose deadline <= now. Until ALL the stale entries' deadlines arrive, they stay in the heap.

The Ord impl at lines 17-30 already includes a `generation` field that tiebreaks equal deadlines, suggesting the original author considered uniqueness across reschedules but did not implement removal.

Fix direction:
  1. Add a `cancel(&mut self, task: TaskId)` method that walks the heap removing all entries for the task. O(N) per cancel; acceptable for the cancel cold path.
  2. Better: switch from BinaryHeap to an indexed binary heap (e.g., keyed_priority_queue crate or hand-rolled `HashMap<TaskId, heap_index>`) so cancel is O(log N).
  3. For reschedule: provide a `reschedule(task, new_deadline)` that updates the existing entry in place rather than inserting a duplicate.
  4. Add a regression test: schedule the same task with three different deadlines, call pop_expired with now between the second and third deadline, assert exactly ONE TaskId is returned (not three duplicates of the same task).

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/runtime/io_op.rs + timer.rs + io_driver.rs (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in commit 223f479da: TimerHeap now uses per-task generation map. insert bumps generation (dedup); cancel removes the per-task entry (silence). pop_expired_into skips stale entries via generation comparison. 5 regression tests cover dedup, cancel, re-arm, reschedule-storm-1000, multi-task independence.

title: [ALIEN][TRACE][GEO] Exact solver for bounded traces (A*/IDA*)
description:
## Purpose

Compute *optimal* minimum-switch linear extensions for bounded traces.

This is used for:
- small counterexamples
- producing canonical minimal-entropy replay traces

## Algorithm sketch

State = set of executed nodes + current owner.
- Available set = minimal elements not yet executed.
- Transition = pick one available node.
- Cost = +1 if owner changes.

Use A* or IDA*:
- g = switches so far
- h = admissible lower bound on remaining switches (e.g., 0; or count of distinct owners remaining minus 1 in best case, carefully bounded)

## Determinism

- Priority queue ordering is deterministic: (f,g,tie_break).
- tie_break uses event key and stable owner ordering.

## Acceptance criteria

- For small n (e.g., n<=30 configurable), solver returns a schedule with cost <= Foata-flatten cost.
- Proof-by-check: returned schedule is a linear extension.
- Exhaustive test on tiny traces: compare solver output cost to brute force enumeration for n<=10.
close_reason: A* exact solver implemented in src/trace/geodesic.rs. All 3 acceptance criteria met: (1) exact_search for n<=30 returns optimal schedule via A* with admissible heuristic, (2) is_valid_linear_extension proof-by-check validates output, (3) brute_force_min_switches exhaustive test passes for n=10 two-chain trace. 12 tests pass.

title: [perf] runtime/scheduler/worker.rs: seen_io_tokens HashSet grows unbounded — memory leak proportional to lifetime I/O sources
description: src/runtime/scheduler/worker.rs:52,109,164 Worker::seen_io_tokens is a HashSet<u64> seeded with capacity 32 and inserted-into on every distinct I/O token observed in drive_io_phase. There is NO eviction. For a long-running process (a SaaS server with hours/days of uptime) the set grows monotonically with the cumulative count of distinct tokens registered with the reactor — every TCP connection's read token, every file descriptor, every timer wakeup, every unique poll handle. Even at 24 bytes/entry (HashSet overhead + u64) and 100k tokens/day, that's 2.4 MB/day per worker × N workers leaked silently. The dedup intent (only emit io_requested trace event once per token) is correct, but the unbounded set is a memory regression. Mitigation: (a) bounded LRU (the trace dedup tolerates re-emission of an old token's first-sight event after eviction); (b) move dedup to the IoDriver where token lifetime is bounded by deregister; (c) use a probabilistic structure like a Bloom filter sized to acceptable false-negative rate. Severity HIGH for long-running services; MEDIUM for short-lived processes.
close_reason: Bounded seen_io_tokens at MAX_SEEN_IO_TOKENS=65_536 with full-clear-on-overflow strategy. Worst-case footprint ~1.5 MiB per worker. 3 unit tests cover cap-trigger, dedup short-circuit, and constant regression guard. Commit 3d6bb2104.

title: [metamorphic-gap] codec/framed: missing exhaustive split-input invariance — encode N items, then split the resulting bytes at every byte position and feed split halves sequentially MUST emit all N items in order
description: src/codec/framed.rs and src/codec/framed_read.rs cover happy-path round-trip but lack the EXHAUSTIVE split-input invariance metamorphic property: for any encoded byte stream B = encode([item1, item2, ..., itemN]), splitting B at position k (for ALL valid k from 1 to B.len()-1) and feeding (B[..k], B[k..]) sequentially through poll_next MUST yield [item1, item2, ..., itemN] in order. This catches: (a) decoder state machine bugs where a partial-frame parse mutates state non-recoverably; (b) length-prefix bugs where the decoder consumes header bytes prematurely; (c) buffer-management issues where a sub-buffer carryover loses bytes between calls. length_delimited.rs has metamorphic_decoder_boundary_fragmentation_preserves_multi_frame_arrival_order which covers SOME splits, but not exhaustively across all positions. Recommend a proptest with 3-10 frames, exhaustive split-position iteration, asserting all frames emerge byte-identical to inputs. Severity HIGH for codec robustness on real network streams (TCP delivers data in arbitrary chunk sizes — every frame boundary IS a split point in production).
close_reason: Added mr_exhaustive_split_input_invariance: 4 frames, every split position 1..total_len, all frames byte-identical.

title: static_files serve_range returns 416 before checking If-None-Match precondition
description: src/web/static_files.rs:327 serve_range parses the Range header first (lines 352-369). When parse_ranges returns Err(InvalidSyntax) or Err(NotSatisfiable), the function returns 416 Range Not Satisfiable BEFORE evaluating the If-None-Match conditional at lines 378-387. RFC 9110 §13.2.2 requires preconditions (If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Range) to be evaluated before Range processing: 'An origin server that supports Range MUST evaluate the request preconditions before doing so.' Real impact: a client with a cached resource whose If-None-Match still matches but who sends a stale or malformed Range header gets 416 instead of 304, causing unnecessary full-body refetches and cache thrashing. Fix: read the file once, compute the ETag, evaluate If-None-Match, and only then parse the Range header. Add regression test: send Range: bytes=99999-100000 + If-None-Match matching the current ETag → expect 304 Not Modified, not 416.

title: [Kafka] consumer/producer Drop + facade hardening follow-ups (Findings 2-5 from fresh-eyes review)
description:
Fresh-eyes Kafka review follow-ups (Finding 1 = begin_transaction Active-wedge fixed separately in tx3wq9). All line numbers verified independently against HEAD.

FINDING 2 (CONFIRMED, primary): KafkaConsumer::Drop runs a blocking C poll loop on the executor thread. kafka_consumer.rs:711 Drop → leave_group_bounded (690) loops up to LEAVE_GROUP_DRAIN_POLLS=100 × consumer.poll(50ms) = ~5s of BLOCKING librdkafka polls on the DROPPING thread when a consumer with an active assignment is dropped WITHOUT close() (panic unwind, early ?-return, region teardown). In a no-tokio runtime the dropping thread is an executor worker, so every other task on that worker stalls (typ ~50-100ms; worst ~5s). close() (1895) offloads the identical leave_group_bounded via spawn_blocking_on_thread (1867); Drop cannot (can't await). FIX TRADEOFF: Drop can't await; a compat-safe option is to take() the Arc<BaseConsumer> and run leave_group_bounded on a detached std::thread — but that weakens the current 'group left before drop returns' guarantee on process-exit races. Needs a design decision, not a mechanical fix. Minimum: a doc comment acknowledging the executor-stall cost.

FINDING 3 (SUSPECTED, latent/facade): KafkaClient/TopicAwareConsumer use the DEFAULT ConsumerContext (KafkaContext, kafka.rs:188 impl ConsumerContext for KafkaContext {}) with NO leave_group_bounded and NO Drop — the exact un-hardened shape kafka_consumer.rs:556-565 documents as the infinite-close-hang root cause. Mitigated because KafkaConsumerTrait exposes no poll/consume, so this consumer is likely never assigned/driven, and KafkaClient has zero internal callers (public-API facade). Fix: give KafkaContext the fixed-protocol rebalance treatment like BrokerConsumerContext, or add a bounded-leave Drop.

FINDING 4 (SUSPECTED, narrow): transaction commit/abort soft-cancel can diverge local state from broker. kafka.rs:2259-2311 — region cancel during librdkafka commit_transaction: the background thread completes the commit (soft-cancel runs to completion, result discarded), but the wrapper future is dropped so mark_transaction_idle never runs → Transaction::Drop sets NeedsAbortRecovery → next begin's recover aborts an already-committed txn → spurious error. Low probability (cancel precisely during the commit round-trip). Genuine soft-cancel/exactly-once tension; behavior-sensitive.

FINDING 5 (SUSPECTED, minor): rebalance(cx, &[]) uses eager unassign() on a cooperative consumer. kafka_consumer.rs:1360-1376 — empty assignment → consumer.unassign() with no cooperative guard, whereas close() (1908-1923) guards RD_KAFKA_RESP_ERR__STATE on cooperative. With a cooperative-sticky consumer, rebalance(cx,&[]) returns a Broker(STATE) error. Manual deterministic-assignment API; limited impact. Fix: mirror close()'s cooperative-protocol guard.

Review VERIFIED SOUND (no bug): delivery callback→async bridge (parking_lot, no panic on callback thread), producer send/flush (non-blocking + checkpoint-bridged, no executor block), consumer poll (spawn_blocking_on_thread ≤50ms slices, bounded cancel latency, single-slot buffered_outcome not unbounded channel), transient UnknownTopicOrPartition/PartitionEOF handled as non-fatal, rebalance TOCTOU atomic under state lock, no lock inversion, no panic-on-broker-metadata.

Filed by SapphireHill.

title: Define independence relation I over TraceEvent labels
description:
# Independence Relation I over Trace Labels

## Purpose
DPOR and trace equivalence require a precise definition of which actions commute.

Independence is a relation `I ⊆ Label×Label` that is:
- symmetric
- irreflexive

Two adjacent actions can be swapped without changing observational meaning iff they are independent.

## Asupersync-Specific Independence Rules
We must define independence at the level of *semantic resources*:
- region IDs
- task IDs
- obligation IDs
- channel IDs (or similar)

Examples:
- actions in disjoint regions often commute
- `reserve(o)` does not commute with `commit(o)`/`abort(o)`
- `cancel(r, …)` does not commute with `spawn(r, …)`

## Acceptance Criteria
- The independence relation is explicit and implemented as a function:
  - `fn independent(a: &TraceEvent, b: &TraceEvent) -> bool`
- Unit tests cover key non-commuting and commuting pairs.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Macaroons for Decentralized Capability Attenuation
description: Asupersync's Cx capability context is a natural fit for Macaroons (§11.8) — bearer tokens with decentralized attenuation. Currently, Cx capabilities are checked at runtime but cannot be attenuated (restricted) without creating new Cx instances. Macaroons allow any holder to add caveats (restrictions) to a capability token without contacting the issuer. This enables: (1) Delegation with restriction — pass a capability to a child task with reduced authority, (2) Time-limited capabilities — add expiry caveats, (3) Context-dependent capabilities — add caveats that check runtime conditions. Implementation: Extend Cx with HMAC-based macaroon chains. Each caveat is a predicate checked at capability use time. Key papers: Birgisson et al. 2014 'Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats'. Acceptance criteria: (1) Cx capabilities support caveat chains, (2) Any task can attenuate (but not escalate) capabilities, (3) Caveat verification is O(n) in number of caveats, (4) Evidence ledger records capability checks and caveat evaluations.

title: io_uring multishot polls (ac01e7857 review): an outside final -ECANCELED disarms an edge registration for good; no lane builds the io-uring tests (skips report ok); orphaned multishot SQEs on submit failure; CQ overflow uncounted
description:
## Findings (read-only review of ac01e7857 by a SapphireHill subagent, 2026-10-01, at origin f4bcaba9c)

No correctness bug in the main multishot path. Impact limit: nothing in production src/ registers EDGE_TRIGGERED today; only tests and the conformance suite do.

1. (medium, medium-high confidence) An outside -ECANCELED on a live multishot poll leaves the registration permanently disarmed (src/runtime/reactor/io_uring.rs ~1970-1972, ~1984-1986, ~1996).
   - register submits the PollAdd from the calling thread (submit_poll_add ~1358), and io_uring ties a request to its submitting task.
   - When that thread exits (a short-lived block_on, test or blocking-pool thread), the kernel ends the poll at its next wakeup with a final -ECANCELED and no F_MORE.
   - The reactor sends ERROR, clears the active poll and does not queue a re-arm. An edge-triggered user that reads, gets WouldBlock and waits for the next edge without calling modify hangs.
   - Fix: the reactor never cancels its own active poll (modify swaps first; deregister unmaps first). So treat a final ECANCELED/ENOENT on the ACTIVE multishot poll as "ended": push it to ended_multishots, re-arm from the polling thread with the fd identity check, and do not report ERROR. One-shot polls already lose the same wakeup silently (~1986).

2. (medium, high) No automated lane runs the new tests.
   - scripts/main_watchdog.py maps modules only through `mod x;` lines and `#![cfg]`. The io-uring gate sits on inline `#[cfg(feature)] mod imp {` blocks (io_uring.rs ~18, ~4266), so targeted-lib runs runtime::reactor::uring with default features: the 5 cfg-off fallback tests only.
   - The conformance target also runs without io-uring, so every io_uring row collapses into one Skip.
   - The live tests' skip helpers (~2026-2049, ~3458-3470) return early, so on a host without io_uring every live test reports ok.
   - Fix: map io_uring.rs to the io-uring feature, or teach the mapper about inline cfg'd modules. Add a `--features io-uring,test-internals` lane for `--lib -- runtime::reactor::uring` and `--test conformance -- reactor`. Add an env flag such as ASUPERSYNC_REQUIRE_IO_URING=1 that turns a skip into a panic in that lane.

3. (low) The re-arm path is tested only by simulation. test_ended_multishot_poll_is_rearmed_and_keeps_delivering (~3786) feeds a fake final completion while the real poll is live. Swapping AsyncCancel back to PollRemove would not be caught either (the modify/deregister tests use idle sockets). Fix: a live test that overflows the CQ (more than 2x the CQ entries in writes without polling), then checks the re-arm and the next edge.

4. (low, low-medium confidence) Orphaned multishot polls are permanent. If the SQE push succeeds but ring.submit() fails (EBUSY with an overflow backlog on 5.x, ENOMEM for a new thread's context), the next poll() submits it, but register or the re-arm has already returned Err and never mapped its user_data. A multishot orphan lives until the reactor drops. It holds a file reference, so closing the fd does not close the socket and the peer never sees FIN. A failed AsyncCancel in deregister (`let _`) leaves the same orphan. Fix: once pushed, treat the request as committed (map user_data), or queue an AsyncCancel for it when submit fails.

5. (low) Dropped completions are not counted. poll() never reads the CQ overflow counter and does not handle EBADR. A dropped CQE (or, on 5.13-5.18, a failed F_MORE post that ends the multishot) leaves the registration marked armed forever. Fix: check completion().overflow() each poll; when it grows, re-arm every multishot poll and send a readiness hint.

## Verified sound by the same review
- user_data never reused (monotonic u64); post-deregister CQEs dropped; replaced multishot reserved until its final CQE; old CQEs filtered by the active-poll check.
- modify arms the new poll before cancelling the old (AsyncCancel, not PollRemove which can -EALREADY); overlap events dropped, not duplicated.
- No CQE storm on a level condition (5.19+ implies EPOLLET unless IORING_POLL_ADD_LEVEL); one-shot and EDGE|ONESHOT unchanged; the 6.1+ downgrade to one-shot is covered by the re-arm.
- Pre-5.13 kernels: EINVAL is cached as Unsupported, register returns ErrorKind::Unsupported, the conformance row reports Skip, inconclusive probes fail closed.
- The live redelivery test (~3618-3657) would fail without the fix; the quiet-window test shows no level storm.

title: gRPC legacy streaming (8ca9aead8): a request sink held at the response window ignores deadline and cancellation (hang); byte-unbounded response buffer; clone wakeups; pooled-unary LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of the legacy GrpcClient streaming transport (src/grpc/client/legacy_native.rs, the native paths in src/grpc/client.rs) added by 8ca9aead8 (br-asupersync-6pc7xg), on origin 8ca9aead8..7f6915855 (SapphireHill rc_20260923 audit agent, 10-09). No HIGH, no compile problem. Line numbers on origin/main 7f6915855.

## MEDIUM
M1. A request sink held at the response window ignores the call's deadline and cancellation (hang). legacy_native.rs drive(): when MAX_STREAM_BUFFERED (1024) responses are unread, a Sink poll returns Pending before polling the call. The deadline and cancel checks live only in the native gate() inside poll_event, so when the deadline timer or a cancel fires the fan-out waker, the sink wakes, hits the window check again and parks again. RequestSink::send / close never return; the task cannot finish its cancellation, so its region cannot close. Tests missed it: the lockstep and reader-task cases never fill the window and no streaming test checks a deadline. Fix: at the window, run the call's cancellation and deadline checks (no keepalive progress, no transport I/O) and end the call on error. Test: bidi call whose server pushes more than MAX_STREAM_BUFFERED responses, sender never reads, channel timeout or caller abort -> send returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED / CANCELLED; old code hangs.

M2. The response buffer is bounded by count, not bytes (legacy_native.rs drive window, push_back): during a bidi upload the sink decodes and keeps up to 1024 responses of up to max_recv_message_size (default 4 MiB) each, about 4 GiB per call. The native owner bounds retained DATA (body_limit) and lets HTTP/2 flow control push back; the legacy layer drains the owner, which returns window credit. Fix: bound by bytes (about one max_recv_message_size) or a small count. Test: client codec whose decoded value tracks live bytes in a counter; echo 256 KiB messages, send 64 without reading, assert the peak stays near 4 x 256 KiB (today about 16 MiB).

M3. Concurrent ResponseStream clones lose wakeups (Fanout keeps one waker slot per role; client.rs poll_native wakes only ResponseStreamState waiters, which the native path never registers). Two tasks each polling a clone: the second registration replaces the first, which is never woken, not even at the end. The in-memory ResponseStream supports multiple waiters, so this regresses clones. Fix: keep a small deduplicated list of Response wakers in Fanout, or register in ResponseStreamState waiters and wake them from the fan-out. Test: two tasks drain clones of an Echo stream that sends 2 messages then ends; both finish within LIMIT.

## LOW
L4. A unary call from a cancelled task closes every pooled connection (client.rs native_h2_unary/refresh/exchange): no up-front checkpoint; TcpStream::poll_read returns Interrupted under a cancelled Cx, so refresh() fails and drops each healthy pooled connection; a cancel during the first flush is labelled unprocessed and redials. Fix: checkpoint before taking from the pool; treat a cancelled Cx as return-to-pool + CANCELLED.
L5. The sink reports FAILED_PRECONDITION "native gRPC request slot is unavailable" instead of the server's status when the server's end arrives in the same read as a message (settle_request records nothing because status() is None). Fix: when the refusal leaves no status, drive the call to its end and return ended_call_status.
L6. Hardening: two fallbacks in legacy_native.rs use unwrap_or_else(Status::ok) (Ready(None) arm, poll_single_response). Unreachable today (both owners always record a final status) but should fall back to INTERNAL.
L7. Performance: any non-OK grpc-status classes the pooled unary connection as processed and drops it.

API note: into_native_* consume the client and only then refuse while a legacy call is alive; the client and channel are lost.

## Test gaps
Reuse tests pass even without refresh() (the GOAWAY case is rescued by the retry). Untested: 30 s idle expiry, cancel/deadline during reuse, PING while idle, the max_idle cap, reuse after an error status. Legacy tests never fill the response window, never poll clones concurrently, never test a streaming deadline. src/grpc/server/duplex/tests.rs lib unit tests have never run (lib-test OOM on the author's host).

Checked and sound: pool exclusivity, reusability classification, pool hygiene, streaming cleanup (no detached task; cancel/drop closes the dedicated connection), trailers-only handling, client-streaming 0/2+ responses -> INTERNAL, size limits both ways, deadline/cancel wakers registered through the fan-out, lock order (call state, then codec).

title: [fresh-eyes] raptorq/metamorphic_tests.rs: MR14 'idempotence' is actually monotonicity, accepts Err on extended symbol set, hides Ok->Err regression
description:
src/raptorq/metamorphic_tests.rs ~line 1320 — MR14 mr_decode_completion_idempotence accepts both Ok(same_block) AND Err(_) outcomes when more symbols are supplied. Comment admits 'more symbols should never make decode FAIL after fewer symbols succeeded. We allow it but don't require it.' This is monotonicity, not idempotence; a future regression where additional symbols cause decode to flip Ok→Err would silently pass MR14.

Fix: tighten the Err arm to prop_assert!(false, "MR14 violation: extended symbol set degraded decode from Ok to Err"). If transient solver instability is real (variable seeds), narrow the data-size/seed strategy until the property holds deterministically.

Test-only finding (no production-correctness impact). Filed at P4 because it weakens MR14's bug-detection power without leaving a wire-visible bug.

Fresh-eyes 14-day-diff audit by SapphireHill 2026-04-26.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ahead. Err arm of MR14 mr_decode_completion_idempotence now prop_assert!(false, ...) with detailed diagnostic; previously was a permissive no-op turning the property into monotonicity-pretending-to-be-idempotence. 17 metamorphic_tests pass; clippy --lib -D warnings clean. title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Unit and E2E tests for choreographic projection and codegen
description:
Comprehensive test suite for the choreographic programming pipeline (DSL -> projection -> codegen).

**Unit tests:**
(1) DSL parser correctness — roundtrip property: parse(pretty_print(ast)) == ast for randomly generated choreographies (proptest).
(2) Projection completeness — for each participant in a choreography, verify that the projected local type accounts for all messages the participant sends/receives.
(3) Deadlock-freedom verification — generated session types must be deadlock-free; verify by model-checking projected types against the global choreography.
(4) Knowledge-of-choice detection — verify that the compiler rejects choreographies where a participant makes a choice but affected participants are not notified (the 'knowledge of choice' problem).

**E2E tests:**
(5) End-to-end saga generation — take 5+ real saga protocols, compile through the full pipeline, execute with FrankenLab, and verify correct behavior under normal conditions.
(6) Fault injection on generated sagas — crash a participant mid-protocol; verify compensation handlers fire correctly and saga rolls back cleanly.
(7) Equivalence test — hand-written saga vs choreography-generated saga must produce identical outcomes across 100 random schedules (deterministic replay).
(8) Regression suite — golden output checksums for all generated code; any change to the compiler must update golden outputs with justification.

**Logging requirements:**
- Each test must log: choreography_name, participant_count, projection_step_count, generated_code_hash, execution_outcome.
- On projection failure, log the specific participant and message that caused the issue.
- On codegen equivalence failure, log both execution traces for diff analysis.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Parser roundtrip holds for 10,000 randomly generated choreographies.
- All 5+ real saga protocols generate correct, working code.
- Generated code matches hand-written equivalents in behavior.
- No deadlock detected in any generated protocol.

**Rust implementation notes:**
- Use proptest for grammar-aware fuzzing of the choreography DSL.
- Use trybuild for compile-fail tests (invalid choreographies should produce clear compiler errors).
- Use insta for snapshot testing of generated code.

title: Implement join_all combinator (N-way join)
description:
# join_all (N-way Join)

## Purpose
Provide an N-ary join combinator derived from the primitive join semantics (⊗):
- run all branches
- wait for all to complete
- aggregate outcomes under policy

This should be a thin, lawful layer on top of Phase 0 kernel primitives.

## Semantics
Given futures `f[0..n)`:
1. spawn each as a child in a subregion (or equivalent structured grouping)
2. await all join handles
3. aggregate outcomes according to policy (default: max severity)

## Requirements
- Must not abandon any branch.
- Must preserve region close = quiescence.
- Must be deterministic in lab runtime.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All branches complete before join_all returns.
- If policy is fail-fast, siblings are cancelled/drained as specified.
- No task leaks and no obligation leaks.

## Testing
- Unit test: 3 tasks complete, join_all returns aggregated result.
- E2E: one branch errors under fail-fast policy; others cancelled and drained.
close_reason: Implemented JoinAll combinator with marker struct, JoinAllResult, JoinAllError, make_join_all_result(), join_all_to_result(), and 20 comprehensive tests. All 33 join module tests pass.

title: [swarm-perf] Add signed profile bundle shadow-run rollout gate
description:
Background:
- The current signed profile bundle lane emits dry-run and verify artifacts, rollback receipts, and digest-only integrity checks, but it still lacks the default adoption wedge recommended by the alien graveyard and runtime ascension doctrine: shadow-run against the conservative baseline before any promotion.
- Massive swarm operators on 64+ core / 256 GiB hosts need a proof-carrying answer to: if we promoted this bundle, would it actually beat the conservative profile on the measured workload, and by how much on the metrics that matter?
- This bead adds that rollout gate without introducing live apply semantics or hidden mutable state.

Required design:
1. Extend the signed profile bundle execution posture with a shadow-run mode that compares the selected bundle against the conservative fallback profile on the same evidence snapshot.
2. Compile the result into deterministic operator artifacts: explicit promote-or-hold verdict, counterfactual loss/regret deltas, dominant reasons, and safe-fallback recommendation.
3. Keep the same artifact vocabulary and runner stack used by the current signed-profile bundle smoke contract; do not fork a second reporting dialect.
4. Preserve existing dry_run and verify behavior exactly unless the new shadow-run path is explicitly selected.
5. Default failure behavior is fail-closed: missing evidence, stale evidence, or no-win outcomes must hold the conservative profile and explain why.

Artifact expectations:
- Contract-backed scenario for a positive shadow-run win and a no-win hold scenario.
- Report fields for baseline profile, candidate profile, promote decision, loss deltas, regret margin, and hold reasons.
- Rollback receipt remains deterministic and must still reference the conservative fallback.

Proof / validation:
- rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check on touched Rust files.
- rch exec -- cargo test -p asupersync --test signed_profile_bundle_contract --features test-internals -- --nocapture
- bash -n scripts/run_signed_profile_bundle_smoke.sh
- bash scripts/run_signed_profile_bundle_smoke.sh --scenario <shadow-run-win> --dry-run
- bash scripts/run_signed_profile_bundle_smoke.sh --scenario <shadow-run-win> --execute
- bash scripts/run_signed_profile_bundle_smoke.sh --scenario <shadow-run-hold> --execute

Success criteria:
- Operators can evaluate a signed profile bundle in shadow-run mode and see a deterministic promote-or-hold verdict with counterfactual deltas against the conservative baseline, using the existing signed-profile bundle artifact surface and fail-closed semantics.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests cover shadow-run request parsing, baseline-vs-candidate loss calculation, promote decision, hold/no-win decision, missing evidence fail-closed, stale evidence fail-closed, host fingerprint mismatch fail-closed, unsupported controller version fail-closed, capacity-certificate mismatch rejection, manual override precedence, secret redaction, deterministic dominant-reason ordering, rollback receipt linkage, digest-only integrity limitation reporting, and disabled/no-runtime-impact behavior. Golden/snapshot coverage must pin at least one promote report and one hold report including baseline profile, candidate profile, fallback profile, candidate loss, baseline loss, regret margin, hold reasons, dominant reasons, capacity certificate reference, child proof hashes, artifact paths, rollback receipt path, sanitized operator note, and projection hash. Deterministic e2e/script coverage must exercise scripts/run_signed_profile_bundle_smoke.sh with --list plus shadow-run-win and shadow-run-hold scenarios in dry-run and execute modes, logging scenario ID, contract version, host fingerprint, CPU/core count, RAM budget, candidate profile ID, baseline profile ID, worker-count sweep, agent-count sweep, evidence artifact IDs/hashes, p50/p95/p99 wake-to-run latency, throughput, queue depth, cancellation debt, memory pressure, brownout risk, candidate loss, baseline loss, regret margin, promote-or-hold verdict, fallback/no-win reason, rollback receipt path, generated artifact paths, exact rch command, and final pass/fail operator verdict. The runner must fail closed if the shadow-run path only emits a recommendation without a baseline comparison, if the report omits rollback/fallback fields, if digest-only limitations are hidden, or if repeated runs produce different projection hashes for the same scenario. - conformal_binary_upper_bound (l227) returns conformal_quantile() of BINARY {0.0,1.0} novelty scores, so conformal_upper_bound is ALWAYS exactly 0.0 or 1.0 (or 1.0 when uncalibrated).
- target_met = conformal_upper_bound <= target_residual_rate, where target_residual_rate = 1 - target_coverage in (0,1).
- => target_met always reduces to (bound == 0.0): 0.0<=r is always true (r>0), 1.0<=r always false (r<1). Independent of the specific target_coverage value.
- recommended_additional_runs / target_reached_after_existing_hits (l269) have the same degeneracy (bound 0/1 vs 1-target_coverage).
- NET: estimate_from_*(.. target_coverage=0.5) and (.. target_coverage=0.9999) produce IDENTICAL target_met / recommended_additional_runs given the same data + alpha. The real convergence criterion is governed solely by alpha (via the conformal quantile rank ceil((1-alpha)(n+1)) landing in the zeros region).

EVIDENCE: every test asserts conformal_upper_bound in {0.0,1.0} (l314,342,361); no test varies target_coverage independently of alpha on fixed data, so the defect is uncaught. The tests even set target_coverage = 1-alpha (config 0.20/0.80), conflating the two.

WHY IT MATTERS: target_coverage is a prominent ExplorationBudgetConfig::new(alpha, target_coverage) knob and the field doc says 'target_met: True when the conformal bound is at or below the target residual rate' — implying it is an active threshold. A configurable parameter that silently does nothing is a footgun.

FIX OPTIONS (owner's call — statistical-method change, not done unilaterally):
(a) Make the bound GRANULAR: replace the binary conformal quantile with a finite-sample upper confidence bound on the novelty PROPORTION at confidence 1-alpha (e.g. Clopper-Pearson exact, or empirical-Bernstein / Hoeffding p_hat + sqrt(ln(1/alpha)/(2n))), then compare against target_residual_rate. This makes target_coverage meaningful and keeps finite-sample validity.
(b) If the binary conformal stopping rule is intentional, REMOVE target_coverage (or document it as metadata only) and drive convergence purely from alpha, so the API doesn't imply an inert threshold.

Code is otherwise mechanically sound (conformal quantile rank/infinity guards, count->flag reconstruction order-insensitivity, edge cases all correct).

title: Implement Tower feature flag and optional dependency
description:
## Overview

Make Tower integration optional via feature flag to avoid mandatory dependencies.

## Requirements

### Feature Flag
```toml
# Cargo.toml
[features]
default = []
tower = ["dep:tower", "dep:tower-service"]

[dependencies]
tower = { version = "0.4", optional = true }
tower-service = { version = "0.3", optional = true }
```

```rust
// src/tower/mod.rs
#![cfg(feature = "tower")]

mod adapter;
mod service;

pub use adapter::{AsupersyncAdapter, TowerAdapter};
```

```rust
// src/lib.rs
#[cfg(feature = "tower")]
```

title: Fix hanging test: sync::notify::tests::notify_one_wakes_waiter
description:
The test notify_one_wakes_waiter hangs indefinitely. The test uses thread::spawn with a 50ms sleep before calling notify_one(). After joining the thread, the second poll should return Ready but it appears the test hangs after the first poll returns Pending correctly.

Investigation shows:
1. First poll registers waiter with noop_waker, returns Pending ✓
2. Thread sleeps 50ms, calls notify_one()
3. notify_one() sets notified=true, takes waker, calls wake() (noop)
4. Main thread joins (wait for thread completion)
5. Second poll checks notified flag - should return Ready

Needs investigation into why the test hangs at step 4 or 5.
notes: Fixed deadlock in Notified::poll Waiting state - was calling cleanup() while holding waiters lock, but cleanup() also tries to acquire the lock. Restructured to release lock before calling cleanup.

title: Watch channel blocks worker threads via Condvar::wait_timeout
description: watch::Receiver::changed() at src/channel/watch.rs:335-377 uses std::sync::Condvar::wait_timeout(10ms) which blocks the calling OS thread. If called from async tasks on scheduler worker threads, this can cause throughput collapse or deadlock with small worker pools. Same pattern in sync/rwlock.rs and sync/barrier.rs. Need async-aware waiting (waker-based notification) instead of blocking. Found during code audit.
notes: Fixed: replaced Condvar::wait_timeout(10ms) with async waker-based notification in watch channel. Receiver::changed() now returns a ChangedFuture that implements Future instead of blocking the OS thread. Sender::send/send_modify/drop wake all registered wakers. WatchStream properly delegates to the future. 24 tests pass including 2 new async-aware tests (Pending→Ready after send, sender drop wakes). Conformance test updated to .await the future.

title: HTTP/1.1 client: POST on a pooled connection the server closed while idle always fails (no liveness check); early 413 lost on body write failure; Retry-After HTTP-date retries immediately
description:
Read-only audit of the HTTP/1.1 client (src/http/h1/http_client.rs, client.rs, client-side codec) at origin/main 2ad2e55c8 (2026-10-02, SapphireHill subagent). No high-severity framing or pool-desync defect was found. Item 1 is confirmed by reading and is being fixed; the rest are high-confidence code readings.

1. Idle pooled connections were reused without a liveness check. Fix in progress.
   - acquire_connection_with (~2369-2380) wrote straight onto a pooled idle connection. Recovery after a failure exists only for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/TRACE (~3072-3077, ~1716-1735). The pool's idle timeout defaults to 90 s; Node and Apache close idle keep-alive connections after 5 s.
   - POST, idle 10 s, server closes, POST again: the write succeeds, the read hits EOF, and the caller gets Io(UnexpectedEof, "connection closed before response headers"). It is not retried, and it happens every time.
   - A server's unsolicited `408 Request Timeout` + close on an idle connection was returned as the NEXT request's response.

2. A server's early response is lost when the request-body write fails.
   - Without Expect: 100-continue, client.rs ~822-827 writes the whole request before reading.
   - A server answering 413 + Connection: close after the head and closing gives Io(BrokenPipe/ConnectionReset), with the 413 unread. A server that answers before draining a large body can deadlock with the client until a timeout.
   - The Expect path already handles this (upload_error).

3. Retry-After given as an HTTP-date retries immediately. http_client.rs ~635 does retry_after_delay(..).unwrap_or(ZERO), and parse_retry_after_delta (~3094-3101) accepts digits only. So a 503 with "Retry-After: <date one hour ahead>" under retry_idempotent_statuses(3) gives 3 back-to-back retries. The rustdoc says a wait longer than 60 s returns the response instead.

4. A header-supplied Proxy-Authorization is dropped on a cross-origin redirect through a forward proxy (http targets; ~2081-2085, ~2110-2114, strip_sensitive_headers_on_redirect ~3258), so the second hop gets 407. https targets keep it (caller_proxy_authorization ~1922). The two are inconsistent.

5. obs-fold in responses is rejected (client.rs ~851-858, codec.rs ~517). RFC 9112 section 5.2 says a user agent replaces it with SP.

6. Relative Location values are not resolved per RFC 3986 section 5.2 (~3185-3199): `?page=2` from /list?page=1 gives /?page=2; `../login` is sent literally; `#x` gives the directory.

7. Any Upgrade header disables connection reuse (~3026-3031). Apache mod_http2 advertises `Upgrade: h2,h2c` on ordinary 200s, so every request opens a new connection. Performance only.

8. The chunked parser rejects whitespace before a chunk extension (codec.rs ~1246-1261; RFC 9112 BWS). This is deliberate anti-smuggling hardening; low priority for a client.

9. A restricted trailer field (Expires, Date, Vary, ...) fails an already complete response (client.rs ~1286-1288) and the body is lost.

10. An HTTP/1.0 response with Transfer-Encoding: chunked and keep-alive is decoded and pooled. RFC 9112 section 6.1 says treat the framing as faulty and close.

Minor:
- Expired idle sockets are closed only on the next acquire, so CLOSE_WAIT sockets can linger.
- PoolExhausted is returned at once instead of waiting (intended).
- Proxied and streaming requests bypass the pool.
- PUT and DELETE are not retried after a stale reuse (conservative).

The auditor found these sound: response framing (CL/TE conflicts, duplicates, digits-only CL, chunked strictness), bodyless responses, 1xx handling (with a cap), Expect: 100-continue, reuse decisions (read-until-close bodies never pooled, prefetched data fails closed, streaming responses never pooled), cancellation guards, deadline composition, pool lock order, redirect method and credential rules, header limits, CONNECT and SOCKS5, request encoding.
close_reason: done

title: WebSocket split review (r20): a retried recv never flushes a retained Close (peer sees 1006); close() budget counts retained bytes (v0.4.3 regression); a discarded committed frame tail corrupts framing
description:
Read-only review (SapphireHill e8 round r20, 10-10) of the API lane's d4f3b61b1 and f926d654b (WebSocket split halves) at origin fbb67e5f6; full report /data/tmp/rc_20260923/audit_r20/B1_websocket_split.md. Neither commit was compiled or run when it landed. Permit FIFO, cancellation registration, lock discipline and single-Close-on-the-wire are sound.

MEDIUM:
- W1. The read half never resumes a retained Close flush (split.rs ~689-692: flush_control ignores close_flush_pending; ~817-833; ~861-865: is_closed returns Ok(None)). If recv is dropped or cancelled while flushing our Close, a retried recv returns Ok(None) (crossing case) or parks until EOF (echo case): our Close is never written and the peer sees 1006; Message::Close is never delivered. The unsplit recv flushes write_buf at the top of every loop.

LOW:
- W2 (regression from v0.4.3). The split close() budget check counts retained write_buf bytes (split.rs ~1153-1166): a retained DATA tail plus the Close exceeds max_pending_write_bytes, so close() returns OutboundBufferFull (Wait) or force-closes without a Close (CloseWithTryAgainLater). v0.4.3 flushed the tail first.
- W3 (pre-existing, 1fde5c571). A committed frame tail is discarded when the tail budget check fails after a partial write (split.rs ~431-440) while the reader appended an echo: part of the frame is on the wire, the echo follows it, and the peer parses the echo as payload (framing corrupted).
- W4 (pre-existing). Control frames (ping(), heartbeat Ping, pongs) can follow our Close; the fence covers DATA only.
- Test gaps: no test retries through recv; no close() with a non-empty retained write_buf; the close_flush_pending empty-buffer guard is unexercised.

title: quic_native stream reassembly keeps one heap slice per STREAM frame: tiny in-order frames cost ~50-100 B resident per credited byte (memory amplification; split from dvdvyi)
description:
## Defect (split from dvdvyi; source-audited at origin 0314a6752, SapphireHill)
src/net/quic_native/streams.rs keeps received STREAM data per contiguous run as `RecvRun { pieces: VecDeque<Bytes>, len }`, one `Bytes` per received frame. The 4096 run cap (projected_recv_chunk_count / RecvPacketRuns::exceeds) bounds HOLES (the number of runs), never the number of pieces inside one run. STREAM frame data is decoded with `Buf::copy_to_bytes` (quic_frames.rs copy_to_bytes_from_buf), so each frame gets its own heap allocation.

A peer that sends in-order 1-byte STREAM frames the application has not read yet costs, per credited byte: one allocation (the allocator minimum, about 16-32 B) plus a 32 B Bytes handle in the VecDeque, about 50-100 B resident per byte of flow-control credit. A 1 MiB stream window is then about 64-100 MiB per stream, multiplied across open streams and connections. Flow control bounds credited bytes, not bytes resident.

## Fix design
Coalesce small frames into a growable tail: `RecvRun` gains a `tail: BytesMut`. A piece under a small threshold (for example 256 B) is appended to the tail (amortized O(1) per byte), and the tail is frozen into `pieces` when it reaches a flush size (for example 16 KiB) or before a large piece is pushed (preserving order). `read` drains pieces and then the tail. `append` flushes the receiver's tail before joining runs and adopts the other run's tail. Large frames keep their zero-copy slice. Resident overhead becomes about 1 B per credited byte plus one handle per flush-size of small frames. Audit every other `pieces` user (prefix discard on reset, split, etc.) for the tail.

## Tests
Push 100,000 contiguous 1-byte frames into one stream without reading: retained slice handles stay at or below len/1024 + 2 (old: 100,000), and reading returns the exact bytes in order. Also mixed small/large frames and interleaved partial reads return exact bytes. Old-red: the handle count equals the frame count.
close_reason: Landed f9c089320 (main=master). RecvRun joins its slices into one buffer whenever the slice handles would cost more than the bytes they hold (slices x 64 B > run length), so tiny frames in either order no longer keep one slice per credited byte, and frames of 64 B or more stay zero-copy. Old red: control ca413d649 failed tiny_frames_do_not_keep_one_retained_slice_per_credited_byte with "100000 slices retained for 100000 one-byte frames". title: QUIC TransportParameters lacks RFC 9000 §10.1 effective max_idle_timeout negotiation
description: RFC 9000 §10.1: 'Each endpoint advertises a max_idle_timeout, but the effective value at an endpoint is computed as the minimum of the two advertised values (or the sole advertised value, if only one endpoint advertises a non-zero value).' QUIC §18.2 says max_idle_timeout=0 means no advertised limit. src/net/quic_core/mod.rs::TransportParameters has only encode/decode — no helper to compute the effective timeout from (local, peer) pairs. Without it, callers must hand-roll the min() and the zero-vs-None semantics, and we have zero tests asserting the negotiation rule. Add TransportParameters::effective_max_idle_timeout(local, peer) -> Option<u64> with a full truth table.

title: Fix scheduler wake-state futurelock on failed local routing
description: Deadlock-finder audit found two concrete futurelock paths in src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs. In inject_cancel(), a local task record calls wake_state.notify() before local routing is proven; if current-worker and pinned-worker enqueue both fail, the function returns without clearing the wake bit.
