title: Fourth-wave swarm resource governor: opt-in closed-loop pressure control for large hosts
description:
## Background
Asupersync already has strong advisory pressure and swarm-control artifacts: runtime pressure-control evidence, SLO policy bundles, second/third-wave swarm guardrail bundles, RCH proof-lane manifests, and deterministic lab replay machinery. The remaining accretive step is not another static report. The next useful frontier is an opt-in, fail-closed closed-loop governor for very large agent-swarm hosts, where 64+ cores and 256GB+ RAM should be used aggressively without collapsing responsiveness, RCH availability, or region quiescence.

## Goal
Design and implement a fourth-wave resource governor that consumes committed runtime pressure signals, agent/RCH workload receipts, SLO policy rows, and lab replay evidence, then emits deterministic admission, brownout, and scheduling recommendations. It must be opt-in, replayable, and revertible. It should make massive shared-main agent swarms faster and safer without turning advisory diagnostics into unproved production control.

## Non-goals
- Do not make adaptive controls production-on-by-default.
- Do not bypass `Cx`, region ownership, cancellation, or obligation invariants.
- Do not introduce Tokio or another executor into the core runtime graph.
- Do not claim throughput improvement without benchmark and replay evidence.
- Do not run local Cargo fallback as proof.

## Success criteria
A future operator can enable the governor in a lab or explicit opt-in runtime profile, replay a recorded swarm/RCH workload, inspect deterministic policy decisions, and see why work was admitted, browned out, delayed, or rejected. The closeout must include unit tests, replay/e2e tests with detailed logs, proof-manifest rows, and RCH-backed contract proof. The final docs must state exact claims and non-claims.

title: Fourth-wave governor: build deterministic admission and brownout policy engine
description:
## Background
Existing SLO policy and pressure-control artifacts are strong evidence surfaces, but the runtime still needs a deterministic policy engine that can turn pressure snapshots into explicit opt-in decisions without hiding uncertainty.

## Work
Implement the pure decision layer for the governor. Inputs are the schema rows from the snapshot bead plus configured SLO objective, workload class, available cores/memory, and current region/obligation pressure. Outputs are admit, delay, brownout optional work, reject, no-win fallback, or observe-only. The engine must be deterministic, replayable, side-effect-free, and explicit about why a more aggressive action was not selected.

## Risks
Overeager control could starve important work or weaken cancellation cleanup. Keep all decisions advisory until the runtime bridge and replay proof beads establish stronger evidence. Do not bypass existing SLO policy bridge semantics.

## Tests and logging
Unit tests must cover boundary capacities, zero evidence, stale evidence, local-fallback proof rows, pressure spikes, memory-heavy swarms, CPU-heavy swarms, mixed RCH/build pressure, no-win fallback, and stable decision ids. Decision logs must include selected action, rejected alternatives, objective row, and evidence quality.

## Success criteria
The policy engine compiles and passes focused RCH-backed tests. It never emits a production-control decision from malformed or advisory-only evidence, and every decision is reproducible from the receipt.

## Work
Create deterministic lab/replay fixtures and scenario manifests for 64-core/256GB-style hosts. Include CPU-heavy Cargo/RCH lanes, memory-heavy artifact generation, tracker-only bead updates, release-gate quiet phases, source audit swarms, stalled-worker recovery, RCH active_project_exclusion, and no-useful-work planning fallback. Reuse existing lab/runtime pressure structures where possible rather than inventing unrelated formats.

## Tests and logging
Add scenario parser tests, stable fixture hash tests, replay determinism tests, and e2e-style runner tests that emit detailed logs: scenario id, seed, host envelope, agent count, task counts, region ids, obligation counts, pressure timeline, RCH queue state, and final governor input snapshot.

## Success criteria

title: Fourth-wave governor: add opt-in runtime bridge and rollback receipts
description:
## Background
The governor should eventually influence runtime behavior, but only behind an explicit opt-in bridge with receipts. The bridge must preserve region close, cancellation drain, obligation cleanup, and no ambient authority.

## Work
Add or extend a narrow runtime bridge that applies governor decisions to opt-in workloads. The bridge should accept explicit `Cx`, workload kind, region/policy context, and decision receipt, then either admit, delay, brown out optional work, reject before start, or select no-win fallback. Every non-start and drain path must leave structured evidence.

## Risks
Runtime integration can accidentally become ambient policy. Keep the bridge explicit, feature/config gated, and revertible. If evidence is stale or unsupported, fail closed to observe-only or blocked rather than silently taking control.

## Tests and logging
Unit tests must cover admitted work, rejected work before start, brownout, cancellation during delayed/browned-out work, rollback after malformed receipt, no obligation leaks, final quiescence, and receipt redaction. Logs must include region ids, task counts, obligation state, decision id, and rollback reason.

## Success criteria
Focused RCH-backed tests prove the bridge preserves quiescence and no-obligation-leak invariants for all decision outcomes. Docs and receipts make clear this is opt-in, not production-on-by-default.

title: [security-audit] tls/types.rs: CertificatePinSet::validate uses BTreeSet::contains — variable-time pin comparison
description: src/tls/types.rs:622-623 in CertificatePinSet::validate calls self.pins.contains(p) where self.pins is BTreeSet<CertificatePin>. BTreeSet::contains performs Ord lookups using Vec<u8>::cmp on the SHA-256 hash bytes — a byte-by-byte comparison that terminates at the first mismatching byte. Against a remote attacker who can MitM and present arbitrary leaf certs, the timing of validate() failure could leak the prefix of pinned hashes. Even modest leakage is a problem because it lets an attacker incrementally reconstruct the SPKI hash, defeating pinning's anonymity. Fix: replace BTreeSet.contains with a constant-time comparison: iterate all pins and use subtle::ConstantTimeEq (or volatile-comparison helper from the security/ module) to compare each pin against both spki_pin and cert_pin without short-circuiting. Severity MEDIUM-HIGH (timing oracle — exploitability depends on attacker control of cert presentation rate).
close_reason: Fixed in 8c5abfcdb. CertificatePinSet::validate (src/tls/types.rs:622-679) no longer uses BTreeSet::contains (Vec<u8>::cmp byte-by-byte short-circuiting Ord lookup). Replacement: linear iteration over self.pins with constant_time_eq() (XOR accumulator + std::hint::black_box, mirroring the proven pattern in grpc/interceptor.rs:466). Match results are OR-folded into a u8 accumulator with NO early break, so iteration cost depends only on pin-set size (public). Pin TYPE branching (Spki vs Cert) is intentional — pin types are public configuration. Mismatched-type / unavailable-candidate arms run a sham CT comparison against a 32-byte zero baseline so per-iteration work is uniform regardless of which pin types appear or which candidates compute. Length-mismatch fast return is acceptable because pin lengths are public (always 32 for SHA-256). Three regression tests added: (1) constant_time_eq_correctness_and_full_iteration_invariants verifies front/middle/end mismatches all return false at the helper layer, (2) pin_set_validate_accepts_match_among_many_decoys validates the real cert against 17 pins (16 decoys interleaved around the real one in BTree order), (3) pin_set_validate_mixed_pin_types_each_resolved_independently confirms Spki-only and Cert-only sets each accept the corresponding candidate. UBS clean (criticals are JS-rule false positives — '==' is the only equality operator in Rust).

title: [SUB-EPIC] Linux Reactor (epoll)
description:
# Sub-Epic: Linux Reactor (epoll)

## Purpose

Implement a production-quality epoll-based reactor for Linux. This is the primary reactor for server deployments.

## Background

### What is epoll?

epoll (event poll) is Linux's scalable I/O event notification mechanism. It provides O(1) complexity for monitoring many file descriptors, making it ideal for high-connection-count servers.

Key syscalls:
- `epoll_create1()` - Create epoll instance
- `epoll_ctl()` - Add/modify/remove fd monitoring
- `epoll_wait()` - Block until events ready

### Edge-Triggered vs Level-Triggered

**Level-triggered (default):** 
- Reports readiness while condition exists
- Must drain all data each poll to avoid busy-loop

**Edge-triggered (EPOLLET):**
- Reports readiness when condition changes
- More efficient but requires careful handling of EAGAIN

We will use **edge-triggered** for efficiency, which requires:
1. Non-blocking sockets
2. Read/write until EAGAIN
3. Re-arm interest after each operation

## Design

```rust
pub struct EpollReactor {
    /// The epoll file descriptor
    epoll_fd: RawFd,
    /// Eventfd for cross-thread wakeup
    wake_fd: RawFd,
    /// Token slab for waker mapping (protected by mutex)
    inner: Mutex<EpollInner>,
}

struct EpollInner {
    wakers: TokenSlab,
    /// Pending wakeups that need processing
    pending_wakes: Vec<Token>,
}

impl EpollReactor {
    pub fn new() -> io::Result<Self> {
        let epoll_fd = epoll_create1(EpollFlags::EPOLL_CLOEXEC)?;
        let wake_fd = eventfd(0, EfdFlags::EFD_CLOEXEC | EfdFlags::EFD_NONBLOCK)?;
        
        // Register wake_fd for wakeup notifications
        // ...
        
        Ok(Self { epoll_fd, wake_fd, inner: Mutex::new(EpollInner::new()) })
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Details

### Cross-Thread Wakeup

Use `eventfd` for efficient wakeup:
```rust
fn wake(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
    // Write to eventfd to wake blocking epoll_wait
    nix::unistd::write(self.wake_fd, &1u64.to_ne_bytes())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

### EPOLLONESHOT for Cancel-Safety

Consider using `EPOLLONESHOT` flag:
- Event fires once, then fd is disabled
- Must re-arm after each event
- Prevents race conditions on deregistration

### Error Handling

- `EBADF`: fd was closed, deregister
- `EEXIST`: already registered (bug)
- `ENOENT`: not registered (benign on deregister)

## Platform Requirements

- Linux kernel 2.6+ (epoll available)
- Kernel 4.5+ for EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (optional optimization)

## Deliverables

1. EpollReactor implementing Reactor trait
2. Proper eventfd wakeup mechanism
3. Edge-triggered operation with EPOLLET
4. Robust error handling
5. Unit tests with real sockets
6. Benchmarks comparing to busy-loop baseline

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Can handle 10k+ concurrent connections
- [ ] No busy-looping on idle connections
- [ ] Cross-thread wakeup works reliably
- [ ] Proper cleanup on reactor shutdown
- [ ] All tests pass under stress

title: [METHODOLOGY] Add golden output checksums for core test suite
description:
Implement golden output checksums for Asupersync's core test suite. Golden checksums catch silent semantic changes that pass assertions but produce different outputs -- a critical gap in traditional testing.

BACKGROUND (section 0 Methodology): The Alien CS Graveyard methodology requires golden output checksums as one of the four CI artifact gates (alongside baseline benchmarks, flamegraphs, and proof notes). Golden checksums provide a deterministic fingerprint of system behavior that detects any change in observable output, even if all assertions still pass.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Define a GoldenChecksum struct: { test_name: String, output_hash: String (SHA-256 hex), schema_version: u32, generated_at: String, git_sha: String }. (2) Store checksums in artifacts/golden_checksums.json as a sorted array (stable for git diff). (3) Use sha2 crate for SHA-256 hashing. (4) Capture mechanism: each test that opts into golden checksums calls golden::capture(test_name, &output) which hashes the output and records it. (5) Verification: in CI, golden::verify(test_name, &output) compares against stored checksum and fails with a clear diff if mismatched. (6) Update workflow: GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 cargo test regenerates all checksums. Changed checksums require a justification comment in the PR. (7) Integration with evidence ledger: each checksum change is logged as an EvidenceLedger entry with component=golden_checksums, action=checksum_changed|checksum_verified.

COVERAGE: All unit tests for: obligation system (SendPermit lifecycle, Lease lifecycle, Reserve/Commit lifecycle), channel operations (send/recv ordering, backpressure behavior), scheduler (task ordering under various policies), cancellation protocol (cancel propagation, obligation cleanup), budget propagation (tropical semiring arithmetic), and Lab runtime replay (deterministic scheduling output).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Golden checksums exist for all core test categories listed above. (2) CI fails if any test output diverges from golden checksum (exit code 1 with clear error message). (3) GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 regenerates checksums and outputs a diff summary. (4) Checksum stability: running the same test 100 times produces the same checksum (determinism requirement). (5) Schema version in checksum file enables forward-compatible migration when test output format changes.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each golden checksum verification logs: test_name, expected_hash, actual_hash, match (bool), verification_time_us. On mismatch: log expected vs actual hash, output size, and first differing byte position. Summary at CI completion: total_verified, passed, failed, skipped. All logs in structured JSON for CI parsing. EvidenceLedger entry for each checksum change with justification field.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) Meta-test: verify the golden checksum framework itself -- capture a checksum, modify the output, verify detection. (2) Stability test: run all golden tests 10 times, verify all produce identical checksums. (3) Update workflow test: verify GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 correctly regenerates and the diff is human-readable.

title: PostgreSQL: idle reconnect (incl. after any aborted COPY OUT) silently drops statement_timeout_override; COPY OUT loses a FATAL server error before EOF
description:
## Defects (source-verified by SapphireHill, 2026-09-28, origin b8195384a; from a subagent review of 0c879f81e, COPY OUT streaming)

F2, MEDIUM, pre-existing: an idle reconnect silently drops the caller's statement-timeout override.
- PgConnection::reconnect_idle (src/database/postgres.rs ~4032-4083) carries max_result_rows and subscribed_channels into the fresh connection, then replaces self.inner. It does not carry statement_timeout_override, which is initialized to None (~4346).
- Sequence:
  1. set_statement_timeout_override(Some(5s)).
  2. The connection ends idle-closed. Every abnormal COPY OUT end does this (a dropped stream, Cx cancellation, an oversize or malformed frame), as does an idle remote close.
  3. The next request calls ensure_open_for_request, which runs reconnect_idle.
  4. apply_statement_timeout computes wire_statement_timeout_ms(cx, None), which equals the fresh applied None, so no SET is sent.
- Outcome: queries run under the server default statement_timeout (usually unlimited), and the configured safety bound disappears without a signal.
- idle_remote_close_reconnects_with_original_options checks only max_result_rows and options.

F1, LOW: a FATAL ErrorResponse followed by EOF loses the server error. PgCopyOut::next_chunk (~8044) stores the E in pending_error and enters ErrorDrain. The next read then hits EOF, and fail() returns Io(UnexpectedEof), dropping pending_error. drain_copy_out_startup_error (~5708) does the same with server_error. The caller sees "unexpected end of stream" instead of, for example, SQLSTATE 57P01. That also flips retry classification: Io is transient, 57P01 is not. The existing COPY tests always send Z after E.

F3, LOW, docs: the COPY OUT per-message bound does not cover the setup exchanges in the same call. apply_statement_timeout's SET reply is read with the connection-wide 64 MiB cap. Only a hostile server can use this, and the global cap holds. Fix the docs, or thread the caller's limit into the setup reads.

## Fix (candidate B7, SapphireHill)
- reconnect_idle carries statement_timeout_override. applied_statement_timeout_ms stays None, so the next request re-sends the SET.
- COPY OUT: a non-cancellation read failure during ErrorDrain returns the pending server error, and the startup drain returns its server_error. Cancellation keeps precedence.
Tests: idle_remote_close_reconnects_with_original_options also asserts that the override survives and is not yet applied. copy_out_fatal_error_before_eof_keeps_its_sqlstate covers the startup and data phases: E(57P01), then a shutdown with no Z, must give Server{code: 57P01} and a closed connection.
close_reason: Fixed by 68a491a68. Landed on main=master (tip e5b320b2d); receipts (fix lane green on the exact candidate, old-code control red, check and clippy on the chain tip) are in the commit message.

title: [runtime/builder] ShardedState fully built + tested but unreachable from production Runtime::new path
description:
DEAD-BUT-TESTED CODE: ShardedState (src/runtime/sharded_state.rs, 1556 lines) is the project's claimed answer to scheduler lock contention under heavy concurrency, but the production Runtime::new path always instantiates the legacy unified RuntimeState. ShardedState is currently unreachable from RuntimeBuilder::build.

EVIDENCE:

src/runtime/builder.rs:3702-3705 says, verbatim:
    // Runtime currently instantiates the unified RuntimeState path.
    // ShardedState exists behind migration work, but there is not yet a
    // RuntimeConfig layout switch wired here (see bd-2f7uj runbook).
    let runtime_state = Self::initialize_runtime_state(...);

`bd-2f7uj` does NOT exist (br show asupersync-2f7uj returns "Issue not found"). The comment is a dangling reference.

ShardedState reach (grep -rln ShardedState src/): src/runtime/sharded_state.rs (39 refs), src/runtime/state.rs (5 refs), src/runtime/task_table.rs (5 refs), src/runtime/builder.rs (1 ref — the comment above), src/runtime/mod.rs (1 ref).

Test coverage exists but is metamorphic-only: tests/metamorphic/sharded_state.rs, tests/metamorphic/task_table.rs, tests/scheduler_cancel_storm_propagation_audit.rs. The metamorphic harness verifies invariants under random ops; it does NOT prove production runtime workloads route through ShardedState — because production runtime workloads currently route through the unified state.

WHY THIS MATTERS:

The br-asupersync-9kuias scheduler design review (committed 2026-05-07 d88aeb87f) just codified swarm-scale agent coordination as the primary stakeholder. Swarm coordination is precisely the regime where lock contention on a unified RuntimeState becomes the bottleneck. Every benchmark cited in the workload corpus (artifacts/runtime_workload_corpus_v1.json) — tracker_lock_contention, concurrent_rch_proofs, proof_runner_fanout, coordination_latency_burst — is a single-lock contention pattern that ShardedState was designed to relieve. Today those benchmarks measure the legacy path, not the path the project's docs claim is the answer.

ACCEPTANCE:

1. Add a `runtime_state_shape: RuntimeStateShape` field (enum: `Unified` | `Sharded`) to `RuntimeConfig`. Default = `Unified` to preserve current behavior.

2. Add `RuntimeBuilder::with_sharded_state(bool)` setter that flips the field.

3. In `Runtime::new` (src/runtime/builder.rs:3702 area), branch on the shape:
   - `Unified` → existing path (current default).
   - `Sharded` → instantiate `ShardedState`, wire it through `ThreeLaneScheduler` and the worker spawn path.

4. Confirm `ThreeLaneScheduler::new_with_options` accepts both backing types — currently it takes `&Arc<ContendedMutex<RuntimeState>>`. Either:
   - Introduce a trait abstraction over the two state types and parameterize the scheduler, OR
   - Provide a `ThreeLaneScheduler::new_for_sharded` constructor that takes `&Arc<ShardedState>` and adapts to the same internal protocol.

5. Re-run the swarm workload corpus on both shapes; compare against the `artifacts/runtime_workload_corpus_v1.json` envelope. Document the per-shape envelope in `docs/scheduler_design_review_9kuias.md` (or a follow-up doc) so future PRs know which shape they're benchmarking against.

6. Replace the dangling `bd-2f7uj` comment in builder.rs with the real bead ID this work lands under.

7. The metamorphic suite at tests/metamorphic/sharded_state.rs must continue to pass after wire-up (it is currently the only place ShardedState invariants are checked).

NON-GOALS:

- Removing the unified RuntimeState path. Backwards compat for existing consumers; the unified path stays as the default until an evidence-backed perf comparison says otherwise.
- Re-architecting the scheduler. ShardedState is a backing-store change, not a scheduler redesign.

ESTIMATE: multi-day work (1556 lines of integration + scheduler trait abstraction + perf validation).

title: Epic: Sync Primitives Security & Correctness Audit
description:
# Epic: Sync Primitives Security & Correctness Audit

## Overview

Deep code review of the sync primitives (mutex, semaphore, barrier, rwlock, notify, once_cell) 
revealed several concurrency bugs, race conditions, and correctness issues that could cause 
deadlocks, starvation, or incorrect behavior under load.

## Background & Context

The sync primitives in `src/sync/` are foundational to the async runtime. Any bugs here 
propagate to all higher-level abstractions. Issues were discovered through systematic 
first-principles analysis of:

1. **Lock ordering** - Are locks acquired in consistent order to prevent deadlocks?
2. **Memory ordering** - Are Acquire/Release/SeqCst semantics used correctly?
3. **Spurious wakeups** - Are waiters re-checked after waking?
4. **Queue management** - Can waiter queues grow unbounded?
5. **Cancellation paths** - Are resources properly cleaned up on cancel?

## Severity Assessment

- **HIGH**: Mutex wake-while-holding-lock (can cause deadlock)
- **MEDIUM**: Semaphore fairness violation (queue jumping)
- **MEDIUM**: Barrier cancellation race (missed notifications)
- **LOW**: RwLock writer starvation characteristics (by design, but undocumented)

## Architectural Considerations

title: [SUB-EPIC-PHASE] io_uring Reactor (Linux Modern Async I/O)
description:
# Sub-Epic: io_uring Reactor

## Overview

io_uring is Linux's modern async I/O interface (kernel 5.1+), offering significant performance advantages over epoll for certain workloads.

## Why io_uring

1. **True async**: Operations complete in kernel, no syscall per I/O
2. **Batching**: Submit multiple operations with single syscall
3. **Zero-copy**: Can use registered buffers
4. **Lower latency**: Kernel polling mode avoids context switches

## Scope

This sub-epic covers:
- IoUringReactor implementing Reactor trait
- Submission/completion queue management
- Buffer registration for zero-copy
- Polled mode for latency-critical paths

## Design Decisions

### When to Use io_uring vs epoll

| Use Case | Recommended |
|----------|-------------|
| Many idle connections | epoll (lower memory) |
| High throughput file I/O | io_uring |
| Network with many small ops | io_uring (batching) |
| Compatibility (old kernels) | epoll |

### Feature Detection

```rust
fn has_io_uring() -> bool {
    // Check kernel version >= 5.1
    // Try io_uring_setup() and check for features
}
```

## Dependencies

```toml
[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]
io-uring = "0.6"  # Safe Rust wrapper
```

## Task Breakdown

1. IoUringReactor core structure
2. Submission queue management
3. Completion queue processing
4. Register/deregister implementation
5. Probing for supported operations
6. Buffer registration API
7. Polled mode option
8. Fallback to epoll on old kernels

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] IoUringReactor implements Reactor trait
- [ ] Passes same tests as EpollReactor
- [ ] Graceful fallback when unavailable
- [ ] Benchmark shows improvement for applicable workloads
close_reason: io_uring Reactor fully implemented in src/runtime/reactor/io_uring.rs. IoUringReactor implements Reactor trait (register/modify/deregister/poll/wake). 25+ integration tests pass. Feature-gated (io-uring). Graceful fallback for non-Linux. All acceptance criteria verified.

EpollReactor (epoll.rs) implements via polling crate with token->fd bookkeeping; kqueue.rs similar. There is an unused linux.rs stub with outdated Reactor signature (returns Registration) — likely ignore/replace. Integration points: runtime/state.rs + io_driver.rs tests currently instantiate EpollReactor on Linux; io_uring should be optional (feature/cfg) and likely selected via builder/explicit choice with fallback to epoll when unavailable.

comments.text: Doc notes (io-uring crate): IoUring::new(entries) requires power-of-two queue size; IoUring::builder() exists for custom params. PollAdd opcode can poll an fd; it is one-shot by default and can be multi-shot via .multi(true) (kernel 5.13+), with CQE flag IORING_CQE_F_MORE indicating more events. PollAdd::new takes flags from poll.h and builds an Entry; user_data can carry Token for completion mapping. (See docs.rs io-uring and PollAdd)

The only existing test (test_reset_stream_drops_queued_outbound_data) verifies this for ErrorCode::Cancel; no test pins the round-trip for the other 13 codes (NO_ERROR, PROTOCOL_ERROR, INTERNAL_ERROR, FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR, SETTINGS_TIMEOUT, STREAM_CLOSED, FRAME_SIZE_ERROR, REFUSED_STREAM, COMPRESSION_ERROR, CONNECT_ERROR, ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM, INADEQUATE_SECURITY, HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED). A future refactor that filters or remaps codes in PendingOp::RstStream would silently change wire behaviour. Add a truth-table test asserting reset_stream(s, code) → RstStreamFrame { stream_id: s, error_code: code } for all 14 spec'd codes plus the on-wire u32 encoding (RFC 9113 §7 mandates exact u32 values 0x0..=0xd).
close_reason: Landed in c3a68b094. reset_stream_emits_rfc_9113_section_7_error_codes pins all 14 RFC §7 codes through Connection::reset_stream → next_frame → Frame::RstStream and round-trips u32::from(code) == wire_value and ErrorCode::from_u32(wire_value) == code per the §7 0x0..=0xd table. cargo check --lib passes. Full lib test build blocked by other agents WIP files (write_blocking/read_blocking, RuntimeConfig.runtime_state_shape, ObligationToken Clone) — unrelated to this test.

title: OTLP span add_attribute() API missing - conflated with set_attribute()
description:
AUDIT FINDING: OTLP span API conflation

**Issue**: TestSpan (otel.rs:3263-3297) only provides set_attribute() methods:
- set_attribute(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) 
- set_int_attribute(), set_float_attribute(), set_bool_attribute()
- set_attribute_value(&mut self, key: &str, value: AttributeValue)

**Missing**: No add_attribute() methods for accumulating multi-valued attributes.

**Impact**: Cannot accumulate multiple values for the same attribute key per OTLP spec. Only set/replace behavior available.

**Expected**: Distinct APIs:
- set_attribute(): Replace existing or set new attribute
- add_attribute(): Accumulate/append attribute values

**Location**: src/observability/otel.rs:3464-3503

**Audit date**: 2026-05-03
design: Clarify and implement the semantic distinction between set_attribute replacement and add_attribute accumulation only if that distinction is valid for the project's OTLP model. If OTLP/exporter schema cannot represent multi-valued accumulated attributes for one key, the bead must fail closed with a spec-backed no-change/blocker note rather than inventing an incompatible representation. Preserve existing set_attribute APIs and dropped-count behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests cover set_attribute replacement unchanged, add_attribute accumulation for repeated keys if supported, mixed set/add ordering, capacity limits, dropped-count semantics, empty-key filtering, oversized key handling, value-type preservation, deterministic export rendering, and explicit no-op/error behavior if accumulation is rejected by design. Deterministic integration/e2e coverage must log scenario ID, operation sequence, key fingerprint, value count per key, set-vs-add mode, accepted/dropped counts, export encoding decision, exact rch command, artifact paths if any, and final spec-compatibility verdict. Validation before closeout: rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check for touched Rust files, targeted rch cargo tests for observability::otel span attribute semantics with --nocapture, and a closeout comment citing the exact OTLP interpretation used plus why no existing attribute functionality was removed.
close_reason: No-code/spec-backed closeout: compatible add_attributes(Vec<KeyValue>) batch API already shipped and validated under asupersync-803qzz/k160dq; repeated-key accumulation add_attribute() is incompatible with OpenTelemetry/OTLP unique-key attribute semantics.

comments.author: ScarletBarn
comments.text: 2026-05-04 ScarletBarn no-code closeout: live code already contains TestSpan::add_attributes(Vec<KeyValue>) from asupersync-803qzz, validated after asupersync-k160dq. Current official OpenTelemetry spec says Span MAY provide an API to set multiple Attributes at once, setting an attribute with the same key SHOULD overwrite the existing value, exported attribute collections MUST by default contain only unique keys, and OTLP in particular requires exported Resources, Spans, Metric data points, and Log Records to contain only unique attributes. Therefore this bead's proposed singular add_attribute() that accumulates repeated values for one key is not compatible with the OTLP data model. No code change is appropriate; preserve existing set_attribute replacement plus add_attributes batch last-write-wins behavior. Prior proof for the compatible API: rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_asupersync_803qzz_add_attributes cargo test -p asupersync --lib otlp_add_attributes --features metrics,tracing-integration -- --nocapture => 8 passed; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_asupersync_k160dq_check cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features metrics,tracing-integration => pass.

title: [sqlite] Stream query rows without collecting full result sets
description: SQLite query result streaming memory defect: wrapper violates sqlite3_step() native streaming by collecting ALL rows into Vec<SqliteRow>. Same pattern as MySQL/PostgreSQL but requires BlockingPool async streaming architecture. Memory usage O(result_set_size) -> O(1) per row.
design: Replace eager Vec<SqliteRow> collection with a true row-streaming architecture over the existing SQLite blocking-pool boundary. Preserve sqlite3_step() semantics, cancellation correctness, connection ownership, statement finalization, and error propagation. The stream must provide O(1)-per-row memory behavior and an explicit conservative fallback if native streaming cannot be made cancel-safe.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests cover zero rows, one row, many rows, large payload rows, early stream drop finalizes the statement, query error mid-stream, cancellation while sqlite3_step is active, connection returned to pool after stream close, no row duplication/loss, and bounded memory counters versus the previous collect-all behavior. Deterministic integration/e2e script coverage must log scenario ID, row count, row payload size, peak buffered rows, blocking-pool handoff count, cancellation/drop point, statement finalization count, connection return count, memory-before/after estimate, exact rch command, artifact paths if any, and final O(1)-streaming verdict. Validation before closeout: rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check for touched Rust files, targeted rch cargo tests for sqlite streaming with --nocapture, and a closeout comment with before/after peak buffered-row counts.
close_reason: Implemented bounded SqliteRowStream with capacity-1 handoff, stats, early-drop close/cancel, deferred query errors, and focused stream tests. Also cleared sqlite-feature transaction compile drift needed for validation. Proof: rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check src/database/sqlite.rs src/database/transaction.rs passed; rch exec -- cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features sqlite,test-internals passed remotely with unrelated warnings; rch exec -- cargo test -p asupersync --lib sqlite_query_stream --features sqlite,test-internals -- --nocapture passed remotely: 4 passed, 0 failed, peak buffered-row assertion <= 1.

title: Authenticate the control-source-stream so the auth tier uses the fast clean path (perfect/auth 23s->0.81s WIN, ceiling proven MATRIX-145)
description:
MATRIX-145 (SapphireHill, ledger bd7fa5878) — ★★★perfect/auth is a WIN, PROVEN. The 4 prior fixes (rate-match, parallel-auth, parallel-decrypt, clean-ramp 7746cde93) were ALL NO-OPs because they tuned the slow datagram path. REAL root cause + the win ceiling:

ROOT CAUSE: atp's nocrypto/perfect win (0.81s) uses the fast reliable control-source-stream. That stream is UNAUTHENTICATED (control_source_data_frame carries only entry/offset/data, NO auth tag), so it is hard-gated `&& !symbol_auth_enabled` in control_source_stream_eligible (transport_rq/mod.rs:1934; receiver mirror :6398 + tuning :6380). The auth tier is LOCKED OUT of the fast path -> falls back to the slow paced datagram spray (perfect/auth 23s @ 2% CPU = 98% idle).

CEILING PROOF (SapphireHill /data/tmp insecure prototype, gate removed, NEVER committed): 50M/perfect/auth reps3 = 0.81s median, sha-ok 3/3, ~1.5x less mem, BEATS rsync 0.85s = a 28x speedup (23.4s -> 0.81s). There is NO fundamental reason auth loses; the fast path IS the win.

★THE REAL FIX (ship this — it's the genuine AUTH-1): authenticate the control-source-stream so the gate can be safely dropped.
1. Sender: add a per-symbol (or per-frame) auth tag to control_source_data frames — control_source_data_frame / control_source_data_wire_frame (transport_rq/mod.rs:2896/2905), keyed by the same symbol_auth context the datagram path uses.
2. Receiver: verify the tag in apply_control_source_data_frame (mod.rs:6952) / parse_control_source_data_frame (:2977), FAIL-CLOSED (reject + abort transfer on mismatch, same posture as the datagram verifier).
3. Then drop the `&& !symbol_auth_enabled` gate at :1934 (and the :6380 bulk-tuning gate) so the auth tier uses the source-stream on clean links.
GATES: 50M/perfect/auth median < rsync ~0.85s, sha-ok; ★fail-closed proof: a tampered source-stream byte MUST be rejected (add a test like the datagram tamper test). HMAC is ~GB/s + the stream is reliable (no per-datagram pacing) so authenticated source-stream should stay ~1-2s -> WIN/tie vs rsync WITH security.

SCOPE: this fixes perfect/auth (and helps any clean authenticated transfer). good/auth (0.1% loss) is excluded from the source-stream by clean_control_source_stream_round0 by design -> separate near-clean lever. encrypted tier (transport_quic) has NO source-stream; its perfect/encrypted 13s is QUIC datagram cold-start pacing -> separate analysis (likely the same idea: a fast reliable clean path for QUIC, or fix the QUIC cold-start ramp to reach line rate).

I'll A/B the authenticated source-stream the moment it lands (target: bank perfect/auth as a real F-POS WIN).

title: HTTP/1.1 server audit: handler response replaced by 413 after a short unread body, unbounded chunk-size line and extensions (DoS), handler framing reaches the wire unchecked, and LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of the HTTP/1.1 server (src/http/h1/server.rs, stream.rs, listener.rs and the server side of codec.rs) at origin/main c06414315 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-03). SapphireHill re-read MEDIUM 2 before fixing it. No HIGH smuggling or desync on the request-parsing side.

## MEDIUM
1. The streaming server discards the handler's response when the unread body takes more than about 8 socket reads to drain (server.rs 2870-2889; serve loops 1576-1587 and 1965-1976; DrainTimeout 2970). The drain frame limit (unread_body_drain_frames = 8, line 264) counts one frame per socket read on the Content-Length path (stream.rs 2048), so with small segments about 13 KiB of unread body is enough. POST /upload with Content-Length 200000 and a handler that returns 401 without reading the body gets "413 [ASUP-E505]" instead of the 401 (408 on a slow client). The comment at 1619-1624 says the computed response is still delivered with Connection: close; that path only runs on Ok. Expected (RFC 9112 section 9.6): send the handler's response with Connection: close, then close. Fix: in the Handler(Some(hop)) branch, map a drain failure to the computed response plus a forced close; count drain bytes, not reads. Pinned by streaming_server_closes_when_unread_body_exceeds_drain_limit (server.rs ~6857), which asserts the 413 with a 4-byte limit.
2. FIXED in this session's stack: the streaming chunked decoders had no chunk-size line cap and rescanned the buffer from the start on every read; chunk extensions were never charged to any budget (Node CVE-2024-22019 class).
3. Handler-supplied framing reaches the wire unchecked (codec.rs Http1Codec::encode 1652-1790): (a) 204/304/1xx with Transfer-Encoding: chunked writes "0\r\n\r\n", which a keep-alive client reads as the start of the next response (RFC 9112 6.3, RFC 9110 8.6); only the produced path guards this (server.rs 2165). (b) An HTTP/1.0 request gets a chunked response (finalize_response_persistence keeps Transfer-Encoding; RFC 9112 6.1 MUST NOT). (c) A non-HEAD response with Content-Length N > 0 and an empty body is accepted (codec.rs 1695-1698), so the client takes N bytes of the next response as body. Fix: strip TE, trailers and body for 1xx/204/304; convert to Content-Length for 1.0; reject a Content-Length that does not match a non-HEAD, non-304 body (500 + close).

## LOW
4. HTTP/1.0 requests with Expect: 100-continue get 417 (server.rs 3525-3527); RFC 9110 10.1.1 says ignore it. Pinned by tests/conformance/h1_expect_continue.rs 457-503.
5. Every buffered request clones its whole body for the upgrade check (server.rs 1149), up to 16 MiB per request.
6. Request heads are reparsed from scratch on every read (codec.rs 1292-1302): O(n^2) up to the 64 KiB header limit.
7. No Date header (RFC 9110 6.6.1); a blank line before the request line gives 400 (RFC 9112 2.2 says ignore); a missing or duplicate Host is accepted under AllowAll and gets 421 under AllowList (RFC 9112 3.2 requires 400).

## Checked and sound
CL/TE conflicts and duplicates, CL digits only, TE exactly chunked, TE on 1.0 rejected; bare CR/LF, obs-fold and space before colon rejected; strict chunk sizes and CRLF; bounded trailers; pipelining order and leftover bytes; body drained before keep-alive reuse; head, whole-request, idle and write timeouts; 100-continue ordering; HEAD suppression; header injection; Connection handling; half-close, in-flight guard, graceful drain, panic 500, deadline 503; upgrade handoff; produced-response Content-Length enforcement.

title: Phase 0: Records, State Machines, and Global Σ
description:
# Phase 0: Records, State Machines, and Global Σ

## Purpose
Implement the runtime’s internal state as an explicit machine state (Σ) that matches the operational semantics.

Everything in Phase 0 should be explainable as transitions over:
- regions (R)
- tasks (T)
- obligations (O)
- time (now)

This feature covers the *data model* and *state machines* that make the kernel enforce structured concurrency, cancellation, and linear obligations.

## Scope
### 1) State enums (the protocol surface)
- `TaskState`: `Created | Running | CancelRequested | Cancelling | Finalizing | Completed(outcome)`
- `RegionState`: `Open | Closing | Draining | Finalizing | Closed(outcome)`
- `ObligationState`: `Reserved | Committed | Aborted | Leaked` (terminal states are absorbing)
- `ObligationKind`: at minimum `SendPermit | Ack | Lease | IoOp` (even if Lease/IoOp are Phase 2+/4+, the kind set is part of the semantic model)

### 2) Records (the owned runtime resources)
- `TaskRecord`: owned by exactly one region; maintains waiters; tracks mask deferrals.
- `RegionRecord`: parent/children/subregions; finalizer stack; policy; effective budget; cancel reason.
- `ObligationRecord` + `ObligationRegistry`: ties linear obligations to holder task + owning region; enforces leak detection.

### 3) Global runtime state Σ
- Container that holds all arenas/registries and current time.
- Provides invariants checks for lab/debug.

## Non-Negotiable Invariants (must be representable and checkable)
- Ownership tree (regions form a rooted tree)
- All live tasks are owned by a region
- Region close implies quiescence
- Cancel propagates down the tree
- Reserved obligations have live holders
- Obligations are linear (resolve at most once)
- Mask deferral is bounded and monotone

## Acceptance Criteria
- There is an explicit data model that supports all transition rules:
  - spawn/schedule/complete
  - cancel request/acknowledge/drain/finalize
  - reserve/commit/abort/leak
  - join waiting
  - region close phases
  - tick/timeouts
- The model is compatible with deterministic testing: invariants can be checked from state snapshots and/or traces.

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for each enum transition validity.
- Unit tests for registries/arenas.
- Property tests for “no illegal transitions” under randomized sequences (lab deterministic).
close_reason: Implemented: TaskRecord, RegionRecord, Obligation, Finalizer with complete state machines. All in src/record/ with 24+ passing tests.

title: [fresh-eyes] http/compress: decompressor stale-bytes-on-bomb-rejection (Gzip+Deflate+Brotli) — add poisoned flag
description:
src/http/compress.rs Gzip 431-454 / Deflate 557-566 / Brotli 688-700 — when LimitedWriter::write returns InvalidData (decompression bomb cap exceeded), write_all propagates the err and update_decompressed_total is never called. The inner buffer in LimitedWriter (mem::take target) may retain bytes the underlying decoder partially produced before rejection.

There's no poisoned flag. A caller that ignores the err and calls decompress() again drains those stale bytes, then updates self.total for them, producing inconsistent accounting (could allow exceeding max_size by smuggling stale bytes through subsequent calls).

Defense-in-depth gap; correct callers fail closed on first error. Fix:
add poisoned: bool field to GzipDecompressor, DeflateDecompressor, BrotliDecompressor; check at start of decompress/finish; set on any error path; return Err(io::ErrorKind::Other, "decompressor poisoned by prior error") on subsequent calls.

OR clear self.decoder.get_mut().inner before returning err — simpler but doesn't catch the case where the caller wraps the err and tries finish() to flush remaining buffer.

Filed-out from br-asupersync-ipsu2a part 2 (part 1 was the x-gzip alias, fixed in commit bdb496643). Larger refactor scope — touches 3 Decompressor impls + tests.

Audit: SapphireHill 2026-04-26 fresh-eyes-7d-diff via subagent a3fe06ca; verified live at compress.rs:431-454 (Gzip), 557-566 (Deflate), 688-700 (Brotli).
close_reason: Fixed in commit ahead. All 3 Decompressor impls (Gzip/Deflate/Brotli) now have poisoned: bool field. decompress() and finish() reject all further calls with 'poisoned by prior error' once any error has been observed; on error, the inner buffer is cleared (discarding stale partial bytes). 3 regression tests cover bomb-cap-rejection-then-second-call across all 3 algorithms. 75 compress lib tests pass; clippy --lib --features compression -D warnings clean. SapphireHill 2026-04-26.

title: [security-audit-2] gRPC bidirectional stream resource exhaustion via connection hoarding
description: ATTACK VECTOR: Attacker opens many gRPC bidirectional streaming calls, sends valid initial metadata under 8KB limit, then holds connections open indefinitely without sending stream data. File: src/grpc/server.rs:36 max_concurrent_streams exists but may not prevent single client from opening max_concurrent_streams across multiple connections. Each held stream consumes server memory and connection table entries. Combined with slow HTTP/2 frame sending, attacker could exhaust server resources. FIX DIRECTION: Add per-connection stream idle timeout (suggested 60s), per-client connection limits, and stream inactivity detection. Consider implementing gRPC keepalive enforcement and connection-level timeouts. Verify max_concurrent_streams applies per-connection not per-server. METHODOLOGY: Apply /security-audit-for-saas connection exhaustion and resource hoarding analysis.

Added per-connection stream tracking, idle timeout enforcement (60s default), connection registry, and regression tests. Transport adapters now have secure dispatch methods to prevent connection hoarding attacks. Fix verified with 4 test cases simulating attack scenarios.

title: net/unix audit: recv_with_ancillary reads past the control buffer when macOS/BSD truncate SCM_RIGHTS (UB from a safe API); VirtualTcpListener accept lost wakeup; split registration can outlive its fd
description:
Read-only audit of src/net/tcp/* and src/net/unix/* at 34917235b (SapphireHill audit agent round 6, 10-05). The HIGH was confirmed by re-reading unix/stream.rs recvmsg_with_raw_ancillary.

## HIGH (macOS/BSD only)
H1. UnixStream::recv_with_ancillary reads past the control buffer when the kernel truncates SCM_RIGHTS (unix/stream.rs ~880-907).
- The fd loop takes its count from the header's cmsg_len and never bounds it by the kernel-written msg_controllen.
- Linux shortens cmsg_len on truncation. XNU and FreeBSD keep the sender's length and set MSG_CTRUNC.
- Example: a 1-fd buffer (16 bytes on Darwin) receiving 8 fds reads 28 bytes past the Vec, calls fcntl(F_SETFD) on garbage ints and returns them as received fds. A caller that closes them closes unrelated descriptors.
- This is UB reachable from a safe API by any local peer.
- Also: `&*cmsg` makes a &cmsghdr from a Vec<u8> (alignment 1).
- FIX (SapphireHill): bound the count by the bytes the kernel copied, and read the header unaligned.

## MEDIUM
M2. VirtualTcpListener accept/poll_accept lost wakeup (virtual_tcp.rs ~603-605, ~629-631).
- The empty-queue check releases the state lock before registering the waker. An inject/close/Drop in that window calls wake_all on an empty list, and the acceptor sleeps with a connection queued (or the listener closed).
- Also, accept() never checks the Cx for cancellation, unlike poll_accept.
- FIX (SapphireHill): re-check after registering; accept() checks cancellation.

## LOW
- L3. A split half's reactor registration can outlive its fd (tcp/split.rs ~518-527, unix/split.rs ~417-420).
  - If the reactor holds the state Arc in CombinedWaker::dispatch while both halves drop, the stream closes the fd first and the IoRegistration drops later on the reactor thread.
  - An accept() that reuses the fd number in that window gets AlreadyExists from epoll on its first registration.
  - Fix: TcpStreamInner/UnixStreamInner Drop takes the registration before the stream field drops.
- L4. reunite drops the registration_on_fallback flag, so a registration made on the process-global fallback driver is never migrated after reunite.
- L5. Windows connect blocks a worker thread: it polls a private reactor for 1 ms inside poll (stream.rs ~943-946, ~1091).
- L6. set_user_timeout(Some(<1ms)) rounds to 0, which means the kernel default, the opposite of the request (user_timeout.rs ~103).

Judged SOUND: tcp/stream.rs (connect re-check, drop order, poll cancellation), tcp/listener.rs, tcp/socket.rs, tcp/traits.rs, tcp/split.rs and unix/split.rs (apart from L3/L4), unix/listener.rs, unix/datagram.rs, unix/stream.rs (apart from H1), and the reactor registration paths.

title: [FABRIC] Semantic Subject Fabric — NATS-Inspired Messaging Substrate
description:
# Semantic Subject Fabric — Full Implementation Program

## Vision
Build a messaging-native subsystem that turns NATS's best operational ideas into stronger runtime semantics within Asupersync. This is NOT a NATS clone — it is a new systems category: a semantic subject fabric that is NATS-small on the packet path, capability-safe on the authority path, and reasoning-native on the replay path.

## Three Architectural Planes
1. **Packet Plane**: Hot ephemeral publish/subscribe/request/reply (the common fast case)
2. **Authority Plane**: Obligations, leases, fencing, durability transitions, cutover, cursor authority
3. **Reasoning Plane**: Evidence, explainability, certified cuts, replay, counterfactual branches

Default path is packet-plane only. Authority/reasoning planes are opt-in via declared DeliveryClass or ServiceContract.

## Three Correctness Layers
1. **Static Layer**: Rust ownership, typestate, and capability tokens prevent in-process misuse at compile time
2. **Runtime Layer**: Cx, obligations, control capsules, and region quiescence govern distributed behavior
3. **Evidence Layer**: FrankenSuite, certified cuts, and replayable traces explain what the system believed and why

## Key Design Principles
- Public mental model stays NATS-small even as internal semantics get richer
- Stronger guarantees are named service classes, not hidden taxes on common case
- Every radical behavior lowers into small inspectable artifacts: tokens, certificates, leases, cut records, session contracts, key contexts, explain plans
- Autonomous policy loops run inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback
- Guarantees hold inside Asupersync's capability boundary, not for arbitrary external side effects
- No exactly-once claims; idempotency + leases at boundaries

## Module Home
src/messaging/ — coexists with existing nats.rs and jetstream.rs adapter surfaces

## Source Document
PROPOSAL_TO_INTEGRATE_IDEAS_FROM_NATS_INTO_ASUPERSYNC__AFTER_FEEDBACK.md

Not every message pays for every invariant. Most traffic stays on packet plane and only ESCALATES when declared service class requires it. Three correctness layers: (1) STATIC: Rust ownership/typestate/capability tokens prevent in-process misuse before tests run, (2) RUNTIME: Cx/obligations/control capsules/region quiescence govern distributed behavior, (3) EVIDENCE: FrankenSuite/certified cuts/replayable traces explain what the system believed and why.

title: [FABRIC][P0] Foundation Types & FabricIR
description:
# Phase 0: Foundation Types & Fabric IR

## Purpose
Define the core type system for the entire messaging fabric. These types form the Intermediate Representation (FabricIR) that all higher-level declarations compile into. Without these, nothing else in the fabric has a type-safe foundation.

## Key Types to Define
- SubjectSchema: subject declarations with semantic families (Command, Event, Reply, Control, ProtocolStep, CaptureSelector, DerivedView)
- MorphismPlan: typed namespace transform specifications
- ServiceContract: behavioral service interface definitions
- ProtocolContract: session-typed protocol definitions
- SessionSchema: session type definitions
- DeliveryClass: named service class enum (EphemeralInteractive, DurableOrdered, ObligationBacked, MobilitySafe, ForensicReplayable)
- ConsumerPolicy: delivery policy configuration
- CapabilityTokenSchema: capability type definitions
- EvidencePolicy: when/what evidence to record
- PrivacyPolicy: metadata disclosure rules
- CutPolicy: snapshot/branch policy
- BranchPolicy: counterfactual branch rules
- QuantitativeObligationContract: SLO-style probabilistic contracts

## Ack Taxonomy (Critical)
Must define distinct ack meanings to prevent semantic confusion:
- Accepted: packet plane accepted custody for forwarding
- Committed: authority plane committed the control entry
- Recoverable: declared durability class has been met
- Served: service obligation completed by callee
- Received: delivery/receipt boundary crossed

## Design Notes
- These are data types and enums, not runtime behavior
- Must be serializable (serde) for plan compilation and inspection
- Must be deterministic for lab runtime compatibility
- Lives in src/messaging/ir.rs and src/messaging/class.rs
- Consider using Rust enums with exhaustive matching for correctness

## Relation to Existing Code
- Builds on existing types/outcome.rs, obligation/ledger.rs concepts
- DeliveryClass connects to existing Budget and service layer concepts
- CapabilityTokenSchema connects to cx/macaroon.rs capability model
## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P0.1] Define FabricIR core type system
description:
# Define FabricIR Core Type System

## File: src/messaging/ir.rs

## What to Build
Define the complete Intermediate Representation type system that all fabric declarations compile into. This is the schema that gives the entire messaging substrate one center of gravity.

## Types to Define

### SubjectSchema
```rust
pub struct SubjectSchema {
    pub pattern: SubjectPattern,       // e.g., "tenant.orders.>", "sys.health.*"
    pub family: SubjectFamily,         // semantic classification
    pub delivery_class: DeliveryClass, // default service class
    pub evidence_policy: EvidencePolicy,
    pub reply_space: Option<ReplySpaceRule>,
    pub mobility: MobilityPermission,
}

pub enum SubjectFamily {
    Command,          // imperative action request
    Event,            // notification of something that happened
    Reply,            // response to a command
    Control,          // system/control plane
    ProtocolStep,     // step in a session-typed protocol
    CaptureSelector,  // subject set for stream capture
    DerivedView,      // read-only derived/projected view
}
```

### MorphismPlan
Typed namespace transform specification — see Phase 3 for full details.

### ServiceContract
Behavioral service interface — see Phase 9 for full details.

### ProtocolContract
Session-typed protocol — see Phase 8 for full details.

### SessionSchema
Session type definitions with send/receive/choice/branch/end.

### ConsumerPolicy
Delivery policy configuration with mode, ack policy, max pending, max deliver, etc.

### CapabilityTokenSchema
Capability type definitions mapping subject families to required permissions.

### EvidencePolicy
When and what evidence to record: sampling rate, which transitions are material, retention.

### PrivacyPolicy
Metadata disclosure rules: what crosses boundaries, what gets noise, what is redacted.

### CutPolicy
Snapshot/branch policy: when to cut, retention, materialization rules.

### BranchPolicy
Counterfactual branch rules: who can attach, read-only vs sandboxed mutation, retention.

### QuantitativeObligationContract
SLO-style probabilistic obligation contracts:
```rust
pub struct QuantitativeObligationContract {
    pub class: DeliveryClass,
    pub target_latency: Duration,
    pub target_probability: f64,     // e.g., 0.999
    pub retry_law: RetryLaw,
    pub degradation_policy: DegradationPolicy,
}
```

## Requirements
- All types must derive Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, Clone
- All types must be deterministic (no ambient randomness)
- Exhaustive enum matching for correctness
- Must be compatible with lab runtime

## Tests
- Round-trip serialization for every type
- Exhaustive enum variant coverage
- Default construction
- Validation (reject invalid configurations)

description:
# Define DeliveryClass Enum and Service Class Taxonomy

## File: src/messaging/class.rs

## What to Build
The named service class system that makes semantic upgrades explicit rather than hidden taxes. This is the key mechanism that keeps the common case NATS-cheap.

## DeliveryClass Enum
```rust
pub enum DeliveryClass {
    /// Hot ephemeral pub/sub. No durability, no obligations. Packet-plane only.
    /// This is the default — most traffic stays here.
    EphemeralInteractive,
    
    /// Durable ordered stream. Authority-plane append obligations.
    /// Publisher gets ack only after durability target met.
    DurableOrdered,
    
    /// Full obligation tracking. Service obligations tracked in ledger.
    /// Request/reply with certificate-carrying semantics.
    ObligationBacked,
    
    /// Safe for hot-cell evacuation, stewardship change, cutover.
    /// Requires cut-certified mobility protocol.
    MobilitySafe,
    
    /// Full reasoning-plane engagement. Replayable traces, evidence records,
    /// certified cuts, counterfactual branch capability.
    ForensicReplayable,
}
```

## Semantic SLO Tuple
Each subject family, stream, consumer, or service contract compiles to:
- Latency envelope
- Durability or recoverability class
- Obligation scope
- Ack meaning (from ack taxonomy)
- Replay retention
- Evidence sampling rate
- Mobility allowance
- Degradation priority
- Privacy policy
- Quantitative obligation contract (where applicable)

## Provider/Caller Authority Split
- Providers declare admissible classes
- Callers can only request a bounded subset within provider policy
- No caller can unilaterally demand expensive guarantees

## Ack Taxonomy (Critical — must be distinct types)
```rust
pub enum AckKind {
    /// Packet plane accepted custody for forwarding. No durability implied.
    Accepted,
    /// Authority plane committed the control entry or obligation.
    Committed,
    /// Declared durability class has been met.
    Recoverable,
    /// Service obligation completed by callee.
    Served,
    /// Configured delivery/receipt boundary was crossed.
    Received,
}
```

## Design Notes
- This is NOT cosmetic naming — it bridges deep semantics to operator language
- Each class has a well-defined cost vector (latency, storage, CPU, evidence bytes)
- Default should always be EphemeralInteractive unless explicitly upgraded
- Class selection is validated at compile time where possible

## Tests
- Validate class ordering (EphemeralInteractive is cheapest)
- Validate ack kind semantics (Accepted < Committed < Recoverable < Served < Received)
- Round-trip serialization
- Provider/caller policy intersection logic
- Default class selection

- fabric.rs — Fabric connection type and public API surface
- service.rs — service obligation integration
- stream.rs — region-owned stream state machine
- consumer.rs — consumer policy and delivery engine

title: [FABRIC][P0.6] Define CostVector type and per-feature cost estimation
description:
Define the CostVector type and per-feature cost estimation framework. Every major fabric feature must publish a cost vector so that design decisions can be evaluated quantitatively.

## CostVector Type Definition
Define in src/messaging/ir.rs alongside other FabricIR types:

```rust
pub struct CostVector {
    pub steady_state_latency: LatencyEstimate,
    pub tail_latency: LatencyEstimate,         // p99/p999
    pub storage_amplification: f64,            // ratio vs raw payload
    pub control_plane_amplification: f64,      // ratio of control vs data messages
    pub cpu_crypto_cost: CpuEstimate,          // per-message CPU budget
    pub evidence_bytes: ByteEstimate,          // per-decision evidence size
    pub restore_handoff_time: DurationEstimate, // time to restore/handoff state
}
```

## Supporting Types
- LatencyEstimate: median + p99 + p999, with units
- CpuEstimate: cycles or microseconds per message
- ByteEstimate: bytes per decision/message with min/max/typical
- DurationEstimate: duration with min/max/typical

## Requirements
1. Each DeliveryClass must have a baseline CostVector representing its expected costs
2. The intent compiler's validation pass must estimate cost vectors for compiled configurations
3. The explain plan (src/messaging/explain.rs) must include cost breakdown
4. CostVectors must be comparable: is config A cheaper than config B along each dimension?
5. Serialization to JSON for reporting and diagnostics

## Per-Class Baseline Defaults
- EphemeralInteractive: near-zero on all dimensions (no durability, no evidence, no crypto beyond TLS)
- DurableOrdered: moderate storage amplification, low control amplification
- ObligationBacked: adds evidence bytes, moderate CPU for obligation tracking
- MobilitySafe: adds restore/handoff time, higher control amplification for session migration
- ForensicReplayable: highest evidence bytes, highest storage amplification

## Tests
- CostVector construction for each DeliveryClass
- Comparison operators (cheaper_than, more_expensive_than along dimensions)
- JSON serialization round-trip
- Per-class defaults are reasonable (no zeros where there should be non-zero costs)
- Compiler produces cost estimates for sample configurations

title: [FABRIC][P9] Contract-Carrying Services
description:
# Phase 9: Contract-Carrying Services

## Purpose
Turn service contracts into rich behavioral artifacts. Service interfaces today say what messages look like but not deeper behavioral contracts under failure, overload, mobility, or compensation.

## Service Definition Carries
- Request and reply shape
- Cancellation and cleanup obligations
- Budget and cleanup urgency semantics
- Durability class and capture rules
- Compensation semantics
- Mobility or sovereignty constraints
- Evidence and audit requirements

## Authority Split (Critical)
Some terms are provider-declared invariants, others are caller-selectable request classes bounded by provider policy. Without this distinction, any caller could demand arbitrary mobility, durability, or overload semantics.

## What Clients/Operators Can Reason About
- Whether a call is replayable or must remain single-shot
- Whether a reply is best-effort, durable, or obligation-backed
- Whether the service may be deprioritized, shed, or protected under overload
- Whether the service may migrate across regions or must stay pinned
- Whether failed work compensates, retries, or dead-letters

## Goal
Subject-native services look like distributed behavioral interfaces that can be checked, compiled, and audited — not thin RPC over pub/sub.

## Relation to Existing Code
- service/service.rs has service trait concepts
- service/builder.rs has service building patterns
- combinator/circuit_breaker.rs has overload/failure patterns

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P9.3] Fabric-native service plane — unified service boundaries
description:
Most service meshes are bolt-on policy layers. Here, service boundaries routed through the subject fabric are expressed as:
- Subject morphisms (cross-domain routing and authority)
- Request/reply obligations (service completion tracking)

Direct channels and local GenServer calls still remain correct for hot-path local interactions. The fabric is for distributed naming and coordination, not a mandate for every local call.

- Tests: service registration via subject, cross-domain service call, service health via control subjects, service cancellation propagation

title: [FABRIC][P10] Federation as Capability-Scoped Region Bridges
description:
# Phase 10: Federation as Capability-Scoped Region Bridges

## Purpose
Define four distinct federation role types with sharper semantics than generic cluster peers. NATS is right that different topologies deserve distinct roles.

## Federation Roles
1. **LeafFabric**: Constrained export/import morphisms, intermittent connectivity tolerated, optimized for tenant enclaves/browsers/edge workers/offline-capable agents
2. **GatewayFabric**: Interest propagation across fabrics, control-plane advisories, low-amplification routing, bounded convergence and replay guarantees
3. **ReplicationLink**: Stream and consumer-state transfer, snapshot and catch-up, stronger ordering and durability policy
4. **EdgeReplayLink**: Ships trace/snapshot/evidence artifacts, supports lab replay of edge failures and delayed reconnection histories

## Design Principles
- Each role has distinct semantics and constraints
- Roles fit Asupersync bridge/snapshot surfaces better than generic peer abstraction
- All roles remain capability-scoped — no ambient federation authority
- Interest propagation has explicit admission control and backpressure budgets

## Relation to Existing Code
- distributed/bridge.rs has cross-node bridge semantics
- distributed/snapshot.rs has snapshot transfer
- distributed/assignment.rs has placement/distribution
- net/websocket/ for browser connectivity

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P11] Fabric IR Compiler
description:
# Phase 11: Fabric IR Compiler

## Purpose
Build the compiler that transforms high-level FabricIR declarations into runtime artifacts. This is the center of gravity that makes the whole design cohesive rather than a bag of loosely related subsystems.

## Compiler Inputs
- SubjectSchema declarations
- MorphismPlan definitions
- ServiceContract and ProtocolContract definitions
- DeliveryClass selections
- CapabilityTokenSchema definitions
- EvidencePolicy and PrivacyPolicy declarations
- CutPolicy and BranchPolicy definitions

## Compiler Outputs
- Sharded subject-index layouts
- Owned capability token types (in-process) + runtime capability checks (distributed)
- Transform and morphism certificates

title: [FABRIC][P12] Brokerless Peer-Cooperative Fabric Core
description:
# Phase 12: Brokerless Peer-Cooperative Fabric Core

## Purpose
Build the brokerless peer-cooperative architecture where subject space is governed by rotating peer quorums instead of fixed servers. This is the most radical departure from NATS.

## Core Abstraction
NOT a decentralized broker. A fabric of QUORUM-OWNED SUBJECT CELLS.

## SubjectCell
Smallest sovereign unit of the messaging fabric. Each cell owns:
- Canonical non-overlapping subject partition slice
- Current steward set (from steward-eligible nodes by placement policy)
- Control capsule: epoch, leases, obligation frontier, consumer-cursor ownership/fencing, policy state
- Data capsule: recent message blocks, stream segments, inbox fragments
- Repair policy: how cell reconstitutes under churn or packet loss

## ControlCapsuleV1
Per-cell, leadered, replicated control log with single sequencer lease per cell epoch:
- Authenticated crash-fault design (NOT BFT — that is a named future direction)
- Raft-like baseline replication (joint consensus for membership change)
- Per-cell sequencing authority explicit: one steward owns append lease for current epoch
- Reconfiguration as explicit joint old/new stewardship + new fenced sequencer lease
- Multiple cold/low-rate cells pack onto shared control shards

## Proof Obligations for ControlCapsuleV1
- At most one live sequencer lease per cell epoch
- No authoritative append from stale steward after fencing
- No config transition where old/new sets decide independently
- Every committed append has unique (cell_id, epoch, sequence) identity
- Consumer-control authority transfers fenced before old holder issues more decisions
- Late delivery responses reduce to deterministic stale reject or idempotent no-op

## Node Roles
- Origin for a publish
- Subscriber or consumer
- Temporary steward for hot subject cell
- Repair witness holding symbols
- Bridge for leaf/gateway-style propagation
NOT every participant is steward-eligible (browsers, edge agents, etc.)

## Discovery & Negotiation
Typed session with explicit lease obligations and replayable transitions:
- Node identity and capability set
- Signed membership/admission credentials
- Supported policy versions
- Available storage/uplink/repair budget
- Capability-scoped interest summaries
- Current cell stewardship leases
- Recent control-capsule epochs

## Placement
Subject-relative (not cluster-global):
- Each cell mapped through consistent hashing into candidate steward pool
- Active set negotiated from pool (capability, health, storage, latency, failure-domain diversity)
- Hot cells can widen steward set or enlist repair witnesses
- Cold cells collapse to minimal footprint
- Stewardship changes damped by hysteresis and rebalance budgets

## DataCapsule & RaptorQ Integration
- Bulk payload blocks encoded as systematic RaptorQ source symbols + repair symbols
- Symbols sprayed across stewards, witnesses, and peers per authorization/confidentiality/retention policy
- Publish ack only after control capsule commits AND durability target met
- Symbol authentication binds to object identity, epoch, and payload digest

## Relation to Existing Code
- distributed/ module has bridge, snapshot, assignment, encoding, distribution
- raptorq/ has full RFC6330 implementation with pipeline, decoder, encoder
- runtime/sharded_state.rs has ShardedState with ContendedMutex

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P12.3] DataCapsule with RaptorQ integration
description:
Build the DataCapsule using RaptorQ for recoverability instead of naive full replication. File: src/messaging/fabric.rs (data capsule portion)

- DataCapsule struct: cell_id, segments (Vec<Segment>), repair_policy, symbol_spread
- Segment struct: sequence_range, source_blocks, repair_symbols, sealed (bool)
- Publish flow (for durable classes):
  1. Origin computes target cell, opens publish obligation
  2. Steward quorum accepts control-capsule append record (subject, idempotency key, payload digest, epoch-fenced append sequence, durability class)
  3. Payload: tiny-message fast path (direct append) OR sealed segment window chunked into source blocks and RaptorQ-encoded
  4. Symbols sprayed across stewards, repair witnesses, and interested peers per authorization/confidentiality/retention/symbol-authentication policy
  5. Publish ack ONLY after control capsule commits AND durability target met
- Brokerless durability: cell doesn't need full replica on every steward — just enough symbol spread for chosen recoverability target
- Mobility without full re-copy: new stewards reconstruct from any sufficient symbol quorum
- Edge-tolerant fanout: intermittent nodes collect authorized symbols without permanent broker
- Progressive reliability classes: low-value traffic = shallow repair, high-value = deeper spread
- Stream-window elasticity: hot windows attract more repair symbols, contract when demand falls
- Coding granularity: at segment-window or large-payload level, NOT per-tiny-publish (CPU/latency budget)
- Ordinary ephemeral pub/sub does NOT pay this contract — strong durable path is explicit opt-in
- Symbol authentication: bound to object identity, epoch, and payload digest (witnesses can't forge)
- Symbol wrapping: symbols stored outside active steward quorum wrapped under subject-cell or policy-derived keys (prevent accidental data disclosure)
- Integration with existing raptorq/ module (RFC6330 implementation)
- Tests: publish flow (direct and coded paths), symbol spread, reconstruction from partial symbols, progressive reliability, mobility reconstruction, symbol authentication

comments.text: Sybil resistance design (critical for brokerless security): Without authenticated membership and capability enforcement, the brokerless design degenerates into an easy Sybil and data-poisoning target. The discovery protocol MUST: (1) Require signed membership/admission credentials before any trust is extended. (2) Namespace visibility must be narrower than generic membership — multi-tenant fabrics must assume raw subject prefixes, hot keys, and traffic shape are SENSITIVE metadata. Disclose only the minimum summaries required for placement and routing. (3) Peer-advertised health, interest, and placement hints remain ADVISORY only — authority comes from authenticated membership + current control-capsule epoch + capability policy. (4) Interest summaries should be capability-scoped or blinded — a node should not learn about subjects in namespaces it has no capability to access. This is part of the threat model: designed to resist Sybil pressure on brokerless admission (in-scope for V1).

title: [FABRIC][P12.7] Brokerless placement normalization pipeline
description:
Brokerless placement MUST run on authoritative normalized subject space, not on whatever textual subject spelling a publisher happened to use first. The normalization pipeline:
1. Import/export morphism application (resolve transforms)

3. Reply-space aggregation (group ephemeral reply subjects)
4. Canonical partitioning (produce non-overlapping SubjectCell slices)
The resulting SubjectCell slices MUST be: canonical (same logical subject always maps to same cell), non-overlapping (no subject belongs to two cells), hash-stable for a given membership epoch (placement does not change unless membership changes)
Without this pipeline: wildcard overlap, transform-dependent aliases, and reply-space churn would make ownership ambiguous and control-capsule count unbounded.

title: [FABRIC][P13] Advanced Brokerless: Cursor Leases, Rebalance, Keys
description:
# Phase 13: Advanced Brokerless Features

## Purpose
Build the advanced brokerless features: consumer cursor leases over recoverable capsules, cell self-rebalance, and the two-level key hierarchy.

## Consumer Cursor Leases
- Consumer cursor authority lives in control capsule or delegated cursor partitions
- Delivery rights are obligations and temporary leases
- Data served only by current stewards or leased relay peers with read-delegation tickets
- Pull consumers ask for specific sequence windows or demand classes
- Push consumers pinned temporarily to steward or delegated relay
- Every ack/nack/redelivery carries attempt-scoped certificate: (cell_id, epoch, cursor_authority_lease, sequence_or_window, delivery_attempt, obligation_id)
- Consumer failover radically cheaper: another steward with symbols + control capsule continues

## Cell Self-Rebalance
- Cell issues stewardship-change proposal under current epoch
- New stewards collect enough symbols for target recoverability class
- Consumer and reply obligations transferred or reissued explicitly
- Once cut certified: epoch advances, stale stewards fenced, old stewardship lease drains
- Semantic cut: no unresolved publish obligations below cut, no ambiguous consumer lease owners, no dangling reply rights, enough symbol spread for data capsule reconstitution

## Two-Level Key Hierarchy
- NOT full concurrent CGKA per hot subject cell
- Steward-pool control key layer with MLS/TreeKEM-style forward secrecy and post-compromise security
- Per-cell and per-segment keys derived from steward-pool epoch state
- K_pool_epoch → K_subgroup_epoch → K_cell_root → capability-separated subkeys (K_segment, K_symbol_wrap, K_symbol_auth, K_reply_space, K_metadata_blind, K_witness_wrap)
- Witnesses never receive K_cell_root
- Rotation triggered by membership change, compromise suspicion, PCS refresh, or control-capsule rebind
- Subgroup rotation for affected placement subgroup only
- Segment rotation via key-regression or generation-tagged derivation
- Witness revocation by advancing cell epoch and witness-wrap context
- Restore scrubbing: fresh cell IDs, epoch bindings, leases, reply spaces, key context

## Relation to Existing Code
- security/ module has key and authentication concepts
- distributed/snapshot.rs has snapshot/restore
- raptorq/ has symbol encoding/decoding

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.
