title: [FABRIC][P13.3] Two-level key hierarchy
description:
Implement the two-level key hierarchy for the brokerless fabric. File: src/messaging/privacy.rs (key hierarchy portion)

- NOT full concurrent CGKA per hot subject cell
- Steward-pool control key layer: MLS/TreeKEM-style forward secrecy and post-compromise security
- Key derivation chain:
  - K_pool_epoch: steward-pool epoch secret
  - K_subgroup_epoch = HKDF(K_pool_epoch, "subgroup-epoch" || placement_pool_id || subgroup_epoch || subgroup_roster_hash)
  - K_cell_root = HKDF(K_subgroup_epoch, "cell-root" || cell_id || cell_epoch || roster_hash || config_epoch_hash || cell_rekey_generation)
  - Capability-separated subkeys from K_cell_root: K_segment, K_symbol_wrap, K_symbol_auth, K_reply_space, K_metadata_blind, K_witness_wrap
- Witnesses NEVER receive K_cell_root (only ciphertext symbols, HPKE-wrapped material, or narrowly scoped witness tokens)
- Non-steward read serving requires bounded read-delegation tickets with explicit epoch scope, cacheability, and revocation
- Rotation semantics: epoch rotation (membership change, compromise, PCS refresh, rebind), subgroup rotation (only affected placement subgroup), segment rotation (key-regression or generation-tagged), witness revocation (advance cell epoch + witness-wrap context)
- Retroactive revocation honesty: revocation protects future epochs immediately but does NOT unread old ciphertext without rewrite/expiry
- Restore scrubbing: fresh cell IDs, epoch bindings, leases, reply spaces, and key derivation context before communication with real peers
- Optional cold-path extension: proof-of-retrievability for witnesses to prove fragment storage without replaying whole object
- Tests: key derivation correctness, rotation for each trigger type, subgroup isolation, witness key narrowing, restore scrubbing, read-delegation ticket lifecycle
close_reason: Existing privacy.rs implementation matches two-level key hierarchy requirements; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/asupersync/target-olive-privacy cargo test -p asupersync --lib --features messaging-fabric privacy -- --nocapture passed (18/18) covering deterministic derivation, rotation, witness narrowing, read-delegation lifecycle, and restore scrubbing

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Research-informed design justification: MLS/TreeKEM and TreeSync give strong foundation for authenticated group state, forward secrecy, and post-compromise security. BUT recent CGKA work (DeCAF, fork-resilient CGKA) shows decentralized concurrent rekey remains subtle and expensive. Therefore: do NOT run full concurrent CGKA per hot subject cell. Instead: steward-pool level MLS-like machinery with HKDF-derived per-cell keys underneath. The key hierarchy in summary: MLS for steward-group secrecy + HKDF for cell/segment keys + HPKE for witness access + optional PoR for cold-path audit. Retroactive revocation honesty: revocation protects future epochs immediately but does NOT unread old ciphertext without rewrite or expiry.

title: [FABRIC][P13.5] Delegated cursor partitions for high-fanout consumers
description:
ControlCapsuleV1 is bounded-fanout and bounded-ack-rate. Once consumer cardinality gets large, cursor state MUST NOT collapse into one monolithic control capsule. Solution: delegated cursor partitions.
- Control capsule delegates cursor authority for specific consumer subsets to partition leaders
- Each partition leader manages cursor state for its consumers within the delegated authority
- Partition leaders report coarse batched summaries back to control capsule
- AttemptCertificate specializes cursor_authority_lease into cursor_partition_lease for delegated variants
- Partition assignment: by consumer group, by subject sub-range, or by hash bucket
- Partition rebalance: explicit authority transfer with fencing (same protocol as cell rebalance but at cursor level)
- This is what makes ControlCapsuleV1 honest: it admits its bounded scope and defines the scaling mechanism
- File: src/messaging/consumer.rs (partition portion)
- Tests: partition creation, consumer assignment, coarse checkpoint reporting, partition rebalance, authority fencing
close_reason: validated targeted consumer partition/delegation selectors after fresh-eyes summary invalidation fix

title: [FABRIC][P13.6] Read-delegation tickets for non-steward serving
description:
Non-steward read serving requires bounded read-delegation tickets, not "any authorized peer can serve" (which is NOT a safe V1 default).
ReadDelegationTicket struct:
- cell_id, epoch (bound to current cell epoch)
- cursor_lease_ref (which cursor authority this delegates from)
- segment_window (which segments this ticket covers)
- expiry (bounded time)
- cacheability_rules (how long can served data be cached)
- revocation_handle (how to revoke this ticket)
Only current stewards or peers carrying valid read-delegation tickets bound to current cell epoch may serve data. Broader opportunistic serving waits until delegation/revocation model is proven.
- File: src/messaging/consumer.rs (delegation portion)
- Tests: ticket creation, ticket validation, ticket expiry, ticket revocation, reject serving without valid ticket, reject stale-epoch ticket
close_reason: Code complete: privacy.rs ReadDelegationTicket with is_usable_for validation and issuance

title: [FABRIC][P13.7] Proof-of-retrievability for cold-path witness audit
description:
Cold-path extension for long-lived witnesses or archival repair lanes: system can optionally use proof-of-retrievability or succinct erasure-coding proofs so a witness can prove it still stores fragments consistent with a committed capsule WITHOUT replaying the whole object.
Use cases:
- Cold durability audits
- Migration safety checks
- Delayed rebalance verification
- Hostile or weakly trusted witness pools
This MUST stay off the hot publish path. It is for audit/verification, not steady-state latency.
- File: src/messaging/fabric.rs (witness portion)
- Tests: witness stores fragments, witness proves retrievability, verify proof without full reconstruction, detect missing/corrupted fragments

title: [FABRIC][P14] CRDT-Augmented Mergeable Control Plane
description:
# Phase 14: CRDT-Augmented Mergeable Control Plane

## Purpose
Add delta-CRDT convergent state for non-authoritative metadata surfaces. The proposal gets materially stronger by saying exactly where strong sequencing is required and where convergent merge is enough.

## Authoritative State (remains in fenced leadered control capsules)
- Appends, authority transfer, reply rights, cursor authority, epoch changes

## Non-Authoritative Surfaces (converge as delta-CRDTs)
- Interest summaries
- Coarse cursor checkpoints
- Membership views
- Lag and load sketches
- Selected advisory aggregates
- Delegated-partition aggregates

## Design Sweet Spot
- Strong consistency where ambiguity would be dangerous
- Convergent merge where centralization would become bottleneck
- Concrete answer to hardest practical question: preventing control plane from becoming global metadata bottleneck

## Scaling Story
- Optimistic propagation across stewards and relays
- Leaderless convergence on cold paths and during transient partitions
- Dramatically cheaper high-fanout consumer churn
- Much lower pressure on authoritative sequencer lease

## Guardrails
- CRDTs ONLY on explicitly non-authoritative, mergeable surfaces
- Never absorb authoritative state into CRDT
- CRDTs are complement to RaptorQ data capsules and fenced control capsules

## Relation to Existing Code
- obligation/crdt.rs already has CRDT concepts
- distributed/ module has convergent state patterns

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P14.1] Delta-CRDT types for non-authoritative metadata
description:
Define delta-CRDT types for mergeable non-authoritative control surfaces. File: src/messaging/control.rs (CRDT portion)

- InterestSummary: delta-CRDT for subscriber interest aggregation (subject patterns with counts). Join-semilattice with merge. Compressible. Used for routing optimization.
- CursorCheckpoint: delta-CRDT for coarse consumer cursor positions. Convergent merge across stewards. Used for load estimation and routing.
- MembershipView: delta-CRDT for node membership and health status. Eventually consistent view. Used for placement decisions.
- LagSketch: delta-CRDT for consumer lag and load estimation. Bounded-error sketch. Used for backpressure and routing.
- AdvisoryAggregate: delta-CRDT for advisory count/rate summaries. Window-based aggregation. Used for monitoring.
- All CRDTs: implement JoinSemilattice trait with merge(), delta(), apply_delta()
- Guardrails: CRDTs ONLY on non-authoritative surfaces. Authoritative state (appends, authority transfer, reply rights, cursor authority, epoch changes) remains in fenced leadered control capsules.
- Tests: merge correctness for each type, delta generation and application, convergence (eventually same value regardless of delivery order), bounded error for sketches

title: [FABRIC][P15] Advanced Semantic Features
description:
# Phase 15: Advanced Semantic Features

## Purpose
Build the advanced features that make the fabric a new category of distributed systems substrate: evidence-native data plane, cut-certified mobility, workflow/saga kernel, counterfactual control, distributed supervision, bounded-regret reliability, consistency certificates, recoverable service capsules, intent-compiled operations, etc.

## Features
1. Evidence-Native Data Plane: FrankenSuite evidence for routing/delivery decisions
2. Cut-Certified Mobility: hot-cell evacuation with proof no obligations orphaned
3. Subject-Native Workflow/Saga Kernel: durable workflow steps as subject transitions + obligations
4. Continuous Counterfactual Control: shadow branches from certified cuts, compare candidate worlds
5. Distributed Supervision Compiler: supervision graphs + subject morphisms + failure domains
6. Bounded-Regret Reliability Control: adaptive tuning within declared safety envelopes
7. Local-to-Global Consistency Certificates: sheaf/obstruction-based topology checking
8. Recoverable Service Capsules: portable hosted state with authority-scrubbing on restore
9. Intent-Compiled Operations: operator intent surface compiled to policy artifacts
10. Commutativity-Aware Sharding: semantic independence partitioning above canonical cell ownership
11. Branch-Addressable Reality: live/lagged/replayed/canary/forensic branch attachment
12. Causality-Native Streams: partial-order views above linear control kernels
13. Budget-Carrying Traffic: overload decisions driven by semantic damage not just load
14. Certified Cut Lattice & Reality Index: policy-scoped retained index of meaningful cuts
15. Privacy-Budgeted Metadata Surfaces: differential-privacy noise on exported metadata
16. Quantitative Obligation Contracts: SLO-style probabilistic contracts above binary obligations
17. Reactive Protocol Synthesis: generate handler skeletons from protocol contracts
18. Speculative Subject-Cell Execution: tentative publish with deterministic rollback

Each of these is a separate task within this epic.

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

- NOT replacing per-cell append sequencing or control-capsule linearity

title: [FABRIC][P15.13] Budget-carrying traffic and obligation-aware degradation

Drive overload decisions by semantic damage, not just load. File: src/messaging/policy.rs (degradation portion)

- Preserve cutover/cleanup/reply-critical work before lower-value traffic
- Prefer degradation paths minimizing orphaned obligations
- Widen repair for work whose failure creates largest semantic debt
- Degrade read models/low-value fanout/expensive replay before violating stronger contracts
- Keep operator-intent and recovery channels alive under pressure by design
- Tests: degradation ordering by semantic value, reserved capacity for control lanes, obligation-minimizing degradation paths

- Enables: 'attach to latest cut causally before incident X', 'fork canary from last certified cut under policy Y', 'show smallest cut explaining this user-visible outcome', 'restore only subtree whose obligations can still be lawfully resumed'

The runtime starts to look like a "secure, replayable, distributed namespace kernel."
This is NOT about pretending to solve full CPU/memory/storage isolation — it is the namespace analogy applied to subject-based addressing. The capability model (Cx + tokens) provides the authority enforcement. The morphism system provides the namespace mapping.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Implementation guidance: This builds on Asupersync's existing sheaf and obstruction infrastructure (see trace/distributed/sheaf.rs). The key insight is that each component (cell, morphism, cursor partition, federation edge, supervisor domain) emits a LOCAL consistency section. The fabric then checks whether these local sections can be GLUED into a global section. If not, the obstruction certificate tells the operator exactly where and why global consistency fails. Specific gluing checks: (1) Morphism composition: if A→B and B→C exist, the composed A→C must respect all facets of both morphisms. (2) Reply-space closure: every reply obligation from an import/export edge must be resolvable within the declared reply-space. (3) Cursor partition disjointness: delegated cursor partitions must not overlap. (4) Obligation coverage: a cutover plan must account for every live obligation below the cut. (5) Witness placement: selected witness set must satisfy BOTH durability target AND confidentiality constraints (these can conflict). Test each gluing check independently and in combination.

title: [FABRIC][P16] Testing, Verification & E2E Validation
description:
# Phase 16: Testing, Verification & E2E Validation

## Purpose
Comprehensive unit tests, lab runtime integration tests, deterministic replay tests, E2E integration test scripts, and conformance tests for the entire fabric.

## Test Categories
1. Unit tests for every module (inline #[cfg(test)])
2. Lab runtime integration tests (deterministic scheduling, virtual time)
3. Deterministic replay tests (verify schedule-replayability)
4. E2E integration test scripts with detailed logging
5. Conformance tests for protocol contracts and session types
6. Property-based tests (proptest) for critical invariants
7. Benchmark tests for hot-path performance

## Critical Invariants to Test
- No task leaks in fabric tasks
- No obligation leaks in request/reply, streams, consumers
- Region close = quiescence for all fabric components
- Losers drained after races in delivery
- Cancel-correctness of all fabric paths
- Interest state cleanup on cancelled subscribers
- Morphism reversibility where required
- Session type duality and compatibility
- Control capsule proof obligations (single sequencer, no stale appends, etc.)
- Key hierarchy derivation correctness

## E2E Test Scenarios
- Multi-node publish/subscribe
- Request/reply with obligation tracking
- Stream capture, mirror, and source
- Consumer failover and cursor transfer
- Federation across fabric roles
- Brokerless cell rebalance
- Snapshot fork and restore
- Control-plane advisory flow
- Concurrent morphism changes under load

## Logging Requirements
All tests must produce detailed structured logs for post-mortem analysis.

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][CROSS] Threat model, fault model, and economic envelope
description:
Document the threat model, fault model, and economic envelope for the Semantic Subject Fabric. This is CRITICAL for V1 scoping — every design decision must be evaluated against these boundaries.

## In Scope and Designed to Resist
1. **Crash-fault participants**: stewards/relays that fail silently without Byzantine behavior
2. **Honest-but-curious stewards and witnesses**: follow protocol but attempt to infer tenant/traffic info
3. **Stale or slow participants**: appends/acks/cursor decisions from past epochs
4. **Unauthorized namespace access**: clients using subjects/reply spaces without capabilities
5. **Replay attacks**: old messages/tokens/certificates replayed across epochs
6. **Sybil pressure**: unauthorized nodes attempting to bias placement/stewardship

## Partially Addressed but Not Eliminated
1. **Network-level traffic analysis**: bounded with DP summaries and blinded metadata
2. **Colluding protocol-compliant stewards**: bounded by key narrowing and trust scoping

## Explicitly Out of Scope for V1
1. **Byzantine-fault stewards** — ControlCapsuleV1 is NOT BFT
2. **Microarchitectural side channels** on crypto ops
3. **Legal coercion** of steward operators
4. **Full physical resource isolation** between tenants on shared hardware

## Documentation Requirements
- Document in src/messaging/mod.rs as module-level doc comments
- Create a standalone design document (docs/FABRIC_THREAT_MODEL.md or similar)
- Reference from every phase epic that touches security boundaries

## Economic Envelope — Cost Vector Requirement
Every major feature MUST publish a cost vector with these 7 dimensions:
- steady-state latency
- tail latency (p99/p999)
- storage amplification (ratio vs raw payload)
- control-plane amplification (ratio of control vs data messages)
- CPU/crypto cost (per-message CPU budget)
- evidence bytes (per-decision evidence size)
- restore/handoff time (time to restore/handoff state)

## Implementation Risks to Track
1. **Hot-path latency explosion** → keep authority-plane coordination narrow and class-gated
2. **Hidden global metadata plane** → CRDT summaries + delegated cursor partitions + strict control-capsule budgets
3. **Developer overwhelm** → progressive disclosure with no-footgun guarantees
4. **Class proliferation** → small named service-class vocabulary
5. **Privacy/reporting distortion** → DP only on exported summaries, never on authoritative control
6. **Speculative fast-path misfire** → opt-in, low-conflict only, kill-switchable

## Deliverables
- Module-level doc comments in src/messaging/mod.rs
- Standalone design document
- CostVector struct defined in src/messaging/ir.rs (coordinate with P0.6 bead)
- Tests: N/A (documentation task), but CostVector struct should compile

title: [FABRIC][CROSS] Design guardrails — enforceable invariants checklist
description:
Document and enforce the complete set of design guardrails for the Semantic Subject Fabric. These MUST be documented, enforced by code review, and tested.

## Do NOT Copy from NATS
- Goroutine-per-connection mental model
- Ambient authority over time/storage/network
- Protocol-first internals
- Lock-heavy shared mutability
- Casual cancellation semantics

## DO Preserve from NATS
- Disciplined bring-up order
- Subject-first API design
- Layered routing caches
- Explicit topology roles
- Stream capture through same substrate as ordinary messaging
- System advisories as native fabric messages
- The operational simplicity of NATS's public mental model

## Soundness Frontier Honesty (30+ Rules)
Every one of these must be documented and enforced:
1. Guarantees hold inside Asupersync's capability boundary, NOT for arbitrary unmanaged external side effects
2. Convergence-to-quiescence assumes runtime's usual cooperative conditions (checkpoints, bounded masking, fair progress)
3. Local region quiescence does NOT imply globally consistent distributed cut; cross-node needs explicit cut/lease/snapshot protocol
4. Replayable snapshots and counterfactual runs MUST model remote peers, clocks, and external effects explicitly
5. Branch-addressable views MUST keep unmanaged external side effects fenced or explicitly modeled
6. Branch/cut indexes MUST stay retention- and access-policy scoped (not infinite history)
7. Distributed execution uses idempotency + leases; NO magical global exactly-once claims
8. Evidence/decision recording is policy-driven and selective; NOT sprayed everywhere by default
9. Reasoning-plane evidence/branch/query MUST NOT leak into default packet path; elevation is explicit and attributable
10. Service-class vocabulary stays small, named, inspectable; NO team-invented one-offs
11. Subject routing/fanout needs explicit admission control and backpressure budgets
12. In-band control subjects are NOT the only recovery path; break-glass path preserved
13. Causality-native views don't eliminate linear control streams; they sit above dependency metadata
14. Don't force every peer to decode/store everything; data capsule split lets recoverability replace replication
15. Keep control capsules small enough for cheap stewardship changes; don't accrete policy/telemetry
16. Certified cut/branch indexes need explicit retention, compaction, materialization policy
17. Don't let high-fanout consumer state collapse into monolithic control capsule; need shard/hierarchy
18. ControlCapsuleV1 doesn't handle arbitrary hot-cell fanout before delegated cursor partitions exist
19. Publish ack certifies chosen recoverability class, NOT impossible downstream guarantees
20. Bind repair symbols to epoch and retention generation (no resurrection of expired data)
21. Require authenticated membership and capability for discovery/stewardship (prevent Sybil/data-poisoning)
22. Not all participants can/should steward; eligibility is capability + policy question
23. Don't synchronously RaptorQ-encode every tiny publish; use direct/batched fast paths
24. Don't run full concurrent CGKA per hot subject cell; put agreement at steward-pool layer
25. CRDTs ONLY on non-authoritative surfaces; never absorb authoritative state
26. Don't claim BFT from Raft-based ControlCapsuleV1; BFT is named future direction
27. Don't claim DP eliminates traffic analysis; it bounds leakage per disclosure
28. Session type checking covers in-process Rust (static) + distributed (dynamic); NOT arbitrary unmanaged participants
29. Reactive synthesis produces correct scaffolding, NOT correct business logic
30. Speculative execution is for low-conflict classes with rollback and kill switches only
31. Keep heavy crypto proofs off default path; compliance lanes only
32. No hot-path homomorphic transforms; encrypted payloads + blinded metadata is practical plan
33. Progressive disclosure fails if Layer 0/1 become footguns requiring Layer 3/4
34. Keep randomized/irreversible transforms OUT of authority-bearing import/export edges

## Deliverables
- Create docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md with the complete checklist
- Add enforcement summary in src/messaging/mod.rs module docs
- Each guardrail should be testable or reviewable — tag with [TESTABLE] or [REVIEW-ONLY]
- Code review checklist referencing guardrail numbers for every PR in the messaging module

title: [FABRIC][P1] Core Subject Fabric
description:
# Phase 1: Core Subject Fabric

## Purpose
Build the subject primitive as a first-class runtime object with a Sublist-style routing engine, wildcard matching, interest state tracking, and subject semantic families. This is the foundation that all messaging, federation, and control-plane features build on.

## Key Components
1. **Subject Primitive** (src/messaging/subject.rs): Subject type with dot-separated token paths, SubjectSchema compilation, semantic family classification
2. **Sublist Routing Core**: Trie-based subject matching engine (inspired by NATS server/sublist.go) with generation-invalidated caches for literal-subject hot lookups and per-link hot caches
3. **Wildcard Matching**: Support for * (single token) and > (tail match) wildcards, compatible with NATS subject language
4. **Interest State Tracking**: Cancel-correct subscriber interest registration — cancelled subscribers must not leave ghost interest behind. Interest state changes are explicit events with trace-visible invalidation epochs.
5. **Queue Groups**: Multiple subscribers sharing work under one subject (one message per group delivery)

## Design Principles
- Subject fabric is for DISTRIBUTED naming and coordination, not a mandate that every local hot-path use subjects
- Direct channels, sessions, and GenServer calls remain correct for local hot-path interactions
- The subject fabric provides: distributed actor naming/rendezvous, service addressing, stream capture coordination, control-plane advisories, distributed federation
- All sharing one primary address model where distributed naming and policy matter

## Physical Design
- Actor-side mutation semantics own the canonical subject-index contract
- Index itself should be physically sharded and read-optimized, not funneled through one monolithic mutable authority
- Interest registration is cancel-correct via the existing cancel/drain/finalize protocol

## Relation to Existing Code
- transport/router.rs has RoutingTable with TTL, EndpointId routing — this extends that concept to subject-based addressing
- distributed/assignment.rs has placement concepts — subjects extend these with semantic families

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P1.1] Build Sublist trie-based routing engine
description:
## Overview
Build a trie-based subject matching engine in src/messaging/subject.rs (routing portion), inspired by NATS server/sublist.go.

## Requirements

### Subject Matching
- Subjects are dot-separated token paths (e.g., `foo.bar.baz`)
- Support literal match: exact token equality at each level
- Support single-token wildcard (`*`): matches exactly one token at that position
- Support tail wildcard (`>`): matches one or more tokens from that position to end of subject
- Examples: `foo.*` matches `foo.bar` but not `foo.bar.baz`; `foo.>` matches `foo.bar` and `foo.bar.baz`

### Trie Structure
- Internal trie nodes keyed by token string
- Each node has: children map, wildcard child (`*`), tail-wildcard child (`>`), and subscriber set
- Insert/remove operations maintain structural invariants (prune empty branches on remove)
- Lookup walks the trie, collecting all matching subscribers across literal, wildcard, and tail-wildcard branches

### Caching
- Generation-invalidated literal-subject hot caches: cache full match results for literal (no-wildcard) subjects
- Per-link hot caches: each link (connection/session) maintains its own cache of recently resolved subjects
- Cache entries tagged with a generation counter; any mutation to the trie bumps the generation, invalidating all caches
- Cache hit path should be sub-microsecond (simple HashMap lookup + generation check)

### Concurrency
- Thread-safe concurrent reads with write-serialized mutations
- Read path: lock-free for cached lookups (AtomicU64 generation check + cached result)
- Write path: single writer at a time (Mutex or similar), bumps generation after mutation
- No reader starvation: writes must not block reads for extended periods

### Cancel-Correctness
- Interest registration is cancel-correct: when a subscriber is cancelled (Cx cancelled, task dropped), its interest MUST be removed from the trie
- No ghost interest: a cancelled subscriber must never appear in match results
- Implementation: tie subscriber lifetime to a guard/handle that removes interest on drop
- Test: subscribe, cancel the subscriber's Cx, verify the subscriber no longer appears in any match results

### Queue Groups
- Multiple subscribers can register under the same subject with a queue group name
- For a given message, only ONE subscriber per queue group receives delivery
- Queue group selection should be round-robin or random (not always the same subscriber)
- A subscriber can be in at most one queue group per subject

### Performance
- O(tokens) lookup where tokens = number of dot-separated segments in the subject
- Cache hit should be sub-microsecond
- Benchmark: 1M lookups/sec for cached literal subjects on modern hardware

## File Location
src/messaging/subject.rs (routing portion)

## Tests (in this file or tests/)
- Literal match: exact match, no match, partial match
- Single wildcard: `*` at various positions, multiple wildcards
- Tail wildcard: `>` at various depths, `>` alone matches everything
- Combined: `foo.*.>`, `*.bar.>`, etc.
- Edge cases: empty subject, single token, very deep nesting (100+ levels)
- Queue groups: single group delivery, multiple groups, group removal
- Cache: hit/miss, invalidation on mutation, generation rollover
- Concurrency: concurrent subscribe/unsubscribe/lookup from multiple threads
- Cancel-correctness: subscribe, drop guard, verify removal
- At least 20+ test cases total
close_reason: Code complete: subject.rs Sublist with TrieNode, wildcard matching, 60 tests

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: NATS implementation reference: server/sublist.go implements the trie-based matching. Key patterns to adapt: (1) the Sublist struct with Insert/Match/Remove operations, (2) result caching with generation-based invalidation, (3) queue group handling where one subscriber per group receives each message, (4) the SublistResult type with subscription lists. The Asupersync version must additionally make interest registration cancel-correct — NATS doesn't have this because Go's GC handles cleanup. In Asupersync, a cancelled subscriber MUST NOT leave ghost interest behind, which means interest removal must participate in the cancel/drain/finalize protocol.

title: [FABRIC][P1.2] Subject index sharding and read optimization
description:
## Overview
Implement physical sharding of the subject index for read optimization in src/messaging/subject.rs. The index must NOT be funneled through one monolithic mutable authority — instead, it is physically sharded so that reads on different shards are fully independent.

## Requirements

### Shard Assignment
- Shard by subject prefix hash: take the first N tokens of a subject, hash them, and map to a shard index
- Number of shards configurable at construction time (default: num_cpus or a reasonable power of 2, e.g., 16)
- Shard assignment is deterministic: same subject always maps to same shard
- Hash function: use a fast, well-distributed hash (e.g., FxHash, AHash) — not cryptographic

### Read Path (Lock-Free for Cached Lookups)
- Each shard has its own generation counter (AtomicU64)
- Cached lookups check the shard's generation counter — if unchanged, return cached result directly
- No mutex acquisition on the read hot path for cache hits
- Read path for cache miss: acquire a read lock (RwLock) on the shard's trie, perform lookup, update cache
- Reads on different shards are fully independent — no cross-shard synchronization

### Write Path (Serialized Per-Shard)
- Write operations (subscribe, unsubscribe) acquire a write lock on the target shard only
- Writes to different shards can proceed concurrently
- After mutation, the shard's generation counter is bumped (Acquire/Release ordering)
- No global write lock — only the affected shard is locked

### Actor-Side Mutation Semantics
- The actor (GenServer, task, etc.) that owns a subscription is the canonical authority for mutation
- Subscribe/unsubscribe operations originate from the owning actor
- The subject index is the shared read-optimized projection of actor-owned state
- This means: actors do NOT read-then-write the index; they issue write commands and the index applies them

### Generation-Based Cache Coherence
- Each shard maintains its own monotonically increasing generation counter
- Cache entries store the generation at time of lookup
- On read, compare cached generation with current shard generation
- If generations match, cache hit; if not, re-lookup from trie and update cache
- Generation overflow: use wrapping arithmetic (u64 won't overflow in practice, but handle gracefully)

## File Location
src/messaging/subject.rs (sharding portion)

## Tests
- Shard distribution uniformity: subscribe 1000 random subjects, verify no shard has >2x the average load
- Concurrent reads during writes: spawn readers and writers on different shards, verify no data races (Miri if possible)
- Concurrent reads during writes on SAME shard: verify correctness (readers see pre-write or post-write state, never partial)
- Generation advancement: subscribe, check generation, unsubscribe, check generation increased
- Cross-shard independence: write to shard A does not bump shard B's generation
- Cache coherence: cached lookup returns correct results after mutation on same shard
- Actor mutation semantics: verify that subscribe/unsubscribe from the owning actor correctly updates the index
close_reason: Code complete: subject.rs ShardedSublist with per-shard RwLock, generation counters

title: [FABRIC][P1.3] Subject semantic family classification and validation
description:
## Overview
Implement SubjectSchema compilation and semantic family classification in src/messaging/subject.rs. Subject declarations compile into SubjectSchema artifacts with semantic family assignment. The family choice constrains admissible transforms, default service class, reply-space law, evidence policy, and mobility permissions.

## Requirements

### Semantic Families
Define the following subject semantic families (enum SubjectFamily):
- **Event**: fire-and-forget notifications (e.g., `system.events.user.created`)
- **Request**: request-reply pairs expecting a response (e.g., `api.users.get`)
- **Reply**: response subjects auto-generated for request-reply (e.g., `_INBOX.abc123`)
- **Stream**: ordered, potentially persistent message streams (e.g., `data.orders.us-east`)
- **Control**: internal control-plane subjects (e.g., `$SYS.server.ping`)
- **Service**: service discovery and health (e.g., `$SVC.auth.health`)
- **CaptureSelector**: subjects used as subscription patterns with wildcards for capture (e.g., `orders.*.status`)

### SubjectSchema
A SubjectSchema contains:
- `pattern`: the subject pattern string (may contain wildcards for CaptureSelector family)
- `family`: the semantic family (SubjectFamily enum)
- `service_class`: default QoS/service class (e.g., BestEffort, AtLeastOnce, ExactlyOnce)
- `reply_space_rule`: for Request family, how reply subjects are generated (e.g., InboxPrefix, Deterministic)
- `evidence_policy`: whether messages on this subject require evidence/audit trail (e.g., None, Log, Prove)
- `mobility`: whether the subject can be federated across cluster boundaries (Local, Federated, Global)
- `transforms`: list of admissible transforms (e.g., Map, Filter, Aggregate) — family constrains which are valid

### SubjectSchema Compilation
- `SubjectSchema::compile(declaration) -> Result<SubjectSchema, SchemaError>`
- Validates family-specific constraints:
  - Reply subjects MUST have a ReplySpaceRule
  - Control subjects MUST be in the `$SYS` namespace (pattern starts with `$SYS.`)
  - Service subjects MUST be in the `$SVC` namespace
  - CaptureSelector MUST contain at least one wildcard (`*` or `>`)
  - Event subjects MUST NOT have ExactlyOnce service class (fire-and-forget semantics)
  - Request subjects MUST have a reply_space_rule set
- Returns descriptive SchemaError on validation failure

### SubjectRegistry
- `SubjectRegistry::new() -> SubjectRegistry`
- `register(schema: SubjectSchema) -> Result<(), RegistryError>`: register a compiled schema; error if conflicting pattern already registered
- `deregister(pattern: &str) -> Option<SubjectSchema>`: remove a schema by pattern
- `lookup(subject: &str) -> Option<&SubjectSchema>`: find the most specific matching schema for a concrete subject
- `list_by_family(family: SubjectFamily) -> Vec<&SubjectSchema>`: list all schemas of a given family
- Thread-safe: concurrent lookups with serialized mutations (similar pattern to routing trie)

### Family Constraints Table
| Family          | Admissible Transforms    | Default Service Class | Reply Rule    | Evidence | Mobility  |
|-----------------|--------------------------|----------------------|---------------|----------|-----------|
| Event           | Map, Filter              | BestEffort           | None          | None     | Federated |
| Request         | Map                      | AtLeastOnce          | Required      | Log      | Federated |
| Reply           | None                     | AtLeastOnce          | N/A (is reply)| None     | Local     |
| Stream          | Map, Filter, Aggregate   | AtLeastOnce          | None          | Log      | Global    |
| Control         | None                     | BestEffort           | Optional      | Prove    | Local     |
| Service         | None                     | AtLeastOnce          | Optional      | Log      | Local     |
| CaptureSelector | Filter                   | BestEffort           | None          | None     | Local     |

## File Location
src/messaging/subject.rs

## Tests
- Compile valid schemas for each family: verify all fields populated correctly
- Compile invalid schemas: Reply without ReplySpaceRule -> error, Control not in $SYS -> error, CaptureSelector without wildcard -> error, Event with ExactlyOnce -> error, Request without reply_space_rule -> error
- SubjectRegistry: register, lookup, deregister, list_by_family
- Lookup specificity: more specific pattern wins over less specific
- Concurrent registry operations: concurrent register/lookup from multiple threads
- Transform validation: verify family constrains admissible transforms (e.g., Event cannot have Aggregate transform)

Bead text is partially stale relative to current architecture because ir.rs already owns SubjectSchema/SubjectFamily; this slice therefore stayed confined to the ownerless subject.rs registry semantics.

title: [FABRIC][P1.4] Unit tests for subject fabric
description:
## Overview
Comprehensive unit and integration tests for the subject fabric (P1.1 routing, P1.2 sharding, P1.3 semantic families). This task depends on P1.1, P1.2, and P1.3 being complete.

## Requirements

### Routing Correctness (30+ test cases)
Test the trie-based routing engine from P1.1:
- Literal match: exact match returns subscriber, non-match returns empty
- Single wildcard (`*`): `foo.*` matches `foo.bar`, not `foo.bar.baz`
- Tail wildcard (`>`): `foo.>` matches `foo.bar` and `foo.bar.baz`
- Combined wildcards: `*.bar.>`, `foo.*.baz`, `foo.*.>`
- Multiple subscribers on same subject
- Overlapping patterns: `foo.bar`, `foo.*`, `foo.>` all match `foo.bar`
- Edge cases: empty subject handling, single-token subjects, very long subjects (100+ tokens)
- `>` alone matches all subjects
- `*` alone matches single-token subjects only
- No partial matches: `foo.bar` does not match `foo.bar.baz`
- Unsubscribe: remove subscriber, verify no longer in results
- Re-subscribe: unsubscribe then subscribe again, verify works correctly

### Queue Group Tests
- Single queue group: 3 subscribers in group `workers`, verify only 1 receives per lookup
- Multiple queue groups: groups `A` and `B` on same subject, verify 1 from each group
- Queue group removal: remove one member, verify remaining members still work
- Queue group + non-group: non-group subscribers AND group subscribers on same subject — non-group gets every message, group gets one-per-group
- Round-robin or distribution verification: over 100 lookups, all group members should receive roughly equal share

### Cancel-Correctness Tests
- Subscribe via guard, drop guard, verify subscriber removed from trie
- Subscribe via guard, cancel the Cx, verify subscriber removed
- Subscribe multiple, cancel one, verify only the cancelled one is removed
- Rapid subscribe/cancel cycles: no ghost interest accumulates
- Concurrent cancel + lookup: cancel in one thread while looking up in another — lookup must never return the cancelled subscriber after the cancel completes

### Sharding Tests (P1.2)
- Distribution uniformity: 1000 random subjects, verify no shard >2x average
- Concurrent reads during writes: spawn readers and writers, verify no panics or incorrect results
- Generation counters: verify generation bumps on mutation, cache invalidation works
- Cross-shard independence: mutation on shard A does not affect shard B's generation or cache

title: [FABRIC][CROSS] Strategic north star — five success criteria
description:
Document and enforce the five strategic success criteria that determine whether the Semantic Subject Fabric is worth building. Every design decision must be tested against these criteria.

## Five Success Criteria
1. **The public mental model MUST remain NATS-small** even as internal semantics get much richer. If a developer needs to understand subject cells, stewardship, or fountain coding to publish a message, the design has failed.
2. **Stronger guarantees MUST be named service classes, NOT hidden taxes on the common case.** The default (EphemeralInteractive) path must have zero overhead from durability, session types, or evidence recording. Stronger classes are opt-in and explicitly named.
3. **Every radical behavior MUST lower into small, inspectable artifacts**: tokens, certificates, leases, cut records, session contracts, key contexts, or explain plans. No magic — everything is tangible and debuggable.
4. **Autonomous policy loops MUST always run inside declared safety envelopes** with replay, evidence, and rollback. No autonomous action without declared bounds, recorded evidence, and the ability to undo.
5. **The first product wedge should be systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation at the same time.** This is the unique value proposition — not competing with NATS on simple pub/sub.

## Anti-Goal
A grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower, the rare case magical, and the operator story less legible than NATS would be a MISTAKE. This is the failure mode to actively guard against.

## Target
A fabric whose default path is simpler than today's stack, while its stronger paths are dramatically more auditable and compositional.

## Enforcement
- Document in src/messaging/mod.rs module-level docs
- Reference in every phase epic's description
- Every PR in the messaging module must state which criteria it advances
- Periodic review: does the current implementation still satisfy all 5?

## Tests
- No automated tests (this is a design-governance task)
- But every feature bead should reference which north star criteria it serves

title: [FABRIC][CROSS] Progressive disclosure model — layered API with no-footgun guarantees
description:
Design and enforce the progressive disclosure model for the fabric API. Users must be able to start simple and adopt stronger semantics incrementally, with each layer independently correct.

## Layer Definitions
- **Layer 0**: Connect, publish, subscribe — NATS-simple, EphemeralInteractive class, no obligations. This is the default. A user who never reads beyond Layer 0 docs should be productive and safe.
- **Layer 1**: Request/reply with timeouts — still simple, optional service obligations. Adds structured request/reply but no durability requirements.
- **Layer 2**: Durable streams, consumers, acks — DurableOrdered class, obligation-backed. Introduces persistence, consumer groups, and acknowledgment protocols.
- **Layer 3**: Session-typed protocols, service contracts, decision contracts — ObligationBacked/MobilitySafe classes. Introduces static protocol checking and formal service contracts.
- **Layer 4**: Counterfactual branches, intent compilation, forensic replay — ForensicReplayable class. Full reasoning-plane capabilities for post-incident analysis and what-if exploration.

## Critical Invariant
Layer 0 and Layer 1 MUST NOT become footguns that silently require Layer 3 or Layer 4 to be safe. Each layer must be independently correct within its declared service class. Specifically:
- Layer 0 publish MUST NOT silently drop messages in a way that only Layer 2 durability can prevent
- Layer 1 request/reply MUST NOT have failure modes that only Layer 3 session types can catch
- No accidental implementation leakage from higher layers into lower layers
- No performance tax from higher layers on lower layers

## Design Rules
- Default is always Layer 0 (EphemeralInteractive) unless explicitly upgraded
- Moving between layers is visible, attributable, and caused by declared DeliveryClass or ServiceContract
- Each layer's types are in separate modules (not all mixed together)
- Documentation for each layer stands alone — Layer 0 docs never reference Layer 4 concepts
- Error messages at each layer use that layer's vocabulary only

## Tests
- Layer 0 works without any higher-layer configuration or imports
- Each layer independently compiles and functions
- No type from Layer N+1 appears in Layer N's public API
- Performance benchmarks: Layer 0 has zero overhead from higher layers
- Feature flags can gate higher layers without breaking lower layers

title: [FABRIC][P2] Static Capability Layer & Cx Integration
description:
# Phase 2: Static Capability Layer & Cx Integration

## Purpose
Make capability possession a compile-time property for in-process Rust code and a runtime property at process boundaries. This is a two-layer capability architecture that goes far beyond ACLs.

## Static Layer (Compile-Time)
Rust ownership and typestate as zero-cost capability layer beneath Cx:
- PublishPermit<S>: owned non-Copy token consumed to publish to subject family S
- SubscribeToken<S>: owned token for registering interest in S
- SessionToken<P, State>: linear protocol-state token for typed conversations
- CursorAuthorityLease: owned authority for cursor operations
- AppendCertificate: owned authority for stream appends
- FenceToken: owned authority for fencing operations

These prevent stale-token reuse, missing permit consumption, and illegal local protocol steps at compile time.

## Dynamic Layer (Runtime)
- Cx integration: each subject prefix or transform space granted through explicit capabilities in Cx
- Capability grant lowers to both owned token type (in-process) and runtime check (distributed)
- Capability-checked routing programs for export/import plans
- The obligation ledger tracks capability grants and revocations

## Why Two Layers
- Static: prevents in-process misuse as compile errors
- Dynamic: prevents distributed misuse as capability errors, stale-certificate rejects, or obligation violations
- Neither layer alone is sufficient; together they produce the strongest practical guarantee

## Relation to Existing Code
- cx/cx.rs already has capability context, checkpoint/cancel/mask, macaroon attenuation
- cx/registry.rs has capability registry with commit_permit
- security/ module has authenticated, tag, context, key types
- This extends those concepts into the messaging domain

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P2.1] Define static capability token types
description:
Define the compile-time capability token types that form a zero-cost capability layer beneath Cx. File: src/messaging/capability/tokens.rs

- PublishPermit<S>: owned non-Copy token consumed to publish to subject family S. Must be consumed (moved) to publish — prevents reuse. Phantom type S ties to subject family.
- SubscribeToken<S>: owned token for registering interest in S. Consumed on subscription creation.
- SessionToken<P, State>: linear protocol-state token for typed conversations. P is protocol type, State is current protocol state (typestate pattern). Non-Copy, must be advanced through protocol steps.
- CursorAuthorityLease: owned authority artifact for cursor operations. Carries cell_id, epoch, and lease expiry.
- AppendCertificate: owned authority for stream appends. Carries cell_id, epoch, sequence.
- FenceToken: owned authority for fencing operations. Epoch-bound.
- All tokens: non-Copy, non-Clone (linear), carry metadata for validation, have Display for debugging
- Tests: compile-time linearity (use-after-move prevented), token metadata validation, Display formatting

title: [FABRIC][P3] Import/Export Morphisms & Transform Algebra
description:
# Phase 3: Import/Export Morphisms & Transform Algebra

## Purpose
Model cross-domain namespace edges as typed namespace morphisms instead of plain routing rules. Each morphism carries independently checkable facets for authority, reversibility, secrecy, cost, and observability.

## Morphism Classification
Every morphism is classified as one of:
- **authoritative**: reversible, reply-authoritative, capability-bearing
- **derived-view**: may redact/summarize/reorder within declared law, but cannot originate authority
- **egress**: one-way export into weaker trust or replay domains
- **delegation**: temporary sub-language handoff with bounded time, budget, and revocation semantics

## Morphism Specification
Each morphism defines:
- Source and destination subject language
- Allowed transform algebra (wildcard capture, deterministic hash-based partitioning, split/slice, left/right extraction)
- Reversibility requirements
- Capability requirements
- Sharing policy for metadata and identity
- Privacy and metadata disclosure policy
- Optional attestation or private-compliance proof policy
- Response policy
- Quota and budget policy

## Five Independently Checkable Facets
1. Authority
2. Reversibility
3. Secrecy and metadata exposure
4. Cost and quota envelope
5. Observability and evidence obligations

## Transform Algebra Design
- Must stay finite, decidable, and explainable (not an embedded scripting problem)
- Deterministic core for authority-bearing edges
- Randomized or irreversible transforms ONLY on one-way non-authoritative fanout paths
- Reversible transforms required for authority-bearing edges
- NATS-inspired: wildcard capture, hash-based partitioning, split/slice, left/right extraction, strict mode

## Key Features
- Definition-time validation of reversibility where required
- Cycle detection with semantic classes (not just string collision)
- Explicit policy + enforcement that cross-domain requests produce replies only in permitted reply spaces
- Auditable reasoning about what metadata crosses a boundary
- Compiled morphism certificates as inspectable artifacts

## Relation to Existing Code
- distributed/bridge.rs has cross-node bridge concepts with sequence advance
- distributed/encoding.rs has encoding/distribution logic
- transport/router.rs has RoutingTable with EndpointId routing

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P4] Certificate-Carrying Request/Reply
description:
# Phase 4: Certificate-Carrying Request/Reply

## Purpose
Elevate request/reply from a pattern to a contract by integrating with the obligation ledger. NATS request/reply is cheap and elegant — preserve that ergonomics on the default path while making stronger contracts available when opted into.

## Core Mechanism
- Each request allocates at least one service obligation
- When stronger semantics needed: separate reply-delivery or receipt obligation
- Callee must: commit service obligation with reply payload, abort with typed failure, or transfer per policy
- Forwarded requests carry service obligation through import/export morphisms
- Reply-delivery obligations resolved only when configured delivery receipt boundary crossed
- Timeouts are explicit aborted obligations with traceable cause, not "absence of message"

## Ack Semantics (from ack taxonomy)
- Accepted: packet plane custody for forwarding
- Committed: authority plane control entry committed
- Recoverable: durability class met
- Served: service obligation completed
- Received: delivery/receipt boundary crossed

## Operational Consequences
- Silent lost replies become protocol violations (in domains with durable tracking)
- Service export latency measured separately for service completion vs reply-delivery lifecycle
- Streamed/chunked replies become obligation families with bounded cleanup semantics

## Integration Points
- Strong fit with gen_server.rs (already has disciplined reply behavior)
- Obligation ledger (obligation/ledger.rs) tracks all service obligations
- Morphisms carry obligations across import/export boundaries
- Budget system provides cleanup bounds

## Design Notes
- Default path should be NATS-cheap (packet-plane only)
- Stronger contracts are opt-in via DeliveryClass
- No exactly-once claims; idempotency + leases at boundaries

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P5] Quiescent Streams with Active Storage Semantics
description:
# Phase 5: Quiescent Streams with Active Storage Semantics

## Purpose
Build region-owned durable streams where storage and shutdown are semantically strong. JetStream shows that a stream is capture policy + storage + consumer coordination. Asupersync makes all of this cancel-correct and region-owned.

## Core Design
- Stream = region-owned durable state machine
- Stream capture is OPT-IN on selected subject sets; uncaptured traffic stays on lighter Core-NATS-like path
- Publish is two-phase: reserve persistence budget, then durably commit append
- Publisher-visible ack emitted only when append obligation commits at requested durability boundary
- Storage backends participate in cancel/drain/finalize
- Mirror and source are child regions, not detached background loops
- Metadata and placement control separated from per-stream append and consumer hot path

## Standard Features (matching JetStream)
- Limits retention, work-queue retention, interest retention
- Dedupe windows, filtered capture
- Replay and catch-up
- Mirror and source pipelines

## Novel Semantics
- No half-acknowledged append under cancellation
- No orphan mirror/source worker on shutdown
- Replay and repair behavior exercisable under lab runtime
- Snapshot as first-class runtime operation

## Forkable Snapshots
- Capture stream + consumer state at logical cut inside Asupersync capability boundary
- Only permit cheap fork at quiescent or cut-certified points (or include in-flight obligations explicitly)
- Restore into lab runtime or staging region
- On restore: rebind epochs, strip/replace live reply spaces, leases, subject-cell keys, import/export credentials
- Replay counterfactual delivery policies against frozen state
- "Git branches for live event systems" under deterministic runtime semantics

## Relation to Existing Code
- distributed/snapshot.rs already has snapshot infrastructure
- stream/ module has 31 stream combinators
- channel/mpsc.rs has two-phase reserve/send pattern to extend

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

StreamState: msg_count, byte_count, first_seq, last_seq, consumer_count, created_at. Stream capture is OPT-IN on selected subject sets; uncaptured traffic stays on lighter packet-plane path. Storage backend trait: StorageBackend with append(), get(), range(), truncate(), snapshot(). Mirror and source are CHILD REGIONS of the stream region (not detached background loops). On region close: wait for quiescence of all mirrors/sources/consumers. Tests: stream lifecycle (create, append, read, close), region ownership, mirror as child region, quiescence on close.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Restore scrubbing detail (critical for safety): When restoring a snapshot into lab runtime or staging, the system MUST: (1) Mint fresh CellIds (if brokerless) — never reuse live cell identifiers. (2) Rebind all epochs to avoid stale-epoch collisions with live system. (3) Strip or replace ALL live reply spaces — restored instance must not accidentally respond to real requests. (4) Invalidate all leases (cursor, stewardship, delegation) — they reference live-system entities. (5) Strip import/export credentials — restored instance must not have authority over live namespaces. (6) Replace subject-cell keys — key material from live system must not leak into test/staging. title: [FABRIC][P6] Consumers as Policy-Driven Delivery Engines
description:
# Phase 6: Consumers as Policy-Driven Delivery Engines

## Purpose
Build fabric-hosted consumers as region-owned delivery engines backed by obligations, not just counters. NATS consumer policy is richer than most realize — preserve all of that richness and make it even stronger with decision contracts.

## Core Design
- Consumers are region-owned delivery engines
- Ack state backed by obligations, not only counters
- Delivery attempts carry explicit attempt identity and stale-ack idempotence rules
- Pull requests, flow control, pause windows, heartbeats, and scheduling policies are explicit policy objects
- Delivery selection incorporates budgets, backlog, ack debt, and fairness policy

## Decision-Contract-Driven Scheduling
The deepest NATS-inspired move: treat consumers as scheduling entities
- Pull-consumer priority groups → typed demand classes
- Pull-consumer pinned-client policy → temporary capability leasing
- Pull-consumer overflow policy → bounded fallback rule with evidence
- Redelivery policy → decision contract recording why retry/delay/dead-letter was chosen

## Adaptive Consumer Kernel
- Stable deterministic default policies
- Optional advanced policies that remain audit-backed and replayable
- No hand-wavy exactly-once claims
- Very strong reasoning about pending work and retry causality

## Consumer Modes
- Push mode: messages pushed to subscriber with backpressure
- Pull mode: consumer pulls specific sequence windows or demand classes
- Priority groups within pull consumers
- Pinned-client delivery
- Overflow and prioritized policies

## Relation to Existing Code
- combinator/circuit_breaker.rs has similar adaptive policy patterns
- service/retry.rs has retry policy concepts
- obligation/ledger.rs tracks ack obligations
- franken_decision has decision contract infrastructure

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Adaptive consumer kernel concept (from proposal): The adaptive consumer kernel has these properties: (1) STABLE defaults: deterministic, well-understood delivery policies that require no configuration. (2) OPTIONAL advanced policies: operator can opt into smarter delivery scheduling, but these are always audit-backed and replayable. (3) NO exactly-once claims: the system is honest about at-least-once delivery with idempotency + leases at boundaries. (4) STRONG reasoning about pending work: because ack state is backed by obligations, the system can always answer 'what is still owed?' precisely. (5) RETRY CAUSALITY: because redelivery decisions are captured in decision contracts, the system can explain the full chain of why a message was redelivered N times and what happened at each attempt. This last point is the key differentiator: most systems can tell you a message was redelivered 5 times, but Asupersync can tell you WHY each redelivery happened, what the competing considerations were, and what evidence justified the decision.

title: [FABRIC][P7] Control Plane as First-Class Subjects
description:
# Phase 7: Control Plane as First-Class Subjects

## Purpose
Model the control plane as first-class subjects in the same fabric, not a separate imperative API. NATS's $SYS.* pattern is powerful — extend it with region-owned handlers, FrankenSuite evidence, and capability domains.

## Control Subject Families
- Fabric health
- Import/export changes
- Route and gateway advisories
- Lameduck and drain state
- Auth and capability failures
- Consumer pause and unpin events
- Stream snapshot creation and restore
- Repair, replay, and rebalance advisories

## Design Guardrails
- System/control subjects live in dedicated capability domain
- Control handlers run with reserved budget and priority (not competing with user traffic)
- Minimal bootstrap and break-glass recovery path available even when ordinary fabric is degraded
- Advisory subjects do NOT automatically feed policy loops without explicit damping/stratification/operator intent

## Asupersync-Unique Additions
1. Control-plane handlers and advisories are region-owned and replayable (once external inputs modeled)
2. Material decisions emit FrankenSuite evidence and decision records

Operators see more than "gateway detached" — they see:
- Which capability graph edges were affected
- Which obligations were transferred, aborted, or replay-scheduled
- Which policy decided the failover path
- What evidence justified it

## Relation to Existing Code
- grpc/health.rs has health check infrastructure
- server/shutdown.rs has graceful shutdown with mark_stopped wakeup
- signal/graceful.rs has graceful signal handling
- franken_evidence and franken_decision provide evidence/decision machinery

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [FABRIC][P8] Session-Typed Protocol Contracts
description:
# Phase 8: Session-Typed Protocol Contracts

## Purpose
Ground the "protocol-carrying subjects" idea in session types. Each protocol-carrying subject family registers a global session type; the fabric projects that into each participant local type with duality and compatibility checking.

## Core Model
- Each protocol-carrying subject family registers a GLOBAL session type
- Fabric PROJECTS that global type into each participant local type
- Duality and compatibility checked when services are imported, exported, or versioned
- Obligation ledger mechanically derives reply, timeout, compensation, and cutoff obligations from protocol contract

## Scope
Start with two-party protocols, grow later into multiparty session types (MPST). Practical goal: move wrong-message-order / missing-reply / incompatible-conversation-shape failures from runtime incidents toward compiler errors and registration-time rejects.

## Protocol Compilation
A protocol definition compiles into:
- Subject families and reply-space rules
- Obligation transitions and timeout law
- Compensation and cutoff paths
- Admissible state transitions
- Evidence checkpoints for material control moves

## Key Use Cases
- Request/reply, streaming reply, reservation handoff
- Cursor delegation, compensation workflows, cutover protocols
- Multi-party: consumer-group coordination, stewardship handoff, split-brain arbitration

## Protocol Compatibility Tooling
- Import/export registration rejects incompatible conversation shapes before any message sent
- Protocol evolution as type-level change forcing adapters or updates (not silent drift)
- Trace-level conformance checking runs session automaton alongside lab runtime execution
- Obligation derivation mechanical for large protocol classes

## Relation to Existing Code
- obligation/session_types.rs already has session type concepts
- obligation/choreography/ has pipeline and codegen infrastructure
- channel/session.rs has session channel concepts

## FABRIC North Star Reference
This phase is governed by the five cross-cutting FABRIC success criteria defined in `src/messaging/mod.rs` and `docs/FABRIC_GUARDRAILS.md`:
1. Keep the public mental model NATS-small.
2. Make stronger guarantees explicit named service classes, never hidden taxes on the common case.
3. Lower radical behavior into small, inspectable artifacts.
4. Keep autonomous policy loops inside declared safety envelopes with replay, evidence, and rollback.
5. Target the first product wedge at systems that need sovereignty, durable partial progress, and post-incident explanation together.

If work in this phase violates those criteria, or drifts toward the anti-goal of a grand unified fabric that makes the common case slower and less legible than NATS, it must be redesigned.

title: [h3-grpc-deepest-4th] http/h3_native.rs:2085-2087 H3RequestStreamState::on_frame catch-all rejects DATAGRAM frames — breaks RFC 9297/9298 CONNECT-UDP interop despite project's own allow-list permitting them
description:
src/http/h3_native.rs:2085-2087 — H3RequestStreamState::on_frame()'s catch-all `_` arm rejects DATAGRAM frames with `H3NativeError::ControlProtocol("only HEADERS/DATA are valid on request streams")`. This contradicts the project's own per-frame-type allow-list at lines 609-618 (`validate_bidirectional_frame`), which explicitly returns Ok for `H3Frame::Datagram { .. }` per RFC 9297, citing the same RFC inline (line 615 comment: "DATAGRAM frames are sent on bidirectional streams per RFC 9297"). The bidirectional dispatch path at line 578 also lists `H3Frame::Datagram { .. }` among permitted frames. So the framework KNOWS DATAGRAM is allowed on bidi streams; the per-stream state machine just forgot.

Concrete reproduction:
  T0 — client opens a bidirectional stream, sends Extended CONNECT HEADERS (`:method CONNECT`, `:protocol connect-udp`, `:path /target/host/port`).
  T1 — server accepts; the CONNECT-UDP session is established. Per RFC 9298 §3 the client may now send `H3Frame::Datagram { quarter_stream_id: <derived-from-stream-id>, payload: <UDP payload> }` on the same stream.
  T2 — H3RequestStreamState::on_frame is called with the DATAGRAM frame.
  T3 — `match frame { H3Frame::Headers(_) ⇒ ..., H3Frame::Data(_) ⇒ ..., _ ⇒ Err(...) }` — the catch-all fires and returns `ControlProtocol("only HEADERS/DATA are valid on request streams")`.
  T4 — connection-level handler treats this as a fatal stream-state error and aborts the CONNECT-UDP session.

Impact:
  (a) HTTP/3 + RFC 9297 DATAGRAM interop is broken on the per-stream path. Any peer attempting CONNECT-UDP via Extended CONNECT (RFC 9298) gets RST'd at the FIRST datagram.
  (b) Cross-implementation interop with browsers, MASQUE clients, and HTTP/3 datagram-aware proxies fails immediately on the datagram-flow handshake.
  (c) The validate_bidirectional_frame "allow-list" is dead code for the per-stream path — the state machine never consults it; instead it duplicates the allow-list inline (HEADERS, DATA) and forgets the DATAGRAM entry. Any future RFC that adds new bidi-allowed frame types (e.g., CAPSULE-related extensions) will hit the same shape.

Fix direction:
  1. Add `H3Frame::Datagram { .. } => Ok(()),` to the match arm in on_frame (between the existing HEADERS and DATA arms or just before the catch-all `_`).
  2. Optionally: add the standard RFC 9114 §7.2.8 "ignore unknown frame types" handling for `H3Frame::Reserved { .. }` (or whatever the unknown-frame variant is) so reserved frame types don't fatal-error the stream.
  3. Better still: route on_frame through validate_bidirectional_frame for the per-stream allow-list, then layer ordering checks (HEADERS-first, DATA after HEADERS, trailers after DATA) on top. That makes the allow-list the single source of truth across the bidirectional code path.
  4. Add a regression test: feed an H3Frame::Datagram into H3RequestStreamState::on_frame after a HEADERS frame; assert Ok.

Severity HIGH because (a) RFC 9297 + 9298 interop is fully broken on this code path — any CONNECT-UDP peer fails to handshake, (b) the bug is silent at the type-checker level (the catch-all compiles fine and looks like a defensive check), and (c) the project's OWN allow-list at line 618 documents the correct behavior — this is a self-inconsistency, not a spec ambiguity.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/http/h3* + src/grpc/* DEEPEST 4th-pass (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Added explicit H3Frame::Datagram arm to H3RequestStreamState::on_frame at h3_native.rs:2071+. Accepts DATAGRAM after initial HEADERS per RFC 9297/9298, rejects DATAGRAM-before-HEADERS with clear diagnostic. Does NOT advance the HEADERS+DATA*+TRAILERS state machine (DATAGRAMs are out-of-band sidecar). Catch-all error message updated to mention DATAGRAM. 4 tests added/updated. Commit 8dfbeeb5d.

title: [bug-hunt] io/copy: cancel returns Err without draining buffered prefix; data read from reader but not yet written is lost
description:
Severity: HIGH (silent data loss on cancel-mid-copy when an in-flight read had already produced bytes the writer never saw).

src/io/copy.rs:88-95 (`Copy::poll`) and the parallel block at 423-430 (`CopyWithProgress::poll`):

    loop {
        if crate::cx::Cx::current().is_some_and(|c| c.checkpoint().is_err()) {
            this.completed = true;
            return Poll::Ready(Err(std::io::Error::new(
                std::io::ErrorKind::Interrupted,
                "cancelled",
            )));
        }
        ...
        // If we have buffered data, write it
        if this.pos < this.cap { ... }

The cancel check fires at the TOP of every loop iteration, BEFORE the
"if we have buffered data, write it" block. So when cancel arrives
while `this.pos < this.cap` (i.e. we already read N bytes from
`reader` into `this.buf` but didn't yet write them), the function
returns `Err` and ABANDONS those bytes in the local buffer. Reader's
internal cursor has presumably advanced past them; writer never saw
them. Net effect: a clean cancel can lose up to one buffer-full of
data WITHOUT any error or count signal, since the io::Error returned
does not carry `this.total` and the buffered prefix was never
counted.

The existing tests at lines 956-1023
(`copy_partial_write_interrupt_preserves_committed_prefix` and
`copy_with_progress_interrupt_reports_only_committed_prefix`)
validate that "committed" (already-written) bytes are visible —
they're silent on the buffered-but-unwritten case. The naming hints at
the contract: only the committed prefix is preserved. But the
contract is unstated in the public docstring, and the loss is silent
(no error variant, no count returned alongside).

Fix shapes (any one):

  (a) Reorder the loop so cancel is checked AFTER attempting one final
      drain of the buffered window. On cancel detection, if `pos < cap`,
      do one non-blocking `poll_write` of the remaining buffer (no
      retry loop) before returning Err. Simple, no API change, but
      doesn't help if the writer returns Pending.

  (b) Return `(u64, Option<io::Error>)` instead of
      `io::Result<u64>` so the caller always sees both the byte
      count and the error. Breaking API change.

  (c) Add a `bytes_copied(&self) -> u64` method on `Copy` /
      `CopyWithProgress` so the caller can recover `this.total`
      after Err. Less disruptive but requires the caller to remember
      to query.

  (d) Document loudly that on cancel, `this.pos..this.cap` bytes are
      LOST and the caller MUST account for it via the
      `bytes_remaining_in_buffer()` accessor. (Add said accessor.)

Same pattern applies to `copy_bidirectional` at line 753 — both
directions can have un-drained buffered data on cancel.

`copy_buf` (line 252) uses the AsyncBufRead API and may be different;
worth a separate audit pass.
