title: Whole-file hash pins are perpetually red: 547 of 1547 artifact pins stale on main (62 artifacts, all with test consumers); owner decision on freshness vs correctness
description:
## Finding (static census, origin a764e10eb, 2026-09-26)
Whole-file sha256 pins in artifacts are perpetually red on a live main. A census of every JSON under artifacts/ and tests/fixtures/ counted each object that carries a `path` in the tree beside a 64-hex `sha256` / `source_sha256` / `blob_sha256` / `file_sha256`:
- 878 JSON files scanned; 1547 path+hash pin records in 75 artifacts.
- 547 records no longer match the file's bytes at head. They sit in 62 artifacts, and every one of those artifacts is read by at least one test under tests/.
- The most-staled files, by how many artifacts' pins on them are stale: Cargo.toml 52, Cargo.lock 44, src/observability/mod.rs 13, artifacts/dependency_capability_registry_v1.json 12, src/lib.rs 11, src/observability/otel.rs 11, src/messaging/kafka.rs 9, src/bin/asupersync.rs 9.
- Worst artifacts (drifted/total): dependency_capability_baseline 45/81, kafka_downstream_user_journey_inventory 38/225, time_utc_capability_inventory 31/101, base64_capability_inventory 28/80, scheduler_join_batch_inventory 23/25, hex_capability_inventory 20/87, cli_clap_surface_inventory 16/31, scheduler_hot_read_inventory 16/26.
- Full table, with each artifact's consuming tests: /data/tmp/rc_20260922/pin_drift_census_a764e10eb.md.

Caveat: some records may be historical receipts that no test compares with live bytes. For futures_lite (7fw928), scheduler_join_batch (bi2462.169), base64 (bi2462.147.7) and dependency_capability_baseline (bi2462.136) the consuming test does hash live bytes and is red. A sample run of 8 consumers on main is recorded in the comments.

## Why this matters
- These pins guard files that the swarm edits every hour (Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, cx.rs, state.rs, observability/mod.rs). Each pin reds on the first unrelated edit and stays red until its owner re-captures it. In practice nobody re-captures, so the gate is permanently red and protects nothing.
- Worse, it masks. A pin assertion that fails first hides every later assertion in the same test fn: futures_lite's manifest-resolution checks never run behind its pin loop. Real regressions land behind already-red targets unseen.
- The main watchdog cannot see this class. It maps a changed src/ file to lib test filters only. Selecting every integration test that names a changed path as text would cost about 300 targets per batch (README 71+92, cx.rs 43+74, state.rs 28+56 referrers, direct + via artifacts), so it is not a per-batch fix either.

## Owner decision needed (recommendation first)
1. RECOMMENDED: split freshness from correctness.
   - Semantic assertions stay blocking in cargo test and must be green: anchors, counts, manifest resolution, census partitions.
   - Byte-freshness pins move out of the blocking path, into one freshness report that the main watchdog computes statically per batch. It needs no build: git blobs vs pins. It attributes each newly stale pin to the commit that changed the file and posts that on the commit's cited bead.
   - Win/lose split: wins = every consuming contract becomes runnable and able to go green, and pin drift gets per-commit attribution it has never had. Loses = a stale pin no longer fails `cargo test`. The effective loss is small, because these gates are already red and ignored.
2. Keep blocking byte pins but only for cold files. Replace pins on hot files (Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, cx.rs, state.rs, builder.rs, observability/*) with semantic anchors, the way 84d6b6c48 re-anchored bi2462.169's audits.
3. Status quo plus owner re-capture after every landing. Not viable at the current landing rate: 547 stale records today.

Until decided: nobody bulk re-pins. That would be gate weakening, and it would be red again within the hour.

## Acceptance
Owner decision recorded here; per-artifact follow-up beads filed for the chosen option; the watchdog change (if option 1) landed with a contract test; the census script committed under scripts/ so the numbers are reproducible.

title: Implement two-phase watch channel for state broadcasting
close_reason: Watch channel implemented with version tracking, cancel-safe changed() waits, multiple receiver support, and comprehensive tests. All tests pass.

title: [memory-ordering] observability/resource_accounting.rs: update_peak uses Relaxed — races with snapshot readers on weakly-ordered targets
description:
src/observability/resource_accounting.rs:447 — update_peak(peak: &AtomicI64, new_value: i64) calls peak.fetch_max(new_value, Ordering::Relaxed). All four peak gauges (pending_peak, tasks_peak, children_peak, heap_bytes_peak) update with Relaxed; snapshot() reads them with Relaxed too.

On weakly-ordered architectures (ARM64, PowerPC, RISC-V), Relaxed provides no synchronization between the writer and the snapshot reader. A thread that just observed a high water-mark via fetch_max may not propagate its write to a concurrent snapshot() reader before the readers load — the snapshot returns a stale peak, missing the just-recorded high-water update.

The asupersync project pattern (see closed asupersync-bd-2wds9 / channel waker dedup work) is: writers publish via Release, readers acquire via Acquire. fetch_max with Release semantics on the writer side AND .load(Acquire) on the reader side restores the happens-before that the gauge contract assumes.

Threat model: this is observability — operators reading peak gauges in production for capacity-planning may see stale values. Lab replay determinism on x86-64 is preserved by accident (TSO), but cross-arch (ARM CI shards) can flake.

Fix direction:
  - update_peak: peak.fetch_max(new_value, Ordering::Release)
  - snapshot readers: peak.load(Ordering::Acquire)
  - the corresponding +1 / -1 counter updates may also need Release on writes, Acquire on reads if downstream code reads them in lockstep with the peak.

title: Reactor audit (r13): two runtimes sharing one reactor steal each other's events (MEDIUM); io_uring register/re-arm stall under the driver lock (HIGH, io-uring only); lab reactor lacks one-shot arming and I/O error injection (MEDIUM)
description:
Read-only audit round r13 (SapphireHill e0155ea8 audit agents, 2026-10-08, origin/main a8bb25747) of the Linux epoll reactor core (src/runtime/reactor/{epoll,mod,registration,token,interest}.rs) and of src/runtime/io_driver.rs plus the lab reactor (reactor/lab.rs).

Summary:
- epoll core: no HIGH. F1 MEDIUM: two runtimes that share one reactor (a RuntimeBuilder cloned after with_reactor, or two IoDriverHandle::new on one Arc) steal each other's events and wakes, and their tokens collide, so tasks hang. LOWs F2-F5 (a recycled fd refused while a dead registration holds it; no reactor-side generation; TokenSlab::clear recycles retired slots; poll holds the event-buffer lock across epoll_wait).
- io_driver / lab reactor: HIGH (io-uring feature only): register, re-arm and deregister can stall up to 250 ms, or indefinitely on the fallback pump, while holding the driver lock, because the io_uring poller holds its ring lock through submit_and_wait. The lock structure was confirmed by SapphireHill on origin. MEDIUM: the lab reactor has no one-shot arming or level readiness, so lab tests cannot catch a missing re-arm. MEDIUM: lab fault injection only sets readiness bits, so error-recovery paths never run under lab chaos. LOWs: a registration outliving its driver never deregisters; lab fault RNG not tied to the seed; lab accepts one fd under several tokens; rearm trusts a cached waker after update_waker.
Fix constraints: epoll.rs, token.rs and registration.rs carry fresh sha256 pins, and epoll.rs has unsafe-ledger line pins (re-pin or stay line-neutral). The io_uring HIGH needs a design change (queue mutations for the poller thread instead of taking the ring lock). The lab reactor items change lab semantics under every lab test.

Both reports verbatim follow.

# E1

# E1: Linux epoll reactor correctness audit (origin/main a8bb25747)

Scope: `src/runtime/reactor/{epoll,mod,registration,token,interest}.rs` at
a8bb25747, plus the parts of `src/runtime/io_driver.rs` (and the builder) that
call into them. All code was read with `git show a8bb25747:<path>`. To check
backend semantics I also read the resolved dependency sources: polling 3.11.0
(`src/epoll.rs`, `src/lib.rs`) and rustix 1.1.5 (`epoll_wait`,
`Timespec::as_c_int_millis`), from `~/.cargo/registry`. Nothing was built or
run.

Bottom line: the epoll backend itself is sound in the default configuration.
Within one `IoDriver` there is no lost wakeup, no wrong-task delivery and no
busy loop. The one real hazard is at the boundary between the reactor and its
driver. A reactor has one flat token namespace and one event stream, but
nothing stops two `IoDriver`s from attaching to the same reactor (F1). The other
findings are edge cases.

| # | Severity | Title |
|---|----------|-------|
| F1 | MEDIUM | One reactor shared by two IoDrivers: the driver that polls takes the other driver's events and wakes (lost wakeup or hang), and the two drivers' tokens collide |
| F2 | LOW | A recycled fd number cannot be registered while a provably dead registration still maps it (AlreadyExists), even though the reactor already stores the identity that would prove it stale |
| F3 | LOW | No reactor-side generation: with raw tokens, an event harvested for a deregistered fd is delivered to a new registration that reuses the token |
| F4 | LOW | `TokenSlab::clear()` puts retired (generation-exhausted) slots back on the free list, which defeats the ABA guard |
| F5 | LOW | `EpollReactor::poll` holds `poll_events` across the kernel wait, so a concurrent `poll(Some(ZERO))` blocks for the leader's whole wait. Through the public `IoDriverHandle::lock().turn()` this also holds the driver lock |

Fix constraints that apply to every finding:
- **Hash pins.** `epoll.rs` (sha256 `28522a60…`, 2385 lines), `token.rs`
  (`77ace1e6…`) and `registration.rs` (`3965fe16…`) currently match their
  sha256 pins in `artifacts/polling_socket_platform_decision_v1.json`.
  `epoll.rs` is also pinned in `artifacts/dependency_capability_baseline_v1.json`
  and `artifacts/io_uring_capability_inventory_v1.json`. Any edit drifts those
  pins.
  - The same artifacts already carry stale pins for `reactor/mod.rs`,
    `reactor/interest.rs` and `io_driver.rs`. Their checkers
    (`tests/polling_socket_platform_decision_contract.rs:437`,
    `tests/io_uring_capability_inventory_contract.rs:218`,
    `tests/dependency_capability_baseline_contract.rs:132`) are therefore
    probably red on origin already, so an edit adds no new red.
    UNCONFIRMED: I compared blob hashes but did not run the checkers.
  - The owner still has to re-pin.
- **Unsafe-ledger line pins.** `artifacts/unsafe_boundary_ledger_v1.json`
  pins `epoll.rs` lines 68, 102, 103, 367, 375, 453 and 528, plus test lines
  682, 683, 694, 695, 717, 1290, 1297, 1389, 1396, 1466, 1499, 1532, 1560, 1572
  and 1624. Keep edits line-neutral above those lines, or update the ledger in
  the same commit.
- **API compatibility.** v0.4.3 compatibility means additive changes only: no
  new required trait methods and no signature changes on public types
  (`Reactor`, `IoDriverHandle`, `TokenSlab`, `RuntimeBuilder`).

---

## F1 (MEDIUM): One reactor shared by two IoDrivers: the driver that polls takes the other driver's events and wakes; the two drivers' tokens collide

The outcome is a HIGH-class hang. I rate it MEDIUM because it needs one
`Arc<dyn Reactor>` under two drivers. The public API allows that without any
warning, but the default build path never does it.

### Where

1. `RuntimeBuilder` is `Clone` and stores the reactor as a shared `Arc`. Each
   `build()` wraps that reactor in a new driver:
   - `src/runtime/builder.rs:2612-2616`:
     ```rust
     #[derive(Clone)]
     pub struct RuntimeBuilder {
         config: RuntimeConfig,
         scoped_cpu_worker_limit: Option<usize>,
         reactor: Option<Arc<dyn Reactor>>,
     ```
   - `builder.rs:3587-3589`: `pub fn with_reactor(mut self, reactor: Arc<dyn Reactor>) -> Self { self.reactor = Some(reactor); ...`
   - `builder.rs:6057`: `state.set_io_driver(IoDriverHandle::new(reactor));`
   - The same pattern exists in `src/runtime/state.rs:2455`, and
     `IoDriverHandle::new` is public.
2. Each driver has its own token slab and its own leader flag:
   - `io_driver.rs:219-220`: `let slab_key = self.wakers.insert(waker); let io_token = Token::new(slab_key.to_usize());`
     Both drivers start at `SlabToken(0,0)`, so both produce `Token(0)` first.
   - `io_driver.rs:632-635` (`IoDriverHandle::new`):
     `inner: Arc::new(Mutex::new(IoDriver::new(reactor.clone()))), ... is_polling: Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false)),`
3. The reactor keys everything by the bare token and delivers every harvested
   event to whoever is polling:
   - `epoll.rs:346-351`: `if state.tokens.contains_key(&token) { return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists, "token already registered")); }`
   - `epoll.rs:580,594,596`: `let mut poll_events = self.poll_events.lock();` … `self.poller.wait(&mut poll_events, timeout)?;` … `let state = self.state.lock();`
   - `epoll.rs:311-315`: `translate_poll_event` looks up `state.tokens.get(&token)` with no owner check.
4. The polling driver drops events whose token is not in its own slab, after
   the oneshot has already disarmed the fd:
   - `io_driver.rs:477-484`:
     ```rust
     let slab_key = SlabToken::from_usize(event.token.0);
     if let Some(waker) = restorer.driver.wakers.get(slab_key) {
         ...
     } else {
         restorer.driver.stats.unknown_tokens += 1;
     }
     ```

### Scenario

`let b = RuntimeBuilder::new().with_reactor(create_reactor()?); let rt_a = b.clone().build()?; let rt_b = b.build()?;`

1. **The second runtime's first registration fails.** A task on `rt_a` reads
   socket SA and registers `Token(0)`. A task on `rt_b` reads socket SB; its
   driver also allocates `Token(0)`. `epoll.rs:346-351` returns
   `AlreadyExists "token already registered"`, and `io_driver.rs:230-233`
   frees the slot. The read on `rt_b` fails with a misleading error. Its retry
   gets `Token(1<<32)` and succeeds.
2. **Both leaders reach the same reactor.** The idle workers of both runtimes
   call `io.try_turn_with(..)` (`three_lane.rs:5486`). The two leader flags are
   independent, so both reach `self.reactor.poll` (`io_driver.rs:772`).
   `EpollReactor::poll` serializes them on `poll_events`, which it holds across
   the blocking `epoll_wait` (`epoll.rs:580-594`). Say `rt_a`'s leader is in
   the kernel and `rt_b`'s leader is blocked on the parking_lot mutex.
3. **The event goes to the wrong driver.** SB becomes readable. The kernel
   reports key `1<<32` to `rt_a`'s `epoll_wait` and, because the registration
   is oneshot, disarms it. Translation succeeds because the token is in the
   shared map. `rt_a`'s driver then finds no slab entry for it
   (`io_driver.rs:477-484`), increments `unknown_tokens` and wakes nothing.
   - The task on `rt_b` waiting on SB is never woken.
   - Its registration stays disarmed, so no later poll on either runtime
     reports SB again. The task hangs until something unrelated (a timeout or
     a cancel) polls it.
4. **The wake goes to the wrong driver too.** `rt_b` spawns a task or
   publishes a timer and calls `reactor.wake()`. The eventfd write wakes
   `rt_a`'s `epoll_wait`. polling then drains the eventfd and clears its
   `notified` flag (polling 3.11.0 `src/epoll.rs:232-237`, `src/lib.rs:765`).
   `rt_b`'s leader, still blocked on the mutex, then enters `epoll_wait` with
   no pending notification. It sleeps for its full timeout, up to the next
   deadline or 250 ms (`three_lane.rs:200`).

Sequential reuse (building a second runtime on the same reactor after the first
was dropped) has a milder variant, which F2 covers. A registration that outlives
its driver skips `reactor.deregister` entirely (`io_driver.rs:1049`), so its
token and fd number stay in the reactor's maps for the next driver to collide
with.

### Fix shape (additive)

Fail closed when a second driver attaches.
- Option A: add a defaulted trait method `Reactor::attach_driver(&self) -> io::Result<()> { Ok(()) }`.
  - `EpollReactor` overrides it with an `AtomicBool` and releases it in a
    `Drop` for `IoDriver`. `ObservedReactor` forwards it.
  - `IoDriverHandle::new` records the result. A handle that did not attach
    returns an error from `register` and `try_turn_with`, with a clear message
    ("reactor already driven by another IoDriver").
- Option B: keep the same guard as a process-wide weak set keyed by
  `Arc::as_ptr(&reactor)` inside `io_driver.rs`. This needs no trait change.

Also document on `with_reactor` that the reactor must not be shared, or make
`RuntimeBuilder::clone` drop an injected reactor. An injected `io_driver`
(`with_io_driver`) can be shared safely, because one handle means one slab and
one leader flag.

### Failing test sketch

Add to `io_driver.rs` `mod tests::epoll_integration`, reusing the existing
`create_test_waker`.

```rust
let reactor: Arc<dyn Reactor> = Arc::new(EpollReactor::new().unwrap());
let h1 = IoDriverHandle::new(reactor.clone());
let h2 = IoDriverHandle::new(reactor.clone());   // "the other runtime"
let (sock, mut peer) = UnixStream::pair().unwrap();
sock.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let (waker, flag) = create_test_waker();
let _reg = h1.register(&sock, Interest::READABLE, waker).unwrap();
peer.write_all(b"x").unwrap();
let _ = h2.try_turn_with(Some(Duration::from_millis(100)), |_, _| {}); // other leader turns first
let _ = h1.try_turn_with(Some(Duration::from_millis(100)), |_, _| {});
assert!(flag.flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst), "h1's event must reach h1's waker");
```

Today the test fails: `h2.stats().unknown_tokens == 1` and the flag stays
false. After the fix, `h2` refuses to poll, so `h1`'s turn delivers the event.

---

## F2 (LOW): A recycled fd number cannot be registered while a provably dead registration still maps it

### Where

- `epoll.rs:353-358` rejects the fd number with no staleness check:
  ```rust
  if state.fds.contains_key(&raw_fd) {
      return Err(io::Error::new(
          io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists,
          "fd already registered",
      ));
  }
  ```
- The reactor already holds the evidence that would prove the mapping stale:
  - `epoll.rs:340` captures the new source's identity:
    `let pre_identity = FdIdentity::from_fd(raw_fd)...`
  - `epoll.rs:402-409` stores `fd_identity: post_identity` for every
    registration.
  - `epoll.rs:266-268` defines `fd_no_longer_matches` for exactly this purpose.
- The behaviour is deliberate and pinned by the test
  `reused_fd_cannot_register_under_new_token_until_stale_token_removed`
  (`epoll.rs:1549-1640`).

### Scenario

Two routes reach this state.

1. **A caller closes the fd before deregistering it.**
   - This happened before as br-asupersync-8vrx8q. It was fixed at each call
     site separately: see the comments at `net/tcp/split.rs:529-538` and
     `net/unix/split.rs:422-431`.
   - Thread X drops the last owner of socket A (fd 7) before A's registration
     T1 deregisters. Thread Y calls `accept()`, gets fd 7 (Linux hands out the
     lowest free fd) and registers it.
   - `register` fails with `AlreadyExists "fd already registered"`, even though
     `fstat(7)` now names a different inode than the one stored for T1. The new
     connection's first read or write fails.
2. **An IoDriver drops while registrations are still alive, then its reactor
   is reused (F1, sequential case).**
   - `IoRegistration::drop` only deregisters when it can still reach its
     driver (`io_driver.rs:1049`:
     `if let Some(driver) = self.driver.upgrade() {`). Otherwise it never calls
     `reactor.deregister`, so the reactor keeps `fds[7] -> T1` indefinitely.
   - Once the stream closes fd 7, every socket that later receives number 7 on
     that reactor fails to register. Lowest-free-fd allocation makes this
     recur, possibly on every accept.

### Fix shape

In `register`, when `state.fds` already maps `raw_fd` to an old token, compare
`state.tokens[old].fd_identity` with `pre_identity`.

- If they differ, the old mapping is provably dead: the number now names
  another file.
  - Remove it from both maps.
  - Add the old token to `orphaned`, so the eventual `deregister(old)` returns
    `Ok` without touching the kernel.
  - Proceed with the ADD.
- Do **not** issue a kernel DEL for the evicted token. It would target the new
  file. Any leftover kernel entry from a dup'd old file dies when that file is
  released.
- Keep the duplicate-*token* check strict. Evicting by token could let a late
  `deregister(old)` delete the new registration.

The fix must stay line-neutral above line 367 (ledger pins). The pinned test at
`epoll.rs:1583-1596` flips: its assertion becomes "registration succeeds and
the stale token's deregister is idempotent".

1. Register `dup(A)` as T1, then close that dup.
2. `dup2(B, same_number)`.
3. `register(B_at_same_number, T2)`. Today this returns

4. Write to B's peer and poll. Assert an event for T2.
5. Assert `deregister(T1)` returns `Ok`.

## F4 (LOW): `TokenSlab::clear()` puts retired (generation-exhausted) slots back on the free list

### Where

- `token.rs:349-366`: `remove` retires a slot whose generation reached
  `MAX_GENERATION`. The slot becomes `Vacant { next_free: FREE_LIST_END, generation: 0 }`
  and is not linked into the free list:
  ```rust
  let new_generation = current_generation.wrapping_add(1) & SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION;
  let recycle_slot = current_generation != SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION;
  ```
- `token.rs:405-420`: `clear()` keys only off the *current* generation:
  ```rust
  self.free_head = FREE_LIST_END;
  for index in (0..self.entries.len()).rev() {
      let current_generation = self.entries[index].generation();
      let generation = current_generation.wrapping_add(1) & SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION;
      if current_generation == SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION {
          ... retire ...
      } else {
          self.entries[index] = Entry::Vacant { next_free: self.free_head, generation };
          self.free_head = index as u32;
      }
  ```
  A retired slot sits at generation 0, which is not `MAX`, so `clear()` links
  it back into the free list at generation 1.

### Scenario

1. A slot cycles until its generation reaches `MAX`: 2^32 cycles on 64-bit, or
   only 65,536 on 32-bit (`token.rs:144-145`). It is then retired.
2. Any `clear()` while `len > 0` brings the slot back. The next `insert` hands
   out `(index, 1)`, a token value that was already issued during the slot's
   first lifetime.
3. A stale token held from that lifetime now matches the new entry. `get`
   returns the new waker, so the event goes to the wrong task.

Reachability: `TokenSlab` is a public export (`reactor/mod.rs:146`).
`IoDriver` and `mpsc` never call `clear()` (checked with `git grep`), so the
runtime cannot reach it. `retain()` (`token.rs:428-464`) handles retirement
correctly.

### Fix shape

In `clear()`:
- Turn `Occupied` entries into `Vacant` exactly as `remove` does, including
  retirement at `MAX`.
- Leave `Vacant` entries' generations unchanged.
- Rebuild the free list only from non-retired vacant slots.
- Alternatively, track retirement explicitly with
  `Vacant { retired: bool, .. }`.

Note that `token.rs` has a fresh hash pin.

### Failing test sketch

In-module, so the test can seed the generation:

```rust
let mut slab: TokenSlab<u32> = TokenSlab::new();
slab.entries.push(Entry::Occupied { value: 1, generation: SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION });
slab.len = 1;
assert_eq!(slab.remove(SlabToken::new(0, SlabToken::MAX_GENERATION)), Some(1)); // retires slot 0
assert_eq!(slab.insert(2).index(), 1);
slab.clear();
let (a, b) = (slab.insert(3), slab.insert(4));
assert!(a.index() != 0 && b.index() != 0, "retired slot must stay retired across clear()");
```

Today this fails: `clear()` relinks slot 0 at generation 1.

## F5 (LOW): `EpollReactor::poll` holds `poll_events` across the kernel wait, so a concurrent zero-timeout poll blocks for the leader's whole wait

### Where

- `epoll.rs:580` and `594`:
  `let mut poll_events = self.poll_events.lock();` … `self.poller.wait(&mut poll_events, timeout)?;`.
  The lock is held for the whole blocking `epoll_wait`.
- The trait promises otherwise:
  - `reactor/mod.rs:921-922`: "All methods use interior mutability and are safe to
    call from multiple threads concurrently".
  - `mod.rs:1061`: "`Some(Duration::ZERO)`: Non-blocking poll, return
    immediately".
- The module doc acknowledges the limitation (`epoll.rs:36-40`: "Concurrent
  `poll()` callers are expected to be serialized externally").
- `IoDriverHandle::try_turn_with` serializes callers, but the public
  `IoDriverHandle::lock()` (`io_driver.rs:809-811`) plus `IoDriver::turn`
  (`io_driver.rs:353`) bypass the `is_polling` flag.

### Scenario

1. A scheduler leader is in `try_turn_with` → `reactor.poll(Some(T))`, holding
   `poll_events`. The driver lock is released at this point.
2. A task calls `handle.lock().turn(Some(Duration::ZERO))`, expecting a
   non-blocking drain.
3. That call takes the **driver** lock, then blocks on `poll_events` until the
   leader's wait ends: the next I/O event, a wake, or `T`.
   - `T` can be up to 250 ms when idle, or longer with a far-off timer.
4. Meanwhile every `rearm`, `set_interest` and `deregister` on every worker
   blocks on the driver lock.
   - Since 2bf1feb5a, an epoll rearm no longer wakes the reactor, so those
     blocked rearms do not shorten the stall. Only `register`'s unconditional
     wake (`io_driver.rs:665`) or real I/O does.
5. When the leader returns, it blocks on the driver lock (`io_driver.rs:775`)
   until the second caller's own turn finishes.
6. `IoDriver::turn_with` also runs the batch's wakers while the caller still
   holds the driver guard (`io_driver.rs:395-402`).

### Fix shape

In `EpollReactor::poll`, when `timeout == Some(Duration::ZERO)`, use
`self.poll_events.try_lock()` and return `Ok(0)` if it is held. This mirrors
polling's own `try_lock` semantics (polling `src/lib.rs:751-774`). The leader
harvests the ready events anyway. Keep blocking behaviour for non-zero timeouts.
The change is line-neutral if done on line 580.

### Failing test sketch

1. Thread L runs `h.try_turn_with(Some(Duration::from_secs(5)), ..)` on an
   `EpollReactor` with nothing ready.
2. The main thread waits until `h.try_turn_with(Some(ZERO), ..)` returns
   `Ok(None)`, which proves L is the leader.
3. Measure `let t = Instant::now(); h.lock().turn(Some(Duration::ZERO)).unwrap();`
   and assert `t.elapsed() < Duration::from_millis(200)`.

Today the call blocks about 5 s. After the fix it returns in microseconds.

## Sound (checked and found correct)

- **Token ABA in the runtime path.**
  - `IoDriver` tokens pack index plus generation, losslessly on 64-bit
    (`token.rs:87-100`).
  - `remove` bumps the generation and retires a slot at `MAX`.
  - A live token can never equal polling's `NOTIFY_KEY`: the 64-bit index is at
    most `u32::MAX-1` (`token.rs:260-264`) and the 32-bit index at most `0xFFFE`.
  - The reactor drops events for unknown tokens, and both
    `register`/`deregister` and `poll`'s translation run under the same `state`
    lock (`epoll.rs:345-415`, `503-573`, `596-607`). A `deregister` that has
    returned therefore never has a later event translated for it.
  - An event already translated before `deregister` reaches
    `extract_wakers_and_event_data`, finds the slab entry gone (generation
    bumped) and wakes nobody.
- **Oneshot re-arm with no lost edge.**
  - The default mode is `PollMode::Oneshot` (`epoll.rs:251-263`).
  - `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` re-polls the fd and queues it, and wakes a blocked
    `epoll_wait`, when it is already ready. So readiness that arrived between
    the event and the re-arm is reported.
  - The kernel re-checks each ready item against its *current* mask at
    harvest. An unreported item keeps its oneshot arm.
- **Interest changes racing an in-flight event.**
  - `modify` holds `state` across `epoll_ctl` and the map update
    (`epoll.rs:426-499`).
  - Translation masks the harvested readiness with the current interest under
    the same lock (`epoll.rs:277-316`).
  - A narrowed direction is dropped only when nobody re-armed it. A widened one
    is re-reported by the kernel.
  - HUP, ERR and PRI are added regardless of the mask, PRI only when it was
    requested (`epoll.rs:295-305`).
- **Wakeup mechanism** (polling 3.11.0).
  - It uses an eventfd, falling back to a pipe, coalesced by the `notified`
    compare-and-swap.
  - A notify sent before `epoll_wait` makes that wait return, because the
    eventfd stays readable and the notifier is re-armed after every wait.
  - A notify that lands during the current invocation is absorbed by it. The
    contract is "wakes the current or the following call", which is correct
    when the caller re-checks its state after `poll` returns.
  - With one write per CAS and a drain on every wait, the pipe cannot fill.
  - `NOTIFY_KEY` events are filtered out (polling `lib.rs:895`).
- **Re-arm wake removal (2bf1feb5a)** is correct for epoll.
  - `ep_modify` wakes a blocked wait when the re-armed fd is ready.
  - `poll` does not hold `state` during the kernel wait.
  - `register`, `deregister` and drop keep their unconditional wakes.
- **6f8ee76ed accumulation.**
  - Every harvested event wakes the token's current waker *after* any
    concurrent `rearm_accumulating`, because dispatch needs the driver lock.
    So a reset of the union cannot strand a direction the woken task still
    needs; the worst case is one spurious wake.
- **Timeouts.**
  - polling uses a timerfd with nanosecond precision, so a 0.5 ms deadline
    neither rounds to 0 nor busy-loops.
  - `Some(ZERO)` gives a non-blocking `epoll_wait` with the timer disarmed.
  - `None` gives an infinite wait with the timer disarmed.
  - `Instant` overflow becomes an infinite wait.
  - Without a timerfd, rustix rounds *up* to whole milliseconds
    (`timespec.rs:193-205`) or uses `epoll_pwait2`.
  - `EINTR` is retried internally against a fixed deadline (polling
    `lib.rs:751-769`).
- **Batch sizing.**
  - Unreported ready items stay on the kernel ready list.
  - `Events::push` grows (`mod.rs:317-323`).
  - The poll buffer is sized to `events.capacity()` with resize hysteresis
    (`epoll.rs:320-322`, `578-592`). No event is ever dropped for capacity.
- **ctl errors.**
  - On `MOD`/`DEL`, `ENOENT`, `EBADF` or an identity mismatch clears the
    bookkeeping and records an orphan tombstone. A retried `deregister` is
    therefore idempotent, and hard errors keep the bookkeeping
    (`epoll.rs:465-498`, `545-571`).
  - `EEXIST` on `ADD` surfaces as `AlreadyExists`.
  - The fd-identity check cannot tell anon-inode fds apart (eventfd and timerfd
    share one inode). The `ENOENT` errno still covers that case.
- **Lock order and re-entrancy.**
  - Driver lock → reactor `state`; `poll_events` → `state`.
  - `try_turn_with` releases the driver lock before `reactor.poll` and releases
    `poll_events`/`state` before re-taking the driver.
  - The reactor never invokes wakers.
  - `try_turn_with` runs callbacks and wakers after dropping the driver lock,
    with panic containment from cf3a632ba and 922594cd2.
  - No cycles.
- **b5322376c.** Failed polls are counted. In practice no kernel-harvested
  event is lost on the error path: polling's only failure after `epoll_wait` is
  a `MOD` on its own eventfd, and `ep_modify` does not allocate.
- **registration.rs.** `Registration` can only be constructed under
  `cfg(test)` (`registration.rs:99-100`), and `ReactorHandle` has no production
  implementation, so the file has no runtime exposure.
- **`registration_count`** uses Relaxed ordering but is diagnostics-only. It is
  never used to decide whether to poll.
- **fd leaks.** The reactor owns only polling's epoll fd, eventfd and timerfd,
  all closed on drop. Kernel entries for a dup'd file whose registered number
  was closed before `DEL` disappear with the file. They are oneshot, so they
  fire at most once and translation drops them.

## 1. HIGH (io-uring builds): waking before a mutation does not stop an io_uring poller from re-entering its ring-locked wait; the mutation then blocks while holding the IoDriver mutex

**Where**
- `io_driver.rs:661-669` (`IoDriverHandle::register`)
- `io_driver.rs:868-881` (the wake helpers)
- `io_driver.rs:959-980` (`rearm_with`)
- `io_driver.rs:1001-1006` (`deregister`) and `io_driver.rs:1043-1054` (`Drop`)
- `io_driver.rs:838-846`, the stated rationale

In each path, the reactor wake happens *before* the driver lock is taken and before the reactor mutation:

```rust
// io_driver.rs:661-668
// Always nudge the reactor before mutating registrations. Relying on a
// sampled `is_polling` flag is racy: a poller can transition into the
// blocking wait right after this load, which is especially harmful for
// io_uring because register/modify also need access to the shared ring.
let _ = self.reactor.wake();
let token = {
    let mut driver = self.inner.lock();
    driver.register(source, interest, waker)?
```
```rust
// io_driver.rs:965-978 (rearm_with)
self.wake_polling_reactor_for_interest_change();   // true for every non-Epoll backend (io_driver.rs:675)
...
let mut guard = driver.lock();
...
    guard.modify_interest(self.token, interest)?;
```

The io_uring backend holds its ring mutex for the whole blocking wait. Every mutation needs that mutex:

```rust
// io_uring.rs:1697-1701 (poll)
let mut ring = self.ring.lock();
match timeout {
    None => { ring.submitter().submit_and_wait(1)?; }
// io_uring.rs:1350 (submit_poll_add, reached from register at 1611 and modify at 1658)
let mut ring = self.ring.lock();
// io_uring.rs:1366 (submit_poll_remove, reached from deregister at 1679)
let mut ring = self.ring.lock();
```

The poller calls `reactor.poll` without the driver lock (`io_driver.rs:772`). The process-global fallback pump re-polls with no timeout, in a tight loop:

```rust
// udp.rs:1593-1594
let turned = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
    driver.turn_with(None, |_, _| {})
```

**Scenario** (fallback driver, `--features io-uring`; `create_reactor` prefers io_uring at `reactor/mod.rs:1184-1197`)
1. Pump thread P is blocked in `submit_and_wait(1)` and holds `ring`.
2. Thread M re-arms a socket on the fallback driver. `rearm_with` calls `wake()`, P's wait returns, and P drops `ring`.
3. M loses the CPU, or loses the driver-lock race. P's extraction holds `inner` (`io_driver.rs:775`). parking_lot lets the running P take `inner` again for `take_events` (`io_driver.rs:766`) before the parked M runs.
4. P completes its turn. Back in the pump loop, it calls `turn_with(None)`, takes `ring` and blocks again. The wake from step 2 has already been consumed.
5. M takes the driver lock (`io_driver.rs:972`), and `modify` takes io_uring `state` and then blocks on `ring.lock()` (`io_uring.rs:1350`).

**Outcome**
- M is a runtime worker, or any thread polling a driverless socket. It hangs until some other fallback fd completes or another thread issues a wake.
- While it hangs, M holds the fallback IoDriver mutex and io_uring `state`. Every other register, rearm or deregister on that driver queues behind it.
- If the socket M is re-arming is the only fallback activity, the hang is permanent.
- On scheduler workers the same race stalls the worker for up to `IDLE_IO_POLL_MAX_TIMEOUT` = 250 ms (`three_lane.rs:200`, `three_lane.rs:5486`), or until the next timer deadline.
- The comment at `io_driver.rs:838-845` ("io_uring needs the wake") assumes that a wake issued before the mutation is enough. It is not: the poller can re-enter its wait between the wake and the mutation.

**Confidence**
- The lock structure is confirmed by reading.
- The interleaving is a race that I did not reproduce. It is most likely on the fallback pump, which re-enters its wait immediately after each turn.
- The epoll backend is not affected. Its poll holds only `poll_events` across `epoll_wait` (`epoll.rs:580-596`).

**Fix shape** (additive)
- *Preferred, in the I/O driver.* Add a private `pending_mutations: AtomicUsize` to `IoDriverHandle`, shared with each `IoRegistration`.
  - A mutator does: increment, `wake()`, lock, mutate, decrement.
  - `try_turn_with` replaces a non-zero `timeout` with `Some(Duration::ZERO)` while the counter is non-zero.
  - This closes the window. Either the poller sees the count before it blocks, or the mutator's wake arrives after the check and ends that wait.
- *Alternative, in io_uring.* `submit_poll_add` and `submit_poll_remove` loop on `self.ring.try_lock_for(~200µs)` and call `self.wake()` after every failed attempt.

**Failing test sketch** (`io_driver.rs` tests)
- Build a stub `RingLikeReactor`:
  - It has a `ring: parking_lot::Mutex<()>`. `poll` holds `ring` and waits on a condvar until a wake flag is set or the timeout expires.
  - `register`, `modify` and `deregister` lock `ring`.
  - It reports the default `injected` backend, so `interest_change_wakes_reactor` is true.
  - Hook: after `arm_hook()`, the next `wake()` sets the flag and then blocks on a `Barrier` until `poll` has been *entered a second time*. This models M being descheduled right after its wake.
- Run a pump thread that loops `handle.turn_with(None, |_, _| {})`.
- In the test body:
  1. Register a source.
  2. Call `arm_hook()`.
  3. Spawn a thread that runs `reg.rearm(Interest::READABLE, &w)` and then sends on a channel.
  4. Assert `rx.recv_timeout(2s).is_ok()`.
- Today: times out. After the fix: passes.
- Teardown: set a stop flag and wake the stub so the pump thread exits.

## 2. MEDIUM: LabReactor has no one-shot arming and no level readiness, so lab results diverge from epoll in both directions

**Where:** `lab.rs:233-239` (socket state), `lab.rs:739-751` (`modify`), `lab.rs:808-817` and `lab.rs:960-971` (delivery).

```rust
// lab.rs:234-239
struct VirtualSocket {
    interest: Interest,
    /// Per-token fault injection state.
    fault: Option<FaultState>,
}
// lab.rs:961-971
let mut ready = delivered_event.ready & registered_interest;
...
if !ready.is_empty() {
    delivered_events.push(Event::new(token, ready));
}
```

The real contract is one-shot:
- `reactor/mod.rs:930-933`: "The Unix reactor backends default to oneshot delivery".
- `epoll.rs:259-261`: non-edge registrations map to `PollMode::Oneshot`.

The lab never disarms a registration after delivering an event, and `modify` only stores the new mask. It never re-evaluates readiness, whereas `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` on a ready fd queues an event. The I/O driver keeps the waker in the slab after dispatch (`io_driver.rs:477-481`), so every later delivery wakes it again.

**Scenario A: false pass**
1. A task's `poll_read` gets WouldBlock. Because of a bug, one path returns `Poll::Pending` *without* re-arming. Typical causes: a partial-read path, an early return, or a path that only buffers.
2. In production, the first event disarmed the one-shot registration, so nothing ever wakes the task again. It hangs.
3. In a LabRuntime test, the test calls `lab_reactor().inject_event(token, Event::readable(token), ..)` for each step it wants. Every injection is still delivered to the stale slab waker, the task advances, and the test passes.

Every lab-driven I/O test therefore misses this class of lost-wakeup bug.

**Scenario B: lab-only hang**
1. A registration is armed for `WRITABLE` only, for example a split half using plain `rearm` with only the write half waiting.
2. The test injects `READABLE`. It is popped and dropped, because `READABLE & WRITABLE` is empty.
3. The read half then re-arms with `READABLE | WRITABLE`. On epoll, `MOD` reports the pending readability at once. The lab reports nothing, so the reader hangs unless the test happens to inject again after the re-arm.

Lab results then depend on whether an injection lands before or after a re-arm.

The conformance harness already records the gap (`tests/conformance/reactor_conformance.rs:55-60`: "it keeps no arming state … oneshot re-arming and edge triggering do not apply"). Neither `lab.rs` nor the LabRuntime documentation warns about it, and nothing in the lab compensates.

**Fix shape** (opt-in, additive)
- Add `LabReactor::with_oneshot_fidelity()`, plus a `LabConfig` switch that LabRuntime passes through.
- Give `VirtualSocket` two private fields: `armed: bool` and `latched: Interest`.
- `register` and `modify` set `armed = true`.
- Delivering an event to a non-`EDGE_TRIGGERED` registration clears `armed`.
- Readiness that cannot be delivered, because the socket is disarmed or its mask does not cover the readiness, is ORed into `latched`.
- `modify` delivers `latched & new_interest` immediately as a level re-check, mirroring `EPOLL_CTL_MOD`. A delivery clears the latched bits it delivered.
- Keep the current behaviour as the default. Existing tests such as `tests/lab_determinism.rs` inject several events without re-arming.

**Failing test sketch**
- (A)
  1. `IoDriverHandle` on `LabReactor::with_oneshot_fidelity()`. Register `READABLE` with a counting waker.
  2. `set_ready`, `turn`: 1 wake.
  3. Do not re-arm. `set_ready` again, `turn`: assert the count is still 1.
  - Today the count is 2.
- (B)
  1. Register `READABLE`, then `reg.set_interest(WRITABLE)`.
  2. `set_ready(READABLE)`, `turn`: 0 wakes.
  3. `reg.set_interest(READABLE)`, `turn`: assert 1 wake.
  - Today 0 wakes.

## 3. MEDIUM: lab fault and chaos injection only change readiness; error kinds never reach I/O, and an injected close repeats HUP forever

**Where:** `lab.rs:854-895` (per-token close, pending and random errors), `lab.rs:932-954` (chaos I/O error), `lab.rs:975-994` (HUP on every poll).

```rust
// lab.rs:892-894
if injected_error.is_some() {
    delivered_events.push(Event::errored(token));
    continue;
}
// lab.rs:935-938
if let Some(kind) = chaos.rng.next_io_error_kind(config) {
    delivered_event = Event::errored(token);
    chaos.last_io_error_kind = Some(kind);
```

- `Event` carries only a token and readiness flags (`reactor/mod.rs:196-203`), so the `ErrorKind` survives only in diagnostics (`last_io_error_kind`, `last_injected_error`).
- The I/O driver does not store readiness at all. It only clones and wakes the slab waker, and passes the event to the trace callback (`io_driver.rs:467-485`, `lab/runtime.rs:5064-5082`).
- Code under test therefore wakes, retries the real syscall or virtual source, and gets data, or WouldBlock, but never the injected error.

The documentation promises otherwise:
- `ChaosConfig::io_error_probability` (`lab/chaos.rs:142-145`): "Probability of I/O operation failing."
- The chaos module table (`lab/chaos.rs:24`): "I/O Errors | Recovery from network/disk failures".
- `inject_error` (`lab.rs:506-508`): "converted to an error event with the specified `ErrorKind`".

The only in-tree check, `lab_runtime_chaos_stats_include_reactor_io_error_injections` (`lab/runtime.rs:7503-7547`), asserts stats and `last_io_error_kind` only. The lab reactor is the only injection site for `should_inject_io_error` (`git grep`).

**Scenario A: error injection does nothing**
1. `LabConfig::new(s).with_heavy_chaos()` (I/O error probability 0.15).
2. Code under test reads a socket. The chaos layer converts its readable event to `ERROR`.
3. The task wakes, reads, gets the data, and never runs its ConnectionReset or BrokenPipe recovery path.
4. A recovery bug, for example a leaked obligation or a missing reconnect, passes under every seed, while `chaos_stats().io_errors > 0` reports that errors were exercised.
5. The original readiness is also replaced (`delivered_event = Event::errored(token)`), so any test reading the trace sees an `ERROR`-only event that a real reset would not produce on its own.

**Scenario B: injected close**
1. A test calls `inject_close(token)` to simulate a peer FIN for a task reading a fd-backed source.
2. Every lab step's `poll_io` emits HUP (`lab.rs:979-994`, sticky by design), so the task is woken on every step.
3. The source is not actually at end of stream, so the read returns WouldBlock, the task re-arms and parks, and the cycle repeats.
4. `run_until_quiescent` spins until `max_steps`, or forever when it is `None`. In production, read returns 0 (EOF) and the task finishes.
5. The conformance harness notes the narrower part of this: "a close as HUP only … end-of-stream read readiness … is not modeled" (`reactor_conformance.rs:2453-2454`).

**Fix shape** (additive)
- Add a per-token pending-error slot that the I/O path consumes:
  - `Reactor::take_error(&self, token) -> Option<io::Error>` as a **default method returning `None`** (additive trait method);
  - `IoRegistration::take_error()`;
  - TcpStream, UdpSocket and Unix-socket poll paths call it after a wake, before retrying the syscall.
- `LabReactor` stores the injected kind there (chaos, pending and random errors), plus a sticky "EOF" flag for `inject_close` that reads observe.
- Until that lands, the `io_error_probability` documentation should say it is readiness-only.

**Failing test sketch** (LabRuntime, `cfg(unix)`)
1. `ChaosConfig::new(1).with_io_error_probability(1.0).with_io_error_kinds(vec![ConnectionReset])`.
2. Spawn a task doing `UnixStream::read` on one end of `UnixStream::pair()`.
3. Step until `lab_reactor().registration_count() == 1`. The token is the only one; on a fresh runtime it is `Token::new(0)` (first slab key).
4. Write 1 byte to the peer, inject a readable event, and step.
5. Assert the read returned `Err(ConnectionReset)`.
- Today it returns `Ok(1)`.

---

## 4. LOW: `IoRegistration` skips reactor deregistration when the driver is gone, although it holds the reactor

**Where:** `io_driver.rs:827-828` (fields), `io_driver.rs:1036-1039` (`deregister` else branch), `io_driver.rs:1049-1063` (`Drop` has no else branch).

```rust
// io_driver.rs:1036-1039
} else {
    self.deregistered = true;
    Ok(())
}
// io_driver.rs:1049
if let Some(driver) = self.driver.upgrade() { ... }   // nothing when the driver is gone
```

`IoRegistration` keeps `reactor: Arc<dyn Reactor>` (`io_driver.rs:828`). When it outlives its driver, it never calls `self.reactor.deregister(self.token)`. `IoDriver` has no `Drop` that deregisters its registrations either.

**Scenario**
1. A runtime shuts down while `TcpStream`s it created live on, for example moved to a std thread, or stored in a struct dropped later.
2. Dropping a stream frees nothing in the reactor, which stays alive through the remaining orphaned registrations.
3. On epoll:
   - the token and fd entries and `registration_count` leak (`epoll.rs:402-418`);
   - if the same reactor `Arc` is handed to a new driver (`RuntimeBuilder::with_reactor`, `builder.rs:3587`, or `IoDriverHandle::new(reactor.clone())`), registering a new socket whose fd number was reused fails with "fd already registered" (`epoll.rs:353-358`).
4. On io_uring, the `POLL_ADD` for the closed fd stays armed. UNCONFIRMED: an armed io_uring poll may hold a file reference, so the socket is not released and no FIN is sent until the ring is dropped.

**Fix shape:** in both the else branch and `Drop`, call `let _ = self.reactor.deregister(self.token);` and treat `NotFound` as success. This is additive.
- Caveat: two live drivers on one reactor already collide on token values, because each slab starts at index 0. That sharing is unsupported in practice, and the change does not make it worse.

**Failing test sketch**
1. A `CountingReactor` stub counts `deregister` calls.
2. `let h = IoDriverHandle::new(r.clone()); let reg = h.register(&src, READABLE, w)?; drop(h); drop(reg);`
3. Assert `r.deregister_calls() == 1`.
- Today the count is 0.

---

## 5. LOW: lab fault randomness is not derived from the lab seed

**Where:** `lab.rs:197-209`, `lab.rs:469-475`, `lab.rs:249-257` with `lab/runtime.rs:2427-2431`.

```rust
// lab.rs:198-203
fn new(token: Token, config: FaultConfig) -> Self {
    // Create deterministic RNG seeded from token for reproducibility
    let seed = token.0 as u64;
    Self { config, rng: ChaosRng::new(seed), ...
// lab/runtime.rs:2427-2430
let chaos_rng = config.chaos.as_ref().map(ChaosRng::from_config);
let lab_reactor = config.chaos.as_ref().map_or_else(
    || Arc::new(LabReactor::new()),
    |chaos| Arc::new(LabReactor::with_chaos(chaos.clone())),   // LabChaos::new -> ChaosRng::from_config(&config): same seed
```

**Scenario**
1. A test sweeps `LabConfig::new(seed)` over 1..1000 with `set_fault_config(token, FaultConfig::new().with_error_probability(0.3) ..)`.
2. Token values come from the slab, so they are identical across seeds, and every seed sees the *same* per-token error pattern. The sweep explores schedules, never fault placements.
3. `tests/lab_determinism.rs:445` works around this by deriving the *token* from the seed (`Token::new((seed % 1024) as usize + 1)`).
4. `set_fault_config` builds a fresh `FaultState` (`lab.rs:473`), so each reconfiguration replays the same decision sequence from the start.
5. The reactor's chaos RNG is a byte-identical copy of the runtime's chaos RNG stream. The k-th reactor decision (delay or I/O error) uses the same uniform value as the k-th runtime decision (cancel, delay, budget), so the two kinds of injection are correlated rather than independent.

Determinism holds. Seed-driven exploration, which the task asked about, does not.

**Fix shape** (additive)
- Add `LabReactor::with_seed(seed)`. LabRuntime passes `config.seed`.
- `FaultState` seeds from `mix(lab_seed, token)`; a reconfiguration keeps the existing RNG state.
- `LabChaos::new` derives `ChaosRng::new(scramble(config.seed ^ REACTOR_STREAM_TAG))`.
- Do not add pub fields to `FaultConfig` or `ChaosConfig` (struct literals).
- Note that this changes recorded chaos replays, so gate it behind a `LabConfig` flag or bump the replay format version.

**Failing test sketch:** run `run_fault_stats` with a *fixed* token under two LabRuntime seeds and assert the error patterns differ. Today they are identical.

---

## 6. LOW: LabReactor ignores source identity

**Where:** `lab.rs:720-737`. `register(&self, _source: &dyn Source, token, interest)` checks only the token. Real backends reject a second registration of the same fd (`epoll.rs:353-358`, io_uring at `io_uring.rs:1599-1604`).

**Scenario**
1. A migration or split path registers one fd twice. This is the bug class `ReactorRegistration::arm` step 1 (`udp.rs`, "migrate a fallback registration") and split/reunite guard against.
2. In the lab both registrations succeed and the test passes. In production the second returns AlreadyExists and the I/O call fails.

Evidence that this matters:
- `split.rs:1542` had to build a `SourceExclusiveReactor` test double to catch exactly this.
- `lab.rs:1991-1999` registers one `TestFdSource` three times.
- The conformance harness acknowledges the gap (`reactor_conformance.rs:2290-2291`).

**Fix shape:** add an opt-in `LabReactor::with_source_exclusivity()` that keys an fd-to-token map by `source.raw_fd()` on Unix. Leave the default unchanged, because existing tests depend on the current behaviour.

**Failing test sketch:** on the opt-in reactor, register one source under `Token(1)` and `Token(2)`, and expect the second to return `AlreadyExists`. Today it returns `Ok`.

---

## 7. LOW (latent, public API): `rearm` trusts `cached_waker`, so after `update_waker` the slab keeps the wrong waker

**Where:** `io_driver.rs:921-928` and `io_driver.rs:983-995`.

```rust
// io_driver.rs:923-927: updates the slab, cannot touch self.cached_waker (&self)
pub fn update_waker(&self, waker: Waker) -> bool { ... guard.update_waker(self.token, waker) ... }
// io_driver.rs:983-995
if self.cached_waker.as_ref().is_none_or(|w| !w.will_wake(waker)) {
    ... slot.clone_from(waker) ... else { return Ok(false); }
}
Ok(true)
```

**Scenario**
1. `reg.rearm(R, &w_a)` sets the slab and the cache to `w_a`.
2. `reg.update_waker(w_b)` (or `IoDriverHandle::update_waker(token, w_b)`) sets the slab to `w_b`; the cache stays `w_a`.
3. `reg.rearm(R, &w_a)` sees `cached.will_wake(w_a)`, skips the slab update and returns `Ok(true)`.

The next event wakes `w_b`'s task, and `w_a`'s task, which just parked, is never woken.

Similarly, after a low-level `IoDriver::deregister_waker(token)` (reachable through the public `IoDriverHandle::lock()`), `rearm` returns `Ok(true)` for a removed slot. The documented contract (`io_driver.rs:938-939`) is `Ok(false)`, so the caller parks on a token with no waker.

There are no in-tree callers today; the only `update_waker` call is in `io_driver_conformance_tests.rs:994`, on `IoDriver`.

**Fix shape:** compare against the slot under the lock that is already held. Use `match guard.wakers.get_mut(key) { Some(slot) => if !slot.will_wake(waker) { slot.clone_from(waker) }, None => return Ok(false) }` and drop `cached_waker`. Pointer comparison costs the same, and nothing is cloned when the waker is unchanged.

**Failing test sketch:**
1. On `LabReactor`, perform the three steps of the scenario.
2. `set_ready`, `turn`.
3. Assert `w_a` was woken and `w_b` was not.
- Today the reverse happens.

---

## Sound (checked, no defect found)

- **Dispatch outside locks.**
  - `try_turn_with` polls without the driver lock (`io_driver.rs:772`).
  - It extracts wakers under the lock (`io_driver.rs:774-783`).
  - It runs callbacks and wakers after releasing it (`io_driver.rs:791-800`).
  - `PollingGuard` restores the event buffer before clearing `is_polling` (`io_driver.rs:600-612`).
- **Waker and readiness edge.**
  - `rearm` holds the driver lock across the reactor `modify` and the slab waker store (`io_driver.rs:972-995`), and extraction reads the slab under the same lock, so an event dispatched after a re-arm sees the new waker.
  - The driver keeps no readiness cache, so there is no "clear readiness after WouldBlock" race.
  - On epoll, one-shot plus `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` re-reports level readiness that arrived between the WouldBlock and the re-arm.
- **Skipping the reactor wake on epoll interest changes** (`io_driver.rs:675`, `io_driver.rs:838-846`) is correct for epoll: its poll holds only `poll_events` across the wait (`epoll.rs:580-596`). This is the epoll half of finding 1; the io_uring half is broken.
- **Panics.** 922594cd2 (`wake_each`) and cf3a632ba (`run_callbacks_then_wake`, `io_driver.rs:1092-1119`) wake every waker of a batch before re-raising. The callback's panic takes precedence. Both dispatch paths use them.
- **6f8ee76ed (`rearm_accumulating`, `undispatched`)** is correct under its single-waiter contract.
  - The union is set at registration, extended by accumulating re-arms, cleared by dispatch on both paths (`io_driver.rs:381`, `io_driver.rs:470`) and dropped at deregistration.
  - A stale event that clears the union after a concurrent re-arm only shrinks the next arming, and every wake re-polls all directions of the one waiter, which rebuilds it.
  - `&self` sockets that several tasks wait on use shared waiter lists (`udp.rs:1932` `arm_shared`). Every `TcpStream` and `UdpSocket` method that parks takes `&mut self`.
- **Tokens carry generations** (`token.rs`). Stale events after deregister and re-register find no waker; `deregister` treats `NotFound` as success and always cleans local maps (`io_driver.rs:302-321`).
- **b5322376c.** A failed poll dispatches nothing and is counted and traced. io_uring returns `Ok` when it has already dequeued completions (`io_uring.rs:1797-1815`), so the "error drops the batch" contract loses nothing. db02202a3 is a cfg attribute only.
- **Lab determinism.**
  - Same-time events are ordered by sequence (`lab.rs:78-86`), and the `deregister` heap rebuild keeps that total order.
  - HUP fan-out over the `HashMap` is sorted (`lab.rs:975-994`).
  - The chaos RNG is seeded from the config.
  - LabRuntime always polls with `Some(ZERO)` (`lab/runtime.rs:5064`), so the reactor clock moves only through `advance_time` and `advance_time_to`, together with the runtime clock (`lab/runtime.rs:3076-3104`).
  - `wake()` never advances virtual time.
  - Each step processes timers, then polls I/O, in a fixed order (`lab/runtime.rs:4509-4512`).
  - No wall clock or unseeded RNG is used in either file.

Not reported, because it is not a correctness issue: `extract_wakers_and_event_data` deduplicates with a linear `SmallVec::contains` (`io_driver.rs:474`), which is O(n²) for a 1024-event batch.

title: [Runtime] Implement spawn(), spawn_local(), spawn_blocking()
description:
# Spawn Variants Implementation

## Overview
Implement the three spawn variants that cover different execution requirements.

## spawn() - General Purpose

### Signature
```rust
impl Scope {
    pub fn spawn<F>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, future: F) -> TaskHandle<F::Output>
    where
        F: Future + Send + 'static,
        F::Output: Send + 'static;
}
```

### Behavior
- Task can run on any worker
- Work-stealing enabled
- Uses region's current budget
- Returns handle for awaiting result

### Implementation
```rust
pub fn spawn<F>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, future: F) -> TaskHandle<F::Output>
where
    F: Future + Send + 'static,
    F::Output: Send + 'static,
{
    let task_id = cx.runtime.create_task(self.region_id, future);
    cx.runtime.scheduler.schedule(task_id);
    TaskHandle::new(task_id)
}
```

## spawn_local() - Non-Send Tasks

### Signature
```rust
impl Scope {
    pub fn spawn_local<F>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, future: F) -> TaskHandle<F::Output>
    where
        F: Future + 'static,
        F::Output: 'static;
}
```

### Behavior
- Task pinned to current worker
- Cannot be stolen
- Useful for \!Send types (Rc, RefCell, etc.)
- Panics if called from blocking thread

### Implementation
```rust
pub fn spawn_local<F>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, future: F) -> TaskHandle<F::Output>
where
    F: Future + 'static,
    F::Output: 'static,
{
    let worker_id = cx.current_worker()
        .expect("spawn_local must be called from async context");
    
    let task_id = cx.runtime.create_task_local(self.region_id, worker_id, future);
    cx.runtime.scheduler.schedule_local(task_id, worker_id);
    TaskHandle::new(task_id)
}
```

## spawn_blocking() - Blocking Operations

### Signature
```rust
impl Scope {
    pub fn spawn_blocking<F, R>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, f: F) -> TaskHandle<R>
    where
        F: FnOnce() -> R + Send + 'static,
        R: Send + 'static;
}
```

### Behavior
- Runs on dedicated blocking thread pool
- Does NOT block async workers
- Useful for CPU-bound or legacy sync code
- Pool auto-scales (bounded)

### Implementation
```rust
pub fn spawn_blocking<F, R>(&self, cx: &mut Cx, f: F) -> TaskHandle<R>
where
    F: FnOnce() -> R + Send + 'static,
    R: Send + 'static,
{
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel();
    
    cx.runtime.blocking_pool.spawn(move || {
        let result = f();
        let _ = tx.send(result);
    });
    
    // Wrap receiver in async task
    let task_id = cx.runtime.create_task(
        self.region_id, 
        async move { rx.await.unwrap() }
    );
    
    TaskHandle::new(task_id)
}
```

## Blocking Thread Pool

```rust
pub struct BlockingPool {
    sender: crossbeam_channel::Sender<Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send>>,
    threads: Vec<JoinHandle<()>>,
    config: BlockingPoolConfig,
}

pub struct BlockingPoolConfig {
    pub min_threads: usize,
    pub max_threads: usize,
    pub keep_alive: Duration,
    pub stack_size: usize,
}
```

## Invariants
- All spawned tasks are owned by a region
- spawn_local tasks cannot migrate
- blocking tasks complete before region close

## Testing
- spawn many tasks, verify completion
- spawn_local with \!Send types
- spawn_blocking for CPU-bound work
- Cancel propagation to all variants
- Region close waits for all variants

## Files
- src/cx/scope.rs (spawn methods)
- src/runtime/blocking_pool.rs (new)
- src/runtime/scheduler/mod.rs (local scheduling)
close_reason: Implemented spawn(), spawn_local(), spawn_blocking() variants in Scope. All tests pass.

title: [EPIC] Phase 2: Real Async I/O Reactor Implementation
description:
# Epic: Real Async I/O Reactor Implementation

## Background & Context

asupersync is a spec-first, cancel-correct, capability-secure async runtime for Rust. It is currently in **Phase 0**: a single-threaded deterministic kernel with no real I/O reactor. Instead, networking primitives use a "busy-loop on WouldBlock" pattern via `yield_now()`.

### Current Phase 0 Behavior (src/net/tcp/stream.rs)
```rust
// Phase 0: Busy-loop on WouldBlock
Err(ref e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => {
    cx.waker().wake_by_ref();  // Re-poll immediately
    Poll::Pending
}
```

This works for deterministic testing but is unsuitable for production:
- No efficient I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)
- Wastes CPU cycles spinning
- Cannot scale to many concurrent connections

## Why This Epic Matters

For rchd (remote compilation helper daemon) and similar production uses, we need:
1. **Unix socket server** - Real async accept/read/write for local IPC
2. **HTTP server capability** - Foundation for axum/hyper integration
3. **SSH connections** - Foundation for openssh-rs integration
4. **Event streaming** - Concurrent broadcast to multiple clients

## Design Philosophy (CRITICAL - Must Be Preserved)

This implementation MUST respect asupersync's core design principles:

1. **Structured Concurrency by Construction**
   - Tasks owned by regions forming a tree
   - Region close guarantees quiescence
   - No orphaned work possible

2. **Cancellation as a Protocol**
   - Not silent drops but explicit request → drain → finalize
   - Bounded cancellation budgets
   - Cancel-correct I/O operations

3. **Capability Security**
   - All effects flow through explicit `Cx` tokens
   - No ambient authority
   - IoCap<'r> capability tier for I/O operations

4. **Deterministic Testing**
   - Lab runtime with virtual time
   - Deterministic scheduling
   - Trace replay capability
   - LabReactor for simulated I/O

5. **Two-Phase Effects (Reserve/Commit)**
   - I/O operations should follow the reserve/commit pattern where applicable
   - ObligationRecord tracking for in-flight I/O

## Phase Roadmap Context
```
Phase 0: Single-thread deterministic kernel    ✅ COMPLETE
Phase 1: Parallel scheduler + region heap      🔜 In Progress
Phase 2: I/O integration                       📍 THIS EPIC
Phase 3: Actors + session types                Planned
Phase 4: Distributed structured concurrency    Planned
Phase 5: DPOR + TLA+ tooling                   Planned
```

## Implementation Strategy

We will build:
1. **Core Reactor Abstraction** - Platform-agnostic trait + IoDriver integration
2. **Linux Reactor (epoll)** - Primary target, most common production env
3. **macOS Reactor (kqueue)** - Developer machines
4. **Lab Reactor** - Deterministic testing with simulated I/O
5. **TCP/UDP Primitives Rewrite** - True async with reactor registration
6. **Unix Domain Sockets** - UdsListener/UdsStream for local IPC
7. **Integration Tests** - Prove correctness across platforms

## Success Criteria

- [ ] TCP server can accept thousands of connections efficiently
- [ ] Unix socket server works with real async I/O
- [ ] Lab runtime still provides deterministic testing
- [ ] Cancellation works correctly (tasks can be cancelled mid-I/O)
- [ ] Obligations are tracked for all in-flight I/O operations
- [ ] No CPU spinning on idle connections
- [ ] All existing tests still pass

title: [fresh-eyes] http/h2/stream.rs: reject_pseudo_headers_in_trailers is pub fn but only called from tests — dead production surface
description:
src/http/h2/stream.rs:42 — pub fn reject_pseudo_headers_in_trailers(headers: &[Header]) -> Result<(), &'static str> was introduced in commit 3d75e38c2 (br-asupersync-of0l5f) as a free function intended for the connection.rs HEADERS-dispatch path to call when stream.would_be_trailer_block() returns true. Production wiring landed differently: connection.rs uses validate_h2_pseudo_headers(headers, is_trailers=true) (the same module-private validator that handles the initial header block), and reject_pseudo_headers_in_trailers is now ONLY called from the of0l5f unit tests within stream.rs (lines 2691 + 2704).

Threat (P3, NOT a security bug):
  - Dead public-API surface: any external caller that imports this function gets it, but the asupersync internal code path doesn't go through it. The two paths could drift — a future bugfix to validate_h2_pseudo_headers's trailer branch would not propagate to reject_pseudo_headers_in_trailers, and external consumers using the latter would see different validation behaviour than the gateway itself applies.
  - Dual-implementation surface for a security-sensitive check (trailer pseudo-header rejection) violates the 'one canonical validator' principle.

Fix direction (one of):
  1. Demote to pub(crate) and document that it's a test-only helper that mirrors the production validator at connection.rs:1636.
  2. Wire it into the production HEADERS dispatch as the canonical trailer validator (would require removing the is_trailers branch from validate_h2_pseudo_headers, leaving that fn focused on initial-block validation only — a small refactor).
  3. Remove it entirely (the tests can call the production path directly; the helper is redundant).

Two non-bug observations from the same audit (recorded for completeness, not filed):
  - Stream::initial_headers_decoded() method shares its name with the field it accesses (cosmetic/style).
  - Commit caa468177's message describes the parameter as 'allow_extended' (RFC 8441 extended-CONNECT) when the actual parameter is is_trailers (RFC 9113 §8.1) — historical-context inaccuracy, no code impact.

Source: fresh-eyes 24h-diff audit on h3_native + h2/stream + grpc/web (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed: demoted to #[cfg(test)] pub(crate); production trailer validation goes through connection::validate_h2_pseudo_headers (commit b1318475f)

title: Implement pipeline combinator for staged processing
description:
## Purpose
The pipeline combinator chains a sequence of transformations where each stage's output feeds the next stage's input. Unlike simple sequential composition, pipeline supports concurrent execution of stages on different data items (streaming pipeline parallelism).

## Design Philosophy
Two modes of pipeline operation:
1. **Sequential pipeline**: Stage N+1 starts only after stage N completes (simple chaining)
2. **Streaming pipeline**: Stages run concurrently, connected by channels (higher throughput)

For Phase 0 (single-threaded), implement sequential pipeline. Streaming pipeline deferred to Phase 1.

## Semantic Model (Sequential)

```rust
pub async fn pipeline<A, B, C, E>(
    cx: &mut Cx<'_>,
    input: A,
    stage1: impl FnOnce(&mut Cx<'_>, A) -> impl Future<Output = Result<B, E>>,
    stage2: impl FnOnce(&mut Cx<'_>, B) -> impl Future<Output = Result<C, E>>,
) -> Outcome<C, E>
```

### Behavior
1. Execute stage1(input) → intermediate
2. If Ok: execute stage2(intermediate) → output
3. If any stage fails: propagate error, do not run subsequent stages
4. If cancelled: stop at next stage boundary

### Generalization
Pipeline can be generalized to N stages using a macro or builder pattern:
```rust
pipeline\!(cx, input,
    |cx, x| stage1(cx, x),
    |cx, x| stage2(cx, x),
    |cx, x| stage3(cx, x),
)
```

## Cancellation Handling
- Check cancellation between stages
- If cancelled before stage N: return Cancelled, stages N..end never execute
- Each stage may have internal checkpoints for finer-grained cancellation
- Stage cleanup runs if stage was started

## Budget Composition
Total pipeline budget = Σ(stage_budgets)
This follows the tropical semiring: budgets add sequentially.

## Future: Streaming Pipeline (Phase 1+)
When parallel scheduler available, support concurrent stages:
```
Input → [Stage1] → Channel → [Stage2] → Channel → [Stage3] → Output
```
- Each stage runs in its own task
- Channels are two-phase (reserve/commit)
- Backpressure through bounded channels
- Cancellation propagates downstream

## Invariant Support
- **Sequential ordering**: Output of stage N is input to stage N+1
- **Error short-circuit**: First error stops pipeline
- **No partial results**: Either all stages complete or none
- **Cancel-correctness**: Respects cancellation at stage boundaries

## Testing Requirements
1. All stages succeed
2. Early stage fails (later stages not called)
3. Late stage fails
4. Cancellation before first stage
5. Cancellation between stages
6. Type flow verification (A → B → C)
7. Budget accounting

## Example Usage

```rust
// Image processing pipeline
let result = scope.pipeline(
    cx,
    raw_image,
    |cx, img| async move { decode_image(cx, img).await },
    |cx, img| async move { resize_image(cx, img, 800, 600).await },
    |cx, img| async move { compress_image(cx, img, Quality::High).await },
).await?;
```

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §5.7 Derived Combinators
- Unix pipeline model
- Reactive streams / backpressure patterns
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: §3.2 Sequential composition

## Acceptance Criteria
- Pipeline stages are executed under structured concurrency (no detached tasks) and respect region close.
- Backpressure/queueing uses cancel-safe two-phase primitives where data loss is otherwise possible.
- Cancellation propagates through stages and drains all in-flight work deterministically.
- E2E tests cover cancellation mid-pipeline and no-obligation-leaks.
close_reason: Pipeline combinator implemented with staged processing, error short-circuit, cancellation checks, and comprehensive tests. All tests pass.

title: [security-saas HIGH] trace/event.rs: redact_browser_trace_event has partial variant coverage AND has zero production callers — sensitive strings (cancel reasons, IoError kinds) leak unredacted through browser trace exports
description:
src/trace/event.rs:738-761 — redact_browser_trace_event handles ONLY two TraceData variants:

```
pub fn redact_browser_trace_event(event: &TraceEvent) -> TraceEvent {
    let mut redacted = event.clone();
    match (&event.kind, &event.data) {
        (TraceEventKind::UserTrace, TraceData::Message(_)) => {
            redacted.data = TraceData::Message("<redacted>".to_string());
        }
        (TraceEventKind::ChaosInjection, TraceData::Chaos { kind, task, detail: _ }) => {
            redacted.data = TraceData::Chaos { kind: kind.clone(), task: *task, detail: "<redacted>".to_string() };
        }
        _ => {}      // BUG: every other variant passes through verbatim
    }
    redacted
}
```

Two HIGH-severity gaps:

1. PARTIAL COVERAGE. TraceData has many variants that carry potentially sensitive strings:
   - TraceData::Cancel { reason } — cancel reasons can include stack-frame-derived paths, originator IDs, user-tagged messages.
   - TraceData::RegionCancel { reason } — same shape.
   - TraceData::IoError { kind } — std::io::Error kind strings can include filesystem paths in some std impls.
   - TraceData::Region { reason }-style variants (when present).
   None of these are redacted by the function. A browser-side trace consumer (which sees redacted output) gets the unredacted value of every non-{UserTrace,Chaos} variant — including reason strings that may contain credentials emitted by careless production code.

2. NEAR-ZERO PRODUCTION USAGE. The only caller in the repo is at src/trace/event.rs:3765 (a test). Every browser/external trace exporter that simply iterates self.events() and serializes each event RAW bypasses the redactor entirely. The function is publicly re-exported (trace/mod.rs:111) but the export path doesn't enforce its use. So even if a future consumer is supposed to call it, today they don't, and the redactor is dead-code in the production graph.

Concrete attack:
  1. Production handler emits a CancelReason with kind=User and message="invalid token sk_live_ABC123".
  2. The runtime records a TraceEvent with TraceData::Cancel { reason: "User: invalid token sk_live_ABC123" }.
  3. Browser-side exporter (e.g., the wasm-browser-preview surface) reads runtime trace events and ships them to a collector for tab-side debugging.
  4. The exporter calls trace.snapshot() but NOT redact_browser_trace_event.
  5. The bearer token leaks to whatever destination the browser collector forwards to.

Fix direction:
  1. Make redact_browser_trace_event total over TraceData variants — for every variant that carries a String field, replace with "<redacted>" (or a hash-with-prefix for diagnostic continuity).
  2. Plumb the redactor into the production browser-trace export path (BrowserCaptureSource::Runtime path) so that no caller can ship raw events. The non-redacted snapshot remains available for in-process consumers (oracles, replays, lab analyses) where the sensitive data stays inside the trust boundary.
  3. Add a regression test that constructs a TraceEvent for every TraceData variant carrying a String field and asserts the redacted output contains "<redacted>" not the original value.
  4. Use a deny-by-default model: the function should NOT have a "_ => {}" fallthrough; missing-variant should be a compile error so future additions to TraceData are forced to declare their redaction policy.

Severity HIGH for the same reasons as br-asupersync-65gy5c: traces routinely cross trust boundaries, the surface is wide, and the data-flow graph from cancel reasons to browser export is long and easy to lose track of.

Source: /security-audit-for-saas on src/observability/* + src/trace/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: redact_browser_trace_event now total over TraceData variants (no _=> fallthrough = compile-error guarantee for future variants); helpers redact CancelReason, DownReason, PanicPayload; wired into browser_trace_log_fields_with_capture so every export path gets redacted output; 5 regression tests
