title: [metamorphic-gap] codec/length_delimited: missing encoded-length monotonicity property — input1.len() <= input2.len() => encoded(input1).len() <= encoded(input2).len()
description: src/codec/length_delimited.rs has 6 metamorphic tests (round_trip, partial_frame_state, max_frame_size_rejections, boundary_fragmentation, oversized_prefixes, byte_order_consistency) but NONE assert encoded-length monotonicity: feeding a SMALLER input must NOT produce a LARGER encoded output. This is the canonical sanity check for any framing codec — violations indicate either non-deterministic header sizing (length_field_length should be const per codec instance) or a bug where the adjustment field accidentally inverts the encoded ordering. Concretely: for a fixed LengthDelimitedCodec, encode(payload_a) and encode(payload_b) where payload_a.len() < payload_b.len() must produce encoded outputs satisfying encoded_a.len() <= encoded_b.len(). The property holds trivially for the current implementation (header is fixed-width, body is appended verbatim) but lack of an explicit test means any future variable-length header refactor or compression integration could regress without detection. Recommend a proptest with payloads of varying lengths asserting the inequality. Severity HIGH for any codec the user expects to behave like an injective length-preserving function.
close_reason: Added mr_encoded_length_monotonicity in src/codec/length_delimited.rs: sweeps length_field_length ∈ {1,2,4,8} × payload grid, asserts smaller payload → smaller-or-equal encoded output, plus encoded == header + payload invariant.

title: [CONTROL] Online change-point detection on runtime metrics — regime-shift alarms with conservative fallback
description:
WHY: the EXP3 cancel-preemption controller and Lyapunov governor adapt WITHIN a regime; none of the existing machinery detects that the regime itself shifted (workload phase change, deploy, traffic pattern flip) — the known failure mode of adaptive controllers is confidently optimizing for yesterday. ADWIN/CUSUM/Page-Hinkley are the buried-standard online detectors: O(1)-ish updates, provable false-positive bounds, exactly the missing complement (graveyard tier-A, failure-signature matched).

WHAT: (1) a ChangePointMonitor over selected runtime series (ready-queue depth, wake-to-run latency, cancel-streak reward drift, drain-rate): pluggable detector per series (CUSUM for known-shift-size mean changes, Page-Hinkley as cheap default, ADWIN where window adaptivity pays), deterministic arithmetic (integer/fixed-point accumulators — no float nondeterminism in replay); (2) ACTIONS, strictly bounded: on detection -> (a) emit a structured regime-change trace event + diagnostic, (b) optionally reset the EXP3 weight state + decision-contract posterior to priors (forgetting stale learning — the conservative response), (c) NEVER takes aggressive scheduling action directly; (3) per the composition discipline: interference analysis vs EXP3/governor documented (timescale separation: detector acts on reset-events at epoch granularity, controllers act per-epoch — no shared-variable fighting), validated in H5's harness; (4) off by default; RuntimeBuilder opt-in with per-series config.
design: FILES: new src/runtime/changepoint.rs (detectors as pure structs: update(x)->Option<Detection>, exhaustively unit-testable), wiring in scheduler snapshot path (where governor already samples — same cadence, zero extra locking), reset hooks into three_lane EXP3 state + decision_contract. Detector params (drift sensitivity, thresholds) as config with documented ARL (average run length) tradeoffs. Galaxy-brain card per detector: equation, substituted defaults, ARL intuition.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Pure-detector unit suite: synthetic step/drift/no-change series -> detection delay + false-positive rates match documented ARL bounds (table-driven, seeded). 2. Determinism: detector state evolution byte-identical across replays (fixed-point proof test). 3. Integration: lab scenario with a mid-run workload flip -> regime event emitted + EXP3 reset observed + post-reset adaptation faster than no-reset baseline (measured, seeded). 4. False-positive cost: steady-workload soak shows zero resets at default params (seed corpus). 5. Interference: timescale-separation statement documented + H5 harness scenario green. 6. Off-by-default verified; config docs + galaxy-brain cards committed.
notes: RELATION: H5 validates composition; recon notes decision-contract already models regime states (healthy/congested/unstable/partitioned) — the detector feeds it evidence rather than competing with it (design alignment note required). FALLBACK: feature is itself the fallback-trigger mechanism; its own failure mode (false resets) bounded by ARL params.

title: [CONTROL] Queueing-theoretic pool autosizing — replace min/max guesses with M/G/k-grounded bounds
description:

Graveyard/alien-artifact family: queueing theory, highest practical-fit entry for this codebase.

WHAT: (1) a sizing module: given observed arrival rate, service-time mean+variance (EWMA-estimated from existing pool metrics), and a target (P(wait) <= p or E[wait] <= w), compute recommended k via square-root staffing with documented approximation error; (2) TWO consumption modes: advisory (default: recommendation exposed via metrics/inspector + logged when actual diverges >2x from recommended — operators act) and managed (opt-in: blocking pool min/max + DB pool size track the recommendation within configured floors/ceilings, adjusting at bounded cadence with hysteresis — no flapping); (3) deterministic in lab (estimators on virtual time); (4) galaxy-brain card: the staffing formula, substituted live values, plain-English 'why 7 threads'.
design: FILES: new src/runtime/pool_sizing.rs (pure math + estimator), consumers: src/runtime/blocking_pool.rs (managed-mode hooks honoring its existing atomic claim/retire invariants — audit memory: expansion/retire logic has subtle invariants, integrate via its existing config surface only), src/database/pool.rs (D5's v2 surface). Estimators: integer-friendly EWMA. Hysteresis: recommendation must move >=20% before action; cadence floor 1 epoch.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Math unit suite: staffing outputs vs known Erlang-C table values (golden, with documented approximation tolerance). 2. Advisory mode: divergence warning fires correctly in a lab scenario with deliberate undersizing (asserted log + metric). 3. Managed mode: lab load ramp -> pool follows recommendation within bounds, no flapping (hysteresis proof: action count bounded), blocking-pool invariants preserved (its existing test suite green). 4. Determinism in lab replay. 5. Floors/ceilings always win over recommendations (safety test). 6. Galaxy-brain card + ops docs. 7. Interference: managed-mode + H1 detector scenario in H5 harness (regime change -> estimator reset -> resize cadence respected).
notes:

title: [CONTROL] Lineage-driven fault injection — target the faults that could actually break invariants
description:
WHY: chaos mode injects faults blindly (seeded but undirected); LDFI's insight (graveyard entry): a SUCCESSFUL execution's trace reveals which events supported the outcome — compute minimal fault sets that could remove that support, inject exactly those, and either find a real bug or build evidence of fault-tolerance. Orders of magnitude fewer experiments than blind chaos for distributed/cancellation invariants.

WHAT: (1) lineage extraction from lab traces: for a target invariant outcome (e.g. 'message delivered', 'region closed clean', 'saga compensated'), compute the support graph (which sends/acks/timer-fires/leases the outcome causally depended on — happens-before machinery in trace/dpor.rs + causality.rs provides the edges); (2) fault-hypothesis generation: minimal hitting sets over the support graph (bounded enumeration, budgeted — hitting-set is NP-hard, use the standard bounded-depth iterative approach from the LDFI literature); (3) experiment loop: re-run with each hypothesis injected via the existing chaos/fault machinery (channel/fault.rs, lab/chaos.rs) -> violation found (=> auto-crashpack, C3) or hypothesis refuted -> iterate to deeper sets; (4) frankenlab ldfi <scenario> --invariant <oracle> --depth N CLI; deterministic end-to-end.
design: FILES: new src/lab/ldfi.rs (lineage + hitting sets + loop), frankenlab subcommand, consuming trace/causality + chaos injection points. Support-graph soundness: over-approximate dependence is safe (more hypotheses), under-approximation misses bugs — document the extraction rules per event type. Budgets: depth cap + experiment cap + per-run step cap, exhaustion reports coverage achieved.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Seeded fixture with a KNOWN single-fault vulnerability (e.g. drop-one-specific-ack breaks delivery): LDFI finds it within depth-1 experiments, vastly fewer runs than blind chaos baseline (count comparison committed). 2. Fault-tolerant fixture (the F1 ECC channel is perfect): LDFI exhausts depth-k refuting all hypotheses -> emits a coverage certificate ('no <=k-fault counterexample exists for this trace corpus' — honest scoping: per-corpus, not universal). 3. Determinism end-to-end. 4. Budget exhaustion paths tested. 5. CLI with --json; docs + galaxy-brain card. 6. Composes with C3 auto-crashpack on found violations (e2e-checked in C7 extension or here).
notes: LDFI hypothesis-layer PROVEN by runnable test: tests/ldfi_fault_hypothesis_proof.rs (cargo test --test ldfi_fault_hypothesis_proof --features test-internals -> 3/3 PASS). Behaviorally validates src/lab/ldfi.rs: AC1 known-single-fault fixture (e1 supports all 19 derivations) -> LDFI returns exactly {e1} = 1 hypothesis vs blind-chaos 20 single-fault experiments (count comparison committed); disjoint support -> minimal size-2 hitting sets; AC2 unbreakable fixture -> coverage_certificate(Some(3)). title: [CONTROL] Learning-augmented scheduling hints — consistency/robustness-bounded predictions (SPECULATIVE; design study first)
description:
WHY (and why cautious): graveyard tier-A entry — learning-augmented algorithms wrap classical policies with predictions while PROVING worst-case bounds when predictions fail (the consistency-robustness tradeoff). Candidate applications here: predicted task service times improving EDF tie-breaks / steal-target selection / proactive worker wake. BUT: asupersync's determinism + replay guarantees make online-learned state in the SCHEDULER a hazard (EXP3 threaded this needle carefully), and the EV is unproven for our workloads. Hence: this bead is a DESIGN STUDY, not an implementation commitment.

WHAT: (1) a written study: candidate prediction points, the consistency/robustness bounds achievable (cite the ski-rental/scheduling-with-predictions literature), determinism-preservation strategy (predictions as pure functions of replayable state ONLY), and the measured headroom (profile: how much do mispredictions of service time actually cost on our benches today?); (2) a go/no-go recommendation with the EV matrix; (3) IF go: a follow-up implementation bead gets filed with the study as its spec (not implemented under this bead).
design: Deliverable is docs/design/learning_augmented_scheduling_study.md + profiling evidence. Hard constraints stated upfront: deterministic replay non-negotiable; predictions must come from replay-stable inputs; worst-case bounds must be PROVEN not vibed; H5 registry compliance mandatory for any actuation.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Study covers: >=3 candidate injection points with headroom measurements from real benches (the profile-first rule). 2. Bounds analysis per candidate (consistency c, robustness r, the tradeoff curve). 3. Determinism strategy per candidate or explicit infeasibility finding. 4. EV matrix + go/no-go with reasoning. 5. If go: follow-up bead filed referencing the study; if no-go: closed as documented-negative-result (equally valid).
notes: DEPENDS on E7 (benches for headroom measurement). P3 speculative by explicit design — the anti-pattern this structure prevents is novelty-driven controller creep.
close_reason: Design study completed as a documented NO-GO. docs/design/learning_augmented_scheduling_study.md identifies three source-grounded injection seams, formal consistency and robustness bounds, deterministic replay and H5 controller-registry gates, an EV screen, and explicit reopen criteria. title: Implement cross-thread wake dedup and atomic task state transitions
description:
# Cross-Thread Wake Dedup + Atomic Task State

## Purpose
Parallel scheduling requires task state and wake signals to be safe under concurrency.

Phase 0 can use plain booleans and single-thread invariants. Phase 1 needs:
- atomic wake flags
- atomic task lifecycle transitions (or lock-protected transitions)
- clear happens-before relationships for trace correctness

## Constraints
- Core crate forbids unsafe code.
- Prefer correctness and determinism over extreme lock-free optimization.

## Plan-of-Record
- Start with lock-protected task records (e.g., per-task `Mutex`) if needed.
- Ensure wake dedup prevents:
  - double-enqueue
  - missed wakeups

## Acceptance Criteria
- Under heavy contention:
  - no missed wakeups
  - no duplicate polls beyond what semantics allow
  - cancellation transitions remain monotone

## Testing
- Parallel stress tests with randomized but deterministic scheduling in lab.
close_reason: TaskPhaseCell + TaskWakeState implemented in src/record/task.rs with atomic transitions and wake dedup tests

title: [REVIEW][HIGH] CDC mask bit calculation non-deterministic leading to chunking inconsistency
description:
**Issue**: The CdcEngine::compute_mask_bits_from_constant() function on line 127 of src/net/atp/chunk/dedupe.rs uses modulo arithmetic that makes chunking non-deterministic:

```rust
let bits = (constant % 16) + 8; // Range: 8-23 bits (256B to 8MB average)
```

**Problem**: Different normalization constants that have the same modulo 16 value will produce identical mask bits, making chunking behavior non-deterministic and potentially breaking content-defined chunking guarantees.

**Impact**: This could cause chunk boundary inconsistency across transfers with different normalization constants, breaking deduplication effectiveness.

**Fix**: Use a proper hash-based approach or direct mapping from the normalization constant to ensure deterministic mask bit selection.
close_reason: done

title: Implement Outcome type with severity lattice
description:
# Outcome Type with Severity Lattice

## Purpose
The Outcome type is the fundamental result type for all tasks and regions in Asupersync. Unlike Result<T, E>, it has FOUR variants ordered by severity, enabling monotone aggregation where "worse always wins."

## The Four Outcomes (Severity Order)
```rust
enum Outcome<V, E, R, P> {
    Ok(V),           // Severity 0: Success with value
    Err(E),          // Severity 1: Application error
    Cancelled(R),    // Severity 2: Cancelled with reason
    Panicked(P),     // Severity 3: Panic (unrecoverable)
}
```

## Why Four Values?
Traditional async runtimes conflate cancellation with errors or ignore it entirely. This causes:
- Silent data loss when cancellation drops in-progress work
- No distinction between "I failed" vs "I was stopped"
- Panics and errors treated the same way

Asupersync makes cancellation a first-class citizen because:
1. **Explicit Reasoning**: Code can pattern match on WHY something stopped
2. **Monotone Aggregation**: When combining outcomes, we want consistent behavior
3. **Policy-Aware**: Different outcomes may trigger different policies (restart, propagate, etc.)

## Mathematical Structure: Severity Lattice
The outcomes form a lattice under severity ordering:
```
Panicked
    ↑
Cancelled
    ↑
  Err
    ↑
  Ok
```

The lattice operations:
- **Join (⊔)**: Returns the more severe outcome (used for aggregation)
- **Meet (⊓)**: Returns the less severe outcome (rarely used)

## Key Operations

### severity() -> u8
Returns 0-3 for comparison. Must be implemented as a const fn for performance.

### combine(self, other) -> Self (for same V types)
Implements the join operation: `max_by_severity(self, other)`

This is used when:
- A region aggregates child outcomes
- A join combinator combines results
- Supervision decides on escalation

### is_terminal() -> bool
All variants are terminal (a task/region has finished).

### is_success() -> bool
Only Ok is success.

### into_result() -> Result<V, CombinedError<E, R, P>>
Converts to traditional Result for interop.

## Implementation Requirements

1. **Generic over all four type parameters**: V (value), E (error), R (cancel reason), P (panic payload)

2. **Default type parameters**:
   - E = Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>
   - R = CancelReason
   - P = Box<dyn Any + Send>

3. **Must implement**:
   - Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq (when inner types do)
   - PartialOrd, Ord based on severity
   - From<Result<V, E>> for easy interop

4. **Combinators**:
   - map, map_err, map_cancelled, map_panicked
   - and_then, or_else
   - unwrap_or, unwrap_or_else
   - ok(), err(), cancelled(), panicked() extractors

## Invariant Preservation

This type supports INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR: outcomes are absorbing states. Once a task reaches Completed(outcome), it cannot transition again.

## Testing Requirements

1. Severity ordering is correct: Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked
2. combine() always returns the more severe outcome
3. Lattice laws hold (associativity, commutativity, idempotence)
4. From<Result> conversions are correct

## Performance Considerations

- Outcome should be repr(u8) discriminant for fast severity checks
- No heap allocation for the Outcome enum itself
- Clone should be cheap (inner types may heap-allocate)

## Example Usage
```rust
let child_outcomes = vec![
    Outcome::Ok(42),
    Outcome::Err(MyError),
    Outcome::Ok(17),
];
let region_outcome = child_outcomes.into_iter()
    .reduce(|a, b| a.combine(b))
    .unwrap_or(Outcome::Ok(()));
// Result: Outcome::Err(MyError) - worst wins
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.2 (Outcomes)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.1 (Outcomes form a severity lattice)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Outcome has variants Ok/Err/Cancelled/Panicked with a total severity order (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked).
- Provides `severity()` and ordering/aggregation helpers used by region close + combinators.
- Aggregation is monotone: combining outcomes never yields a "less severe" result.
- Unit tests cover ordering, lattice laws (assoc/comm/idempotent), and conversions.

- Provides aggregation helper(s) used by region close and join.

1. current_source_review.sources[regex_lowering.rs] (sha256, bytes, review text) in both lowering artifacts. Only current_source_review may change; the historical-JSON digest guard hashes the artifact without that key.
2. live_source_pins[4,5] in regex_private_compile_api_map_v1.json (sha256, line_count, revision).
3. VM_SOURCE_SHA256 (tests/regex_vm_terminal_receipt_contract.rs:56) and sources[regex_vm.rs] (sha256, bytes) in artifacts/regex_vm_terminal_receipt_v1.json.

   - regex_vm_terminal_receipt_v1.json's digest is in the api map's producer_artifact_pins (~line 1911);

   Then run all 9 tests/regex_*contract* binaries plus the privacy inventory test.

- L-B1: execute_capture_mode (regex_vm.rs ~3793-3815) now runs program.validate before invariants_hold. A call with both an invalid program and invalid limits returns a compile error instead of InvalidLimits, unlike execute_full and find_iter. No test covers this.

- L-A3: the tightened reconnect test is a wall-clock window with about 400 ms of slack. About 1400 ms, or an ordering assertion, would not flake on loaded workers.
Found sound: NATS PING/PONG accounting across confirmation, keepalive, user ping() and reconnect; a timed-out attempt closes its socket at once; cancellation wins over the timeout.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Convert Lease/Release obligation to session types
description:
Convert the Lease->Release protocol to session types. This is more complex than SendPermit because leases have timeout semantics, creating a branching protocol.

BACKGROUND (Session Types with Choice, Graveyard section 5.2): Binary session types support choice (branching) via offer/select. When a protocol has multiple possible continuations, the type system tracks which branch was taken. This maps naturally to lease protocols where a lease can be released or can expire.

CURRENT STATE: Lease and Release are runtime-checked. A task acquires a lease, holds it for some duration, then either releases it explicitly or lets it expire. Timeout detection is handled by a separate watchdog.

TARGET STATE: Channel<LeaseActive> offers two transitions: (1) release() -> Channel<Done> for explicit release, (2) The timeout watcher can force-transition to Channel<Expired> via an external event. This tests the choice/branching encoding in the typestate system.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Define state types: struct LeaseActive; struct LeaseExpired; struct Done;. (2) Choice encoding: use an enum for the branch outcome: enum LeaseOutcome { Released(Channel<Done>), Expired(Channel<LeaseExpired>) }. (3) Timeout integration: impl ObligationChannel<LeaseActive> { async fn hold_or_expire(self, deadline: Instant) -> LeaseOutcome } uses tokio::select! internally. (4) Renewal as recursion: impl ObligationChannel<LeaseActive> { fn renew(self, new_deadline: Instant) -> ObligationChannel<LeaseActive> } consumes and re-creates the channel in the same state. (5) Cx deadline propagation: the lease deadline is derived from Cx::deadline(), ensuring attenuated capabilities cannot extend leases beyond their parent budget. (6) Use typestate macros from bd-3u5d3.2 to generate from protocol spec.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Calling release() on Channel<LeaseActive> compiles and returns Channel<Done>. (2) Accessing the channel after expiry produces a compile error (moved value). (3) Renewal resets the deadline without releasing the lease (same logical channel, new timeout). (4) Lease duration respects Cx deadline propagation. (5) Zero runtime overhead vs current implementation. (6) All transitions logged to EvidenceLedger.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each lease lifecycle event emits structured log: lease_id, event_type (acquired|renewed|released|expired), remaining_budget_ms, trace_id. EvidenceLedger entry on lease completion: component=lease_manager, action=lease_released|lease_expired, includes hold_duration_ms, renewal_count, was_within_budget.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) trybuild compile-fail tests for invalid lease operations. (2) Unit tests: acquire, hold, release -- verify Done state. (3) Timeout test: acquire lease with short deadline, verify expiry path fires correctly. (4) Renewal test: acquire, renew 5 times, release -- verify all transitions. (5) Virtual time test via FrankenLab: verify lease expiry is deterministic under virtual clock. (6) Concurrent leases: 100 leases with staggered deadlines, verify no cross-contamination.

title: [cardinality-leak] observability/cancellation_debt_monitor.rs entity_queue_depths HashMap unbounded by user-controllable entity_id
description:
src/observability/cancellation_debt_monitor.rs:146,543-545 — DebtSnapshot (public struct) carries:

  entity_queue_depths: HashMap<String, usize>

populated at lines 543-545 from work.entity_id during record_pending_work(). Same shape as the cancellation_tracer.rs and cancellation_visualizer.rs leaks (filed separately): user-controllable key, no cap, public structure exported via snapshot interfaces.

Threat: enqueue pending work with distinct entity IDs across calls; the HashMap grows one entry per unique value. Snapshots widen over time. Operators who export DebtSnapshot to monitoring systems see bloat in every snapshot payload.

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) Heap growth in the debt monitor; eventual OOM.
  (b) Snapshot serialization grows without bound.
  (c) Inter-snapshot diffs (used for change detection) grow expensive as the cardinality climbs.

Fix direction:
  1. MAX_ENTITY_QUEUE_DEPTHS cardinality cap with LRU eviction on least-recently-touched entity.
  2. Or: drop entity_queue_depths entries when the corresponding work completes (size-couple to actual pending state).
  3. Add a regression test mirroring the entity_throughput one.

Severity HIGH — same reasoning as the sibling beads on cancellation_tracer.rs and cancellation_visualizer.rs (this is the same pattern applied to a third structure in the same module family). All three should be fixed in a single sweep applying a shared CardinalityCappedMap helper from crate::util.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/observability/* deepest pass (2026-04-26).

Regression test af24n5_entity_queue_depths_cap_with_overflow_bucket at line 1279 covers cap behavior. Closing as already-applied.

title: [codec] src/codec/tests/mod.rs:105 capacity_growth_bounded can miss per-call over-allocation regressions
description: capacity_growth_bounded reuses a single BytesMut across size tiers [100, 1000, 10000] and checks cap_after <= buffer.len() * 4 after each append. Because buffer.len() is cumulative and the buffer is never cleared, a later encode can over-reserve badly relative to the incremental write and still pass as long as the total buffer length stays large enough. Example: a buggy encode that grows to 32_768 on the 10_000-byte append still satisfies the current bound once total len reaches 11_100. Suggested fix: run each size against a fresh destination buffer or assert on incremental slack relative to cap_before/newly-appended bytes instead of cumulative len.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION to my own fix sketch, after reading scripts/scan_stubs.sh properly rather than inferring from its output. Two of my three structural claims were imprecise; the diagnosis and the 18-marker enumeration stand.

WRONG IN MY FILING: 'Add the 18 rows to artifacts/stub_placeholder_inventory_v1.json'. That artifact has no rows array -- rows[] is the OUTPUT (row_inventory_output). The input is `selectors`: 35 rules keyed on path/path_prefix + term list, each carrying disposition, support_class, blocker_bead_id, notes. So the fix is a handful of selector entries, not 18 hand-written rows. Smaller and better than I described.

WORTH NOTING: those selectors match on PATH + TERM, with no line or text anchoring. That is the same blindness class as the no-mock allowlist before asupersync-pzfwf5 -- a selector added for one justified marker silently covers every future marker of that term in that file. Whoever takes this should not widen a selector's path_prefixes to make the count go to zero.

WRONG IN MY FILING: I suggested giving scan_stubs.sh the cfg(test) awareness from pzfwf5 as if it had none. It has two mechanisms, and they are unevenly applied:
  - check_production_deferred_comments_are_tracked uses production_lines(), which IS cfg(test)-aware: it tracks #[cfg(test)] and #[test] scope by brace depth and bails out entirely on a top-of-file #![cfg(test)]. Its own comment concedes the approximation ('marker comments/strings should not control test scope') -- brace_delta() counts raw { and } per line, so a brace inside a string or comment shifts its depth. That is the exact failure mode cfg_test_regions()/rust_code_mask() in scripts/check_no_mock_policy.py now handles, so the upgrade is still worth doing, but as a precision fix to something that exists.
  - build_rckstb_inventory_summary (the check that reports the 18) has NO such awareness. Its only test filter is is_src_rust_test_module(), a FILENAME heuristic: name.endswith('_test.rs') or name.startswith('test_'). src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs matches neither, so all 9 of its in-file #[cfg(test)] markers are scanned as production. That asymmetry is the whole reason check 1 reports 18 while check 2 reports 1.

REVISED FIX ORDER:
  (A) Point the rckstb inventory at the same production_lines() filter check 2 already uses. That alone should drop 9 of the 18 without classifying anything, and removes the recurring burden rather than paying it once.
  (B) Add narrow selectors for the remaining 9 production markers, with blocker_bead_id set (z01bbr.8.3 for the three atp.rs ssh-tunnel markers, which already hold a no-mock waiver expiring 2026-10-31).
  (C) The 'tracked-marker entry' for src/bin/atp.rs:2695 is a hardcoded shell branch in check_production_deferred_comments_are_tracked -- currently a single literal if matching one nats.rs string mapped to asupersync-jh9g1j. Adding a second branch works but that registry does not scale; consider moving it to data alongside the selectors.

Sequence matters: do (A) before (B), or you will write selectors for markers that (A) removes from the surface entirely.

title: [perf] runtime/state.rs: live_task_count() does O(N) arena scan despite incremental counters available via task_table
description: src/runtime/state.rs:2062 RuntimeState::live_task_count() does self.tasks_iter().filter(|(_, t)| !t.state.is_terminal()).count() — full O(N) scan over the task arena on every call. The xxcss5 work (commits 1f942f8e0/86d9793a2/665de00fe/adadea72) wired O(1) incremental counters into TaskTable (tasks.live_task_count(), count_in_phase, etc.) precisely so callers like LyapunovGovernor's StateSnapshot::from_runtime_state could avoid the O(N) scan. RuntimeState::live_task_count was apparently missed by that wiring. If anything still calls RuntimeState::live_task_count (e.g., diagnostics, region close checks, doctor/observability), every call eats O(N) where N is the arena size, even when the answer is cached one method dispatch away. Fix: delegate to self.tasks.live_task_count() (the O(1) incremental accessor). Severity HIGH if hot paths still call this; even MEDIUM-as-tech-debt because the duplicated semantics will silently drift from each other.
close_reason: RuntimeState::live_task_count() now delegates to TaskTable::live_task_count() — phase_counts.iter().sum() — replacing the O(N) tasks_iter().filter(!is_terminal()).count() arena scan with O(1) incremental-counter access. Soundness verified: TaskState::is_terminal == matches!(Completed(_)), TaskPhase::is_terminal == TaskPhase::Completed, and the LIVE_PHASE_COUNT=5 phase_counts buckets cover {Created, Running, CancelRequested, Draining, Finalizing} — Completed is the only excluded bucket, mirroring is_terminal exactly. Edge cases preserved: claim-but-not-spawned (Created bucket), in-flight cancel (CancelRequested/Draining/Finalizing buckets), and the terminal Completed transition. Stress regression test 'live_task_count_matches_arena_scan_under_churn' creates 32 tasks, partial-cancels every other one, completes all of them, and asserts at every step that the new O(1) method agrees with the original O(N) arena-scan oracle. State.rs edits compile clean; the lib's overall default-feature build is still blocked by pre-existing concurrent-agent regressions (Outcome<()> 2-generic and Waiter rename in record/task.rs:55,715) that are completely unrelated to this fix (0ba45c264)

title: [AGENT-DX] Agent-Native Developer Experience — machine-readable surface, error codes, self-explaining failures
description:
WHY: asupersync's primary consumers are increasingly AI coding agents (the repo even ships skills/asupersync-mega-skill). Agents fail with this library for predictable reasons found in recon: (1) no machine-readable API map — agents must grep 1900-line README or source; (2) runtime panics like "obligation leaked: ObligationLeak {...}" carry no remediation; (3) compiler errors from missing Send bounds or absent `__state` in macros are generic Rust errors that never mention the asupersync concept that fixes them; (4) doctest coverage on the 10 core types is patchy so agents can't pattern-match working code.

GOAL: an agent that has never seen this repo can (a) discover the API surface from a checked JSON artifact, (b) turn any ASUP-Exxx error code into a documented fix, (c) copy a working doctest for every core type, and (d) follow one short agent-targeted testing guide to write a passing deterministic test on the first try.

CHILD TASKS: machine-readable API surface map + contract test; ASUP-Exxx error-code registry wired into Display/panic paths; actionable diagnostics for the big three failure classes (obligation leak, region close timeout, futurelock); doctest + examples-metadata coverage; TESTING_FOR_AGENTS guide + mega-skill sync; e2e agent-affordance validation script.

SUCCESS METRIC: scripted "agent smoke test" (child bead) passes: parse API map, resolve 3 error codes to remediation docs, compile+run every doctest, follow the guide to author a lab test.

title: [AGENT-DX] Machine-readable API surface map — checked JSON artifact agents can navigate
description:
WHY: agents adopting asupersync today must grep source or parse rustdoc HTML. The repo already has a strong pattern for this problem: checked JSON contract artifacts (artifacts/*.json + tests/*_contract.rs). Apply the same pattern to the public API itself.

WHAT: artifacts/api_surface_map_v1.json — generated (not hand-written) from rustdoc JSON output (cargo +nightly rustdoc -- --output-format json, or rustdoc-types crate) and post-processed into a curated schema: modules -> exported items {name, kind, signature, one-line doc, stability class (core/feature-gated/preview/test-internals), feature flag, example pointer}. Plus an entry_points section listing the blessed starting calls per use-case (run async main, spawn, channel, lab test, HTTP server, HTTP client, RaptorQ transfer...) — the 'what do I call first' table agents need most. A generator script (scripts/generate_api_surface_map.py or rust tool) + a contract test (tests/api_surface_map_contract.rs) that fails when the public surface drifts from the artifact — forcing regeneration, which keeps the map perpetually truthful.
design: FILES: new scripts/generate_api_surface_map.* , artifacts/api_surface_map_v1.json, tests/api_surface_map_contract.rs, docs pointer from README + AGENTS.md. Schema gets a schema_version field from day one. Curation layer: a small config (kept next to the generator) lists modules to exclude (internal) and the entry_points table content — config is the human-judgment part, generation is mechanical. Contract test compares the artifact against freshly-extracted symbols (names+kinds at minimum; signatures hashed to avoid churn noise).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Artifact generated, committed, <300KB, schema-versioned. 2. Contract test red when a public symbol is added/removed without regenerating (prove by temporary mutation in review). 3. entry_points covers >=10 use-cases each pointing at a real compiling example/doctest. 4. Generator runs via one documented command (rch-wrapped) in <2 min. 5. README + AGENTS.md reference the artifact as the canonical surface map. 6. jq-validated in CI (well-formed, required fields present).
notes: RISK: rustdoc JSON format is nightly-unstable — pin handling in the generator and treat format breaks as generator-maintenance, never as blocking the API itself (contract test compares the committed artifact, not live rustdoc, in the default lane). RELATION: B6 smoke test consumes it; [DX-CORE] A13 examples index feeds example pointers.

title: [AGENT-DX] ASUP-Exxx error-code registry — every runtime failure maps to a documented remediation
description:
WHY: recon's strongest agent-DX finding: failures like 'obligation leaked: ObligationLeak {...}' or generic SpawnError give an agent nothing to act on. Error CODES with a stable registry turn every failure into a lookup -> remediation -> fix loop. The repo's own doctor/error-taxonomy work for WASM (docs/wasm_dx_error_taxonomy.md, ASUPERSYNC_BROWSER_NATIVE_* codes) proves the pattern works here — extend it to the core runtime.

WHAT: (1) define the ASUP-Exxx namespace (E0xx core runtime: spawn/region/budget; E1xx obligations; E2xx channels/sync; E3xx cancellation/drain; E4xx lab/replay; E5xx net/http; E6xx db; E7xx distributed/remote; E8xx raptorq; E9xx config/build) — allocate in a registry file docs/error_codes/registry.json {code, name, summary, probable_causes[], remediation[], doc_path, since}; (2) per-code markdown page under docs/error_codes/ (template-driven; start with the ~25 highest-traffic failures found in recon: obligation leak, region close timeout, futurelock, spawn errors, channel closed/lagged, budget exhausted, lock-order violation, replay divergence, decode failure...); (3) wire codes into Display/Debug of the corresponding error types + panic messages ('[ASUP-E101] obligation leaked... see docs/error_codes/ASUP-E101.md'); (4) contract test: every code referenced in src/ exists in the registry and has a doc page, and vice versa (no dead codes).
design: FILES: docs/error_codes/registry.json + pages, src/error.rs, src/obligation/graded.rs (leak panic text), src/runtime/state.rs (leak handler messages), src/lab/runtime.rs (futurelock/replay messages), tests/error_code_registry_contract.rs. Keep code-in-message format machine-parseable: leading '[ASUP-ENNN]' token. The registry.json IS the machine surface; markdown pages are the human/agent deep-dives.
acceptance_criteria: 1. >=25 codes registered with complete remediation pages on day one (list reviewed at close against recon's failure-class inventory). 2. Contract test enforces bidirectional registry<->source<->docs consistency. 3. Display/panic wiring verified by unit tests asserting the [ASUP-ENNN] token appears (golden text tests). 4. Remediation pages follow a fixed template (symptom/cause/fix/example/related) — lint check in the contract test. 5. Registry schema-versioned; jq-validated in CI.
notes: RELATION: [DX-CORE] A9 SpawnError taxonomy lands codes E001-E0xx; B3 diagnostics rewrite consumes this; B6 smoke test resolves 3 codes end-to-end. Scope discipline: this bead builds the SYSTEM + initial 25 codes; long-tail code assignment happens organically per-bead afterwards (note in AGENTS.md bead-workflow conventions).

title: [AGENT-DX] Actionable diagnostics for the big three: obligation leaks, region-close timeouts, futurelocks
description:
WHY: these three failure classes are where users/agents actually get stranded (recon Part C). Each currently reports WHAT without WHO/WHY/HOW-TO-FIX, even though the runtime KNOWS the answers (task ids, obligation kinds, wait edges, last checkpoints are all tracked internally — diagnostics just don't surface them).

WHAT (per failure class, reusing [INTROSPECT] surfaces where available):
1. ObligationLeak: report kind (permit/ack/lease), creating task + region, creation backtrace-lite (creating call site if cheaply available via track_caller on reserve paths), age, and the 3-step remediation from the error-code page. Include the nearest checkpoint message of the leaking task.
2. RegionCloseTimeout: report WHICH children are still live (task names/ids, their states, their last checkpoint message, what they are waiting on via wait-edge lookup) — turning 'region stuck' into 'task fetch-user-42 is Running, last checkpoint "connecting to db", waiting on TcpStream readable'.
3. FuturelockViolation: report held obligations + the await point class it stalled in, plus the standard fix patterns.
All three: emit as structured trace events AND human text with the ASUP code; in lab mode, attach to the run report automatically.
design: FILES: src/observability/diagnostics.rs (CancellationExplanation/TaskBlockedExplanation/ObligationLeak already exist — extend + actually wire them into the failure paths), src/runtime/state.rs (leak handler), src/lab/runtime.rs (futurelock emission), src/record/task.rs (last-checkpoint access). #[track_caller] on reserve() entry points for creation-site capture (zero-cost; verify no hot-path regression with bench). Determinism: diagnostic text stable across same-seed runs (it feeds goldens).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Each failure class has a lab test that triggers it and asserts the diagnostic contains: ASUP code, responsible task/region ids, last checkpoint message, and at least one wait-edge/holding fact. 2. Golden snapshot tests for the rendered text (scrubbed of volatile ids per the repo's snapshot-scrubbing idiom). 3. track_caller additions show zero p50 regression on the channel/obligation benches. 4. Diagnostics emitted as structured TraceEvents validated in trace tests. 5. Error-code pages for the three classes updated with real rendered examples.
notes: DEPENDS on error-code-registry (codes) and benefits from [INTROSPECT] J1/J3 (ledger queries + checkpoint history) — sequence after those where convenient, but do not block: degrade gracefully to the data available. RELATION: directly serves [LAB-DX] auto-crashpack content quality.

title: Multipath aggregator: dropped late symbol stays deduped (dead rollback wiring)
description: src/transport/aggregator.rs: ReorderProcessResult.rollback_dedup_record is ONLY ever constructed false (accepted(), :1481), so the rollback at process() :1922-1923 (self.dedup.rollback_record) is DEAD CODE. process() records a symbol in the dedup 'seen' set FIRST (:1902), then the reorderer's late-symbol branch (diff<0, :1626-1628) DROPS it without delivery and without rollback, so the symbol stays in 'seen' and any retransmission is rejected forever. git 297cc5c3f added rollback_record intending exactly this fix but never wired the producer side. NUANCE: simply setting rollback=true on the late branch is INSUFFICIENT — once the give-up/timeout paths (:1603-1623, flush_timeouts :1680-1682) advance next_expected past a missing slot, a retransmission still hits diff<0 and is re-dropped, so rolling back dedup alone does not make it deliverable. The real fix is semantics-dependent: decide whether the RaptorQ decoder consumer wants every unique symbol regardless of order (then the reorderer should DELIVER late-but-unique symbols, not drop them) vs strictly ordered delivery (then distinguish 'behind a delivered slot' = keep deduped from 'behind an abandoned slot' = rollback). Needs a design decision + test.

title: quic_core: implement RFC 9000 §A.2 packet-number decode-reconstruction algorithm + conformance vectors
description:
Conformance audit of src/net/quic_native/transport.rs + src/net/quic_core/mod.rs (packet number). Existing tests cover sender-side width selection (rfc9000_packet_number_encoding_length, rfc9000_packet_number_truncation_algorithm, rfc9000_packet_number_edge_cases, rfc9000_packet_number_width_validation) and round-trip encode/decode when encoded_pn == decoded_pn (rfc9000_packet_number_in_headers). Two genuine gaps remain:

GAP 1 (conformance) — RFC 9000 §17.1 receiver-side decode algorithm is not implemented.

read_packet_number at quic_core/mod.rs:707 extracts the width-byte suffix into a u32 but does NOT reconstruct the full packet number from context. Per RFC 9000 §A.2 ('Sample Packet Number Decoding Algorithm'), a receiver must use the 'largest packet number received' (expected_pn) to reconstruct the full PN from the truncated suffix:

  expected_pn = largest_pn + 1
  pn_nbits = pn_len * 8
  pn_win = 1 << pn_nbits
  pn_hwin = pn_win / 2
  pn_mask = pn_win - 1
  candidate_pn = (expected_pn & ~pn_mask) | truncated_pn
  if candidate_pn <= expected_pn - pn_hwin and candidate_pn < (1 << 62) - pn_win:
      candidate_pn += pn_win
  elif candidate_pn > expected_pn + pn_hwin and candidate_pn >= pn_win:
      candidate_pn -= pn_win
  return candidate_pn

Well-known RFC 9000 §A.2 test vectors:
  - largest_pn = 0xa82f30ea, truncated = 0x9b32, pn_len = 2 -> 0xa82f9b32
  - largest_pn = 0xa82f30ea, truncated = 0xac5c02, pn_len = 3 -> 0xa82fac5c02 ... (validate against the spec's exact examples)

Without this algorithm, a long-lived connection whose PN exceeds 2^(pn_len*8) cannot decode peer-sent packets; only the wire suffix is returned. If the caller treats that suffix as the full PN (which read_packet_number's signature invites), ack tracking silently misattributes acks to the wrong packets.

GAP 2 (inconsistency) — wire encoder uses u32, ack tracker uses u64.

- quic_core::LongHeader.packet_number and ShortHeader.packet_number are u32 (line 175, 205)
- transport.rs TrackedPacket.packet_number is u64 (line 32)

Per RFC 9000 §17.1 the protocol allows PN up to 2^62 - 1. Truncating at the wire layer to u32 means long-lived connections (> 2^32 packets) cannot be encoded without wrapping. The transport u64 side already assumes the reconstructed PN is full; the wire u32 forces callers to bridge.

Recommended fix (single work item):
1. Add pub fn decode_packet_number_reconstruct(truncated: u32, pn_len: u8, largest_pn: u64) -> u64 next to read_packet_number, implementing RFC 9000 §A.2 exactly.
2. Add a conformance test module quic_core::tests::rfc9000_a2 with the exact §A.2 examples as a table-driven #[test].
3. Widen LongHeader.packet_number / ShortHeader.packet_number to u64; keep ensure_pn_fits u64-aware. Existing round-trip tests stay valid because the encoder still writes only pn_len bytes; the u64 just prevents silent wrap.
4. Wire transport.rs ack tracker to feed largest_acked_pn into the decode path.

References: RFC 9000 §17.1 (encoding), §A.2 (decoding pseudocode and examples), §A.3 (sample encoding). The existing asupersync tests in quic_core/mod.rs lines 1506-1790 are the right place for the conformance harness.

Audit commit: 3e4616c2 (CRDT MRs) — no code changes in this bead filing.
close_reason: RFC 9000 §A.2 packet number reconstruction implemented: (1) Added decode_packet_number_reconstruct() function with exact algorithm, (2) Added comprehensive conformance tests with RFC examples, (3) Widened packet_number fields from u32 to u64 in headers, (4) Updated related functions. Core functionality complete.

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 0 - Single-Thread Deterministic Kernel
description:
# Phase 0: Single-Thread Deterministic Kernel

## Overview
This is the foundational phase of Asupersync. It establishes the core runtime semantics on a single thread with deterministic execution, enabling rigorous testing and validation of the fundamental invariants before adding complexity.

## Why Single-Thread First?
1. **Correctness Before Performance**: Multi-threading adds non-determinism and complexity. By starting single-threaded, we can prove our semantic model is correct.
2. **Deterministic Testing**: Single-thread execution with virtual time enables perfect reproducibility - the same test always produces the same behavior.
3. **Simpler Debugging**: When something goes wrong, there's only one execution path to analyze.
4. **Foundation for Parallelism**: Everything built here transfers directly to Phase 1's parallel scheduler.

## Core Components
- **Outcome Type**: The four-valued severity lattice (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked)
- **Budget System**: Product semiring for deadline/quota propagation
- **Region Tree**: Structured concurrency ownership hierarchy
- **Task System**: Task lifecycle and state machine
- **Cancellation Protocol**: Request → Drain → Finalize with bounded cleanup
- **Obligation System**: Two-phase effects with linear resource tracking
- **Cx Capability Boundary**: All effects through explicit capabilities
- **Scheduler**: Cancel > Timed > Ready lane priority
- **Lab Runtime**: Virtual time and deterministic scheduling

## Success Criteria
- All 6 non-negotiable invariants hold in all reachable states
- All progress properties verified under fair scheduling
- Test oracles verify: no task leaks, no obligation leaks, quiescence on close, losers drained, all finalizers ran, no ambient authority
- Trace capture/replay works perfectly
- Derived combinators (join, race, timeout) behave according to algebraic laws

## Mathematical Foundations Implemented
- Severity lattice for outcome aggregation
- Near-semiring operations for join/race
- Product semiring for budget combination
- Linear resource discipline for obligations
- Mazurkiewicz trace equivalence (foundation for Phase 5 DPOR)

## The 6 Non-Negotiable Invariants (from AGENTS.md)

| # | Invariant | Oracle |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | **Structured concurrency** – every task is owned by exactly one region | no_task_leaks |
| 2 | **Region close = quiescence** – no live children + all finalizers done | quiescence_on_close |
| 3 | **Cancellation is a protocol** – request → drain → finalize | (state machine tests) |
| 4 | **Losers are drained** – races must cancel AND fully drain losers | losers_always_drained |
| 5 | **No obligation leaks** – permits/acks/leases must be committed or aborted | no_obligation_leaks |
| 6 | **No ambient authority** – effects flow through Cx and explicit capabilities | no_ambient_authority |

Additionally, **Determinism** is a first-class property of the lab runtime that enables testing.

## Key Implementation Beads (Phase 0)

### Core Types
- Outcome type with severity lattice
- CancelReason with severity ordering
- Budget with product semiring semantics
- Core identifiers (RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time)

### State Machines
- TaskState: Pending → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed
- RegionState: Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed
- ObligationState: Reserved → Committed/Aborted/Leaked

### Records
- TaskRecord, RegionRecord, ObligationRecord and registries

### Runtime
- Global RuntimeState (Σ)
- Scheduler with 3-lane priority
- Waker (std::task::Wake) and wake deduplication (no unsafe)
- Timer heap for sleep operations

### Cx/Scope
- Scope API for user-facing region handles
- Cx capability boundary

### Cancellation/Finalization
- Cancellation protocol transitions
- Finalization system (defer_async, defer_sync, bracket)

### Combinators
- join (parallel composition)
- race (alternative composition with loser draining)
- timeout (race with deadline)

### Lab Runtime
- Virtual time
- Deterministic scheduling
- Trace capture/replay

### Test Oracles
- 6 oracles matching the 6 invariants

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §21 (Phase-0 kernel reference implementation plan)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md (complete operational semantics)
- AGENTS.md (non-negotiable invariants)
close_reason: Phase 0 complete. All 10 sub-beads closed: Scaffolding (akx.1), Semantics Types (akx.2), Records & State Machines (akx.3), Scheduler & Waker (akx.4), Cancellation & Finalization (akx.5), Cx Capability (akx.6), Trace & Lab Runtime (akx.7), Combinators (akx.8), Verification (akx.9), Two-Phase Primitives (akx.10). 2145+ lib tests, 23 E2E tests, all invariants verified.

title: Phase 0: Scaffolding & Core Utilities
description:
# Phase 0: Scaffolding & Core Utilities

## Purpose
Establish the *non-negotiable* foundations that every other Phase 0 component will build on:

- A clean crate/module layout and lint configuration
- Deterministic, dependency-minimal utilities that preserve the lab runtime’s determinism
- Internal data-structure utilities (arenas/queues/small collections) needed to implement the kernel without pulling in large crates or ambient globals

This feature exists to keep the core runtime implementation **small, deterministic, and dependency-disciplined**.

## Why This Needs Its Own Feature
The design documents repeatedly demand:
- **Determinism** (lab runtime, replay)
- **No ambient authority** (no hidden globals)
- **Minimal dependencies** (avoid pulling in large ecosystems)
- **Hot-path performance** (avoid unnecessary allocations)

These are easiest to satisfy when we explicitly plan and implement “supporting utilities” *before* we write the scheduler and state machine.

## Scope (What This Feature Covers)
### 1) Crate scaffolding
- Cargo workspace + `src/` module layout that mirrors runtime concepts (ids, outcomes, budgets, records, scheduler, trace, lab)
- Strict lints: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, clippy pedantic/nursery as configured by project policy
- A project structure that makes it hard to accidentally introduce ambient globals or side-effectful logging

### 2) Deterministic PRNG (lab-only)
We need deterministic tie-breaking (e.g., choosing among runnable tasks) and deterministic jitter (e.g., backoff). We **must not** rely on OS entropy or global RNG.

Plan-of-record:
- Implement a tiny internal PRNG (e.g., `SplitMix64`/`XorShift`-class) with:
  - explicit seed in `LabConfig`
  - reproducible `next_u64()` and `gen_range(n)`
  - no external dependencies

### 3) Internal arenas / IDs / small collections helpers
The kernel needs “arenas” for `RegionRecord`, `TaskRecord`, `ObligationRecord` and stable IDs.

Plan-of-record:
- Implement an internal `Arena<T>` backed by `Vec<Option<T>>` (or equivalent) that provides:
  - `insert -> Id`
  - `get/get_mut`
  - `remove` (only when safe; e.g., after close/quiescence or for tests)
  - deterministic iteration order when needed (or explicit “order is unspecified”)
- Avoid pulling `slab`/`slotmap` unless we can justify it under the dependency policy.

### 4) Test-only helpers
- Minimal helpers to run deterministic tests and print/format traces **only inside tests**.

## Non-Goals
- Implementing the runtime itself (scheduler, cancellation, region close) — those are separate features.
- Adding any new executor runtime dependency (tokio/async-std/etc.)

## Acceptance Criteria
- We can build an empty crate and pass the quality gates:
  - `cargo check --all-targets`
  - `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
  - `cargo fmt --check`
- Deterministic PRNG utility exists and is used anywhere “randomness” is required.
- Arena utility exists and is used for runtime records (no ad-hoc `Vec` indexing scattered everywhere).
- No external dependency is introduced without explicit justification.

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for PRNG determinism: same seed => identical sequence.
- Unit tests for arena safety: insert/get/remove invariants, ID reuse policy documented and tested.
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met: quality gates pass, deterministic PRNG (det_rng.rs) and Arena utilities (arena.rs) implemented with tests, no external dependencies added.

title: Implement deterministic PRNG utility (no deps)
description:
# Deterministic PRNG Utility (No Dependencies)

## Purpose
The lab runtime and some combinators require deterministic tie-breaking and deterministic jitter. We must not introduce ambient randomness or rely on external heavy RNG crates unless justified.

This task introduces a tiny internal PRNG used *only* when determinism is required:
- lab scheduler tie-breaking among runnable tasks
- deterministic jitter/backoff (retry, hedge) in lab mode
- any future schedule exploration tooling

## Constraints
- No `rand` crate in core unless explicitly justified.
- Must be reproducible across platforms and Rust versions.
- Must be fast and simple.

## Plan-of-Record Design
### Algorithm
Use a small, well-known PRNG suitable for deterministic testing:
- `SplitMix64` as a seed expander and/or direct generator
- optionally layer `xoroshiro`-class generator if needed later

SplitMix64 is attractive because:
- trivial to implement
- good statistical properties for non-crypto use
- deterministic by construction

### API
```rust
pub struct DetRng {
    state: u64,
}

impl DetRng {
    pub fn new(seed: u64) -> Self;
    pub fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64;

    /// Deterministic range selection.
    /// Must be unbiased (use rejection sampling) unless we explicitly accept modulo bias.
    pub fn gen_index(&mut self, len: usize) -> usize;

    /// Deterministic u32 convenience.
    pub fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u32;
}
```

### Unbiased `gen_index`
- Implement rejection sampling to avoid modulo bias for small domains.
- Document performance tradeoff and why it’s acceptable in lab scheduling.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Same seed yields identical sequences across runs.
- `gen_index(len)` never panics for `len > 0` and is deterministic.
- Unit tests cover:
  - golden vectors for a few seeds
  - determinism
  - range correctness

## Testing
- Unit test: generate first N outputs for a fixed seed and compare against hard-coded expected values.
- Property test: `gen_index(len) < len` for many seeds/lengths.
close_reason: Implemented in src/ (tests + clippy clean)

title: Implement internal Arena<T> utilities for runtime records
description:
# Internal Arena<T> Utilities

## Purpose
Phase 0 needs stable, compact IDs and fast lookup for runtime records:
- regions
- tasks
- obligations

We want the benefits of a slab/arena without bringing in external crates unless necessary.

## Design Requirements
- Deterministic behavior (no hash-randomized iteration relied on for semantics)
- O(1) insert/get/get_mut by ID
- Clear policy about ID reuse (reuse allowed only after safe removal; documented)
- Ergonomic newtype IDs (e.g., `TaskId(u32)`) with explicit conversion

## Plan-of-Record Design
### Arena storage
Use a `Vec<Option<T>>` plus a free list:
- `slots: Vec<Option<T>>`
- `free: Vec<u32>`

Insert:
- if `free` non-empty, pop index and fill
- else push new slot

Remove:
- set slot to None
- push index to free list

### ID types
- `RegionId`, `TaskId`, `ObligationId` are newtypes around `u32`.
- Reserve `0` as root region if desired (explicit constant).

### Safety / invariants
- All public APIs that accept an ID must validate existence (in debug/lab) or be carefully audited.
- Removal rules must be documented:
  - Phase 0 may keep records forever (no removal) to simplify.
  - If we do remove, it must only happen after quiescence/closure.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `Arena<T>` supports:
  - `insert -> Id`
  - `get/get_mut`
  - `contains`
  - `iter` for debugging
- Unit tests validate:
  - no accidental reuse while still live
  - removed IDs become invalid
  - insertion after removals reuses indices (if we choose reuse)

## Notes
We should avoid depending on iteration order of arenas for semantics. If order matters for determinism, we must explicitly sort by IDs or use ordered structures.

title: Phase 0: Semantics Types & Policy
description:
# Phase 0: Semantics Types & Policy

## Purpose
Codify the core semantic “atoms” that the runtime is built from. These types are *not* incidental—they are the engineering surface that enforces the spec’s reasoning principles:

- Outcomes form a **severity lattice** so aggregation is monotone (“worse wins”).
- Cancellation reasons have an **ordering** so multiple cancels **strengthen** deterministically.
- Budgets form a **product semiring** so limits propagate down the region tree (“stricter wins”).
- Policies define how regions aggregate and respond to child outcomes (fail-fast, supervision-like behavior).

If these are wrong, everything above them becomes confusing or unsound.

## Scope
### Outcome
- 4-valued terminal outcome: `Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked`.
- Must support monotone aggregation across join, region close, supervision.

### CancelReason / CancelKind
- Ordered cancel kinds (at minimum): `User < Timeout < FailFast < ParentCancelled < Shutdown`.
- **Strengthening** operation is idempotent + monotone.
- Must carry enough context for trace/debug (optional message, source, timestamp).

### Budget
- Product structure with componentwise meet (min) except priority (max):
  - deadline
  - poll quota
  - cost quota
  - priority
- Combines parent/child budgets so children cannot exceed parents.

### Policy (MISSING TODAY — MUST ADD)
Policy is required by the spec’s region semantics:
- Region close computes its terminal outcome by aggregating:
  - child outcomes
  - finalizer outcomes
  - policy-defined escalation rules

Plan-of-record policy surface:
- Default aggregation: **max severity wins**.
- Optional overrides:
  - fail-fast: error cancels siblings
  - panic handling: propagate vs isolate vs convert to error (explicitly decided)
  - cancellation handling: whether child cancellation cancels siblings

We should explicitly document which policies are part of Phase 0 versus later phases.

## Critical Spec Properties
- Monotonicity: combining information cannot make outcomes “better.”
- Determinism: repeated runs with same seed/config yield same combined results.
- Local reasoning: users can predict what happens on region close, join, and race.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Types are fully specified with:
  - ordering semantics
  - combine/strengthen semantics
  - debug/trace representation
- Property tests cover:
  - lattice laws for Outcome combine
  - idempotence/associativity/monotonicity for CancelReason strengthen
  - associativity/commutativity/idempotence for Budget meet (where applicable)
- Policy is implemented (or at least specified) sufficiently for Phase 0 region close and join/race semantics.

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for each type.
- Property tests for algebraic laws.
- Integration tests that validate policy effects (e.g., fail-fast cancels siblings and losers are drained).
close_reason: Implemented: Outcome<T,E> severity lattice, CancelKind/CancelReason, Budget product semiring, Policy. All in src/types/ with passing tests.

title: Define and implement Policy for region outcome aggregation
description:
# Policy (Region Outcome Aggregation + Escalation)

## Purpose
The runtime needs a *policy surface* that defines how a region responds to child outcomes and how it computes its own terminal outcome.

This is essential for:
- region close semantics
- join semantics (⊗)
- fail-fast behavior (cancel siblings on error)
- later supervision/actors (Phase 3)

## What Policy Must Decide (Phase 0)
### 1) Outcome aggregation
Given:
- outcomes of child tasks
- outcomes of child regions
- outcomes of finalizers (if modeled as tasks)

Compute region outcome.

Default rule (from spec): **max severity wins** under the lattice:
`Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked`.

### 2) Response to child failure during execution (not only at close)
We need at least one policy suitable for Phase 0:
- `Policy::default()` (no fail-fast; region closes normally)
- `Policy::fail_fast()` (on first Err or Panicked, request cancellation of siblings)

This connects directly to join/race correctness.

### 3) Monotonicity
Policy decisions must be monotone:
- new information cannot downgrade the “worst” outcome already observed.

## Plan-of-Record API
```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub struct Policy {
    pub on_err: ChildOutcomeAction,
    pub on_cancel: ChildOutcomeAction,
    pub on_panic: ChildOutcomeAction,
    pub aggregate: AggregateStrategy,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
pub enum ChildOutcomeAction {
    Ignore,
    CancelSiblings,
    EscalateToParent,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
pub enum AggregateStrategy {
    MaxSeverity,
    // Future: more structured aggregation for supervision/actors
}
```

Implementation sketch:
- On child completion, apply `on_*` action to decide whether to request cancellation on siblings.
- Region close computes final outcome according to `aggregate`.

## Edge Cases to Specify
- If multiple children fail with different severities, aggregation returns the max severity.
- If a child panics:
  - Phase 0 default: treat as `Outcome::Panicked` and (optionally) cancel siblings.
- Finalizer outcomes:
  - If finalizers can panic, how is this recorded? (Prefer: capture as Panicked outcome and continue running remaining finalizers.)

## Acceptance Criteria
- `Policy` exists and is used by:
  - join combinator
  - region close logic
  - fail-fast cancellation (if enabled)
- Unit tests cover:
  - aggregation behavior
  - fail-fast sibling cancellation triggers
  - determinism under repeated runs

## Testing
- E2E: join two tasks where one errors; with fail-fast policy, other is cancelled and drained.
notes:

- `src/runtime/state.rs`: added `RuntimeState::apply_policy_on_child_outcome` hook that applies policy and requests sibling cancellation.
- `src/combinator/join.rs`: added `aggregate_outcomes(policy, outcomes)` helper to make join semantics explicitly policy-driven.
- Tests: policy unit tests (ordering + aggregation), and runtime-state sibling cancellation tests.
