title: [IDEA-WIZARD][ARTIFACT-GOV] Artifact ownership and citation hygiene program
description:
## Background
Asupersync now has a very large corpus of checked artifacts, proof contracts, dashboards, runbooks, and signoff packets. Existing validation-frontier and proof-evidence-debt work governs proof-lane evidence, but future agents still need a whole-corpus answer to: who owns this artifact, is it current, what bead produced it, what tests keep it checked, what claims may cite it, and what supersedes it when it goes stale.

This idea-wizard pass deliberately avoids duplicating DX-CORE, AGENT-DX, SCHED-PERF, SERVER, LAB-DX, INTROSPECT, LOCK, AppSpec, unsafe-ledger, RaptorQ, Lean coverage, validation-frontier, proof-reuse, and runtime-pressure lanes. The uncovered value is artifact governance across all those lanes.

## Goals
- Every durable artifact under artifacts/, docs proof surfaces, and checked operator report has a machine-readable owner/citeability/freshness row or an explicit exclusion.
- Agents can tell whether an artifact is citeable for a claim, advisory only, superseded, blocked, or missing a proof lane before referencing it in Beads, README, AGENTS, or mail.
- Supersession and retirement are non-destructive: this program never deletes files; it marks status, successors, and no-claim boundaries.
- The output complements proof_evidence_debt_graph instead of replacing it: proof-debt ranks proof evidence, while artifact governance assigns ownership and citation semantics to the broader artifact corpus.

## Non-Goals
- Do not weaken proof-lane guarantees or treat stale artifacts as green evidence.
- Do not delete or rewrite existing artifacts as cleanup.
- Do not create a second tracker or replace br/bv, proof_status_snapshot, validation_frontier, or proof_evidence_debt_graph.

## Success Criteria
- A checked artifact-governance ledger exists with schema, contract tests, and a deterministic Markdown/JSON operator report.
- The ledger has enough coverage to catch orphan artifacts, uncited signoff packets, stale/superseded artifacts with no successor, and artifacts cited beyond their no-claim boundaries.
- Future artifact-producing beads include an update step for the ledger and citeability class.

## Idea-Wizard Rationale
Phase 2/3 generated many candidates around RCH, validation, large-host control, AppSpec, operator cockpit, proof reuse, and coordination. Phase 4 overlap checks showed those are already covered by existing beads/artifacts. This program survived winnowing because it stitches those surfaces together without duplicating their implementation scopes.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A1] Ledger schema, citeability taxonomy, and exclusion policy
description:
## What
Design the first artifact-governance ledger schema and taxonomy. The ledger should describe durable artifacts with path, owning bead or producing lane, responsible domain, checked-by tests, citeability class, freshness policy, superseded_by, no-claim boundaries, and explicit exclusion reason when a file should not be tracked.

## Why
Agents currently encounter hundreds of artifacts and must infer whether a file is current, advisory, proof-bearing, stale, or superseded. Existing proof evidence debt ranks proof evidence, but it does not define whole-corpus artifact ownership and citation semantics.

## How
Create a schema artifact such as artifacts/artifact_governance_ledger_v1.json with a small but representative seed set covering proof manifests, validation-frontier artifacts, RCH stale receipts, runtime pressure evidence, swarm/agent artifacts, browser/wasm artifacts, and RaptorQ artifacts. Include citeability classes such as proof-bearing, advisory, blocked-frontier, superseded, generated-fixture, operator-report, and excluded.

## Risks
The schema can become another stale artifact if it is too broad or too vague. Keep v1 strict enough to be checked, but allow explicit exclusions so the first pass is practical.

## Success Criteria
- Ledger schema and v1 artifact exist.
- Every field has a clear meaning and no-claim boundary.
- Exclusion policy is explicit and non-destructive.
- Initial rows cover multiple existing artifact families without claiming full corpus coverage yet.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A2] Corpus scanner for artifact ownership, checks, and citation references
description:
## What
Build a deterministic scanner that inventories durable artifact paths and links them to owners, tests, docs references, proof manifest rows, proof status rows, and Beads identifiers when those references are discoverable.

## Why
Manual artifact review does not scale in this repo. Agents need a checked way to discover orphan artifacts, artifacts cited in README/AGENTS without an ownership row, and artifacts with tests but no citeability guidance.

## How
Use structured parsing where possible: JSON for artifact files, manifest/status JSON for proof rows, grep/rg-style reference collection only as input to a deterministic parser/report, and explicit ledger overrides for ambiguous cases. The scanner should produce stable JSON and a concise Markdown report. It must not rewrite or delete artifacts.

## Risks
Naive filename matching can create false owners. Require confidence levels: exact bead_id field, proof manifest source path, README/AGENTS reference, test constant path, or manual override.

## Success Criteria
- Scanner finds artifact paths and reference sites deterministically.
- Output separates exact ownership from inferred ownership.
- Orphan, ambiguous, stale, and excluded artifacts are reported as distinct categories.
- Unit tests cover malformed JSON, missing owner fields, duplicate paths, and supersession chains.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A3] Citation policy checks and no-claim boundary enforcement
description:
## What
Add contract checks that prevent artifacts from being cited beyond their ledger-declared citeability class and no-claim boundaries.

## Why
Asupersync has many artifacts that are advisory, fixture-only, stale-frontier, or narrow proof evidence. Future agents need machine-checked guardrails so a green fixture contract is not accidentally cited as broad runtime health, release readiness, performance proof, or RCH fleet availability.

## How
Define citation contexts such as README/AGENTS discoverability, proof_status claim, bead closeout, release signoff, operator runbook, and internal fixture. Validate that each context only cites artifacts whose ledger class permits it. Include negative fixtures for overclaims: fixture-only cited as release proof, stale-frontier cited as green proof, and advisory pressure row cited as production enforcement.

## Risks
Too strict a policy could block useful documentation. Allow explicit advisory citations, but require the text to carry no-claim wording and the ledger to identify the allowed context.

## Success Criteria
- Contract tests reject at least three overclaim fixtures.
- Allowed advisory citations remain possible with explicit no-claim text.
- README/AGENTS/proof_status references to representative artifacts are checked against ledger rows.
- The policy clearly complements validation-frontier and proof_evidence_debt_graph instead of duplicating them.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A4] Operator report for orphan, stale, superseded, and citeable artifacts
description:
## What
Generate a deterministic operator report from the artifact-governance ledger and scanner output. The report should summarize citeable artifacts, advisory-only artifacts, stale/superseded rows, orphan artifacts, ambiguous ownership, and missing tests.

## Why
The raw ledger is for machines; operators and future agents need a compact report that says what is safe to cite, what needs rerun, what needs an owner, and what should be superseded without deleting anything.

## How
Produce both JSON and Markdown report forms with stable ordering, scrubbed volatile fields, and examples that include proof manifest artifacts, runtime pressure evidence, browser/wasm package artifacts, RaptorQ artifacts, and validation-frontier artifacts. Include a golden summary fixture that demonstrates the expected wording for no-claim boundaries.

## Risks
Reports can become noisy. The first version should group by action: citeable, advisory, blocked, stale/superseded, owner-missing, and excluded. Avoid giant wall-of-file output by default; allow full JSON for tooling.

## Success Criteria
- Report generator has deterministic JSON and Markdown outputs.
- Golden tests pin a representative operator summary.
- Report clearly tells agents the next action for each problematic category.
- No destructive cleanup is suggested; supersession is metadata-only.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A5] Producer checklist and CI guard for new durable artifacts
description:
## What
Add a lightweight producer checklist and checked guard so future beads that add durable artifacts also declare ownership, citeability, freshness, and no-claim boundaries in the artifact-governance ledger.

## Why
The ledger only works if new artifacts cannot silently appear without metadata. This repo constantly adds proof contracts, signoff packets, runbooks, and dashboards; artifact governance must be part of the producer workflow, not a one-time audit.

## How
Document the update rule in the relevant operator/runbook docs and add a contract test that detects newly referenced artifacts in artifacts/, README/AGENTS proof sections, proof_lane_manifest, or proof_status_snapshot without a ledger row or explicit exclusion. Keep the guard precise enough to avoid blocking throwaway logs or generated local output.

## Risks
A too-broad guard can create busywork. Scope v1 to durable checked artifacts and docs/proof references, with explicit exclusions for transient logs, snapshots that are already governed elsewhere, and local target output.

## Success Criteria
- New durable artifacts require a ledger row or explicit exclusion.
- Docs explain the producer workflow for future beads.
- Contract tests include positive and negative fixtures.
- The guard never suggests deleting files; it only asks for ownership metadata.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A6] End-to-end signoff lane, proof-status row, and closeout runbook
description:
## What
Create the final signoff lane for artifact governance: a manifest/status mapping, an e2e contract command, and a runbook section explaining how future agents cite the ledger and close artifact-producing beads.

## Why
The program should end with one documented procedure and one checked proof lane, not scattered comments. Future agents need to know exactly what the artifact-governance signoff proves and what it does not prove.

## How
Add a final signoff artifact that cites A1-A5 deliverables, the exact RCH-required command for the contract lane, and proof-status snapshot rows. The runbook should explain closure decisions: citeable, advisory, stale-frontier, superseded, owner-missing, excluded, and no-win when RCH admission is unavailable.

## Risks
Signoff rows can overclaim. The final artifact must explicitly not prove broad workspace health, runtime correctness, performance, release readiness, or RCH fleet availability unless those are separately proven by their own lanes.

## Success Criteria
- Final signoff artifact is checked by a contract test.
- Proof manifest/status include the artifact-governance lane with no-claim boundaries.
- Runbook gives future agents a deterministic closeout checklist.
- RCH-required validation command is documented, with no local fallback semantics.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A7] Seed backfill across high-value artifact families
description:
## What
Backfill the artifact-governance ledger with representative rows from the highest-value existing artifact families, enough to prove the schema handles real repo diversity without claiming whole-corpus completion.

## Why
A schema-only program would be too abstract. Future agents need real examples for proof manifests, validation-frontier artifacts, RCH stale/quiet/admission receipts, proof reuse, runtime pressure, swarm guardrails, browser/wasm package evidence, unsafe boundary ledger, and RaptorQ performance/correctness artifacts.

## How
After A1/A2, add curated seed rows with exact owner/citeability/freshness/no-claim metadata. Prefer artifacts with explicit bead_id, proof_status row, or README/AGENTS reference. Mark ambiguous artifacts as owner-missing or advisory instead of guessing. Do not delete, rename, or rewrite the original artifacts.

## Risks
Backfill can overclaim coverage. The ledger and report must say this is a representative seed set, not complete certification of the entire corpus until a later coverage threshold is explicitly added.

## Success Criteria
- Seed rows cover at least eight artifact families.
- Each row has ownership confidence and citeability class.
- Ambiguous rows are represented explicitly without fake owners.
- Operator report demonstrates useful output from real repo artifacts.

title: [ARTIFACT-GOV][A8] Unit, fixture, and e2e validation harness with structured logs
description:
## What
Build the dedicated validation harness for artifact governance: unit tests for schema/parser edge cases, fixture tests for citation overclaims and supersession chains, and an e2e script or manifest lane that emits structured JSON/Markdown logs for the full ledger -> scanner -> report -> signoff flow.

## Why
The program should not rely on scattered test mentions. Future agents need one obvious validation bead that proves the ledger and reports work together and produces useful logs when something is blocked or overclaims a proof.

## How
Use checked fixtures for malformed artifacts, missing owners, duplicate paths, stale/superseded rows, advisory-only citations, blocked RCH evidence, and valid citeable proof rows. The e2e output should include command, artifact counts by class, first blocker, no-claim boundary violations, and recommended next action. Heavy Cargo validation stays RCH-only and must document no-local-fallback behavior.

## Risks
A broad e2e can become slow or flaky if it scans the whole corpus by default. Keep default fixtures deterministic and cheap; make whole-corpus scans opt-in or report-only until their budget is proven.

## Success Criteria
- Unit tests cover schema and parser failures.
- Fixture tests include both allowed and rejected citation examples.
- E2E/logging output is deterministic and golden-checked.
- The final signoff bead depends on this harness before closure.

title: [bound-violation-transient] cancel/symbol_cancel.rs mark_seen inserts before eviction — set transiently exceeds max_seen by one
description:
src/cancel/symbol_cancel.rs:1027-1040 (mark_seen) and line 882 (max_seen = 10_000) — mark_seen inserts the new key into seen_sequences BEFORE checking whether the set exceeds max_seen. The eviction loop condition `while seen.set.len() > self.max_seen` then evicts back down to max_seen, but during the brief window between insert and eviction the set holds max_seen + 1 entries. The bounded-memory contract is technically violated by one entry per call.

Why this matters: max_seen is documented as a memory bound. If operators tune max_seen against a tight memory ceiling (e.g., embedded targets, tight container memory limits), the actual peak is one entry larger than the configured cap. For max_seen = 10_000 and entry size ~32 bytes, that's a ~32-byte transient over-allocation per call — small, but technically a contract violation.

The deeper concern: this is the same anti-pattern as the recently-filed observability/cancellation_tracer.rs unbounded HashMap (br-uae0hk family). The asupersync pattern (per the bs92bg / 65gy5c fixes) is to enforce caps as PRE-conditions, not POST-conditions. Future maintainers refactoring this code may copy the pattern thinking it's correct.

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) Operator's memory monitor alerts on max_seen + 1 instead of max_seen — alert noise.
  (b) Under high concurrent insert load (mark_seen is held under a write lock so this is single-threaded, but multiple instances of the broadcaster compound) the over-allocations sum up.
  (c) Future refactor that exposes the seen-set externally observes the over-allocation as user-visible.

Fix direction:
  1. Reorder: check `if seen.set.len() >= self.max_seen { evict }` BEFORE inserting the new entry.
  2. Or: pre-allocate `set.reserve(0)` after eviction — no functional effect but makes the bound explicit.
  3. Or: change the loop condition to evict BEFORE the insert: `while seen.set.len() >= self.max_seen { evict_oldest }; seen.set.insert(...)`.

Severity LOW because the overage is single-entry and transient under the held write lock; impact is limited to documentation-vs-implementation disagreement.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting deepest 9th-pass on src/cancel/* + src/cx/* + src/obligation/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: mark_seen reordered to evict-before-insert. The seen_sequences set now never exceeds max_seen, even transiently; the bounded-memory contract holds at every observable moment under the held write lock. Test: mark_seen_never_exceeds_max_seen_transiently with cap=5 and 15 inserts, asserting len <= max_seen after every call. Commit b59300136.

title: [security-audit-for-saas] InterceptorLayer leaks RateLimit slots when inner interceptor fails
description:
Security/correctness defect in grpc interceptor cleanup.

Problem:
- InterceptorLayer can acquire a RateLimit slot before invoking an inner interceptor.
- If a downstream interceptor rejects, errors, or is cancelled before normal request admission, the acquired slot can remain held.
- Under repeated auth/validation failures this can become a user-visible denial of service because future legitimate requests are throttled by leaked capacity.

Required design:
1. Make RateLimit acquisition an obligation with exactly one commit or abort path across success, error, and cancellation.
2. Cover nested interceptor stacks where a failure can occur at any depth.
3. Preserve existing successful-call behavior and status mapping.
4. Emit deterministic internal diagnostics or test-observable counters for acquired, released, committed, aborted, and leaked slots.
5. Keep the fix scoped to interceptor/resource cleanup; do not change unrelated gRPC routing or auth policy.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests cover inner interceptor success, immediate failure, failure after outer acquisition, nested failure at every stack depth, cancellation during interceptor evaluation, panic/error mapping if applicable, and repeated failures returning the RateLimit count to baseline. Integration/e2e script coverage must run a deterministic stack with detailed logs for request ID, interceptor depth, acquisition order, failure point, slot count before/after, release reason, returned status, and final no-leak verdict. Validation must include rch rustfmt plus targeted rch cargo test/check for grpc interceptor and rate-limit surfaces.
close_reason: Released gRPC rate-limit slots on request drop with idempotent generation-aware leases

title: ATP Channel Bonding — multi-donor RaptorQ fountain spray (next-gen BitTorrent)
description:
# ATP Channel Bonding — multi-donor RaptorQ fountain spray ("next-gen BitTorrent")

## What this is
A new ATP capability: let MULTIPLE source machines (each holding a COMPLETE, byte-identical
copy of a file/tree) simultaneously spray FUNGIBLE RaptorQ symbols — with STAGGERED, disjoint
ESI ranges so their symbols never overlap — at one (later: several) recipient machine(s). The
recipient aggregates symbols arriving from all donors into a single per-entry RaptorQ decoder
set and reconstructs the object far faster than any single source could deliver it. Think
BitTorrent, but built on a fountain code: no piece selection, no rarest-first, no tit-for-tat —
because RaptorQ symbols are fungible (ANY K(1+epsilon) linearly-independent symbols decode a
source block), the only coordination needed is "don't generate the same ESI twice."

## Why RaptorQ makes this categorically better than BitTorrent
RaptorQ (RFC 6330) is a systematic fountain code. From a source block of K symbols you can
generate a practically unbounded stream of repair symbols at ESI = K, K+1, K+2, ... Each ESI
deterministically yields a distinct linear combination; ANY K(1+epsilon) independent symbols
recover the block. Consequences:
- Two donors emitting DIFFERENT ESIs always produce INDEPENDENT, useful symbols. Two donors
  emitting the SAME ESI produce the SAME symbol (deterministic) = wasted. So coordination
  collapses to "assign disjoint ESI sets" (staggered starting points).
- The receiver does not care which symbols it gets or from whom — only that it collects enough
  independent ones per block. No chunk map, no piece negotiation, no rarest-first.
- Loss is absorbed for free: if donor A's symbols drop, donor B's still help; no per-donor
  retransmit coordination needed (donors keep spraying until the receiver says "complete").
- Aggregate intake ≈ sum of donors' send rates, bounded only by the receiver downlink and
  single-core decode rate → near-linear speedup in donor count for upload-bottlenecked sources.

## The staggering rule (core invariant)
All donors agree on the SAME object parameters (symbol_size, max_block_size → same K and
byte-layout per (sbn, esi)). This agreement is FREE and VERIFIABLE: donors hold byte-identical
copies, so they compute the same per-entry SHA-256, the same merkle root, hence the same
transfer_id and per-entry object_id; symbol (sbn, esi) names the identical byte range on every
donor. Given N donors indexed 0..N-1, the canonical static rule: donor i emits symbols at every
ESI e where e ≡ i (mod N), e = 0,1,2,...  This uniformly partitions BOTH the systematic source
range (e < K) AND the unbounded repair range (e ≥ K). Zero overlap, full coverage, all fungible.
Phase E upgrades this to dynamic receiver-allocated disjoint ESI windows to survive donor churn.

## Why it serves the over-arching goal (beat rsync over ANY connection)
rsync is point-to-point: one source, one sink, one TCP stream; it CANNOT aggregate bandwidth
across sources — a categorical limit, not a constant factor. Channel bonding pulls from N
sources at once, so when the bottleneck is any single source's UPLINK (seeding a release to a
fleet; pulling a big artifact from an upload-limited host), ATP delivers ~N× rsync's throughput.
It is also strictly more robust on bad/spotty links: donors traverse independent paths/ISPs, so
a lossy path is masked by others, and the fountain needs no cross-path retransmit coordination.
This is a capability-level win — something rsync structurally cannot do.

## Transports (all three required)
1. Direct IP: donor → receiver reachable IP:port (TCP control + UDP spray).
2. SSH: when reachable by SSH but not direct UDP (NAT/firewall). SSH is the CONTROL/bootstrap
   plane — orchestrator SSHes each donor to launch the donor process, which sprays UDP direct to
   the receiver; if direct UDP is blocked, fall back to an SSH-forwarded TCP symbol stream.
3. Tailscale-native: same tailnet → Tailscale IPs / MagicDNS for control and UDP (NAT traversal
   + WireGuard encryption free). Already modeled as PathKind::TailscaleIp in src/lab/atp_path/
   (preferred over relay). Prefer Tailscale > direct IP > SSH-tunnel.

## Security model (defense in depth)
- Symbol HMAC (existing): HMAC-SHA256 over (domain||object_id||sbn||esi||kind||len||payload)
  binds every symbol; all donors share the transfer auth key → receiver rejects forged/corrupt
  symbols cheaply; a donor without the key cannot inject useful symbols.
- End-to-end content integrity (existing): manifest per-entry SHA-256 + merkle root → wrong
  decoded content FAILS CLOSED (never committed). Even unauthenticated multi-source cannot yield
  corruption — only wasted work. Auth prevents waste; content-addressing prevents corruption.
- Transport encryption: Tailscale (WireGuard) or SSH provides on-wire confidentiality.

## Phasing (child phase issues A..I)
A design/invariants → B donor spray → C receiver aggregation → D transports →
E coordination/liveness → F CLI/SDK → G multi-recipient/swarm cascade → H testing/benchmarks →
I security/hardening. B+C are the core MVP (single recipient, N donors, direct IP); the rest
layer capability + robustness.

## Acceptance (definition of done)
Cross-machine demo: 3+ donors (mixed direct-IP + Tailscale) bond to one recipient and deliver a
large file with byte-identical SHA-256, wall-clock materially below the best single-donor
transfer AND below tuned rsync from the fastest single donor, bounded receiver memory, and clean
fail-closed behavior on donor death. All work on main, green gates, deterministic lab tests + a
beyond-reproach benchmark (Phase H).

## Cross-references
Relates to epic atp-dataplane-redesign-317hxr (the beat-rsync data-plane work; channel bonding is
the multi-source extension of that single-source transport). Reuses transport_rq fountain
(src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs), the auth tag (src/security/tag.rs), and the path/Tailscale
abstraction (src/lab/atp_path/). NOTE: the existing transfer_brain "relay" concept is path
selection through ONE intermediate — NOT multi-source; do not conflate.
notes:
CROSS-CUTTING TESTING & LOGGING STANDARD (applies to EVERY child bead — do not skip):
1. UNIT TESTS: every implementation bead ships inline #[cfg(test)] tests covering happy path, edge
   cases (0/1/N donors; last/partial block; empty file; single-block; multi-block directory tree;
   K=1), and error/failure conditions. New logic is NOT done without tests.
2. DETERMINISTIC LAB TESTS: multi-donor behavior tested under asupersync LabRuntime (virtual time,
   deterministic schedule) — see H1. Concurrency-sensitive paths use the lab runtime, not wall clock.
3. E2E SCRIPTS: real-socket loopback (netns/veth) + cross-machine proofs via the H6 detailed-logging
   harness; failure-injection via H7.
4. DETAILED LOGGING (C5): every bead touching the data/control path emits structured ATP_BOND_TRACE
   timeline events + counters (per-donor goodput, cross-donor duplicate-rate, source-memcpy vs
   FEC-decode split, per-block coverage map, donor liveness, window/residue assignment). 'Works' must
   be PROVABLE from logs + asserted counters, never eyeballed — with N donors you cannot eyeball it.
5. INTEGRITY: every test asserts SHA-256 byte-identical result, OR correct fail-close with EMPTY
   committed paths (never a partial/corrupt commit). NEVER compare to old/broken atp; benchmark only
   vs best-single-source ATP + tuned rsync from the fastest donor (ledger ★★★ integrity standard).
6. ISOMORPHISM: donor_count=1 must be byte-identical to today's single-source path (H5).
7. NO FEATURE LOSS: bonding must preserve all single-source capabilities (auth, directories/trees,
   bounded memory, fail-closed, pacing) — it is a superset, not a fork.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Central bench SapphireHill (MATRIX-116): multi-stream bonding is a SEVERE REGRESSION on lossy, not a win. 50M/bad/nocrypto --streams 4 = atp 23.77s (5/5 sha) vs --streams 1 = 10.86s on the IDENTICAL cell — 2.2x SLOWER, flipping atp's 0.76x win into a 1.67x loss vs rsync (14.24s). Splitting one file's transfer into 4 RaptorQ streams shrinks per-stream K (worse FEC efficiency + more repair rounds), the streams contend on the shared sender/reactor, and 2% loss x4 streams multiplies repair. Correctness is fine (sha 5/5) but throughput collapses. CONCLUSION: bonding as currently wired (splitting a single transfer) is net-negative; do NOT default streams>1. If bonding is meant to aggregate INDEPENDENT flows (many files / many connections) rather than split one RaptorQ stream, it needs that design + a cell that tests it. I bench centrally.

title: Bonding Phase A — design, descriptor & invariants
description:
Phase A: lock the wire/data invariants that make multi-donor fountain correct BEFORE writing
donor/receiver code. Deliverables are types + a short design note inline in the beads (no
separate markdown — the beads ARE the plan).

Scope:
1. BondTransferDescriptor: the small, signed/agreed object every donor + the receiver share.
   Fields: transfer_id (= merkle-root-derived, already computed by transport_rq), root_name,
   is_directory, total_bytes, merkle_root_hex, per-entry {index, rel_path, size, sha256_hex},
   symbol_size, max_block_size, auth-key id/material reference. This is essentially the existing
   TransferManifest + object params; Phase A's job is to confirm it is sufficient and identical
   across donors and to define how a donor PROVES it holds the matching bytes (recompute merkle
   locally; mismatch ⇒ refuse to donate).
2. ESI partition scheme (canonical): donor i of N emits ESI e with e ≡ i (mod N), for e=0,1,2,...
   spanning systematic source (e<K) and repair (e≥K), per block, per entry. Document the math,
   the fungibility guarantee, and the "same ESI on two donors = duplicate" waste rule. Define the
   DonorAssignment { donor_index, donor_count, optional explicit esi windows for Phase E }.
3. Identity agreement: prove all donors compute the same (transfer_id, per-entry object_id, K per
   block, byte-layout). object_id derivation = entry_object_id(transfer_id, entry_index) (existing).
   Because copies are byte-identical, merkle_root and thus transfer_id are identical → free agreement.
4. Security model spec: shared symbol auth key across donors; receiver fail-closed on merkle/SHA;
   what an authenticated-but-malicious donor can/can't do (can waste bandwidth by spraying junk
   that fails auth → rejected cheaply; cannot corrupt output). Decide key distribution (out of
   band / via the orchestrator's SSH/Tailscale control plane).

Reasoning: getting the invariants exactly right here is what lets Phases B and C be simple and
independent. The fungibility + identical-object-params guarantees are the whole reason this is
easier than BitTorrent; write them down so future-self does not re-derive them.

Acceptance: a reviewed inline spec (in this bead + comments) for the descriptor, ESI scheme,
identity proof, and security model; the Rust types compile (struct stubs) and have unit tests for
the ESI partition function (disjointness + full coverage for N donors).
close_reason: Completed Phase A tracker closeout: A1/A2/A3/A4 are closed and current bonding module exposes descriptor, ESI partitioning, donor assignment/security model, and handshake negotiation with unit coverage. Downstream Phase B/C/I remain open as separate follow-on beads.

title: A1: BondTransferDescriptor type + donor byte-match (merkle) proof
description:
Define the descriptor every donor + receiver share, and how a donor PROVES it holds the matching
bytes. Largely a confirmation/repackaging of the existing TransferManifest + object params.

Implementation notes:
- Reuse TransferManifest (transfer_id, root_name, is_directory, total_bytes, merkle_root_hex,
  entries[{index, rel_path, size, sha256_hex}]) + symbol_size + max_block_size. Add a thin
  BondTransferDescriptor wrapper if needed (or just reuse the manifest + an ObjectParams view).
- Donor side: on enrolment, recompute per-entry SHA-256 + merkle root over its LOCAL copy
  (hash_file_streaming + flat_merkle_root_from_digests already exist). If the computed
  merkle_root_hex != descriptor.merkle_root_hex ⇒ REFUSE to donate (typed error). This guarantees
  every donor that participates is spraying symbols for byte-identical content → (sbn,esi) means the
  same bytes everywhere → fungibility holds.
- transfer_id is already merkle-derived (transfer_id_hex). per-entry object_id =
  entry_object_id(transfer_id, index). Confirm these are deterministic across donors (they are,
  given identical bytes).

Why: this is the foundation of fungibility. If two donors disagreed on object params or bytes,
their (sbn,esi) symbols would mean different things and the decode would be garbage. The
merkle-recompute is a cheap, total guarantee that this never happens.

Acceptance: BondTransferDescriptor compiles; donor-side verify refuses on byte mismatch (unit test
with a tampered copy); identical descriptors produced independently from identical bytes (test).

title: A2: ESI partition function + disjointness/coverage tests
description:
Implement and TEST the canonical staggering math: donor i of N owns ESI residue class
{ e : e ≡ i (mod N) }, applied per block, spanning source (e<K) and repair (e≥K).

Implementation notes:
- Pure function esi_for_donor(donor_index, donor_count, seq) -> esi, or an iterator
  donor_esi_stream(i, N) = i, i+N, i+2N, ... Plus a predicate owns_esi(i, N, esi) = esi % N == i.
- Used by the donor (Phase B) to filter which symbols to emit, and (Phase E) generalized to
  receiver-allocated explicit windows.
- Document the fungibility guarantee inline: distinct ESIs ⇒ independent symbols (w.h.p. for repair;
  exactly for systematic source); identical ESIs ⇒ identical symbol ⇒ duplicate waste.

Why: this tiny function is the heart of bonding. Its correctness (disjoint + total coverage) is
what makes N donors cooperate with zero negotiation.

Acceptance: unit tests proving, for N in {1,2,3,5,8}: (a) the union of all donors' ESI sets covers
0..M with no gaps; (b) pairwise-disjoint (no ESI owned by two donors); (c) N=1 owns every ESI
(isomorphism with single-source).

title: A3: DonorAssignment type + security model + key distribution spec
description:
Define DonorAssignment (the per-donor instruction) and write down the security model so future-self
does not re-derive it.

Implementation notes:
- DonorAssignment { donor_index: u32, donor_count: u32, esi_windows: Option<Vec<(u32,u32)>> (Phase E),
  receiver_udp_endpoints: Vec<SocketAddr> (direct + tailnet), auth_key_ref }.
- Security model (encode as bead comments + a doc/ section):
  * Symbol HMAC (existing src/security/tag.rs) binds (object_id,sbn,esi,kind,len,payload); all donors
    share the transfer auth key; receiver rejects forged/corrupt symbols in constant time.
  * Content-addressing (merkle/SHA) ⇒ wrong content fails closed; even unauthenticated multi-source
    cannot corrupt output, only waste bandwidth.
  * Key distribution: the auth key travels ONLY over the encrypted control plane (Tailscale WireGuard
    or SSH), never in argv on shared hosts — pass via env var or keyfile path.

Why: opening a transfer to N sources widens trust; recording exactly what each layer guarantees keeps
later phases honest and prevents accidental downgrades.

Acceptance: DonorAssignment compiles; security model documented in this bead's comments + referenced
from Phase I; a test that a donor with the wrong key produces only rejected symbols.

title: A4: bonded handshake protocol version + capability negotiation
description:
Add an explicit protocol version + capability set to the bonded handshake so mixed-version fleets do
not silently corrupt or hang.

Why (gap found in review): the original design assumed all hosts run the same atp build. Real fleets
drift. Without version/capability negotiation, a newer receiver + older donor (or vice versa) could
disagree on the ESI scheme, dynamic-window support, transports, or auth and fail confusingly.

Scope:
- Handshake carries: bonding_protocol_version (semver/int), supported_transports (ip|ssh|tailscale),
  supports_dynamic_windows (Phase E), supports_resume (E5), auth_required, max_donor_count.
- Receiver + donor compute the intersection; refuse with a CLEAR typed error if incompatible (e.g.
  "donor bonding v1 < receiver requires v2"); degrade gracefully where safe (e.g. fall back to static
  residue if a donor lacks dynamic windows).
- Forward-compat: unknown capability flags are ignored, not fatal.

Acceptance: handshake negotiates version+capabilities; incompatible pair refuses with a clear error;
a donor lacking dynamic-windows still works via static residue (degrade path tested). Unit tests for
the negotiation matrix (compatible / degrade / refuse).

title: Bonding Phase B — donor-side partitioned fountain spray
description:
Phase B: a donor process/library entrypoint that, given a local file/tree + a BondTransferDescriptor
+ a DonorAssignment {donor_index, donor_count} + a receiver UDP endpoint, sprays ONLY the ESI
residue class assigned to it. This is the producer side of bonding.

Scope:
1. New library API in transport_rq (e.g. donate_path / spray_assigned): reuse the existing
   encoder + spray loop, but filter emitted symbols to e ≡ donor_index (mod donor_count) per block.
   Reuse the systematic source emission for e<K (so the receiver gets the fast memcpy path) and the
   unbounded repair generation for e≥K. MUST reuse existing pacing (token bucket / qdisc-overrun
   guard) per donor so each donor self-paces to its own path rate.
2. Donor verifies it holds the matching bytes (recompute per-entry SHA / merkle; refuse on mismatch).
3. Donor honors receiver feedback: on NeedMore(block, count) keep emitting its residue class for
   that block; on ObjectComplete/Close, stop. (Dynamic per-round windows arrive in Phase E.)
4. Stagger START offset so donors do not all begin at the same symbol (reduces head-of-line
   collisions even before residue filtering steady-states).

Reasoning: the donor is intentionally dumb — it knows only its index/count and the descriptor.
All cleverness (allocation, churn) lives in the receiver/coordinator (Phase C/E), keeping donors
fungible and trivially scalable.

Depends on Phase A (descriptor + ESI scheme). Acceptance: unit test that a single donor with
donor_count=1 reproduces today's single-source spray (isomorphism); a test that donor i only emits
its residue class; integrates with the existing encoder with byte-identical symbols.

title: B1: donate_path / spray_assigned — residue-filtered fountain

- Emit systematic source for e<K (keeps the receiver's memcpy fast path alive when sources arrive)
  AND unbounded repair for e≥K, both filtered by residue.
- MUST reuse the existing per-donor pacing (token bucket + qdisc-overrun guard) so each donor paces
  to its own link rate independently.
- Control: connect to the receiver, handshake, receive DonorAssignment (or take it from CLI), spray.

Why: keep the donor dumb and reuse the proven single-source encode/spray/pacing so bonding inherits
all the existing correctness + speed work.

burst.

title: B4: source-range-first collective coverage (keep receiver on memcpy fast path)
description:
CRITICAL PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION found in review. The whole benefit of bonding (N× ingress) is
throttled by the receiver's SINGLE-CORE RaptorQ decode (~0.8 MB/s per the ledger). If donors flood
repair symbols, the receiver becomes decode-bound and bonding's gain caps almost immediately.

Key insight: RaptorQ is SYSTEMATIC — if the receiver collects ALL K source symbols of a block, it
reconstructs by MEMCPY with NO decode (try_complete_from_source_symbols, decoding.rs:736). With N
donors PARTITIONING the source range (ESI 0..K-1) round-robin, the receiver collects all K source in
~1/N the time → memcpy → zero decode cost. Repair/decode is then needed ONLY to cover actual packet
loss, not as the primary delivery mechanism. This keeps the common case OFF the decode wall.

Scope:
- Donors collectively cover the SOURCE range (e<K) FIRST for every block before spending bandwidth on
  repair (e>=K). With static residue this is automatic if each donor emits its residue in ascending
  ESI order (source ESIs come first). Make this ordering explicit + guaranteed.
- The receiver, on NeedMore, prefers requesting MISSING SOURCE symbols (cheap, keeps memcpy path) over
  generic repair for the first source_retransmit rounds (mirrors the existing single-source source-first
  policy), and only escalates to repair/FEC when source holes persist.
- Document the math: with N donors and loss p, expected time-to-all-source ≈ (1/N)·(K/rate)·(1/(1-p))
  + retransmit tail; memcpy reconstruct = O(size) with no GF(256) work.

Why it serves the goal: this is what makes bonding actually deliver N× and not collapse to decode-bound.
It is the bonding-specific application of the source-first fast path that already wins on single-source.

Acceptance: with N donors on a clean link, the receiver completes via memcpy (feedback_rounds low,
0 FEC decodes) — assert 0 inactivation-solves in the trace; throughput scales ~linearly with N up to
the link/memcpy ceiling (not the decode ceiling). Unit + loopback tests.
close_reason: Source landed in c37e4b7ce: receiver-side bonding prefers source holes/source-first collective coverage before repair, preserving the memcpy fast path for clean N-donor links. Final shared-tree RCH cargo check -p asupersync passed on vmi1264463; later origin/main includes c37e4b7ce and 0160824c5.

title: Bonding Phase C — receiver-side multi-donor aggregation
description:
Phase C: the receiver accepts symbols from N donors into ONE per-entry decoder set and drives a
single fountain feedback loop across all of them. This is the core of bonding and the MVP with
Phase B.

Scope:
1. Bonded control: accept N control connections (one per donor) instead of exactly one (today's
   receive_once accepts a single control conn at transport_rq/mod.rs:2757). Each donor handshakes,
   receives its DonorAssignment {index, count} and the shared UDP spray endpoint.
2. Single decoder set: all donors spray to the same UDP port; the receiver feeds every accepted
   symbol into the same EntryDecoder set keyed by (entry, sbn, esi). Existing dedup by (object_id,
   sbn, esi) means a duplicate ESI from two donors is harmlessly dropped (but the staggering should
   make duplicates ~zero). NOTE: coordinate with E-9 fix — the source+FEC completion accounting must
   be correct under multi-source too.
3. Aggregate feedback: track per-block symbol counts across ALL donors; when a block needs more,
   broadcast NeedMore to all donors (Phase E refines to targeted per-donor windows). On verified
   ObjectComplete, broadcast Close to all donors.
4. Receiver bandwidth/decode are the bottleneck: ensure recv_batch drain + bounded memory hold
   under N× inbound rate (reuse E-8.2 bounded retention).

Reasoning: the receiver is the coordinator; it owns correctness and completion. Keeping ONE decoder
set (not per-donor) is what makes symbols truly fungible across sources.

Depends on Phase A; pairs with Phase B for the MVP. Acceptance: loopback test with 2-3 in-process
donors bonding to one receiver → byte-identical decode, symbols_accepted ≈ sum of donor emissions,
near-zero duplicate ESIs.

title: C1: receiver accepts N donor control connections
description:
Generalize the receiver from exactly-one control connection (receive_once, transport_rq/mod.rs:2757)
to N donor control connections feeding one transfer.

Implementation notes:
- A bonded control listener accepts up to expect_donors connections (or accepts donors as they arrive
  within a window). Each donor handshakes; the receiver assigns DonorAssignment {index, count,
  endpoints} and tracks the connection for feedback broadcast.
- Index assignment: receiver hands out 0..N-1 as donors connect (and renumbers/uses dynamic windows in
  Phase E for churn).

title: C6: receiver decode throughput must keep up with N× ingress (parallel per-block decode)
description:
RISK + MITIGATION found in review. Even with source-first (B4), real loss forces SOME FEC decode, and
under N× ingress the single-core decoder can become the bottleneck that erases bonding's benefit.

Scope:
- Quantify: measure receiver decode MB/s vs aggregate ingress for N donors; identify the donor count
  at which decode saturates (this is the real bonding ceiling and MUST be reported in H4).
- Mitigation 1 (primary): source-first memcpy (B4) avoids decode in the common case.
- Mitigation 2: PARALLEL per-block decode — blocks are independent, so FEC solves for different blocks
  can run on the blocking pool concurrently (asupersync spawn_blocking). This ties to the existing
  317hxr F6.3 parallel-decode work (peer-owned feed_symbol); coordinate, do not duplicate. Bonding makes
  parallel decode MUCH more valuable because ingress is N× — the decode queue fills faster.
- Mitigation 3: backpressure — if decode falls behind, the receiver shrinks donor windows (E4) so
  ingress tracks decode capacity instead of overflowing memory (C4).

Why: without this, "way faster" claims would be false beyond a small N. Honesty (ledger ★★★) requires
us to find and report the saturation point AND push it out with parallel decode.

Acceptance: a microbench of receiver decode MB/s vs N; parallel per-block decode raises the saturation
donor count measurably; backpressure keeps memory bounded when decode is the bottleneck. Documented
ceiling reported to H4.

title: Bonding Phase D — transports (direct IP / SSH / Tailscale-native)
description:
Phase D: make bonding work across the three required reachability models. Each donor independently
negotiates its best path to the receiver.

Scope:
1. Direct IP: donor connects to the receiver's reachable IP:port (control TCP + UDP spray). Already
   the default once B+C exist; just expose endpoints.
2. SSH: SSH is the CONTROL/BOOTSTRAP plane. The orchestrator SSHes into each donor host and launches
   the donor process (atp bond-donate ...) pointed at the receiver. UDP symbols go DIRECT donor→
   receiver when possible. If direct UDP is blocked (NAT/firewall), fall back to an SSH local-forward
   carrying a TCP symbol stream to the receiver (slower; correctness preserved). Detect and choose.
   Reuse contabo/ovh SSH key conventions already in the repo for the cross-machine proof.
3. Tailscale-native: if all hosts share a tailnet (detect via `tailscale status --json` / presence of
   100.64.0.0/10 addrs / MagicDNS), use Tailscale IPs for BOTH control and UDP — free NAT traversal +
   WireGuard. Build on the EXISTING PathKind::TailscaleIp in src/lab/atp_path/ (already preferred over
   relay in the lab path selector). Prefer Tailscale > direct IP > SSH-tunnel.
4. Per-donor path selection: extend/reuse atp_path so each donor picks its best path; the receiver
   advertises all of its reachable endpoints (public IP, tailnet IP) in the handshake.

Reasoning: real fleets are a mix of directly-reachable, NAT'd-but-SSH-able, and tailnet hosts.
Supporting all three is what makes bonding usable in practice, not just on a LAN.

Depends on B+C (need a working bonded transfer first). Acceptance: cross-machine bonded transfer
proven over (a) direct IP, (b) SSH-bootstrapped donors, (c) Tailscale — each in its own e2e.

Acceptance: bonded transfer over direct IP on a LAN/netns; receiver advertises endpoints; donor picks one.
Depends on C1.

title: Bonding Phase E — coordination, liveness & dynamic ESI windows
description:
Phase E: robustness for real networks — donor churn, fairness, and liveness.

Scope:
1. Dynamic ESI windows: upgrade from static residue classes to the receiver allocating fresh
   DISJOINT [esi_lo, esi_hi) windows per donor per block per feedback round. This guarantees
   disjointness under churn (donor join/leave) without renegotiating a global N, and lets the
   receiver give faster donors larger windows (proportional-fair allocation by observed goodput).
2. Donor liveness: detect dead donors (control EOF + no UDP symbols within a beacon interval) and
   reallocate their pending windows to survivors. Build on WIRE-5 BeaconScheduler
   (src/net/atp/datagram/beacons.rs) for UDP keepalive/probe — bonding NEEDS peer-liveness because a
   silent dead donor must not stall completion (this is the multi-donor analogue of the known QUIC
   no-liveness gap).
3. Donor join mid-transfer: a late donor can be handed currently-unmet windows → graceful scale-up.
4. Cross-donor fairness/congestion: each donor self-paces (Phase B), but the receiver caps total
   inflight so aggregate intake does not exceed its downlink/decode rate (reuse CongestionControl
   WIRE-2). Avoid the N-donor incast collapse (synchronized bursts overflowing the receiver buffer).

Reasoning: the simple static scheme (Phase B/C) works on a stable donor set; Phase E makes it
production-grade against the messy reality of machines coming and going and heterogeneous link rates.

Depends on C (feedback loop) and benefits from WIRE-5 (beacons) + WIRE-2 (congestion). Acceptance:
e2e where a donor is SIGKILLed mid-transfer and the transfer still completes (survivors cover the
gap), and where a donor joins mid-transfer and measurably accelerates completion.

title: E1: dynamic receiver-allocated disjoint ESI windows
description:
Upgrade from static residue classes to the receiver allocating fresh DISJOINT [esi_lo,esi_hi) windows
per donor, per block, per feedback round.

Implementation notes:
- Receiver maintains a per-block ESI high-water mark; each round it hands each live donor a fresh
  window above the high-water mark, sized proportional to that donor's observed goodput
  (proportional-fair). Windows are disjoint by construction (the receiver is the sole allocator).
- NeedMore carries the per-donor window instead of "keep doing your residue."
- This subsumes static residue (Phase B) and handles churn: a dead donor's unmet window is simply
  reassigned next round; a new donor gets a fresh window.

Why: static residue leaves gaps when a donor dies and cannot rebalance for heterogeneous link speeds.
Dynamic windows are robust + fair, at the cost of a little control traffic.
Depends on C3. Acceptance: windows provably disjoint across donors/rounds; faster donors get larger
windows (test with asymmetric simulated rates); completion under churn.
acceptance_criteria: Unit: allocated ESI windows are PROVABLY disjoint across donors AND rounds; faster donors get proportionally larger windows (test with asymmetric simulated rates). Lab: completion under churn. Logging: trace each window allocation {donor, block, [lo,hi)}.

title: E2: donor liveness via beacons + reallocate on death (uses WIRE-5)
description:
Detect dead donors and reassign their pending windows so a silent donor cannot stall completion.

Implementation notes:
- Build on WIRE-5 BeaconScheduler (src/net/atp/datagram/beacons.rs) for UDP keepalive/probe. A donor is
  dead if its control conn EOFs OR no UDP symbols + no beacon arrive within an interval.
- On death: reallocate that donor's outstanding ESI window (E1) to survivors next round; renumber if
  using static residue.
- This is the multi-donor analogue of the known QUIC no-peer-liveness gap — bonding REQUIRES liveness
  because a stalled donor must not wedge the transfer.

Why: real machines die mid-transfer; the transfer must complete from survivors without manual
intervention.
Depends on E1 + WIRE-5 (datagram/beacons.rs). Acceptance: SIGKILL a donor mid-transfer → transfer
still completes from survivors, bounded extra time; byte-identical result.
acceptance_criteria: e2e/lab: SIGKILL a donor mid-transfer -> transfer completes from survivors, bounded extra time, byte-identical; dead donor's outstanding window reallocated. Depends on WIRE-5 beacons. Logging: trace liveness state transitions + reallocation events.

title: E3: donor join mid-transfer (graceful scale-up)
description:
A late donor can enroll mid-transfer and immediately help.

Implementation notes: the receiver accepts a new control conn after start, verifies the descriptor
(A1), assigns it a fresh ESI window (E1) for currently-unmet blocks, and it begins contributing. No
global renumber needed with dynamic windows.
Why: capacity should grow as donors come online (and is the substrate for the Phase G swarm cascade).
Depends on E1. Acceptance: adding a donor mid-transfer measurably accelerates completion; result
byte-identical.
acceptance_criteria: Lab/e2e: add a donor mid-transfer -> it verifies descriptor, gets a fresh window for unmet blocks, and measurably accelerates completion; result byte-identical. Logging: trace join + first contribution.

title: E4: cross-donor congestion / incast control (reuse WIRE-2)
description:
Cap aggregate inflight so N synchronized donors do not overflow the receiver's downlink/buffer (incast
collapse).

Implementation notes:
- Each donor self-paces (Phase B). The receiver additionally bounds TOTAL inflight across donors by
  sizing the per-donor windows (E1) to the measured aggregate goodput, and/or by a global token budget
  reusing CongestionControl (src/net/atp/datagram/congestion.rs, WIRE-2).
- Watch for synchronized round-start bursts (all donors emit a new window at once) → stagger window
  starts (ties to B3 staggered start).

Why: N donors can easily exceed the receiver's capacity and cause loss/buffer overflow that wastes the
bonding benefit. Aggregate control keeps intake near the receiver's true ceiling.
Depends on E1 + WIRE-2. Acceptance: with N donors whose summed send rate >> receiver downlink, the
receiver caps intake near its capacity with low loss; throughput does not collapse vs fewer donors.
acceptance_criteria: Lab/loopback: N donors whose summed send-rate >> receiver downlink -> receiver caps aggregate intake near capacity with LOW loss; throughput does NOT collapse vs fewer donors (incast-safe). Reuses WIRE-2 congestion. Logging: aggregate inflight + per-round loss.

title: E5: resume from partial staging (rsync-parity, supercharged by bonding)
description:
FEATURE found in review — a major user benefit and rsync-parity item. If a recipient already holds a
PARTIAL copy (a prior interrupted bonded/single transfer left a staging file, or it has an older
version), it should request only the MISSING blocks, not the whole file.

Scope:
- On start, the receiver scans any existing staging file for the transfer_id and determines which
  source blocks are already present + valid (per-block hash or the existing source_blocks accounting).
- It advertises "already have blocks {set}" so donors skip those ESI ranges entirely — donors only
  spray symbols for UNMET blocks. With bonding this is extremely powerful: N donors converge on just
  the missing blocks.
- Interacts with the protocol-version capability (A4 supports_resume) and dynamic windows (E1: windows
  are allocated only for unmet blocks).
- Delta/diff against an OLDER version of the file (rsync-style rolling-hash) is OUT OF SCOPE here (note
  it as a possible future bead); this bead is block-level resume of the SAME object.

Why: interrupted large transfers are common; resuming only the gap (across N donors) is a decisive UX
+ speed win and matches what users expect from rsync.

Acceptance: interrupt a bonded transfer at 60%, restart → only the remaining ~40% of blocks are
sprayed/decoded, result byte-identical, wall-clock ≈ proportional to the remaining fraction. Tests for
partial-staging detection + unmet-block-only spray.

title: Bonding Phase G — multi-recipient & swarm cascade
description:
Phase G: scale beyond one recipient — the true BitTorrent-like swarm.

Scope:
1. Multiple recipients: donors spray to several recipients at once. Simplest: per-recipient unicast
   UDP (donor duplicates its assigned ESIs to each recipient endpoint). Better: detect when recipients
   share a broadcast/multicast-capable segment and use it. Document the bandwidth tradeoffs.
2. Finished-recipient-becomes-donor (cascade): once a recipient fully reconstructs + verifies the
   object, it can immediately enroll as a NEW donor (it now holds a byte-identical copy → same
   transfer_id → can be assigned a fresh ESI residue/window). This is the swarm flywheel: capacity
   grows as the file propagates, exactly like BitTorrent but with fungible symbols.
3. Coordinator/tracker (lightweight): a registry of who-has-the-file and who-needs-it so the
   orchestrator can assign donor indices and rebalance as the swarm grows. Could be a tiny in-repo
   service or piggyback on the existing mailbox/agent-mail style coordination.

Reasoning: single-recipient bonding already beats rsync for fan-in; the cascade is what lets a
release propagate to an entire fleet in ~log(N) waves instead of N sequential rsyncs.

Depends on C (receiver) + F (CLI/orchestrator) + E (dynamic allocation for churn). Acceptance:
3+ machines where a file seeded on 1 reaches all others via cascade faster than star-topology rsync;
byte-identical everywhere; fail-closed throughout.

broadcast/multicast segment and use it.

title: Bonding Phase H — testing, benchmarks & beyond-reproach proof
description:
Phase H: prove it correct and prove it fast, honestly.

Scope:
1. Deterministic lab tests (asupersync LabRuntime): N in-process donors → one receiver over the
   in-memory/loopback path; assert byte-identical decode, near-zero duplicate ESIs, correct completion
   under simulated per-donor loss + donor death. Cover mixed source+FEC completion (guards the E-9 class
   under multi-source).
2. Loopback N-donor e2e (real sockets): netns/veth with N donor namespaces + 1 receiver; SHA-256 verify.
3. Cross-machine proof: OVH + Contabo (+ more) as donors bonding to one receiver; mixed direct-IP +
   Tailscale. Measure wall-clock, peak/avg RSS (both ends), per-donor goodput, aggregate.
4. BENCHMARK INTEGRITY (per docs/atp_rq_beat_rsync_ledger.md ★★★): compare bonding ONLY against the
   honest baselines — (a) best SINGLE-donor ATP transfer, (b) tuned rsync from the FASTEST single
   donor — never against a crippled baseline. Headline = "N-donor bond vs best single source." Show the
   speedup scales with donor count until the receiver downlink/decode saturates; report where it
   saturates (that ceiling is the real story).
5. Isomorphism: donor_count=1 bonded path must be byte-identical to today's single-source transport.

Reasoning: a multi-source speed claim is meaningless unless measured against the best honest single
source. This phase is where we make the "way faster" claim beyond reproach.

Depends on B+C (then D/E/G as they land). Acceptance: a recorded scorecard in the ledger:
N-donor bond vs best-single-donor vs tuned-rsync, with the saturation point identified.

title: H7: chaos / failure-injection test matrix (correctness under adversity)
description:
A comprehensive failure-injection matrix proving bonding stays CORRECT (byte-identical or clean
fail-close) and LIVE (completes from survivors) under adversity. Drives scripts/atp_bond_chaos.sh (H6).

Failure dimensions (each a deterministic lab case AND a loopback case where feasible):
1. Donor death: SIGKILL a donor at 25%/50%/75% -> survivors complete; byte-identical; bounded extra time.
2. Donor join mid-transfer (E3) -> accelerates; correct.
3. Control-channel failure: a donor's control TCP drops but UDP continues (and vice versa) -> handled.
4. Descriptor mismatch: a donor with wrong/old bytes -> refused at handshake (B2/I2); others complete.
5. Byzantine waste: a donor sends valid-auth duplicate/old-ESI symbols -> throttled (I2); honest complete.
6. Junk/auth-fail donor: random or wrong-key payloads -> rejected cheaply (I1); honest complete.
7. Severe per-donor loss/asymmetry: one donor at 30% loss, others clean -> completes; fair windows (E1).
8. Incast burst: all donors start simultaneously -> no buffer-overflow collapse (E4); bounded mem (C4).
9. Slow control feedback: delayed NeedMore/Close -> no premature stop, no runaway spray.
10. Resume (E5): interrupt + restart -> only-missing-blocks; byte-identical.

Each case asserts: SHA-256 byte-identical (or correct fail-close with EMPTY committed paths — never a
partial/corrupt commit), bounded memory, bounded time, and emits the C5 timeline on failure.

Why: multi-source widens the failure surface; this matrix is how we KNOW it is robust, not hope so.

Acceptance: every matrix cell has a test (lab + loopback where feasible); all pass; documented results.

title: Bonding Phase I — security & hardening
description:
Phase I: make multi-source safe against hostile/buggy donors and abuse.

Scope:
1. Shared-key vs content-addressed: confirm BOTH layers hold under multi-source — (a) symbol HMAC
   rejects forged symbols from a donor without the key; (b) merkle/SHA fail-closed rejects any wrong
   decoded content regardless of source. Add tests where one donor sends junk/auth-fail symbols and the
   transfer still completes correctly from the honest donors (junk rejected cheaply).
2. Malicious/byzantine donor: a donor that sends VALID-auth but useless duplicate ESIs (waste) — the
   receiver should detect low novelty per donor and shrink/revoke its allocation (ties to Phase E
   fairness). A donor that claims a wrong descriptor must be refused at handshake (merkle mismatch).
3. Rate-limit / amplification: the receiver must bound per-donor and aggregate inflight to avoid being
   used as an incast amplifier; donors must verify the receiver actually wants the transfer (handshake
   token) so bonding cannot be abused to flood a third party.
4. Auth-key distribution hardening: keys travel only over the encrypted control plane (Tailscale/SSH),
   never in argv on shared hosts (use env/keyfile); document.

Reasoning: opening a transfer to N sources widens the trust surface. This phase keeps the fail-closed
guarantee and prevents bonding from becoming a DoS primitive.

Depends on A (model) + B+C (impl) + E (fairness for byzantine-waste handling). Acceptance: tests for
junk-donor tolerance, descriptor-mismatch refusal, per-donor novelty throttling, and a documented
abuse-resistance note.

title: ATP receivers send committed:true before a file's data is fsynced (TCP/RQ/QUIC-unpacked never sync staged file data); power loss can leave zero-length committed files
description:
Found by a read-only fresh-eyes review (SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-07) of 21682b3fa (r02ssd), verified on origin/main 921d94484. This predates that commit; r02ssd's directory batching itself is sound.

Defect: an ATP receiver can send `committed: true` for a file whose data is not on disk.
- Before a staged file is renamed into place, only QUIC packed members call sync_all on their data (src/net/atp/transport_quic/native_link.rs ~9701, ~9790).
- QUIC unpacked entries only flush() the staging file (native_link.rs ~9413-9420).
- The TCP receiver (src/net/atp/transport_tcp/mod.rs) and the RQ receiver (src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs) have no sync_all or sync_data anywhere.
- r02ssd's argument ("the receipt is sent only after every committed directory is on disk") holds for directory entries only.

Failure: power loss after the receipt. On ext4 or XFS with delayed allocation, a newly created file can come back zero-length under its fsynced name, although the sender was told it was committed. A related, smaller and also older gap: directories made by create_dir_all are never fsynced into their own parents.

Fix shape:
- sync_data (or sync_all) each staged file before its rename, in every commit path (TCP, RQ, QUIC unpacked). The per-directory batching of r02ssd stays.
- Or, as a batched alternative, fsync the staged files of a batch before renaming any of them.
- fsync newly created directories into their parents.
This costs one data fsync per file; measure it against the r02ssd baseline. The test must be able to fail on a sync() that does nothing (r02ssd's test only checks which parents were recorded).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SapphireHill (c7), 2026-10-07: assessed, NOT implemented; releasing the claim. This needs an owner decision on ATP's durability contract, because every fix option trades against the tree benchmarks vs rsync.

What the code promises today. The receipt docs promise atomic installation, not power-loss durability: ReceiveReceipt.committed is "whether the receiver atomically committed the transfer", and the TCP receipt says regular files use atomic rename from staging. Behavior is inconsistent across paths:
- QUIC packed members (small files) sync_all each member file (native_link.rs ~9701, ~9790; arrived 2026-07-10 inside the bonding commit 0cefc9f3a with no stated rationale; MATRIX-233 on 07-09 still recorded "NO per-file fsync").
- QUIC unpacked entries only flush(); TCP and RQ never sync file data.
- All three fsync each destination parent once per batch (r02ssd, 21682b3fa).

Measured on this box (ext4 on NVMe, 1000 x 4 KiB files, Python probe, write+rename then one parent fsync):
- no data sync: 0.12-0.48 s
- fsync each file before its rename: 15.8 s (about 15 ms per file)
- fsync each file after all renames: 12.5 s
- one global sync() before the renames: 0.40 s
- one global sync() after the renames: 0.17 s
Tuned rsync (-aW --inplace, the benchmark baseline) does no fsync at all.

Options:
A. Durable by default, per file: sync_data each staged file before its rename in TCP, RQ and QUIC unpacked. Simple and scoped, but about 100x slower on many-small-file trees on this disk. QUIC packed already pays this.
B. Durable by default, batched: stage every file of a batch, then flush once per destination filesystem (Linux syncfs(2) via nix::unistd::syncfs on a parent dir fd; per-file sync_data elsewhere), then rename, then the parent fsyncs. QUIC packed would drop its per-member sync_all. Cost about one flush per batch, but syncfs also flushes other processes' dirty data on that filesystem, and the receivers' commit loops must stage before renaming.
C. Keep the documented contract (atomic install, no power-loss guarantee, the same as rsync without --fsync): say so in the receipt docs, make QUIC packed consistent (drop its per-member sync_all), and add an opt-in durable mode later (additive builder option, A or B).

Recommendation: C now (documents reality, removes an inconsistent per-file cost, no benchmark asymmetry), with B as the opt-in durable mode. If the owner wants durable-by-default, B rather than A. Whatever is chosen, the test must fail on a sync that does nothing; r02ssd's test only records which parents were synced.

title: ATP RaptorQ data-plane redesign: cross-machine QUIC convergence + parallel encode (DEFAULT-ON, beats rsync)
description:
# ATP RaptorQ data-plane redesign — converge cross-machine + parallelize encode (DEFAULT-ON)

## Overarching goal (why this epic exists)
atp's raison d'etre (asupersync-mixdaw): a universal data mover RADICALLY faster + more robust than
rsync, using QUIC (fast, encrypted) + RaptorQ (fungible erasure-coded symbols) to saturate the pipe
across multiple streams/connections/peers. Two MEASURED failures block that.

PROBLEM 1 — QUIC fails cross-machine. `atp --transport quic` OVH(fmd 51.222.245.56)->Contabo
(vmi1149989 212.90.121.76): handshake + control STREAM cross the open internet fine, but the symbol
DATAGRAM data plane NEVER converges. tcpdump: 564,564 symbol datagrams ARRIVE at the receiver NIC,
yet it decodes ZERO blocks and times out ("transport timeout during receive symbol round after
60s"); sender spins 99% CPU re-spraying forever. Path MTU fine (1400B DF pings pass). Loopback
passes 5/5 — masking the bug.

PROBLEM 2 — large-file CPU-bound. `atp --transport rq` (the transport that DOES work cross-machine)
vs tuned rsync (-r --whole-file --inplace --no-compress + aes128-gcm ssh), OVH->Contabo, sha256 OK
both: 512K rsync2.38/atp0.43 (atp WINS); 1M 2.79/1.83 (atp WINS); 10M 3.86/11.76; 100M 8.44/164.75
(99% CPU, 224MB RSS); 1G 176.84/~28min. atp wins small-file latency, loses BADLY on large files.

## Root cause — ONE shared root, TWO masks (VERIFIED, corrected from first-pass)
Shared root: DEFAULT_MAX_BLOCK_SIZE=8MiB + MTU-capped ~1KiB symbols => K up to ~8192 symbols/block.
- QUIC mask (Problem 1): QUIC NEVER applies the block sizer => stuck at K~=8192, while the receiver
  inbound DATAGRAM queue is 256 drop-oldest (quic_native/connection.rs:234/1229). Needing 8192
  survivors but staging <=256 => P(a block ever reaches rank K) ~= 0 => 0 decode. Open-loop spray
  (SPRAY_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=1 + 1ms/8sym, native_link.rs) + drop-oldest are the AMPLIFIERS that turn
  "slow" into "never": sender answers loss by spraying MORE into an overrun receiver, the reliable
  control STREAM feedback starves behind the datagram firehose => 60s timeout.
- rq mask (Problem 2): rq ALREADY targets K~=512 (TARGET_SOURCE_SYMBOLS_PER_BLOCK / sizer in
  transport_rq/adaptive.rs, used at mod.rs:1100). So rq's bug is NOT block size — it is SERIAL,
  super-linear GF(256) encode on ONE core (encoding_parallelism:1, mod.rs:1486), serialized with
  send => 100M = 164.75s @ 99% CPU, NIC idle; plus whole-object Vec materialization => 224MB RSS.

## Keystone fix (validated, 6/6 design lenses survived adversarial review)
QUIC: bound K to ~512 on BOTH ends + decode-on-arrival with backpressure instead of drop-oldest.
rq: parallelize + pipeline the encode across cores (native BlockingPool) + on-demand block read.
Both: close the spray loop with capacity-matched repair + delivery-rate pacing + reliable control.
The composition: bounded-K makes a block FIT the staging buffer; decode-on-arrival + backpressure
stop survivor eviction; a decode-matrix RANK monitor makes NeedMore exact (1-2 rounds);
capacity-matched repair stops the 99% re-spray; pacing turns the firehose into a closed loop;
parallel encode-ahead makes the sender network-bound; reliable control stops one lost marker from
wedging the transfer.

## CRITICAL load-bearing constraint (found in verify)
The QUIC receiver REJECTS a mismatched block size (transport_quic/mod.rs:2316:
hello.max_block_size != receiver_max_block_size => Hello fails). So the K-shrink MUST land in
QuicConfig::default on BOTH ends, not just the sender; mixed-version transfers fail the Hello check
(fail-closed, NOT silent mis-decode). The QUIC encoders also never call the sizer
(encoders_from_entries / encoders_from_prepared_source, mod.rs:1035/1644) — that is the wiring gap.

## EV-ranked levers (adjusted EV from verified cards)
1. Receiver decode-on-arrival + drain/backpressure (Little's law / queueing) — EV 16.7, Tier S. THE
   QUIC convergence fix: replace 256 drop-oldest with an mpsc reserve/permit reorder buffer that
   PARKS the pump on overflow (never evicts); drain-until-empty; feed each symbol to its per-block
   DecodingPipeline (decoding.rs:383 feed_symbol).
2. Encode-ahead pipeline + bounded memory (Little's law + Amdahl) — EV 16.7, Tier S. rq throughput +
   RSS: parallel per-(entry,SBN) encoders on spawn_blocking feeding a bounded mpsc ring consumed by
   a paced sender; on-demand block read drops the whole-object Vec.
3. Bounded-K + capacity-matched repair (coding theory / concentration) — EV 6.6, Tier S. QUIC
   K 8192->512; repair = ceil(K*p/(1-p) + z*sqrt(K*p/(1-p)) + 2) instead of blind max(K/4,16).
4. Reliable self-resync control (self-stabilization / ARQ) — EV 5.2, Tier S. round_seq + PTO resend
   + KeepAlive beacon so a lost marker self-heals (<250ms) instead of wedging.
5. Delivery-rate pacing + flow control (BBR / control theory) — EV 4.9, Tier S. pace to measured
   delivered rate; cap inflight <= receiver flow-control credit.
6. Parallel + SIMD per-block encode (Amdahl + GF(256) SIMD) — EV 4.7, Tier S. S(p)~9x on 16 cores;
   PSHUFB kernels already exist (gf256.rs:2743/1933/2201, ledger row unsafe-src-raptorq-gf256-rs).

## NON-NEGOTIABLE PRODUCT DIRECTIVE (user, 2026-06-16, verbatim intent)
"we don't want to gate this stuff behind non-default flags, the default atp cli tool MUST support by
default ALL optimizations and features/functionality!" => ALL optimizations are DEFAULT-ON in the
shipped atp CLI / RqConfig::default / QuicConfig::default. The conservative modes are AUTOMATIC
runtime safety fallbacks keyed on runtime conditions, NOT opt-in flags. KEY RECONCILIATION with lab
determinism: spawn_blocking runs INLINE (M=1, deterministic SBN order, replay-identical) when the Cx
has NO blocking pool — which is exactly the lab runtime. Production has the pool => M>1 parallel.
So "default-on" + "lab-deterministic" coexist via the pool-presence runtime gate, not a user flag.
Any temporary internal switch is debug/bisection-only and MUST default to the optimized path.

## asupersync invariants (EVERY child must honor)
No tokio / no rayon-in-prod: fan-out via crate::runtime::spawn_blocking -> region BlockingPool
(cx.rs blocking_pool_handle); backpressure via crate::channel::mpsc reserve/SendPermit
(mpsc.rs:426/495). Cancel-correct: per-block handles region-scoped; on cancel CancelOnDrop cancels
tasks + SendPermit::Drop releases slots + finalize awaits drain within one block's work;
cx.checkpoint() between blocks; staging-dir cleanup on cancel (native_link.rs:1474). Lab-determinism:
inline-when-no-pool (above) + estimators/pacer are PURE value types taking cx.now()/micros
explicitly (mirror the pure RttEstimator at transport.rs:94 — do NOT reuse CongestionController's
Instant::now() body). #![deny(unsafe_code)]: SIMD reuses existing ledgered gf256 kernels; keep the
coefficient matrix Vec<u8> so systematic.rs addmul-slice adds ZERO new unsafe. Edit in place
(no _v2). Library silent — telemetry only via cx.trace_with_fields.

## Relationship to existing beads (overlap-checked)
Advances asupersync-mixdaw + asupersync-arq-quic-epic-b0k8qo (benchmark gate b0k8qo.7.2; fleet
bring-up b0k8qo.7.1; lab tests b0k8qo.9.3). Generalizes asupersync-ro853b (RQ single-block
cross-machine convergence — same congestion-collapse family). RaptorQ-crate correctness/perf under
RAPTORQ-RFC6330 (bd-*).

## Epic DONE when
1. `atp --transport quic` converges OVH->Contabo: sha256 match, sender CPU returns to ~0 after K
   reached, ZERO symbol-round timeouts. (First working ATP-over-QUIC WAN transfer.)
2. atp <= rsync at 10M/100M/1G (100M <=~25s from 164.75s; 1G < rsync 176.84s; RSS < 64MB) AND keeps
   small-file wins, on scripts/atp_quic_vs_rsync_benchmark.sh, all sha256 OK.
3. ALL optimizations default-on; loopback e2e 5/5 green (non-regression floor); cargo build (no simd)
   clean under #![deny(unsafe_code)]; cancel-leak + determinism-replay tests green.

title: F0 (Phase 0): QUIC bounded-K — shrink K to ~512 on both ends via existing sizer (convergence keystone)
description:
# F0 — Phase 0: QUIC bounded-K (shrink K to ~512 on BOTH ends) — the convergence keystone, ship now

## Why (the QUIC convergence fix, pure config)
QUIC is stuck at K~=8192 because its encoders never call the block sizer, while the receiver can
stage only 256 symbols => P(block reaches rank K)~=0 => 0 decode (the 564k-arrive/0-decode symptom).
rq already does this (K~=512); QUIC must too. See epic asupersync-atp-dataplane-redesign-317hxr.

## Change (verified code sites)
1. Call the existing sizer (transport_rq/adaptive.rs effective_max_block_size_for_largest_entry —
   currently 0 QUIC callers) inside transport_quic encoders_from_entries (mod.rs:1035) and
   encoders_from_prepared_source (mod.rs:1644) so QUIC blocks target K~=512.
2. Set QuicConfig::default().max_block_size so K->~512 on BOTH ENDS. CRITICAL: the receiver rejects
   a mismatch (transport_quic/mod.rs:2316: hello.max_block_size != receiver_max_block_size => Hello
   fails). So this is a coordinated default change to encode AND decode config; mixed-version
   transfers fail the Hello check (fail-closed, never silent mis-decode) — document that interop
   requires both ends >= this build.

## Reasoning
Bounded-K makes a block FIT the (to-be-fixed) staging buffer and converge in O(1) feedback rounds.
This is the single highest-leverage, lowest-risk change: a pure clamp that strictly improves
queue-fit, no estimator, no concurrency.

## Default-on / fallback
K~=512 is the default. Any ATP_QUIC_ADAPTIVE kill-switch is debug-only and defaults to ON.

## Success criteria
loss-injecting QUIC unit test shows blocks reach rank K and decode; loopback e2e 5/5 stays green.
(Full cross-machine convergence needs F1 too.)

title: G1: Multi-stream + multi-connection QUIC fan-out (saturate the pipe; reuse rq EXP3 tuning)
description:
# G1 — Multi-stream + multi-connection QUIC fan-out (saturate the pipe)

## Why (mixdaw core; do not lose this)
asupersync-mixdaw's headline: "leverage multiple streams from multiple connections ... to fully
saturate the pipe." rq already sprays across udp_fanout sockets with EXP3 adaptive arm-grid tuning;
QUIC is single-connection-per-port today (ATP_QUIC_INITIAL_DCID constant, native_link.rs). After
convergence (F1) lands, a single QUIC flow will be congestion-window-limited and leave bandwidth on
the table on a fat WAN pipe. This bead makes QUIC fan out so throughput scales with the pipe.

## Change
1. Multi-stream within one connection: interleave source blocks across N concurrent DATAGRAM flows /
   QUIC streams so the pacer (F5) can keep more bytes in flight than one stream's window.
2. Multi-connection fan-out: open N QUIC connections (configurable, default scaled to pipe/cores),
   each with its own DCID — REQUIRES per-connection DCID demux on the short header (today the accept
   path is single-conn-per-port; see native_link.rs ATP_QUIC_INITIAL_DCID note). Symbols are fungible
   so any connection can carry any block's symbols.
3. Adaptive fan-out tuning: reuse rq's EXP3 arm-grid (transport_rq/adaptive.rs arm_grid_fanout
   [1,2,4,8]) to pick the fan-out that maximizes measured goodput without inducing loss.

## asupersync invariants
Each connection/stream is a region-owned task; cancel drains all; pacing (F5) is shared/coordinated
across flows so aggregate offered load stays <= aggregate delivered rate (no per-flow flood).

## Default-on / fallback (user mandate)
Fan-out ON by default (adaptive degree). AUTOMATIC fallback to single connection when the adaptive
controller has <3 samples or DCID demux is unavailable. NOT a user flag.

## Success criteria
Aggregate throughput scales with fan-out up to the pipe/CPU limit on the OVH->Contabo benchmark
(measurably closer to line rate than single-flow); correctness unchanged (sha256 + merkle); no
increase in loss-induced feedback rounds at the chosen degree.

title: G2 (Phase 5): Multi-source/multi-peer fungibility — wire MultipathAggregator (any K from anyone)
description:
# G2 — Multi-source / multi-peer fungibility (any K symbols from anyone)

## Why (mixdaw core; do not lose this)
mixdaw: "the same object graph fetched as symbols from MULTIPLE peers simultaneously (fungibility =
any K symbols from anyone)." This is atp's biggest differentiator vs rsync: pull a file from several
mirrors at once and decode from the union. src/transport/aggregator (MultipathAggregator: dedup +
reorder + path-select) EXISTS but is standalone with zero refs in the transports. This wires it in.

## Change
1. Receiver: feed symbols from MULTIPLE source connections/peers into ONE per-block decoder via
   MultipathAggregator (dedup by (sbn,esi), reorder, path-select). Decode succeeds on the UNION
   reaching rank K regardless of which peer sent which symbol.
2. Symbol scheduling: avoid redundant work across peers (coordinate which ESIs each peer favors) while
   preserving fungibility (no peer is on the critical path; any peer can drop out).
3. Coordinate with F5 pacing per-peer + capacity-matched repair (F4) across the aggregate.

## Phase
Phase 5 — depends on single-path convergence (F1) and ideally multi-connection (G1). Most ambitious
lever; sequence last. Relates to asupersync-mixdaw.

## Default-on / fallback
When only one peer is configured, behaves exactly like single-source (automatic). Multi-peer engaged
when the caller supplies >1 source.

## Success criteria
Multi-peer loopback test: object decodes from the union of two lossy peers when neither alone has K;
cross-machine: pull from two fleet senders simultaneously, sha256 + merkle match, throughput >
single-peer.
