title: perf(channel/broadcast): reduce lock hold and waker fanout cost under high receiver count
description:
Profiling-software-performance audit of src/channel/broadcast.rs under high-fanout lag tracking. No benches run (rch round-trip unreliable for micro-benchmarks this session); hotspot ranking is static-evidence-only with code citations. Hand-off candidate for /extreme-software-optimization.

SCENARIO FINGERPRINT (proposed for baseline when harness lands):
- N receivers in {1, 10, 100, 1000}; 1 sender; capacity in {16, 1024}
- Workload: burst of M=100k sends, half the receivers lag (never call recv until end)
- Metric: send p50/p95/p99 latency, peak RSS, allocator Bytes/sec

HOTSPOT TABLE (static evidence, unranked p95 — ordered by expected impact):

| Rank | Location | Metric | Expected Cost | Category | Evidence |
|------|----------|--------|---------------|----------|----------|
| 1 | SendPermit::send line 336 | alloc/send | 1 Vec<Waker> per send, spills to heap when live_wakers > 4 | CPU/alloc | broadcast.rs:336 SmallVec<[Waker; 4]> from drain_values().collect() |
| 2 | Shared::inner Mutex contention | wait_ns | Single parking_lot::Mutex gates both send and ALL recv paths | lock | broadcast.rs:129,303,376,434 |
| 3 | Waker::wake in send loop | tail-p99 | Sequential wake of N receivers in send critical path; inline-poll executors amplify | CPU | broadcast.rs:341-343 |
| 4 | Lag check on hot recv path | fixed | inner.buffer.front().map_or(total_sent, .index) on every recv, even no-lag case | CPU | broadcast.rs:379,437 |

HYPOTHESIS LEDGER:
- waker-drain-alloc dominates high-fanout send : likely supports — O(N) allocation per send, worst case 1000 heap allocs/sec × send rate
- single-mutex contention dominates over alloc : unknown — needs contention profile (off-CPU flame) to disambiguate
- receiver side try_recv allocates : rejects — try_recv holds lock briefly and only lag-branch copies data
- capacity overflow pop_front is hot : rejects — VecDeque::pop_front is O(1), not a leaf in any expected flame

CANDIDATE LEVERS (for extreme-software-optimization):
1. Replace drained-Vec waker wake with in-place waker slots + mark-and-sweep; avoid SmallVec spill.
2. Separate sender commit lock from receiver cursor Mutex — publish total_sent via AtomicU64, keep Mutex only for buffer push+evict.
3. Wake broadcast via an MPSC fanout task instead of sender thread; bounds sender p99 even when a waker is slow.
4. Precompute and cache earliest-index under atomic publish so hot recv path avoids the Mutex when the receiver is caught up.

Not filing sub-beads per lever — the EvExtreme skill scores Impact × Confidence / Effort ≥ 2.0 before any change. This bead is the intake.

Cite for hand-off: broadcast.rs:100-170 (Shared/channel layout), 210-346 (send paths), 375-445 (recv paths). No regression test gap identified in this audit; conformance at tests/conformance/broadcast_lag.rs + tests/metamorphic/broadcast_slow_receiver.rs cover correctness.

title: ClockSkew jitter bounds above i64 range invert direction and magnitude
description: ClockSkewConfig exposes jitter_max_ns as u64, but compute_skew samples an inclusive u64 magnitude, casts it to i64 with as, then multiplies by a signed direction. For magnitude greater than 2^63 the cast wraps negative, inverting both requested directions and emitting magnitude 2^64-m. At exactly 2^63, the positive direction already becomes i64::MIN; the negative calculation is an overflow hazard if the RNG sequence changes, though the current xorshift successor parity makes that exact panic unreachable today. No UB, but extreme public configs inject the wrong fault deterministically. Reject jitter_max_ns above i64::MAX in both with_jitter and SkewClock::new because config fields are public; use i64::try_from and direct conditional negation rather than a wrapping cast and sign multiplication. Accept i64::MAX; reject i64::MAX+1 and u64::MAX through builder and direct-config construction; test signed conversion endpoints and correct the existing sampled-bound oracle to inclusive <= max. Originated in fe49bbaf9 and endpoint exposure in 78fd30548; no open duplicate. Independently confirmed by two source reviews on 2026-07-15.

title: gRPC native server streaming: response HEADERS awaited under the 5 s connect timeout (breaks watch RPCs against grpc-go/java lazy-header servers); 0..=3 byte receive windows never refill; admit_started deadline untested
description:
## Findings (fresh-eyes review of 9b5df80ae by SapphireHill, 2026-10-01; verified by reading at origin 787bbd36f)

### 1. into_native_server_streaming waits for response HEADERS under the connect/setup timeout (interop, medium)
- src/grpc/native_stream/connect.rs ~409: `setup.run(async { stream.headers().await.map(|_| ()) })`.
- The Setup deadline is min(call deadline, start + setup_timeout) (~508). client.rs ~918/921 passes config.connect_timeout (default 5 s) as setup_timeout.
- grpc-go and grpc-java servers send response HEADERS lazily, with the first message or an explicit SendHeader/sendHeaders. Their clients therefore read headers lazily.
- Failing case: a Watch/subscribe RPC whose first event comes after more than connect_timeout, against a grpc-go or grpc-java server (for example etcd or Kubernetes style watches). The call fails with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED "native gRPC connection setup deadline exceeded" at 5 s, even when the caller set no deadline or a longer one.
- This behavior is pinned on purpose: native_setup_timeout_closes_stalled_header_wait_without_cancelling_parent (connect/tests.rs ~559) asserts DEADLINE_EXCEEDED for a peer that withholds headers. The rustdoc also says "Setup includes DNS, TCP, TLS, encoding and response headers". So the change needs an owner/API-lane decision.
- Proposed fix: end setup once the H2 connection is established (server SETTINGS received) and the request headers are flushed. Await response headers under the call deadline only; NativeServerStream::poll_headers already runs `gate`, which applies it. Alternatively, read them lazily on the first message(), as duplex does. Change the stalled-peer test to assert that the call deadline, not connect_timeout, bounds the wait. Keep a separate test showing that a stalled TCP/TLS/H2 handshake is still bounded by connect_timeout.
- Related: the unary path maps a blackholed host to UNAVAILABLE (client.rs ~1410), while streaming reports DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, so retry policies treat them differently.

### 2. Receive windows of 0..=3 are accepted, then can never be refilled (low)
- src/grpc/native_stream.rs ~93-96 rejects only stream windows above 2^31-1.
- The automatic stream WINDOW_UPDATE fires when the receive window drops below initial/4 (src/http/h2/stream.rs ~614). For an initial window of 3 or less that threshold is 0, so it never fires.
- `.initial_stream_window_size(0..=3)` then blocks every message until the deadline, or forever for a watch without a deadline. The unary path shares the flaw but is bounded by its timeout.
- Fix options: reject windows that can never be refilled during config validation, or make the update threshold max(1, initial/4) with initial > 0. The second touches HTTP/2 flow control shared with the H2 client and server.

### 3. Test gap (low)
native_stream_interceptor_cannot_restart_the_call_deadline (client.rs ~4369) advances past the entire deadline. It therefore fails in preparation and never reaches admit_started (connect.rs ~454-471), which is what applies the original deadline to the connected stream. Removing admit_started's min(at) fails no test. Missing case: an interceptor that uses 3 s of a 5 s budget and rewrites grpc-timeout to 50S.

### Verified sound by the same review
- Deadline capture before interceptors, and recomputed grpc-timeout.
- Bounded buffering; gzip output capped at the receive limit.
- Status and trailers mapping (trailers-only, missing or malformed grpc-status, EOF before trailers, RST codes).
- Cancel and drop close the dedicated connection.
- Interceptors run once; reserved metadata is rejected.
close_reason: All findings handled: 1 (setup ends at SETTINGS) c9fc35dc7, 2 (windows) c9fc35dc7, 3 (admit_started test) 205580544, review regression (setup past HEADERS) f6545963c

title: E-15: ATP tree per-entry overhead — loses rsync on perfect+bad trees
description:
MEASURED 2026-06-18 (idle-109 netns+netem, atp_e14 rq-auth vs rsync-ssh aes128gcm, 3-rep median, byte-identical OK/OK both sides, harness /tmp/atp_tree_bench.sh). atp's single-small-FILE dominance (500K 2.9-4.9x) does NOT carry to many-small-files-in-a-TREE:
  perfect tree_small(2000f): atp 1.11s vs rsync 0.51s (rsync 2.17x)
  good    tree_small:        atp 2.12s vs rsync 2.02s (~tie 1.05x)
  bad     tree_small:        atp 19.1s vs rsync 6.8s (rsync 2.80x)
  perfect tree_big(400f):    atp 1.21s vs rsync 0.61s (rsync 1.98x; atp 1.5x less RSS)
  good    tree_big:          atp 1.84s vs rsync 2.42s (atp WINS 1.31x + 1.67x less RSS)
  bad     tree_big:          atp 30.3s vs rsync 14.3s (rsync 2.12x; atp 1.4x MORE RSS = FEC retention)
ROOT CAUSE: each file is its own RaptorQ OBJECT (own object_id, manifest entry, per-entry staging file, per-entry handshake/auth/spray/feedback). 2000 files = 2000 objects, each paying fixed per-object overhead, while rsync pipelines all small files over ONE connection. atp WINS good (the realistic regime, esp tree_big) but loses perfect (rsync raw pipelining) + bad (per-entry x loss-recovery compounds + FEC retention RSS). LEVER IDEAS (profile-first, dream big): (a) PACK small entries into fewer/larger RaptorQ objects (tar-like coalescing of sub-threshold files into a combined object, split on receive by manifest offsets) — amortizes per-object overhead across many files, likely the biggest win; (b) pipeline/overlap per-entry handshake+spray so 2000 entries don't serialize their setup; (c) shared per-transfer auth/keying instead of per-object; (d) bound FEC retention on multi-entry bad-link transfers (the tree_big-bad RSS regression). GATE: byte-identical sha (tree_digest both sides) + before/after on idle-109 across perfect/good/bad x tree_small/tree_big; must not regress the good-regime WIN. title: [fresh-eyes] grpc/status.rs: AddrInUse io::Error misclassified as ConnectFailed→Unavailable + TransportErrorKind missing #[non_exhaustive]
description:
Two related grpc/status.rs hardening issues, both verified live:

(1) src/grpc/status.rs:438 — From<std::io::Error> maps Ek::AddrInUse → TransportErrorKind::ConnectFailed (which → Status::unavailable, retryable). AddrInUse means the local port is already taken — it's a server-bind failure, NOT peer unreachability. Surfacing as Unavailable (retryable) is misleading: the local conflict won't go away without operator action, but client-side retry policy will keep retrying.

Fix: route AddrInUse to TransportErrorKind::ProtocolViolation (→ Status::internal, non-retryable) since it's a local-config error that won't recover via retry. Document the rationale.

(2) src/grpc/status.rs:355 — TransportErrorKind enum lacks #[non_exhaustive]. Adding new variants (e.g. TlsHandshakeFailed) would be a breaking change to all match-on-kind callers. Add #[non_exhaustive] so future taxonomy growth is non-breaking.

title: Combinators/time audit: Scope::timeout cannot stop a sleeping operation (owner decision), reports caller cancellation as timeout, circuit breaker re-opens on the recovering success, CircuitBreakerMiddleware leaks the probe, wasm32 timer clock never advances, and LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of src/combinator and src/time (and Scope::timeout) on origin/main b573259aa (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-03). SapphireHill re-read item 1 (scope.rs 2080-2124, sleep.rs 763-792).

OWNER DECISION on item 1 (Scope::timeout vs a sleeping operation). The two documented rules conflict:
- Sleep (sleep.rs ~770) deliberately does not end early on a Timeout/Deadline cancel, "so that letting the handler continue after its sleep would [not] turn a timeout into a successful response".
- Scope::timeout aborts with CancelReason::timeout() and joins, and its docs (and tests/scope_timeout_e2e.rs) say an operation that observes the cancel and returns Ok during the drain is Completed(Ok).
Aborting with a kind Sleep honours (e.g. ParentCancelled with the timeout as cause) makes the sleep return at once; the operation's code then runs on (`sleep(1h); write(); Ok(())` writes immediately) and is reported Completed(Ok) — the outcome Sleep's exclusion exists to prevent. Keeping the kind keeps today's behaviour: the join waits out the sleep's own deadline. A third option is a Sleep variant (or Scope-aware path) that ends the wait AND makes the operation see an error (e.g. timeout-aware sleep returning Result). Not changed until the owner picks.

I found one HIGH, four MEDIUM (one already tracked) and a set of LOW issues at origin/main b573259aa. Everything below comes from reading the code: nothing was built or run, and no file was edited. I re-read the code myself for every HIGH and MEDIUM item. Most LOW items were reported by three parallel slice audits; I re-read the cited lines for about half of them, and the rest are their read-only reports.

## HIGH

**1. `Scope::timeout` cannot stop an operation parked in `sleep`, so it returns hours late or never.** Untracked; related to asupersync-pev2xi, which recommends `Scope::timeout` as the fix for waits that must end.
- **Where:** `src/cx/scope.rs:2111-2120` cancels the operation with `CancelReason::timeout()` (kind `Timeout`) and then joins it uninterruptibly. `src/time/sleep.rs:779-785` deliberately does not complete a sleep whose cancel kind is `Timeout` or `Deadline`. `Sleep` is the only wait that excludes these kinds.
- **What happens:** the abort wakes the task, but `Sleep` sees a `Timeout` cancel, re-parks and keeps its timer. The join waits for the sleep's own deadline, so `loop { sleep(1s).await; work() }` never ends.
- **Scenario:** `scope.timeout(&cx, 10ms, |c| async move { sleep(c.now(), 3600s).await; Ok::<(),()>(()) })` returns after about 3600 s.
- **Contract:** its doc says the task "is protocol-cancelled … and then joined … so the operation's cleanup has run", and the README maps `tokio::time::timeout` to it.
- **Fix:** abort with a kind that `Sleep` honours (e.g. `ParentCancelled`, with `timeout()` as the cause), or have `Sleep` exclude only cancellations that come from the task's own budget.
- **Test:** under `LabRuntime`, run the scenario and assert `cx.now() - start < 1s`. Today it is about 3600 s.

## MEDIUM

**2. `Scope::timeout` reports the caller's own cancellation as a timeout.** Untracked.
- **Where:** `scope.rs:2095` polls its timer with the cancel-aware `Sleep::poll`. When the caller is cancelled, that poll returns Ready before the `cx.checkpoint()` check at 2098, so `caller_cancelled` stays false.
- **Effect:** the operation is aborted with `Timeout` instead of the caller's reason, which also triggers #1 if it is sleeping. The result is `TimedOut` although the deadline never passed. Every other deadline user calls `poll_deadline` (e.g. `timeout_future.rs:259/305`).
- **Fix:** check `cx.checkpoint()` first, then call `sleep.as_mut().poll_deadline(poll_cx)`.
- **Test:** the operation parks on `mpsc::recv(&c)` and records `c.cancel_reason().kind`. Abort the owner with `CancelReason::user`. It should see `User`; today it sees `Timeout`.

**3. The circuit breaker re-opens on the very success that proves recovery.** Untracked.
- **Where:** `src/combinator/circuit_breaker.rs:912-917` writes every counted failure into the sliding window before looking at the state. `:772-782` checks the window after a success.
- **What happens:** opening the breaker clears the window, but calls admitted while Closed that fail later (while Open) refill it. When the half-open probe succeeds and the breaker closes, the window rule immediately trips it again.
- **Scenario:** `failure_threshold=1000, success_threshold=1, open_duration=10s, window{60s, minimum_calls=4, rate=0.5}`.
  - Take 8 Normal permits at t=0. Four fail at t=0, which opens the breaker and clears the window.
  - The other four fail at t=1s and land in the window.
  - The probe succeeds at t=10s, so the breaker closes. The window now holds 4 failures and 1 success (80%), so it is Open again and `times_opened == 2`.
- **Contract:** test `opening_circuit_clears_sliding_window_before_half_open_recovery` treats clearing on open as the intended behaviour.
- **Fix:** record Normal-permit outcomes into the window only while Closed, re-checked under the window lock.
- **Test:** the scenario above, asserting the state is still Closed.

**4. `CircuitBreakerMiddleware` leaks the half-open probe and stamps outcomes with a stale time.** Related to asupersync-5vzqse (closed), which added `acquire_guarded`; this caller was never moved to it.
- **Where:** `src/web/middleware.rs:607-648` takes a bare `should_allow` permit.
- **Leak:** if the handler future is dropped (client disconnect, timeout) or panics, the probe slot is never released. Half-open has no timeout, so every later request gets 503 `HalfOpenFull`.
- **Stale time:** `record_*` reuses the `now` read at request start. A failing call that ran at least `open_duration` sets `Open.since` in the past, so the Open phase is skipped.
- **Fix:** use `acquire_guarded`, and record with a fresh `(self.time_getter)()`.
- **Test:** `{failure_threshold:1, open_duration:0}`. Request 1 returns 500. Request 2's handler is `pending()`: poll it once with a never-waking waker, then drop it. Request 3 should be admitted as a probe; today it gets 503.

**5. On wasm32, the runtime timer clock never advances, so every sleep and timeout hangs.** Untracked.
- **Where:** `src/time/driver.rs:101-272` (`BrowserMonotonicClock::now()` moves only via `observe_host_*`) and `src/runtime/builder.rs:3569, 5860, 5908`. The builder hands an un-retained `Arc` to the driver.
- **Defect:** no code outside tests calls `observe_host_*`, so `timer.now()` and `wall_now()` under a `Cx` stay at `Time::ZERO`. Any nonzero `sleep` or `timeout` never fires.
- **Reach not established:** the shipped JS Browser Edition goes through the ABI dispatcher, not this builder path. It would be HIGH if the wasm32 `RuntimeBuilder` lane is expected to work.
- **Fix:** feed `wasm_monotonic_nanos()` into the clock each pump turn, or wrap it in a `TimeSource` that samples the host.
- **Test:** extract the builder's driver construction into a helper and assert `now()` advances after 20 ms of real time.

**6. (Already tracked: asupersync-e66q35 item 2, in_progress.)** `TimeoutFuture::with_time_getter` and `Sleep::with_time_getter` compare a custom-clock deadline against the runtime's timer clock (`timeout_future.rs:285-293`, `sleep.rs:801-805, 874-932`). Inside a runtime task they fire immediately, late, or never. I confirmed this independently.

## LOW

- **Hedge timer starts at construction** (`hedge.rs:608-617`). A `HedgeFuture` built and first polled 150 ms later, with a 100 ms delay, launches the backup alongside the primary. Fix: arm the timer on the first poll.
- **Retry backoff jump** (`retry.rs:210-213`). `exponent > 60` is forced to infinity, so with `multiplier 1.0` attempt 62 jumps from 100 ms to `max_delay`, contradicting the documented formula. Fix: drop the short-circuit; `powi` plus the `is_finite` check handle overflow.
- **`RetryTokenBucket::refill` clock rewind** (`retry.rs:464-469`). It sets `last_refill = now` even when `now` is earlier, so the same interval is credited twice. Fix: return early when `now <= last_refill`. Separately, `RateLimitedRetryPolicy` is never connected to `Retry`.
- **Policy fields that are ignored:**
  - `RateLimitPolicy.algorithm` (`rate_limit.rs:70`) is never read, and FixedWindow has no implementation.
  - `BulkheadPolicy.weighted` (`bulkhead.rs:62`) is never read.
- **Rate limiter queue growth** (`rate_limit.rs:623-670`). The wait queue has no size limit and no drop guard, so abandoned entries pile up and are scanned on every call.
- **`first_ok!` macro** (`first_ok.rs:429-485`). It never checks cancellation, although the module docs (44-48) promise a check before each attempt.
- **Quorum (`quorum.rs`):**
  - Display at lines 147-151 prints "required 0 exceeds total" for `needed == 0`.
  - `quorum_to_result` (lines 418-424) returns `InsufficientSuccesses` instead of `Cancelled` when the caller's reason is RaceLost.
- **`Bracket::drop`** (`bracket.rs:284-308`). The match temporary keeps the use future alive while `release_fn` runs, contrary to the comment. A release that takes a lock held by the use future deadlocks.
- **Timer wheel (`wheel.rs`):**
  - `max_wheel_duration(ZERO)`: `refill_overflow` (843-856) never promotes, so timers never fire.
  - Coalescing fires timers up to one window early, while the docs (19-21, 116-118) say they fire at the boundary.
  - The doc's 37.2 h range and "rejected" wording are wrong for `register()`, which clamps.
- **Driver `update()` on a fired handle** (`driver.rs:489-506`). It silently does nothing and returns the old handle; the trait and handle docs don't say so.
- **Interval and the tokio-parity claims:**
  - There is no awaitable tick, and `tick(now)` before the deadline returns the future deadline without advancing it. The natural "await the returned tick" loop therefore processes each tick twice. Example: `tick(0)`, `tick(5ms)` and `tick(100ms)` return 0, 100ms, 100ms.
  - `Delay` resets from `now` on every tick. Tokio does that only when more than 5 ms late, so ours drifts by the poll latency each period.
  - `reset` means "now", where tokio's means now + period.
  - The `poll_tick` doc says it "Waits", and the "tick() is cancel-safe" line is meaningless for a sync call. Yet the README and `docs/tokio_compatibility_limitation_matrix.md` mark Interval as full parity.
- **`Elapsed` doc** says the inner future was dropped. `TimeoutFuture` keeps it, and a repoll after `Ok` returns `Err(Elapsed)`.

## Checked and sound

- **Time arithmetic:** fully saturating, including `Duration::MAX` and `Time::MAX`.
- **Interval missed-tick modes:** Burst and Skip maths match tokio.
- **Sleep:** waker replacement on re-poll, horizon re-arm (youlxs), reset, and drop or completion cancelling the registration.
- **Fallback pump:** the unpark-on-arm path.
- **`deadline.rs`:** min-composition and jitter.
- **Timer wheel:** cascade at level boundaries, overflow promotion, no early fire from rounding, minimum taken across all levels, generation-based cancel.
- **Driver and virtual clock:** `next_deadline` is clamped to now; pause, set and advance are correct.
- **Circuit breaker:** the half-open probe cap is enforced by CAS, epoch checks discard stale probes, and `PermitGuard` releases the slot on drop and panic.
- **Rate limiter:** refill carries the fractional remainder (no truncation loss) and is capped at burst; wait-time maths rounds up.
- **Bulkhead:** CAS accounting and `QueuedAcquire` drop cancellation.
- **Retry:** attempt counting, jitter range, and the deadline taken from the same driver clock.
- **Race, select, join and JoinSet:** losers are cancelled and drained, there is no poll after completion, and quorum k/n edge cases are handled.
- **Combinator `timeout`:** `effective_deadline` takes the earlier deadline.
- **`commit_section`:** the mask is restored if the poll panics.

Only #6 is tracked in a bead (asupersync-e66q35). Everything else above has no bead; #1, #3, #4 and #5 are related to pev2xi, an existing test and 5vzqse as noted.

title: ContendedMutex labels rolling suffix percentiles as exact all-history metrics
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found LockMetricsSnapshot documents p95/p999 wait and hold fields as exact for observed acquisitions, while Metrics batch-evicts samples and retains only a sawtooth suffix of 7,501 to 10,000 observations. Counts, totals, and maxima remain all-history, so the snapshot silently mixes horizons and exposes no sample count or window metadata. Deterministic example: 2,500 waits at 1,000ns then 7,500 at 1ns reports p95=1,000ns; one more 1ns sample evicts every high sample and reports p95=1ns even though the exact percentile across all 10,001 observations remains 1,000ns. This can downgrade swarm atlas and resource-monitor severity. This semantic-contract defect is distinct from the open batch-eviction hot-path cost and concurrent snapshot/reset coherence beads, though a shared redesign may close all three. Either retain true all-history exact data, or explicitly define last-N rolling percentiles with horizon/sample metadata and label sketches approximate. Cross the 10,001 boundary in deterministic wait and hold tests and assert the documented horizon.

title: ContendedMutex snapshots and resets can publish impossible metric tuples
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found Metrics::snapshot loads six atomics and then clones and sorts each live sample population separately for p95 and p999, while recorders continue mutating them. A later sample can make a percentile exceed the earlier loaded max, and eviction or insertion between percentile clones can yield p95 greater than p999. Metrics::reset likewise performs six SeqCst stores followed by two independent clears; SeqCst does not make the compound reset atomic, so an overlapping recorder can produce nonzero count/max with erased samples or zero count/max with later samples. These tuples feed the live swarm contention atlas and heatmap severity. Establish one coherent recording/snapshot/reset boundary or an epoch-swap design, freeze each population once, and compute both percentiles from it. Test-only barriers should force the load/record and store/clear interleavings and assert p95 <= p999 <= max plus linearizable reset outcomes.
close_reason: Fixed in 966198cbe: per-domain lock-boundary recording; snapshot freezes each population once (counters read in the same critical section) and computes both percentiles from the one frozen sorted vec so p95<=p999<=max by construction; reset zeroes counters + clears samples under the lock so store+clear is atomic. Verified sync::contended_mutex 21/21 (lock-metrics) + 12/12 (default), incl new metrics_snapshot_and_reset_coherent_under_concurrency stress test.

title: ContendedMutex try_lock order panic poisons untouched data
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found both lock-metrics and no-metrics ContendedMutex::try_lock success arms acquire the raw std::sync::MutexGuard before calling the panic-based lock-order check. Holding a higher-ranked tasks lock and catch_unwind around a successful lower-ranked regions try_lock triggers ASUP-E205 while the raw regions guard is live; unwinding drops that guard as panicking and poisons otherwise untouched data. This is distinct from the open eager failed-try checks in async Mutex/RwLock because the raw acquisition succeeds here. Expose non-panicking validation or otherwise capture the violation, drop the raw guard while the thread is not unwinding, and only then raise the diagnostic; prechecking before try_lock is incorrect because WouldBlock must remain an ordinary result. Regression for both feature configurations: catch the inversion, release the higher rank, then require the lower mutex to remain unpoisoned with unchanged data.
close_reason: Fixed in faae22879: both try_lock success arms (lock-metrics + no-metrics) now run the lock-order check inside catch_unwind, drop the raw guard cleanly on violation (thread not unwinding), then resume_unwind. No more poisoning of untouched data. Regression try_lock_order_violation_does_not_poison_lower_mutex. sync::contended_mutex 12/12 pass (default/no-metrics, the shipping path); lock-metrics arm structurally identical + compiles, its run blocked by an unrelated lock-metrics-only build break in cx/scope.rs (record_task_spawn).

title: ContendedMutex sample eviction creates a periodic locked hot-path cliff
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found Metrics::record_acquire drains the oldest 2,500 entries whenever the 10,000-sample Vec is full. This first occurs on acquisition 10,001 and repeats every 2,500 acquisitions, shifting roughly 7,500 u64 values while the target std::sync::MutexGuard is still held and before the wrapper guard is returned. That convoys waiters and contaminates measured hold latency. Snapshot also clones and sorts each 10,000-element wait and hold population twice. Existing 4,096-operation overhead evidence explicitly does not cross or assert the threshold. Replace batch drain with a preallocated fixed-capacity ring or VecDeque using O(1) replacement, and compute both quantiles from one frozen clone. Add structural tests across several wrap boundaries for constant cardinality/capacity and one-at-a-time FIFO replacement, plus a strict remote performance gate that spans eviction boundaries.

title: Copy future-drop cancellation loses read-ahead despite cancel-safe proof claim
description: Copy, CopyWithProgress, and both directions of CopyBidirectional read into private 8192-byte buffers before writing. If a race/select drops the future after poll_read succeeds but poll_write returns Pending, the future buffer is destroyed while the underlying reader cursor remains advanced, silently skipping up to one buffer per direction when the caller resumes or retries. The new checkpoint path from closed bead asupersync-8ww5b0 only best-effort drains when the future is polled after Cx cancellation; Drop has no such path. Canonical docs/tokio_io_codec_cancellation_correctness.{md,json} explicitly declare future drop as the Copy cancel model, mark all three cancel_safe/all_cancel_safe=true, yet also admit nonzero in_flight_loss, which is internally contradictory. RLD-1 polls only a reader-Pending case and never exercises read-success/write-Pending; the metamorphic test checks only that writer output is some prefix, not that unread plus buffered data remains recoverable. Either redesign the cancel-safe API around caller-owned/buffered input so uncommitted read-ahead survives Drop (copy_buf provides the relevant shape), or remove the false guarantee and expose a distinct explicitly lossy primitive. Add deterministic read-ready/write-pending drop regressions that then continue from the same reader and prove no skipped bytes for every API still labeled cancel-safe; update proof artifacts and summaries fail-closed. This is the future-drop remainder missed by asupersync-8ww5b0, not a duplicate of its explicit checkpoint path.
close_reason: Shipped truthful future-drop safety contracts and deterministic loss/recovery regressions in 4bd332a94; scoped remote tests/checks green.

title: [INTROSPECT] Core-model introspection — obligations, capabilities, budgets, and checkpoints become queryable
description:
WHY: recon found the core model (obligations, capabilities, budgets, checkpoints) enforces its invariants invisibly: obligation leaks are only observable via panic or the hidden PANIC_LEAK_TRACKER (src/obligation/graded.rs:244-263); there is no public ledger query API; Cx capability narrowing (CapSet const-generics, wrappers.rs) cannot be introspected at runtime so code discovers restrictions only by getting None; budget consumption (polls used, deadline remaining, cost) is opaque; checkpoint messages keep only the latest value. For debugging, for the deadline monitor, and especially for AI agents diagnosing their own code, the model must answer questions about itself.

CHILD TASKS: (1) ObligationLedger audit/query API (per-region, per-task, per-kind pending/leaked/resolved counts + records); (2) Cx::capabilities() introspection + Cx::budget_stats() (deadline remaining, polls used/remaining, cost used/remaining); (3) bounded checkpoint history ring + last-N retrieval, wired into deadline-monitor warnings; (4) unified RuntimeInspector: one call dumps region tree + tasks + obligations + wait edges as deterministic JSON, exposed through the existing debug-server feature and usable from tests.

DISCIPLINE: all introspection surfaces are read-only, deterministic (stable ordering), zero-allocation-on-hot-path (snapshot on demand, not continuous), and additive (no behavior change).

SUCCESS METRIC: a test can assert "region R holds exactly these 2 obligations of kind Lease" via public API; the e2e debug-server scenario returns a schema-stable JSON dump validated by contract test.

title: CORS preflight broken via Router::layer: OPTIONS to a route without an OPTIONS handler returns 405 before CORS runs
description:
Fresh-eyes audit (2026-06-12) of the just-landed web middleware/router layer (commit 4c772a47c, eeexl1.3).

Root cause: Router::layer applies middleware by re-wrapping each EXISTING per-method handler entry in MethodRouter.handlers (src/web/router.rs:113-119 map_handlers). MethodRouter::dispatch (router.rs:122-133) looks up req.method in that map and returns 405 METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED (line 131) when there's no entry. A browser CORS preflight is OPTIONS /resource; the preflight logic lives INSIDE CorsMiddleware::call (src/web/middleware.rs:342-394). So for a route that registered only GET/POST (the common case), an OPTIONS preflight finds no OPTIONS handler entry, returns 405, and the CORS-wrapped handler is never invoked — the documented 'Router::layer(CorsLayer)' style (middleware.rs:42-46 module doc) silently fails preflight. CORS only works today if the caller also registers an explicit .options(...) per route, or composes CORS as a whole-router MiddlewareStack handler. No router-level CORS/preflight test exists in tests/e2e_web.rs.

Fix options (design decision — deferred because the peer is actively iterating on the web layer): (a) auto-OPTIONS at the MethodRouter/Router level that runs the registered layer stack; (b) have Router::layer wrap MethodRouter::dispatch rather than only the individual method handlers; or (c) document that CorsLayer must be paired with an explicit .options() route.

Also from the same audit (LOW, defense-in-depth / docs):
- middleware.rs:370-383: CorsMiddleware preflight sets access-control-allow-methods/headers/max-age via raw resp.headers.insert(...), bypassing sanitize_header_value that apply_common_headers uses for the reflected Origin. Values are server-config (not attacker-controlled) so LOW, but route them through resp.set_header for parity.
- middleware.rs:826-864: RetryMiddleware struct doc says non-idempotent (POST/PATCH/DELETE) retried by default, but new() sets idempotent_only=true and is_idempotent() includes DELETE+TRACE; the safe behavior is correct, the doc is wrong/misleading. Fix the doc and align the idempotent-method list.
close_reason: Resolved on HEAD: Router::layer now wraps method_not_allowed so OPTIONS preflight reaches CorsMiddleware (204 not 405); regression test cors_layer_handles_preflight_without_options_route committed (router.rs:2036); both LOW items (preflight set_header sanitization, RetryMiddleware doc/is_idempotent) also addressed.

title: [label-injection] observability/otel.rs format_labels does not escape quote/backslash in label values — Prometheus output corruption
description:
src/observability/otel.rs:428-434 — format_labels() builds the labels portion of metric output as:

  format!("{k}=\"{v}\"")

where v is the user-supplied label value. If v contains a literal '"' or '\\' character, the result violates Prometheus text-exposition-format quoting:
  Prometheus text format: label_name="label_value" with backslash-escaped " inside.
  This implementation: label_value embedded verbatim, so a value of \"foo\"bar produces label_name=\"foo\"bar\" — a malformed two-label sequence.

Threat: a metric with attacker-influenced label values (e.g., URL path, header name, error message embedded in a Tag) corrupts the entire metrics endpoint output. Specifically:
  (a) A label value containing '"' breaks the parser at every downstream Prometheus / OpenMetrics scraper.
  (b) A label value containing '=' followed by '"' can inject spurious labels — a counter labeled {path="/api\"; user="admin\"} becomes interpretable as two labels {path="/api"} and {user="admin"}.
  (c) Newlines in label values break the line-based exposition format entirely.

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) /metrics endpoint becomes unparseable; alerting based on those metrics fires false-positives or silent-fails.
  (b) Adversarial label injection: user input that includes attacker-chosen label values ends up in dashboards/alerts.
  (c) Cross-metric pollution: malformed line affects parsing of ALL subsequent metrics in the same scrape.

Fix direction:
  1. Sanitize label values per Prometheus text format rules: escape '\\', '"', and '\n' as '\\\\', '\\"', '\\n' respectively. Reject characters that have no valid escape (e.g., raw NUL bytes).
  2. Or: validate label keys/values at registration time and reject violations.
  3. Constants for a safe-character allowlist (label names match [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*).
  4. Regression test: register a metric with label value containing each special character and assert the rendered output is well-formed by parsing it back via prometheus-parse.

Severity MEDIUM (not HIGH) because (a) the metrics endpoint is typically auth-walled, (b) the impact is observability output corruption rather than runtime correctness, and (c) the recently-filed pdu7wg already addressed escape extension in a sibling code path — this is a remaining gap in the otel-specific format_labels function.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/observability/* deepest pass (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Verified in HEAD: src/observability/otel.rs:467 defines fn escape_label_value(value: &str) -> String implementing the Prometheus exposition trio (\\, \n, \") plus CR; line 521 in format_labels routes every label value through escape_label_value(v). The fix is in place — closing as already-applied. Verification recorded for traceability.

title: [EPIC] Chaos Testing Mode for Lab Runtime
description:
# Overview

An extension to LabReactor that can inject random delays, spurious wakeups,
simulated I/O errors, and cancellations at configurable rates - to stress-test
application code's resilience.

## Why This Matters

Production systems face chaos constantly:
- Network partitions
- Slow responses  
- OOM kills
- Race conditions
- Random failures

A chaos mode lets developers find these bugs BEFORE production. Combined with
deterministic replay, failures become REPRODUCIBLE.

## How It Works

```rust
Lab::new()
    .with_chaos(ChaosConfig {
        cancel_probability: 0.01,      // 1% random cancellation
        delay_probability: 0.05,       // 5% random delay
        delay_range: 1ms..100ms,
        io_error_probability: 0.02,    // 2% I/O error
        wakeup_storm_probability: 0.001, // 0.1% spurious wakeups
        seed: 12345,                   // REPRODUCIBLE chaos!
    })
    .run(|cx| async {
        // Application code with injected chaos
    });

// On failure:
// "Test failed with seed 12345. Replay with same seed to reproduce."
```

## Chaos Types

1. **Random Cancellation**: Inject CancelRequested at random times
2. **Random Delays**: Add latency at poll points
3. **I/O Errors**: Fail I/O operations randomly
4. **Wakeup Storms**: Spurious wakeups to test idempotency
5. **Budget Exhaustion**: Randomly exhaust budgets
6. **Clock Skew**: Virtual time jumps (for distributed scenarios)

## Determinism is Key

The chaos MUST be deterministic:
- Same seed = same chaos sequence
- Same test = same failures
- Enables debugging of intermittent issues

This is the killer combination: chaos + deterministic replay.

## Integration with Existing Features

- Uses LabReactor's virtual time
- Uses LabReactor's deterministic scheduling
- Integrates with cancellation injection (#1)
- Reports via tracing (#2)
- Verified by oracles

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Configurable chaos parameters
- [ ] Deterministic with same seed
- [ ] All chaos types implemented
- [ ] Integrates with Lab infrastructure
- [ ] Clear failure reporting with seed
- [ ] Documentation with examples
notes: Chaos testing mode complete: (1) ChaosConfig with all builder methods for configurable parameters; (2) Deterministic chaos with seed-based reproducibility; (3) All core chaos types implemented - cancellation, delays, I/O errors, wakeup storms, budget exhaustion; (4) Full Lab infrastructure integration via LabConfig.with_chaos(); (5) ChaosStats for clear failure reporting; (6) Comprehensive documentation and examples (asupersync-mzsl). Clock skew deferred to Phase 4 distributed work.

title: [codec] src/codec/tests/mod.rs:155 recovery test clears the buffer and masks LinesCodec post-error state bugs
description:
src/codec/tests/mod.rs:154-156 claims to test LinesCodec recovery after InvalidUtf8, but it calls src.clear() before appending the recovery line. That discards any stale bytes or discard-state evidence left by the failed decode, so the test passes even if the codec cannot recover when valid data arrives immediately after an invalid UTF-8 line in the same buffer.

Concrete repro reasoning: if a future LinesCodec regression leaves unread tail bytes or stale over-limit/discard state after Err(InvalidUtf8), this test still goes green because line 155 wipes the buffer and effectively constructs a brand-new happy-path decode.

Suggested fix: preserve the original buffer and append the valid line without clearing, or use a single buffer containing invalid line + valid recovery line and assert the second decode succeeds after the first error.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
Scope and method (SapphireHill, 2026-09-10T18:25Z): fresh-eyes review of code landed by other agents since mid-August (five read-only review agents over runtime obligations, native QUIC, HTTP/1+2/web, combinators/supervision/cancel, ATP CLI/SDK/remote/regex; every claim re-read in the code by me before any edit) plus my own deep read of src/fs/file.rs. Fixes in the working tree, verified by lane_review (check --all-targets --all-features, lib units for every touched module, web/h1/h2/combinator e2e targets, clippy lib+bins, fmt):
- fs::File::into_std lost the caller's cursor after a poll-trait read (read-ahead / in-flight read) since the 2026-09-02 poll-offload change; now settles and rewinds. Two white-box tests; RED "expected 2, got 6" / "expected 0, got 4" on the old code; GREEN fs:: 72/0. The tree sweeper committed this file as 5a3c5165d under the user's identity before the GREEN receipt existed; the receipt above covers exactly those bytes (--no-overlay on 5a3c5165d). poll_shutdown now settles a pending write (its error was lost); try_clone documents that read-ahead is per wrapper.
- ATP SDK transfer.rs: removed two content heuristics that overrode the hash check (zero-length file "passes" iff its path contains "empty"; any 512-aligned file ending in ten zero bytes was "corrupt" even with a matching hash); the daemon reachability probe (blocking std connect_timeout inside async fns) moved to the blocking pool.
- atp CLI: a rejected RQ key's error no longer echoes the offending byte value/frequency of the key.
- remote.rs: (1) an unauthenticated TCP connect held a connection slot for ever when the TlsAcceptor had no handshake timeout (slot registered before the handshake; nothing bounded it): the handshake is now bounded by initial_frame_timeout; (2) a failed Cancel exchange surfaced as TransportError/Failed instead of Cancelled because take_cancel had cleared the reason the mapper re-read; (3) a V3 child-region close failure returned early past the idempotency commit, leaving the key in flight for the peer's record budget; (4) admit_tls_peer discarded validate's Ok(false) (report-only mismatch) and admitted; (5) a V3 client got a bare wire response for the inline-mode LifecycleUnavailable refusal and failed to decode it; the envelope now follows the hello version.
- HTTP/1 streaming server: the head read timeout restarted on every read (slowloris: 64 KiB x idle windows); one deadline per head now; body reads had no timeout at all and now carry the idle timeout. Buffered server: max_body_size above 8 MiB was unreachable because Framed's default buffer cap fired first (io error instead of 413); the buffer is sized from the config. Live SSE: the produced-body frame cap (64 KiB) was below the stream's event bound (16 MiB), so any larger event ended the stream without a terminator; the cap now follows the stream's limit (new StreamingSse::event_bytes_limit getter).
- HTTP/2 listener: request bodies were bounded per stream only (256 x 16 MiB = 4 GiB pinned per connection by a peer that sends bodies just under the cap and stays silent); a per-connection cap of 4 x max_body_size resets the offending stream with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.
- Combinators/supervision: the bounded join sweeps (64 slots in map_reduce, 32 in pipeline and in the managed supervisor's wait_exit) lost the wake of a child that terminated at an index the multi-poll sweep had already passed (coalesced with the sweep's self-wake) and could park forever with no other child left to wake them. Every child future now carries a TerminationTally guard (crate::combinator::TerminationTally, fires on completion, cancel-before-poll and unwind) and the coordinators rescan whenever the tally is ahead of the joins they observed. No busy loop: every terminated child is joined by the next sweep, so the counters converge.
- record/region.rs: the checked-credit release path used expect on counter underflow inside ObligationToken::drop (a panic there during an unwind aborts the process); it now saturates with a debug_assert like resolve_obligation.
- Native QUIC: (1) admission aborted on any spoofed/corrupted/oversized datagram from the peer's address (RFC 9000 §12.2 says discard) and counted such junk toward the accepted-packet bound; the standalone client/server drive loops had the same arm. Unauthenticated packets (AEAD failure, length overrun, malformed header, oversized) are now discarded, only authenticated packets count, and the PTO clock still bounds a handshake nobody drives. Unit test: corrupted Initial + length-overrun Initial are discarded and the real Initial still authenticates. (2) STREAM data after RESET_STREAM or after our STOP_SENDING was a hard error that failed the whole packet on ordinary reordering (§3.2/§3.5 say discard; only a final-size violation is an error); now discarded, and the packet-level reassembly screen admits such frames. Unit test added.
Larger review findings not fixed here are filed as separate beads (list follows in the next comment).

title: CrashController Cold restart mode has no operational effect
description: RestartMode is stored on CrashController but only read by its accessor; restart never branches on it. title: Concurrent CrashSender sends overshoot exact deterministic crash point
description: CrashSender::send loads send_count and checks crash_after_sends before awaiting inner.send, then increments only after the await succeeds. Concurrent futures can all pass the same stale count and later commit, so the promised crash after exactly N successful sends overshoots by the number of in-flight sends. Deterministic limit=1 repro: prefill a capacity-one inner channel without incrementing the wrapper count; poll sends A and B so both observe zero and park; drain the sentinel and complete A, then drain A and complete B. Count becomes two and the controller remains live until a third attempt. Serialize the decision-through-commit section—crashed check, exact-N check, inner send completion, and success increment—with a non-poisoning cancel-aware one-permit Asupersync gate at the same scope as the counter. A pre-await fetch_add is insufficient because cancelled or failed sends are not successes. Regress the forced two-pending-send schedule plus cancellation, disconnect, unwind recovery, and exact delivery/count/stat totals. Closed audits asupersync-35ajl and asupersync-4bvab noticed this TOCTOU but dismissed it; nothing fixed it and no open duplicate exists. Independently confirmed by two source reviews on 2026-07-15.

title: [swarm-perf] Add adaptive batch sizing for cancel and inject burst handling
description:
Background:
- Fixed batch sizes are easy to reason about but often wrong under swarm-scale burstiness: small batches waste throughput, large batches create queueing tails and fairness damage.
- This is distinct from the combiner-path bead: here the target is adaptive sizing of existing ready/cancel/inject drains under changing pressure.
- The decision rule should be evidence-backed and bounded, not a pile of magic constants.

Candidate surfaces:
- src/runtime/scheduler/priority.rs
- src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs
- src/runtime/scheduler/global_injector.rs
- benches/scheduler_benchmark.rs

Required design:
1. Measure where fixed batch sizes hurt under bursty mixed-lane pressure.
2. Add bounded adaptive sizing using queue depth, retry pressure, or wake backlog as inputs.
3. Preserve the current fixed-size behavior as an explicit fallback/profile.
4. Make tuning observable with counters or traces for selected batch sizes and fallback reasons.

Proof / validation:
- Bench comparisons across burst sizes and worker counts.
- Deterministic regression proving no starvation and no queue corruption.
- Safe-mode pinning to current fixed sizes when the adaptive rule is disabled.

Success criteria:
- Batch sizing responds to burst shape in a way that improves throughput or tails without introducing fairness regressions.
design: Adaptive batch sizing is a bounded lane-local cadence controller, not an admission or brownout controller. It may adjust only ready/cancel/inject drain quanta within explicit min/max limits after consuming the shared wake-to-run and retry-pressure evidence from asupersync-99if94 and the stabilized combiner counters from asupersync-g0kwgh. It must not write admission_window, tail-risk admission knobs, brownout phase, topology placement, task ownership, region lifecycle, or cancellation protocol state. Controller safety requirements from asupersync-b4guhs apply: use hysteresis, cooldown, deterministic epoch/window updates, fixed-profile fallback, and a no-win safe profile when adaptive sizing is noisy or loses. Cancel-drain service gets a hard floor whenever cancellation debt is present, so throughput tuning can never starve cancellation finalization.
acceptance_criteria:
Unit tests cover per-lane min/max bound enforcement, hysteresis, cooldown and deterministic epoch reset, fixed-profile fallback, disabled-mode equivalence, no starvation, no queue corruption, no double enqueue or task loss, no cancellation-drain starvation, cancel-debt service floor, deterministic behavior under repeated seeds, controller-boundary proof that adaptive sizing does not write admission_window or brownout/tail-risk knobs, and serialization/redaction of selected-batch evidence. Deterministic scenario or e2e coverage must compare fixed profiles vs adaptive profiles under mixed ready/cancel/inject pressure and log scenario ID, contract version, workload seed, selected batch size per lane, queue depth, retry/CAS pressure, combiner mode state, fairness counters, cancellation debt, cancel-drain latency p50/p95/p99, wake-to-run p50/p95/p99, fallback reason codes, no-win trigger, safe fallback profile, generated artifact paths, and final pass/fail operator verdict. Add a versioned smoke contract and runner, expected names artifacts/adaptive_batch_sizing_smoke_contract_v1.json and scripts/run_adaptive_batch_sizing_smoke.sh unless a better existing contract is reused explicitly. The runner must support --list, --scenario, --dry-run, --execute, --output-root, default Rust validation through rch, report markers recoverable from --nocapture output, deterministic repeated-run hash/projection checks, and artifacts that show when adaptive batching wins, when it loses, and when operators should keep fixed sizes pinned. Validation before closeout: bash -n for the runner, runner --list, jq/schema validation for the contract, rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check for touched Rust files, targeted rch cargo tests for unit coverage, rch-backed execution of every smoke scenario, benchmark evidence for 1/8/32/64 producer or equivalent burst profiles, and bounded graph-health check via bv robot mode or br dep cycles with timeout.

Plan-space refinement, 2026-05-04 AmberElk: adaptive batching must include an explicit controller-stability proof and tail-risk comparator, not just benchmark wins. Additional unit/property tests must cover phase-shift workloads, adversarial burst alternation, bounded update frequency, anti-windup or equivalent state reset after saturation, oscillation/flapping detection, cooldown enforcement across epoch boundaries, sample-size insufficiency fallback, stale telemetry rejection, and timescale separation from admission, brownout, combiner, and capacity-envelope controllers. Scenario/e2e coverage must include fixed-vs-adaptive comparisons for p50/p95/p99/p999 wake-to-run and cancel-drain latency, throughput, fairness, cancellation debt, mode-switch count, batch-size variance, controller decision input hash, calibration or telemetry-sufficiency verdict, and stable-projection hashes across repeated runs. Closeout must include a no-win artifact when adaptive sizing does not beat the named fixed profile by a deterministic margin, and final signoff must fail closed on any controller that improves throughput while worsening p99/p999, cancellation-debt service, fairness, or composition stability.
notes: Plan-space revision by PeachLantern on 2026-05-03: keep this bead downstream of the closed combiner and telemetry work. Read the asupersync-g0kwgh closeout before implementation so adaptive batch sizing reuses combiner pressure counters instead of adding a second private hot-path measurement system. Read the asupersync-b4guhs controller matrix before selecting update cadence; this bead must be lane-local and must not become another same-timescale writer to admission or brownout controls. Preserve all existing fixed-size behavior as a named safe profile and require explicit no-win evidence when adaptive sizing does not beat fixed sizes.

title: Kafka exactly-once: stale consumer snapshot error in send_offsets_to_transaction leaves the transaction committable without its offsets
description:
## Defect (source-verified by SapphireHill, 2026-09-28, on origin 17f130960; introduced by 850af98a6)
TransactionalProducer's Transaction::send_offsets_to_transaction (src/messaging/kafka.rs ~2683-2700) runs metadata.prepare_offsets(offsets)? BEFORE TransactionOperationGuard::claim_offsets. prepare_offsets (src/messaging/kafka_consumer.rs ~580-587) calls validate_membership (~619-635), which fails when:
- the consumer's rebalance generation or assignment changed after the snapshot ("consumer group metadata is stale after a rebalance", KafkaError::Transaction), or
- the consumer was closed or dropped.
That early return leaves the transaction Active with pending_offsets == None. The doc (~2678) says "Local validation errors before enrollment leave the transaction usable", and that is what makes it fail-open.

## Failure sequence (exactly-once violated)
begin_transaction; send the output records; a rebalance is observed (another task polls the shared consumer, or the snapshot predates the poll); send_offsets_to_transaction returns Err. KafkaError::Transaction reports is_transient() == true, so a retry wrapper, or an app that logs and continues, calls commit(). commit() passes ensure_active_transaction, and the broker commits the output with NO input offsets. After a restart the input is re-read from the old committed offset, so the output is duplicated.
librdkafka's own TxnOffsetCommit fails the same condition with ILLEGAL_GENERATION or UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID, which require an abort. This wrapper's mock test (kafka.rs ~4269) already maps UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID to NeedsAbortRecovery. The in-worker offsets.validate_current() (~2709) runs the identical membership check after the claim, and there a failure DOES move the transaction to NeedsAbortRecovery. So whether a stale snapshot blocks the commit currently depends on whether the rebalance lands before or after the claim.

## Why tests miss it
transactional_offsets_validate_batches_and_membership_before_enrollment checks only that prepare_offsets returns Err. No test inspects the producer's state after a stale, closed or dropped-consumer error through the public method.

## Fix direction
Run the membership check first. On a stale, closed or dropped consumer, call self.producer.mark_transaction_dropped(self.generation) (or the equivalent), so an Active transaction with no operation in flight moves to NeedsAbortRecovery, and return the error. Pure input-shape errors (empty, negative, duplicate, unassigned partition, regression) stay non-poisoning. Update the doc near ~2678.
Test (default features, guard-level, plus the kafka-feature mock): after a rebalance between snapshot and enrollment, commit() must be refused and the next begin_transaction must run abort recovery. The current code is the old red.

## Also (LOW, same review)
1. No rewind after abort: the doc (~2665) says "Aborting discards both", but nothing seeks the consumer back. An app that keeps the same consumer skips the aborted input permanently. Document the required seek/restart, or provide one. After a failed enrollment, Transaction::abort() returns "must be aborted before reuse"; the actual abort happens on the next begin_transaction.
2. Possible teardown deadlock: group_metadata alone uses the runtime blocking pool (run_kafka_blocking, kafka.rs ~576), while the other consumer operations use spawn_blocking_on_thread. A cancelled queued pool task keeps its consumer lease until a pool worker runs it. With blocking_threads(1,1) and the pool busy, scoped-consumer teardown can wait forever in retire_and_wait (kafka_consumer.rs ~951). Fix: use spawn_blocking_on_thread for group_metadata too.
3. The kafka-feature mock test commits offset 2 after consuming 0..2 (off by one; protocol-only claims). The real-broker test runs nothing unless REAL_KAFKA_TESTS is set.

Source: independent read-only review of 850af98a6 and a19e2c5e5 (subagent); the MEDIUM claim was re-checked against the cited lines.

Filed from asupersync-server-stack-hardening-eeexl1.12 item 8 after source verification. src/net/tcp/socket.rs currently supports address family selection, bind, SO_REUSEADDR, and Unix SO_REUSEPORT. It does not expose nodelay/TCP_NODELAY, keepalive idle/interval/count convenience configuration, or tests proving those options are applied to both connect and listen/accepted stream paths where supported.

Goal: add portable TCP socket option ergonomics matching the runtime capability posture: supported platforms apply the socket options before connect/listen, unsupported options return typed unsupported errors or are explicitly documented as unavailable.

Acceptance criteria:
1. TcpSocket exposes set_nodelay and keepalive configuration methods with deterministic error behavior per platform.
2. connect() applies configured options before dialing; listen()/accepted streams document and test the supported option propagation path.
3. Tests cover IPv4 and IPv6 where available, invalid family behavior remains unchanged, and unsupported keepalive knobs skip or fail deterministically.
4. Docs describe defaults and why options are explicit rather than ambient globals.
5. No Tokio or alternate runtime dependencies are introduced.

title: [SUB-EPIC] Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver
description:
# Sub-Epic: Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver

## Purpose

Define the platform-agnostic reactor interface and integrate it with the runtime's IoDriver. This is the foundation upon which all platform-specific reactors (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) are built.

## Background

The reactor abstraction already exists in stub form at `src/runtime/reactor/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub trait Reactor {
    fn register(&self, source: &dyn Source, interest: Interest) -> io::Result<Registration>;
    fn deregister(&self, registration: Registration) -> io::Result<()>;
    fn poll(&self, events: &mut Events, timeout: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<usize>;
    fn wake(&self) -> io::Result<()>;
}
```

We need to:
1. Finalize this trait design
2. Implement proper Registration/Token management
3. Integrate with IoDriver for waker coordination
4. Design the Source trait for I/O sources (sockets, pipes, etc.)

## Design Considerations

### Waker Efficiency
Phase 0 uses `wake_by_ref()` which causes immediate re-poll. Real reactor needs:
- Slab-based waker storage (like mio/tokio)
- Token → TaskId mapping for targeted wakeups
- Batch processing of ready events

### Cancel-Correctness for I/O
When a task is cancelled mid-I/O:
- Deregister interest immediately
- Any in-flight data may be lost (documented behavior)
- Registration cleanup must be atomic

### Two-Phase I/O Operations
For cancel-safety, consider:
```rust
// Reserve phase: register interest, get permit
let permit = stream.reserve_read(cx).await?;
// Commit phase: perform actual read
let bytes = permit.read(buf)?;  // Linear, must happen
```

This is optional for basic I/O but important for advanced patterns.

## Key Types to Define/Refine

1. **Registration** - Handle to registered I/O source
2. **Token** - Compact ID for mapping events to wakers
3. **Interest** - Bitflags for READABLE/WRITABLE/ERROR
4. **Source** - Trait for things that can be registered (sockets, pipes)
5. **Events** - Container for ready events from poll()

## Integration Points

- `RuntimeState`: Hold reactor instance
- `IoDriver`: Bridge between reactor events and task wakers
- `Cx`: Provide IoCap capability tier for I/O registration
- `Scheduler`: Wake tasks when their I/O is ready

## Deliverables

1. Finalized `Reactor` trait with complete documentation
2. `Source` trait for registerable I/O sources
3. `Registration`, `Token`, `Interest`, `Events` types
4. `IoDriver` implementation with slab-based waker storage
5. Runtime integration (reactor in RuntimeState)
6. Unit tests for token allocation/deallocation
close_reason: All sub-tasks completed: Reactor trait (hqpl), Registration (553y), Interest/Events (kja2), Token slab (uxt9), Source trait (ufm5), RuntimeState integration (3utu), IoDriver (tk79)

title: CurrentCxGuard must preserve restrictions under out-of-order drop
description: CurrentCxGuard::drop unconditionally pops the top CURRENT_CX_STACK frame. Because CurrentCxGuard is public and two same-thread guards can be dropped in any Rust-valid order, dropping an outer full-authority guard while an inner restricted guard remains alive pops the restriction instead. Cx::current then exposes the outer full-capability frame during the restricted scope. Fix must give every frame a unique guard identity and remove only that frame, keeping the LIFO fast path. Preserve public signatures and add an old-red/new-green regression that asserts IO, remote, time, and fetch capability remain masked after outer-first drop and that the stack is empty after both guards drop.
acceptance_criteria: Public API regression proves dropping an outer CurrentCxGuard before an inner restricted guard does not remove or widen the inner restriction; all gated capabilities remain unavailable; dropping the remaining guard leaves no ambient Cx; ordinary LIFO behavior and existing restriction tests remain green; focused RCH and UBS pass.
notes: Repaired CurrentCxGuard with a unique per-thread frame identity so Drop removes only its own frame while preserving the LIFO fast path and all public signatures. Permanent public native regression drops an outer full-authority guard before an inner cap::None guard, verifies IO/remote/time/fetch remain masked, then verifies no ambient Cx remains after the inner guard drops. Exact old-red: base before repair on vmi1293453 job 29980111176466578 exited 101 at time authority must remain masked. Exact current green: pure clean-overlay/no-overlay base c2c896520591c6ebe17c9d635b43bf36ad010a67 on vmi1293453 ran 1/1 green. Existing same-runtime and restriction coverage remained green in the focused integration target. UBS targeted changed files surfaced only pre-existing repository warning inventory, with no new actionable changed-hunk defect.

title: Excluded fuzz lock resolves rustls 0.23.43, inside RUSTSEC-2026-0285 (GH #78); the root lock already has 0.23.45
description:
GH #78. The excluded fuzz workspace's committed lock (fuzz/Cargo.lock, line 2428) resolves rustls 0.23.43, which is inside RUSTSEC-2026-0285 / GHSA-2mjx-qc3c-rqvc (affected >= 0.23.13, < 0.23.45; patched >= 0.23.45): rustls can accept TLS 1.3 handshake messages across encryption-level changes within one record. The root lock already resolves 0.23.45, so the runtime graph is not affected; only the fuzz harness graph is.

Fix (bounded, as the issue asks): move only rustls in fuzz/Cargo.lock to 0.23.45, within the fuzz manifest's existing requirement (rustls = "0.23.38", default features off, std/ring/tls12). rustls 0.23.45 needs nothing newer than the fuzz lock already resolves (rustls-webpki >= 0.103.14: 0.103.15; rustls-pki-types >= 1.12: 1.15.1; zeroize >= 1.8: 1.9.0; once_cell >= 1.16; subtle >= 2.5; ring 0.17), and its dependency list under these features is the same as 0.23.43's. So the lock delta is two lines: version and checksum. The checksum 0d41d731... equals the root lock's rustls 0.23.45 entry and the sha256 of the cached crates.io archive.

Verification plan: cargo tree --locked on the fuzz manifest (the lock is complete as written), and cargo check --locked of TLS fuzz targets on RCH.

Not done here (governance owners): the dependency_supply_chain_policy fingerprints for both root and fuzz lockfiles were already stale before this change (policy f301a96e.../d304c648... vs origin 4696080b.../0c37f50c...), so checked_manifest_and_lockfile_fingerprints_match was already red; this change does not re-pin another owner's inventory. A cargo-audit/cargo-deny run against the current RustSec database is not part of this fix.
close_reason: fuzz lock rustls 0.23.45 landed in 41f21d29e; --locked fuzz check green; no new contract red

title: [db-bug-hunt] database/postgres.rs: prepare() generates unbounded server-side named statements — connection-scoped memory leak
description: src/database/postgres.rs:3335 PgConnection::prepare allocates a statement name '__asupersync_s{id}' via let stmt_name = format!(...self.inner.next_stmt_id) and increments next_stmt_id with wrapping_add. There is NO statement cache (no LRU, no max-size eviction, no dedup against previously-prepared SQL). Every distinct prepare() call creates a new server-side prepared statement entry that lives until DEALLOCATE or session end. For long-running pooled connections (default max_lifetime 3600s in src/database/pool.rs) the server-side pg_prepared_statements table grows monotonically with the cumulative count of distinct prepares ever issued on that connection — a real connection-scoped memory leak with NO upper bound. The doc comment at line 3308 says callers should call close_statement(...) but provides no enforcement. Worse: if next_stmt_id is u32 (verify width) and wraps after 2^32 prepares, the synthetic name could collide with a still-active server statement, causing a duplicate-name error or — worse if duplicate names silently overwrite — accidental statement substitution. MySQL (src/database/mysql.rs:2565 prepare) has the same pattern using server-assigned statement_id. Mitigation: add a bounded LRU cache keyed by SQL hash; on eviction, send DEALLOCATE/COM_STMT_CLOSE for the evicted statement. SQLite already does this via rusqlite's set_prepared_statement_cache_capacity (src/database/sqlite.rs:72). Severity HIGH for long-lived connections in pooled deployments.
close_reason: Implemented PreparedStatementCache (HashMap + VecDeque LRU) with DEFAULT_MAX_PREPARED_STATEMENTS=256. prepare() fast-path on cache hit; DEALLOCATE-on-eviction for LRU. 5 unit tests cover cap-trigger, LRU promotion, miss, zero-cap edge, duplicate-SQL replacement. Latest commit on main+master.

title: [runtime-deep] timer.rs: current_gen entry leak for incomplete timer lifecycles
description:
LOCATION: src/runtime/timer.rs, TimerHeap::insert (line 131-142) and pop_expired_into (lines 184-209).

ISSUE: The per-task generation map current_gen tracks the most-recent generation for each task (br-40mcc2). The map is populated on insert() [line 136] and cleared on two paths: (a) when a timer fires and is popped live (line 204), and (b) when cancel(task) is called (line 153). However, a timer that is inserted but never fires AND never cancelled leaves current_gen[task] permanently in the map. In a long-running runtime with many ephemeral tasks, each unfired timer accumulates a leaked entry.

CONCRETE SCENARIO: Task T inserts a timer deadline=tomorrow, but the runtime shuts down before the deadline is reached. The timer is never popped; current_gen[T] remains. Over millions of task lifecycles, current_gen grows without bound.

FIX OUTLINE: (1) Add a clear() call in pop_expired_into for stale entries that are popped (already done at 204, but only for LIVE entries). For stale entries (line 207 path), also remove current_gen if present. (2) Alternatively, reference-count or epoch-scan to reap entries for tasks that no longer exist (requires task-lifetime integration). Option (1) is simpler: stale entries are already being skipped; eagerly clean their generation entries.
close_reason: Fixed in 63f6fbc93: TimerHeap::cancel now physically reaps heap entries for the task via BinaryHeap::retain in addition to bumping current_gen. Long-deadline timers on short-lived tasks no longer accumulate stale heap entries proportional to cancel volume. Tests: cancel_before_fire_releases_both_current_gen_and_heap_entry, many_cancel_without_fire_does_not_leak (1024 cycles, 0 retained), cancel_does_not_disturb_other_tasks_heap_entries.

title: atp-rq-auth 50M/perfect 60s completion stall (accept/connect timeout not cancelled on fast-link completion)
description:
MEASURED by SapphireHill central bench (ledger MATRIX-138, commit 0dd7159f8). 50M/perfect AUTH tier (atp-rq-auth) takes a DEAD-EXACT 60.5s to complete (60.557/60.562/60.496s across 3 reps, variance <0.1s, rounds=0, sha_ok=true, peak RSS only 10MB) vs rsync-ssh ~0.85s = ~60-70x LOSS on a CLEAN AUTHENTICATED transfer.

CHARACTERIZATION:
- The DATA transfers fine (sha_ok=true, tiny 10MB RSS, rounds=0) — it is COMPLETION that blocks ~60s, not the transfer.
- PERFECT-LINK-SPECIFIC: auth/bad=17.7s, auth/good=20.9s complete promptly. Only the perfect (no-loss, no-delay) link stalls.
- AUTH-SPECIFIC: nocrypto/perfect=0.82s, encrypted/perfect=13s. Only the auth tier (--rq-auth-key-hex) stalls.
- The dead-exact 60.5s (sub-100ms variance x3) is a FIXED TIMEOUT firing, not load/noise.

ROOT-CAUSE CANDIDATE: src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs:155 DEFAULT_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT and :158 DEFAULT_CONNECT_TIMEOUT are both Duration::from_secs(60). On a sub-second perfect-link auth transfer, an accept/connect wait (likely the auth control/handshake channel or a second connection the auth path opens) is NOT cancelled when the data transfer completes, so it runs to the full 60s timeout before the process exits/commits. On lossy links the netem delay changes the timing so the wait resolves normally. This was HIDDEN because prior auth benching was bad/good only (never perfect).

FIX DIRECTION: cancel/short-circuit the accept/connect wait on transfer completion (or detect peer-done promptly) so clean auth transfers finish in <1s like nocrypto/perfect. 

WHY IT MATTERS: fixing this turns 50M/perfect AUTH from a ~60x LOSS into a likely WIN vs rsync — the data already arrives in <1s, and nocrypto/perfect already beats rsync (0.82s vs 1.23s). High EV, isolated, well-characterized.

REPRO: sudo env BIN=<atp> ATP_MATRIX_TIMEOUT=90 timeout 360 bash scripts/atp_bench/matrix_bench.sh --execute --generate-workloads --workloads 50M --regimes perfect --tiers auth --reps 3 --run-cell-command 'bash scripts/atp_bench/run_matrix_cell.sh'. Evidence: runs 20260627T2144*/2150*.
close_reason: 60s accept/connect-timeout completion stall verified fixed by cc76330e5 (50M/perfect auth 60.5s->20.7s, sha 3/3, MATRIX-139). Residual auth-CPU-wall tracked separately.

title: Capability escalation: a type-restricted Cx regains Cx<cap::All> via open_child_region (ChildRegion::cx returns &Cx<All>)
description:
## Defect (source-verified by SapphireHill, 2026-09-28, origin 17f130960)
A type-restricted context can recover full compile-time authority by opening a child region.
- Cx::restrict::<NewCaps>() is a type-level re-typing only. retype() keeps runtime_mask unchanged (src/cx/cx.rs ~1204-1226, br-asupersync-5ckssb), so the SPAWN bit is still set at runtime.
- Cx::open_child_region is in the unbounded `impl<Caps> Cx<Caps>` block (cx.rs ~949; method ~4115). It checks only `self.runtime_mask.has(cap::CapMask::SPAWN)` (~4123).
- ChildRegion::cx() returns `&crate::cx::Cx`, which is `Cx<cap::All>` (src/cx/child_region.rs ~263). Publication narrows only the runtime mask to the parent's (~191).

Trigger (compiles and runs):
    let pure: Cx<cap::None> = cx.restrict();
    let child = pure.open_child_region(ChildRegionSpec::inherit()).await?;
    child.cx().spawn(..); // also timer_driver(), blocking_pool_handle(), other HasX-gated APIs
The compile-time capability model ("all effects flow through explicit Cx; no ambient authority") is bypassed by any code that holds a restricted Cx. Present since open_child_region was added (first seen v0.4.11; not in v0.4.3).

## Fix options (the API policy is the owner's; 0.5/0.6 compatibility policy pending, bi2462.138)
(a) Compatible narrowing: make it ChildRegion<Caps = cap::All>, with cx() -> &Cx<Caps> (and the opening future generic the same way). Callers holding Cx<All> are unchanged, since the default param keeps `ChildRegion` meaning All. Only already-restricted callers, the ones currently escalated, get a narrower type.
(b) Stricter: require `Caps: cap::HasSpawn` on open_child_region, because opening a region is spawn authority. This breaks restricted callers at compile time; it needs owner approval.
Audit the siblings in the same pass: any API that takes a restricted Cx and returns or exposes a Cx<All> (Scope, spawn gateways, dynamic_supervisor, resource_bracket, worker_readiness). Census with git grep for `-> &crate::cx::Cx` and `-> crate::cx::Cx`.

## Tests
- compile-fail (trybuild, asupersync-macros style or tests/compile_fail): restricted cx -> open_child_region -> child.cx().spawn(..) must not compile under (a) or (b).
- Runtime: the child's runtime mask never exceeds the parent's (already true; keep a regression).
Source: independent read-only review of 888020a6b's neighbourhood (subagent); every claim re-checked against the cited lines.
close_reason: fixed in 05f6ab6c6 (compatible narrowing ChildRegion<Caps>); old-red f69ad94b7 compile_fail compiled; new-green doctests, lib 15/0, all-features check clean

title: Cx cancellation-Waker registry has ABA ownership and callback-under-lock hazards
description: Independent review of the Barrier detached-cancellation fix exposed a shared Cx registry defect. Cancellation-Waker ownership is identified only by Waker::will_wake plus a count. After Waker A is replaced by B and later A is registered again, a stale owner of the first A epoch can clear the later A registration, leaving its pending future unwakeable. Separately, register_cancel_waker clones arbitrary RawWaker payloads while holding CxInner.write, and clear_cancel_waker_if_current can retire the stored Waker under that non-reentrant lock. Acceptance: add an opaque generation token for each installed-Waker epoch; atomically refresh a callers ownership only when its token is stale; clear only the exact generation plus Waker identity; perform arbitrary Waker clone/final retirement outside Cx locks; advance the generation on direct runtime/lab replacement and cleanup paths; migrate Barrier and OnceCell cancel-aware waits; add deterministic ABA, same-Waker refcount, changed-Waker, callback-unlocked, detached cancellation, terminal, and Drop regressions. Preserve the single-slot scheduler contract and no unsafe expansion.

title: W3C trace context is never propagated: add web middleware/layer and gRPC interceptor that continue or start the trace (n0zqlh built only the parser)
description:
W3C Trace Context was never propagated by the web or gRPC stacks.

Evidence (origin f3e76f3f4): `git grep` finds no caller of extract_from_http, extract_propagation_from_http, inject_to_http or inject_to_grpc anywhere in src/ outside w3c_trace_context.rs itself; only the re-export list in observability/mod.rs names them. No web middleware and no gRPC interceptor reads `traceparent`. asupersync-n0zqlh ("W3C trace context propagation implemented for HTTP->gRPC boundaries") delivered the parser and an audit test that calls the parser directly, not a propagation path, so a server built on asupersync drops every incoming trace and every request starts unrelated.

Plan (additive, v0.4.3-compatible):
1. observability::w3c_trace_context::continue_or_start_trace(headers): the context one hop runs under. A valid traceparent continues as a child span (keeps tracestate and baggage); a missing or invalid one starts a new trace and drops tracestate (W3C: a vendor that cannot parse traceparent must not use tracestate); malformed baggage is ignored instead of discarding a valid trace.
2. web::middleware::W3CTraceContextMiddleware + W3CTraceContextLayer + MiddlewareStack::with_w3c_trace_context: puts traceparent / tracestate / baggage of the handler's span in the request extensions, and sets extensions trace_id (32-hex) unless an outer layer set one, so RequestTraceMiddleware and CatchPanicMiddleware logs carry the W3C trace id.
3. grpc::W3CTraceContextInterceptor / w3c_trace_context_interceptor(): replaces traceparent / tracestate / baggage metadata with a child span (removes stale keys first, so an invalid traceparent's tracestate does not survive).

Acceptance:
- Positive: a request carrying a valid traceparent reaches the handler (web) / leaves the interceptor (gRPC) with the SAME trace id and a NEW span id, tracestate and baggage kept; two interceptor passes (client then server) keep one trace with distinct spans and exactly one traceparent entry.
- Negative: missing or invalid traceparent -> new trace, tracestate dropped; a trace_id set by an outer RequestIdMiddleware is kept.
- Control: a combined control that disables continuation (always new_root), tracestate filtering, the stale-key removal and the trace_id guard must turn the new tests red.

No-Claim: this does not create or export OpenTelemetry spans, and does not inject traceparent into outgoing HTTP client requests automatically; the handler copies the extensions/metadata onto its outgoing calls.
close_reason: Landed in 814157d5c: web middleware, layer and gRPC interceptor continue incoming W3C trace
