title: JoinSet audit (10-09): an owner's waker can outlive a dropped JoinSet in a member's retirement barrier; register-before-scan ordering untested
description:
Read-only audit of JoinSet collection and wakeups (src/combinator/join_set.rs, join_set/collector.rs, join_set/owner/, candidate_tests.rs, waker_tests.rs), focused on 5f8303a12 and b3d54ec0f (landed uncompiled 10-07; since compiled under 3d9c36acc and cf817d12b), at origin 27893f71f (SapphireHill rc_20260923 audit agent, 10-09). No HIGH or MEDIUM: candidate bookkeeping, lost-wakeup ordering (refresh before scan; MemberWake inserts the candidate then reads the waiter), waker ownership, fail-fast precedence and drain, owner APIs, accounting and drop were checked and are sound; the new tests would fail on the pre-fix code.

## LOW
L1. An owner's executor waker can outlive a dropped JoinSet inside a member's retirement barrier: join_all_cancel_on_owner / join_all poll members with the owner's own waker (owner.rs ~48-49; join_set.rs ~433), register_and_is_open stores a clone in the barrier's single slot, and TaskHandle has no Drop, so after the owner future is dropped (e.g. by a timeout) the slot keeps that waker (and its task allocation) until the member retires, then wakes it spuriously. join_next / try_join_all leave only MemberWake there, so 5f8303a12's promise holds on those paths. Fix: TaskHandle Drop clearing a waker this handle registered (or a registration token). Test: member with RetirementBarrier::pending() and a published result, poll join_all_cancel_on_owner once with a counting waker, drop it, assert the waker's strong count fell back and open_and_wake does not wake it.
L2. join_next / try_join_next have no per-poll budget (join_set.rs ~273-286, ~370-379): the first collection after N spawns polls all N in one poll (try_join_all caps at 64). Not a regression.
L3. summary() (~415-417) says it counts outcomes observed by join_next; try_join_next and the owner APIs count too. Some 1sngsf lines are not rustfmt-shaped.

## Test gaps
G1. Nothing tests the register-before-scan ordering in next_outcome (join_set.rs ~360): moving collector.refresh after the scan would pass every test (and in try_join_all the runnable self-wake at fail_fast.rs ~188 would mask it). A deterministic test: park member 2 with a waker whose Drop fires MemberWake for member 1, park member 1 with a waker whose Drop publishes member 0's result, remove 1 from candidates, poll join_next once with a counting waker; the waker must be woken (with scan-then-register the set hangs).
G2. Fail-fast precedence: no test for try_join_all with owner cancel first and a sibling panic during the drain (expect Panicked), none for two failures in the same poll (expect the lower spawn index), no multi-thread stress of completion against collector parking.
close_reason: done

comments.text:
SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-09: two more LOWs from a read-only audit of src/combinator/join_set/owner.rs and owner/fail_fast.rs at 8213ebf5c (round r17-d0 B1; report /data/tmp/rc_20260922/audit_r17_B1_join_set_owner.md). No HIGH or MEDIUM. Not claimed.

Collecting n members one at a time is O(n^2). The doc (~83-86) says "not a full repeated scan". Fix: track how far the cancellation has been sent and redo the full pass only when the owner's reason strengthens. Members spawned between calls still need the reason, so it cannot simply be dropped. (fiber::scope had the same pattern; fixed there in f7cae0578 with a pass-once flag plus inheritance at spawn.)
- LOW-2, fail_fast.rs try_join_all (64-per-poll cap ~141, owner verdict ~168-178): the owner is cancelled, 64 members are running and member 64 already returned Err("boom"). The first poll stops at the cap and picks the owner's cancellation, so the result is Cancelled(owner); with 63 running members it is Err("boom"). The batch size changes the verdict, against the docs (~92-94 "a parked early member cannot hide a later member's error"; ~106-108). Fix: choose the owner verdict only after a full pass over the ready members (cancellation of running members can still be sent at once).

title: [channel] src/channel/atomicity_test.rs:245 shared cancellation injector loses RNG updates under concurrency
description: CancellationInjector::should_cancel reads rng_state with load(Relaxed), computes the next LCG state, and writes it back with store(Relaxed). The injector is shared across concurrent producer tasks, so two callers can read the same old state and both store the same next state, collapsing RNG progression and correlating cancellation decisions. That distorts the intended cancellation distribution and weakens stress coverage. Suggested fix: advance rng_state with an atomic fetch_update / compare_exchange loop (or use fetch_add on a bijective counter-based PRNG) so each call consumes a unique state even under concurrency.

title: [oneshot] Sender::poll_closed bypasses waiter identity system causing waker races
description:
ISSUE:
Sender::poll_closed method directly overwrites inner.waker without using the established waiter identity system (waker_id/next_waiter_id), while RecvUninterruptibleFuture properly uses this system.

IMPACT:
1. Waker race: Receiver future registers waker with ID X, sender poll_closed overwrites it without ID, receiver future thinks it still owns the waker but doesn't
2. Stale waker cleanup: Cancelled receiver futures can't properly clear their waker since poll_closed bypassed identity tracking  
3. Inconsistent state: waker_id points to receiver registration but waker contains sender's waker
4. Lost wakeups: Receiver might not get notified if its waker gets overwritten by sender

LOCATION:
src/channel/oneshot.rs:335-346 (Sender::poll_closed method)

FIX:
poll_closed should either:
- Use a separate sender_waker field, OR  
- Implement proper waiter identity coordination, OR
- Use a different notification mechanism that doesn't conflict with receiver wakers

TEST: Create a scenario with concurrent receiver recv and sender poll_closed to verify proper wakeup behavior.
close_reason: Fixed oneshot Sender::poll_closed waker race by adding separate sender_waker field

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Region Tree Property Testing
description:
## Overview

Implement comprehensive property-based testing for the region tree using proptest, verifying structural invariants hold under arbitrary operation sequences.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Unit tests check specific scenarios but may miss edge cases. Property-based testing generates thousands of random scenarios, finding bugs that humans wouldn't think to test.

**Invariant Verification**: The region tree has critical invariants (no orphans, proper parent-child relationships, cancellation propagation). Property tests verify these hold for ALL possible operation sequences.

**Confidence**: With property tests, we can refactor region tree internals confidently, knowing the invariants are continuously verified.

## Key Invariants to Test

### Structural Invariants
1. **No orphan tasks**: Every task has a valid parent region
2. **Tree structure**: No cycles, single root, proper parent pointers
3. **Child tracking**: Parent's children list matches children's parent pointers
4. **ID uniqueness**: No duplicate RegionId or TaskId

### Behavioral Invariants
5. **Cancel propagation**: If parent cancelled, all descendants cancelled
6. **Close ordering**: Region cannot close until all children closed
7. **Outcome collection**: All child outcomes collected before parent completes

### Resource Invariants
8. **No leaks**: After full close, all resources freed
9. **Budget inheritance**: Child budgets never exceed parent budgets

## Property Test Strategy

### Arbitrary Operations
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Arbitrary)]
enum RegionOp {
    CreateChild,
    SpawnTask,
    CancelRegion(RegionSelector),
    CompleteTask(TaskSelector),
    CloseRegion(RegionSelector),
    AdvanceTime(Duration),
}
```

### Test Harness
```rust
proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn region_tree_invariants(ops: Vec<RegionOp>) {
        let mut tree = RegionTree::new();
        
        for op in ops {
            tree.apply(op);
            tree.assert_invariants();  // Check after EVERY operation
        }
    }
}
```

### Shrinking
Proptest automatically shrinks failing cases to minimal reproductions. A failure with 1000 ops might shrink to 3 ops that reproduce the bug.

## Test Categories

### Category 1: Structure Tests
- Random create/close sequences maintain tree structure
- Deep nesting (100+ levels) works correctly
- Wide trees (1000+ children) work correctly

### Category 2: Cancellation Tests  
- Random cancel at any node propagates correctly
- Cancel during close is handled
- Multiple concurrent cancels are idempotent

### Category 3: Completion Tests
- Random task completions with various outcomes
- Panic in child doesn't corrupt parent
- All outcomes eventually collected

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Arbitrary impl for RegionOp
2. assert_invariants() checks all 9 invariants
3. At least 5 property test functions
4. Tests run 10,000+ cases each
5. Shrinking produces minimal reproductions
6. CI runs property tests (with fixed seed for reproducibility)

## Dependencies

- Uses proptest (already in dev-dependencies)
- Tests region tree internals

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #14 because while extremely valuable for correctness, property tests are a testing technique rather than user-facing feature. The runtime works without them, they just increase confidence.
notes: All 4 child tasks closed: asupersync-s4hw (property tests written), asupersync-kbg7 (shrinking/seeds), asupersync-7ljc (E2E/CI), asupersync-9w45 (coverage measurement). Region tree property testing infrastructure is complete.

title: [swarm-perf] Add hot-cold arena tiers and optional large-page cold evidence slabs
description:
Background:
- The swarm-perf plan already covers arena pre-sizing, task-record pooling, scheduler evidence artifacts, and large-memory trace profiles, but it does not yet have an explicit allocator/substrate bead for separating hot runtime metadata from cold evidence retention on 256GB-class hosts.
- Canonical graveyard guidance points to hot/cold region separation, allocator selection by expected throughput-latency-fragmentation loss, and optional hugepage-backed slabs for cold buffers as the natural next lever once simple capacity hints exist.
- Large hosts should be able to spend RAM intentionally to reduce allocator interference on scheduler and cancellation hot paths without silently changing semantics for default hosts.

Candidate surfaces:
- src/util/arena.rs
- src/runtime/state.rs
- src/trace/* and/or cold evidence buffer owners
- src/runtime/config.rs and builder.rs for explicit opt-in policy wiring

Required design:
1. Define an explicit hot-vs-cold arena policy so scheduler/task metadata stays on the low-latency path while evidence/trace payloads can use a separate cold tier.
2. Keep any large-page / hugepage / far-memory tactics strictly optional and profile-gated; the conservative fallback must remain the current allocator behavior.
3. Reuse the capacity-hint family from asupersync-2b5y3w and compose cleanly with the large-memory profile work in asupersync-yaj7g6 instead of inventing disconnected knobs.
4. Emit operator-visible accounting for hot/cold bytes, allocation source, fallback activation, and retained evidence cost so the policy is explainable.

Proof / validation:
- Deterministic tests for placement rules, accounting, fallback behavior, and disabled-mode equivalence.
- A large-host scenario or e2e script comparing default vs tiered allocation on hot-path latency, allocator contention, RSS, retained evidence bytes, and fallback counts.
- Artifact pack must make it obvious when the cold-tier policy loses and the conservative allocator path should remain pinned.

Success criteria:
- 256GB-class swarm hosts can spend RAM intentionally for lower hot-path allocator interference and longer evidence retention, while default hosts preserve exact behavior and operators can explain every memory-tier decision.
design: Hot/cold arena tiering is the storage-temperature substrate. It must not choose NUMA placement and must not become the user-facing large-memory profile planner. It consumes capacity hints and NUMA locality outputs, then classifies allocations by access temperature: hot scheduler/task/region/obligation metadata stays on the lowest-latency path, while cold evidence and trace slabs may use separate profile-gated storage. Hugepage, large-page, far-memory, or cold-slab tactics are optional, explicitly gated, and must fall back to current allocator behavior when unsupported, over budget, or slower.
acceptance_criteria:
Unit tests cover hot/cold classification, capacity-hint integration, locality-policy integration, disabled-mode equivalence, zero cold budget, very large evidence buffers, accounting totals, fallback reason serialization, unsupported-platform fallback, restoration after disabling the policy, hot metadata never routed into cold slabs, and deterministic report rendering. Scenario or e2e coverage must compare default vs tiered allocation and log scenario ID, contract version, selected storage-temperature policy, capacity hints, locality profile input, hot bytes, cold bytes, allocation source, hugepage or cold-slab status, RSS, retained evidence bytes, allocator contention, hot-path latency p50/p95/p99, fallback counts, no-win trigger, safe fallback profile, generated artifact paths, and final operator verdict explaining whether the tiered policy won or should stay disabled. Add a versioned smoke contract and runner, expected names artifacts/hot_cold_arena_tiers_smoke_contract_v1.json and scripts/run_hot_cold_arena_tiers_smoke.sh unless a better existing contract is reused explicitly. The runner must support --list, --scenario, --dry-run, --execute, --output-root, default Rust validation through rch, report markers recoverable from --nocapture output, deterministic repeated-run hash/projection checks, and a real-host template that clearly marks hugepage or large-memory assumptions as optional. Validation before closeout: bash -n for the runner, runner --list, jq/schema validation for the contract, rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check for touched Rust files, targeted rch cargo tests for unit coverage, rch-backed execution of deterministic smoke scenarios, and bounded graph-health check via bv robot mode or br dep cycles with timeout.

Plan-space refinement, 2026-05-04 AmberElk: hot/cold arena tiering must prove hot-path isolation under memory-pressure and cold-retention storms. Additional unit/property tests must cover monotonic memory-budget enforcement, cold-slab exhaustion, hugepage/large-page refusal, TLB/large-page unsupported fallback, cold evidence burst retention while scheduler metadata remains hot, repeated enable/disable cycles without leaked slabs, hot metadata migration refusal, allocator-fragmentation accounting, and stale locality-profile rejection. Scenario/e2e coverage must add p999 hot-path latency, allocation tail variance, cold-tier pressure transitions, retained-evidence admission/refusal counts, slab fragmentation, fallback trigger ordering, and no-flapping proof when memory pressure crosses thresholds repeatedly. Closeout must include a no-win artifact if tiering increases p99/p999 hot-path latency, allocator contention, RSS instability, or fallback churn; final signoff must fail closed if a large-memory profile can route task/region/obligation hot metadata into cold slabs or if unsupported hugepage assumptions are treated as required.
notes: Plan-space revision by PeachLantern on 2026-05-03: this bead remains the temperature layer between NUMA-local arena placement and large-memory trace profiles. Do not absorb NUMA-local shard placement from asupersync-nxd9xm or operator profile composition from asupersync-yaj7g6/c1qfr9. Preserve all functionality: opt-in profile gate, disabled-mode equivalence, unsupported-platform fallback, optional large-page/cold-slab behavior, precise accounting, detailed e2e artifacts, and an operator-readable no-win verdict.
close_reason: Implemented on main across 90d8eda39, 360842bdd, and c896ea729. Current HEAD validation passed: runner bash -n, runner --list, contract jq shape check, rch rustfmt, rch arena_temperature lib tests (8 passed), and hot/cold smoke runner --execute with repeat projection stability. Bounded br dep cycles graph-health checks timed out at 30s with no output; recorded as control-plane timeout, not hhlhjv code failure.

title: CI integration for conformance tests
description:
## Overview

Integrate conformance tests with CI/CD pipeline for continuous validation.

## Requirements

### CI Script
```yaml
# .github/workflows/conformance.yml
name: Conformance Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run conformance tests
        run: |
          cargo test --package conformance --features all-runtimes -- --nocapture
          
      - name: Generate coverage report
        run: |
          cargo run --bin conformance-report > conformance.md
          
      - name: Check coverage threshold
        run: |
          COVERAGE=$(cargo run --bin conformance-coverage)
          if [ "$COVERAGE" -lt 90 ]; then
            echo "Coverage $COVERAGE% below threshold 90%"
            exit 1
          fi
          
      - name: Upload report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: conformance-report
          path: conformance.md
```

### Performance Bounds CI
```yaml
  performance-bounds:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run performance conformance
        run: |
          cargo test --package conformance --features performance -- --nocapture
          
      - name: Compare with baseline
        run: |
          cargo run --bin conformance-perf-compare baseline.json current.json
```

### Runtime Matrix
Test against multiple runtime implementations:
- Lab runtime (always)
- Production runtime (Linux only)
- Mock runtime (for negative tests)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. GitHub Actions workflow
2. Coverage threshold enforcement
3. Performance bounds testing
4. Multi-runtime matrix
5. Artifact upload for reports
6. Failure notifications

## Test Requirements
- Test CI script locally with act
- Test coverage threshold logic
- Test performance comparison

title: [security-saas] web/session.rs: no session ID regeneration / rotation API — session fixation vulnerability on login/privilege change
description: src/web/session.rs has no public regenerate() / rotate_session_id() API. After a successful login (or any privilege escalation — role change, MFA verification), the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet REQUIRES generating a fresh session ID and invalidating the old one to prevent session fixation: an attacker pre-logs-in to the application, captures their own session ID, tricks the victim into using that ID (via a planted cookie or an URL parameter), then waits for the victim to authenticate — the now-authenticated session ID is in the attacker's hands. The current SessionMiddleware (session.rs:617+) only mints new IDs on (a) brand-new sessions (first request, no cookie) and (b) session_cleared (session_data.is_empty + is_modified). Login flows that authenticate WITHIN an existing pre-auth session reuse the same session_id, leaving the application vulnerable. Mitigation: (a) add Session::regenerate(&mut self) that clears server-side state under the old ID, mints a fresh cryptographic ID, marks modified=true so the cookie is reissued; (b) document the contract that callers MUST call regenerate() at every privilege boundary. Severity HIGH for any SaaS with auth flows.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 5e1ebd1bf: Session::regenerate() rotates ID + invalidates old store entry + preserves data + rotates CSRF token in lockstep. End-to-end test middleware_regenerate_rotates_id_and_preserves_data locks all 3 properties.

title: [correctness] raptorq/rfc6330.rs: tuple_indices asserts panic on degenerate tuple.d=0 — malformed FEC-OTI is a DoS vector
description:
src/raptorq/rfc6330.rs:419-425 — assert!((1..=RFC6330_MAX_LT_DEGREE).contains(&tuple.d), ...) panics if tuple.d=0. The deg() function (line 354) is documented to return 1..30 only, so internally this assertion holds — but a malformed FEC-OTI that influences the tuple-expansion boundary OR a future caller that passes a tuple with d=0 directly turns this into a panic-on-input vector.

For a network-receivable FEC code, panic-on-malformed is the wrong shape: a hostile peer can crash the receiver by sending FEC parameters that route to this assertion.

Fix direction: replace the assert! with a Result-returning early return ('SystematicError::DegenerateTupleDegree { d: 0 }') and propagate the error up through the public encode/decode entry points. Validates the RFC compliance contract WITHOUT giving an attacker a panic surface.

title: [WEDGE] Unit and E2E tests for FrankenLab runtime and CLI
description:
Comprehensive test suite for the FrankenLab standalone testing harness, covering the deterministic scheduler, virtual time, scenario YAML format, and CLI.

**Unit tests:**
(1) Deterministic scheduler reproducibility — run the same program with the same seed 100 times; verify bit-identical scheduling decisions each time.
(2) PRNG scheduling strategies — verify that random, round-robin, DPOR, and PCT strategies each produce valid (non-deadlocking) schedules for a standard test program.
(3) Virtual time correctness — verify that sleep(Duration::from_secs(N)) with virtual time completes instantly in wall-clock time but advances virtual clock by exactly N seconds.
(4) Auto-advance semantics — when all tasks block on sleep, virtual time advances to the minimum next wake-up point (not further).
(5) YAML scenario parser — roundtrip property: parse(serialize(scenario)) == scenario for randomly generated scenarios (proptest).
(6) JSON Schema validation — verify that all example scenarios pass schema validation and that intentionally invalid scenarios are rejected with clear errors.
(7) Fault injection determinism — the same fault schedule with the same seed produces identical fault timing across runs.

**E2E tests:**
(8) Full scenario execution — run all 10+ example scenarios through the CLI and verify all assertions pass.
(9) Record/replay round-trip — record an execution trace, replay it, and verify bit-identical outcomes.
(10) Cross-machine reproducibility — generate artifact hashes on CI and verify they match expected golden values (proves determinism is not hardware-dependent).
(11) CLI error handling — verify that malformed YAML, missing files, and invalid seeds produce clear, actionable error messages with non-zero exit codes.
(12) Performance regression — FrankenLab overhead vs direct execution must stay below 10% for small tests (criterion.rs benchmark).

**Logging requirements:**
- Each test must log: scenario_name, seed, strategy, virtual_time_final, wall_time_ms, assertion_results, fault_count.
- On replay divergence, log the first diverging scheduling decision with full context.
- All logs in structured JSON to EvidenceLedger.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- 100% deterministic replay across 1000 runs.
- All example scenarios pass.
- Overhead below 10% for small tests, below 5x for large tests.
- All CLI error cases produce exit code != 0 with human-readable message.

**Rust implementation notes:**
- Use proptest for YAML schema fuzzing.
- Use assert_cmd + predicates for CLI integration tests.
- Use tempfile for isolated test directories.

title: [profiling-perf-hotpath] runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs:3993 b: Arc::clone wake_state per task poll (2 sibling sites)
description:
CATALOGUE: 1st-pass hot-path audit. Two sibling sites in src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs both call `Arc::clone(&record.wake_state)` inside the per-task dispatch path:

  - line 3993 — finish_dispatch (called once per task poll)
  - line 4034 — local task dispatch (TLS-stored task removed, dispatch path)

Concrete reasoning: Arc::clone is an atomic refcount fetch_add (~5ns on x86-TSO, plus a cacheline write that may invalidate the L1 cacheline that holds the refcount counter on cores reading it). With a 100k task-poll/sec workload this is ~1M atomic ops/sec just for waker construction. The wake_state Arc is held by the scheduler, so most clones could be replaced with a borrowed `&Arc<WakeState>` if the downstream Waker construction is lifetime-compatible, or with a pre-cached Waker stored on the TaskRecord that's cloned once at spawn time and reused across polls.

Profile evidence or microbenchmark outline:
  - criterion bench in benches/scheduler.rs measuring next_task() throughput with 1000 ready tasks. Compare baseline vs a stub variant that bypasses the Arc::clone (e.g., uses a pre-cached Waker on TaskRecord). Expect 5-10% wall-clock reduction.
  - perf-stat measuring atomic ops per dispatch: pre-fix should show ≥1 per dispatch from this site alone.
  - flame graph on three_lane scheduler under uniform-load: Arc::clone should appear in the top-15 self-time contributors.

Class: (b) Arc::clone in hot path that could be borrowed.

Source: /profiling-software-performance 1st-pass hot-path audit on src/runtime/scheduler/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Verified against current three_lane.rs:3987-4078: Arc::clone(&record.wake_state) at line 3993 is REQUIRED, not extraneous. The local wake_state binding is consumed after the with_task_table closure at lines 4247 (wake_state.clear()), 4303 (wake_state.finish_poll()), and 4384 (wake_state.clear()) — all of which run AFTER the task-table guard is released. Eliminating this clone requires either (a) caching wake_state on StoredTask (invasive: StoredTask is a Box<dyn Future>, would need a wrapper struct breaking the type's Box-trait-object shape), (b) ManuallyDrop pattern (does not help; the issue is owned Arc lifetime past lock release, not Drop ordering), or (c) Arc::as_ptr (returns a raw pointer; cannot be reconstituted as an owned Arc). When cached_waker is Some (the common warm-path), the outer clone IS still consumed by clear()/finish_poll() — there is no waker-cached fast path that avoids it. Tradeoff: 1 atomic refcount inc+dec (~3-5ns) per poll, intrinsic to the current Arc<wake_state> lifecycle. Closing as already-optimized; future invasive refactor tracked separately if profiling shows this dominates.

title: [conformance] raptorq/rfc6330.rs: V0-V3 lookup tables lack byte-exact regression pin (sub-area #1 of lc0anl)
description:
src/raptorq/rfc6330.rs lines 14-159 hardcode 4 256-entry u32 tables (V0/V1/V2/V3) per RFC 6330 §5.5.2. There is no test that verifies these arrays match the RFC byte-exact: a single transcription error (e.g. one digit off in any of the 1024 values) silently corrupts every Rand(y,i,m) call and therefore every encode/decode operation.

Existing tests in rfc6330.rs exercise rand_function with sample (y,i,m) triples but those triples don't isolate which V-table is wrong — a hash collision or off-by-one wouldn't be reliably detected.

Fix: add a deterministic hash-pin or insta snapshot of the four arrays so any byte-level change in src/raptorq/rfc6330.rs trips. This is sub-area #1 of br-asupersync-lc0anl (RaptorQ conformance epic) and stands alone.

title: [oracle-correctness HIGH] lab/oracle/region_leak.rs: pervasive Instant::now / SystemTime::now means the entire oracle is non-replayable and threshold-based detection is wall-clock-dependent
description:
src/lab/oracle/region_leak.rs is structurally non-replayable: every timing path uses ambient wall-clock primitives.

Sites identified:
  - line 275 RegionLeakOracle::new: `start_time: Instant::now()`
  - line 318 on_region_created: `now = Instant::now()` for `creation_time`/`last_activity`
  - line 325, 614, 630, 646, 663, 695: `detected_at: SystemTime::now()` in violation records
  - line 368, 459, 471, 491, 501: `region.last_activity = Instant::now()` on every state transition
  - line 383, 415, 430, 512, 581: `now = Instant::now()` for threshold comparisons against `max_creation_delay`, `max_closing_time`, `max_finalizing_time`, `max_task_lifetime`, `max_idle_time`

Two failure modes flow from this:

  (a) **Detection threshold non-determinism.** `max_idle_time = Duration::from_secs(2)` and similar thresholds (with_strict_timeouts at line 298 ratchets these tighter to 10ms / 100ms / 500ms / 1s / 2s). The detection compares `now.duration_since(creation_time)` to the threshold. A lab run on a busy CI host takes 5x longer than on a dev workstation; the oracle reports a leak in CI that does NOT exist in dev — or vice versa. The asupersync core invariant 'lab replay is byte-identical given the same seed' is silently violated.

  (b) **Violation record non-determinism.** Even when the same set of leaks is detected, the `detected_at: SystemTime::now()` field puts a different timestamp in every replay. Trace certificates and crashpack hashes that include violation records become unstable. Users comparing crashpacks across two runs see noise.

This is a HIGH severity oracle-correctness regression: the oracle's entire purpose is to detect and document leaks, and it cannot do either deterministically.

Fix direction:
  1. Replace every `Instant::now()` with `now: Time` parameters threaded from the caller (LabRuntime::check_invariants already has `now` in scope — see lab/runtime.rs:1408 `hydrate_temporal_from_state(&self.state, now)`).
  2. Replace every `SystemTime::now()` with the same Cx-supplied Time. Where the schema demands SystemTime (e.g., for serialised crashpack consumers), normalise to `Time`'s nanosecond representation and document that the field is virtual-time, not wall-clock.
  3. Add a regression test that runs the oracle through a deterministic LabRuntime with a virtual-time clock and asserts two replays produce byte-identical violation records.

Related: br-asupersync-qu7yet (minimizer ambient time), br-asupersync-h0vru4 (crashpack ambient time). This finding is the same shape but in an oracle hot path, which is the worst location for this bug class because the lab's whole value proposition is replay determinism.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/lab/oracle/* + lab/explorer.rs (2026-04-26).

Violation records are now byte-stable across replays for crashpack-hash and trace-certificate equivalence. Internal Instant::now() threshold sites remain — converting those to Time is structural follow-up.

title: [TESTING] Loom-based concurrency tests for scheduler queues
description:
Implement Loom-based concurrency tests for Asupersync's scheduler queues and lock-free data structures. Loom exhaustively explores all possible thread interleavings to find concurrency bugs that are nearly impossible to catch with random testing.

BACKGROUND (Tier C Formal Assurance, Graveyard section 0.14): Loom provides model-checked concurrency testing by controlling thread scheduling and exploring all valid interleavings. Unlike stress tests that probabilistically find bugs, loom guarantees that if a bug exists within the exploration bound, it will be found. This corresponds to Tier C (Deductive Verification) on the formal assurance ladder because it provides exhaustive coverage within bounds.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Add loom as a dev-dependency behind a cfg(loom) feature flag. (2) Replace std::sync::atomic with loom::sync::atomic in testable code using conditional imports: #[cfg(loom)] use loom::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize; #[cfg(not(loom))] use std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize. (3) Create a separate test binary: tests/loom_tests.rs that only runs under cargo test --features loom. (4) Use loom::model(|| { ... }) to wrap each test case. (5) For work-stealing deque: test push/pop from owner thread, steal from multiple thief threads, verify no lost items and no duplicates. (6) For MPSC channel: test concurrent sends from N producers, single consumer recv, verify total ordering within each producer and no message loss. (7) For task state machine: test concurrent wake/cancel/complete transitions, verify exactly one terminal state is reached. (8) For budget counter: test concurrent decrements from N threads, verify counter never goes below zero and final value equals initial minus total decrements.

COVERAGE TARGETS: (1) Work-stealing deque: all push/pop/steal interleavings with 2 threads, 3 operations each. (2) MPSC channel: all send/recv interleavings with 3 senders, 1 receiver, 2 messages each. (3) Task state machine: all wake/cancel/complete interleavings with 2 threads. (4) Budget counter: all decrement/check interleavings with 3 threads, 2 decrements each.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) All loom tests pass with max_preemptions=2 (CI fast mode). (2) All loom tests pass with max_preemptions=4 (nightly thorough mode). (3) No data races detected by loom (loom catches these automatically via its memory model). (4) No deadlocks (all model executions terminate within bounded steps). (5) Correct final state in all explored interleavings. (6) Loom tests complete in < 5 minutes for CI, < 30 minutes for nightly.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each loom test logs: test_name, max_preemptions, total_interleavings_explored, execution_time_ms, pass_fail. On failure: log the specific interleaving that caused the failure (loom provides a trace of scheduling decisions). Summary at test suite completion: total_tests, total_interleavings, unique_bugs_found. All output in structured JSON for CI parsing.

TESTING APPROACH (meta): (1) Start with the simplest data structure (budget counter) to validate the loom test infrastructure. (2) Progressively add more complex structures. (3) Use loom::thread::yield_now() at critical points to increase exploration coverage. (4) Compare loom results against tokio-test stress tests to validate that loom catches bugs stress tests miss.

title: Expose/auto --max-block-size to chunk big single files into small RaptorQ blocks (collapse decode wall)
description: MATRIX-1 evidence (ledger 2026-06-19): atp WINS rsync at 5M (perfect 1.27x, bad/2% 1.10x, sha-clean) but LOSES 50M at every regime (perfect 3.55x, bad 4.89x) and FAILS 50M/broken (exit 144). Root cause = single-core RaptorQ FEC-repair DECODE WALL ~0.8MB/s: a 50M file is one large block-set, so decode time dominates once loss triggers repair rounds (50M/perfect 0-rounds=4.36s vs 50M/bad 4-rounds=68s). Competitiveness scales as 1/block-size — trees of <=1MB files and the 5M file clear the wall. LEVER: cap RaptorQ block size (e.g. ~4-8MB) so a 50M file decodes as ~7-12 independent small blocks (like the winning 5M cell / a tree), which (a) collapses the per-block decode wall, (b) enables parallel per-block decode (see z01bbr.3.5 / 317hxr.7.3), (c) bounds receiver memory (50M/bad recv peak 483MB), and (d) likely clears the 50M/broken exit-144. Verify byte-identical (isomorphism) + re-run matrix 50M/500M/5G; target: 50M tracks the 5M win-profile. Complements parallel-decode beads (block size is the prerequisite that makes them effective).

title: Implement core identifier types (RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time)
description:
# Core Identifier Types (RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time)

## Purpose
Define the fundamental identifier and time types used throughout the runtime.

These types are simple but critical:
- they appear on hot paths (scheduling, tracing, registry lookups)
- they are embedded in most runtime records
- they must be deterministic, copy-friendly, and easy to debug

The operational semantics uses these identifiers directly:
- `r ∈ RegionId = ℕ`
- `t ∈ TaskId = ℕ`
- `o ∈ ObligationId = ℕ`
- `τ ∈ Time = ℕ` (discrete ticks in lab)

## The Identifier Types

### RegionId
```rust
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct RegionId(u32);
```
Identifies a region in the region tree (arena key).

### TaskId
```rust
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct TaskId(u32);
```
Identifies a task. Used for:
- wake scheduling (`Waker` built via `std::task::Wake`, carrying a `TaskId`)
- join handles / waiters sets
- tracing (task lifecycle events)
- obligation ownership tracking (holder task)

### ObligationId
```rust
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct ObligationId(u32);
```
Identifies an obligation in the obligation registry. Used for:
- tracking reserved/committed/aborted/leaked state
- leak detection
- tracing/debugging

### Time
```rust
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct Time(u64);
```
Represents a point in time.

Normative semantics:
- in the lab runtime, time is **discrete ticks** advanced only by explicit `tick` transitions
- in production, time may map to real instants, but Phase 0 treats `Time` as an abstract, comparable scalar

## Representation Choices

### Why `u32` for IDs?
- 4 billion IDs is plenty for Phase 0 / Phase 1
- trivially copyable, no heap allocation
- cache-friendly, good for arena indexing

### Generation counting (optional enhancement)
To harden against stale-id bugs, we can extend IDs with a generation counter:
```rust
pub struct TaskId {
    index: u32,
    generation: u32,
}
```
This catches use-after-free bugs if arena slots are reused.

Phase 0 plan-of-record: keep IDs as a single `u32` until we have evidence reuse is common or bugs justify the extra storage.

## Time Semantics

### Lab Mode (Deterministic)
- time starts at `Time(0)`
- time advances only by explicit `tick` transitions
- sleeps are expressed as "wake at or after Time(t)" in the timer heap

### Production Mode (Later Phases)
- `Time` may represent a real instant or monotonic clock reading
- mapping from OS time → `Time` must be explicit and capability-gated (no ambient authority)

## Key Operations

### For all ID types
- constructors are internal (IDs originate from arenas)
- `index()` accessor for arena lookup

### For Time
- `from_ticks(u64)` (lab)
- arithmetic helpers are saturating or checked; no silent overflow

## Display / Debug Formatting
Readable formatting is required for trace debugging:
- `task-42`, `region-7`, `obligation-100`, `t1000`

## Acceptance Criteria
- All ID types are `Copy + Eq + Ord + Hash` and `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- No heap allocation is required to create/copy/compare IDs.
- `Time` supports deterministic lab tick arithmetic (checked/saturating helpers as needed).
- Unit tests cover:
  - ordering and hash/Eq consistency
  - formatting stability
  - basic time arithmetic edge cases

## References (context only)
- `asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md` §1.1 (Identifiers)
- `asupersync_plan_v4.md` §21 (arenas for tasks/regions/obligations)
close_reason: Implemented in src/ (tests + clippy clean)

title: FlowControlMonitor collapses concurrent waits on the same task-channel edge
description: FlowControlMonitor represents blocked_channels, blocked_tasks, and DeadlockDetector.task_to_channel as sets even though one task can have multiple producer/reserve waits on one channel. Deterministic repro: ReserveBlocked(T,C,P1), ReserveBlocked(T,C,P2), ReserveUnblocked(T,C,P1). P2 remains pending, but every blocked set/graph edge is erased; stats report zero and starvation, cancellation, indefinite-blocking, and deadlock checks miss the live wait. pending_permits is keyed only by permit_id and atomicity checks ignore channel_id, so ReserveBlocked(T,C1,P) followed by Commit(T,C2,P) is accepted and corrupts unrelated state. first_block_time is also one task-wide value and is not recomputed when the earliest of several waits ends; record_task_cancel drops cancellation when no state exists yet. Use canonical identity-preserving wait records keyed by kind/task/channel/reason-or-permit, derive refcounted edges and earliest times, validate exact unblock/commit/abort identity, and persist cancellation independently. Regress two permits on one edge, mixed producer/reserve waits, channel/permit mismatch, earliest-wait removal, and cancel-before-first-block. No duplicate found; 3bdda0c5c and ea26665cd added the lossy shapes, while later nearby fixes addressed only history/cleanup/averaging. Independently confirmed by two source reviews on 2026-07-15.
close_reason: Replaced lossy set-only wait tracking with canonical task/channel/kind identities and refcounted task, channel, and deadlock edges. Exact producer reason and reserve permit/channel completions now remove only their matching live wait; invalid and duplicate terminal events leave state and duration totals unchanged. Earliest live wait time is recomputed, cancellation before the first block is retained, duplicate begins are idempotent, and disabled monitors remain allocation-free. Added deterministic coverage for two permits on one edge, both mixed producer/reserve completion orders, wrong-channel unblock/commit/abort classification, reason mismatch, starvation-clock rebasing, duplicate events, early cancellation, and disabled mode. Source commit 75b09d9a7. Verification: focused RCH job j-29955796225753309 passed 18/18; cargo check --all-targets RCH job j-29955796225753310 exited 0; cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings RCH job j-29955796225753311 exited 0; cargo fmt --check and git diff --check passed locally. Final independent review found no high- or medium-severity issues. The separate active-control lifecycle bead asupersync-wvihh8 remains open and is not claimed by this closure.

title: [PERF] Replace PacketAssembler priority insertion scan

No write/flush timeout anywhere on H1 (1259, drive_produced_response) unless request_timeout is set. join_streaming_handler_and_body (2627) drops the handler's response on DrainTimeout / DrainLimitExceeded (pinned by streaming_server_closes_when_unread_body_exceeds_drain_limit, 6109), so every route that does not extract the body loses its 401/404/413 when the request body exceeds 512 KiB / 8 frames / 500 ms; RFC 9112 section 9.6 says write it with Connection: close, then close. add_connection_close (3171-3191) rewrites the first Connection value instead of adding the close token (a forced-close 101 loses upgrade). src/web/multipart.rs:2300: the buffered parser accepts a body whose last part is followed by a non-closing delimiter and EOF, which the streaming decoder rejects. src/http/h2/listener.rs:3468: stream_idle_timeout defaults to None. src/http/h1/stream.rs:1140-1143: push_bytes returns ConsumerDropped without buffering the data and the driver then calls discard_bytes on an empty slice (2543-2549), a framing desync on a kept-alive connection if the consumer is dropped from another task mid-push. title: Http1Listener::run_tls: TLS handshake has no time bound with a default TlsAcceptor (handshake_timeout None); half-open TLS clients pin registered connection slots until shutdown
description:
Http1Listener::run_tls registers the TCP connection with the connection manager and then awaits the TLS handshake with no time bound of its own. TlsAcceptor defaults to handshake_timeout: None, so with a default acceptor a client that opens TCP and never finishes (or trickles) its ClientHello pins a registered connection slot until listener shutdown force-close. The plain-TCP H1 path bounds the equivalent phase (first head read) by Http1Config::idle_timeout, 60 s by default; the TLS path bounds nothing.

Evidence (7fc9e53a4):
- src/tls/acceptor.rs 63, 94, 591: handshake_timeout is Option and both constructors default it to None; 237-250: accept applies a timeout only when Some.
- src/http/h1/listener.rs 1068-1086 (spawn_tls_connection): the ConnectionGuard is moved into the task at 1069, then acceptor.accept(stream) is polled against only the ForceClosing phase; Http1Config::idle_timeout is not applied to the handshake. The doc at 713-716 says "the normal connection limit and drain accounting cover slow or silent TLS peers", but the limit only counts them; nothing evicts them.
- src/server/connection.rs 227-246: register refuses new connections once len() >= max_connections (default 10_000 in Http1ListenerConfig 276) by dropping the accepted stream, so honest clients are refused while half-open handshakes hold the slots. drop_idle_connections (308) exists but has no production caller.
- This is the only TLS accept site in the server stacks (grep over src/http, src/server, src/web, src/grpc, src/net); the streaming, produced and SSE listeners have no TLS variant.

Impact: reliability / connection-slot exhaustion on run_tls deployments that did not set TlsAcceptorBuilder::handshake_timeout. Equivalent in class to asupersync-1to1qw (streaming body trickle); this one is simpler because the handshake phase has a natural single deadline.

Suggested repair (additive, no public-API change): in spawn_tls_connection, wrap the handshake in timeout(idle_timeout) when config.idle_timeout is Some and the acceptor has no handshake_timeout of its own (or always apply min(idle_timeout, acceptor timeout)); on expiry drop the stream so the guard releases the slot and count it in listener stats (a new record_handshake_timeout or the existing transient counters). Changing TlsAcceptor's default from None to a finite value would also close it but is a documented-behavior change under the v0.4.3 compatibility gate, so the listener-level bound is the safer first step; document in run_tls that the acceptor timeout, when set, wins if shorter.

Repro test sketch (native, loopback): run_tls with a default TlsAcceptor and max_connections = 1; open a raw TCP connection and send nothing; a second client attempting a real TLS handshake is refused (register returns None) for as long as the first socket stays open. After the repair the first slot is released after idle_timeout and the second client is served.

Found during the read-only fresh-eyes pass (asupersync-cqzuzt) while source is frozen; no edits made.
close_reason: Fixed in 6580764f9: run_tls handshake bounded by acceptor handshake_timeout else Http1Config::idle_timeout; slot released on expiry. RED (base listener, exit 101) / GREEN (20/20 e2e) receipts in comments.

title: [bug-hunt] messaging/redis: no cluster-mode redirect handling for -MOVED / -ASK
description:
Severity: MEDIUM (feature gap; surfaces as user-visible RedisError::Redis on every misrouted command in a clustered Redis deployment).

src/messaging/redis.rs has no MOVED / ASK / cluster-redirect logic. `grep -n "MOVED|ASK|cluster|hash_slot|crc16"` returns zero hits across 3160 LOC. Every Redis Cluster command that lands on the wrong node returns:

    -MOVED <slot> <host>:<port>      (permanent reshard)
    -ASK <slot> <host>:<port>        (transient migration in progress)

The current code passes these through as `RedisError::Redis(msg)` exactly like any other server error, leaving the caller to:
  - parse the error string by hand,
  - look up or open a connection to the new node,
  - re-issue the command (and remember the ASKING prefix for ASK),
  - track slot ownership for future commands so the same slot doesn't keep bouncing.

Most production-grade Redis clients (redis-rs, fred, ioredis, lettuce) fold this into a transparent `ClusterClient` layer that:
  1. Maintains a slot → node map (queried via `CLUSTER SLOTS` / `CLUSTER SHARDS`).
  2. Computes CRC16 of the key (or the hash-tag if present) to pick the slot.
  3. On MOVED, updates the slot map and retries against the new node.
  4. On ASK, sends `ASKING` then the command against the indicated node, but does NOT update the slot map (the migration is transient).

Fix shape: a `RedisCluster` type that wraps a pool of `RedisClient`s plus a slot map. The single-node `RedisClient` API stays unchanged. Detection of `-MOVED` / `-ASK` happens at the response layer; the redirect logic lives in the cluster wrapper.

This is filed as a feature gap rather than a bug because single-node Redis deployments work correctly. Anyone running this client against a cluster discovers the limitation on the first cross-slot command.

title: h2 listener: FrameCodec accept limit (16384 default) never tied to local advertised SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE
description: Found in deep review (SapphireHill 2026-06-29). src/http/h2/listener.rs:1316 Framed::new(stream, FrameCodec::new()) — codec accept limit stays at DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_SIZE (16384) and set_max_frame_size (connection.rs:112) is never called from the listener. The SEND path is fine (consults remote_settings.max_frame_size directly, connection.rs:1710-1835; the Setting::MaxFrameSize let _=size at 1481 is harmless since remote_settings is already committed at 1464). The gap is the ACCEPT limit: if a deployment configures local settings.max_frame_size > 16384, the listener advertises it (queue_initial_settings) but the codec still rejects frames >16384 (connection.rs:140) -> spurious FRAME_SIZE_ERROR for conformant peer frames. Fail-closed (default-safe), config-only. FIX: create the codec with the local accept limit, e.g. let mut codec=FrameCodec::new(); codec.set_max_frame_size(settings.max_frame_size); Framed::new(stream, codec). Only ever the LOCAL value, never the peer's. Add an e2e test driving a >16384 frame with a large local max_frame_size.
close_reason: Fixed (SapphireHill, commit pending): h2 listener inbound FrameCodec accept limit was stuck at DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_SIZE (16384) regardless of the locally advertised SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE. Added frame_codec_for(max_frame_size) helper wired with settings.max_frame_size (captured before settings moves into Connection); serve_h2_connection now builds the codec via it. Always the LOCAL value, never the peer's. Test frame_codec_for_honors_local_max_frame_size: a 20000-byte DATA frame is accepted at a 32768 local limit and rejected (FRAME_SIZE_ERROR) at the default. clippy clean; tests green.

title: [security-audit] grpc/server.rs: ServerConfig has no max_header_list_size / max_metadata_size — memory exhaustion via long header lists
description: src/grpc/server.rs ServerBuilder exposes max_recv_message_size, max_send_message_size, initial_connection_window_size, initial_stream_window_size, max_concurrent_streams, keepalive_*, default_timeout, send_compression — but NO max_header_list_size, max_metadata_entries, or per-key max_value_size. RFC 9113 (HTTP/2) §6.5.2 specifies SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE; without enforcing it, an attacker can send a HEADERS frame with arbitrarily long field-name and field-value pairs, forcing the HPACK decoder to allocate unbounded memory PER CONNECTION. Combined with the lack of a max_concurrent_connections cap (also missing from ServerConfig), a single client can exhaust server RAM. Trailer manipulation (audit dimension 3) is the same surface — gRPC trailers are HTTP/2 HEADERS frames at end-of-stream, subject to the same lack of bounds. Severity HIGH (P1). Suggested fix: add max_header_list_size: u32 (default 8KiB per gRPC convention) to ServerConfig; enforce in the h2 transport adapter when it gets wired. Document trailer-size limit explicitly.
close_reason: Header-list DoS gap fixed in 967c52abe. ServerConfig now carries max_metadata_size: usize with default 8 KiB (DEFAULT_MAX_METADATA_SIZE constant, matching grpc-go MaxHeaderListSize). ServerBuilder.max_metadata_size(usize) setter for override. New canonical enforcement helper enforce_metadata_size_limit(&Metadata, limit) -> Result<(), Status> returns Status::resource_exhausted (gRPC equivalent of HTTP 431) when sum(key.len()+value.byte_len()) > limit. metadata_byte_size(&Metadata) -> usize is the standalone size accessor. Five regression tests landed: default-cap, under-cap-accepts, over-cap-rejects-with-RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, zero-disables, builder-override. Cargo check on grpc/server.rs clean; lib build has 1 unrelated pre-existing error in src/record/task.rs from concurrent-agent WIP. Companion bead asupersync-mfk14i (CRITICAL — Server::serve never invokes the interceptor chain) is the wiring follow-up that must CALL enforce_metadata_size_limit at the request-reception boundary; until then this fix provides the helper transport adapters need.

comments.text: Found during c5d0q fresh-eyes audit of transport_tcp/mod.rs. (1) transport_tcp/mod.rs:1407 'apply_entry_metadata(&out_path, meta).await?' propagates errors, but the comment at 1404-1405 says metadata application is 'best-effort ... never fatal'. If apply_entry_metadata returns Err (e.g. set_permissions failing on a file the receiver does not own — metadata.rs ~447), the commit aborts AFTER the staging file was already renamed into the destination (1402) => partial commit + the transfer reports failure despite the file being on disk. (2) The multi-file commit loop (~1306-1423) renames/links entries one at a time; a mid-loop error (create_dir_all, rename, symlink, hard_link, or apply_entry_metadata) leaves a PARTIALLY-populated destination with no rollback, while the module doc (lines 29-32) claims it 'atomically rename[s] the staging files into the destination'. FIX OPTIONS: make metadata application non-fatal in the commit loop (treat apply_entry_metadata Err as a traced skip, matching the doc) AND/OR soften the doc to 'per-file atomic rename, not transfer-atomic'. The metadata-error-contract fix needs metadata.rs (apply_entry_metadata error vs skip semantics) which is currently a HOT file (active editor) — deferred to avoid collision. transport_quic has the analogous metadata path (not yet wired per validate_quic_manifest).

title: [obs-reality-check] observability/cancellation_debt_monitor.rs: pending_work HashMap unbounded + cancel_reason stored as Debug-formatted String per entry — memory leak proportional to lifetime work-item count
description: src/observability/cancellation_debt_monitor.rs:219 pending_work: HashMap<WorkType, HashMap<u64, PendingWork>> has NO cap, NO time-based eviction, NO per-WorkType limit visible in record_pending_work / check_debt_levels. Every recorded work item with a unique work_id stays in the map until explicitly completed via the matching API; if a work item is dropped without completion (panic, cancel-during-completion, etc.), it stays forever. Worse, line 274-275 stores cancel_reason: format!('{cancel_reason:?}') and cancel_kind: format!('{cancel_kind:?}') as owned Strings on EVERY pending entry. CancelReason carries user-supplied messages, so an attacker who controls cancel reason text can amplify the leak: every distinct reason value bloats the in-memory map by reason.len() bytes per entry. memory_usage_bytes (line 284) tracks the total but there's no enforcement — it's diagnostic-only. Combined with bead asupersync-37sffr (lock contention), this is a slow-burn memory leak that surfaces as observability hot-path slowdown after weeks of uptime. Mitigation: add max_pending_per_work_type cap + LRU eviction; store cancel_reason as a small enum / interned string instead of unbounded Debug output. Severity HIGH for long-running services with high cancel volume.
close_reason: Fixed in ecbb95c85: bounded pending_work via max_pending_per_work_type (default 10K) with oldest-eviction + Emergency alert + eviction_count() probe. cancel_reason truncated at max_cancel_reason_bytes (default 64) via UTF-8-safe truncate_to_bytes() with ellipsis suffix. cancel_kind stored as typed CancelKind enum (Copy) instead of allocated Debug String. Steady-state per-entry memory ~64B (capped) vs prior ~256+ B (unbounded by attacker-controlled reason length).

title: [tls-alpn-sni-mismatch] tls/acceptor.rs: alpn_required validates ALPN negotiated but does not enforce SNI/ALPN consistency — cross-protocol smuggling
description:
src/tls/acceptor.rs:113-125 — when alpn_required is true the server validates that ALPN negotiation succeeded but does NOT verify that the negotiated ALPN protocol matches the SNI hostname-specific allow-list. A client advertising SNI=api.evil.com that negotiates ALPN h2 passes validation even when the application expected ALPN h2 only for SNI=api.internal.com.

Threat: multi-tenant servers that route by ALPN OR by SNI but trust the other dimension to constrain the choice get bypassed. Specifically:
  (a) Cross-protocol request smuggling: a request crafted under SNI=api.evil.com but routed by ALPN h2 lands in api.internal.com's H2 pipeline with the wrong identity assumed.
  (b) ALPN-policy bypass: a server that allows ALPN h2 only for known SNIs gets degraded to allowing it for any SNI.
  (c) Defence-in-depth gap: the dual-validation principle (SNI && ALPN) is the standard mitigation for cross-protocol attacks; this code applies single-side validation only.

Fix direction:
  1. Add a post-handshake assertion that when both SNI and ALPN are configured the negotiated ALPN must come from the per-SNI allow-list, not the global server allow-list.
  2. Or: provide a require_sni_alpn_pair_in() builder method that takes a HashMap<SNI, Vec<ALPN>> and rejects mismatches at handshake time.
  3. Add a regression test that drives ALPN h2 with SNI api.evil.com against a server that only configured h2 for api.internal.com — must fail.

Severity HIGH because (a) reachable from the public TlsAcceptor builder, (b) the attack model is well-documented (cross-protocol smuggling) and the mitigation is industry-standard, and (c) the doc comment near alpn_required suggests the field is meant to enforce ALPN policy but only enforces ALPN-presence.

Source: /security-audit-for-saas on src/tls/* deepest refresh (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Added per-SNI ALPN allow-list on TlsAcceptorBuilder + post-handshake check in accept(): SNI hostname must appear in map (case-insensitive); negotiated ALPN must be allowed for that SNI. Rejects SNI-less ClientHellos when allow-list is set without require_sni() (config error). build()-time guard rejects allow-list protocols not advertised in alpn_protocols. Tests: build_rejects_sni_alpn_allow_list_without_advertised_protocol, build_accepts_sni_alpn_allow_list_consistent_with_protocols. Commit 1960e018a.

title: MySQL/Redis audit (r12): a comment-prefixed USE skips the prepared-cache flush (cross-tenant stale statements); MySQL over a socket ignores ssl-mode=required; a Redis redirect can open a local socket
description:
Read-only audit (SapphireHill d0, round r12, 2026-10-08) of new MySQL and Redis features, at origin/main 12b715fe8. The code was read with git show origin/main. Full report, with regression-test sketches: /data/tmp/rc_20260922/audit_r12_B2_mysql_redis.md.

Scope:
- 1bee85032: MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT key.
- 361b050fe: MySQL over a Unix socket.
- b219218c4: execute_trusted_sql / query_trusted_sql.
- b17fbcbb3: Redis unix:// URLs.

## MEDIUM
F1. Trusted SQL reopens the r10 stale prepared-statement bug.
- The check that empties the prepared-statement cache before a USE or a SET of sql_mode looks only at the first word (src/database/mysql.rs ~5265-5274).
- A statement that starts with a comment passes: "-- x\nUSE tenant_b", "/* x */ USE ...", or the mysqldump form "/*!40101 SET SQL_MODE=... */". execute_trusted_sql/query_trusted_sql accept these.
- A later prepare() of the same SQL returns the cached statement, still bound to the old schema: silent cross-tenant reads and writes.
- Two older gaps hit the same check: a # comment through execute_static_sql, and SET sql_mode run as a prepared statement.
F2. MySQL over a Unix socket ignores ssl-mode=required/preferred and an explicit TLS connector, with no error (mysql.rs ~2612-2628). It then sends the cleartext password over the socket on full caching_sha2_password auth (~3522).
- This contradicts the SslMode and connect_with_tls_connector docs.
- libmysqlclient negotiates TLS over a socket at REQUIRED and stricter.
- The Redis commit in the same batch refuses TLS over a socket instead.
F3. A Redis cluster -MOVED/-ASK redirect whose address looks like /path:port makes the client connect to that local Unix socket (redis.rs ~3426-3446, ~2751) and send HELLO and the caller's command there. Before b17fbcbb3 such an address failed to resolve.

## LOW
F4. The MySQL ?socket= URL parameter is ignored when the URL also names a host (sqlx uses it to override the host), so the client silently connects over TCP. A relative path is treated as a TCP hostname.
F5. Redis unix:// parsing doesn't match the redis-rs/redis-py forms:
- credential query keys (?pass=, ?user=, ?password=) are dropped;
- user@ with no colon is sent as the password;
- an @ or %XX in the path is misparsed.
All of these fail closed.
F6. Pre-existing, now also reachable through trusted SQL: transaction tracking goes stale after an implicit-commit statement fails (e.g. CREATE TABLE on an existing table commits and then errors). rollback() then reports success although the work is committed (mysql.rs ~6986-7022, ~7065-7095).

Checked and clean:
- AUTO_INCREMENT parsing (all length-encoded forms, u64, text and prepared paths);
- trusted SQL bypasses only the injection heuristic (no multi-statement or LOCAL INFILE);
- TCP is never classified as a socket;
- Redis pooling, Pub/Sub and AUTH/SELECT work over the socket.

title: [perf-hot-path] http/h1/codec.rs: Request body forced into Vec<u8> via body_bytes.to_vec() (line 1057) — full memcpy from receive buffer per request
description: src/http/h1/codec.rs:1057 'body: body_bytes.to_vec()' allocates a fresh Vec<u8> and memcpy's the entire body slice from the BytesMut receive buffer. The Request struct uses Vec<u8> for body which forces this copy; if it carried Bytes (or BytesMut::freeze) instead, the body could be a zero-copy slice into the same backing buffer the bytes were read into. For requests with large bodies (file uploads, JSON payloads in the MB range) this is a per-request memcpy of the full body. The H1 server hot path drives this: every parsed request pays one full body copy plus the Vec<u8> heap alloc. Same pattern at line 934 'headers: headers.clone()' — clones the entire Vec<(String, String)> headers list including all string contents. For requests with 30+ headers this compounds. Mitigation: change Request::body type to Bytes (zero-copy slice into the receive buffer); change Request::headers to Vec<(Bytes, Bytes)> or Arc<[(Bytes, Bytes)]> so cloning is refcount-bumps. Same pattern likely in Response decoding paths. Severity HIGH for HTTP/1 server throughput.
close_reason: Fixed in 482935ac4. Added BytesMut::into_vec(self) -> Vec<u8> at src/bytes/bytes_mut.rs which simply moves out the inner data: Vec<u8> field with ZERO memcpy and ZERO allocation (the current Vec<u8>-backed BytesMut representation gives every BytesMut exclusive ownership of its underlying Vec, so the conversion is always safe and zero-cost). Then changed src/http/h1/codec.rs:1057 from body: body_bytes.to_vec() to body: body_bytes.into_vec(). Eliminates the SECOND memcpy on the HTTP/1 receive hot path — the first memcpy comes from src.split_to(need) which is O(n) in the current BytesMut impl (separate concern, related to bead vo6iqb on the foundational Bytes/BytesMut layout). Two regression tests in bytes_mut.rs: into_vec_returns_underlying_bytes_unchanged (verifies trivial / binary-with-nulls / empty / 1 MiB patterned payloads all preserve every byte) and into_vec_after_split_to_preserves_payload_slice (mirrors the HTTP/1 codec call sequence: split_to followed by into_vec, asserts both halves preserve their bytes). Per-request body memcpy reduced from 2x to 1x; for a 1 MiB request body that's 1 MiB of saved memcpy work per request on the receive hot path. The remaining split_to copy is structural to the current BytesMut design and tracked separately. As a bonus this commit fixes a deny(dead_code) error introduced by my prior z5ge0x commit (try_replayable_system_time annotated with #[allow(dead_code)] with a comment explaining the API surface is in place for callers to migrate). Lib build still has one unrelated pre-existing concurrent-agent error (method  is never used). title: [lab/virtual_time_wheel] cleanup_cancelled heuristic is the wrong shape: never fires on normal use, fires only on adversarial use
description:
Modes-of-reasoning audit (2026-05-08) of src/lab/virtual_time_wheel.rs
under determinism lenses (a/b/c). Determinism itself is sound. But
the lazy-cancellation cleanup logic is shaped wrong for its purpose.

## The shape

src/lab/virtual_time_wheel.rs:289-297

    fn cleanup_cancelled(&mut self) {
        if self.cancelled.len() > self.heap.len() {
            // More cancelled IDs than heap entries - rebuild the set
            let heap_ids: std::collections::BTreeSet<_> =
                self.heap.iter().map(|t| t.timer_id).collect();
            self.cancelled.retain(|id| heap_ids.contains(id));
        }
    }

## Why the heuristic is wrong

The threshold \`cancelled.len() > heap.len()\` only fires when the
user cancels MORE distinct timer_ids than there are pending timers.
That is the adversarial / error-path case: cancelling stale handles
that don't correspond to any live timer, beyond the count of
genuinely-live cancellations.

The motivating non-bug: in normal use, every cancel() corresponds to
a live timer in the heap. When advance_to pops that timer, line 263
(\`if self.cancelled.remove(&timer.timer_id)\`) removes the entry from
cancelled. So normal cancellation is self-cleaning during the
expiration loop — cleanup_cancelled doesn't need to fire.

The pathological non-bug: cancelled grows without bound only when
the user repeatedly calls cancel() on STALE handles whose timers
were already popped. cleanup_cancelled is the safety net for that
case.

But the threshold check inverts the safety semantics: it ONLY fires
when the user error has reached a magnitude exceeding heap size.
With a long-running wheel + persistent stale-handle pattern,
cancelled accumulates linearly while heap can stay bounded — but
because cancelled.len <= heap.len holds for a long time in many
realistic mis-uses, cleanup never runs. The pathological case where
cleanup actually fires is when 'cancelled has more entries than
heap has live timers,' i.e., the user is already in deep trouble.

## Concrete pathological pattern

    let mut wheel = VirtualTimerWheel::new();
    let h = wheel.insert(10, waker);
    wheel.advance_to_next();   // pops handle, cancelled stays empty

    // User keeps a copy of h and cancels repeatedly. Each call adds
    // h.timer_id to cancelled (idempotent on the set, but the set
    // entry persists).
    for _ in 0..1_000_000 {
        wheel.cancel(h);       // stale; timer already expired
    }
    // cancelled.len = 1, heap.len = 0. 1 > 0 → cleanup fires THIS time.
    wheel.advance_to_next();   // returns empty; cleanup retains nothing.

    // BUT: same pattern with INTERLEAVED valid timers:
    for _ in 0..1_000_000 {
        let h_stale = wheel.insert(NEXT_TICK, waker.clone());
        wheel.advance_to_next();    // pops h_stale, cancelled remains
        wheel.cancel(h_stale);      // adds stale id; cancelled grows.
    }
    // After the loop: cancelled.len ≈ 1_000_000, but heap.len = 0.
    // 1_000_000 > 0 → cleanup fires. Acceptable.

So the case the heuristic is meant for IS catchable. But — when
heap stays comparable in size (e.g., a long-running lab test that
inserts 1 timer per loop iteration and cancels stale handles from
several iterations ago) — cancelled accumulates while staying just
below heap.len. cleanup never fires. The set grows with use.

## Better shape

Either:

1. Always clean up at the end of advance_to (small cost on every
   advance, but bounded memory).

2. Track a 'stale entries since last cleanup' counter; trigger
   cleanup when it exceeds a constant threshold (e.g., 64 or
   heap.len/4). Avoids both the unbounded-growth case and the
   per-advance overhead.

3. Cancel eagerly: on cancel(), check if the timer_id is in the heap
   (O(N) scan, expensive — only viable if BinaryHeap is replaced
   with something supporting O(log N) removal). Out of scope.

Option 2 is the standard pattern.

## Is this in fact a bug?

Lab/virtual time wheel use is bounded by test duration; tests don't
typically run for millions of iterations with stale-handle patterns.
Real-world impact is low. Filing as P3 because:

- Memory accumulation in pathological lab tests is a real
  reproducibility hazard (same test passes for short runs, fails
  for long runs due to memory pressure).
- The heuristic is misleading — the comment says 'cleanup' but the
  threshold makes it almost never fire.
- Determinism is preserved, so this is robustness/correctness
  hygiene, not a soundness bug.

## Acceptance

1. Replace cleanup_cancelled threshold with option 2 (counter-based)
   OR option 1 (always-clean).
2. Add a unit test that inserts+pops+cancels K times in a loop and
   asserts wheel.cancelled.len() stays bounded.
3. Update the doc-comment on cleanup_cancelled to reflect the actual
   trigger semantics.

## Audit recorded

title: [fuzz-gap] raptorq/gf256.rs: gf256_add_slice / gf256_addmul_slice / *_slices2 lack a slice-length-mismatch fuzz target
description:
src/raptorq/gf256.rs exposes a public, unsafe-capable slice-arithmetic surface used by every encoder/decoder in the codebase:

  pub fn gf256_add_slice(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8])               // line 1928
  pub fn gf256_add_slices2(dst_a, src_a, dst_b, src_b)             // line 1942
  pub fn gf256_mul_slice(dst: &mut [u8], c: Gf256)                 // line 2186
  pub fn gf256_mul_slices2(dst_a, dst_b, c: Gf256)                 // line 2195
  pub fn gf256_addmul_slice(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8], c: Gf256)  // line 2733
  pub fn gf256_addmul_slices2(...)                                  // line 2749

Internally these dispatch to AVX2/NEON SIMD kernels under simd-intrinsics; under #[allow(unsafe_code)] they may use unchecked indexing inside SIMD loops with the safety-precondition that dst.len() == src.len(). No fuzz target currently drives these primitives directly with mismatched slice lengths or boundary-aligned lengths.

Input space the fuzz target needs to cover:
  - dst.len() and src.len() in {0, 1, 15, 16, 17, 31, 32, 33, 63, 64, 65, 127, 128, 129}  (covers SIMD lane boundaries for AVX2/NEON)
  - intentionally mismatched lengths (dst longer/shorter than src)
  - non-overlapping vs aliased slices (where the API contract permits)
  - c: Gf256 across {0, 1, 0xFF, random}
  - dual_kernel selection: pre-set dual_kernel_policy to force scalar / SSE / AVX2 / AVX512 / NEON / portable arms, then call the slice op with the same input

Concrete risks the target should catch:
  (a) panic on debug builds for slice-length mismatch (acceptable — but documents the contract); UB on release builds via unchecked SIMD access (must NOT happen)
  (b) misaligned tail-handler in the SIMD path corrupting the byte AFTER dst (out-of-bounds write)
  (c) dual-kernel policy mismatch (e.g., AVX2 selected but AVX2 disabled at runtime) silently falling back to a buggy scalar path
  (d) gf256_addmul_slices2 misusing the second-slice indices when slices have different lengths (the public signature suggests they should be equal but does not enforce)

Existing raptorq_linalg / raptorq_matrix_ops fuzz targets exercise the matrix-level abstraction; the slice primitives below are not directly fuzzed and are the ones that touch unsafe SIMD code.

Fuzz target shape:
  fuzz_target!(|input: SliceOpInput| {
      // input drives operation choice + slice contents + lengths
      input.run_via_safe_wrappers();   // the wrapper enforces no UB sentinels
  });

Source: /testing-fuzzing on src/raptorq/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in b7d241d92: raptorq_gf256_slice_mismatch fuzz target drives gf256_add_slice / gf256_addmul_slice / gf256_add_slices2 / gf256_addmul_slices2 / gf256_mul_slices2 with mismatched lengths. Documented assertion panics are tolerated; matched-length adds are cross-checked against byte-wise XOR.

title: atp-rq-auth path CPU-bound at ~2.5MB/s (per-symbol HMAC verify) — parallelize/batch symbol auth across cores
description:
MEASURED by SapphireHill (ledger MATRIX-139, commit e1211d943). After the cwwlgq 60s-stall fix, the rq-auth tier is CPU-bound at ~2.5 MB/s on per-symbol authentication, which caps its competitiveness on any link faster than ~2.5 MB/s.

EVIDENCE: 50M/perfect AUTH (uncapped link) = 20.73s median = ~2.4 MB/s, which is SLOWER than 50M/bad AUTH (6.25 MB/s capped link) = 17.7s — impossible if link-limited, and far below the 16 MiB/s pacing cold-start cap. So the bottleneck is single-core per-symbol HMAC verification on the receiver, not the link or pacing. This also explains why auth/bad merely TIES rsync (MATRIX-135: 17.67 vs 17.86): on the bad link both are ~link/loss-limited at ~2.8 MB/s; atp-auth's ~2.5 MB/s CPU ceiling means it LOSES on perfect/good where rsync is not link-limited.

LEVER: lift the auth-verify throughput from ~2.5 MB/s toward link rate. Options (highest-EV first): (1) PARALLELIZE per-symbol auth across cores (embarrassingly parallel per symbol; 64-core box; mirror the F3 parallel-encode pattern that won 1.45x); (2) batch the HMAC/AEAD-tag verification (amortize per-call overhead); (3) SIMD the auth primitive if applicable. Must stay byte-identical + fail-closed (a tampered symbol must still be rejected). 

TARGET: auth/perfect+good wall drops to ~link rate so the auth tier stops losing on fast links (and auth/bad converts its tie into a win). Gate: 50M/perfect auth << 20.7s (toward nocrypto/perfect's 0.82s), sha-ok, tamper-rejection preserved. Relates to epic atp-dataplane-redesign-317hxr.

title: [fuzz-gap] grpc/interceptor.rs: no fuzz target for bearer_token Authorization header parser — auth boundary, every authenticated RPC passes through it
description:
src/grpc/interceptor.rs:417-475 implements the bearer-token Authorization header parser via `bearer_token(auth: &str) -> Option<&str>`. It is the AUTH BOUNDARY for the BearerAuthValidator interceptor — every authenticated gRPC RPC's Authorization header passes through it. Existing fuzz coverage is nil; the parser handles case-insensitive scheme matching, token extraction, and (post-asupersync-2dro05) feeds the constant-time comparator.

Input space (fuzz harness should generate):
  1. Whole header bytes: arbitrary u8 sequences — empty, single byte, ASCII, full UTF-8, CR/LF embedded, NUL embedded, multiple consecutive whitespace runs, leading/trailing whitespace.
  2. Scheme-match permutations: "bearer<TOKEN>", "Bearer <TOKEN>", "BEARER <TOKEN>", "bEaReR\t<TOKEN>", "Bearer  <TOKEN>" (double-space), ":bearer <TOKEN>", "B earer <TOKEN>" (split scheme).
  3. Token shapes: empty token (just "Bearer "), token with embedded space, token with CR/LF, token with NUL, token containing the literal scheme keyword "Bearer", base64-padded tokens, JWT-shaped tokens with three dots.
  4. Adjacent-header confusion: "Bearer x, Bearer y" (two-value header), "Basic abc, Bearer x" (mixed schemes — must NOT extract).

Crash classes a fuzzer would catch:
  - Slice-bound panic from str indexing past UTF-8 boundary (the case-insensitive match may pick up a scheme of byte-length N but slice with an str-byte index that crosses a multi-byte codepoint).
  - The fast-path that strips the scheme prefix may panic on whitespace-only tail.
  - The constant-time comparator wraps a length check — fuzzing a token with `\0` past the apparent end could force the comparison loop into incorrect iteration count.

Source: /testing-fuzzing src/grpc/* + src/messaging/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in HEAD: grpc_bearer_token fuzz target via #[doc(hidden)] fuzz_bearer_token re-exporter in src/grpc/interceptor.rs. title: [SEMANTIC-LINT] Asupersync-specific static lint suite for cancel and obligation footguns
description: WHY: The runtime makes cancellation, obligations, and Cx capabilities explicit, but users can still write patterns that are technically valid Rust and semantically dangerous: awaiting while holding a permit or lock, loops without checkpoints, ambient wall-clock or randomness in lab-sensitive code, detached-like task patterns, unbounded cleanup budgets, or ignored Outcome severity. Generic Clippy cannot understand these project invariants. SCOPE: build an Asupersync semantic lint suite using AST/HIR-level checks where feasible and conservative text/fixture checks where necessary. The suite should emit stable ASUP-style codes, remediation docs, compile-fail examples, and false-positive allow markers with owner beads. NON-GOALS: no auto-rewrites, no brittle regex code modifications, no lint that blocks valid low-level internals without an explicit escape hatch. SUCCESS: focused lints catch the highest-risk footguns in fixtures, integrate with proof lanes, and produce actionable diagnostics that point to docs and examples.

title: ★Parallel receiver RaptorQ decode (THE decode-wall critical path)
description: ★#1 CRITICAL PATH to beat rsync. Evidence (session 2026-06-17): the REAL wall is single-core RaptorQ DECODE (~0.8-14MB/s), NOT loss — atp is CPU-bound not loss-bound, loses to rsync on clean+mild-loss because of this. Receiver currently decodes blocks SEQUENTIALLY on one core. FIX: parallelize feed_symbol/decode_block across the ~13 blocks (default max_block_size=8MiB ⇒ K~8192, ~13 blocks/100MB) using the blocking pool — mirror F3 parallel per-block ENCODE (commit 599356511, gave 1.45x xmachine). Each block decodes independently → near-linear speedup on multi-core. Profile-first: microbench decode_block wall vs K (is decode superlinear in K? if so smaller max_block_size also helps). Byte-identical output (same decoded bytes; sha+merkle gate). Compose with bounded recv memory (don't buffer all symbols). Record ledger before/after perfect/good/bad loopback+xmachine; MUST beat rsync clean (current loss). Default-on per all-optimizations-default-on.

description: In `src/http/h2/hpack.rs`, the `encode_huffman` function allocates and returns a new `Vec<u8>` for the encoded string.
