title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Trace ring: four lifecycle records per task under one global mutex; make recording contention-free
description:
## Why
Each spawned task writes about four trace records (TaskSpawnEnqueued at spawn_mailbox.rs ~1671-1676; Spawn
and TaskAdmitted at state.rs ~974/~1038; Complete at completion) into the instrumentation ring
(src/trace/buffer.rs ~246-254), a 4096-slot buffer behind a single `parking_lot::Mutex`. All workers contend on
that mutex for every task lifecycle event. The only production knob is the TraceStorageProfile
(Default/LargeMemory; runtime/config.rs ~598-640); there is no way to keep the ring off the hot path.

## Work
1. Confirm who reads the production ring (crashpacks, debug server, diagnostics APIs) and whether ordering
   across workers is part of any documented behavior. The LabRuntime's deterministic trace must not change.
2. Behavior-preserving option A: per-worker rings (no cross-worker contention), merged by sequence number on
   read; the global sequence comes from one `fetch_add` (already cheaper than a mutex).
3. Option B (additive, owner-visible): a `TraceStorageProfile` variant that records only non-lifecycle events
   in production. Default stays as today unless the owner approves a change.
Pick A unless reading shows a hard cross-worker ordering contract; record the choice.

## Tests
Trace/crashpack tests and lab replay determinism goldens green; new native test with 8 workers spawning 50k
tasks asserting every lifecycle record is present exactly once and sequence numbers are strictly increasing
after merge.

## Measurement
spawn_join rows vs tokio before/after (8-worker variant especially).

## Done when
No global mutex on per-task trace recording (or the owner-approved alternative), tests green, ratios
recorded.

- TraceBufferHandle::push_event is 2.0% self time;
- parking_lot RawMutex::lock_slow does not appear (no caller samples).
So the global trace-ring mutex is not contended on this path, and moving to per-worker rings would recover about 2% at most. This bead is low priority compared with the allocation and memmove costs; see .1.9. Sample count was modest (about 300 samples per profile), so this rules out a large cost, not a small one.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Local wake fast path: a task woken on its own worker goes to that worker's queue, not the global injector
description:
## Why
`ThreeLaneWaker::schedule` (three_lane.rs ~8840-8870) always does `self.global.inject_ready(...)` (or
`inject_cancel`) followed by `self.coordinator.wake_one()`, regardless of which thread performs the wake. In
the very common pattern "task A sends on a channel, task B on the same worker becomes ready" this pays a
shared-queue push, a cross-worker unpark, and cache misses. tokio routes a wake from the current worker into
its local run queue (with a LIFO slot for the most recently woken task) and only uses the injector for wakes
from outside the runtime. This is the largest remaining structural difference after the lock/allocation fixes.

## Fix (riskier; do after the dispatch-lock, next_task audit and region-set beads)
- In `schedule()`, if the current thread is a worker of THIS runtime (thread-local worker context already
  exists for owner-pinned locals; reuse it), push to that worker's local ready queue and skip `wake_one`
  unless that worker is parked. Otherwise keep today's path.
- Preserve cancel-lane priority: cancelling tasks still route to the cancel lane (local cancel lane if one
  exists, else global).
- Preserve `!Send` local-task pinning rules (local tasks must stay on their owner worker; never move them).
- Starvation guard: if a LIFO slot is used, cap consecutive LIFO pops (tokio uses 3) and keep the existing
  `cancel_streak_limit` fairness accounting.
- LabRuntime is unaffected (it does not use ThreeLaneWaker); assert that explicitly in a test.

## Tests
three_lane_tests, work-stealing fairness metamorphic tests, priority inversion oracle, native parked-task
cancellation lane, golden_outputs. New native tests: ping-pong between two tasks on a 1-worker and 4-worker
runtime completes and records local wake counts; a task hogging LIFO cannot starve the injector (bounded
wait); a woken `!Send` local task never runs on another worker.

## Measurement

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Default-on UCB1 cancel-preemption controller: measure its benefit and stop it taking the global lock every epoch
description:
## Why
The README headline table advertises "Adaptive preemption fairness: default-on discounted UCB1 policy". It is
on by default (runtime/config.rs ~2236), runs per worker every 128 dispatches, and at each epoch
`capture_adaptive_snapshot` (three_lane.rs ~4955-4975) locks the global RuntimeState (and possibly the task
table) to compute a Lyapunov snapshot. The only benchmark (benches/scheduler_benchmark.rs ~2048) measures
policy OVERHEAD, never benefit over the fixed `cancel_streak_limit = 16`. LabRuntime uses a fixed 16, so lab
replay does not exercise it (asupersync-gap-ucb1-lab-replay-my2vov). Nobody has shown it earns its cost.

## Work
1. Make the epoch snapshot lock-free: read the counters it needs from atomics the scheduler already
   maintains (or add relaxed counters), no RuntimeState lock. Behavior identical (same arm choices on the same
   inputs; the golden `golden_test_lab_runtime_replay_determinism` in three_lane_tests.rs replays it).
2. Benefit measurement in the same invocation: cancel-heavy workloads (benches/cancel_storm.rs,
   cancel_drain_bench.rs) and the head-to-head suite with adaptive ON vs a fixed limit of 16 (builder
   config toggle), reporting cancel-drain latency, ready-lane fairness (max wait), and throughput.
3. Report to the owner: keep default-on (if it wins somewhere and never loses), or propose default-off (a
   documented-behavior change; needs explicit approval). Do not flip without approval.

## Tests
Existing UCB1/adaptive tests and replay golden green after step 1.

## Done when
No global lock in the epoch path; measured benefit table recorded in a comment; owner decision recorded.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
OWNER DECISION (delegated), recorded 2026-10-02 by SapphireHill.

The owner wrote, verbatim: "and for this stuff, please YOU decide the optimal, smartest way to handle it that doesn't compromise the ambition of the project or its goals". This covered the list item "Production defaults: whether the scheduler monitors, epoch tracker, UCB1 and blocking pool keep their current defaults".

Decisions:
- **Verification-only machinery stays on in tests and debug builds and goes off in release production builds:**
  - the scheduler FairnessMonitor and SchedulerInvariantMonitor;
  - the runtime-state EpochConsistencyTracker (also kept on with `tracing-integration`, which is the only way its receipts reach anyone);
  - the CancelProtocolValidator.

  Rationale: nothing in the runtime acts on their output, but in release builds they cost locks, map updates, clock reads and allocations on every spawn, enqueue and completion. The fairness map also degrades to an O(10,000) scan per enqueue once stolen tasks fill it. The lab runtime keeps its own oracles, unaffected.
- **UCB1 is evidence-gated.** The epoch snapshot must stop taking the global lock in any case. UCB1 stays default-on only if it beats a fixed limit of 16 on cancel-heavy benches without losing anywhere else; otherwise the default becomes a fixed 16, which is also what the lab runs.
- **A bare RuntimeBuilder gets an on-demand blocking pool:** zero threads until first use, small cap. This matches what `#[main]` already configures. `blocking_threads(0, 0)` stays available as an explicit opt-out.

- It is slower on spawn+join, yield and ping-pong: 23-29% on hz3, 1-16% on hz4. Spawn from four producers is within noise.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Publish honest asupersync-vs-tokio numbers in the README (win or lose)
description:
## Why
The README has a "How We Made It Fast" section that lists optimizations but no comparison against the runtime
everyone actually compares to, and the "How Asupersync Compares" table (README ~480-503) compares only against
async-std and smol, omitting tokio. Critics concluded the runtime is too expensive for servers; the honest
answer is a measured table, whatever it shows.

## Work
After the P1 perf levers in this epic land (dispatch lock, next_task audit, region set, monitors, epoch
tracker; others as they land), run the head-to-head suite on two different RCH hosts at the same commit and
publish in README:
- A "Performance vs tokio" table: row, asupersync p50, tokio p50, ratio, host class, date, commit.
- A plain-English reading: where asupersync is slower and why (structured-concurrency bookkeeping it does and
  tokio does not), and where it is comparable.
- Replace or qualify any README perf sentence that the numbers contradict (e.g. "This runtime got fast
  through...").
- Add a tokio column to "How Asupersync Compares" (see the README plain-English bead; coordinate so only one
  of them edits that table).
Keep the README-reading tests green (see the README marker inventory bead).

## Done when
README shows the table with receipts (commit, command, hosts) in the bead comment; no unmeasured performance
claims remain in README.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Server-shaped benchmark: loopback TCP request/response and HTTP/1.1 throughput + p99
description:
## Why
The critic's claim is specifically "does not fit servers". Spawn microbenchmarks are necessary but not
sufficient; servers are dominated by accept, per-connection task spawn, readiness I/O, and small writes. The
repo has no requests/sec or latency-percentile measurement anywhere (benches/reactor_benchmark.rs has a TCP
echo latency bench with no recorded results; protocol_benchmark.rs is parsing-only). A downstream project
(midas_edge_api/Cargo.toml ~113) notes the asupersync HTTP client "hangs during outbound nonblocking connect
under the server runtime" and uses ureq instead; a server bench may also surface such issues.

## Work
Add to the head-to-head suite (or a sibling bench target with the same rules):
1. `tcp_rr/{1,64}`: loopback; server task per connection echoing 64-byte requests; client tasks issue
   request/response round trips for a fixed count; asupersync TcpListener/TcpStream vs tokio::net (enable the
   tokio dev-dependency features "net" and "io-util"; check the dependency budget contract first).
   Report throughput and p50/p99 latency (HDR-style histogram computed in-bench; no new dependency if a
   simple sorted-sample percentile suffices).
2. `http1_hello/{64}`: asupersync's H1 server (src/http/h1 / web Router) answering GET / with a fixed body,
   driven by an in-process keep-alive client over loopback; absolute req/s and p99. A hyper comparison is
   desirable but only if it can be done without adding hyper to the dependency graph beyond what
   asupersync-tokio-compat already pulls; otherwise record absolute numbers only and say so.
3. Run under RCH on one host; record numbers in a bead comment and feed the README table bead.

## Done when
Bench lands, runs, numbers recorded; any functional failure found (hang, error) filed as its own bug bead.
close_reason: Both items landed (tcp_rr earlier; http1_hello 08bcd77ba in 43155708a); numbers recorded; no functional bug (421 = default host policy by design, docs fixed in 97341363d). Self-verified close.

What the bench does:
- tcp_rr/{1,64} opens that many loopback connections. Each connection gets a server echo task and a client task, and each client makes 200 round trips of a 64-byte request. Connection setup is not timed, and TCP_NODELAY is set on both sides.
- asupersync runs TcpListener/TcpStream through Cx::spawn on the default runtime, which uses the platform reactor. tokio runs tokio::net on a 4-worker runtime with enable_io (tokio_multi_io).
- Criterion reports throughput. p50/p99 come from 10 recorded batches per row and print as "tcp_rr latency ..." lines when the filter selects tcp_rr.
- Cargo.toml: tokio's dev features gain net and io-util. Cargo.lock is unchanged. On the 64 Cargo.toml-reading test targets, origin and the candidate give identical results.

Numbers. Run on vmi1149989, base 22063e1a8 (same bench code), remote exit 0. This is the in-repo feature set (conformance dev-dep features unified), not production defaults.

| tcp_rr/64 | 54.5K/s, p50 547 us, p99 15.8 ms | 40.8K/s, p50 614 us, p99 20.4 ms | 1.34x |

Criterion medians: tcp_rr/1 4.359 ms vs 8.661 ms per 200 round trips; tcp_rr/64 234.8 ms vs 313.7 ms per 12,800.

Reading:
- No hang or error on either runtime. No functional bug to file.
- On a steady-state request/response path, asupersync is 1.3-2x tokio's throughput cost. The spawn+join microbenchmarks show 8-33x, and this path does not spawn per request.
- The single-connection p99 (264 us vs 57 us) is the weakest number and is worth profiling.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Server footgun: a bare RuntimeBuilder has no blocking pool, so fs I/O runs inline on async workers
description:
## Why
README (tokio mapping table) states a bare `RuntimeBuilder::new()` ships `blocking_threads(0, 0)`; with no
pool, `spawn_blocking_io` runs the closure inline on the async worker (runtime/spawn_blocking.rs ~576-600:
"A context without a pool runs the closure inline"). `File::open`, `fs::*` helpers and other blocking-backed
facades therefore block a scheduler worker for the duration of the syscall in any server built from a bare
builder. `#[main]`/`#[test]` configure a pool on demand, so only builder users are affected. Changing the
default is a documented-behavior change (owner approval required).

## Work (additive)
1. Ensure the server-oriented presets (`RuntimeBuilder::multi_thread()` documented as equivalent to new();
   check the "high-throughput server" preset in builder.rs ~3680) configure a non-zero blocking pool; if a
   preset is documented to have none, leave it and add a new preset instead.
2. Emit one diagnostic (trace event, plus an ASUP error-code warning only if the registry rules allow a
   warning-class code) the first time blocking I/O runs inline on an async worker of a multi-thread runtime.
3. README/rustdoc: state the inline behavior next to RuntimeBuilder::new and File::open.
4. Owner decision recorded: should `RuntimeBuilder::new()` get a small default pool? Do not change without
   approval.

## Tests
Native test: multi-thread runtime without pool performs File::open and observes the diagnostic exactly once;
with the preset, the work runs on a pool thread (assert thread identity differs from the worker).

## Done when
Preset/diagnostic/docs landed, owner decision recorded.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
OWNER DECISION (delegated), recorded 2026-10-02 by SapphireHill.

The owner wrote, verbatim: "and for this stuff, please YOU decide the optimal, smartest way to handle it that doesn't compromise the ambition of the project or its goals". This covered the list item "Production defaults: whether the scheduler monitors, epoch tracker, UCB1 and blocking pool keep their current defaults".

Decisions:
- **Verification-only machinery stays on in tests and debug builds and goes off in release production builds:**
  - the scheduler FairnessMonitor and SchedulerInvariantMonitor;
  - the runtime-state EpochConsistencyTracker (also kept on with `tracing-integration`, which is the only way its receipts reach anyone);
  - the CancelProtocolValidator.

  Rationale: nothing in the runtime acts on their output, but in release builds they cost locks, map updates, clock reads and allocations on every spawn, enqueue and completion. The fairness map also degrades to an O(10,000) scan per enqueue once stolen tasks fill it. The lab runtime keeps its own oracles, unaffected.
- **UCB1 is evidence-gated.** The epoch snapshot must stop taking the global lock in any case. UCB1 stays default-on only if it beats a fixed limit of 16 on cancel-heavy benches without losing anywhere else; otherwise the default becomes a fixed 16, which is also what the lab runs.
- **A bare RuntimeBuilder gets an on-demand blocking pool:** zero threads until first use, small cap. This matches what `#[main]` already configures. `blocking_threads(0, 0)` stays available as an explicit opt-out.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-03: HELD. The default-pool change was implemented and tested, and it is not landing. Here is why.

Staged change (candidate B6 83e198987; full tree C14 dc016293d):
- RuntimeBuilder::new() starts with blocking_threads(0, 512);
- #[main(blocking = 0)] emits blocking_threads(0, 0);
- docs, CHANGELOG, and a positive/planted-negative test pair for offload and placement.
All of its own tests passed, and clippy all-targets was clean.

What the full-tree lane found: several components read the PRESENCE of a pool as a capability or sizing signal, so a default pool changes their behavior. In detail:
1. ATP RaptorQ (net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs).
   - rq_decode_core_limit_for_cx (~7992) takes pool.current_max_threads() as the decode core limit, which is 512 under the default. The parallel round-0 encode (~9740) and auth-verify width (~15484) switch on when a pool exists.
   - tests/atp_rq_loopback_e2e.rs::loss_injection_recovers_via_repair_symbols, with both runtimes built by bare RuntimeBuilder::multi_thread():
     - origin ff3798158: 0 of 20 runs fail;
     - C14: 18 of 20 fail, all with the sender error "Connection refused (os error 111)" during send under 1/7 symbol loss.
   - A diagnostic probe comparing pool and no pool on the same tree is running (3a5dc5133).
   - The likely reading is that ATP's parallel path does not survive loss recovery. If so, ATP runtimes that size a pool explicitly (the CLI and daemon) would hit the same failure under real loss. That is worth its own bead once the diagnostic confirms it.
2. PressureGovernor: the blocking-pool signal becomes available, so pressure_governor_records_partial_fallback_and_decision_latency sees a different fallback verdict.
3. Durable membership and symbol services stop refusing work (intended), and drained_blocking_native's "missing pool" case needs an explicit opt-out.

Decision: hold B6. The default must not change until:
- ATP sizes parallelism by real cores (min(pool cap, available cores)) and its parallel path passes loss injection;
- every other pool-presence branch has been audited for the same assumption.
v0.4.3 compatibility is a hard gate, and a default that changes ATP's data-plane execution shape for every bare-builder user fails it today.

The deadline-monitor fix that was staged with B6 (asupersync-2zubyr) is independent and lands without it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-03, diagnosis of the ATP failure noted above (probe 3a5dc5133 on C14):
- with a pool, 7 of 8 runs report "Connection refused" on the sender while the receiver COMMITS (115 symbols accepted);
- without a pool, 0 of 8.
The transfer succeeds and the sender reports a false failure. Its parallel path keeps spraying UDP after the receiver closes its socket, and it treats ECONNREFUSED as fatal. Filed as asupersync-fjg6ng (P1), which now blocks this bead: the default pool must not land while ATP misreports under a pool.

SapphireHill 2026-10-04, data point: the flagship examples/production_service.rs hit this footgun.
- It built its runtime with RuntimeBuilder::new().worker_threads(2), which has no blocking pool, so GET /users ran its SQLite open, seed and query inline on an async worker.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-04: still HELD; a finding for whoever retries B6.

fjg6ng (the ATP sender misreport under a pool) was fixed on 10-03. What remains is the sizing signal. ATP reads pool.current_max_threads() as CPU parallelism in three places:
- rq_decode_core_limit_for_cx: transport_rq/mod.rs ~8011;
- the parallel encode width: ~9769;
- packet_unprotect_parallel_width_for_cx: quic/packet_protection.rs ~196.

The ATP CLI and atpd size their pools from host parallelism: bin/atp.rs build_runtime clamps available_parallelism to [workers, 64], and atpd_live uses workers. The #[main]/#[test] expansion, however, already configures blocking_threads(0, 512) today (asupersync-macros/src/entry.rs DEFAULT_BLOCKING_THREADS).

So any #[main] program that runs ATP already fans RaptorQ decode out 64 wide (the RQ_MAX_PENDING_DECODE_JOBS_PER_TRANSFER_HARD cap). Unprotect can fan out up to 512 minus busy chunks. Both are independent of the host's core count. A B6 default would extend this to bare-builder users.

Retry plan:
- give CPU-bound fan-out one helper that bounds width by min(pool max, a cores estimate);
- keep the CLI's "explicit pool size wins" behavior for pools that are sized explicitly.

That helper touches ATP transport files where four agents hold in-progress beads, so I am not starting it now.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] mpsc one-call send: stop registering a runtime obligation for the internal permit it commits in the same poll
description:
## What

`mpsc::Sender::send` (the one-call convenience path) currently runs the same `Reserve` future as the explicit two-phase `reserve()`, so every message registers a `SendPermit` runtime obligation through the obligation gateway (`Cx::try_register_obligation`) and then commits it a few instructions later. Each message therefore costs two obligation-mailbox posts, each applied by a worker under the runtime state lock, for an obligation that can never leak.

## Why the obligation can never leak in `send`

`send` awaits the reserve, and registration happens only in the poll that grants capacity (`Reserve::poll_with_registration`). The returned permit is consumed by `permit.try_send(value)` in that same poll, with no `.await` in between. Cancellation of `send` while it waits for capacity happens before any permit exists. So the `send` path has no window in which an obligation is outstanding across a suspension point, and no cancellation point between "permit granted" and "permit committed". The obligation tracking adds pure overhead there.

Explicit `reserve()` / `reserve_checked()` permits are handed to user code, which may hold them across awaits, forget them, or be cancelled. They MUST stay tracked, and this change keeps them tracked exactly as before.

## Change

- Add a private `TransientReserve` wrapper in `src/channel/mpsc.rs`. It polls `Reserve::poll_with_registration(ctx, |_| Ok(None))`, giving identical channel semantics (FIFO waiter queue, capacity, cancellation, disconnect, waker handoff) but no runtime registration.
- `Sender::send` uses it. Nothing else changes.
- `try_send`, `try_reserve` and `UnboundedSender::send` never registered obligations. `reserve`, `reserve_checked` and every other channel are unchanged.

## Observable differences (audited 2026-10-02 against origin/main 2ad2e55c8)

- Exact obligation counts for a workload that uses one-call `send` on a runtime `Cx` drop by one reserve/commit pair per message. Leak, quiescence and balance invariants (`pending_obligation_count()==0`, `reserved == committed + aborted`, leak oracle passes) are unaffected because the removed pair always balanced.
- **One test depends on the count:** `tests/oracle_report.rs::lab_runtime_oracle_feeding_census` asserted `obligation_leak.entities_tracked > 0` with a one-call `send` as its only obligation. Its workload now uses an explicit `reserve` + `permit.try_send`, matching its own comment ("a task in a region using a channel permit").
- **No impact found** on goldens, snapshots, replay fixtures, golden_checksums or Foata fingerprints. All of them use `try_send`/`try_reserve`, have no participants, or compare runs to each other.
- **Also affected:** actor/GenServer cast, session endpoints and stream forwarders ride on mpsc `send`, so they stop registering transient obligations too. No test pins their counts.
- **Pre-existing stale pins:** `tests/server_incoming_body_contract.rs` and `tests/crossbeam_queue_safe_experiment_contract.rs` hash-pin `src/channel/mpsc.rs`. Both pins were already stale on origin/main (sha 39406c, 2096 lines, vs current 373c9f, 2106 lines, since 2d326554b). This change does not create a new red, and re-pinning belongs to those inventories' owners.

## Tests

- Added `tests/channel_permit_runtime_obligations_e2e.rs::mpsc_one_call_send_posts_no_transient_obligation_but_reserve_still_does`. Two one-call sends plus one explicit reserve must give `assert_clean(lab, reserved=1, committed=1, aborted=0)`, with no leak, no refusal and quiescence.
- The existing explicit-reserve leak tests in the same file (permit forgotten → `SendPermit` leak; sent/dropped → resolved) still pass and prove the two-phase path is still tracked.

## Acceptance

- Measured in the same process against tokio, with `benches/runtime_vs_tokio.rs` mpsc_ping_pong and the zz probe:
  - `send` ping-pong must move toward the `try_send` ping-pong figure, which is the no-obligation floor.
  - Report the numbers win or lose. If there is no measurable gain, do not land it: the tracking would then cost nothing worth removing.
- `channel_permit_runtime_obligations_e2e`, `oracle_report`, `mpsc_tests` and the native parked-task cancellation lane (`runtime_abort_vs_cancel_semantics_audit`, which covers MPSC cancellation publication) must be green through RCH.

Measured ping-pong 2.7-4.1x faster vs origin eae501b83 with tokio in the same process (default features, vmi1227854). RCH receipts in the commit body (native cancel contract 42/0, obligation e2e 14/0, mpsc lib 113/0, clippy 0 warnings).

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Stop taking the global RuntimeState lock on every scheduler dispatch (drain_spawn_admissions)
description:
## Bug
`ThreeLaneScheduler::next_task` (three_lane.rs ~6422) calls `self.drain_spawn_admissions()` on every
dispatch on every worker. Its first block (three_lane.rs ~6045-6059, working tree; origin/main ~6050-6064):

```
{
    let mut state = self.state.lock().unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner);
    if state.has_pending_obligation_posts() {
        let _ = state.drain_obligation_posts_with_task_table(OBLIGATION_POST_BATCH, self.task_table.as_ref());
    }
}
```

takes the global `ContendedMutex<RuntimeState>` unconditionally just to check whether obligation posts are
pending. Only after that does it perform the cheap `spawn_mailbox.spawn_requests_are_empty()` atomic check.
The comment at the call site (~6436) says "One atomic emptiness check in direct mode / idle mailbox", which is
false. Introduced by commit 582195258 (2026-09-03, asupersync-bi2462.13 obligation seam D1), i.e. AFTER all
recorded spawn-throughput numbers, so current per-task cost is likely worse than the July 6-33 us figures.
Every worker serializes on this mutex once per dispatch even when completely idle of obligation work.

## Fix
Maintain an atomic pending-post indicator next to the obligation post queue (wherever posts are enqueued:
find the producer of `has_pending_obligation_posts`' backing queue in RuntimeState / the obligation mailbox).
Producer: push the post, then `fetch_add(1, Release)` (or set a flag). Consumer in drain_spawn_admissions:
`if indicator.load(Acquire) != 0 { lock; drain; decrement by drained count }`. Keep the drain semantics,
batch size (64), and post ORDER identical. If the queue already lives in a lock-free structure with an
`is_empty()` that is safe to read without the state lock, use that instead of a new counter. Fix the
misleading comment.

Scan the other PHASE steps of next_task in the same pass only if trivially identical; the general audit is the
sibling bead "[ISSUE-65][PERF] audit remaining next_task phases".

## Tests
- Existing obligation-post ordering tests from asupersync-bi2462.13 must stay green (find them with
  `rg -n 'obligation_post' tests src --type rust`).
- New native test: multi-worker runtime (4 workers), tasks reserve/commit/abort obligations concurrently
  while other workers dispatch; assert every post reaches RuntimeState exactly once, in per-producer order,
  and the obligation-leak oracle sees no leaks. Must run on the native runtime, not only LabRuntime.
- Lab determinism goldens unchanged (golden_outputs integration test).
- Mandatory native parked-task cancellation lane stays green
  (`cargo test -p asupersync --locked --test runtime_abort_vs_cancel_semantics_audit`).

## Measurement
Head-to-head suite rows spawn_join/* and spawn_join_structured/* before vs after, same host, reporting the
asup/tokio ratio. Also `cargo bench --bench spawn_throughput -- join_handle_completion/`.

## Done when
No global-state lock on an idle dispatch (verifiable by code reading plus a test hook or lock-metrics
counter if one exists), tests green through RCH, ratios recorded.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Audit the remaining next_task phases: idle paths must cost one atomic load, not a lock
description:
## Why
`next_task` (three_lane.rs ~6422) runs several phases before it pops work:
PHASE -0.6 `drain_handle_cancel_requests()`, PHASE -0.5 `drain_deferred_cancel_dispatches()`,
PHASE 0 `timer.process_timers()`, PHASE 0.5 `drain_spawn_admissions()` (fixed by the sibling bead), PHASE 0.6
owner-pinned local spawn admission, then lane pops. Any phase that takes a lock or allocates when it has
nothing to do is paid on every dispatch on every worker. The sibling bead found one such phase; assume there
are more until proven otherwise.

## Work
For each phase: read the code, write down (in a bead comment) whether its idle path takes a lock or
allocates, and if so add an atomic emptiness indicator (Release on produce, Acquire before lock) exactly as in
the drain_spawn_admissions fix. Specifically check:
- `drain_handle_cancel_requests` / `drain_deferred_cancel_dispatches`: do they lock RuntimeState or a queue
  mutex when empty?

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Region task membership O(1): replace Vec<TaskId> contains/retain with an order-preserving indexed set
description:
## Bug
`RegionRecord` stores member tasks as `tasks: Vec<TaskId>` (src/record/region.rs ~325).
- `add_task_internal` (~1128-1171) does `inner.tasks.contains(&task)` (O(N)) under the region RwLock write
  guard on every spawn.
- `remove_task` (~1190-1193) does `inner.tasks.retain(|&t| t != task)` (O(N)) on every task exit.
- While a region is closing, `can_region_finalize_in` (state.rs ~7463) clones the whole task-id Vec
  (region.rs ~1008) on every advance.
A server that keeps its connection tasks in one region (the root region, or the listener's region) pays O(N)
per accept and per close: O(N^2) total. With 10k live connections that is ~10k comparisons per spawn and per
exit, under a write lock that every spawn into that region contends on. Related: asupersync-5om2tj (lab
still scales ~N^1.4 from remaining per-completion O(tasks) costs).

## Fix (behavior-preserving)
Introduce a small private `TaskMembership` type in src/record/region.rs:
- O(1) insert, O(1) remove, O(1) contains, len(), and iteration in INSERTION ORDER (iteration order feeds
  cancel propagation and therefore traces, lab replay determinism and golden checksums; it must not change).
- Suggested shape: `slots: Vec<Option<TaskId>>` + `index: DetHashMap<TaskId, u32>` (crate's deterministic
  hasher, src/util) + `live: usize`; remove = tombstone; compact (stable, preserving order) when
  tombstones > live and > 64. Alternative: store the slot index in TaskRecord. Choose whichever needs fewer
  lock-order changes; document the choice.
- Keep `max_tasks` limit semantics (counts live tasks), idempotent add, cleanup-task bypass in Finalizing.
- Replace the Vec clone in can_region_finalize_in with a borrow-scoped check or a `live == 0` fast path.

## Tests
- Unit tests in region.rs: add/remove/contains/idempotent add/limit/cleanup bypass/iteration order equals
  insertion order across interleaved removals and compaction.
- golden_outputs integration test and lab replay determinism tests unchanged (byte-identical).
- Scaling test (native): spawn 1k vs 16k sleeping tasks into one region; per-spawn and per-exit cost ratio
  between the two sizes must stay within 2x (it is ~16x today if O(N) dominates). Use relative timing within
  one test to stay host-independent; mark `#[ignore]` only if runtime > 30 s and wire it into the perf lane.

## Measurement
spawn_join/10000 and spawn_join_structured/10000 rows (one region holds 10k tasks) before/after vs tokio.

## Done when
No O(N) operation on region add/remove; determinism goldens byte-identical; ratios recorded; comment on
asupersync-5om2tj with the lab-scaling effect.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] JoinSet::join_next: O(1) completion-order collection instead of an O(N) scan + Vec::remove per call
description:
## Why
`JoinSet::join_next` (src/combinator/join_set.rs ~229-260) polls every owned handle in a loop
(`for index in 0..self.handles.len()`) and removes the finished one with `self.handles.remove(index)` (O(N)
shift). Collecting N members in completion order is therefore O(N^2), and every parking poll re-polls all
members. benches/spawn_throughput.rs documents this ("join_next costs more than join_all by construction:
each parking poll scans the members it still owns"). tokio's JoinSet uses an idle/notified set so join_next
is O(1) amortized. JoinSet is the blessed fan-out helper the README maps from `tokio::task::JoinSet`, so this
is exactly the comparison critics will make.

## Fix
Keep the public API and semantics; change the internals:
- Each member gets a completion notification (index pushed to a shared ready queue, e.g. an
  `Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<usize>>>` or lock-free queue, plus the JoinSet's stored waker) when its terminal result
  is published. join_next pops a ready index and takes that member's outcome without touching the others.
- Handles stored in a slab (O(1) remove, stable indices).
- Preserve: cancel-safety (dropping a join_next future must not lose an outcome; the earlier hang fixed in
  asupersync-tncxj9 came from deregistering the waker); `join_all` spawn-order semantics; `cancel_all` drain
  semantics; Outcome mapping; Drop sends aborts to unfinished members (join_set.rs ~354-369).
- Lab determinism: when several members complete in the same step, pop order must be deterministic (e.g. the
  order notifications were published, which is deterministic in the lab).

## Tests
Existing JoinSet tests (tests/join_set_* and inline) green. New: 10k members join_next completes with linear
total work (relative timing 1k vs 10k within ~12x, not ~100x); drop a pending join_next future mid-flight then
call join_next again and get every outcome exactly once; lab test with a fixed seed yields identical
completion order across two runs.

## Measurement
`spawn_throughput` bench `join_set_fanout/join_next/{1000,10000}` before/after plus a tokio JoinSet row in the
head-to-head suite.

## Done when
join_next O(1) amortized, semantics tests green, ratios recorded.

- The absolute gap (13-15x) matches the plain spawn+join gap recorded on kpmoy5.1.1: 14.2x at n=1000 and 16.9x at n=10000 for the Cx::spawn structured row. That run was on a different host, so only the ratios compare, not the microseconds. join_next no longer adds its own multiplier. What remains is per-task spawn/join cost, which is kpmoy5.1 and its children (5.1.2-5.1.12).

Not met as written: "join_next O(1) amortized".
- Members live in BTreeMap<u64, Member> and the ready set is BTreeSet<u64> (src/combinator/join_set.rs:101,121). Each collection is O(log N), and collecting N members is O(N log N) in total. The c109aadf5 landing comment said so.
- The BTree is there to keep the existing earliest-spawned tie-break when several members are ready at once. That is the v0.4.3 behavior (the old 0..len scan returned the lowest ready index). join_next_ready_order_is_deterministic_across_replays pins it for members that are all ready before the first poll.
- A slab plus a FIFO ready queue would be O(1) but would return members in wake order rather than spawn order whenever wakes arrive out of spawn order between polls. The test above would not catch that; the behavior change would still be real. A slab plus a min-heap over the ready set only would keep the tie-break at O(log k) for k simultaneously ready members, but spawn-order join_all/cancel_all would then need separate ordering.
- At n=10000 a BTreeMap step is tens of ns against about 13 us per member end to end, so neither change would move these rows measurably.

Owner decision: accept O(log N) with the preserved tie-break as meeting the intent (then close on this comment), or require literal O(1) (then this stays open for the slab + ready-heap rework). I am not closing it on my own reading of the criterion.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] Scheduler fairness/invariant monitors: make the default-on per-schedule bookkeeping allocation-free and cheap
description:
## Why
Every local schedule (`schedule_local`, three_lane.rs ~7650-7672) takes three per-worker mutexes in a row:
`self.local.lock()` (the PriorityScheduler), `self.fairness_monitor.lock().record_task_enqueue(...)`, and
`self.invariant_monitor.lock().record_task_enqueue(...)`. Further call sites: ~6816, ~7596, ~7608, ~7697,
~7705, ~7740 (requeue paths). `SchedulerInvariantMonitor::with_defaults()` sets `enable_verification: true`
(invariant_monitor.rs ~65). For each newly tracked task `record_task_enqueue` inserts a `TaskInvariantState`
into a HashMap with `lifecycle_state: "enqueued".to_string()` and `queues: HashSet<String>` populated with
`queue_name.to_string()` (invariant_monitor.rs ~430-447). That is at least two String allocations plus a
HashSet allocation per task on the production hot path, for verification that only tests consume.

## Fix, step 1 (behavior-neutral, do this)
- Replace `lifecycle_state: String` with a small `enum` (or `&'static str`), and `queues: HashSet<String>`
  with a bitset over a fixed enum of queue names (the names are compile-time constants:
  "local_ready_heap", etc.). Same observable stats/violation reports (render names when reporting).
- Make `is_enabled()` an atomic/plain field read that does not require taking the monitor mutex (call sites
  ~4631, ~4681, ~4696 lock just to ask).
- Ensure the FairnessMonitor's record path does not allocate per task either.

## Step 2 (owner decision, do NOT do without approval)
Whether production `RuntimeBuilder::new()` should default `enable_verification` to false (lab, test-internals
and debug builds keep it on). First check whether monitor stats/violations are reachable through public API
(`rg -n 'pub fn .*(invariant|fairness)' src/runtime`); if they are, a default flip changes documented
behavior and needs explicit owner approval per AGENTS.md. Record the analysis and the owner's answer in this
bead.

## Tests
Inline invariant_monitor/fairness tests green; three_lane_tests green; a test asserting zero heap
allocations per `record_task_enqueue` for an already-tracked task and a bounded count (no Strings) for a new
task, using a counting global allocator in a dedicated integration test binary.

## Measurement
spawn_join and yield_storm rows vs tokio before/after.

## Done when
Step 1 landed with ratios recorded; step 2 decision recorded (approved and done, or declined).
close_reason: Step 2 (release default off) landed in c2d7715ae under the delegated owner decision; public-API reachability analysis recorded 2026-10-03; step 1 superseded (allocations no longer on any production path), stated explicitly in the closing comment; ratios in the c2d7715ae body.

title: [ISSUE-65][PERF] CancelProtocolValidator: remove the global mutex + HashMap round-trips from spawn and completion
description:
## Why
RuntimeState builds `cancel_protocol_validator: Arc<parking_lot::Mutex<CancelProtocolValidator::new(CancelValidationLevel::Basic)>>`
by default (state.rs ~2165-2178). Task admission validates and inserts (state.rs ~4374-4387: two lock
acquisitions and a HashMap insert); completion validates and removes (two more). July profiles: 4.0% of spawn
CPU in `validate_task_transition`. History: asupersync-cancelvalidator-leak-mdvuf9 (it leaked one entry per
task forever; fixed), asupersync-1swlf4 (it never observed cancel/drain transitions; fixed),
asupersync-hiqudf (child regions untracked).

## Fix (behavior-neutral)
Move per-task validator state off the global map: store the task's validation state inline (a small enum in
TaskRecord, or an atomic in the task's shared state), so validation is a field transition performed under
locks the path already holds, with no extra mutex and no HashMap. Region/obligation validation can keep the
map if it is not per-task hot. The Basic-level checks and their error reporting must be identical.

## Tests
Validator unit tests (src/cancel/*) and the metamorphic/fuzz-derived tests named in asupersync-4na358 and
asupersync-a5z772 stay green; add a test that an illegal task transition is still rejected with the same
error after the move. Native parked-task cancellation lane green.

## Measurement
spawn_join rows vs tokio before/after.

## Done when
No global validator lock on task admission/completion; same violations detected; ratios recorded.

## Why
Code reading of one `Cx::spawn` + join (2026-10-02) counted about 20 heap allocations. Avoidable ones:
- `Cx::new_with_drivers` (src/cx/cx.rs ~1062-1100) builds `logical_clock: LogicalClockHandle::default()`,
  then RuntimeState immediately installs the real clock (state.rs ~4426 builds `logical_clock_mode.build_handle`)
  through `Arc::make_mut(&mut self.handles).logical_clock = clock` (cx.rs ~1195), which allocates the default
  clock for nothing and may clone the whole CxHandles Arc (~18 fields).
- An `OsEntropy` Arc is forked at admission (state.rs ~4421 `entropy_source.fork(task_id)`) and, per the
  spawn-path reading, again on first poll in the factory path; SpanId is drawn twice from a process-wide
  `fetch_add` (observability/context.rs ~33-36).
- `ObservabilityState` carries a `BTreeMap<String, String>` allocated per task even when no field is ever set.
- The user future sits under three nested Boxes (factory Box, Box::pin(LazyFactoryTask) at state.rs ~4705,
  and the boxed future inside), where one would do.
- `CxInner` holds two `Option<String>` plus a Vec and a VecDeque; check which are allocated eagerly.
Re-verify each item by reading the current code before changing it; drop items that turn out false.

## Fix
Pass the final clock/entropy/span into Cx construction (a builder-style internal constructor), allocate
observability maps lazily on first insert, and remove one level of boxing where the types allow. No public
API change. Keep determinism: entropy forks must remain a pure function of (seed, task_id) in the lab.

## Tests
A dedicated integration test binary with a counting `#[global_allocator]` that spawns+joins 1,000 trivial
tasks on a current_thread runtime and asserts allocations per task <= a recorded target (set to the
measured post-change value; the pre-change value goes in the bead comment). Lab replay determinism tests
unchanged.

## Measurement
spawn_join rows vs tokio before/after; allocation count per task before/after.

## Done when
Allocation count per spawn+join reduced and pinned by the counting test; ratios recorded.

title: [ISSUE-65][SC] Close the verified holes in "no orphan tasks" and "losers are drained"
description:
## Why
The critic's "just use a local executor" is wrong. A dropped local executor gives single-threaded drop-cancel
with no drain, async cleanup, tree propagation or work stealing. But a code audit (2026-10-02) found real holes
in the guarantees the README headlines ("No orphan tasks: every spawned task is owned by a region; region close
waits for all children"; "Losers are drained"):
1. `race_drained`'s partial-spawn-failure path leaves already-spawned branches running (code comment claims
   otherwise).
2. A race drains each losing branch task but not the tasks that branch spawned: branches are spawned into the
   CALLER's region, so a loser's descendants live until the caller's region closes.
3. `RuntimeHandle::spawn` (Clone handle) spawns into the ROOT region from anywhere, including from inside a
   task: effectively `tokio::spawn`, bypassing the task's own region.
4. Runtime-level `spawn_blocking` has no owning region at all (pre-existing asupersync-bi2462.156).
5. Region close waits forever for a non-cooperative child; there is no bounded close with a straggler
   report for child regions (only `Runtime::drain_root_region(bound)` exists).
6. Cleanup budgets are advisory on the production runtime (pre-existing owner decision asupersync-0fvvq9).

## Approach
Fix (1) as a bug. Fix (2) additively and measure the cost. For (3), (4) and (6), the honest-documentation
part lands regardless. Behavior changes wait for owner approval. Add (5) as an additive API. No change to the
default semantics of existing APIs without the owner's written approval.

## Done when
All children closed. The README's ownership and drain claims are stated precisely, with each remaining caveat
named in plain English.

title: [ISSUE-65][SC] race_drained: a branch spawn failure leaves the already-spawned branches running
description:
## Bug
`Cx::race_drained*` (src/cx/cx.rs ~4333-4348) spawns each branch with `self.spawn_in(&scope, ...)`. If a
later branch fails to spawn (e.g. the region hit `max_tasks`, or it is closing), the error path does:

```
// Fail closed: dropping the already-spawned handles requests their cancellation...
drop(handles);
return Err(JoinError::Cancelled(CancelReason::user("race! branch spawn failed")));
```

`TaskHandle` has no `Drop` impl (only `JoinFuture` does, task_handle.rs ~1099), and its rustdoc says "If
the TaskHandle is dropped, the task continues running" (task_handle.rs ~395-397). So the earlier branches keep
running, unobserved and undrained, until the caller's region closes. The comment is false, and the
"losers are drained" invariant is broken on this path.

## Fix
On spawn failure, abort every already-spawned handle with a `RaceLost`-class (or user) cancel reason, then
join each one (drain) before returning the error. Reuse the existing loser-drain helper used by
`Scope::race_all` (scope.rs ~1433/1456) rather than writing a second drain loop. Fix the comment.

## Tests (escaped-defect protocol: old-red/new-green receipts)
Native test on current_thread and a 4-worker runtime:
- Run in a child region with `RegionLimits { max_tasks: Some(k), .. }`.
- Branch 0..k-1 each set a "started" flag, then park on a never-completing cancel-aware wait (for example
  `rx.recv(&child_cx)` on a channel nobody sends to). Each records "cancel observed" and "drop ran" via
  Arc<AtomicBool> guards.
- Branch k fails to spawn because of the limit.
- Assert, at the moment race_drained returns Err:
  - every started branch observed cancellation;
  - every started branch reached terminal state (drop guard ran);
  - the region has zero live tasks.
- Prove the formerly-failing state: assert the started flags are set before the failing spawn, using the test
  hook or the ordering of spawns. Run the test against the pre-fix code (dangling commit with the fix
  reverted) and record the red receipt in this bead.

## Done when
Fix landed with old-red and new-green receipts. The native parked-task cancellation lane and race tests are
green.

Native test race_drained_fails_closed_and_drains_admitted_branches_at_the_task_limit green on 2 runtimes; see comment for receipts and the no-trigger limit.

Cx::spawn_in enqueues to the spawn mailbox, and a region refusal is published on the branch's own handle ("spawn admission failed", User kind). race_all takes that as the race's result and cancels and drains every admitted sibling before returning.

title: [ISSUE-65][SC] Race loser drain should cover the loser's descendants: run each branch in its own child region
description:
## Why
`race_drained` spawns every branch with `self.spawn_in(&self.scope(), ...)`, i.e. into the caller's region
(cx.rs ~4333; `Cx::spawn` uses `self.region_id()`, cx.rs ~4510). When a branch task itself spawns children
(via its `Cx`), those children are siblings in the caller's region, not owned by the branch. The race
cancels and drains the losing branch TASK, but the loser's spawned descendants keep running until the
caller's region closes. Users reasonably read "losers are drained" (README, AGENTS invariant) as "nothing the
loser started is still running when race returns". `Scope::timeout`, `hedge`, `quorum` and `first_ok` should
be checked for the same shape.

## Fix (additive in effect, but it strengthens observable behavior: owner approval required)
Create a lightweight child region per branch (ChildRegion or the internal equivalent). The branch runs as the
root task of that region. Loser cancellation cancels the region, and the drain waits for region quiescence
(not just the branch task). The winner's region closes normally after it completes. Measure the cost: one
region creation is about 0.5 us (artifacts/baseline.json `task_spawn/create_root_region` 524-622 ns). Note it
in the bead.

Owner decision needed before landing: losers' descendants are cancelled at race end instead of at
caller-region close. This tightens behavior to match the documented contract. It is technically observable,
so record approval per AGENTS.md "Backwards Compatibility".

## Tests
Native and lab test: the loser branch spawns a grandchild that parks cancel-aware. Assert that when
race_drained returns, the grandchild observed cancellation and is terminal. The winner's descendants are
unaffected until the winner's own region closes. Repeat for Scope::race, Scope::timeout and Scope::hedge if
they share the shape.

## Measurement
Race micro-benchmark (benches/cancel_drain_bench.rs or the head-to-head suite) before and after; record the
per-race overhead.

## Done when
Owner decision recorded, fix landed with tests, overhead recorded, README "Losers are drained" wording
precise.

This covered the list item "Race losers' children: whether a race should also cancel what a losing branch spawned, which tightens current behavior".

Decision: YES. A race cancels and drains each losing branch's descendants before it returns. This is what "losers are drained" promises.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-03: a design constraint found while scoping this. It is not started, and I have not claimed it.

RegionCommand::Close does not wait for a region's tasks. It cancels them: three_lane.rs ~6503 and lab/runtime.rs ~4140 call close_region_command_in_task_table with CancelReason::user("owned child region body finished"). ChildRegion's Drop backstop enqueues the same Close.

So with one child region per branch:
- Losers: cancel the region and await close(). This drains every descendant, which is the delegated decision.
- Winner: none of the options keeps today's behavior. Today the winner's descendants are siblings in the caller's region and run until that region closes.
  - Closing the winner's region, which is what dropping it does, cancels its descendants when the race returns. That tightens behavior beyond the delegated loser-only decision.
  - Detaching it (defusing the Drop backstop) keeps the descendants alive, but leaves one open, eventually empty region per race until the caller's region closes. That grows without bound in a long-lived region such as a server root running races in a loop.
  - Keeping today's lifetime would need a new close mode, "close when the last task finishes, without cancelling". That is a RegionCommand variant plus handling in both schedulers.

Cost (gylb7i): every open_child_region is a scheduler round trip that also builds a throwaway Cx and a swarm admission receipt. That is p50 8.1 us current-thread and 11.5 us multi-thread per region at cda61043d, so a 2-branch race would add roughly 16-23 us before any fix to gylb7i.

The simplest SC-consistent semantics: a race owns its branches' regions, and nothing a branch started outlives the race, winners included. That needs a decision on winners. If owners of winning branches need background work, they spawn it on an explicit outer scope.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-04: design notes, read-only on origin 2e816db92. Not claimed; nothing implemented.

Facts that decide the design:
- A ChildRegion Close is a cancel cascade: state.rs collect_region_and_descendants_with_depth, then cancel_request_in. A region reaches Closed only after child_count() == 0. So closing a loser branch's region does cancel and drain everything the loser started. That half is mechanical.
- An Open region never closes by itself (advance_region_state_in's Open arm is `_ => {}`). Leaving the WINNER's region open would therefore leak one region record per race into the caller's region until the caller closes. That is unbounded for a long-lived caller, such as a loop doing race!(work, sleep).
- RegionRecord::begin_close(None) is a non-cancelling close: the legacy Scope::region body-done path. Its tasks run to completion, but Closing refuses new spawns. Using it for the winner changes winner semantics: the winner's background work could no longer spawn after the race returns. The 10-02 decision approves tightening LOSERS only.
- Every task completion re-drives advance_region_state_in on its owner (unlink_completed_task_from_region_in), and every child close re-drives the parent. So a "close when quiescent" flag checked in the Open arm would fire at the right moment.
- But cancel_request_in is the only sanctioned emitter of RegionCloseBegin, plus region_cancelled and the cancellation metrics. It needs &mut task access that advance_region_state_in does not have. A seal-close emitted from the Open arm needs its own carefully paired trace/validator events; the lab oracles watch these.

Design I would build:
1. A "sealed" flag on RegionRecord and RegionCommand::Seal. A sealed Open region still admits spawns from its own tasks. Once it has no tasks, children or pending spawns it begins a non-cancelling close and finalizes. RegionCloseBegin is paired as in cancel_request.
2. race_drained / race_drained_with:
   - open one child region per branch (all Create commands enqueued first, so one scheduler round trip);
   - spawn each branch as that region's task, and select and drain through the existing Scope::race_all;
   - close each loser's region (cancel cascade, await Closed) before returning;
   - seal the winner's region.
   - On Err or panic, close all branch regions. Dropping the race future already hits ChildRegion's drop backstop (Close), which is right for a cancelled race.
3. Tests, native and lab: a loser's grandchild parked cancel-aware is terminal when race returns; a winner's grandchild keeps running after the race, can still spawn, and its region closes when it finishes; drain_root_region stays Quiescent.

Cost to measure before landing:
- Per race: N child-region opens, at least one scheduler round trip if batched; N-1 loser closes; one seal.
- race! is the timeout primitive, so its cost matters for issue #65's performance criticism. Measure race_drained(2 branches) before and after on benches/runtime_vs_tokio.rs or a standalone probe, and record per-race overhead. If it is material, the cheaper variant is to create a branch region lazily on the branch's first spawn. That needs a spawn-path hook, so it is a bigger change.

I had an unlanded alternative (race groups: a branch's descendants are tracked as group members on CxInner, and losers' groups are cancelled and drained) that never claimed this bead. It is dropped, not competing.

Regression: a winner's kept context stops working once its sealed region drains.
- Probe (never landed) 0bf40e35d = origin bfd2aefaf plus my tests/race_factory_native.rs, which adds two tests that exercise both halves of the contract. RCH vmi1227854, -j 1: 18 passed, 2 failed.
  - a_race_finishes_what_its_loser_spawned_and_keeps_what_its_winner_spawned, "workers=1 prebuilt=false: the winner's work runs on, uncancelled, after the race" (race_factory_native.rs:1228);
  - lab_a_race_finishes_what_its_loser_spawned, "seed 17: the winner's work ran on after the race" (:1285).
  - Every loser assertion passes: losers' descendants are drained, which is the bead's goal.
- What the test does: the winning branch keeps a clone of its own Cx (stores it, as code does when it returns a client or connection that spawns its reader tasks later). After the race, the winner's spawned task is released; it spawns again, joins that task, and finishes. Then the kept Cx spawns once more and joins, expecting Ok(5). The failing helper combines three checks into one bool: the re-spawn ran, the winner's task saw no cancellation, and the late join returned Ok(5). The kept Cx's spawn call itself returned a handle (its expect did not fire), so the bool does not say which check failed. From the code, the late spawn is the likely culprit: once the winner's last task is gone, advance_region_state_in's Open arm closes the sealed region, and admission into a Closed region is denied.
- v0.4.3 behaviour: a branch's Cx lived in the caller's region, so it worked for as long as the caller's region was open. This is an observable change on the winner side, beyond the owner's decision, which covered losers' descendants.
- A fix that keeps the design: when a spawn's requested region is a sealed branch region that has already closed itself (a winner's), admit it into that region's parent, as the "refused mint falls back to the requested region" path already does. Or unseal the winner's region at race end and close it with the caller's region (the old lifetime). Either way the two probe tests become the regression tests. The test file is in 0a6317ea2:tests/race_factory_native.rs (lines ~1100-1300) for reuse.

title: [ISSUE-65][SC] RuntimeHandle::spawn escapes to the root region from inside tasks: document precisely, diagnose, and prove root drain
description:
## Why
`RuntimeHandle::spawn` / `try_spawn` / `spawn_local` / `spawn_with_cx` (src/runtime/builder.rs ~5040-5160)
spawn into the ROOT region and need no `Cx`. `RuntimeHandle` is `Clone` (~4911), and
`Runtime::current_handle()` is reachable from any task. So any task can bypass its own region, which is
equivalent to `tokio::spawn`. Those tasks are drained only by `Runtime::drain_root_region(bound)`, which
`#[main]` calls with `drain_ms` (default 2000 ms; entry.rs ~43, ~179-197). On drain timeout the remaining work
is dropped without cleanup when the runtime drops (builder.rs ~4497-4500). The README's "No orphan tasks:
every spawned task is owned by a region; region close waits for all children" is technically true (the
root region owns them). It is misleading for nested scopes, because the task's own region close does NOT
wait for root spawns. The flagship example examples/production_service.rs uses `handle.try_spawn` into the
root region.

## Work (additive; no API removal)
1. Rustdoc on every RuntimeHandle spawn method:
   - the task belongs to the root region;
   - it is cancelled and drained only by root drain or runtime shutdown;
   - prefer `cx.spawn` / `Scope` inside tasks.
2. Debug diagnostic: when `RuntimeHandle::spawn*` is called from a thread currently polling a runtime task
   that has a `Cx` (Cx::current() is Some), emit one trace event per call site. Rate-limit it, and add a
   warning-class ASUP code only if the error-code registry rules allow one. Name the alternative in the
   message.
3. Native test proving the root-drain contract:
   - a task spawned via RuntimeHandle from inside a nested ChildRegion is still running after that
     ChildRegion closes;
   - it is cancelled and drained by `drain_root_region(bound)` within the bound;
   - with a non-cooperative task, drain_root_region reports the straggler (RootDrainOutcome) instead of
     claiming success.
4. README: say this in plain English in the "No orphan tasks" row and the tokio mapping table (owned by the
   README plain-English bead; hand the exact wording to it).

## Done when
Rustdoc, diagnostic, native tests and README wording landed.

title: [ISSUE-65][SC] Bounded child-region close: ChildRegion::close_within(bound) returns a straggler report instead of hanging forever
description:
## Why
Cancellation is cooperative. A child that never awaits a cancel-aware operation or a checkpoint keeps
`ChildRegion::close()` (src/cx/child_region.rs ~370-383) and legacy `Scope::region` (scope.rs ~881-907)
pending forever. No timeout and no report exist. Critics contrasted this with tokio's abort: drop-cancel
always terminates at the next yield. The runtime already has the right shape at the root:
`Runtime::drain_root_region(bound) -> RootDrainOutcome` (builder.rs ~4510-4600) cancels, polls until
quiescent or the bound expires, and reports. Child regions have no equivalent, so "scoped cleanup bounds"
cannot be expressed for a subtree.

## Work (additive API)
Add `ChildRegion::close_within(self, cx: &Cx, bound: Duration) -> Result<RegionCloseOutcome, ChildRegionError>`
(names to match existing conventions; mirror RootDrainOutcome fields). It cancels the remaining children
(same as close), waits for quiescence up to `bound`, and returns either Quiescent or `Stragglers { task_ids,
elapsed }`.

On the timeout path, decide between two options and record the decision:
- (a) leave stragglers owned by the still-closing region, which an ancestor close or root drain handles
  later. This is the safest choice, with no forced drop.
- (b) offer an explicit `abandon` mode that detaches them to the root region with a diagnostic.

Default to (a). Never force-drop a future from another thread; that is not sound.

Time must come from the Cx's timer, so the lab's virtual time works.

## Tests
- Native: one cooperative child plus one spinning non-cooperative child (`loop { yield_now().await }` without
  a checkpoint). close_within(50 ms) returns Stragglers naming exactly the spinning task within about 50 ms
  plus scheduling slack. The cooperative child is terminal.
- Lab: the same scenario under virtual time is deterministic across seeds.
- The existing close() behavior is unchanged.

## Done when
API landed with rustdoc, tests green, README "cleanup bounds" wording updated to point to it.

Shape (additive):
- `ChildRegion::close_within(self, bound: Duration) -> Result<ChildRegionCloseReport, ChildRegionError>`.
- `ChildRegionCloseReport` is #[non_exhaustive] with:
  - `outcome: ChildRegionCloseOutcome { Quiescent, TimedOut }`, mirroring RootDrainOutcome;
  - `elapsed: Duration`;
  - `stragglers: Vec<TaskId>`, empty when Quiescent.

- `Cx::now()` and the Cx timer driver give virtual time under LabRuntime. Never use Instant.
- The race must poll both every time. Use a small select future in child_region.rs, not a new combinator.

- ChildRegion only talks to the runtime through `SpawnGateway::enqueue_region_command` and has no state access. So add

title: [ISSUE-65][TYPES] Deliver the promised borrow-friendly "Fibers" tier and stable-by-default builds
description:
## Why
A critic hoped asupersync "uses newer Rust... a better type system" and concluded it does not. A
code-verified assessment (2026-10-02) found:
- **Real type-level pieces exist.** Edition 2024; a const-generic capability row
  `Cx<Caps>` / `CapSet<const SPAWN, TIME, RANDOM, IO, REMOTE: bool>` (src/cx/cap.rs); typestate
  `ObligationToken<K>` with compile_fail tests; 158 `#[must_use]`.
- **The headline structured-concurrency guarantees are runtime-enforced.**
  - Every spawn requires `Send + 'static` (cx.rs ~4498-4502).
  - `cx.scope()` returns `Scope<'static>` (cx.rs ~4074).
  - There is no way to run concurrent child futures that BORROW from the parent's stack frame.
- **The design bible promises exactly that tier.** asupersync_plan_v4.md line ~55: "Fibers: borrow-friendly,
  region-pinned, same-thread execution"; ~424 `FiberCap<'r>`: "spawn fibers, borrow 'r, not Send". The README
  architecture diagram draws a FIBERS column ("Borrow-safe, Same-thread, Region-pinned, Cancel-safe"), but no
  fiber code exists in src/. Phase 0/1 beads that mentioned fibers were closed without it.
- **Default features need nightly.** The default `nightly-outcome-try` feature needs a nightly compiler, so
  `cargo add asupersync` with default features fails on stable. That buys only `?` on `Outcome`.

Delivering fibers answers the type-system critique and the cost critique at the same time:
- Fibers are futures polled inside their parent task, so they need no runtime task record, no global lock
  and no 'static bound.
- They are the cheap tool for fine-grained concurrency; tasks stay the tool for parallelism.
- Region ownership is transitive and sound: the parent task cannot complete until its fiber scope drains,
  and the region waits for the parent task.

## Done when
Fibers shipped with tests, benchmark rows and docs. Default features build on stable. Cancellation errors
carry their reason.

title: [ISSUE-65][TYPES][FIBERS-2] Public fiber scope: borrow-friendly concurrent child futures with cancel-and-drain on exit
description:
## Why
This delivers the design bible's Fibers tier (asupersync_plan_v4.md ~55, ~424): "borrow-friendly,
region-pinned, same-thread execution". Users get structured fan-out that can borrow from the enclosing stack
frame, with no `Send` or `'static` bound and no per-child runtime task.

## API sketch (finalize names against existing conventions; additive only)
```
let total = cx.fibers(|scope| async move {
    let a = scope.spawn(|fcx| async move { parse(&input[..mid], &fcx).await });   // borrows `input`
    let b = scope.spawn(|fcx| async move { parse(&input[mid..], &fcx).await });
    Ok::<_, Error>(a.await? + b.await?)
}).await;   // -> Outcome<T, E>
```
- `Cx::fibers(f)` (or `Scope::fibers`) returns a future. Polling it polls the body plus every live fiber, all
  inside the CURRENT task: same thread, no Send bound, and borrows are fine because everything lives in this
  one future's state.
- Each `scope.spawn` gets a derived Cx from FIBERS-1 and returns a `FiberHandle<T>` that can be awaited
  inside the scope (the result, or Cancelled/Panicked).
- Exit protocol. When the body finishes, errors or panics, or the scope is cancelled:
  1. request cancellation on every live fiber (reason: scope exit, or the parent's reason);
  2. keep polling them until each completes. This allows async cleanup and is the drain;
  3. only then resolve.
  The result aggregates via the Outcome severity lattice (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked), matching join
  semantics.
- Panic in a fiber: catch_unwind around each fiber poll. Record it as Panicked, cancel the siblings, drain,
  and surface as Outcome::Panicked.
- Deterministic poll order (spawn order) so LabRuntime replays are stable.
- Soundness: the fibers live inside the scope future, so nothing outlives the borrow. If the user
  `mem::forget`s the scope future, the fibers are simply never polled again (no UB, nothing dangling). This is
  the moro-style design, not async-scoped's unsafe one. NO unsafe code.
- Region ownership is transitive: the parent task cannot complete while the scope is pending, and region close
  waits for the parent task. No per-fiber runtime records. Add an optional lightweight counter for diagnostics
  only if it costs nothing measurable.
- Not parallel. Document clearly: use `cx.spawn` / JoinSet for parallelism; use fibers for concurrency within
  one task (I/O fan-out, timeouts on parts of work, borrowed-data pipelines).

## Implementation notes
- Store fibers in a slab of `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + 'scope>>` plus result slots.
- Use per-fiber wake flags (an `Arc<AtomicBool>` waker wrapper) so only woken fibers are re-polled. This
  avoids an O(N) poll per wake: never poll all N fibers on every wake.
- Respect the parent's budget and poll quota, since fibers consume the parent task's polls.

## Done when
API landed behind the default feature set with rustdoc and an example (`examples/fibers_borrowing.rs`, or an
extension of an existing onramp example). Tests come in FIBERS-3 (a sibling bead).

comments.author: ubuntu
ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the earlier comment that said the API "landed". What landed in c2d7715ae does NOT meet this bead's spec.

The spec asks for cancel-and-drain on exit:
- remaining fibers are cancelled when the body returns;
- a panicking fiber cancels its siblings;
- each fiber observes its own cancellation through the derived-Cx primitive (FIBERS-1, kpmoy5.3.1).

The landed `cx::fiber::scope` follows `std::thread::scope` instead:
- WAIT on exit: when the body returns, the scope keeps polling the remaining fibers until each completes on its own.
- A panic is caught per fiber. It is reported through that fiber's handle, or re-raised when the scope ends if no handle observed it; siblings are not cancelled.
- Fibers observe only the calling task's cancellation, through the task's Cx. There is no per-fiber cancellation, because FIBERS-1 is not built.
- Dropping the scope future drops its fibers.

The README states the semantics that landed ("the scope waits for all of them") and does not claim cancel-on-exit.

This bead stays OPEN. Two ways to finish it:
(a) build FIBERS-1 and switch body-exit and panic to cancel-and-drain. That changes the semantics of a public API added in c2d7715ae, before any release ships it;
(b) the owner accepts wait-on-exit as the fiber contract, and this bead's spec is amended to match.

The examples/fibers_borrowing.rs example lands with batch 3 regardless.

title: [ISSUE-65][TYPES][FIBERS-3] Fiber scope proof: borrow compile tests, drain/cancel/panic behavior, lab determinism, cost vs tokio
description:
## Tests to add
1. Compile-pass (trybuild or doctest): fibers borrow a local `Vec` and a `&mut` counter through
   non-overlapping borrows. A `!Send` value (`Rc`) used inside fibers compiles.
2. Compile-fail (trybuild, alongside the existing asupersync-macros compile-fail suite or a new
   tests/ui_fibers/ directory):
   - a FiberHandle cannot escape the scope closure (lifetime error);
   - a fiber cannot outlive the borrowed data.
3. Native behavior (current_thread and a 4-worker runtime, with the parent as a spawned task):
   - body returns early: remaining fibers observe cancellation, run async cleanup (await a cancel-aware
     channel send in a masked section, or `commit_section`), and complete before the scope resolves. Assert
     with drop guards and timestamps;
   - parent task aborted through TaskHandle::abort while fibers are parked on cancel-aware waits: every fiber
     observes cancellation with the parent's reason; the scope drains; the TaskHandle reports the documented
     result (follow the native parked-task cancellation contract style: prove the parked state first);
   - a fiber panics: siblings are cancelled and drained, and the outcome is Panicked;
   - outcome aggregation follows the severity lattice.
4. Lab: the same scenarios under LabRuntime with two seeds give identical traces per seed. A fiber parked
   while holding an obligation is visible to futurelock detection (the obligation's holder is the parent task).
5. `mem::forget` of a scope future that contains fibers: the process stays sound, the borrowed data can be
   reused afterwards (the borrow ended), and nothing panics. Run under Miri only if Miri is available on RCH;
   otherwise note it.

## Benchmark rows (in the head-to-head suite)
`fibers_join/{100,1000}`: N trivial fibers awaited in one scope, compared with tokio's
`futures::future::join_all` (if futures-util is already a dev dependency) or a tokio JoinSet. Also
asupersync's own `spawn_join_structured/{100,1000}`. Expect fibers to be much cheaper than asupersync tasks.
Record the ratio.

## Done when
All tests green through RCH, benchmark rows recorded.

comments.text:
Read-only audit (SapphireHill, 10-03) of src/cx/fiber.rs, dynamic_supervisor.rs (+worker.rs), dynamic_service.rs and supervisor_service.rs on origin/main 7564bd965. The supervisors and services held up. Two findings in fiber.rs belong here (fiber scope proof). They are not fixed, because fiber.rs is your in-progress feature:

F1 MEDIUM - a second fiber panic is lost once the first has been observed. UnobservedPanic is a single slot (fiber.rs:188). Completion::finish (:231-235) records only the first panic, and FiberHandle::poll (:286-293) clears the slot when its own panic is observed. So when fibers A and B both panic in one pass, the body awaits A (Panicked) and drops B's handle, and the scope finishes normally: B's panic vanishes. This breaks fiber.rs:42-44, "a panic no handle observed is re-raised when the scope finishes, so it cannot vanish silently". Fix: Arc<Mutex<Vec<(u64, PanicPayload)>>>; finish pushes, poll removes its own id, and scope re-raises the first one remaining. Test: two panicking fibers, await the first, drop the second, and expect the scope to re-raise "second".

F2 LOW - a handle to a fiber dropped with its scope hangs forever. run_fiber calls finish only on completion (:303-317). close_and_drop_fibers / CloseOnDrop (:477-500) drop unfinished fiber futures, so Completion stays Running(Some(waiter)) and nobody wakes it. A handle that escaped the body (stored outside, or sent to another task, since FiberHandle<T> is Send) and is awaited after the scope future was dropped (timeout or select around scope) stays Pending forever. This breaks :251-252, "Awaiting yields Ok(value), or JoinError::Panicked". Fix: a publish-on-drop guard passed into run_fiber that sets HandleState::Abandoned and wakes; poll maps it to JoinError::Cancelled.

Minor: dynamic_supervisor.rs:677-684 returns Region(close_error) instead of the original SpawnError when both submit and close fail; the doc at :366 says Spawn. fiber.rs:57-58 says the table lock is taken twice per poll, but it is taken three times.

title: [ISSUE-65][TYPES] Default features must build on stable Rust: probe for try_trait_v2 in build.rs instead of hard-requiring nightly
description:
## Why
Cargo.toml's default features include `nightly-outcome-try` (Cargo.toml ~137). src/lib.rs ~52-53 then does:
```
#![cfg_attr(feature = "nightly-outcome-try", feature(try_trait_v2))]
#![cfg_attr(feature = "nightly-outcome-try", feature(try_trait_v2_residual))]
```
So `cargo add asupersync` with default features fails to compile on stable. Stable users must know the
incantation `--no-default-features --features proc-macros` (README "Minimum Supported Rust Version"). The
only thing the feature buys is `?` on `Outcome` (`impl Try/FromResidual for Outcome`,
src/types/outcome.rs ~696-745), and FromResidual covers only Outcome/Result with the same E. Critics read
"nightly by default" as immaturity. Downstream evaluators hit it in the first minute.

## Fix (compatible for every existing user)
- build.rs already exists (it embeds the git revision). Add a compiler probe: run `$RUSTC` on a tiny crate
  containing `#![feature(try_trait_v2, try_trait_v2_residual)]` plus a minimal impl. Emit
  `cargo:rustc-cfg=asupersync_try_trait` only if it compiles. Emit `cargo::rustc-check-cfg=cfg(asupersync_try_trait)`
  (the crate's lints set `unexpected_cfgs = warn` and gates run `-D warnings`).
- Respect `RUSTC_WRAPPER` and `RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER` the way autocfg does. Probe with the same target flags
  (`--target` from the `TARGET` env) so cross builds work. Cache nothing between builds.
- lib.rs: `#![cfg_attr(all(feature = "nightly-outcome-try", asupersync_try_trait), feature(...))]`. Gate the
  Try/FromResidual/Residual impls in outcome.rs the same way.
- Keep the feature name and its default status. On nightly, nothing changes. On stable with default features,
  the crate now compiles and `?` on Outcome is unavailable. Code that used it was already uncompilable on
  stable, so this is not a regression.
- Optionally emit a build warning (`cargo:warning=`) when the feature is requested but unsupported. Decide by
  checking that it does not break -D warnings lanes (cargo warnings are not rustc warnings, but verify).
- Docs: README MSRV/feature table and the "Downstream dependency resolution" section. State the stable
  default-feature build plainly, and set `rust-version` in Cargo.toml only if the stable lane proves a
  specific floor.

## Tests
- Extend scripts/run_stable_lane_e2e.sh with a stage that checks the crate with DEFAULT features on
  `cargo +stable`, through RCH. Keep the existing proc-macros-only stage.
- The downstream fixture (tests/fixtures/downstream-consumer-proof) builds on stable with default features
  (add a stage) and on the pinned nightly (unchanged).
- The nightly lane still runs the Outcome `?` unit tests.
- Pins: before editing, check that contract tests reading Cargo.toml features, README MSRV text and the
  stable-lane script (`rg -l 'nightly-outcome-try' tests artifacts`) stay green.

## Done when
`cargo +stable check -p asupersync` with default features passes through RCH, nightly behavior is unchanged,
and the docs are updated.

title: [ISSUE-65][TYPES] checkpoint() cancellation errors drop the CancelReason: attach it and expose an accessor
description:
## Why
The four-valued Outcome and the structured `CancelReason` (kind, origin, cause chain) are a selling point
("cancel attribution"). But `Cx::checkpoint()` returns
`Err(crate::error::Error::new(crate::error::ErrorKind::Cancelled))` with no reason attached (src/cx/cx.rs
~3017; doc ~2485/~2665). Under the default spawn policy, a task that acknowledges cancellation and returns
`Err` through `?` joins as `Ok(Err(cancelled_error))`, not `JoinError::Cancelled(reason)`. So the reason
reaches the join site only for cancellation-blind or never-started tasks. Callers must remember to read
`cx.cancel_reason()` themselves before the Cx is gone.

## Fix (additive)
When checkpoint (and the shared cancellation-error constructor used by cancel-aware primitives, if there is
one) builds the Cancelled error, attach the current `CancelReason`. Use the existing context/source
mechanism of `crate::error::Error` if it has one; otherwise add a private optional field. Add a public
accessor `Error::cancel_reason(&self) -> Option<&CancelReason>`. Error's Display gains no new text unless
existing tests allow it; check the error-code registry contract (tests/error_code_registry_contract.rs) and
any Display goldens.

Do not change JoinError semantics. This only makes the reason recoverable from the error users already get.

## Tests
- Unit: cancel with `CancelReason::timeout()`, then the checkpoint error's cancel_reason() is the timeout
  reason (kind and origin preserved).
- Native: a task cancelled through TaskHandle::abort with a custom reason returns
  `cx.checkpoint()?`-propagated Err, and the joined `Ok(Err(e))` has `e.cancel_reason()` equal to the abort
  reason.

## Done when
Accessor public, documented, tested. The README's "cancel attribution" sentence mentions it.
