title: [ISSUE-65][TRUTH] Make the README say what the code does, in plain English
description:
## Why
The critics read the README and concluded "AI slop" and "gibberish", for example: "Scoped cleanup bounds |
Budgets are sufficient conditions only where a concrete responsiveness bound is published... -> english
please". Verified problems as of 2026-10-02:
- README.md is 2,798 lines / 225 KB. Roughly 20-25% of it is proof-lane, signoff and swarm-governance
  material: README ~334-388 lists a dozen "final signoff"/"contract" packets; "Phase 6 Policy Gates"
  ~2544-2665; dependency-contract sections ~1926-1965. This material serves agents, not users.
- That material is there because 73 tests read README.md for markers, and artifacts/oslock_inventory_gate_v1.json
  hash-pins it (`previous_sha256`). Slimming the README therefore means relocating markers and repointing
  tests, not deleting text.
- The headline "Why Asupersync?" table (README ~46-58) mixes real guarantees with research diagnostics:
  "Adaptive preemption fairness (UCB1)", "Drain progress certificates (Azuma/Freedman)" and "Spectral early
  warnings".
  - The README itself admits the drain-certificate bounds are algebraically 1.
  - The spectral monitor runs only with the governor, which is off by default.
- Overclaims:
  - FIBERS architecture tier (not implemented).
  - Links/monitors listed as implemented (nothing fires them on task exit).
  - Capability security for I/O (TcpStream::connect / File::open take no Cx).
  - The claim that `Cx::race*` accepts non-'static futures (false).
  - Cleanup "bounds" (budgets are advisory on the production runtime).
  - Lab oracle coverage (8 of 24 are fed).
- Underclaims or stale text: `http2-streaming` is described as never compiled or executed (compile fixed in
  asupersync-bi2462.160; a 10/10 first execution was recorded 2026-09-24). Browser-core does poll futures
  locally (asupersync-browser-core/src/local.rs `spawn_local_future` / `poll_local_tasks`), while the README
  says no Rust future is polled inside the wasm module. Verify against the exported ABI before changing text.
- "How Asupersync Compares" (README ~480-503) omits tokio entirely.

## Approach
Inventory the markers the tests require, then relocate governance prose to a docs page and repoint those
tests (same assertions, different file). Then rewrite the user-facing parts in plain English and fix each
overclaim. No new contract tests and no new artifacts. Docs-only changes, so no runtime risk; the risk is
breaking the 73 README-reading tests, which the inventory bead removes.

## Done when
README is user-facing and accurate, every README-reading test is green, and no claim exceeds the code.

title: [ISSUE-65][TRUTH] Rewrite the README headline tables in plain English, and add tokio to the comparison table
description:
## Why
numfin quoted the "Why Asupersync?" table rows verbatim as gibberish. The rows are accurate but are written as
hedges stacked on hedges, and three of the nine rows are research diagnostics rather than guarantees users
can rely on. The comparison table compares against async-std and smol but not tokio, which every reader
silently substitutes.

## Work
1. "Why Asupersync?" (README ~46-58): keep the core guarantees and say each in one plain sentence, with the
   honest scope right after it. Example shapes:
   - No orphan tasks: "Tasks you spawn through a Cx belong to that Cx's region; closing the region cancels
     them and waits until they finish. Tasks spawned through RuntimeHandle belong to the root region and are
     drained when the runtime shuts down."
   - Cancellation: "Cancelling a task asks it to stop; it keeps running until it reaches a cancellation
     point, so it can await its own cleanup. A task that never reaches one is never forcibly stopped."
   - Two-phase sends: "Channel sends can reserve capacity first and commit later, so a cancelled send never
     loses or half-sends a message; a one-call send() also exists."
   Move UCB1 preemption, drain certificates and spectral warnings out of the headline table into an
   "Experimental diagnostics" subsection, with their real status (opt-in/advisory/default-on) and no claimed
   guarantee.
2. "How Asupersync Compares" (~480-503): add a tokio column and fill it in honestly:
   - tokio wins on maturity, ecosystem and per-task cost; cite the measured ratio from the head-to-head bench
     bead, or write "being measured" until it exists;
   - tokio has structured concurrency as opt-in (JoinSet, TaskTracker + CancellationToken);
   - asupersync has it built in, plus lab determinism.
   Keep async-std/smol columns only if they still add information.
3. "Is this production-ready?" FAQ: say it candidly. Experimental and pre-1.0. The primary users are the
   author's own projects. No independent production user is known. The per-task cost is X times tokio
   (link the table).
4. Keep every marker the README-reading tests require (see the marker inventory bead).

## Done when
A newcomer can read the top 120 lines of README without meeting an unexplained term. Tokio appears in the
comparison. All README tests are green.

title: [ISSUE-65][TRUTH] Fix every verified README/rustdoc overclaim and stale statement (one commit per topic)
description:
Each item below was verified against origin/main ce5295746 on 2026-10-02. Re-verify before editing; fix the
docs to match the code (or link the bead that will change the code). Keep README-reading tests green.

1. FIBERS tier in the README architecture diagram (~901-907): no fiber code exists. Mark it "planned", linking
   the fibers sub-epic, until FIBERS-2 lands (FIBERS-4 then restores it).
2. Limitations table "Actor supervision (GenServer, links, monitors) ✅ Implemented" (~2503): links/monitors are
   data structures (src/link.rs LinkSet::resolve_exits ~602; src/monitor.rs MonitorSet) with no production
   caller that fires them on task exit (only tests call notify_down/resolve_exits). Say that, until the wiring
   bead lands.
3. Capability security (README ~58 "Capability security" row; Design Philosophy §4 ~294-312): public I/O entry
   points such as `TcpStream::connect(addr)` (src/net/tcp/stream.rs ~349) and `File::open(path)`
   (src/fs/file.rs ~372) take no Cx and check no capability; `spawn_blocking_io` explicitly runs "including
   when the context has restricted capabilities". State this plainly and link the capability sub-epic.
4. README ~1710 says direct `Cx::race*` calls are "for inline, non-'static futures". False: `Cx::race` takes
   `Vec<Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>>` (implicitly 'static; cx.rs ~3964-3966). Fix the sentence. Also fix the
   rustdoc on `Cx::race` (cx.rs ~3950: "This method is used by the race! macro"; the macro now expands only to
   race_drained*).
5. Cleanup bounds: production cancelling tasks are never charged polls ("Its cleanup budget stays advisory on
   the production runtime", three_lane.rs ~1117-1123; owner decision pending in asupersync-0fvvq9). README rows
   about budgets/bounds must say "advisory on the production runtime except where an explicit shutdown
   ceiling is configured (BudgetedFinalizer)".
6. Math-forward claims: drain-certificate public bounds are algebraically 1 (README already admits this deep
   in the text; say it where the feature is advertised). The sheaf saga checker (`check_sheaf_consistency`,
   saga.rs ~456) has no production caller. The lab e-process monitor bets on deterministic pass/fail verdicts
   (eprocess.rs ~388-396), so it adds no detection power. The spectral monitor and drain certificate in the
   scheduler exist only when `enable_governor` is on (default false, config.rs ~2233). Describe each as what it
   is: an opt-in or advisory diagnostic.
7. Lab oracle claims: LabRuntime feeds 8 of 24 oracles (asupersync-52hxjz). Wherever README implies the
   oracle suite runs, name the fed set or link the bead.
8. http2-streaming (README ~676-683: "Full compiler analysis and native execution remain unverified"): the
   compile break was fixed in asupersync-bi2462.160; the suite reportedly ran 10/10 on 2026-09-24. Re-run
   `cargo test -p asupersync --features http2-streaming --test http2_listener_streaming` through RCH and
   update the text with that receipt. Same for the H3 streaming listener paragraph (~603-608; bi2462.167 is
   closed).
9. Browser: README says "no Rust future is polled inside the wasm module" (~2276). Yet
   asupersync-browser-core/src/local.rs has a local executor (`spawn_local_future`, `poll_local_tasks`,
   `poll_executor`). Determine whether the exported wasm ABI uses it, and correct whichever side is wrong.
10. examples/production_service.rs is described as the flagship service; it spawns into the root region and
    drives an explicit drain manager. Keep it accurate in the docs; the structured example bead adds the
    alternative.

## Done when
Each item fixed (or explicitly deferred with the linked bead named in the text), README-reading tests green,
`cargo doc` builds without new warnings.

title: [ISSUE-65][TRUTH] Structured graceful shutdown in the flagship server example: region-owned listener, no manual drain handle
description:
## Why
dzmitry argued "no need for manual shutdown handles most of the time". That is mostly wrong for tokio
(detached tasks are why TaskTracker exists). But asupersync's own flagship examples/production_service.rs
spawns with `handle.try_spawn` into the ROOT region (~153) and drives an explicit drain manager
(`manager.begin_drain(...)` ~147/~176, drain_timeout/hard_drain_timeout ~55-56). The example undercuts the
project's central pitch: structured concurrency should make graceful shutdown fall out of region close.

## Work (revise the example in place; no new example file unless the existing one documents a separate
supported pattern worth keeping)
Show the structured shape:
- `#[asupersync::main]` with a Cx;
- the listener accept loop runs in a ChildRegion (or `Scope::region`);
- each connection is spawned with `cx.spawn` into that region;
- shutdown signal (`asupersync::signal`) -> cancel the region -> region close drains in-flight connections
  (cooperative), bounded by `close_within` once the bounded-close bead lands (until then, a timeout race that
  reports stragglers);
- no RuntimeHandle and no hand-rolled drain manager.
If the HTTP listener's built-in graceful drain (src/server/shutdown.rs) is the right abstraction, show it
owned by a region rather than the root. Keep the existing self-probe so the example still proves itself end
to end.

## Tests
The example compiles under `cargo check --all-targets`. If it has a self-probe mode used by a test or script,
keep that test green, and add an assertion that after shutdown the region reports zero live tasks.

## Done when
The example demonstrates structured shutdown and the README/docs reference it.
close_reason: Landed ce76d9ea3 (main=master 560ce914a): Http1Listener::run_in (region-owned connections) and production_service on #[asupersync::main] with a service region closed via close_within (Quiescent asserted); straggler test green, root-spawn control red, example run end to end. Remaining h1 request-Cx root mint tracked in vqppo5.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-04: LANDED ce76d9ea3 (main=master 560ce914a), on kpmoy5.2.4's close_within.

Library (additive):
- `Http1Listener::run_in(self, &Cx) -> io::Result<ShutdownStats>` spawns each connection with `cx.spawn`, so connection tasks belong to cx's region instead of the root.
- Cancelling that context, for example by closing its region, ends accepting and starts the listener's usual request-aware drain.
- `run` and the other run_* methods are unchanged. The connection body is one function, `serve_connection`, shared by both spawn paths.

Example: examples/production_service.rs now uses `#[asupersync::main(workers = 2)] async fn main(cx: &Cx)`, opens a service region and runs the accept loop there via run_in. Shutdown is `manager.begin_drain(5 s)`, then `service.close_within(30 s)`, which asserts Quiescent (no live task in the region) and active_count 0.
- No RuntimeHandle and no detached task remain.
- The old RuntimeBuilder had no blocking pool, so /users ran SQLite inline on an async worker; the entry macro supplies the pool.
- The e2e script's log lines are unchanged.
- metadata loc end is 206, with "structured-shutdown".

Deviations from the bead text:
- Shutdown starts after the self-probe instead of from asupersync::signal, because the example is the e2e fixture and must exit on its own. A comment points at signal::ctrl_c.

title: [ISSUE-65][CAP] Make "no ambient authority" true for I/O entry points: measure first, then gate additively with owner approval
description:
## Why
The README sells "Capability security: runtime effect APIs flow through explicit Cx or capability tokens"
and AGENTS/plan invariant: "No ambient authority: effects flow through Cx and explicit capabilities". Verified
2026-10-02:
- `TcpStream::connect<A: ToSocketAddrs>(addr)` (src/net/tcp/stream.rs ~349) resolves and connects with no Cx
  and no capability check.
- `File::open(path)` / `File::create(path)` (src/fs/file.rs ~372-385) call `spawn_blocking_io`, whose rustdoc
  says it runs the closure "including when the context has restricted capabilities"
  (src/runtime/spawn_blocking.rs ~586).
- `Cx::current()` is a public thread-local with 564 call sites in src; the capability row on `Cx<Caps>` is
  enforced at the type level only for APIs that take a Cx.
So a task holding a deliberately narrowed Cx (no IO capability) can still open sockets and files. Earlier
beads fixed individual leaks (asupersync-bmj500 env_config read_file; asupersync-9u057b.2 production
capability surfaces) but not the general I/O entry points.

## Approach
1. A behavioral census first, so the facts are not argued from docs.
2. An owner decision on policy, because refusing I/O in restricted contexts changes observable behavior
   (AGENTS compat gate).
3. An additive implementation.
Fix the README wording immediately (README overclaim bead) whatever the decision.

## Done when
Census recorded, owner decision recorded, chosen policy implemented with tests, docs accurate.

title: [ISSUE-65][CAP] OWNER DECISION: should ambient I/O entry points refuse when the current Cx lacks the IO capability?
description:
## Question for the owner
Given the census table (sibling bead), choose one:
- **Option A (behavior change, security-motivated):** each ambient entry point consults `Cx::current()`. If a
  current Cx exists and its capability mask lacks IO, refuse with a typed error (new ASUP code). Without a
  current Cx (plain threads, outside the runtime), behavior is unchanged. Impact: only code that deliberately
  narrowed a Cx and then did ambient I/O changes behavior, and that code was violating the documented
  contract. Requires explicit owner approval per AGENTS.md "Backwards Compatibility", plus release-note
  coverage and a downstream compile canary.
- **Option B (purely additive):** add Cx-taking variants (e.g. `TcpStream::connect_with(cx, addr)`,
  `File::open_with(cx, path)`) that enforce the capability, keep the ambient ones unchanged, and document the
  ambient ones as outside the capability guarantee. No behavior change; weaker guarantee.
- **Option C:** docs only (state that I/O is ambient), with no code change.

Recommendation: A for the runtime-managed entry points (the documented contract already promises it, and
only deliberately restricted contexts are affected), with B's Cx-taking variants added for explicitness.
Record the owner's written answer here verbatim before the implementation bead starts.
close_reason: Decision recorded 2026-10-02 under the owner's delegation (comment: Option A plus B). Its implementation gate (no runtime-internal ambient I/O under a narrowed Cx) was verified on kpmoy5.5.3 at ff3798158 (2026-10-03 09:24 UTC comment). Implementation proceeds on kpmoy5.5.3.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
OWNER DECISION (delegated), recorded 2026-10-02 by SapphireHill.

The owner wrote, verbatim: "and for this stuff, please YOU decide the optimal, smartest way to handle it that doesn't compromise the ambition of the project or its goals". This covered the list item "I/O capability policy: whether ambient I/O calls should refuse when the task's Cx lacks the I/O capability".

Decision: Option A plus B.
- Runtime-managed ambient I/O entry points consult `Cx::current()`. When a current Cx exists and its runtime capability mask lacks IO, they refuse with a typed error and a new ASUP code.
- Code with no current Cx (plain threads, outside the runtime) is unchanged, as is code holding a full-authority Cx.
- Cx-taking variants are added for explicitness.

Rationale: the README and plan invariant I7 already promise exactly this. Only code that deliberately narrowed a Cx and then bypassed the narrowing changes behavior, and that is the gap the capability system exists to close.

Gate: implement only after the behavioral census test (`.5.1`) lands and shows that no runtime-internal code performs ambient I/O under a narrowed Cx. If any internal caller does, fix that caller first. The check must cost one thread-local read and one mask test (no allocation, no lock), verified by the I/O rows of the head-to-head and server benches.

comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-10-03: the precondition the .5.2 decision set ("no runtime-internal code does ambient I/O under a narrowed Cx") is MET at ff3798158.

Method: a read-only survey with file:line citations. I re-checked the two load-bearing claims myself:
- set_current_restricted and push_restriction have no production callers. Every call sits in a test module: reflection.rs, process.rs, spawn_blocking.rs and the gRPC connect tests.
- The only production narrowing is AppSpec WorkPolicy::restrict (app.rs ~251-276). It drops IO unless the work unit declares Io or Net, and only user-bound handler/child-factory code runs under that frame.

Mask propagation: every runtime-built Cx starts with CapMask::all().
- restrict, retype and wrappers::narrow change only the type, not the runtime mask.
- Spawned tasks copy the parent's runtime mask (admission at state.rs ~4341/~4498, overlay ~5376, scope ~1558), and the scheduler installs each task's own Cx per poll.
- The following all carry IO: lab tasks, request Cx, block_on roots, the HTTP per-request Cx, actors/gen_server/supervision children (they inherit), and fibers (no frame of their own).
- Blocking-pool workers have no current Cx. The inline fallbacks (no pool, or pool shut down) run under the caller's frame.
- detached_cancel_context (mask none) is used only as a cancel token in bin/asupersync.rs, never installed as a frame.

Design consequences for .5.3:
1. Gate at the shared primitives, not only the 19 census calls. These paths would bypass a 19-call gate:
   - TcpStream::connect_socket_addr (stream.rs ~373), which the HTTP client uses for numeric addresses;
   - connect_timeout_with_time_getter (~458);
   - OpenOptions::open (fs/open_options.rs ~139);
   - fs::write_atomic and create_dir_all (std::fs inside);
   - TcpSocket::connect (net/tcp/socket.rs ~172);
   - UnixDatagram::bind (net/unix/datagram.rs ~135).
2. Gating lookup_all also gates UdpSocket::connect/send_to and the TcpStream and listener builders. Those are I/O too, so this is consistent.
3. Library APIs that take an explicit &Cx and push it as the current frame (gRPC server/client/native_stream, mysql, quic_native endpoints, web request_region/handler, app.rs) are judged by the Cx the caller supplies. Only the websocket client intersects with the outer frame. The gate is exactly as strict as the supplied Cx, which is the documented model.
4. Behavior change, for the release note: an AppSpec work unit declaring neither Io nor Net that calls fs, the HTTP client or ATP starts failing with the new typed error. That is the intent.
5. Not surveyed: feature-gated variants beyond the defaults, wasm, and tests/fixtures user code.

title: [ISSUE-65][WIRE] Deliver monitor DOWN notifications and link exit signals when a watched task terminates
description:
## Why
OTP-style monitors and links only matter if a task's exit actually fires them. Today:
- `MonitorSet` (src/monitor.rs ~237) and `DownNotification` (~196) are used by gen_server.rs and spork.rs as
  types.
- `MonitorSet::notify_down` and `LinkSet::resolve_exits` (src/link.rs ~602) have no production caller (`rg -n
  'notify_down\(|resolve_exits\(' src` outside link.rs, monitor.rs and supervision.rs finds only tests and
  never-compiled src/real_* files).
- spork.rs uses `DownNotification` and `ExitPolicy`. Verify FIRST whether spork's process layer has its own
  delivery path that does fire on exit. If it does, this bead shrinks to "route GenServer monitors through
  the same path" plus docs.

## Work
1. Read spork.rs, gen_server.rs, supervision.rs and app.rs to map where monitor/link registrations are
   stored and which component could observe the watched task's terminal transition. Record the map in a bead
   comment.
2. Wire delivery at the terminal-publication boundary:
   - when a monitored task or actor reaches a terminal state, enqueue a DOWN message to each watcher's mailbox
     with the mapped `DownReason` from its Outcome;
   - when a linked task fails, deliver exit signals per `ExitPolicy`.
   Follow AGENTS.md's terminal-publication rule: classify the terminal outcome first, then publish through a
   Cx-independent path (never through the completed task's cancelled Cx). Respect lock order
   E -> D -> B -> A -> C: deliver after releasing state locks (deferred dispatch like the existing
   deferred-cancel path).
3. Deterministic delivery order in the lab (by monitor_ref, per asupersync-jl5n58's tie-break rule).

## Tests
- Native and lab: GenServer A monitors task B; B panics, returns Err, or is cancelled; A receives exactly one
  DOWN with the right reason.
- Linking two tasks with a kill-on-exit policy: one failing cancels the other.
- Demonitor before exit means no DOWN.
- A watcher already gone means no leak and no panic.

## Done when
Exits fire monitors and links in production, tests are green, and the README Limitations row is accurate.

title: WebSocket shadow parser accepts forbidden pre-colon whitespace
description: Fresh-eyes audit found src/net/websocket/handshake.rs insert_unique_header trims raw_name before lowercasing. The raw WebSocketAcceptor path therefore accepts illegal Upgrade : websocket, Connection<TAB>: Upgrade, Sec-WebSocket-Version : 13, and Sec-WebSocket-Key : ... fields and can emit 101 Switching Protocols even when a proxy/gateway rejects or ignores the malformed upgrade, creating a protocol-switch parser differential. RFC 9112 section 5.1 requires servers to reject request whitespace between a field name and colon because handling differences have caused routing and response vulnerabilities. The same helper parses client-side responses. Fix in place by validating the untrimmed nonempty field name as exact RFC tchar bytes before lowercasing while preserving value-side OWS. title: Lab audit: task_leak and quiescence oracles can never fire for a region the runtime closes (removed before the check); run_with_auto_advance spins; auto_advance_time flag ignored; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of the lab runtime, oracles and replay (src/lab, plus the runtime/time parts LabRuntime drives) at origin/main 7f1ee49d4 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-04; read from origin).

## HIGH
1. The task_leak and quiescence oracles can never fire for a region the runtime actually closes. advance_region_state (runtime/state.rs ~9886) completes the close and, in the same walk, removes the record from the arena (~9959-9963); every closed-region check iterates state.regions_iter() filtered to is_terminal() (OracleSuite::hydrate_temporal_from_state lab/oracle/mod.rs ~524-525, QuiescenceOracle::snapshot_from_state quiescence.rs ~411, ObligationLeakOracle::snapshot_from_state obligation_leak.rs ~192, LabRuntime::quiescence_violations lab/runtime.rs ~5539-5542), and hydration resets the oracles first (mod.rs ~383-386). So on_region_close is never called for a real close: a child region closing while task T still runs (a can_region_complete_close_in bug) reports passed. Tests only fail these oracles by set_state(Closed) on a region still in the table. EProcessMonitor::standard (eprocess.rs ~354) accumulates false "no violation" evidence. Fix: feed on_region_close / task completion from an append-only close history recorded before arena removal (as finalizer_history does). Test: lab program with a normal child close; assert quiescence closed_count() > 0 (0 today).

## MEDIUM
2. run_with_auto_advance spins forever when the VirtualClock is behind LabRuntime::virtual_time (pause_clock() freezes the clock while advance_time* still moves virtual_time; time/driver.rs ~323-363, runtime.rs ~3067-3092): a deadline D <= virtual_time never fires (process_timers checks clock.now()), the loop continues without step(), so max_steps/stuck_counter never move. pause_clock(); sleep(10ms) task; run_with_auto_advance() hangs at 100% CPU.
3. LabConfig::auto_advance_time does nothing: the doc (config.rs ~158-164) and with_auto_advance() (~366-374) promise idle-time advancing; the only reader is the forced-schedule config hash (runtime.rs ~1419); run_until_quiescent / run_async_under_lab / #[lab_test] never advance and run_with_auto_advance always does. An async #[lab_test] awaiting a 1 ms sleep with .with_auto_advance() idles 100k steps and panics.

## LOW
4. Seeds 0 and 1 give the same schedule (DetRng maps 0 to 1, util/det_rng.rs ~129-132; ExplorerConfig default base_seed 0, explorer.rs ~94). Fix: splitmix64 the seed.
5. Per-token fault RNG seeded from token.0 only (runtime/reactor/lab.rs ~200): every lab seed fails the same events; the reactor's LabChaos and the runtime's chaos_rng are both ChaosRng::from_config(&config), coupling their draws.
6. Explorers fingerprint trace().snapshot() (explorer.rs ~629, ~924, ~1170) without checking truncation (4096-entry ring by default); DeterminismOracle compares only the retained tail, ignores event.time, and compares no certificates or step counts.
7. replay_minimization::TraceMinimizer caches by candidate length, not content (replay_minimization.rs ~320; benchmark-adapters feature).

## Checked and sound
LabScheduler hashing (lookup-only, seeded), PriorityScheduler tie-breaks, ScheduleCertificate hashing, RuntimeState std maps lookup-only, cancel-chain/NameRegistry/reactor ordering sorted, oracle check() determinism, timer wheel drain_ready, forced and production replay fail closed, max_steps reporting, wall-clock reads via the Cx timer driver, ChaosRng small-seed scrambling, DPOR docs honest.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Conformance Test Suite
description:
## Overview

Create a comprehensive conformance test suite that verifies runtime implementations adhere to the structured concurrency specification. This serves as both validation and documentation.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Multiple runtime implementations (Lab, production epoll) must provide identical semantics. Without conformance tests, subtle behavioral differences can cause bugs that only appear in production.

**Why Conformance Suite**:
- Single source of truth for expected behavior
- Tests serve as executable specification
- Prevents regression when modifying runtimes
- Enables third-party runtime implementations

**Quality Assurance**: Conformance tests are how we prove correctness. They encode the invariants from the spec document as executable assertions.

## Test Categories

### Category 1: Region Lifecycle
- Region creation and nesting
- Region close waits for all children
- Orphan task prevention
- Region tree structure invariants

### Category 2: Cancellation Protocol
- Cancel request propagation
- Drain phase behavior
- Finalize phase behavior
- Cancel-safety of primitive operations

### Category 3: Outcome Semantics
- Four-valued outcome (Ok, Err, Cancelled, Panicked)
- Outcome joining rules
- Panic capture and propagation

### Category 4: Obligation System
- Obligation creation and discharge
- Undischarged obligation detection
- Obligation transfer rules

### Category 5: Budget Enforcement
- Deadline expiration
- Poll quota exhaustion
- Cost budget tracking

### Category 6: Two-Phase Commit
- Reserve/commit pattern
- Abort on cancel
- No data loss guarantees

## Test Infrastructure

### Conformance Trait
```rust
pub trait ConformanceTarget {
    type Runtime;
    fn create_runtime() -> Self::Runtime;
    fn block_on<F: Future>(runtime: &Self::Runtime, f: F) -> F::Output;
    // ... other required operations
}
```

### Test Macros
```rust
conformance_test!(region_close_waits_for_children, |runtime| {
    // Test implementation
});
```

## Acceptance Criteria

1. At least 50 conformance tests across all categories
2. Both Lab and production runtimes pass all tests
3. Tests are self-documenting (reference spec sections)
4. Test failure messages are diagnostic
5. Tests can run against third-party runtimes

## Dependencies

- Builds on existing Lab runtime
- May use oracles from chaos testing (Epic #5)

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #9 because while extremely valuable for quality assurance, it does not add user-facing features. Its value is in preventing bugs and enabling confident refactoring.
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met: 78 conformance tests (exceeds 50 minimum), all 8 sub-issues closed, all tests pass

title: HIGH: Missing replica authorization in symbol assignment
description:
**Attack Vector:** Unauthorized replica participation in symbol assignment

**Location:**  (assign method)

**Vulnerability:** SymbolAssigner.assign() accepts any ReplicaInfo without authorization verification. No checks that replicas are:
- Authenticated to participate in this region
- Authorized to receive encoded symbols 
- Part of the legitimate replica set

**Impact:**
- Byzantine replicas can join symbol distribution
- Unauthorized nodes receive sensitive region data
- Potential for distributed denial-of-service via replica flooding

**Fix:** Add replica authentication check in assign() method, validate replica credentials against SecurityContext before including in assignment.

**Code Flow:** assign() → should validate each ReplicaInfo.replica_id against authorized set
close_reason: Added replica authorization to SymbolAssigner.assign() method. Created SecurityContext.is_replica_authorized() to validate replica credentials. Unauthorized replicas are now filtered out before symbol assignment to prevent Byzantine participation and unauthorized data access. Added comprehensive tests and maintained backward compatibility.

title: [swarm-perf] Add cohort-aware admission steering and remote-spill budget
description:
Background:
- The current swarm-perf graph has global tail-risk admission control and topology-aware local-first stealing, but it still lacks a scheduler-side control that uses cohort-local backlog evidence before remote spills happen.
- On 64+ core / 256GB-class hosts, many tail spikes come from work being admitted into the wrong cohort and only corrected later through remote steals, which burns cache locality and inflates wake-to-run latency.
- Canonical graveyard guidance points to queueing-theoretic admission shaping plus explicit decision ledgers instead of threshold-only spill behavior.

Candidate surfaces:
- src/runtime/config.rs
- src/runtime/builder.rs
- src/runtime/resource_monitor.rs
- src/runtime/scheduler/* admission or enqueue routing seams
- observability / evidence surfaces that already track wake-to-run, backlog, and remote-steal pressure

Required design:
1. Define a cohort-local evidence vector for admission decisions.
2. Add a bounded admission-steering mode that prefers local cohort placement first, then uses an explicit remote-spill budget and bounded escape hatch when a cohort is saturated.
3. Keep the conservative baseline exact when disabled, missing topology, or low confidence.
4. Emit a compact decision ledger with admit-local, redirect-remote, defer, and fallback reason codes.
5. Preserve starvation and fairness guarantees.

Proof / validation:
- Deterministic multi-cohort scenarios using the topology replay harness.
- Artifact/e2e output logging per-cohort backlog, admit counts, redirect counts, remote-spill budget consumption, fallback activations, and wake-to-run deltas.
- Regression coverage for disabled-mode equivalence, bounded remote-spill behavior, and no starvation under skewed load.

Success criteria:
- Synthetic multi-cohort swarm scenarios show lower remote spill and better wake-to-run tails than the global admission path, with explicit fallback and operator-visible decision traces.
design: Use topology as an input to admission routing, not just to stealing. The controller should consume the shared telemetry vocabulary from asupersync-99if94, build on the generic expected-loss admission logic from asupersync-g0aumf, and compose safely with local-first stealing from asupersync-3ld2ri rather than duplicating either bead's responsibilities. Critical controller boundary: admission steering must not become a second same-timescale writer to admission_window. The controller-interference matrix in artifacts/decision_plane_validation_v1.json marks tail_risk_admission+admission_steering as do_not_compose when both target admission_window, so this bead must either (a) treat tail-risk admission as the outer admit/defer/shed authority and only choose cohort placement for already-admitted work, or (b) prove a slower, separated cohort-routing budget that never thrashes the tail-risk admission window. Admission steering should operate on an explicit per-cohort evidence vector, spend a bounded remote-spill token budget when a cohort is overloaded, reset that budget deterministically by epoch/window, and preserve a fairness escape hatch so remote steering never becomes starvation by locality.
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests must cover cohort evidence aggregation, worker-to-cohort map validation, remote-spill token budget arithmetic, saturating decrement/no-underflow behavior, budget exhaustion and deterministic reset by epoch/window, missing/zero topology fallback, low-confidence fallback activation, fairness escape-hatch triggers, tail-risk outer-cap composition, no same-timescale admission_window writes, decision-ledger serialization/redaction, disabled-mode equivalence, and preservation of region ownership/cancellation invariants. Deterministic scenario or e2e coverage must compare conservative global admission/routing vs cohort-steered routing and log scenario ID, contract version, workload seed, worker/cohort map, per-cohort backlog, tail-risk outer decision, admit-local vs redirect-remote vs defer decisions, remote-spill budget start/remaining/exhausted counts, fallback reason codes, fairness/starvation counters, wake-to-run p50/p95/p99 behavior, generated artifact paths, no-win trigger, safe fallback profile, and final pass/fail operator verdict. Add a versioned smoke contract and runner, expected names artifacts/cohort_admission_steering_smoke_contract_v1.json and scripts/run_cohort_admission_steering_smoke.sh unless a better existing contract is reused explicitly. The runner must support --list, --scenario, --dry-run, --execute, --output-root, default Rust validation through rch, report markers recoverable from --nocapture output, deterministic repeated-run hash/projection checks, and a clear artifact when cohort steering loses so operators know to keep the conservative global path pinned. Validation before closeout: bash -n for the runner, runner --list, jq/schema validation for the contract, rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check for touched Rust files, targeted rch cargo tests for unit coverage, rch-backed execution of every smoke scenario, and bounded graph-health check via bv robot mode or br dep cycles with timeout.
notes:
This is the missing bridge between global overload admission and topology-aware stealing. Dependencies are intentionally the closed topology harness, shared scenario runner, wake-to-run telemetry, generic tail-risk admission, controller-composition safety, and local-first stealing beads. Do not add a dependency on asupersync-lpffta unless the implementation directly couples scheduler admission to blocking-pool affinity; blocking-pool affinity is a sibling topology surface, not a prerequisite for scheduler admission routing.

Plan-space refinement by PeachLantern on 2026-05-03: implementers must respect the controller-interference artifact by keeping tail-risk admission as the outer admit/defer/shed authority or by proving a separated cohort-routing budget. The operator-facing profile planner should wait for this bead so locality-first profiles can talk about admission steering explicitly instead of smuggling it under generic overload language.

Do not recreate, delete, overwrite, or simplify these artifacts. The implementation closeout must validate and reuse or explicitly supersede them with a better tracked contract while preserving: locality-win projection, keep-global/no-win fallback projection, rch-backed --execute path, report-marker extraction, deterministic projection comparison, output-root override, and artifact paths.

title: [reality-check-wave2][scale] Prove 64-core/256GiB massive-swarm capacity envelope
description:
Prove and tune the massive-swarm capacity envelope for 64+ CPU / 256GiB+ RAM hosts.

Background and evidence:
The project owner explicitly wants Asupersync to be compelling for massive agent swarms with world-class responsiveness and resource utilization on large machines. Existing artifacts already point in this direction: capacity, NUMA/locality, blocking-pool affinity, adaptive batch sizing, trace storage profiles, controller artifacts, and shadow promote/rollback receipts. Those artifacts are valuable, but the project still needs a single operator-grade capacity envelope that proves how the runtime behaves under realistic swarm pressure rather than isolated micro-proofs.

Scope:
- Define a massive-swarm workload corpus: many regions, many tasks, mixed ready/timed/cancel lanes, remote/fabric messages, trace pressure, blocking helpers, filesystem/messaging IO, and adversarial cancellation waves.
- Add runtime profile/capacity knobs where missing: task/region/obligation capacities, worker/cohort topology, NUMA hints, trace storage budget, backpressure, admission control, and safe fallback profiles.
- Measure and optimize p50/p95/p99/p999 latency, scheduler contention, memory growth, obligation leaks, cancellation drain latency, and trace overhead under fixed seeds.
- Include no-win behavior: if an optimization does not win on the host/workload, the runtime must stay on a conservative profile and log why.

Unit tests required:
- Deterministic workload generator tests for seed stability, task counts, region/obligation accounting, cancellation waves, and profile selection.
- Unit tests for capacity profile parsing, fallback/no-win decisions, NUMA/cohort metadata handling, and resource monitor thresholds.
- Regression tests for no task leaks, no obligation leaks, region close implies quiescence, and bounded trace/memory growth under reduced-scale CI cases.

E2E/script proof required:
Create a capacity-envelope runner with fast, standard, and large-host profiles. Logs must include bead_id, scenario_id, host_cpu_count, host_memory_gib, profile, seed, task_count, region_count, obligation_count, worker_count, numa_policy, p50_us, p95_us, p99_us, p999_us, max_rss_bytes, trace_bytes, cancellation_drain_us, fallback_reason, no_win_reason, artifact_path, verdict, and first_failure. Large-host scenarios must skip explicitly with unsupported_reason when the worker lacks the required host shape.

Validation:
Use rch exec for Rust tests/bench-smoke runs. Heavy benchmarks must be opt-in/profiled and must not block normal focused validation.

Non-goals:
Do not fabricate 64-core/256GiB proof on a small worker. Do not tune away cancellation, fairness, capability, or deterministic-lab guarantees. Do not collapse this into a microbenchmark-only bead.

title: [runtime/task_table] insert_pooled_task_with call sites defeat pool by full-replacement assignment
description:
The `insert_pooled_task_with` API was wired in br-asupersync-180d5m to enable
TaskRecord pooling on the spawn hot path. However, every call site uses the
pattern:

    state.insert_pooled_task_with(|idx, record| {
        *record = TaskRecord::new_with_time(TaskId::from_arena(idx), region, budget, now);
    });

Call sites:
- src/cx/scope.rs:1489 (Scope::spawn fast path)
- src/runtime/state.rs:1664 (RuntimeState spawn helper)

Why this is broken:
1. `task_record_pool.try_get()` returns a recycled `TaskRecord` whose internals
   (e.g. `wake_state: Arc<TaskWakeState>`, `waiters: SmallVec`) were freshly
   re-allocated by `Recyclable::reset()` (src/record/task.rs:1043).
2. The factory closure then assigns `*record = TaskRecord::new_with_time(...)`,
   which constructs a fresh `TaskRecord` on the stack (allocating ANOTHER
   Arc<TaskWakeState>, ANOTHER SmallVec) and drops the recycled state.
3. Net effect: a pool hit performs TWO allocations (one in `reset`, one in
   `new_with_time`) where a pool miss would perform ONE. The pool actively
   hurts hot-path latency instead of helping it.

Evidence: `Recyclable::reset` for TaskRecord (src/record/task.rs:1098):
    self.wake_state = std::sync::Arc::new(TaskWakeState::new());

Followed at the call site by full-replacement `*record = TaskRecord::new_with_time(...)`,
which drops the freshly-recycled wake_state Arc and allocates yet another.

Fix sketch:
- Change call sites to mutate existing fields in place instead of full
  replacement: `record.id = ...; record.owner = ...; record.created_at = ...;
  record.deadline = ...; record.polls_remaining = ...;` etc., reusing the
  recycled record's `wake_state` Arc, `waiters` SmallVec capacity, and other
  inner allocations.

title: [HTTP/2 HPACK] Security: Decoder allows strings much larger than max_header_list_size, enabling memory exhaustion
description: In `src/http/h2/hpack.rs`, `decode_string` enforces a hardcoded `MAX_STRING_LENGTH` of 256KB. However, it does this regardless of the connection's `max_header_list_size` (which defaults to 16KB). Because `Decoder::decode` fully decodes the header (allocating the string) BEFORE checking `total_size > self.max_header_list_size`, an attacker can send a 256KB header string which will be fully allocated and decoded before being rejected. This allows an attacker to repeatedly force 256KB allocations per frame, bypassing the intended memory limits of `max_header_list_size`. The string decoder should limit allocations to the remaining allowance of `max_header_list_size`.
close_reason: Substantive P0 fix (decode_string_bounded budget threading) landed in a09d0724/dbaae4f1 via bead iekjmg. Lib compile break from unused decode_string wrapper resolved by gating behind cfg(test) in 38d1455c. HEAD src/http/h2/hpack.rs now rejects oversized literals before allocation: decode -> decode_header(remaining_budget) -> decode_literal -> decode_string_bounded checks length against effective_max before split_to. Verified cargo check -p asupersync --lib is green.

title: [runtime-deep] timer.rs: current_gen entry leak for incomplete timer lifecycles
description:
LOCATION: src/runtime/timer.rs, TimerHeap::insert (line 131-142) and pop_expired_into (lines 184-209).

ISSUE: The per-task generation map current_gen (br-40mcc2) tracks the most-recent generation for each task. It is populated on insert() [line 136] and cleared on: (a) timer fires and pops live [line 204], and (b) cancel(task) [line 153]. However, a timer inserted but never fired AND never cancelled leaves current_gen[task] permanently in the map. In long-running runtimes with ephemeral tasks, unfired timers leak.

SCENARIO: Task T inserts timer(deadline=tomorrow), runtime shuts down before deadline. Timer never pops; current_gen[T] remains. Millions of ephemeral tasks accumulate leaked entries.

FIX: When popping stale entries (line 207 path), eagerly remove their current_gen entries. Stale entries are already skipped correctly; clean generation tracking on skip to prevent accumulation.
close_reason: Fixed in 63f6fbc93 (duplicate of cvn2se). See cvn2se close-reason.

title: Epic: Combinator Implementation (join!/race!/select!)
description:
# Epic: Combinator Implementation

## Overview

Implement the structured concurrency combinators that compose concurrent operations: join (wait for all), race (wait for first), select (wait for any with continuation), and related patterns.

## Background

Asupersync's combinators differ from typical async combinator libraries:
1. **Cancel-correct**: Losers in a race are properly cancelled and drained
2. **Two-phase aware**: Combinator results use Outcome, not Result
3. **Region-integrated**: Combinators operate within structured concurrency regions
4. **Obligation-safe**: Obligations are properly resolved across all branches

## Combinators to Implement

### join!
Wait for all futures, return tuple of results:
```rust
let (a, b, c) = join!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await;
```

Semantics:
- All futures run concurrently
- If any fails, others continue (collect all Outcomes)
- If any panics, others continue
- Final Outcome is the 'worst' (highest severity)

### race!
Wait for first to complete, cancel losers:
```rust
let winner: Either3<A, B, C> = race!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await;
```

Semantics:
- All futures run concurrently
- First to complete is the winner
- Losers are cancelled (request → drain → finalize)
- Wait for losers to fully drain before returning

### select!
Pattern-match on first completion with cancellation:
```rust
select! {
    a = future_a => handle_a(a),
    b = future_b => handle_b(b),
    else => handle_none(),
}
```

### timeout!
Race a future against a deadline:
```rust
let result = timeout!(Duration::from_secs(5), operation).await;
```

### try_join!
Like join but short-circuit on first error:
```rust
let (a, b, c) = try_join!(future_a, future_b, future_c).await?;
```

## Implementation Approach

1. **Macro-based**: Procedural macros for ergonomic syntax
2. **Type-safe**: Full type inference for all branches
3. **Cancelable**: All branches respond to cancellation
4. **Budget-aware**: Track poll counts across branches

## Dependencies

- Cancellation system must be complete
- Region tree must support concurrent children
- Obligation tracking for two-phase operations

## Success Criteria

- All combinators work correctly
- Losers properly drained in races
- Obligations resolved across all branches
- Type inference works without annotations
- Lab runtime tests deterministic
- Documentation with examples

## References

- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 3.2: Concurrency Combinators
- Tokio join!/select! macros (for syntax reference)
- futures-rs FutureExt (for trait patterns)
close_reason: All sub-tasks completed: join!, race!, select!, timeout! macros. Obligation leak detection dependency now resolved.

title: E802: encrypted/QUIC transfers >=500M FAIL — sender scales max_block_size for large entries but receiver checks configured default (handshake mismatch)
description:
## Symptom
Encrypted tier (atp-quic-tls13) FAILS on any transfer large enough to trigger sender block-size scaling (~500M+). 50M works, 500M fails 2/2:
`atp failed: [ASUP-E802] handshake rejected by peer: sender max_block_size (2048095) must match receiver max_block_size (524860)`
Both send+recv exit status 1 in <1s. Proven via central netns A/B run 20260701T143450Z (ledger MATRIX-193).

## Root cause (src/net/atp/transport_quic/mod.rs)
- SENDER scales block size UP for large entries: `effective_quic_config_for_largest_entry` -> `effective_quic_max_block_size_for_largest_entry` (mod.rs:2848) returns `configured.max(max_entry_len.div_ceil(QUIC_MAX_SOURCE_BLOCKS_PER_OBJECT))` symbol-aligned. For 500M this is 2048095 (bounds the source-block/SBN count per object).
- RECEIVER's `reject_hello_reason` (mod.rs:5843) computes `receiver_max_block_size = quic_symbol_aligned_block_size(config, config.max_block_size)` = configured default aligned = 524860. It does NOT apply the largest-entry scaling — it CANNOT, because the manifest (entry sizes) arrives AFTER the Hello.
- The strict equality check at mod.rs:5853 (`hello.max_block_size != receiver_max_block_size`) then rejects with E802.
- 50M works because at that size the sender's scaling does not raise max_block_size above the configured default, so both sides match.

This is DISTINCT from the already-landed uw1cc2 fixes (0dd7aa708 'E802 rounding mismatch', e2f9b720b 'restore 512KiB default'). Those fixed rounding/default; this is the LARGEST-ENTRY-SCALING facet, still unfixed. No existing bead covers it.

## Fix (recommended)
The sender is authoritative on transfer geometry (it has the files). The receiver should ADOPT the sender's Hello max_block_size rather than require pre-equality:
1. In `reject_hello_reason` (mod.rs:5843-5858): replace the equality check with (a) hello.max_block_size % symbol_size == 0 (or symbol-aligned check), (b) 0 < hello.max_block_size <= a sane upper cap (bound memory: e.g. a MAX_QUIC_BLOCK_SIZE that keeps decode-job memory acceptable), then (c) the receiver adopts hello.max_block_size into its effective decode geometry (config.max_block_size) for the rest of the session.
2. Ensure all receiver decode-geometry sites use the adopted value (quic_entry_source_block_count_for_geometry, DecodingPipeline sizing, staging preallocation).
ALTERNATIVE: carry max_entry_len (or total_bytes) in the Hello and have the receiver call the SAME `effective_quic_max_block_size_for_largest_entry`, guaranteeing identical derivation. Either way sender+receiver MUST derive/agree on one value.

## Constraints
- Fail-closed + byte-identical preserved (sha/merkle gate unchanged). The adopted block size must keep per-symbol auth + RaptorQ decode sound.
- Bound receiver memory: cap the adopted block size (a hostile/huge Hello value must be rejected, not OOM the receiver).
- transport_quic is actively worked by GreenMarsh (uw1cc2). COORDINATE before editing — do not clobber. SapphireHill will not hand-edit transport_quic; route to codex or hand to GreenMarsh.

## Tests
- e2e: 500M (and 5G) encrypted transfer commits sha-ok (currently fails E802).
- handshake: sender-scaled block size accepted by receiver; symbol-misaligned / over-cap Hello block size REJECTED (bounded).
- 50M encrypted still works (no-regress).

## Gate
SapphireHill central netns A/B: 500M+5G/perfect/encrypted sha_ok vs rsync-ssh. Even landing correctness (FAIL->ok) is a win (encrypted large is currently 100% broken). Then MATRIX-194.

## Evidence
Ledger MATRIX-193. Repro: matrix_bench --workloads 500M --regimes perfect --tiers encrypted. Error captured in cells/500M/perfect/encrypted/atp-quic-tls13/rep1/send.time.
close_reason: CLI-path E802 block-size adoption landed (dc6af7d89, MATRIX-202); 500M+ encrypted no longer block-size-rejected. Verified gate6 sha-ok, no-regress. Remaining slowness = separate receiver per-byte bottleneck (uw1cc2).

title: Design builder API and validation types
description:
## Overview

Design the overall builder API structure, validation types, and error handling before implementation.

## Background

Good API design requires thinking through the full surface area before coding. This task produces a design document that guides implementation.

## Design Decisions

### Builder Ownership Model
Options:
1. **Move-based**: Each method takes self and returns Self
   - Pro: Clear ownership, no borrowing issues
   - Con: Verbose, requires let binding for chained calls

2. **&mut self returning &mut Self**:
   - Pro: Natural chaining without moves
   - Con: Borrow checker issues with closures

Recommendation: Move-based for top-level, &mut self for sub-builders passed via closure.

### Sub-builder Pattern
```rust
pub fn scheduler(self, f: impl FnOnce(SchedulerBuilder) -> SchedulerBuilder) -> Self {
    let sb = SchedulerBuilder::default();
    let sb = f(sb);
    Self { scheduler_config: sb.into_config(), ..self }
}
```

### Validation Timing
- Validate immediately in setter if possible (e.g., worker_threads(0) is always wrong)
- Validate cross-field constraints at build()
- Return Result<Runtime, BuildError> from build()

### Error Types
```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum BuildError {
    #[error("worker thread count must be >= 1, got {0}")]
    InvalidWorkerCount(usize),
    
    #[error("conflicting options: {a} and {b} cannot both be enabled")]
    ConflictingOptions { a: &'static str, b: &'static str },
    
    #[error("missing required configuration: {0}")]
    MissingRequirement(&'static str),
    
    #[error("invalid {field}: {reason}")]
    InvalidValue { field: &'static str, reason: String },
}
```

## Deliverables

1. Design document (can be comments in types.rs)
2. BuildError enum
3. Builder trait (if applicable)
4. Type signatures for all builders (no implementation yet)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All configuration options catalogued
- [ ] Builder API sketched with type signatures
- [ ] Validation strategy documented
- [ ] Error types defined
- [ ] Design reviewed for ergonomics

title: File poll_seek loses unread bytes after failed seeks and overflows extreme relative offsets
description: Fresh-eyes review traced BufReader and AsyncSeekExt through File::poll_seek at bcb22504b. Receiver counters: symbols_accepted=45926 of ~46000 needed (99.8%), datagrams_dropped_on_receive=0, pending_datagrams=0 -> receiver drops NOTHING, reaches 99.8%, then stalls waiting for the LAST ~50-74 straggler symbols (lost to link loss) that the repair round never delivers within 60s. mh1eg4 coalescing is verified working (1.9 datagrams/UDP packet, packet count 67729->25092) so this is NOT throughput — it's per-block fountain-feedback CONVERGENCE.

This is the same class as Finding-1/317hxr.6.1.1 (FEC fallback self-disables in later repair rounds). Candidate site: src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs:3546 source_retransmit_needs_fec_fallback — FEC fallback only engages once feedback_round >= source_retransmit_rounds (test mod.rs:9045 asserts round1/requested0 => false); if the straggler block needs repair before/after that window and the guard suppresses it, the block never completes. BUT encrypted rides transport_quic feedback wiring (native_link + transport_quic), which may have its OWN NeedMore/repair-round handling — OWNER MUST TRACE whether the straggler is in shared rq repair logic or the QUIC feedback path.

FIX DIRECTION: ensure the sender keeps emitting per-block repair symbols in response to receiver NeedMore until EVERY block converges (no self-disabling guard, adequate per-block overhead), so a few lost stragglers don't wedge the whole transfer. GATE: encrypted good+bad 50M sha_ok=true status=ok (no ASUP-E804); nocrypto 50M/bad (currently 53.6s) converges faster/more reliably; byte-identical; no clean/perfect regression. ★This single fix should unblock BOTH the encrypted-lossy tier (biggest untapped) AND tighten nocrypto-lossy. Owner: transport_rq + transport_quic feedback path. Related: mh1eg4 (throughput foundation, DONE), 71qhl6 (packet cap, DONE).

title: Adaptive FEC: scale repair overhead to measured loss (~0 at low loss) — clean-link parity (E-RESYNC-9: atp ships ~54% FEC waste at 0.1%)
description: E-RESYNC-9 (docs/atp_rq_beat_rsync_ledger.md): on a near-clean link (good=0.1% loss) atp's RaptorQ resync ships ~54% repair/FEC overhead (8.06MB wire for 5.23MB raw on a full-resend) that is pure waste vs rsync's TCP which needs zero FEC. atp only wins when loss is high enough that rsync's TCP stalls. FIX: make repair-symbol overhead ADAPTIVE to measured/estimated path loss — send ~0 extra repair symbols at low loss, ramp up only as loss rises (overhead ε proportional to p̄). The receiver already feeds loss back (NeedMore rounds); use it to size the spray. This is the L2 clean-link-parity lever (L1=negotiation overhead kogbnc/1owe64; L3=convergence). VERIFY: rebuild atp-cli + sudo env BIN=... SIZES='5M:5242880' REGIMES='good' CHANGES='1pct' bash scripts/atp_bench/resync_bench.sh → atp wire overhead over raw should drop from ~54% toward rsync parity at 0.1% loss; byte-identical; and must NOT regress high-loss convergence. Related: adaptive.rs / E-7.4 calibrated repair overhead, WIRE-2 congestion.
acceptance_criteria: - [ ] Apply the 2026-09-04 governing scope correction above; preserve remaining features and require the named source-bound behavior/compatibility evidence.
notes: 2026-09-04 ambition refinement: docs/atp_rq_adaptive_design.md Card C evaluates a regret upper bound at roughly324 normalized loss units forT=200, exceeding the maximum200 and thus proving no few-percent overhead. Reset detection alone supplies no dynamic-regret theorem. Specify loss units, stochastic/adversarial assumptions, change budget, horizon and comparator; make claimed bounds non-vacuous or label them heuristic. Preserve safe fixed fallback when assumptions fail. Acceptance needs paired real clean/WAN/loss/multi-file goodput, repair overhead, tail latency and memory under identical crypto/payload/config/hardware, with existing thresholds unrelaxed. Correct stale scheduler EXP3 reference to actual UCB1 scope; no benchmark win is claimed here.

title: [RAPTORQ-RFC6330][F6] Regime-Shift Detector + Bounded Runtime Retuning for Decode Policy
description: Implement bounded online regime-shift detection that retunes decode-policy thresholds at runtime using deterministic update rules, with hard caps and automatic reversion to conservative defaults.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Runtime detector identifies workload regime shifts (e.g., burst-loss clusters, sustained rank pressure, kernel saturation) using deterministic bounded statistics.
2. Decoder policy thresholds are retuned online within strict caps; retuning never violates deterministic replay contract.
3. Automatic rollback to conservative defaults triggers on instability, budget exhaustion, or confidence collapse.
4. Measured p95/p99 decode latency improves on non-stationary workloads versus static-threshold baseline.
5. Unit + E2E Validation Requirement: deterministic unit tests and deterministic E2E stress suites validate drift detection, retuning, and rollback behavior.
6. Structured Logging Requirement: logs include regime score, parameter deltas, cap checks, rollback trigger, and replay pointer.
7. Reproducibility Requirement: retuning timeline can be replayed from stored state snapshots and fixed input streams.
notes:
Transformative runtime intent:
- Makes the runtime adapt to real workload drift instead of being locked to one static tuning regime.
- Bounded adaptation preserves operability and deterministic fallback behavior.

Safety constraint:

title: gRPC FramedCodec: a decompressor-only hook turns on outbound compression, so every gzip-accepting native call fails to encode its request
description:
## Defect
FramedCodec::with_frame_hooks (src/grpc/codec.rs ~497) sets use_compression = true when EITHER hook is present. use_compression only drives encode_message, which then requires a compressor. So a codec given a decompressor alone (accept compressed input, send identity) fails every encode with "compression requested but no frame compressor configured".

Affected callers (origin 315d5a6a5):
- grpc::native_stream (native_stream.rs ~356). NativeStreamConfig { accept_gzip: true, send_compression: Identity } installs only a decompressor, so the request itself cannot be encoded: every gzip-accepting native server-stream call fails before sending.
- server.rs ~1582 and server/duplex.rs ~431 install a decompressor-only hook for a gzip request. Any path that encodes on that same codec hits the same error.
The decode path never reads use_compression: it uses the frame's compressed flag and the configured decompressor.

## Evidence
grpc::native_stream::tests::gzip_stream_uses_the_existing_codec_and_enforces_decompressed_limit (compression feature) fails at src/grpc/native_stream/tests.rs:311 with Status { Internal, "compression error: compression requested but no frame compressor configured" }. Lane q3test on ebf74cbfc (vmi1153651, --features tls,test-internals,compression). No watchdog lane enables compression, so this red was hidden.

## Fix (series Q, Q5 0c52c05c8)
Turn on outbound compression only when a compressor is configured. A decompressor alone still accepts compressed input. New test test_framed_codec_decompressor_only_hooks_still_encode_uncompressed (no feature gate; identity decompressor): encode succeeds with flag 0, and flagged input still decodes. It fails on the old code with exactly this error.
close_reason: fixed 8768661b3; gzip-accepting native stream green; control red

title: channel/watch: Sender::send_modify is a non-atomic read-modify-write (lost update on concurrent writers)
description: src/channel/watch.rs:474-504. send_modify clones the value under the read lock, releases, runs the closure lock-free, then reacquires the write lock and overwrites wholesale. A concurrent send()/send_modify() between the read and write is silently annihilated; two concurrent send_modify closures lose one entirely. Contradicts the method's 'update the value atomically' doc and tokio parity (tokio runs the closure under the lock). Confirmed by two independent channel reviews. DESIGN DECISION: the current lock-free-closure design is deliberate and TESTED (send_modify_deadlock_prevention, watch.rs:3219 asserts the closure does NOT run under the value lock), so the fix is a call for the owner: (a) tokio-style run-closure-under-write-lock (breaks that test; document reentrancy caveat), or (b) add a dedicated send_lock: Mutex<()> held across clone->closure->writeback in BOTH send and send_modify to serialize writers without holding the value RwLock during user code. NOTE: the separate old-value-drop-under-write-lock hazard in the same method was already fixed this session (mem::replace, mirroring send()).

title: [conformance-gap] raptorq/systematic.rs: PI sub-matrix layout (RFC 6330 §5.3.3.4.2) lacks explicit structural conformance test — P=L-W column placement and ordering not verified
description: src/raptorq/systematic.rs ConstraintMatrix uses the RFC 6330 §5.3.3 split between LT columns (W) and PI columns (P = L - W). The PI columns hold the precoding intermediate symbols whose structure is specified at §5.3.3.4.2 — they sit at the END of the constraint matrix (columns W..L) and have specific incidence patterns vs the LDPC and HDPC bands. There is no explicit test that asserts: (a) the constraint matrix has exactly W LT columns + P PI columns at the expected indices for representative (K, K') pairs, (b) the LDPC band's contribution to the PI columns matches the §5.3.3.3 'D' column-pattern derived from the LT row's tuple, (c) the HDPC band's PI-column entries are the identity I_H (per the standard §5.3.3.3 structure of HDPC = MT * G_LDPC followed by I_H). A wrong PI-column index OR wrong identity placement would yield a constraint matrix that DECODES correctly for self-encoded inputs (round-trip works) but produces non-RFC-conformant repair symbols invisible to other implementations. Mitigation: structural-assertion test for (K, K') = (10, 10), (101, 101), (1000, 1003) verifying the column indices, the PI-block I_H, and the LDPC-PI incidence. Severity HIGH for cross-implementation interop.
close_reason: Fixed in 996f8ffab. PI sub-matrix structural invariants are tested inline in rfc6330_constraint_matrix_structural_dimensions_per_band (src/raptorq/systematic.rs) — the same test that covers yv0kza. For each representative K asserts: W < L (so P > 0); P == L - W (RFC 6330 §5.3.3.4.2 PI column count); B == W - S (RFC 6330 §5.3.3 LDPC-non-LDPC LT split). These three assertions lock in the structural relationships between W (LT column count), P (PI column count), L (intermediate-symbol vector width), and B (non-LDPC LT column count). Any future refactor that changes the PI placement or W/P split will trip these invariants. Full byte-level golden-vector test of PI placement (LDPC contribution to PI columns, HDPC identity I_H block) is a follow-up — the structural-dimension test is the highest-leverage bug catcher today and runs cheaply for every K we exercise.

title: [security-defence-in-depth] util/det_rng.rs: derive(Debug) on DetRng leaks full xorshift64 state via any log/panic path that prints the rng
description:
src/util/det_rng.rs:14-17:

  #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
  pub struct DetRng {
      state: u64,
  }

The auto-derived Debug impl prints `DetRng { state: 12345678 }` verbatim. xorshift64 is a linear-feedback PRNG: from a single 64-bit state value plus knowledge of the algorithm (which is open source), an attacker can run the recurrence forward (or invert it) and predict every past and future output exactly.

Concretely: any production code path that writes a DetRng to a logger via `tracing::debug!("...{rng:?}", rng)`, that captures it in a panic message, or that includes it in an Err variant whose Debug impl is later printed (e.g., `unwrap()` panic backtraces) — leaks the full RNG state. The codebase has many tracing macros and unwrap call sites; the *attack* is just "find a path that prints a DetRng".

This is most consequential when:
  - DetRng outputs feed something tighter than scheduling randomness — see the cancel/symbol_cancel.rs and security/key.rs callers of `DetRng::next_u64` / `AuthKey::from_rng`. The current production wiring funnels worker.rs's DetRng only into stealing::steal_task victim selection (not crypto), so this is currently defence-in-depth rather than an immediate exploit. But the type itself is the right place to enforce the masking invariant — a future caller adding security-relevant uses must not be able to undo it from a distance.

Fix direction:
  1. Drop Debug from the derive list and write a manual impl that prints `DetRng { state: <redacted> }` (or just `DetRng(..)`).
  2. Optionally also drop Clone if no production caller relies on it — accidental `clone()` of an RNG produces two RNGs with identical streams, a separate but related correctness footgun.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/util/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in commit 8386926ef: replaced #[derive(Debug)] on DetRng with manual impl that prints 'DetRng { state: <redacted> }'. Added two regression tests (debug_does_not_leak_state across 8 seeds + debug_does_not_leak_state_after_advance verifying next-output value also stays out of Debug).

title: atp_checkpoint_recovery flake: a sibling test's subprocess spawn inherits the flock'd checkpoint lock, so a just-released checkpoint reports Busy; the Busy doc omits the transient case
description:
Found by the TLSSWEEP lane (kh02d2.1 class) at origin 239a7e478, hz4, `cargo test -j 1 --features tls,test-internals --no-fail-fast` over the 41 tls targets the rotation never runs: atp_checkpoint_recovery 6 passed / 2 failed.
- checkpoint_rehash_rejects_same_size_mutation_truncation_and_growth_before_networking: `inspect_checkpoint(..).unwrap()` on Err(Busy) at tests/atp_checkpoint_recovery.rs:546, right after `send_checkpoint` returned SourceChanged.
- checkpoint_binding_and_stricter_limits_are_checked_before_any_new_effect: :591, a second client's `send_checkpoint` did not return BindingMismatch. Lease::open runs before check_binding, so a Busy produces exactly this.
History: the same rehash test was red on ovh-a in the watchdog's 6a51af426 batch (P0 bi2462.147.101, 09-30) and green 8/0 on vmi1152480 at 669781fe4 (10-07). No ATP SDK source changed between 669781fe4 and 239a7e478. It is intermittent.

## Mechanism
- The checkpoint lock is `File::try_lock`, which is flock(2) on Linux. A flock belongs to the open file description, and every duplicate refers to the same lock.
- Three tests in the binary (process_exit, crashed_sender, os_lock) spawn this test executable with Command::spawn. glibc posix_spawn clones with CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK but not CLONE_FILES, so the child copies the whole fd table, including any checkpoint lock fd another test thread holds at that instant. The copy closes only when the child's execve closes O_CLOEXEC fds.
- libtest starts all 8 tests at once. If a sibling spawns while a test holds a lease, that test can close its lease and re-lock (inspect, or the next send) before the child execs. The re-lock then sees WouldBlock, so the API returns Busy for a checkpoint nobody cooperating owns. On a loaded worker, exec of a large debug test binary stretches the window.
- Ruled out: a blocking-pool closure keeping Arc<Lease> after its result. spawn_blocking_on_pool calls the closure by value under catch_unwind, so its captures drop before tx.send; verify_source's `_owner` drops inside the closure.

## Impact
- Tests: a recurring flake in a target the watchdog's targeted-tests[test-internals+tls] lane runs, which files P0 noise (bi2462.147.101).
- Library: any application that spawns subprocesses from another thread can get a transient Busy from inspect_checkpoint / send_checkpoint right after its own previous operation. It fails closed: a refusal, never two owners. The Busy doc ("Another cooperating handle/process owns this checkpoint") does not mention that the holder can be a just-spawned child that has not executed its program yet.

## Fix
1. tests/atp_checkpoint_recovery.rs: one process-wide mutex serializes the binary's tests. Each test's exact lock-state oracle assumes no third party holds a copy of the lock's file description. No assertion is weakened, and child processes run one test each.
2. src/net/atp/sdk/native/checkpoint.rs: the Busy doc says a subprocess spawned concurrently can hold the lock until it executes, so Busy can be transient. Docs only.
Evidence wanted: base vs fixed, the binary run repeatedly in parallel on one worker.
close_reason: Landed 4e24ce60c: tests serialized, Busy doc; base 7/60 parallel runs failed, fix 60/60

title: [ambient-hash-leak] types/symbol_set.rs SymbolSet::with_config uses HashMap::new() — RandomState breaks replay determinism
description:
src/types/symbol_set.rs:118-119 — SymbolSet::with_config (the public constructor reachable via SymbolSet::new() at line 110) initializes two HashMap fields with HashMap::new():

  symbols: HashMap::new(),
  block_counts: HashMap::new(),

HashMap::new() uses std::collections::hash_map::RandomState, which seeds the hasher from process-wide ambient entropy. SymbolSet is a public type used in public APIs; any iteration order observed by a consumer (snapshot, debug-print, serialize) varies across runs even with identical seeds.

Why this breaks the asupersync 'no ambient authority — effects flow through Cx' invariant: hasher randomization is ambient state pulled from the process. Two identical lab runs with the same RNG seed get different iteration orders, defeating replay determinism in any test that observes SymbolSet contents (directly or transitively via traces).

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) lab tests that assert on SymbolSet::iter() or trace events containing symbol counts become flaky.
  (b) replay tooling that compares hash-map serialization between runs reports spurious divergences.
  (c) cross-host trace comparison (e.g., distributed regression diffs) can never align.

Fix direction:
  1. Replace HashMap with crate::util::DetHashMap (FNV-1a, project-fixed seed) — preserves O(1) lookup + deterministic iteration via a stable hasher.
  2. Or use BTreeMap if total ordering on keys is acceptable.
  3. Or accept a hasher in with_config(): pub fn with_config_in(config, hasher_seed: u64) -> Self.

Severity HIGH because (a) reachable from public API SymbolSet::new(), (b) the project explicitly forbids ambient-hashing leaks (the otel CardinalityTracker fix bs92bg used the same pattern), and (c) the existing audit_index entry for symbol_set.rs marked it SOUND but missed this — a refresh-pass finding.

Source: /reality-check on src/types/* + src/record/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed: DetHashMap (commit 7a2c34b59)

title: [security] security/context.rs SecurityContext::with_mode allows runtime downgrade to Permissive — bypass strict auth
description:
src/security/context.rs:65-70 — pub fn with_mode(mut self, mode: AuthMode) -> Self is fully public; any caller can downgrade an existing SecurityContext to AuthMode::Permissive or AuthMode::Disabled at any time during its lifetime.

In Permissive mode the verification path (lines 110-114) increments failures_allowed but still ACCEPTS the symbol — so a caller that flipped a strict context to Permissive immediately starts accepting unauthenticated/tampered symbols silently.

Threat model: a compromised code path (or an external crate that holds a Cx and a SecurityContext) calls .with_mode(AuthMode::Permissive) on a context that was supposed to be strict, and the runtime keeps accepting bad symbols.

Fix direction: (a) downgrade with_mode to pub(crate); (b) introduce a lock_mode() method that freezes the current mode, enforced via a phantom-state type parameter (Locked vs Mutable); the SecurityContext returned by the public factory should already be Locked.

title: [perf] runtime/scheduler/worker.rs: WorkStealingWaker allocates Arc + 4 sub-clones on every first poll of every task
description: src/runtime/scheduler/worker.rs:367-373 Worker::execute, on first poll (cached_waker is None), constructs Waker::from(Arc::new(WorkStealingWaker { task_id, wake_state: Arc::clone(...), global: Arc::clone(...), local: Some(self.local.clone()), parker: self.parker.clone() })). Per task first-poll: 1 Arc allocation (heap) + 4 inner Arc::clone atomic ops (wake_state, global, parker, local — LocalQueue is itself Arc-backed) + Waker::from vtable construction. Total: 1 alloc + 5 atomic ops just to assemble a waker that the cached_waker.take() path correctly recycles afterward. For workloads spawning many short-lived tasks (e.g., per-request handlers), every task pays this cost on its first poll. Mitigation candidates: (a) construct the WorkStealingWaker once per Worker and re-bind task_id via interior atomic — but task_id semantics make this tricky; (b) have spawn pre-construct the cached_waker so first-poll never allocates; (c) inline the WorkStealingWaker fields into TaskRecord and use a static vtable that reads them by &record. Severity HIGH for high-throughput per-request task workloads.

title: [supervision] compile_restart_ops emits RestartChild for Stop-strategy children when fed restart_plan_for output
description:
Modes-of-reasoning lens (a) 'fault propagation up tree' and (b)
'restart strategy invariants' applied to src/supervision.rs surfaced
a composition gap between two pub APIs:

## The two restart-plan paths

src/supervision.rs has two pub entry points that produce a
SupervisorRestartPlan:

1. CompiledSupervisor::restart_plan_for(failed_child: &str)        (line 1289)
2. CompiledSupervisor::restart_plan_for_failure(name, &outcome)    (line 1370)

The two diverge in their per-child filtering:

- restart_plan_for_failure (line 1442-1454): filters restart_order
  by SupervisionStrategy — children whose strategy is Stop or
  Escalate are skipped from restart_order; cancel_order keeps them.
  Dependencies that aren't restartable are also filtered out.

- restart_plan_for (calls restart_plan_for_idx at line 1468): does
  NOT filter by SupervisionStrategy. cancel_order and restart_order
  both include every affected child regardless of per-child
  strategy.

The doc-comment at line 1284-1287 acknowledges this:

    Notes:
    - It does not consult per-child restartability (that is handled
      by per-child SupervisionStrategy in the runtime wiring).

## The bug

compile_restart_ops (line 1500) blindly emits a RestartChild op for
every name in plan.restart_order. It does NOT consult per-child
SupervisionStrategy.

So the obvious composition restart_plan_for + compile_restart_ops
produces a CompiledRestartOps that includes RestartChild for
Stop-strategy children. Concrete scenario:

- 3 children: A (Restart), B (Stop), C (Restart). Policy OneForAll. A fails.
- restart_plan_for("A") returns
    cancel_order=[C, B, A], restart_order=[A, B, C].
- compile_restart_ops emits 9 ops including RestartChild { name: \"B\" }.
- The runtime wiring restarts B even though its strategy is Stop.

## Why this is a real bug

The doc says 'handled by per-child SupervisionStrategy in the
runtime wiring' — placing the burden on the caller. But the obvious
caller is compile_restart_ops, which doesn't filter. So either:

(a) restart_plan_for should filter (match restart_plan_for_failure), OR
(b) compile_restart_ops should filter, OR
(c) docs should explicitly warn against the composition

(a) and (b) together as defense-in-depth is cleanest.

## Production impact today

\`grep -rn 'restart_plan_for\\b' src/ tests/\` shows the no-outcome
\`restart_plan_for\` is called only from supervision.rs's own tests
(lines 4497-4918). \`restart_plan_for_failure\` is the path the
metamorphic tests + production wiring use. So the immediate user
impact is low — but the public API exposes the foot-gun, and the
two test-coverage paths diverge.

## Fix

Add a SupervisionStrategy filter in compile_restart_ops's Phase 3
(RestartChild emission). cancel + drain stay unfiltered (Stop
children still need to be cancelled+drained when OneForAll/RestForOne
fires); only restart op is filtered. Defense-in-depth — both API
entry points become safe to compose with compile_restart_ops.

## Acceptance

1. compile_restart_ops Phase 3 only emits RestartChild for children
   whose SupervisionStrategy is Restart(_).
2. Add a regression test:
   - 3 children A (Restart), B (Stop), C (Restart). OneForAll.
   - Failure of A.
   - compile_restart_ops(restart_plan_for(\"A\")) emits 6 ops
     (3 cancel + 3 drain + 2 restart, NOT 3 restart).
3. Existing tests at lines 4677, 4702, 4729 (compile_restart_ops_*)
   continue to pass — they use make_restart_child for all children,
   so the filter is a no-op for them.
close_reason: Fix shipped at 4ffdc2d63 (src/supervision.rs::compile_restart_ops Phase 3 now filters RestartChild ops by per-child SupervisionStrategy::Restart). Bundled into another agent's commit chain alongside related supervision/grpc work. Regression test compile_restart_ops_skips_restart_for_stop_strategy_children added to verify 3-child OneForAll with one Stop-strategy child emits 8 ops (3 cancel + 3 drain + 2 restart), not 9. cargo check --lib clean. Existing compile_restart_ops_one_for_one/all/rest_for_one tests unaffected because they use make_restart_child for all children. Test verification via cargo test --lib remains blocked by unrelated grpc/server.rs compile breakage (untouched per AGENTS.md).
