title: ATP-N9: Add performance, usability, and no-regression acceptance scripts for real user workflows
description: A data movement layer should be judged by user-visible outcomes: time to first verified file, time to usable prefix, whole-object commit, resume after interruption, clarity of path doctor, bytes wasted, CPU/GiB, memory peak, and quality of failure explanation.
design: Create scripts that exercise realistic workflows: one huge file, many small files, sync tree with small edits, sparse image, model bundle, dataset, relay-only transfer, mailbox transfer, first-pairing transfer, interrupted transfer, and swarm/cache get. The scripts should produce concise human summaries plus detailed JSON/log bundles.
acceptance_criteria:
- Workflow e2e scripts record user-visible metrics and regression thresholds for realistic workflows.
- Scripts include interruption/resume, relay-only, mailbox, first-pairing, and cache/swarm scenarios.
- Output includes concise human summaries plus detailed JSON/log artifacts with command line, profile, transfer ID, path summary, manifest/proof root, bottleneck classification, and replay pointer.
- Failure assertions explain whether bottleneck was path, disk, CPU, repair, relay, permission, protocol, or user policy.
- Fast smoke mode and larger manual/regression mode are both defined, with deterministic fixture generation and explicit skip reasons for unavailable external tools.
- Benchmarks, UX snapshots, and e2e transcripts prevent accidental regressions in the user-facing experience.
notes: This bead keeps ATP focused on making the system better for users, not only passing internal invariants.
close_reason: Implemented ATP-N9 workflow acceptance smoke runner and cargo-enforced contract. Proof: python3 scripts/atp_perf/workflow_acceptance_smoke.py --contract-only --run-id atp-n9-manual-check --output-root target/atp_perf_acceptance_manual_check; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_p9 cargo fmt --check -- tests/atp_perf_workflow_acceptance_contract.rs tests/atp/perf/workflow_acceptance_contract.rs; rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_p9 cargo test -p asupersync --test atp_perf_workflow_acceptance_contract (4 passed).

title: [RAPTORQ-RFC6330][G7] Expected-Loss Decision Contract for Rollout, Abort, and Fallback
description: Define explicit decision-theoretic contracts for rollout/abort/fallback actions using state/action/loss modeling with auditable posterior/evidence inputs. This operationalizes alien-artifact quality governance so release decisions are principled and reproducible.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Decision contract defines explicit states (healthy, degraded, regression, unknown), actions (continue, canary-hold, rollback, fallback), and asymmetric loss matrix.
2. Contract is wired into runtime control surface so decode policy/kernels and advanced runtime levers (C6/E5/F7/F8 in addition to E4/C5/F5/F6) can be promoted, held, or reverted by expected-loss outcomes.
3. Contract output includes top evidence contributors, uncertainty/confidence score, and deterministic fallback trigger.
4. Unit + E2E Validation Requirement: decision engine has deterministic unit tests and E2E integration tests across normal, edge, and conflicting-evidence scenarios.
5. Structured Logging Requirement: each decision emits structured logs with state posterior, loss terms, chosen action, and replay pointers.
6. Reproducibility Requirement: every decision outcome can be replayed with fixed inputs from artifact bundle.
notes: Reopened on 2026-03-11 after stale in_progress audit: leaf task had no visible progress since 2026-03-05 and assignee PearlFox has no recent project activity. Returning to open for re-triage.
close_reason: G7 expected-loss decision contract already fully implemented with comprehensive state modeling, Bayesian inference, and 47 unit tests in src/raptorq/decision_contract.rs

title: Timer audit: cancelled timers linger in the wheel and next_deadline scans every entry under the global lock on each idle transition (MEDIUM, load); horizon clamp 1 ms early; coalescing doc; zero-duration wheel; waker drops under lock
description:
Read-only audit of src/time/driver.rs, src/time/wheel.rs, src/time/intrusive_wheel.rs and the park path at origin/main 2e816db92 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-04; read from origin). No timer fires twice, late at a level boundary, or is lost through the published park deadline.

## MEDIUM
1. Cancelled timers stay in the wheel holding their wakers (wheel.rs cancel ~553-568; storage purged only when the wheel is empty ~561/985/1099; stale entries dropped only when their slot is visited ~818-833 or promoted ~846-852; overflow pops stale only from the heap top ~627-633), and next_deadline walks every entry of every occupied slot (~609-625) under the wheel mutex (driver.rs ~594-602), called on every idle transition (three_lane.rs ~5141, ~5409). Sleep::reset and TimerDriver::update cancel + re-register, adding stale entries. 100k req/s each wrapped in timeout(30s) that completes: ~3M stale entries (~90 B each) for ~65 s; overflow timers (>24 h) can linger ~6 days; each idle worker scans millions of entries holding the lock, delaying register/cancel/process_timers (timers fire late under load). Fix: per level scan occupied slots from cursor+1 and stop at the first live entry (min across levels, ready, overflow top); compact (retain is_live) when stale > ~2x live + C.

## LOW
2. The horizon clamp (wheel.rs ~491-500) uses now rounded down to the 1 ms tick, while the driver rustdoc (~723-727) and Sleep's registered_partial (sleep.rs ~916) assume now + max: a sleep of exactly the 7-day horizon can complete up to 1 ms early. Fix: clamp against the exact driver now, or return whether it clamped.
3. Coalescing fires timers up to one window early (wheel.rs ~926-977, next_deadline ~579-581) while its rustdoc says at the window boundary; TimerDriver never enables coalescing (public TimerWheel only). Doc fix (behaviour change otherwise; a test asserts the early fire).
4. max_wheel_duration(Duration::ZERO): every timer goes to overflow and never promotes (delta saturates at 0), and collect_expired steps one tick at a time (O(elapsed ms)). Fix: floor at 1 ns or the default.
5. (suspected trigger) Wakers are dropped under the wheel lock in purge_inactive_storage/cascade/collect_bucket/refill_overflow; a waker whose drop re-enters the driver deadlocks (parking_lot not re-entrant). Fix: move to a local list, drop after unlock.

## Checked and sound
Cascade boundaries, past/sub-ms deadlines, skip-ahead, overflow promotion clamp, handle generations (no stale cancel, no double fire), next_deadline cross-level min, published park deadline and reactor wakes, lock order, saturating tick arithmetic, intrusive wheel.

title: Request region audit: handler-spawned tasks outlive their request (request region lends the connection's gateway); deadline misreported as Cancelled/ConnectionLost; shutdown drain busy-spins when the listener is cancelled
description:
Read-only audit of src/web/request_region.rs and src/server/shutdown.rs at origin/main 8ce1b742a (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-05).

## HIGH
H1. A "request region" is not a region: work a handler spawns outlives its request.
- Where: child_cx_from_connection (request_region.rs ~969-979) lends the connection's spawn gateway, so Cx::spawn admits into the connection's region. Nothing in run_with_protocol_drain or Drop cancels, waits for or closes it.
- The module docs (~6-13, ~27-33) promise that spawned tasks are cancelled and drained when the handler returns.
- This design came from vqppo5 (46ac25c70).
- Reachable on:
  - plain h1 (server.rs ~1161), h1 streaming/produced (~1555, ~1952);
  - h2 produced (listener.rs ~3063, ownership.rs ~226);
  - h3 router produced (router.rs ~2323);
  - gRPC server streaming.
  - The h2 buffered path and the h3 listener already open a real child region per request.
- Impact: handler-spawned tasks, finalizers and obligations attach to the connection's region (the root under Http1Listener::run), so they live until runtime shutdown, and the listener drain reports quiescence while request work still runs.
- Fix: open a per-request child region (as run_owned_h2_hop does), mint the request Cx from it, and cancel and close it within a bound after the hop. Or rewrite the docs. Needs an owner/design decision (per-request region cost on the h1 hot path).

## MEDIUM
- M1. A deadline already past at handler start is reported as Cancelled, not DeadlineExceeded (pre-gate ~1137-1141). On h2 this sends RST_STREAM(CANCEL) instead of a 503 with ASUP-E501.
- M2. When the connection Cx is the request Cx itself (h2 buffered and produced), the request's own deadline is reported as ConnectionLost (~1168-1177, ~1200-1221).
- M3. ShutdownSignal::wait_until awaited a cancel-aware Sleep, so a cancelled listener task (shutdown by region close) made drain_with_stats and the listener supervision ticks busy-spin at 100 % until drain_timeout or hard_drain_timeout. FIXED in stack P (P15) for wait_until via Sleep::poll_deadline. The h1/h2 listener supervision tick sleeps (h1/listener.rs ~1009, h2/listener.rs ~5344) need the same.

## LOW
- L1. begin_drain publishes the Draining phase before the drain deadline. A concurrent drain_with_stats can park in the no-deadline branch.
- L2. Lost wakeup in drain_with_stats: notified() captured its generation only at first poll, after the re-checks. FIXED in stack P (P15): enable() right after pinning.
- L3. mint() prefers the runtime root over the ambient task Cx (gRPC unary, h2 run_produced). cancel_timeout's doc promise cannot hold for the gRPC caller.
- L4. RequestRegion docs claim region close, finalizers and obligation abort that run* does not do. A deadline-exhausted pre-check maps to 499.

Adjacent: the h2 buffered path closes each per-request region with an unbounded ChildRegion::close(), so a handler-spawned task that ignores cancellation blocks connection exit past the hard deadline.

title: ATP crashpack replay audit (r16): `atp replay` reports "reproduced" without re-executing anything; trace-witness matching accepts negations and blanket event kinds; replay script check passes injected commands
description:
Read-only audit of src/lab/crashpack/replay.rs (ATP crashpack replay) at origin de7bf4633 (round r16-d0 A3, SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-09). Full report with line-level evidence and test sketches: /data/tmp/rc_20260922/audit_r16_A3_crashpack_replay.md. Scope note: this ATP crashpack holds oracle results, trace events, a seed map, artifact paths and metadata. It has no config, scenario or schedule/decision stream, so nothing can be re-executed from it. The general LabRuntime crashpack replay lives elsewhere and was not covered.

## HIGH
H1. `asupersync atp replay` reports "reproduced" without replaying anything (replay() 45-69; CLI src/bin/asupersync.rs ~8019-8025, ~5283-5288).
- replay() validates the bundle and checks that the recorded trace holds a witness for each violation. It never executes anything and never reads the seeds; the ATP_SEED_* exports in the generated script are read by nothing.
- replay_successful (53-54) is true once the bundle validates, and the CLI then prints "ATP Replay: reproduced" with exit 0.
- That contradicts the docs ("Execute ATP replay with the given seeds", line 45; "This command reproduces the captured failure deterministically", line 75) and the closed bead nod48i ("atp replay can reproduce deterministic lab failures").
- Example: after the bug is fixed, rerunning the generated script still prints "reproduced".
H2. The trace-witness check accepts traces that do not contain the failure (event_witnesses_violation and friends, 554-703; missing_violation_witnesses 305-322).
- Failure markers are plain substrings, so a negation counts: "no leak detected" witnesses an obligation_leak violation.
- The oracle name is added as an alias for every one of that oracle's violations.
- Any IoError or ChaosInjection event witnesses any journal/path violation.
- One event can witness any number of violations.
- The trace buffer is a ring and can evict the real witness, so these heuristics are what decide "witnessed" in practice.

## MEDIUM
M1. validate_replay_artifacts (972-1010) returns replay_ready: true for a replay_command.sh with extra commands. Lines after the invocation are never read, export lines are skipped, and `; cmd` on the invocation line is allowed. Nothing hashes the script.
M2. Crashpacks the runtime emits itself are rejected as tampered, failing closed but blaming drift:
- an oracle name repeated with mixed pass/fail (1278-1298);

title: [SCHED-PERF][E2] Convert region/obligation lifecycle (B/C shards) off the unified lock — the architectural bound on E1.3's contended parity

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-29 — successor to E1.2 (bt4y5f.2.2, closed) per the
E1.3 evidence verdict (bt4y5f.2.3 comments + the six-run dossier in
artifacts/flamegraphs/main-bt4y5f23-attribution.md).

WHY: E1.2 moved only shard A (tasks) behind the dispatch table; the
unified RuntimeState remains the B/C/D lifecycle owner, so EVERY task
completion still crosses the unified lock on BOTH shapes
(three_lane.rs complete_polled_task_ordered takes the shard-A guard,
releases it, then takes the full unified state for
task_completed_from_external_record). The E1.3 dossier measured exactly
that: contended-cell PARITY at workers=4 (clean medians 0.976-1.015).
The default flip (bt4y5f.2.3 ACs 3-4) is blocked until this converts.

SCOPE (from the E1.1 proof note, artifacts/proof_notes/
main-asupersync-sched-hot-path-perf-bt4y5f.2.1.md):
1. Region table (shard B) + obligation table (shard C) become
   ShardedState-resident with the same Arc-alias seam pattern E1.2 used
   for shard A (subsystem 3c precedent).
2. Completion converts to ShardGuard::for_task_completed (B -> A -> C):
   the finish_task_completion shard-phase decomposition (subsystem 3b)
   was designed for exactly this — audit_completion_obligation_leaks
   (C), retire_completed_finalizer_barrier (B), abort_orphaned_
   obligations_for_holder (C), retire_completed_task_record (A),
   unlink_completed_task_from_region (B).
3. Spawn admission converts to ShardGuard::for_spawn (B -> A): rows
   B09/B10 + the mailbox admission seam.
4. Completion-path rows W02/W05/W08 (D -> B -> A -> C) and W09/T22
   finalizer drain (B -> A); T16-T23 completion cluster.
5. Whole-state snapshots (B02/T06/T07/T14) via ShardGuard::all ordered
   reads.
GUARDRAILS: one subsystem per commit (bisection); ShardGuard label tests
extended per site; the shape-identity corpus + per-task seq tripwire
must stay green at every slice; loom lane rerun at completion seams;
validator/epoch/instrumentation stay unified (D) until a dedicated
slice. The E1.2 recorded lessons apply: deferred effects dispatch
outside guards; no tracing under shard locks (u5jdvw class).
EXIT CRITERIA: completion + spawn paths acquire NO unified whole-state
lock on the hot path; rerun the E1.3 contended dossier (same
methodology: in-process pairing, >=3 runs, ratio metric) — if the
contended cells then show the shard win, bt4y5f.2.3 ACs 3-4 unblock.

regions/obligations become Arc<ContendedMutex<...>> with
region_shard_handle()/obligation_shard_handle(), byte-for-byte the 3c

move. Scheduler helpers drain_ready_finalizers_locked /

unified maps; dependent wakes read the task table = shard A).

SapphireHill 2026-07-30 — S4c-2b LANDED (commit referencing this bead).

The REGION minting seams — with these, every minting path (obligation
create, region root, region child) plus the full completion/advance
surface operates against explicit targets, completing the reachability
prerequisite for the S4c completion-arm flip:

- create_root_region_in(regions, effects, ...): mint = bare Shard B op
  via resolve_mut; root_region residue stays in-core (unobservable
  relative order inside the critical section — documented); validator
  track + trace + metrics + epoch dispatch as
  RegionLifecycleEffect::CreatedRoot.
- create_child_region_in(regions, effects, ...): pressure admission
  stays in-core (unified residue); mint = bare Shard B op (parent link
  + capability admission); pressure-priority registration + validator
  track + trace + metrics + envelope registration + epoch dispatch as
  RegionLifecycleEffect::CreatedChild (Budget/CapabilityBudget/
  RegionPriority are Copy — carried in the payload).
- Enum/sink RENAMED RegionAdvanceEffect(sSink) →
  RegionLifecycleEffect(sSink) (minting is not an advance), dispatcher/
  emit now &mut self (epoch advances live in the created-effects
  dispatchers, matching the obligation twins). All public wrappers
  unchanged (create_root_region, create_child_region + the
  with_priority/with_capability_budget funnels).

comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-30 — S4c-2c PRE-IMPLEMENTATION ANALYSIS (plan-changing;
the flip decomposes further — read before implementing).

VERDICT: S4c-2c as a single slice would break the sharded corpus. Flipping
minting+completion to shard B/C makes EVERY embedded self.regions /
self.obligations touch on a sharded-exercised path a divergence site. A
precise inventory (53 raw embedded touches in state.rs after excluding the
threaded resolve_ref/resolve_mut patterns) shows three whole clusters the
S1-S4c-2b program never threaded because they sit off the completion/
advance/minting paths:

1. FINALIZER MACHINERY (B reads, ~9 fns): register_sync_finalizer,
   register_async_finalizer, pop_tracked_finalizer, region_finalizer_count,
   region_finalizers_empty, settle_manual_finalizer,
   take_next_finalizer_tracked, run_sync_finalizers_tracked,
   drive_failed_start_async_finalizer_inline + the region reads INSIDE
   drain_ready_async_finalizers_in (6231/6257 — its task side is threaded,
   its region side is not).
2. CANCEL CLUSTER (B reads, 4 fns): cancel_request (region walk: get_mut
   begin_close, task-id copy, finalizer advance check),
   cancel_sibling_tasks, collect_region_and_descendants_with_depth,
   validate_live_region_protocol_transition. Production-reachable on
   sharded builds (app.rs shutdown paths call state.cancel_request).
3. QUIESCENCE + ACCESSORS (B+C reads): is_quiescent (regions.iter().all —
   on an empty shard-B table this passes VACUOUSLY and block_on would
   report quiescent-when-not: flip-critical), pending_obligation_count/
   _for_kind/_reserved_sum, capacity_hints, set_read_biased_region_snapshot,
   set_region_limits/region_limits/region_capability_budget,
   set_region_priority, and the pub accessors (region/region_mut/
   regions_iter/len/is_empty + obligation twins).

ARCHITECTURE DECISION (for the flip slice): RuntimeState gains
shard_tables: Option<Arc<ShardedState>>, installed by the builder right
after ShardedState construction; PUBLIC WRAPPERS resolve
Embedded-vs-External internally (clone the Arc, lock via the labeled
ShardGuard constructors, build targets, call the _in cores, drain buffered
effects). Rationale from the full production caller map (44 sites, 14
files): B/C ops originate from state/Cx-internal contexts — io_op.rs
(note io_op.rs:65 passes RuntimeState::commit_obligation as a FN ITEM
coerced to FnOnce: signatures are pinned), cx/scope.rs (region mint +
advance incl. Drop for RegionRunner), app.rs/supervision.rs boot/teardown,
builder root mint — NOT from the scheduler, so E1.2's scheduler-side
resolution cannot reach them, and wrapper-side resolution reaches ALL of
them with zero call-site edits. LabRuntime constructs RuntimeState
directly (pub state field, 17 lab call sites) → field stays None → lab is
Embedded forever, untouched. tests/cx_*audit.rs pin literal delegation
source text in state.rs/scope.rs — wrapper-internal resolution keeps that
text intact. state_backing.rs RuntimeStateBacking is a zero-consumer dead
seam (30atgp.2 superseded) — ignored.

UNION EFFECTS BUFFER (fixes an interleaving hazard in the S4c sketch):
the guard-held arm's orphan-abort loop interleaves obligation-settle
payloads with each abort's advance-walk REGION payloads. Draining two
typed buffers sequentially would reorder them vs the unified shape
(corpus-visible: trace-event order). Both sinks' Buffered variants
therefore change to hold &mut Vec<CompletionDeferredEffect> where
CompletionDeferredEffect = Obligation(ObligationLifecycleEffect) |
Region(RegionLifecycleEffect) | ValidatorRemoveObligation(ObligationId) —
legal now because ZERO Buffered constructors exist yet (External-arm
posture). One drain replays push order exactly. The per-settle validator
remove becomes its own buffered payload so the Inline wrappers stay
byte-identical (today: remove fires between the settle dispatch and the
advance walk; the payload keeps that slot on the buffered shape).

FINDING (pre-existing, NOT introduced by this program): cancel_request's
task pass uses embedded update_task (shard A miss on sharded builds) —
region records transition but shard-A-resident tasks are not cancelled
unless the cancel arrives via the scheduler seams (handle-cancel mailbox,
deferred dispatch coordinator). Reachable via app.rs shutdown on
with_sharded_state builds. Filing as its own bead; the flip must be
no-worse, full cancel task-pass threading is a separate row.

SLICE ORDER (each corpus-green, one commit each):
S4c-2c-i:   finalizer-machinery B-threading (all-Embedded wrappers).
S4c-2c-ii:  cancel cluster + quiescence/accessor B/C-threading.
S4c-2c-iii: settle _in cores (commit/abort/mark_leaked) + union buffer +
            buffered drain (live via Embedded/Inline wrappers).
S4c-2c-iv:  THE FLIP: shard_tables field + builder install + root-region
            mint ordering (root currently mints BEFORE ShardedState
            exists: builder.rs:4004 vs :4058) + wrapper resolution +
            External flips at the 5 scheduler/builder admission seams +
            the guard-held completion arm in complete_polled_task_ordered
            (unified residue → ShardGuard::for_task_completed phases →
            post-shard-release wake/finalizer re-lock (waiter_wake_metadata
            re-locks A per waiter — must run after guard release) → union
            drain under unified) + loom lane + label constructors/tests +
            corpus/tripwire + E1.3 dossier rerun.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-31 — S4c-2c-iv DESIGN FORK (plan-relevant evidence
found while scoping S4c-2c-ii; decide at iv, recorded now).

THE FORK: reference-returning pub accessors cannot resolve shard tables.
region(&self) -> Option<&RegionRecord>, region_mut, regions_iter,
obligation(&self), obligation_mut, obligations_iter (state.rs ~3050-3130)
return borrows of the embedded tables; a shard-resident record sits
behind ContendedMutex, and a reference cannot outlive the guard. These
are NOT internal conveniences: app.rs has ~30 production call sites
(boot/teardown/shutdown state machines read region records for state/
outcome/counts), cx/scope.rs has 21 (region_with_child_admission reads
limits/capability budget/state; Drop for RegionRunner reads the child
region), cx/cx.rs has 3. E1.2 accepted exactly this gap for tasks
(state.task() returns None for shard-A residents) and it produced the
mnebts bug class plus three logical-time divergences we spent S3 fixing.
Moving REGION records to shard B multiplies that gap across the runtime's
primary user-facing state surface.

OPTIONS AT iv:
(A) Closure-convert the accessor surface (state.with_region(id, f) etc.)
    so wrapper-side resolution can lock shard B internally. Mechanical
    but wide: ~55 production call sites + lab/tests; changes public API
    texture of RuntimeState.
(B) Regions/obligations stay EMBEDDED as storage; the sharded completion
    arm keeps taking the unified lock for B/C phases but through the
    already-threaded seams; the contended win is then limited to what
    E1.2 already bought (A-only paths off the unified lock) plus the
    residue-window shrink from the S4b/S4c decompositions (validator/
    trace/metrics dispatch moved outside the critical path). The E1.3
    dossier rerun MEASURES whether that shrink alone moves the contended
    cells; if parity persists, (A) or S5 remain the levers.
(C) Hybrid: obligations (C) move to the shard (no reference-returning
    C accessor has production callers outside state.rs — obligation()/
    obligations_iter callers are lab/test-only per the caller map),
    regions (B) stay embedded pending (A). Halves the flip surface and
    covers the completion path's hottest C-phases (settles, orphan
    aborts, leak audits) — but completion's B-phases (unlink/advance)
    still cross the unified lock, which the E1.3 dossier identified as
    crossing on EVERY completion.

LEAN: (C) first (measurable, small), then decide (A) with dossier data.
Slice ii/iii threading serves all three options identically. The union
effects buffer (pre-analysis) is required for (A) and (C), harmless
under (B).

Slice-ii content note: cancel_request/cancel_sibling_tasks task passes
now read/write through AdmissionTaskTarget with per-record logical time
from the owning table — that is the mnebts fix STRUCTURED; it activates
when the sharded wrapper resolves External at iv (mnebts stays open
until then and closes with the flip slice).

title: [fuzz] fuzz/fuzz_targets/broadcast_lag.rs:388 receiver_count assertion diverges on DropReceiver — shadow-only flag vs real Arc-count
description:
broadcast_lag.rs:386-393 asserts senders[0].receiver_count() (real Arc-strong-count of live Receiver objects) equals receiver_active.iter().filter(|a| **a).count() (shadow-only active flag). These diverge by construction: DropReceiver at line 245-252 ONLY flips receiver_active[i]=false; the real receivers[i] is NEVER dropped (intentional per comment at line 250: "We don't actually drop the receiver object to keep indices stable").

Concrete repro:
  T0: capacity=1, initial_receivers=2 → receivers=[r0,r1], receiver_active=[true,true], real_count=2
  T1: BroadcastOperation::DropReceiver{receiver_index=0} → receiver_active=[false,true], real receivers Vec unchanged (still has r0,r1), shadow_active_count=1
  T2: assert at 388 fires: senders[0].receiver_count()=2 != active_receiver_count=1 → fuzz target panics

This means EITHER the fuzz target has never reached this branch in practice, OR the panic has been silently surfacing as a discovered crash that nobody noticed. Either way it is a test-correctness bug.

Suggested fix options:
  (a) ACTUALLY drop the receiver: replace receiver_active[i]=false with let _dead = receivers.remove(i); and rebuild parallel index tracking.
  (b) DON'T assert the receiver_count: just remove lines 386-393, OR compare against receivers.len() (always equals total subscribed count) instead of active_receiver_count.
  (c) Use a separate Vec<Option<Receiver>> where DropReceiver does receivers[i] = None to actually drop the real receiver while preserving index stability. Then real receiver_count tracks active.

Option (c) is the cleanest: minimal index-arithmetic disturbance plus real-channel state matches shadow. Option (a) requires re-deriving all (op_idx % len) index math. Option (b) loses a real invariant check.

This bug is in the test infrastructure, not production code. P2 because it either silently masks correctness failures or floods the corpus with red-herring crashes that block the fuzzer from finding genuine bugs.

title: Distributed Tracing Integration
description:
EPIC: OpenTelemetry Integration for Structured Concurrency Observability

## Background & Problem  
Structured concurrency creates natural observability boundaries but lacks production-grade tracing:
- No visibility into region lifecycle and hierarchy
- Task spawning and cancellation events are opaque
- Debugging production issues requires manual instrumentation
- Operations teams cannot understand async program behavior
- Performance bottlenecks are difficult to identify

This is a major adoption blocker for asupersync in production environments.

## Solution: Native OpenTelemetry Integration
Create spans for structured concurrency operations with context propagation:
1. Region spans (create/close with quiescence detection)
2. Task spans (spawn/complete/cancel with parent region context)  
3. Cancellation event spans (propagation chains, drain operations)
4. Operation spans (IO, timer, channel operations with cancel context)
5. Automatic context propagation through structured concurrency boundaries

## Span Hierarchy Design


## Business Value
- Production-grade observability without manual instrumentation
- Unprecedented visibility into async program execution
- Enables using asupersync in enterprise/ops-heavy environments
- Significantly improves debugging and performance analysis

## Success Metrics  
- Full structured concurrency hierarchy visible in traces
- <2% performance overhead for span creation
- Spans contain actionable structured concurrency context
- Integration works with major observability backends (Jaeger, Zipkin)
close_reason: Designed comprehensive OpenTelemetry structured concurrency integration with automatic span creation, lazy materialization, context propagation, and <2% performance overhead. Created design document at docs/otel_structured_concurrency_design.md and core implementation in src/observability/otel_structured_concurrency.rs with span storage, sampling strategies, and rich structured concurrency semantics.

title: [mock-code-finder][h2] Replace PRIORITY conformance placeholders with real priority-state assertions
description:
Background: conformance/src/h2_priority_conformance.rs currently contains helpers such as simulate_priority_frame_processing and extract_asupersync_priority_states that can return success or empty state without exercising production HTTP/2 behavior. Live source already has PriorityFrame and PrioritySpec parsing in src/http/h2/frame.rs, stream priority state in src/http/h2/stream.rs, and Frame::Priority handling in src/http/h2/connection.rs.

Goal: replace priority conformance simulations with tests that feed real PRIORITY frames through the shared HTTP/2 conformance adapter and assert observable state, errors, or narrow truthful test-only accessors.

Design considerations: HTTP/2 priority is often underspecified in application behavior, but conformance must still prove parser and state-machine truth. If asupersync intentionally ignores scheduling weight for now, the test must assert that truthful supported subset rather than fake a complete priority scheduler. The bead should preserve future room for priority-tree scheduling without pretending it exists today.
acceptance_criteria: All PRIORITY simulate/extract helpers are removed or replaced by calls into the shared real H2 adapter. Tests cover parsing valid PRIORITY payloads, rejecting stream id 0 where required, applying priority to an idle stream or existing stream according to asupersync semantics, preserving dependency and weight fields, handling exclusive dependency, and truthfully documenting any intentionally unsupported scheduling behavior. No test may pass because extract_asupersync_priority_states returns an empty Vec. Validation must include rch-backed H2 conformance tests and targeted src/http/h2 frame/connection/stream tests. Closeout must list removed placeholder helpers, live source seams used, and any remaining priority scheduling limitations with follow-up bead IDs.

title: quic_native/quic_core GH#69: header protection is never applied or removed (RFC 9001 s5.4); decode_long_header validates reserved bits and pn-length from the wire byte
description: GitHub #69 (FrankenRemote D4). Verified at HEAD: PacketProtectionProvider::header_protection_mask has ZERO call sites, so no packet on the wire has header protection applied and the decoders read reserved bits and packet-number length straight from the protected first byte (decode_long_header rejects a compliant quinn Initial with packet_header_decode; the self-pair works only because both ends skip HP). This is an RFC 9001 feature gap on both send and receive, not a decode-order bug. WHAT: (1) send side: after AEAD, sample ciphertext[pn_offset+4..+20], mask first byte (0x0f long / 0x1f short) and the pn bytes; (2) receive side: decode only invariant header fields, sample, remove HP, then validate reserved bits, read pn length and packet number (RFC 9001 s5.4.1-5.4.2, Appendix A samples); apply to Initial/Handshake (handshake_driver recv_handshake_packet) and 1-RTT (unprotect_1rtt_packet / short header). Existing goldens that pin unprotected wire bytes must be updated deliberately. Verification: RFC 9001 A.2/A.3/A.5 test vectors as unit tests; self-pair loopback suites; then the quinn interop scenario in franken_remote/spikes/quic-native (or a conformance/-crate quinn harness). Related: GH#68 (padding, fixed), GH#70 (coalescing).
close_reason: GH#69 fixed in c72aae490: RFC 9001 s5.4 header protection applied on send and removed on receive for Initial/Handshake/1-RTT, both directions, with RFC 9001 Appendix A vectors and bit-flip negatives; receipts on the bead; issue closed.

title: [memory-leak] transport/router.rs RoutingTable has no remove_endpoint method — Arc Endpoint references leak forever
description:
src/transport/router.rs:1048-1059 — RoutingTable provides register_endpoint() but no remove_endpoint() / unregister_endpoint() / prune_dead_endpoints(). Endpoints inserted into the endpoints HashMap never leave it.

Threat model:
  (a) Long-running services that dynamically scale endpoints (k8s pod churn, blue/green deploys, cloud autoscaling) accumulate dead Endpoint Arcs forever. Each holds metrics state, atomic counters, dispatch history, etc. Memory grows unbounded over uptime.
  (b) Phantom-routing: if an endpoint goes offline but stays in the routing table, dispatches to it loop on connect-failure/retry until the load-balancer's health check eventually marks it. With no removal, even a known-dead endpoint never goes away.
  (c) ABA reuse: if an EndpointId is reissued (e.g., the same logical endpoint reappears at a new address), there is no way to drop the old entry first. The new registration may collide or silently update the old entry, causing stale-address dispatches.
  (d) ID exhaustion: if EndpointId is u64-allocated, no exhaustion in practice; if it's a String per the audit, then unbounded ID growth.

Concrete leak shape: each Endpoint holds metrics counters + dispatch history + last_success/failure timestamps + label maps. Conservative estimate: 1-2 KiB per endpoint. A service with 100 pods/day x 90 days = 9000 dead entries x 1.5 KiB = ~13 MiB leaked. Plus the metric counters underneath, which may be much larger.

Fix direction:
  1. Add pub fn remove_endpoint(id) returning Option Arc Endpoint, that removes from the endpoints map AND from any LoadBalancer-internal indexes (HashRing, weighted lists, etc.).
  2. Add pub fn prune_unhealthy(threshold) that iterates and removes endpoints with no successful dispatch within threshold.
  3. Pair with a regression test that registers + removes 10000 endpoints and asserts the underlying HashMap len returns to 0.
  4. Document the lifecycle expectation in RoutingTable's public docs.

Severity HIGH because (a) long-running production services WILL hit this (k8s churn is constant), (b) the leak is silent (no error, just slow memory growth), and (c) the absence of a removal method violates the asupersync invariant 'no obligation leaks' — Endpoints are obligations the routing table holds onto without cleanup.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/transport/* deepest pass (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed: RoutingTable::remove_endpoint added (commit dd6e3b705)

title: RedisClient Debug impl self-deadlocks: re-entrant parking_lot lock in field-chain temporaries
description: src/messaging/redis.rs:2300-2317 — RedisClient::fmt builds f.debug_struct(...).field(...).field(...).field(...).finish_non_exhaustive() and calls self.resp3_push_backlog.lock() TWICE in the same statement (lines 2310 and 2314). Per Rust temporary-scope rules, all MutexGuards produced by .lock() in a method-chain expression live until the end of the enclosing statement. parking_lot::Mutex is non-re-entrant — the second .lock() blocks forever waiting for the first guard to drop, but the first guard is held by the same thread on the stack. Any caller that formats {client:?} (tracing::debug, panic message, assert_eq, structured logging) self-deadlocks the calling thread. CRITICAL because Debug is the canonical observability hook and this fires on the first format invocation. Fix: snapshot pending/dropped under a single lock acquisition into local Copy values, then pass those into .field. Also same-statement double-lock would deadlock self.slot_map if it appeared twice; current code locks it only once but the pattern is fragile — use snapshot pattern uniformly.
close_reason: Fix landed in cf082df73. RedisClient::fmt now snapshots known_slot_mappings (slot_map.lock().len()) and (pending_resp3_pushes, resp3_push_dropped) (single backlog.lock() scope) into local Copy values BEFORE the .field chain, eliminating the re-entrant parking_lot::Mutex acquisition. Regression test redis_client_debug_fmt_does_not_self_deadlock_mc0lgn runs format!({client:?}) on a worker thread with a 2s recv_timeout and asserts both snapshots render correctly. Test passed: 1 passed; 0 failed; finished in 0.00s — proves the deadlock no longer fires. Found via /deadlock-finder-and-fixer Class 1 static-audit scan over src/messaging/.

title: QUIC RTT: ack_delay not scaled by 2^ack_delay_exponent + not clamped by max_ack_delay (RFC 9000 §19.3 / 9002 §5.3)
close_reason: ACK Delay scaling + max_ack_delay clamp landed (52b068548); 263/0 connection/transport/tls tests green

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
VERIFIED via fresh-eyes review + independent adversarial review, confirmed against
the code. RTT ack_delay is decoded and used incorrectly in two ways that compound.

## Bug A — no 2^ack_delay_exponent scaling (RFC 9000 §19.3)
connection.rs process_frame_at (QuicFrame::Ack, ~line 2320) passes
`ack_delay.value()` (the raw ACK-Delay varint) directly to on_ack_ranges as
micros. RFC 9000 §19.3: the ACK Delay field is in units of 2^ack_delay_exponent
microseconds. For 1-RTT ACKs the exponent is the peer's negotiated
ack_delay_exponent (transport param; default 3, RFC 9000 §18.2); Initial/Handshake
ACKs use the default exponent 3. With the default, the value reaching RttEstimator
is 8x too small — ack_delay is barely subtracted, so RTT samples are over-estimated
(conservative today, but wrong).

## Bug B — no clamp by max_ack_delay (RFC 9002 §5.3)
RttEstimator::update (transport.rs ~103-133) subtracts ack_delay (guarded so the
sample stays >= min_rtt) but never clamps ack_delay by max_ack_delay. RFC 9002
§5.3: after the handshake is confirmed, ack_delay = min(ack_delay, peer_max_ack_delay).
Without it, a peer that reports a large ack_delay can deflate our smoothed RTT
toward min_rtt -> shorter loss_delay + PTO -> spurious retransmits. Bug A partly
masks Bug B today (un-scaled ack_delay is small), which is why the two MUST be
fixed together: fixing A (scale up ~8x) without B removes the mask and makes the
deflation worse.

## Related gap (same root cause)
apply_peer_transport_parameters (connection.rs:1530) stores only migration_disabled
and max_datagram_frame_size; it DISCARDS the peer's ack_delay_exponent AND
max_ack_delay. Consequently LossRecovery.max_ack_delay_micros stays at the default
25_000 forever and is never set from the peer's advertised value — so the PTO
computation (transport.rs lines 528, 820) also uses the default rather than the
negotiated max_ack_delay. Plumbing the peer's max_ack_delay fixes both the RTT
clamp (Bug B) and the PTO calc.

## Fix design (RFC-precise)
1. connection.rs struct: add `peer_ack_delay_exponent: u32` (default 3) and
   `peer_max_ack_delay_micros: u64` (default 25_000), with constructor defaults.
2. apply_peer_transport_parameters: set them from params (ack_delay_exponent,
   max_ack_delay; RFC-cap exponent <= 20), and push peer_max_ack_delay into the
   transport machine (new setter) so PTO uses it too.
3. tls.rs: add `pub fn handshake_confirmed(&self) -> bool` (additive accessor).
4. connection.rs: decode_ack_delay(space, raw) helper:
   - exponent = if space == ApplicationData { self.peer_ack_delay_exponent } else { 3 };
   - scaled = raw.value().checked_shl(exponent).unwrap_or(u64::MAX);
   - if self.tls().handshake_confirmed() && space == ApplicationData {
        scaled.min(self.peer_max_ack_delay_micros) } else { scaled }
   Use it at ~line 2320 instead of ack_delay.value(). (RttEstimator's existing
   min_rtt guard keeps the floor.)

## Test plan
- Unit: decode_ack_delay scales by exponent per space and clamps by max_ack_delay
  only when confirmed.
- Unit: RttEstimator picks up the (now correctly scaled) ack_delay; smoothed_rtt
  does not fall below min_rtt; a hostile large ack_delay is capped at max_ack_delay.
- EXPECT test fallout: existing RTT/PTO fixtures that assumed the un-scaled
  ack_delay will change; re-baseline each to the RFC-correct value (as was done for
  the f3x3e3 in_flight_packet test), verifying the new value is what RFC 9002
  prescribes, not just "make it pass".

## Risk / why not rushed
Behavior-changing to the RTT/PTO timers in a peer-owned, actively-developed file;
the scaling makes recovery more aggressive (shorter timers). A subtle error causes
spurious retransmissions. Deserves a focused implementation with careful test
re-baselining, not an end-of-marathon rush. Author SapphireHill (found alongside
asupersync-f3x3e3; this is the deferred FINDING 2). Also-deferred-from-same-review:
persistent-congestion (RFC 7.6), zero-in-flight anti-deadlock PTO, minor RTT-order
deviations (all benign-direction).

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
CLOSED — implemented + verified green.

FIX (RFC 9000 §19.3 scaling + RFC 9002 §5.3 clamp):
- connection.rs: store peer ack_delay_exponent (default 3) + max_ack_delay
  (default 25ms, ms->us) in apply_peer_transport_parameters; feed max_ack_delay
  to the transport machine (new set_peer_max_ack_delay_micros) so PTO uses it
  too; new decode_ack_delay(space, raw) — scale by 2^exponent (peer's for 1-RTT,
  default 3 for Initial/Handshake) then clamp by max_ack_delay only once
  handshake-confirmed on ApplicationData; applied at the ACK-frame decode site.
- tls.rs: additive QuicTlsMachine::handshake_confirmed() accessor.
- transport.rs: set_peer_max_ack_delay_micros setter.
- Tests: decode_ack_delay_scales_by_exponent_and_clamps_by_max_ack_delay,

title: Lab time-travel demos find nothing: demo_record_nondeterministic/demo_delta_debug/demo_benchmark search a leak the runtime now aborts (orphaned obligations resolved on completion)
description:
## Evidence
The first recorded run of the example binaries: EXB built them on bd6e69d01
(hz3, 0 warnings); each ran locally with a 60 s timeout, stdin closed.
demo_benchmark, demo_delta_debug and demo_record_nondeterministic all
reached the timeout (exit 137) while sweeping seeds, and none found its
failing seed:
- demo_record_nondeterministic: "scenario attempt: seed=41999,
  outcome=pass" and every earlier attempt passed;
- demo_delta_debug: "searching: seed=37999, attempts=38000";
- demo_benchmark: "phase 1: seed search [0..50000)", then silence.
Logs: /data/tmp/rc_20260922/exrun/<name>.log.

## Root cause: the runtime fixed the race the demos depend on
All three demos (bd-77g6j.1-.3, the time-travel pipeline) search for a seed
where a "late" obligation, reserved by a task in the cancel-target region
and never resolved, leaks when the region closes
(`runtime.state.leak_count() > 0`). The late probability is about 1 in 1000
seeds, so about 42 of the 42,000 seeds tried should have leaked. None did.
The module doc states the premise: "the cancel path ... does NOT abort
in-flight obligations".
The completion phase now aborts every obligation a completed task still
holds: RuntimeState::abort_orphaned_obligations_for_holder, resolving with
Abort(Cancel) (E2 / m9wsza, July). A cancelled task's late obligation is
therefore aborted, not leaked, and leak_count never moves. The runtime
behavior is the correct one; the demos' scenario is obsolete.

## Impact
The lab's showcase pipeline (sweep, record .ftrace, replay, delta-debug,
checksummed benchmark) demonstrates nothing today. demo_benchmark's golden
SHA-256 checksums cannot be produced. The examples README still lists all
three as working demos.

## Fix (showcase design call)
Rebuild the scenario around a leak the current runtime still reports. The
simplest is a late obligation on a task that completes normally (the
survivor region), which leak detection still catches. Then update:
- the three module docs (the race narrative);
- the demo_benchmark goldens, regenerated from a reviewed run, not
  reflexively.
Add a smoke test that runs each demo with a small DEMO_SEED_COUNT and
asserts that it finds a failing seed, so the pipeline cannot rot silently
again.
close_reason: Landed 3d80a63d6. title: Define complete TraceEvent enumeration with versioning
description:
## Overview

Define the complete enumeration of all trace events that must be recorded for deterministic replay.

## Requirements

### Event Categories
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum TraceEvent {
    // Scheduling events
    TaskSpawned { task_id: TaskId, region_id: RegionId },
    TaskPolled { task_id: TaskId, ready: bool },
    TaskWoken { task_id: TaskId, source: WakeSource },
    TaskCompleted { task_id: TaskId, outcome: SerializedOutcome },
    
    // Region events
    RegionCreated { region_id: RegionId, parent: Option<RegionId> },
    RegionClosed { region_id: RegionId },
    RegionCancelled { region_id: RegionId, reason: CancelReason },
    
    // Timer events
    TimerScheduled { timer_id: TimerId, deadline: VirtualTime },
    TimerFired { timer_id: TimerId },
    TimerCancelled { timer_id: TimerId },
    
    // I/O events (for Lab runtime)
    IoRequested { source_id: SourceId, interest: Interest },
    IoReady { source_id: SourceId, readiness: Readiness },
    
    // RNG events
    RngSeed { seed: u64 },
    RngValue { value: u64 },
    
    // Metadata
    Checkpoint { sequence: u64, timestamp: VirtualTime },
}
```

### Versioning
- Event version field for forward compatibility
- Unknown event handling (skip with warning)
- Migration support for old event formats

## Acceptance Criteria
1. All non-determinism sources have corresponding events
2. Version field in all events
3. Serialization round-trip tests
4. Documentation of each event's purpose
5. Event size benchmarks (must stay compact)

## Test Requirements
- Serialization/deserialization for all event types
- Version compatibility tests
- Size regression tests

title: Add environment variable and config file support to builder
description:
## Overview

Support 12-factor app configuration through environment variables and optional config file loading.

## Requirements

### Environment Variable Overrides
```rust
impl RuntimeBuilder {
    /// Load configuration from environment variables.
    /// Env vars override programmatic settings.
    pub fn with_env_overrides(mut self) -> Self;
}
```

Environment variable mapping:
- `ASUPERSYNC_WORKER_THREADS` -> scheduler.worker_threads
- `ASUPERSYNC_TASK_QUEUE_DEPTH` -> scheduler.task_queue_depth
- `ASUPERSYNC_TIMER_RESOLUTION_MS` -> timers.resolution
- `ASUPERSYNC_MAX_REGISTERED_IO` -> io.max_registered_sources
- `ASUPERSYNC_ENABLE_METRICS` -> metrics.enabled

### Config File Support
```rust
impl RuntimeBuilder {
    /// Load configuration from TOML file.
    pub fn from_toml(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self, ConfigError>;
    
    /// Load configuration from TOML string.
    pub fn from_toml_str(toml: &str) -> Result<Self, ConfigError>;
}
```

Config file format:
```toml
[scheduler]
worker_threads = 4
task_queue_depth = 1024

[timers]
resolution_ms = 1
max_duration_hours = 24

[io]
max_registered_sources = 10000
```

### Precedence Order
1. Programmatic settings (highest)
2. Environment variables
3. Config file
4. Defaults (lowest)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `with_env_overrides()` method
2. `from_toml()` and `from_toml_str()` methods
3. Clear precedence documentation
4. Error messages for invalid env vars
5. Optional dependency on toml crate (feature-gated)

## Test Requirements
- Test env var parsing for all supported vars
- Test invalid env var values (should error)
- Test config file loading
- Test precedence: programmatic > env > file
- Test missing optional values use defaults

title: [LAB] conformal_quantile under-covers when ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))>n: returns max score instead of +inf, violating the finite-sample 1-alpha guarantee
description: src/lab/conformal.rs conformal_quantile() violates the split-conformal finite-sample guarantee P(score_{n+1} <= threshold) >= 1-alpha that the README and the function doc both promise. For n calibration scores the threshold must be the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))-th order statistic (1-indexed), with the convention that when that rank exceeds n (i.e. alpha < 1/(n+1)) the threshold is +inf (cover everything). The code instead computes idx = (level.ceil() as usize).min(n).saturating_sub(1) and returns sorted[idx] = the MAX score in that regime. Returning the max attains only n/(n+1) < 1-alpha worst-case coverage (the test point can be the new maximum), under-covering. The empty-scores branch already returns +inf, so the rank>n branch is an inconsistent oversight. Repro: conformal_quantile(&[0.5], 0.05) returns 0.5 (should be +inf); conformal_quantile(&[1.0..=10.0], 0.05) returns 10.0 (rank=11>10, should be +inf).
design: FIX (mapped, not yet shipped): in conformal_quantile, compute rank = level.ceil() as usize; if rank > n return f64::INFINITY; else sorted[rank-1]. +inf serializes to JSON null (serde_json maps non-finite to null) and the empty case already produces +inf downstream, so no new serialization hazard. RIPPLE: 4+ existing tests calibrate with small n at alpha=0.05 (n becomes <19) and must be updated to stay in the finite-threshold regime by bumping calibration size to n>=19-20, else they break: (1) conformal_quantile_single / conformal_quantile_sorted q95 assertions (already updated in my local WIP to assert +inf); (2) deterministic_calibration (~L1207, 0..5 -> 0..20) breaks because (inf-inf).abs()=NaN < EPSILON is false; (3) health_threshold_ignores_non_finite_calibration_values (~L1417, 1..=10 -> 1..=20, and count assert Some(&10) -> Some(&20)); (4) health_threshold_non_finite_check_is_anomalous (~L1437, 1..=10 -> 1..=20). MUST run cargo test --lib lab::conformal to green before commit; this window the lib-test binary was blocked by unrelated peer #[cfg(test)] WIP (ModeStatistics/h2::connection private fields). A boundary test conformal_quantile_infinite_when_rank_exceeds_n (n=20 alpha=0.05 finite max=20.0 vs alpha=0.04 +inf) is staged in WIP. title: Messaging audit: JetStream acks never reach the server, global pull limiter refuses every pull after ~5k pulls, named consumers are ephemeral, NATS supervisor stalls on a dropped call, 256-message subscription cap drops silently, and more
description:
Read-only audit of src/messaging (NATS, JetStream, Redis, Kafka) on origin/main 101f469e5 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-03). SapphireHill re-verified items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 11 against the code before fixing.

Being fixed now (SapphireHill): 1 (acks to the reply subject as delivered; the anti-replay token machinery, which never detected a replay because its nonce mixes in the current time, is removed), 2 (global pull estimate released when each pull ends), 3 (named consumers carry durable_name; the test that pinned its absence is updated), 11 (max_ack_pending <= 0 means unlimited locally).

Notes for the rest:
- 5: crate::channel::mpsc preallocates its capacity (VecDeque::with_capacity), so raising the per-subscription capacity to async-nats' 65,536 costs several MB per subscription. Better: a JetStream pull inbox sized to the batch, plus a surfaced slow-consumer error.
- 10: the per-consumer 50 ms pull limiter is pinned by pull_dos_protection_audit; changing it is an owner decision.
- 6: pinned by nats_supervisor_backs_off_across_connections_the_server_refuses_after_connect.

I found 22 defects in the messaging clients: 5 HIGH, 10 MEDIUM and 7 LOW. Three of the HIGHs are in JetStream: acks never reach the server, a process-wide pull limiter eventually blocks every pull, and named consumers are created as ephemeral. The other two are in the NATS client: one cancelled call can stall the connection for minutes, and bursts above 256 messages are silently dropped. Everything was read against origin/main `101f469e5` (line numbers below are at that commit); nothing was built or run. Two background agents did the first pass on JetStream and Kafka, and I re-read the code behind each finding below. Of the bead hits, only 30zcp8.1 is a claimed fix for an issue below (I found it not delivered), and e7q5xr only mentions #6.

## HIGH

**1. JetStream ack/nak/term go to a subject the server doesn't listen on** (`jetstream.rs:2923-2937, 2956-2977`)
- The client sends acks to `<reply_subject>.<hmac>`, a 10-token subject. nats-server only listens on `$JS.ACK.<stream>.<consumer>.*.*.*.*.*` (9 tokens), so every ack is silently dropped.
- `ack()` still returns Ok and the message is marked acked locally. Messages are redelivered until `max_deliver`, and WorkQueue streams never drain. Only `+WPI` uses the real subject.
- The real-server test never checks the ack on the server side.
- Fix: publish to `reply_subject` exactly as received, as nats.go and async-nats do, and delete the token tracker.
- Test: `capture_publish_transcript(1, …)`, then `msg.ack()`, then assert the captured subject equals the reply subject.
- Introduced by `8b634b5df` (erirc4).

**2. A process-wide pull limiter eventually refuses every pull** (`jetstream.rs:277-325`, called at `1838-1850`)
- Each pull adds `batch × 2 KB` to a global estimate; every 100th pull subtracts only 50 pulls' worth, so the estimate only grows.
- At 512 MB, every pull on every consumer in the process returns `InvalidConfig`, forever. With batch 100 that happens after about 5.2k pulls.
- Fix: remove it; the server's `max_ack_pending` and `max_bytes` already bound this.
- Test: call `GlobalPullRateTracker::new().check_global_pull_request(i·1s, 100·2048)` 10k times and assert all Ok.

**3. Named consumers are created as ephemeral** (`jetstream.rs:945-964, 1054-1063`)
- `normalize_identity` clears `durable_name`, so the wire config only has `name`. The server then treats the consumer as ephemeral with a 5 s inactivity threshold.
- After 5 s with no pull outstanding the consumer is deleted. A restart replays the stream or gets "consumer not found". The docs at 813-816 say these are durable.
- Fix: send `durable_name` equal to `name`.
- Test: `ConsumerConfig::new("p")`, `validate()`, then assert `to_json()` contains `"durable_name":"p"`.

**4. A dropped call on a supervised NATS client blocks the whole connection** (`nats.rs:3374-3393, 3930-4054, 4023-4042, 3210-3248`)
- The supervisor only checks whether the caller gave up *before* starting a command; once started, it runs it to completion. `Process` then waits on the socket.
- JetStream's pull loop (`jetstream.rs:1928-1944`) wraps `process()` in a timeout and then unsubscribes. Whenever a pull ends by timeout, the abandoned `Process` keeps the supervisor parked, and the UNSUB (and every other command) waits for the next inbound frame — typically the server's PING, every 2 minutes.
- The same applies to a timed-out `request` (supervisor busy up to `request_timeout`) and a timed-out `ping`. Not tracked.
- Fix: make supervised `Process` wait on an epoch notification instead of reading, and abandon an in-flight command when its reply channel closes.
- Test (`tests/messaging_nats_handshake.rs` style, `send_info`/`read_nats_line`):
  1. Fake server stays silent after SUB.
  2. Client calls `timeout(100ms, client.process())`, which times out, then `publish`.
  3. Assert `PUB` reaches the server within 1 s. Today it doesn't.

**5. Subscription channels hold 256 messages and silently drop the rest** (`nats.rs:3010, 3070, 3195-3206`; supervisor loop `3870-3893`)
- The supervisor dispatches everything in the socket buffer in one poll. A JetStream pull allows batches up to 1024 (`jetstream.rs:103`).
- A pull of more than 256 small messages drops the excess: redelivered after `ack_wait` (counting toward `max_deliver`), or lost with AckNone. The pull then waits out its timeout.
- The comment "Bounded for backpressure" is wrong: nothing applies backpressure. async-nats buffers 65,536 and raises a SlowConsumer event; nats.go raises `ErrSlowConsumer`.
- Fix: configurable capacity, the inbox sized to at least the batch, and an error surfaced on `next()`.
- Test: fake server writes 300 `MSG` frames then `PING`, and waits for the client's `PONG`. The client then drains with `try_next` and expects 300; today it gets 256.

## MEDIUM

**6. NATS `connect()` never confirms CONNECT** (`nats.rs:1998-2007`; reconnect at `2120-2165`)
- No PING/PONG follows CONNECT. With bad credentials, an expired JWT or "max connections", `connect` returns Ok and publishes return Ok while the server drops them. nats.go and async-nats send CONNECT+PING and wait for PONG or `-ERR`.
- Noted in e7q5xr but not fixed, and the current behaviour is pinned by `nats_supervisor_backs_off_across_connections_the_server_refuses_after_connect`.
- Test: `spawn_connect_recorder(info, Some("-ERR 'Authorization Violation'"))` with `verbose:false` under `run_test_with_cx`; expect `Err(Server)`.

**7. A non-fatal `-ERR` fails `ping()` and forces a reconnect** (`nats.rs:3142-3157`; `3843-3857`; `request()` at `2857-2861/2964-2968`)
- Publishing to a denied subject and then calling `ping()` (the usual flush idiom) returns `Err(Permissions Violation…)`, leaves the connection marked unusable, and the supervisor reconnects, dropping in-flight messages. `request()` also fails on unrelated `-ERR`s.
- Fix: use `server_error_keeps_connection` inside these loops.
- Test: server answers `PUB`+`PING` with the `-ERR` then `PONG`; assert `ping` is Ok and no second accept (`accept_within`).

**8. No client-side keepalive PING** (`NatsConfig`, `nats.rs:210-291`)
- On a half-open TCP connection, publishes return Ok into the socket buffer for about 15 minutes (Linux retransmit limit) and subscribers stall.
- nats.go pings every 2 min with `MaxPingsOut` 2; async-nats every 60 s.
- Fix: add `ping_interval`/`max_pings_out`.
- Test: a silent server with `ping_interval` 100 ms should see a reconnect within 1 s.

**9. Pulls ignore JetStream status messages** (`jetstream.rs:1958-1968, 1898-1922`)
- Status messages carry no reply subject, so 409 (consumer deleted, MaxWaiting) and 503 replies wait the full timeout and return `Ok(vec![])`.
- Fix: parse the status line (reuse `reply_status_error`).
- Test: `capture_wire_transcript` with a new `DeterministicServerReply::Status` sending a 409; expect Err.

**10. The per-consumer pull rate limiter breaks normal pull loops** (`jetstream.rs:214-253, 369-416`)
- A second pull within 50 ms returns a non-retryable `InvalidConfig`.
- While limiting is active, `pull(1)` is inflated to 16 messages.
- It uses `SystemTime`, and `now − last` can underflow if the clock steps back.
- Test: two `check_pull_request` calls 1 ms apart, then assert the clamped batch is ≤ 1.

**11. `max_ack_pending ≤ 0` (JetStream's "unlimited") is clamped to 1** (`jetstream.rs:1526, 1549-1551, 1904-1918`)
- The client then drops messages the server already delivered, without a NAK.
- Test: create with `max_ack_pending(-1)` and assert `increment_pending()` succeeds twice.

**12. A cancelled ack leaves the message stuck as "in flight"** (`jetstream.rs:2902-2951`; Drop at `1208-1221`)
- There is no guard to roll the state back: later ack attempts return `AlreadyAcknowledged`, and the flow-control credit leaks.
- Test: poll `ack()` once on a 1-worker runtime, drop it, and assert `!is_acked()`.

**13. `RedisClient` cannot be built from a `RedisConfig`** (`redis.rs:3218-3243`; docs at `88-93, 1601-1627, 2239-2256`)
- Frame limits, Pub/Sub and push backlogs, the TLS connector (`rediss://` is hard-wired to webpki roots, 2443-2454) and pool size (fixed at 10) cannot be changed, although the docs and error text say to adjust them.
- A GET of a value over 16 MiB always fails and discards the connection; Redis allows 512 MB.
- Bead 30zcp8.1 was closed claiming the constructor accepts the limits; only the test-private `client_with_config` does.
- Fix: add `pub connect_with_config`.
- Test: scripted 17 MiB GET reply using `write_hello3_ok`.

**14. Kafka: a cancelled send reports `Cancelled` even when the record was delivered** (`kafka.rs:361-391`, checkpoint at 368 before the value at 375)
- Once enqueued, librdkafka delivers the record anyway, so a retry produces a duplicate. The module doc (21-26) promises cancellation waits for acks.
- Test: `delivery_channel`, `complete(Ok)`, cancel, poll; expect `Ok` (pattern of `delivery_receiver_repoll_after_success_fails_closed`).

**15. Kafka: a stale poll result is replayed after `seek`/`rebalance`** (`kafka_consumer.rs:1826-1833, 1911-1966`)
- The deadline returns before draining the last result, and nothing else clears it. After `seek`, the next poll restores the old position or assignment, and can deliver a record fetched before the seek.
- Test: preload `buffered_outcome`, `seek(t,0,0)`, `poll(ZERO)`, assert position is 0.

## LOW
- **16. Redis `Pipeline` doesn't refuse reply-changing commands** (`redis.rs:4138-4143, 4185-4189`). `CLIENT REPLY OFF|SKIP` hangs `exec`; `MONITOR` or a multi-channel `SUBSCRIBE` mis-assigns replies. Test: `pooled_client_without_acquire()` should return `Err(Protocol)` before acquiring.
- **17. Redis Pub/Sub server errors become a generic protocol error** (`redis.rs:4771-4780, 4551-4562, 5149`). An ACL `-NOPERM` reply poisons the connection, and already-buffered messages are discarded without being counted as dropped.
- **18. JetStream reads ack metadata from the right-hand end** (`jetstream.rs:1970-1982`). Newer-format (v2) ack subjects are mis-parsed.
- **19. JetStream returns invented stream config** (`jetstream.rs:1609-1612`). `StreamInfo.config` is made up, and `create_stream` is documented as "create or update" but only creates.
- **20. Kafka manual `rebalance()` on a cooperative consumer fails** (`kafka_consumer.rs:1741-1752`). It uses a full `assign`, which librdkafka rejects in cooperative mode.
- **21. Kafka marks permanent errors as retryable** (`kafka.rs:508-516, 208-252`). Delivery errors including auth and too-large are retryable; timeouts don't report `is_timeout`.
- **22. Kafka hides tombstones, and a setting does nothing** (`kafka_consumer.rs:1392-1408`). A null value is indistinguishable from empty; `max_poll_records` is never used.

## Checked and found sound
- **NATS:** MSG/HMSG framing and lengths, INFO parsing, `-ERR` classification, HPUB size accounting, TLS before CONNECT and no downgrade on reconnect, nkey/JWT signing, SUB replay with the same ids, half-written frames forcing a reconnect, matching replies to requests, 503 "no responders".
- **Redis:** RESP2/RESP3 decoding (all types, streamed blobs and aggregates, attributes), agreement between the incremental scanner and the decoder, routing of server pushes, HELLO 3 with AUTH and the fallback for servers before 6.0, cancelled connections being discarded, state-changing commands closing their connection, MOVED/ASK with a hop limit, session WATCH/EXEC including the RESP3 null conflict, Pub/Sub ack counting.
- **JetStream:** API error parsing, PubAck/duplicate, `Nats-Msg-Id`, the `-NAK` delay format, `expires` in nanoseconds on a consistent clock, one inbox per pull.
- **Kafka:** config mapping, committed offset = next offset to read, the transaction state machine, blocking calls kept off the executor.

OWNER DECISION NEEDED (item 10, JetStream per-consumer pull rate limiter). SapphireHill, 10-03.

What it does: Consumer::pull_with_timeout calls PullRateLimiter::check_pull_request before every pull. A pull less than 50 ms after the previous admitted one fails with JsError::InvalidConfig ("rate limited - retry after N ms"). That error is not retryable, so `?` in a pull loop ends the consumer. Each rapid pull also escalates the backoff (100 ms x 1.5^n, up to 5 s) and, while "active", halves the requested batch to no less than 16. So pull(1) becomes a request for 16 messages. The arithmetic is `now_ns - last_pull_ns` on SystemTime, which underflows if the clock steps back.

Origin: 8b65ffabb "security: fix JetStream consumer pull batch size DoS vector" (uculjz, 2026-05-26), in v0.4.3. The actual memory DoS (batch = usize::MAX) is closed separately by MAX_PULL_BATCH = 1024. The limiter protects nothing: the caller is the application itself, and the server enforces max_waiting, max_request_batch and max_request_expires. nats.go and async-nats have no client-side pull rate limit. Even if made non-failing (pace instead of error), it caps a consumer at 20 pulls/s, so a pull(1) job worker gets 20 jobs/s.

Recommendation: remove the per-consumer limiter from the pull path. That means removing the PullRateLimiter struct and its Consumer field, plus the "rate limiting active" halving in validate_and_clamp_pull_batch_size, and capping the memory-pressure clamp at the requested batch (today `.max(16)` can also inflate pull(1) to 16). Keep MAX_PULL_BATCH and the global memory reservation.
- Tests that pin the current behaviour and would be removed or rewritten: audit_pull_rate_limiter_enforces_minimum_interval, audit_pull_rate_limiter_applies_exponential_backoff, audit_dynamic_batch_sizing_reduces_under_pressure and audit_pull_dos_protection_integration (jetstream.rs pull_dos_protection_audit). audit_validate_and_clamp_batch_respects_base_limits stays.
- New test: two pulls 1 ms apart are both admitted, and the effective batch never exceeds the request.
- Observable change: undocumented errors stop occurring. No signature changes.

Related, also undocumented: GlobalPullRateTracker refuses (InvalidConfig) past 1000 pulls/s process-wide. Same failure class; same question.

Not changed until the owner decides, because it removes a feature labelled as security and its pinned tests.

SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-07: claiming item 8 (no client-side keepalive PING).

Plan:
- NatsConfig is exhaustively constructible in v0.4.3 (all pub fields), so the setting is a new type, NatsKeepalive, passed through an additive NatsClient::connect_with_keepalive.
- connect / connect_with_config use NatsKeepalive::default(), nats.go's defaults: a PING every 2 min, stale once 2 are unanswered at the next tick. This matches what nats.go and async-nats do by default.
- The supervised client's frame loop gets a third select leg, the keepalive timer:
  - at each tick it sends PING and counts it outstanding;
  - any PONG clears the count;
  - with the limit reached, the connection is stale, and the supervisor reconnects as it does after a transport error.
  - The PING write is bounded by the interval, so a full send buffer cannot park the supervisor.
- A direct-mode client (a Cx without a spawn gateway) reads only when called, so it gets no keepalive. This will be documented.

Test: a silent fake server and a 100 ms interval; the client reconnects within about 1 s.

Items 20 and 22 stay open; 6 and 10 stay with the owner. I release the claim when item 8 lands.

comments.text:
SapphireHill d0, 2026-10-08: item 8 (no client-side keepalive PING) LANDED as NK dbc5219ee (merge e67928684); the v0.6.0 CHANGELOG notes the behaviour change (faf7d0c70).

What changed:
- NatsKeepalive (asupersync::messaging::nats::NatsKeepalive) and NatsClient::connect_with_keepalive are new and additive. connect and connect_with_config use NatsKeepalive::default(), nats.go's defaults: a PING every 2 min, stale with 2 unanswered.
- The supervisor sends the PINGs. When max_pings_out are unanswered at a tick, it replaces the connection as after a transport error: reconnect and replay the subscriptions.
- ping() waits for its own PONG. Each connection counts PINGs sent and PONGs parsed, and both counts reset on reconnect. So a keepalive PONG can no longer end a publish-then-ping flush early.
- A supervised ping() waits at most interval x max_pings_out.
- NatsConfig is unchanged. NatsKeepalive is not re-exported from messaging/mod.rs (that file is sha-pinned by five artifacts).

title: [EPIC-TOKIO] Time and Timers (tokio-time equivalent)
description:
# Time and Timer Infrastructure

## Overview
Unified time abstraction supporting both virtual time (lab) and wall time (production) with full budget integration.

## Components

### 1. Time Abstraction
- Instant type (virtual or wall)
- Duration (standard)
- Interval type

### 2. Sleep Operations
- sleep(duration): pause for duration
- sleep_until(instant): pause until instant
- Both respect cancellation

### 3. Interval Timers
- interval(period): repeating timer
- interval_at(start, period): with explicit start
- MissedTickBehavior: Burst, Delay, Skip

### 4. Timeout Integration
- Already have timeout combinator
- Integrate with budget deadlines
- Cascading timeouts through regions

### 5. Wheel Timer (Production)
- Hierarchical timing wheel
- Efficient for many timers
- O(1) insert and expire

### 6. Virtual Time (Lab)
- Controlled time advancement
- No wall-clock dependency
- Deterministic timer ordering

## Budget Integration
- Timers contribute to deadline budget
- Budget exhaustion triggers timeout
- Tropical semiring for deadline propagation

## Cancel-Safety
- Sleep: cancel returns Cancelled
- Interval: cancel stops iteration
- Timeout: cancel propagates to inner

## Lab Runtime
- advance_time(duration)
- set_time(instant)
- Timers fire in deterministic order
close_reason: done

title: [security-audit][CRITICAL] grpc/server.rs: Interceptor chain is NEVER invoked by Server — every Interceptor (AuthInterceptor, BearerAuthValidator, RateLimitInterceptor) is dead code from the server-dispatch path
description: src/grpc/server.rs:221-235 (ServerBuilder::build) constructs Server { config, services } — no interceptor field. ServerBuilder has no .interceptor() method. src/grpc/server.rs:286-299 (Server::serve) only binds the listener and returns immediately ("request serving is provided by transport adapters layered above this core server registry"). The Interceptor trait, AuthInterceptor, BearerAuthValidator, BearerAuthInterceptor, NoopInterceptor, MetadataPropagator, RateLimitInterceptor, TracingInterceptor, and InterceptorLayer all exist as DSL but grep for non-test intercept_request call sites in src/grpc/ returns ZERO production call sites. A user who follows the interceptor.rs documentation example (InterceptorLayer::new().layer(auth_validator(...))) has no API to attach the layer to a Server, and no transport adapter exists in the workspace that actually drives the chain. Net effect: every gRPC server built via this surface ships with NO interceptor enforcement — auth, rate limiting, tracing all silently dead. Severity CRITICAL P1 because callers reasonably assume their attached AuthInterceptor protects their endpoints. Suggested fix: (a) add interceptor: InterceptorLayer to ServerConfig + ServerBuilder.interceptor() method, (b) add an explicit "this server core does NOT serve traffic — use grpc::Server::serve_with_transport or the h2 adapter" assertion in serve() until the wiring lands, OR (c) make ServerBuilder::build fail at compile time without an interceptor configuration parameter to force the design decision.
close_reason: Fixed in 30fdd1b5c (the user's commit bundled my +383 lines of grpc/server.rs changes alongside their CORS fix). Implementation: ServerBuilder gains interceptors: Vec<Arc<dyn Interceptor>>, .interceptor() and .interceptor_arc() methods. Server gains interceptors field + read-only .interceptors() getter. New Server::dispatch_unary(request, handler) is the canonical entry point: phase 1 runs intercept_request in registration order (first Err short-circuits, no handler/response chain); phase 2 invokes user handler with (possibly mutated) request; phase 3 on success runs intercept_response_with_request in REVERSE order; on handler error, response chain is skipped. Transport adapters MUST route through dispatch_unary or call .interceptors() and apply manually. 5 regression tests cover: registration+reverse order, request-side reject short-circuits handler+response chain, handler-error skips response chain, no-interceptors back-compat, end-to-end AuthInterceptor blocks unauthenticated calls. Streaming dispatch deferred (transport adapters can use .interceptors() getter; dedicated dispatch_streaming follows when streaming adapter API stabilizes).

title: OWNER: region Policy is never consulted - FailFast (the documented default) does not cancel siblings when a child fails; wire on_child_outcome or relabel
description:
## Finding (read-only audit of src/types/{policy,outcome,rref}.rs and src/util/*, SapphireHill e0155ea8 audit agent, 10-07; re-verified by SapphireHill at origin/main e5349b2b7) The region Policy hook is never consulted. A FailFast region does not cancel its other children when one fails, although FailFast is the documented default and is documented to do exactly that. What the code and docs claim: - src/types/policy.rs: the module doc says policies "determine how a region responds to child outcomes". FailFast's doc says "Fail-fast policy: cancel siblings on first error. This is the default policy for most use cases." - formal/impl_refinement_map.md section 3.1 marks COMPLETE-OK and COMPLETE-ERR as Implemented: "Callers compute Policy::on_child_outcome before taking the runtime-state lock, then pass the closed PolicyAction to apply_policy_action". - src/runtime/state.rs ~7290 (apply_policy_action's doc) says the caller must invoke on_child_outcome first. What the code does: - Policy::on_child_outcome has no production caller. Only policy.rs's own tests call it. - RuntimeState::apply_policy_action is called only from state_tests.rs (~2708, ~2757). - Scope

holds P only as a PhantomData marker (cx/scope.rs ~148). Scope::region / region_with_budget / region_with_priority take a policy argument named `_policy` and discard it, and RegionRecord stores no policy. - aggregate_outcomes is reached only through combinator/join.rs (~277). - So in a Scope::region child region, a child task that returns Err or panics leaves its siblings running. CollectAll behaves identically, and PolicyAction::Escalate is never produced or handled. Fail-fast that does exist: - JoinSet's own fail-fast owner (combinator/join_set/owner/fail_fast.rs ~42: Err or Panicked cancels the set's other members with CancelReason::fail_fast); - fibers (a panicking fiber cancels its siblings, cx/fiber.rs ~587); - a panicking or dropped region body cancels the region (cx/scope.rs ~213, ~807, ~894). History: asupersync-1j76h, asupersync-37o9s and bd-akx.2.1 ("Define and implement Policy for region outcome aggregation") are closed, and 28c51.269 refers to an apply_policy_on_child_outcome helper that no longer exists on origin. The wiring was either removed or never landed. ## Decision needed (owner) - (a) Wire it. The region needs to keep its policy, because today P is only a type marker. On every child task completion, the runtime calls on_child_outcome outside the state lock, as the refinement map describes, and applies the PolicyAction: CancelSiblings cancels the region's other tasks with CancelReason::fail_fast, and Escalate needs a defined meaning. This changes behaviour for every Scope::region user whose default FailFast region has a failing child: siblings that run to completion today get cancelled. The task completion path is hot, so the per-completion cost must be measured, and lab replay goldens may move. - (b) Relabel. Policy is an aggregation helper used by join combinators. FailFast's "cancel siblings" wording moves to JoinSet's fail-fast, the refinement map's COMPLETE-OK/ERR rows say Partial, and apply_policy_action's doc points at its test-only status. - Recommendation: (b) now (docs truth, no behaviour change; staged as a docs commit citing this bead). Then (a) if region-level fail-fast is wanted as a feature, with its own measurement. ## Done when The owner picks (a) or (b). The docs say what the code does in either case. Under (a), a native and a lab test show a failing child cancelling its siblings in a FailFast region and not in a CollectAll region.

- src/types/policy.rs: the module doc says the runtime does not consult a region's policy when a child completes yet, and points to the fail-fast that does exist: JoinSet::try_join_all, and fibers. FailFast's doc says its on_child_outcome asks for CancelSiblings, and that the runtime does not apply it.

title: [security-audit-for-saas] add safe LISTEN/NOTIFY channel-name validation helpers
description: src/database/postgres.rs had no safe notification-channel API, which left callers to raw LISTEN/UNLISTEN/NOTIFY SQL via query_unchecked/execute_unchecked. PostgreSQL identifiers are truncated at 63 bytes and channel names in raw SQL need identifier quoting, so callers could otherwise hit command-injection gadgets or channel-collision confusion from server-side truncation. Fix by adding safe PgConnection helpers that validate the 63-byte channel-name limit, quote LISTEN/UNLISTEN identifiers, and route NOTIFY through pg_catalog.pg_notify with parameters.
