title: QUIC encrypted throughput: coalesce many symbol-DATAGRAMs per UDP datagram (one-symbol-per-packet caps tier to ~1MB/s)
description:
EVIDENCE (MATRIX-39, run artifacts/atp_bench_matrix/20260623T011637Z/): after 71qhl6 fix (5a690b975, envelope 16384->65535) the packet-too-large error is GONE (0 occurrences). But encrypted 50M LOSSY still fails 0/3: good+bad hit [ASUP-E804] transport timeout during receive proof/fountain feedback after 60s. perfect works (37.4s, 46000 symbols sha-ok).

ROOT CAUSE: QUIC sender delivers <1 MB/s REGARDLESS of link bandwidth. Receiver counters: perfect 46000 symbols/37.4s=1230 sym/s~1.5MB/s; good (25MB/s link) 45964/46000 in 60s=766 sym/s~0.92MB/s (3.7% util); bad (6.25MB/s link) 34974/46000 in 60s=583 sym/s~0.70MB/s (11% util). Receiver drops NOTHING (datagrams_dropped_on_receive=0, pending_datagrams=0) — it accepts every symbol that arrives; sender just emits too few/sec. native_link.rs:895 'Cap each 1-RTT data packet to carry at most one symbol DATAGRAM' => max_app_payload = one_datagram (symbol_size+header+16 ~1216B). Throughput is packets/sec-bound, not bytes/sec-bound; higher RTT (good 25ms/bad 80ms) => fewer round-trips in 60s => good lands 45964/46000, bad 34974/46000 => timeout. SAME cap explains encrypted-CLEAN 42x loss (perfect 1.5MB/s vs rsync 58MB/s).

FIX: now that ATP_QUIC_UDP_MAX_PACKET=65535, coalesce MANY symbol-DATAGRAM frames per UDP datagram (~53 x 1216B fit in 65535). Each symbol stays its own RFC9221 DATAGRAM frame (per-symbol loss granularity preserved), just packed into one UDP send/sendmmsg. ~50x send-throughput headroom -> should fix BOTH encrypted-lossy convergence AND encrypted-clean speed. PAIR WITH receiver: the 256-deep inbound DATAGRAM queue (original reason for 1-symbol cap, native_link.rs:895 comment) must drain faster or be enlarged to absorb coalesced bursts. GATES: encrypted good+bad 50M converge sha_ok=true status=ok; perfect wall DROPS sharply (toward rsync); byte-identical; no receiver queue overflow. Owner: transport_quic. This is THE encrypted-tier unblocker (lossy + clean).
close_reason: QUIC DATAGRAM coalescing shipped and engaged; performance hypothesis refuted by MATRIX-110

comments.text:
Central trace evidence (SapphireHill, ledger MATRIX-108, committed a5908d19b) for the QUIC encrypted throughput floor. ATP_RQ_TRACE on encrypted 50M/perfect (the proven-good path, parent 5038ba9f8):
  pacing ramp: start_rate_Bps=12,000,000 -> 20,388,608 -> max_rate_Bps=25,165,824 (=24 MiB/s), datagram_fanout=1 datagram_frame_bytes=1200 burst_symbols=2
  BUT measured throughput_bytes_per_sec = ~4.6-6.2 MB/s on BOTH send and recv; decode_micros~11ms; feedback_rounds=0; symbols_accepted=46000.
=> The path runs ~5x BELOW its own pacing allowance (achieves ~5 MB/s, paced for ~25 MB/s). The floor is the protect/send + recv/unprotect/intake machinery, NOT the pacing cap, NOT decode, NOT repair.
Concrete levers:
 (1) burst_symbols=2 is tiny (~2.4KB/burst, ~21k bursts/50MB); rq path uses 16-32. Per-burst fixed overhead likely dominates -> see bead 839ykg (round-0 pacing ramp). Raise the clean-link burst.
 (2) Receiver intake may backpressure below the cap (bounded 256 datagram queue, possibly serial unprotect+intake) -> see beads atp-rq-r1-receiver-intake-trace-drhadc and 317hxr.29. Batch/parallelize recv unprotect+intake.
 (3) Secondary: raise the 24 MiB/s clean-link cap once (1)/(2) let the machinery fill it.
Available win: encrypted-perfect 10.36s (4.8 MB/s) -> toward nocrypto 2.82s (17.7 MB/s), ~3.7x. NOT auth (refuted MATRIX-106/107) and NOT source-stream (DEAD 102/104). I bench centrally on request.

title: Implement pipeline combinator for staged processing
description:
## Purpose
The pipeline combinator chains a sequence of transformations where each stage's output feeds the next stage's input. Unlike simple sequential composition, pipeline supports concurrent execution of stages on different data items (streaming pipeline parallelism).

## Design Philosophy
Two modes of pipeline operation:
1. **Sequential pipeline**: Stage N+1 starts only after stage N completes (simple chaining)
2. **Streaming pipeline**: Stages run concurrently, connected by channels (higher throughput)

For Phase 0 (single-threaded), implement sequential pipeline. Streaming pipeline deferred to Phase 1.

## Semantic Model (Sequential)

```rust
pub async fn pipeline<A, B, C, E>(
    cx: &mut Cx<'_>,
    input: A,
    stage1: impl FnOnce(&mut Cx<'_>, A) -> impl Future<Output = Result<B, E>>,
    stage2: impl FnOnce(&mut Cx<'_>, B) -> impl Future<Output = Result<C, E>>,
) -> Outcome<C, E>
```

### Behavior
1. Execute stage1(input) → intermediate
2. If Ok: execute stage2(intermediate) → output
3. If any stage fails: propagate error, do not run subsequent stages
4. If cancelled: stop at next stage boundary

### Generalization
Pipeline can be generalized to N stages using a macro or builder pattern:
```rust
pipeline\!(cx, input,
    |cx, x| stage1(cx, x),
    |cx, x| stage2(cx, x),
    |cx, x| stage3(cx, x),
)
```

## Cancellation Handling
- Check cancellation between stages
- If cancelled before stage N: return Cancelled, stages N..end never execute
- Each stage may have internal checkpoints for finer-grained cancellation
- Stage cleanup runs if stage was started

## Budget Composition
Total pipeline budget = Σ(stage_budgets)
This follows the tropical semiring: budgets add sequentially.

## Future: Streaming Pipeline (Phase 1+)
When parallel scheduler available, support concurrent stages:
```
Input → [Stage1] → Channel → [Stage2] → Channel → [Stage3] → Output
```
- Each stage runs in its own task
- Channels are two-phase (reserve/commit)
- Backpressure through bounded channels
- Cancellation propagates downstream

## Invariant Support
- **Sequential ordering**: Output of stage N is input to stage N+1
- **Error short-circuit**: First error stops pipeline
- **No partial results**: Either all stages complete or none
- **Cancel-correctness**: Respects cancellation at stage boundaries

## Testing Requirements
1. All stages succeed
2. Early stage fails (later stages not called)
3. Late stage fails
4. Cancellation before first stage
5. Cancellation between stages
6. Type flow verification (A → B → C)
7. Budget accounting

## Example Usage

```rust
// Image processing pipeline
let result = scope.pipeline(
    cx,
    raw_image,
    |cx, img| async move { decode_image(cx, img).await },
    |cx, img| async move { resize_image(cx, img, 800, 600).await },
    |cx, img| async move { compress_image(cx, img, Quality::High).await },
).await?;
```

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §5.7 Derived Combinators
- Unix pipeline model
- Reactive streams / backpressure patterns
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: §3.2 Sequential composition

## Acceptance Criteria
- Pipeline stages are executed under structured concurrency (no detached tasks) and respect region close.
- Backpressure/queueing uses cancel-safe two-phase primitives where data loss is otherwise possible.
- Cancellation propagates through stages and drains all in-flight work deterministically.
- E2E tests cover cancellation mid-pipeline and no-obligation-leaks.
close_reason: Pipeline combinator implemented with staged processing, error short-circuit, cancellation checks, and comprehensive tests. All tests pass.

title: Implement CancelReason type with severity ordering
description:
# CancelReason Type with Severity Ordering

## Purpose
CancelReason encapsulates WHY a task or region was cancelled. Different reasons have different severity levels, which affects how cancellation requests are combined (strengthened) when multiple cancel requests arrive.

## The Cancel Kinds (Severity Order)
```rust
enum CancelKind {
    User,              // Severity 0: Explicit user cancellation
    Timeout,           // Severity 1: Deadline expired
    FailFast,          // Severity 2: Sibling failed, policy triggers cancel
    ParentCancelled,   // Severity 3: Parent region cancelled
    Shutdown,          // Severity 4: Runtime shutdown
}
```

## Why Severity Matters
When a task receives multiple cancel requests, they must be STRENGTHENED (merged):
- A User cancel followed by Shutdown becomes Shutdown
- A Timeout followed by ParentCancelled becomes ParentCancelled

This ensures:
1. **Idempotence**: Multiple cancels don't cause issues
2. **Monotonicity**: Cancel requests only get more severe, never less
3. **Determinism**: Same requests always produce same result

## CancelReason Structure
```rust
struct CancelReason {
    kind: CancelKind,
    message: Option<String>,  // Optional human-readable context
    source: Option<TaskId>,   // Who initiated the cancel (for debugging)
    timestamp: Time,          // When the cancel was requested
}
```

## Key Operations

### strengthen(current: Option<CancelReason>, new: CancelReason) -> CancelReason
The core operation. Combines two cancel reasons:
```rust
fn strengthen(current: Option<CancelReason>, new: CancelReason) -> CancelReason {
    match current {
        None => new,
        Some(old) => CancelReason {
            kind: max(old.kind, new.kind),  // More severe wins
            // Keep both messages? Keep newer? Policy decision
            message: new.message.or(old.message),
            source: old.source,  // Keep original source
            timestamp: old.timestamp,  // Keep original time
        }
    }
}
```

### severity() -> u8
Returns 0-4 for the CancelKind.

### is_shutdown() -> bool
Returns true if kind is Shutdown. Useful for fast-path checks.

## Relationship to Cancellation Protocol

This type feeds into the cancellation state machine:
```
Running → CancelRequested(CancelReason, cleanup_budget) → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled(CancelReason))
```

The cleanup_budget may vary based on CancelKind:
- User/Timeout: Normal cleanup budget
- FailFast: Shorter cleanup budget
- Shutdown: Minimal cleanup budget

## Implementation Requirements

1. **CancelKind must be Copy, Clone, Ord, PartialOrd**
2. **CancelReason must be Clone, Debug**
3. **Display implementation** for human-readable output
4. **No panics**: All operations are infallible

## Invariant Support

Supports I3 (Cancellation is a protocol, idempotent):
- strengthen() is idempotent: strengthen(r, r) = r
- strengthen() is monotone: severity only increases

## Testing Requirements

1. CancelKind ordering is correct
2. strengthen() is idempotent
3. strengthen() is monotone (severity never decreases)
4. strengthen() is associative
5. Default cleanup budgets are appropriate per kind

## Example Usage
```rust
let mut cancel = None;

// First: user requests cancel
cancel = Some(strengthen(cancel, CancelReason::user("please stop")));
// cancel.kind = User

// Then: parent gets cancelled too
cancel = Some(strengthen(cancel, CancelReason::parent_cancelled()));
// cancel.kind = ParentCancelled (more severe, wins)

// This is idempotent
cancel = Some(strengthen(cancel, CancelReason::user("stop again")));
// cancel.kind = ParentCancelled (still, User < ParentCancelled)
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.3 (Cancel Reasons)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.2 (strengthen function)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §7.2 (Idempotent strengthening)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Defines `CancelKind` severity ordering and a `CancelReason` structure suitable for tracing/debugging.
- `strengthen` is monotone + idempotent and produces deterministic results.
- Cancellation reasons propagate downward through the region tree per the spec.
- Unit tests cover ordering, strengthen laws, and key propagation scenarios.
notes: Implemented CancelKind/CancelReason per semantics §1.3 + api skeleton: CancelKind {User, Timeout, FailFast, ParentCancelled, Shutdown} (Ord + severity) and CancelReason { kind, message: Option<&'static str> } with deterministic strengthen. Added unit tests for ordering + strengthen laws (idempotent/associative/monotone message rules). Gates: cargo check/clippy/fmt/test pass.
close_reason: Aligned CancelReason with semantics/skeleton + strengthen law tests; gates pass

title: [validation] Clear runtime config clippy frontier
description:
## Context
The rch-backed lib clippy proof from `asupersync-jm7y3y` now fails only in `src/runtime/config.rs`. The diagnostics are concrete and local to runtime configuration / operator policy code:

- `clippy::derivable_impls` for `BlockingPoolAffinityProfile`, `ArenaTemperaturePolicy`, and `ArenaLocalityPolicy`
- `clippy::case_sensitive_file_extension_comparisons` for JSON artifact path checks at the host-profile, capacity-envelope, and shared artifact validator surfaces
- `clippy::map_unwrap_or` for host-profile evidence validation aggregation
- `clippy::cast_possible_wrap` for signed shadow-run regret margin calculation
- `missing_docs` for public methods added around host-profile planning, capacity envelopes, and signed profile bundle support

## What
Clear the measured `src/runtime/config.rs` clippy frontier without changing runtime behavior or broadening into peer-owned files. Prefer semantic fixes over blanket allows:

1. Derive `Default` on the three policy enums and mark the current default variants with `#[default]`.
2. Centralize or consistently use a JSON-artifact extension helper instead of case-sensitive `.ends_with(".json")` checks. Preserve the existing non-empty, traversal, and character validation. If live tests or docs indicate artifact identifiers must be lowercase-only, keep that behavior with an explicit local lint allow and a comment; otherwise accept `.JSON`/mixed-case extensions as a user-friendly path normalization improvement and cover it with tests.
3. Replace `map(...).unwrap_or(false)` with `is_some_and(...)` for evidence validation aggregation.
4. Replace the u64-to-i64 regret-margin cast with a non-wrapping conversion strategy. The preferred behavior is a saturating signed margin: values above `i64::MAX` saturate instead of wrapping, and ordinary basis-point values keep the same sign and magnitude.
5. Add focused rustdoc for the public methods clippy reports, describing operator-visible semantics rather than filler text.

## Scope guardrails
Touch only `src/runtime/config.rs` plus tracker files for this bead. Do not edit observability tests, grpc tests, dirty peer-owned `tests/*`, smoke artifact directories, OnceCell, scheduler, or blocking-pool files. Do not change defaults, feature gates, hash formats, validation refusal wording unless a test proves the wording is part of the intentional contract.

## Unit tests
Add or update inline `#[cfg(test)]` coverage in `src/runtime/config.rs` only where behavior can change:

- JSON artifact validators accept lowercase `.json`; if case-insensitive behavior is adopted, also test `.JSON`/mixed-case and path strings with directory components.
- JSON validators still reject empty strings, parent-directory traversal, unsupported characters, and non-json suffixes.
- Shadow-run regret margin keeps positive, zero, and negative ordinary margins and saturates instead of wrapping for extreme synthetic loss values if the helper is exposed enough to test directly.
- Default enum tests continue to prove the same default variants are selected.

If existing tests already cover a case, extend them rather than creating duplicate test surfaces.

## E2E / proof scripts and logging
Run CPU-heavy proof through `rch` and keep `--nocapture` for focused tests so the log records the exact config behavior under test:

- `rch exec -- rustfmt --edition 2024 --check src/runtime/config.rs`
- `rch exec -- env CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=0 RUSTFLAGS="-C debuginfo=0" CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_runtime_config_check cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features test-internals`
- `rch exec -- env CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG=0 RUSTFLAGS="-C debuginfo=0" CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_runtime_config_tests cargo test -p asupersync --lib runtime::config --features test-internals -- --nocapture`
- If that filter is too broad, run exact focused tests added or extended by this bead and record why the broader filter was narrowed.
- `rch exec -- env CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=0 RUSTFLAGS="-C debuginfo=0" CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/rch_target_runtime_config_clippy cargo clippy -p asupersync --lib --features test-internals -- -D warnings`

Success means `src/runtime/config.rs` is absent from the lib clippy frontier. If full lib clippy still fails elsewhere, record the exact external files and prove this file is clear.

title: [SCHED-PERF] cancel_request task pass is embedded-A only: region-level cancels miss shard-A tasks on sharded builds
close_reason: Fixed in c3d580312 (m9wsza S4c-2c-iv): sharded cancel_request resolves shard A for the task pass; dep on m9wsza was ordering context, the fix itself is landed and gated

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-30 — found during the m9wsza S4c-2c pre-analysis.

state.rs cancel_request (~5543) second pass cancels the region's tasks via
self.update_task(task_id, ...) — which resolves ONLY the embedded
RuntimeState.tasks table (state.rs ~2903: self.tasks.update_task). On
with_sharded_state builds, task records live exclusively in ShardedState
shard A (the E1.2 dispatch table); the embedded table does not own them.
Consequence: a region-level cancel_request on a sharded build transitions
the REGION records (those are still embedded today) and emits the region
trace events, but the per-task RequestCancel pass silently no-ops for
shard-A-resident tasks — no task cancel flags, no task cancel trace
events, no cancel-lane scheduling from this path.

Reachability: app.rs shutdown/teardown paths call state.cancel_request
directly (app.rs:1521, :1923, :2229) and are runnable on sharded builds.
gen_server/lab/conformance callers run on LabRuntime (always unified) and
are unaffected. Scheduler-originated cancels are unaffected (they flow
through the handle-cancel mailbox / deferred-dispatch coordinator seams,
which are shard-A aware).

Fix shape (suggested): thread cancel_request's task pass through
AdmissionTaskTarget (the E1.2 seam) the way admission/finalizer paths
were threaded, with the wrapper passing Embedded; the sharded resolution
arrives with the m9wsza S4c-2c-iv wrapper-resolution slice (RuntimeState
gains the shard handle bundle there). The B-side region reads of the same
walk are being threaded in m9wsza S4c-2c-ii regardless.

Cross-refs: br-asupersync-m9wsza (E2 program; S4c-2c pre-analysis comment
records this finding), E1.2 = bt4y5f.2.2 (task-table seams).

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-31 — FIXED in c3d580312 (m9wsza S4c-2c-iv).

cancel_request's public wrapper now resolves shard A on
with_sharded_state builds: the task pass writes through
AdmissionTaskTarget::External(shard-A guard) via cancel_request_in, so
region-level cancels transition shard-A-resident task records, emit
their cancel trace events with logical time read from the owning table,
and return them for cancel-lane scheduling. The structural threading
landed in S4c-2c-ii (a97904438); the sharded wrapper resolution that
makes it live landed in c3d580312. Covered by the slice-iv gate set
(1723 lib tests incl. the fingerprint corpus and all sharded_shape
runtime tests; loom 18/18; 48 audit binaries).

title: [SCHEDULER-INVARIANTS] Three-Lane Scheduler Invariant Matrix
description:
GOAL: Comprehensive runtime verification that the three-lane scheduler (priority/normal/cooperative) maintains all its invariants across state transitions, work-stealing operations, and cancellation scenarios.

BACKGROUND: The three-lane scheduler is the heart of asupersync's runtime. It must maintain complex invariants around fairness, priority ordering, work-stealing correctness, and task ownership while handling cancellation and load balancing.

RATIONALE: Scheduler bugs can cause deadlocks, starvation, priority inversions, or lost work. These bugs are often subtle and only manifest under specific load patterns. Comprehensive invariant checking catches these bugs early and provides confidence in scheduler correctness.

IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH:
- Define complete matrix of scheduler invariants for all three lanes
- Instrument all scheduler operations (spawn, steal, complete, cancel)
- Verify invariants hold during state transitions
- Detect violations in real-time with detailed diagnostics
- Integration with existing scheduler infrastructure (three_lane.rs, priority.rs, etc.)
- Support for both development and production monitoring

KEY INVARIANT CATEGORIES:
- Priority ordering: higher priority tasks scheduled before lower priority
- Fairness: cooperative lane gets fair CPU time allocation
- Work-stealing correctness: stealing preserves task ownership and completion
- Task lifecycle: proper state transitions (spawned → running → completed)
- Load balancing: work distributed fairly across available threads
- Cancellation handling: cancelled tasks properly drained from all queues
- Queue consistency: internal queue state remains valid

SPECIFIC INVARIANTS TO VERIFY:
- No task appears in multiple queues simultaneously
- Priority lane always serves highest priority tasks first
- Cooperative tasks don't starve normal/priority work
- Work-stealing doesn't cause double-execution of tasks
- Cancelled tasks are removed from all scheduler queues
- Queue depth metrics match actual queue contents
- Worker thread assignment is consistent and fair

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS:
- Low overhead suitable for production use
- Thread-safe invariant checking across all worker threads
- Integration with ContendedMutex and ShardedState patterns
- Structured logging of all invariant violations
- Stack trace capture for violation attribution
- Configurable enforcement levels (metrics vs assertions)

SUCCESS METRICS:
- Detects all known scheduler invariant violations
- Zero false positives during correct scheduler operation
- Clear diagnostics for debugging scheduler issues
- Measurable improvement in scheduling predictability
- Prevention of scheduler-related deadlocks and starvation

title: [SECURITY] ATP object verify_detached_object_signature: signature_valid.unwrap_or(true) treats ABSENT signature as valid (verified=true) — signature-stripping downgrade bypass
description:
SECURITY verification-bypass found in Phase-C hunt (signature-stripping downgrade).

LOCATION: src/net/atp/sdk/transfer.rs verify_object path (~line 389).

CODE:
  let signature_valid = self.verify_detached_object_signature(object_path, computed_hash, size_bytes).await;  // -> Option<bool>
  let verified = integrity_check_passed && signature_valid.unwrap_or(true);

verify_detached_object_signature (line 672) returns Option<bool>: None when the detached .sig file does NOT exist; Some(true) when present and valid; Some(false) when present but invalid (bad envelope/algorithm/size mismatch) OR file read error. The payload check itself is correct (constant-time ct_eq on algorithm/size, serde envelope parse, fail-closed on malformed).

BUG: signature_valid.unwrap_or(true) makes the ABSENT-signature case (None) resolve to TRUE. So:
  - present-but-invalid signature (Some(false)) -> verified=false  [fail-closed, correct]
  - ABSENT signature (None) -> verified=true (if integrity passes)  [FAIL-OPEN]
This is asymmetric: a forged/invalid signature is rejected, but simply DELETING the signature file yields verified=true. An attacker who cannot forge a valid signature performs a signature-stripping downgrade and the object is still reported verified=true. No require_signature/mandatory-signing config exists in src/net/atp, so signatures are effectively optional and stripping is trivial.

IMPACT: ObjectVerification.verified is the overall verdict consumers use to decide an object is authentic; treating unsigned/strip-attacked objects as verified defeats the detached-signature protection.

FIX OPTIONS: (a) fail-closed: signature_valid.unwrap_or(false) so verified=true REQUIRES a present+valid signature (recommended if ATP objects are expected to be signed); (b) if unsigned objects are legitimately supported, do NOT fold a missing signature into verified=true — keep verified gated on either a valid signature OR an explicit allow-unsigned policy flag, and ensure consumers distinguish 'integrity-only' from 'signature-verified' (the struct already exposes signature_valid: Option<bool> separately). Either way, absent-signature must not be conflated with valid-signature. Filed by SapphireHill 2026-06-14 Phase-C security hunt.
close_reason: Fixed: verified now requires signature_valid==Some(true) (fail-closed); absent/invalid signature -> verified=false. Regression test added. Committed.

title: App/blocking-pool audit: a panicking on_thread_start hook churns threads forever and no job runs; shutdown_and_wait can miss an accepted job; cohort starvation; AppSpec duplicate routes by raw string
description:
Read-only audit of src/app.rs and src/runtime/blocking_pool.rs at origin/main 49fec5364 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-05).

No HIGH.

## MEDIUM
M1. shutdown_and_wait can report a clean shutdown while an accepted job has no worker yet (blocking_pool.rs ~788-801).
- The loop checks only active_threads and replacement_pending. A submitter preempted between enqueue and maybe_spawn on an idle min=0 pool (from a non-runtime thread holding a handle) then spawns a worker that is never joined and runs the job after teardown.
- This is the same class as d679m7, on the submitter side.
- Fix: include pending work in the wait condition, or drain from the shutdown path.

M2. A panicking on_thread_start hook causes endless thread churn, and queued jobs never run, even after shutdown (~1392-1399).
- The start hook runs outside catch_unwind (the stop hook is contained). The exit guard spawns a replacement, which panics again.
- FIXED in stack P (P12): the hook is contained like the stop hook.

M3. With cohort affinity, a job routed to a cohort with no live worker can wait forever under sustained load (~1135-1144, ~206-229). Foreign cohort queues are only checked when the worker's own queue and the global queue are empty.

M4. AppSpecV1 duplicate-route detection compares raw path strings (app.rs ~738-758). Two examples:
- `/users` vs `/users/`;
- `GET /users/:id` vs `DELETE /users/:uid`.
In both, one handler silently shadows the other (405s), and routes_ready() reports true.

## LOW
- pending_count can briefly underflow to usize::MAX: the task is pushed before the count is incremented. A wired-up PressureGovernor then sees a huge load.
- The exit-guard handoff lacks the SeqCst fence that the retirement path has.
- A huge max_threads panics at build time: Vec::with_capacity(max_threads).
- Doc mismatches: priority support; completion suppressed for cancelled tasks; the queue is unbounded.
- Threads are created while the pool mutex is held.
- A Startup job bound as Permanent is re-run on every success.
- Some manifest fields (service resources, actor mailbox_capacity) are silently dropped.
- Spawn and Blocking share one capability bit.
- App stop has no time bound (close_within exists but is unused).

title: [EPIC-INFRA] First-Class Tracing Integration with Structured Causality
description:
# Overview

Integrate deeply with the `tracing` crate to automatically instrument task spawning, region 
entry/exit, cancellation events, obligation lifecycle, and budget consumption - with causality 
links between related spans.

## Why This Matters

Async debugging is notoriously difficult. Traditional tracing shows events but not causality.
Asupersync's structured concurrency model means causality IS explicit (parent regions, child 
tasks). Surfacing this through tracing is low-hanging fruit that transforms debugging.

This is foundational infrastructure that enables:
- Task Tree Visualization Dashboard (#4)
- Deterministic Replay Debugging (#6)
- OpenTelemetry Metrics Export (#15)
- Enhanced Cancel Reason Attribution (#10)

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Feature-gated**: `tracing` is an optional dependency behind a feature flag
2. **Zero-cost when disabled**: No overhead when tracing feature is off
3. **Causality links**: Use `tracing::Span::follows_from()` to link related operations
4. **Structured fields**: All spans include region_id, task_id, budget info
5. **Integration with DiagnosticContext**: Leverage existing observability infrastructure

## What Gets Instrumented

- Region lifecycle: enter, exit, state transitions (Open→Closing→Draining→Closed)
- Task lifecycle: spawn, poll, wake, complete, state transitions
- Cancellation flow: request, propagation path, drain, finalize
- Obligation lifecycle: reserve, commit, abort, leak detection
- Budget checkpoints: remaining quota, deadline proximity
- I/O operations: register, ready, complete

## Expected User Experience

```rust
// Users see spans like:
region[id=42, parent=1, state=Open] {
    task[id=100, region=42, state=Running] {
        checkpoint[remaining_polls=847, deadline_in=4.2s]
        cancel_requested[reason=Timeout, source=budget, propagated_from=region:1]
        obligation[kind=SendPermit, id=55, transition=Reserved→Aborted]
    } // task completed: Cancelled(Timeout)
} // region closed: quiescent
```

## Implementation Estimate

- ~300-400 lines of instrumentation code
- Touches: cx.rs, scope.rs, scheduler, obligation registry, reactor
- Dependencies: tracing crate (optional)

## Success Criteria

- [ ] All region state transitions emit spans
- [ ] All task state transitions emit spans  
- [ ] Cancellation propagation is fully traceable
- [ ] Obligation lifecycle is fully traceable
- [ ] Causality links connect parent/child relationships
- [ ] Zero overhead when feature disabled (verified by benchmark)
- [ ] Integration tests verify span structure

title: Scheduler Performance: benchmark suite and regression tests
description:
# Task: Benchmark Suite for Scheduler Performance

## Overview

After performance improvements, we need comprehensive benchmarks to:
1. Measure baseline performance metrics
2. Track performance regression on every PR
3. Compare against alternatives (Tokio, async-std, smol)
4. Validate fairness guarantees statistically
5. Profile for optimization opportunities

## Benchmark Categories

### Micro-benchmarks

#### Queue Operations
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_empty` - Insert into empty queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_100` - Insert into 100-item queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_10000` - Insert into 10000-item queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_pop` - Dequeue from queue
- [ ] `bench_local_queue_push_pop` - Worker-local queue cycle
- [ ] `bench_global_queue_push` - Global queue insertion
- [ ] `bench_global_queue_drain` - Drain batch from global
- [ ] `bench_work_stealing_solo` - Steal with no contention
- [ ] `bench_work_stealing_contended` - Multiple stealers

#### Synchronization Operations
- [ ] `bench_parker_park_unpark_solo` - No contention park/unpark
- [ ] `bench_parker_park_unpark_contended` - High contention scenario
- [ ] `bench_condvar_signal` - Signaling overhead
- [ ] `bench_wake_state_transition` - Atomic state changes
- [ ] `bench_try_lock_success` - Uncontended try_lock
- [ ] `bench_try_lock_failure` - Contended try_lock

#### Task Operations
- [ ] `bench_task_create` - Task allocation cost
- [ ] `bench_task_schedule` - Push to scheduler
- [ ] `bench_task_poll_noop` - Poll empty future
- [ ] `bench_task_poll_yield` - Poll future that yields
- [ ] `bench_waker_wake` - Waker invocation cost
- [ ] `bench_waker_clone` - Waker cloning cost

### Macro-benchmarks

#### Throughput Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_empty_10k` - 10K empty tasks, measure tasks/sec
- [ ] `bench_throughput_empty_100k` - 100K empty tasks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_yielding_1k` - 1K tasks, 10 yields each
- [ ] `bench_throughput_yielding_10k` - 10K tasks, 10 yields each
- [ ] `bench_throughput_cpu_bound` - CPU-intensive tasks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_mixed` - 70% yield, 30% CPU-bound
- [ ] `bench_throughput_chained` - Tasks spawn subtasks

#### Latency Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_latency_spawn_to_poll` - Time from spawn() to first poll
- [ ] `bench_latency_wake_to_poll` - Time from wake() to re-poll
- [ ] `bench_latency_idle_to_run` - Task on idle worker start time
- [ ] `bench_latency_steal_to_run` - Task stolen, time to run
- [ ] `bench_latency_p50_p99_p999` - Full latency distribution

#### Fairness Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_fairness_equal_priority` - Variance in execution count
- [ ] `bench_fairness_priority_ratio` - Higher priority gets more CPU
- [ ] `bench_fairness_starvation_max_wait` - Max wait time < 10x average
- [ ] `bench_fairness_worker_balance` - Work distributed evenly

#### Concurrency Scaling Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_1` - Single worker baseline
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_4` - 4 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_8` - 8 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_16` - 16 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_ncpu` - Number of CPUs
- [ ] `bench_scale_efficiency` - Throughput per worker

#### Memory Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_memory_task_overhead` - Bytes per task
- [ ] `bench_memory_scheduler_idle` - Idle scheduler footprint
- [ ] `bench_memory_scheduler_loaded` - 10K pending tasks
- [ ] `bench_memory_worker_overhead` - Per-worker memory
- [ ] `bench_memory_allocation_rate` - Allocations/sec under load

### Comparative Benchmarks

```rust
// Compare against Tokio
#[bench]
fn bench_vs_tokio_spawn_throughput() {
    // Same workload, measure relative performance
    // Report: asupersync_ops/sec, tokio_ops/sec, ratio
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_tokio_latency_p99() {
    // Same workload, compare p99 latency
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_async_std_spawn_throughput() {
    // Compare against async-std
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_smol_spawn_throughput() {
    // Compare against smol
}
```

### Regression Test Suite

```rust
// Run on every PR to catch regression
#[test]
fn regression_throughput_baseline() {
    warm_up();
    let ops = measure_throughput_10k_empty();
    let baseline = BASELINE_THROUGHPUT;
    let threshold = baseline * 0.9; // Allow 10% regression
    
    assert!(ops >= threshold,
        "Throughput regression: {} ops/sec < {} (baseline {} * 0.9)\n\
         This PR reduces throughput by {:.1}%",
        ops, threshold, baseline,
        (1.0 - ops as f64 / baseline as f64) * 100.0
    );
}

#[test]
fn regression_latency_p99() {
    warm_up();
    let p99 = measure_p99_latency_us();
    let baseline = BASELINE_P99_LATENCY_US;
    let threshold = baseline * 1.2; // Allow 20% regression
    
    assert!(p99 <= threshold,
        "P99 latency regression: {}us > {} (baseline {} * 1.2)\n\
         This PR increases p99 latency by {:.1}%",
        p99, threshold, baseline,
        (p99 as f64 / baseline as f64 - 1.0) * 100.0
    );
}

#[test]
fn regression_memory_per_task() {
    let bytes = measure_memory_per_task();
    let baseline = BASELINE_MEMORY_PER_TASK;
    let threshold = baseline * 1.1; // Allow 10% increase
    
    assert!(bytes <= threshold,
        "Memory regression: {} bytes/task > {} (baseline {} * 1.1)",
        bytes, threshold, baseline
    );
}
```

### Profiling Integration

#[ignore]

}

#[ignore]

}

### E2E Benchmark Script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# scripts/bench_scheduler_e2e.sh

set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_ROOT="$(dirname "$SCRIPT_DIR")"
LOG_DIR="$PROJECT_ROOT/bench_logs/scheduler_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"

echo "=== Scheduler Performance Benchmark Suite ==="
echo "Machine: $(uname -a)"
echo "CPUs: $(nproc)"
echo "Memory: $(free -h | grep Mem | awk '{print $2}')"
echo "Log directory: $LOG_DIR"
echo "Start: $(date -Iseconds)"

# Disable CPU frequency scaling for consistent results
if command -v cpupower &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Setting CPU governor to performance..."
    sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance 2>/dev/null || echo "Could not set governor"
fi

# Warm up (compile and run once)
echo ""
echo "[0/6] Warming up..."
cargo bench --bench scheduler_micro -- --warm-up-time 5 >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

# Run micro-benchmarks
echo ""
echo "[1/6] Running micro-benchmarks..."
cargo bench --bench scheduler_micro 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/bench_micro.log"

# Run macro-benchmarks
echo ""
echo "[2/6] Running macro-benchmarks..."
cargo bench --bench scheduler_macro 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/bench_macro.log"

# Run comparison benchmarks
echo ""
echo "[3/6] Running comparison benchmarks..."
cargo bench --bench scheduler_compare 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/bench_compare.log" || echo "Comparison benchmarks skipped"

# Run scaling benchmarks
echo ""
echo "[4/6] Running scaling benchmarks..."
for workers in 1 2 4 8 $(nproc); do
    ASUPERSYNC_WORKERS=$workers cargo bench --bench scheduler_scale 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG_DIR/bench_scale.log"
done

# Run regression tests
echo ""
echo "[5/6] Running regression tests..."
cargo test --release regression_ -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/regression.log"
REGRESSION_EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

# Generate report
echo ""
echo "[6/6] Generating report..."

# Extract key metrics
THROUGHPUT=$(grep -oP 'throughput.*?(\d+(?:,\d+)*)\s*ops' "$LOG_DIR/bench_macro.log" | head -1 || echo "N/A")
P99_LATENCY=$(grep -oP 'p99.*?(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*(us|ns|ms)' "$LOG_DIR/bench_macro.log" | head -1 || echo "N/A")

cat > "$LOG_DIR/report.md" << EOF
# Scheduler Benchmark Report

## Date
$(date -Iseconds)

## System
- Machine: $(uname -n)
- Kernel: $(uname -r)
- CPUs: $(nproc)
- Memory: $(free -h | grep Mem | awk '{print $2}')
- Rust: $(rustc --version)

## Summary

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Throughput | $THROUGHPUT |
| P99 Latency | $P99_LATENCY |
| Regression Tests | $([ $REGRESSION_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "❌ FAIL") |

## Micro-benchmark Results

\`\`\`
$(grep -E "^(test|bench)" "$LOG_DIR/bench_micro.log" | head -30)
\`\`\`

## Scaling Results

\`\`\`
$(grep -E "workers|throughput" "$LOG_DIR/bench_scale.log" | head -20)
\`\`\`

## Comparison vs Tokio

\`\`\`
$(grep -E "tokio|asupersync|ratio" "$LOG_DIR/bench_compare.log" | head -10)
\`\`\`

## Criterion Reports

HTML reports available at: target/criterion/

EOF

echo "=== Report Generated ==="
cat "$LOG_DIR/report.md"

echo ""
echo "End: $(date -Iseconds)"
echo "Logs saved to: $LOG_DIR"
echo "=== Benchmark Complete ==="

# Exit with failure if regression tests failed
exit $REGRESSION_EXIT
```

title: Implement deferred cleanup queue system
description:
Implement lockless deferred cleanup queues with epoch-based memory reclamation.

## Requirements  
- Lockless enqueue/dequeue for cleanup work items
- Support for different cleanup work types (obligations, wakers, regions)
- Integration with epoch tracking system
- Bounded memory usage with backpressure on overflow

## Technical Approach
- Use crossbeam-queue SegQueue for lockless operation
- Cleanup work item enum with type-specific cleanup handlers
- Epoch-based memory reclamation for queue nodes
- Backpressure mechanism that blocks allocation on queue overflow

## Testing Requirements
- Stress tests with high enqueue/dequeue concurrency
- Memory leak tests over extended operation
- Performance benchmarks vs current direct cleanup
- Correctness tests ensuring no cleanup work is lost

## Integration Points
- RuntimeState cleanup methods call into deferred system
- IO driver waker cleanup uses deferred queues
- Region cleanup integrates with deferred system

title: Client pooling audit (r12 B2): Http2Client clones with different tls_connector share one connection pool (TLS identity mix-up, HIGH); pool_wait_timeout stale retry can fail PoolExhausted; legacy gRPC stream clones lose wakeups; unix: server streaming refused
description:
Read-only audit round r12 B2 (SapphireHill e0155ea8 audit agent, 2026-10-08, origin/main c37c5ddc6) of the API lane's new client features: HttpClientBuilder::pool_wait_timeout 4515d3a98, Http2Client::reuse_connections 0294e933f, gRPC Channel unix dial 45bf3826f, legacy GrpcClient streaming over native HTTP/2 + unary reuse 8ca9aead8, W3C context through the pooled client and streaming responses ed7ca17a2/08a5add2a. Finding 1 (HIGH) was re-read and confirmed by SapphireHill on origin c44bccc95: Http2Client::tls_connector keeps the clone-shared Arc<ConnectionPool>, keyed only by (https, host, port). Full report verbatim below.

# B2 clients audit (read-only, origin/main c37c5ddc6)

Scope: 4515d3a98 (H1 pool_wait_timeout), 0294e933f (H2 reuse_connections),
45bf3826f (gRPC unix: targets), 8ca9aead8 (legacy GrpcClient streaming over
native H2 + unary reuse), ed7ca17a2 / 08a5add2a (TracedHttpClient W3C).
All code read with `git show c37c5ddc6:<path>`; every scoped commit is an ancestor of
c37c5ddc6. Nothing was built or run. Line numbers are on c37c5ddc6.

Six findings: 1 HIGH, 1 MEDIUM, 4 LOW.

---

## 1. HIGH (security, conditional): `Http2Client` pool is shared by clones even after `tls_connector()` is swapped, so one TLS identity's connection carries another's requests

Files: `src/http/h2/client.rs:183-192` (struct: `tls_connector` and `pool: Option<Arc<ConnectionPool>>`),
`:248-253` (`tls_connector`), `:273-281` (`reuse_connections`), `:368-377` (pool lookup), `:1245` (`type Origin = (bool, String, u16)`).

Code:
```rust
pub fn tls_connector(mut self, connector: crate::tls::TlsConnector) -> Self {
    self.tls_connector = Some(connector);   // self.pool (Arc) is kept as is
    self
}
...
let origin: Origin = (request.url.scheme == Scheme::Https, host.clone(), request.url.port);
if let Some(pool) = &self.client.pool {
    while let Some(mut conn) = pool.take(&origin, pool_now(cx)) { ... conn.request(...) ... }
```
`Http2Client` is `#[derive(Clone)]`, and clones share the `Arc<ConnectionPool>`. The docs say so
("shared by the client's clones"). The pool key is only (https, host, port). It does not include the
connector that authenticated the connection. The only connector check before the pool is
`tls_connector.is_none()` (`:359`).

Scenario:
```rust
let base = Http2Client::new().reuse_connections(4);
let a = base.clone().tls_connector(connector_with_client_cert_A);  // or private-CA trust
let b = base.clone().tls_connector(connector_with_client_cert_B);  // or a pinned/stricter verifier
a.get("https://api.example/x").send(cx).await?;  // dials, mTLS as A, pooled under (true,"api.example",443)
b.get("https://api.example/y").send(cx).await?;  // pool.take() returns A's TLS connection
```
- The server authenticates B's request as tenant A (an mTLS identity mix-up).
- B's trust policy (roots, pins, SNI rules) is never evaluated for that request.

Reachability: it needs two clones with different connectors for the same origin, for example
per-tenant mTLS clients derived from one pooled base.

Fix shape (additive; v0.4.3-compatible):
- Preferred: `tls_connector()` detaches the pool. If `self.pool` is `Some`, replace it with a fresh
  `ConnectionPool { max_idle, idle: Mutex::new(HashMap::new()) }`, and document it.
- Alternative: add a connector identity (for example, the address of the connector's
  `Arc<ClientConfig>`) to `Origin`.

Failing test sketch:
- Unit test in `client.rs` (`cfg(feature = "tls")`):
  - Build `base` with `reuse_connections(2)`, then `a = base.clone().tls_connector(c1)` and
    `b = base.clone().tls_connector(c2)`.
  - Assert `!Arc::ptr_eq(a.pool.as_ref().unwrap(), b.pool.as_ref().unwrap())`. Today they are equal.
- Integration test:
  - Run a TLS h2 server with a self-signed certificate and count accepted connections.
  - `a`'s connector trusts the certificate. `b`'s connector has an empty or other root store.
  - After `a` succeeds, `b.get(url).send(cx)` must fail with `Http2ClientError::Tls`. Today it
    succeeds, and the server accepts only 1 connection.

---

## 2. MEDIUM: with `pool_wait_timeout`, a stale-connection retry that has to wait can never take a connection released to the idle set; it fails `PoolExhausted` after the full wait

Files: `src/http/h1/http_client.rs:2490-2504` (`acquire_fresh_connection` → `reuse_idle = false`),
`:2544` (`if reuse_idle {`), `:2574-2590`, `:2594-2622` (the wait), `:1832-1848` / `:1869` (the retry);
`src/http/pool.rs:471-476` and `:480` (`evict_idle_for`).

Why:
- `acquire_fresh_connection` removes the host's idle connections once (`pool.remove_idle(&key)`).
  It then loops with `reuse_idle == false`, which skips the idle branch on every iteration.
- At the limit it waits on `pool_released`. When the in-flight holder finishes,
  `release_connection` stores the connection as **idle** and notifies.
- The waiter wakes and still cannot use that connection:
  - `reuse_idle` is false, so it skips the idle branch.
  - `evict_idle_for(&key)` returns `None`: it never evicts the same key
    (`.filter(|(host_key, _)| *host_key != key)`), and it returns early when the key is at its own
    per-host limit (`:471-476`).
  - `can_create_connection` counts the idle connection, so it is false.
- The waiter sleeps again. Nothing frees a slot, because releases go back to idle, so it ends at
  `Err(_elapsed) => return Err(exhausted())`. The `observe/until` deadline is fixed, so the whole
  `pool_wait_timeout` is spent.

Scenario (defaults plus the opt-in):
- `HttpClient::builder().max_connections_per_host(1).pool_wait_timeout(30s)`; the default
  `RetryPolicy::SafeMethodsOnStaleReuse` is in effect.
- The server restarts, so idle keep-alive connections go stale.
- GET A reuses stale connection #1, fails, and runs `drop(guard)`. That calls `drop_connection` and
  notifies the waiters.
- On a multi-thread runtime, waiter W (or any new request on another worker) registers the freed
  slot first. A then calls `acquire_fresh_connection` and waits with `reuse_idle = false`.
- W completes and releases #2 to idle.
- A sleeps until the 30 s wait expires and returns `PoolExhausted`, while #2 sits idle and healthy.

Without the wait option the same race already returns `PoolExhausted` at once. The new feature's
promise to wait for a connection is broken on this path. On a current-thread runtime A usually wins,
because nothing awaits between `drop(guard)` and `register_connecting`.

Fix shape (internal only): in `acquire_connection_with`, make `reuse_idle` mutable and set it to
`true` after the first wake (`Ok(true)`). Connections released after the stale failure have just
finished an exchange, so they are not the stale generation. Alternative: when `!reuse_idle`, run
`remove_idle(&key)` (and notify) on every iteration before `can_create_connection`.

Failing test sketch (unit test in the `http_client.rs` tests module, which can reach private items):
- Setup:
  - Start a `std::net::TcpListener` on 127.0.0.1:0 that accepts in a thread.
  - Build the client with `max_connections_per_host(1)` and `pool_wait_timeout(5s)`.
  - Parse the URL to `parsed` and take `key = parsed.pool_key()`.
- Simulate the holder: `let id = client.pool.lock().register_connecting(key.clone(), client.pool_now(), 1);`
- Release from another thread: a std thread sleeps 100 ms, then calls
  `client.release_connection(&key, Some(id), true, loopback_client_io())`.
- Main thread: inside `RuntimeBuilder::current_thread().build().block_on`, time
  `client.acquire_fresh_connection(&cx, &parsed)`.
- Assert `Ok` within 1 s. Today it returns `Err(PoolExhausted)` after about 5 s.

---

## 3. LOW: legacy native `ResponseStream` clones polled from two tasks lose wakeups; one can hang forever

Files: `src/grpc/client/legacy_native.rs:175-189` (`Fanout { wakers: Mutex<[Option<Waker>; 2]> }`, one
slot per role), `:403-416` (`poll_message` registers `Role::Response`);
`src/grpc/client.rs:3130-3136` (the native path returns before `state.register_waiter`),
`:3156-3165` (end-of-call wakes only `state.take_waiters()`).

Why:
- Every `ResponseStream` clone polls as `Role::Response`. `Fanout::register` keeps one waker per
  role and replaces it when `!will_wake`.
- Native polls never join `ResponseStreamState::waiters`. The loopback and legacy `ResponseStream`
  keeps a waiter list, so concurrent clones are a supported pattern there.

Scenario:
- `let (sink, stream) = client.bidi_streaming(path).await?; let s2 = stream.clone();`
- Task T1 awaits `stream.next()` and task T2 awaits `s2.next()`, and both park. The Response slot
  holds only T2's waker.
- The next message wakes only T2.
- When the call ends, T2 sets `closed` and wakes `state.waiters`, which is empty for native polls.
- T1 is never woken, so its `next()` hangs indefinitely.

Fix shape (additive): in `poll_native`, on `Pending` also `state.register_waiter(cx.waker())`. On any
`Ready` (message or end) wake `take_waiters()` so other clones re-poll. Or let `Fanout` hold a
deduplicated `Vec<Waker>` for the Response role.

Failing test sketch:
- Use the legacy_streaming harness in `tests/grpc_http2_e2e.rs`. The server sends 2 messages
  100 ms apart, then OK.
- Clone the stream. Spawn 2 tasks that each await `next()` until `None`, each under a 3 s timeout.
- Assert both finish. Today one task times out.

---

## 4. LOW: gRPC unary `reuse_connections` discards a healthy pooled connection on every non-OK grpc-status

Files: `src/grpc/client.rs:1996-2000`
(`accumulator.finish().map(..).map_err(UnaryFailure::processed)`), `:2044-2045`
(`Err(failure) => return Err(failure.status)`), `:2050-2053` (fresh path `map_err(|f| f.status)?`),
`:2374-2396` (`finish` returns `Err` for `grpc-status != 0`).

Why:
- An application status such as NOT_FOUND or PERMISSION_DENIED comes back as an `Err` from
  `exchange`.
- It is handled the same way as a transport failure. The connection is dropped instead of reaching
  `pool_after_success`, even though the stream closed cleanly both ways.

Scenario:
- `ChannelBuilder::reuse_connections(1)`.
- Three calls to a method that answers trailers-only `grpc-status: 5`.
- The server accepts 3 connections (3 TLS handshakes on https) instead of 1.
- This defeats the opt-in feature on common error paths. There is no leak.

Fix shape: return the completed wire outcome, `(Result<NativeUnaryWireResponse, Status>, stream_id)`,
from `exchange` once `accumulator.is_complete()`. Call `pool_after_success` for any completed stream
whose request side is fully sent and whose connection is `reusable()`. Then return the status.

Failing test sketch:
- Use the raw-H2-peer fixture behind `unary_calls_dial_per_call_by_default_and_reuse_when_enabled`.
  The peer answers `:status 200` with trailers-only `grpc-status: 5`.
- Make 3 calls with reuse on. Assert each one returns NOT_FOUND and the peer's accept count is 1.
  Today the count is 3.

---

## 5. LOW: `Channel::server_streaming_on` refuses every `unix:` channel that 45bf3826f now allows

Files: `src/grpc/native_streaming.rs:148` (`let (scheme, authority) = authority(channel.uri())?;`), `:639-647`:
```rust
let (scheme, rest) = uri.split_once("://").ok_or_else(|| Status::invalid_argument("invalid gRPC URI"))?;
```
Why: `Channel::connect("unix:///run/app.sock")` and `Channel::connect("unix:app.sock")` now succeed
(`parse_channel_uri` → `unix_target_path`, `client.rs:2422-2430`). The caller-supplied-transport API
still parses the URI as `scheme://authority`.

Scenario:
- `channel = Channel::connect("unix:app.sock")`, which has no `://`.
- `channel.server_streaming_on(cx, unix_stream, path, req, codec)` returns `INVALID_ARGUMENT`
  "invalid gRPC URI" before I/O.
- `unix:///run/app.sock` splits to scheme `unix`, which is not http or https, and gets the same
  error.

Fix shape: resolve scheme and authority through `parse_channel_uri`: for `unix:` targets use
`("http", "localhost")`, as `NativeH2Target::unix` does.

Failing test sketch: build a `unix:` channel to the Unix-socket server in
`tests/grpc_http2_unix_socket.rs`. Call `server_streaming_on` with a `UnixStream` to it and assert
the stream yields the service's message. Today it returns INVALID_ARGUMENT.

---

## 6. LOW (interop): `unix:` target paths are used verbatim: not percent-decoded, and `?` / `#` stay in the file name

File: `src/grpc/client.rs:2556-2576` (`unix_target_path` returns `&uri[5..]`, minus `//`, unchanged).

Scenario:
- `Channel::connect("unix:///tmp/my%20app.sock")` dials the literal `/tmp/my%20app.sock`.
- `unix:///run/x.sock?foo` dials `/run/x.sock?foo`. Both end as UNAVAILABLE (ENOENT).
- UNCONFIRMED (from memory): grpc-go builds the unix endpoint from `url.URL.Path`, which is decoded
  and has the query removed, so it dials `/tmp/my app.sock`. The asupersync behavior above is
  confirmed by reading the code.

Fix shape: percent-decode the path for the `unix:/…` and `unix:///…` forms, and reject or strip
`?` and `#`. `ChannelUri.unix_path` then needs an owned `String` (crate-private).

Failing test sketch: `parse_channel_uri("unix:///tmp/a%20b").unwrap().unix_path == Some("/tmp/a b")`.

---

## Sound (checked, no defect found)

- **H1 pool wait (4515d3a98):**
  - The `Notified` is created and `enable()`d at the top of each iteration. Its generation is
    captured in `notified()`, so a release between inspection and the wait still wakes it.
  - Every path that frees a slot notifies: `release_connection` (after the idle IO is stored and the
    pool lock is dropped), `drop_connection`, the `ConnectGuard` drop, and stale-idle removal.
  - The wake is a broadcast with no hand-off, so a waiter that times out or is cancelled cannot
    strand or double-count a connection. `Notified::drop` deregisters it.
  - The limit holds: registration happens under the pool lock.
  - The wait deadline is fixed across re-waits (`wait_until`) and sits inside the request's total
    timeout and budget. A cancelled Cx ends the wait; a masked cancellation keeps it waiting.
  - Not FIFO: documented.
- **H2 reuse (0294e933f):**
  - A pooled connection is owned by one request future; cancellation or deadline drops it.
  - It is put back only when `sent == body.len()`, no frames are pending for the stream, and the
    connection is `Open` with no GOAWAY either way.
  - `refresh()` drains buffered and idle-time frames, including a trailing RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR),
    before reuse.
  - Late frames for earlier streams are ignored once the new stream is open.
  - Retry happens only for a stream refused locally, REFUSED_STREAM, or a GOAWAY that excludes the
    stream.
  - The `exchange` and `send_on` refactor keeps the old logic.
- **gRPC unary pool (8ca9aead8):**
  - `take()` is exclusive.
  - The unprocessed classification is correct for unary: END_STREAM rides on the last message
    frame.
  - `pool_after_success` checks pending frames and GOAWAY. The accumulator ignores frames for other
    streams.
  - The channel is immutable and has a single target, and metadata cannot set `:authority` or
    `host`, so no per-origin key is needed.
  - A timeout drops the connection.
- **Legacy streaming (8ca9aead8):**
  - `request_ready` / `RequestFlushed` slot handoff: the duplex starts with `request_pending = true`,
    so the first event releases the slot.
  - The fan-out waker covers the transport, the Cx cancel waker and timers.
  - Backpressure at `MAX_STREAM_BUFFERED`: the reader's pop wakes the sink.
  - Client-streaming enforces exactly one response.
  - Drop/cancel: a sink dropped after `close()` is a no-op, and `cancel` after finish is a no-op.
  - Lock order: the codec lock is never held while taking the state lock.
- **unix: (45bf3826f):**
  - TLS, `tls_server_name` and `dial_addr` are refused.
  - Connect is bounded by `connect_timeout`: `NativeH2Conn::dial` wraps the dial in a timeout, and
    the streaming path uses `Setup::run`.
  - `:authority` is `localhost` and `:scheme` is `http`. Loopback detection is unaffected. The
    unary pool works over UDS.
- **W3C (ed7ca17a2, 08a5add2a):**
  - Headers appear exactly once: the wrappers drop user-supplied traceparent, tracestate and baggage,
    and the config's default propagation headers are stripped.
  - Retries and same-origin redirects reuse the same `extra_headers`, and `Limited` is narrowed to
    `SameOrigin`. Origin includes the scheme, so an https→http downgrade is not followed.
  - Baggage is opt-in. A CONNECT tunnel gets only Proxy-Authorization.
  - The context is per request, so nothing leaks across callers on a pooled connection.
  - An invalid parent starts a new trace and drops tracestate, as W3C requires.
  - These commits say they were never compiled. I checked that every API they reference exists and
    is visible at c37c5ddc6: `Cx::random_bytes`, `ClientRequestBuilder: Clone` with
    `header`/`json`/`timeout`/`send`, the pub `HttpClientConfig` fields, the `h1::ClientIo` and
    `ClientStreamingResponse` exports, and the W3C helpers. Compilation itself was not verified.

title: Panicking Mutex grantee Waker can freeze FIFO handoff
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found Mutex::unlock pops waiter A, stores granted_waiter=A, and then calls A Waker without an exception-safe handoff. If wake panics before scheduling A, the mutex is unlocked but the grant remains pinned to A; later waiter B stays queued and receives no wake unless the abandoned A future is eventually dropped. The same baton path exists when cleanup_waiter grants a successor, and a Waker panic during guard destruction can become an aborting second panic. Catch wake panics, revoke a failed unconsumed grant under state, continue to the next eligible waiter without re-waking the same payload, and propagate only where unwind-safe. Add A-panics/B-counts regressions for normal unlock and cancelled granted-waiter baton pass, including guard drop during an existing unwind.
close_reason: Fixed 6d3b0e00d: exception-safe wake_granted baton (revoke-and-pass, resume-or-suppress); 3 regression tests green by name, control run red pre-fix

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-07-27 — fixed with exception-safe baton handoff (6d3b0e00d).

MECHANISM (as the bead predicted, both sites): Mutex::unlock and the
cleanup_waiter successor path pinned granted_waiter=A then called A's Waker
bare. A wake panic left the mutex unlocked with the grant pinned to a
never-woken task; the fast path and try_lock refuse while a grant is
outstanding, so all later waiters froze. In guard drops during an existing
unwind, the panic was a process-aborting double panic.

FIX: shared Mutex::wake_granted — per-wake catch_unwind; on panic the failed

title: Mutex and RwLock failed try-lock calls can raise false lock-order panic
description: src/sync/mutex.rs Mutex::try_lock and src/sync/rwlock.rs try_acquire_read_state and try_acquire_write_state call lock_ordering::check_acquire before inspecting poisoned, locked, queued-writer, or active-reader state. In debug or lock-metrics builds, operations that should return TryLockError, TryReadError, or TryWriteError can instead panic with ASUP-E205 and record nonexistent acquisition edges. Independently identified by a semaphore review and confirmed by direct second code-path inspection on 2026-07-15; 501dd8267 introduced the eager precheck and no matching bead exists. Move check_acquire under the state guard into each successful eligibility branch immediately before the state transition, matching async acquisition and the separately tracked semaphore fix. Regression should hold a higher-ranked guard, require unavailable and poisoned lower-ranked nonblocking calls to return their normal Err variants, and require an actually available lower-ranked acquisition to keep enforcing the ordering panic.
close_reason: Fixed in 18dfce24b: moved lock_ordering::check_acquire off the eager precheck into the success branch (under the state guard, before the transition) in Mutex::try_lock (borrowed+owned), RwLock::try_acquire_read_state, try_acquire_write_state — mirroring the async path. Failed try (locked/poisoned/reader-present) now returns Err without a false ASUP-E205 or phantom edge; available lower-ranked acquisition still enforces the ordering panic. +2 regressions (mutex+rwlock). Verified sync::mutex 72/72 + sync::rwlock 72/72 (debug_assertions).

title: Mutex guard drop wakes reentrant code before recording lock-order release
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found Mutex::unlock invokes the selected Waker before all four borrowed, mapped, owned, and owned-mapped guard Drop implementations call lock_ordering::record_release. A synchronous Waker can re-enter lock acquisition while the released rank is still recorded as held, causing a false ASUP-E205 on an otherwise valid lower-ranked acquisition. If the Waker panics, record_release is skipped entirely and leaves a phantom held rank for the thread. Split transition and callback delivery: extract the Waker under state, record the rank release, then invoke user-controlled wake code, consistently for all guard variants. Regressions should use a reentrant Waker that acquires a valid lower-ranked mutex and a panicking Waker followed by a valid acquisition, proving no false violation or phantom rank remains.
close_reason: Fixed in b94dcb5e3 with deterministic four-guard regression coverage

title: Mutex clones and destroys queued Wakers while holding state lock
description: Fresh read-only audit plus direct second review on 2026-07-15 found three Mutex paths that can execute Waker vtable code or destroy the last Waker-owned payload while MutexState is locked: LockFuture::cleanup_waiter binds WaiterChain::remove to _removed inside the state-guard scope; changed-waker polling calls WaiterChain::update_waker, whose clone_from destroys the old Waker in place; and registration/requeue clones the incoming Context Waker under the guard. A safe Drop payload that re-enters the same mutex can self-deadlock. This is the Mutex integration sibling of the existing RwLock and Semaphore retirement beads, not a duplicate of either. Clone incoming Wakers before taking state, replace or remove by value, and carry all retired or unused Wakers beyond the guard before destruction. Add cancellation, timeout, changed-waker, and requeue regressions with Drop probes that require state.try_lock to succeed during retirement.

title: Migration planner: render operator report and risk-scored phase plan
description:
## What
Create the human-readable and machine-readable report layer. It should merge inventory, semantic migration recommendations, compat quarantine rows, proof-pack commands, and residual risks into a phased migration plan that an operator can act on.

## Why
The planner is only valuable if the output is navigable. Large migrations need a short executive summary, precise file/surface pointers, ordered phases, risk scores, and rerun/proof handles that work in CI and during human review.

## Implementation guidance
- Produce stable JSON and Markdown outputs from the same data model.
- Include phase ordering, expected blast radius, confidence score, native/compat/blocker counts, proof commands, residual-risk owner rows, and next recommended bead/task suggestions.
- Make report wording deterministic enough for golden tests while still readable.
- Keep raw details accessible; summaries must point to raw artifacts rather than replacing them.

## Tests and logging
Golden tests should pin representative Markdown and JSON reports for clean, mixed, and blocked migrations. Include malformed input and missing proof-pack scenarios. Logs must include report version, input artifact hashes, generated output paths, recommendation counts, and final verdict.

## Success criteria
A contributor can read the report and understand the migration order, blockers, evidence level, and exact commands without spelunking the raw JSON first.

title: [bug-hunt] raptorq/linalg: solve() vs solve_markowitz() classify same system as Inconsistent vs Singular (5x5 GF(256))
description:
raptorq_gauss_solver fuzz target oracle (br-v57ezp validation run, fuzz job b5en5e4gd) caught a divergence between the two Gaussian-elimination pivot strategies on the SAME input matrix:

```
basic = solve()           → GaussianResult::Inconsistent
markowitz = solve_markowitz() → GaussianResult::Singular
```

Both return values are documented as VALID outcomes for the same trait, but they are SEMANTICALLY DIFFERENT:
- Inconsistent: the system has NO solution (rank(A) < rank([A|b]))
- Singular: the system MAY have infinitely many solutions (rank(A) < cols, but b is in column-space)

A correct solver MUST classify any given system identically; one of the two strategies is misclassifying.

**Crash repro** (saved at fuzz/artifacts/raptorq_gauss_solver/crash-8223d855022c3b77546c9263fb37207069b2c741, 36 bytes):

Hex bytes:
```
0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x17, 0x5b, 0x0d,
0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c,
0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x4c, 0x4c,
0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x00, 0x00
```

Base64: `TExMTExMTBdbDUxMTExMTExMTEwAAAAAAAAAAExMTExMTAAA`

Per the fuzz target's input layout (fuzz/fuzz_targets/raptorq_gauss_solver.rs):
- bytes[0] = 0x4c → rows = 0x4c % 24 + 1 = **5**
- bytes[1] = 0x4c → cols = 0x4c % 24 + 1 = **5**
- bytes[2..27] = 25 GF(256) coefficients (5x5 matrix, mostly 0x4c with a few outliers at indices 5,6,7 = 0x17, 0x5b, 0x0d)
- bytes[27..] = RHS seed for build_rhs

To reproduce locally:
```bash
cd /data/projects/asupersync
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_pane13 rch exec -- cargo +nightly fuzz run raptorq_gauss_solver fuzz/artifacts/raptorq_gauss_solver/crash-8223d855022c3b77546c9263fb37207069b2c741
```

Or as a unit test in src/raptorq/linalg.rs:
```rust
#[test]
fn solve_vs_markowitz_must_agree_on_5x5_singular_v_inconsistent() {
    let coefs: [[u8; 5]; 5] = [
        [0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c],
        [0x4c, 0x4c, 0x17, 0x5b, 0x0d],
        [0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c],
        [0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c],
        [0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x4c, 0x00],
    ];
    // RHS derived from seed bytes 27.. via build_rhs() in the fuzz target.
    // Two solvers built from the same matrix MUST agree on result_kind.
}
```

Severity: HIGH (P1) — the two pivot strategies are documented to solve the SAME systems with the SAME outcomes, just at different cost/quality tradeoffs. A semantic disagreement on classification means one strategy returns INCORRECT information about whether the system has a solution. RaptorQ FEC encoding/decoding makes branching decisions based on these outcomes (proceed-with-solve vs request-more-symbols), so a misclassification can cause spurious decode failures or premature symbol requests.

Investigation hint: the divergence is INSIDE the rank-determination logic. Compare the rank/zero-row checks in solve() (basic pivot, src/raptorq/linalg.rs) vs solve_markowitz() (Markowitz-pivot variant). Markowitz reorders rows/cols differently; if either strategy's post-elimination rank check is wrong, this is where it surfaces.

Fuzz job: b5en5e4gd. Discovery time: ~34470 fuzz iterations into the run. Caught by the consistency oracle at fuzz_targets/raptorq_gauss_solver.rs:77.
close_reason: Fix already shipped in 609f18b36 ('fix(raptorq): proof-trace timing + Gaussian Singular/Inconsistent + regen snapshot'). Verified in src/raptorq/linalg.rs:787 + 843 — both solve() and solve_markowitz() now route the pivot-stall classification through first_inconsistent_row_from(pivot_col) (full scan) instead of the old single-row first_inconsistent_row_at. Regression tests at lines 2418+ (_mwx6zi_class helper, mwx6zi_classifier_agreement_* tests) pin the agreement contract across all 4 classification arms (rank-deficient with late contradiction, rank-deficient no contradiction, solvable, synthetic sweep). My follow-up commit 0ef33b96c only updated the bead state. Lib check passes.

title: quic_native GH#71: ~71% spurious loss and cwnd collapse at ~29 ms RTT (1 MiB in 14.3 s, 736 lost / 1032 acked, pto 0)
description: GitHub #71 (FrankenRemote D6, real tailnet path, direct WireGuard, ~29 ms RTT). Code facts at HEAD: loss detection (transport.rs on_ack_ranges) uses packet threshold 3 and time threshold now-loss_delay with loss_delay = 9/8*max(srtt, latest); the receiver's ack_frame (connection.rs ~3181) always encodes ack_delay = 0 and bounds ranges to MAX_ACK_FRAME_RANGES = 96; smoothed_rtt was reported as 44 ms on a 29 ms path (ACK delay never subtracted); pto_count stayed 0 so the declarations are threshold-based, not PTO. Suspects: (1) ack_delay 0 inflates RTT samples by the receiver's drive cadence, but that widens loss_delay rather than narrowing it — it does not explain the losses alone; (2) the caller-driven drive loop's cadence (receive_wait up to 500 ms, MAX_PACKETS_PER_FLUSH bursts) vs the time threshold: packets generated in a burst ahead of an ACK for a later burst; (3) ack-range truncation or a packet-number bookkeeping mismatch between sent_packets and the ACK frame. WHAT: reproduce deterministically in the lab with a 30 ms one-way delay link (extend tests/quic_h3_e2e_loss.rs's injected-loss harness with delay), assert lost/acked ratio on a lossless delayed path stays near zero, then fix the detector/cadence and re-run the real-path scenario (franken_remote spike serve/connect-remote, or hz3<->vmi at ~88 ms). ACCEPTANCE: near-zero spurious loss on a clean delayed path; throughput bounded by the path.
close_reason: GH#71 fixed in c72aae490: non-in-flight (ACK-only) packets are never declared lost (RFC 9002 A.10/B.8) and receivers keep non-ack-eliciting packet numbers in ACK ranges (RFC 9000 s13.2.1). Delayed-path lab test 29 ms RTT: 13.3 s/369 lost -> 218 ms/0 lost; receipts on the bead; issue closed.

title: [bug-hunt] database/mysql: COM_STMT_EXECUTE parameter type metadata never sets UNSIGNED flag
description:
Severity: HIGH (silent data corruption for unsigned integers > signed-max).

src/database/mysql.rs:3151-3155 (`write_stmt_execute_params`):

    buf.write_byte(0x01);                              // new-params-bound
    for param in params {
        buf.write_u16_le(u16::from(param.mysql_type_code()));
    }

The MySQL binary protocol for COM_STMT_EXECUTE encodes each parameter's
type as 2 bytes:

    low byte (offset 0):  MYSQL_TYPE_xxx
    high byte (offset 1): flags. bit 0x80 = UNSIGNED.

`u16::from(type_code: u8)` is the type in the LO byte and 0 in the HI
byte — i.e., no UNSIGNED flag is ever set. Without it, the server
interprets every numeric parameter as signed:

    u32::MAX           => server reads as i32 = -1
    u64::MAX           => server reads as i64 = -1
    u32 > i32::MAX     => negative i32 on server
    u64 > i64::MAX     => negative i64 on server

Round-tripping such a value through a prepared statement returns the
wrong number on the server (and any `WHERE id = ?` predicate will not
match the row the caller meant to identify).

The `mysql_type` constant module at src/database/mysql.rs:3175-3184
also has no unsigned variants — there is no path to communicate "this
u32 is unsigned" through the `ToSql::mysql_type_code` trait.

Fix shape:
  1. Add `fn is_unsigned(&self) -> bool { false }` (default false) to
     the `ToSql` trait.
  2. Override on the integer impls (u8, u16, u32, u64, usize → true).
  3. In `write_stmt_execute_params`, encode the type field as:
        let mut t = u16::from(type_code);
        if param.is_unsigned() { t |= 0x80_00; }
        buf.write_u16_le(t);
     (0x80_00 = bit 0x80 in the HI byte under little-endian wire.)
  4. Add a fixture test that round-trips u32::MAX and u64::MAX through
     a real (or mock) MySQL server and asserts the server saw the same
     value the client sent.

Pass 1 of this audit verified mysql_native_auth and caching_sha2_auth
formulas SOUND against the canonical RFC-style references, including
input order to the inner SHA1/SHA256 (nonce || double_hash for
mysql_native, double_hash || nonce for caching_sha2). XOR composition,
empty-password short-circuit, and SHA-1 prehash all match.
close_reason: done

title: MySQL client audit (r10): the prepared-statement cache survives USE and pool return (silent cross-schema reads/writes); stale max_execution_time after a cancelled SET; commit Ok after a server-ended transaction; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of the MySQL client (src/database/mysql.rs, mysql_load_data_infile_security_audit.rs, and the pool/transaction parts it uses) at origin/main b94da3ea9, re-checked unchanged at d6208c454 (SapphireHill audit agent round 10, 10-07). Report: /data/tmp/rc_20260923/audit_r10_mysql.md. Overlapping, still-open items stay on asupersync-k3y26t (H3 session reset on pool return, M2 DECIMAL as f64 on the text path, M3 charset echo, L1-L7) and bi2462.112 (static-SQL heuristic).

## HIGH
H1. The prepared-statement cache is keyed by SQL text only and survives USE and pool return. MySQL binds a prepared statement to the default database (and parse-time sql_mode) in effect at prepare time, so after `USE tenant_b` (same checkout, or the next pooled tenant) prepare() returned a statement still reading and writing the earlier schema's tables, with no error. Planned fix: empty the cache and close its statements before a USE or a SET of sql_mode (public query/execute/stream paths, so the client's own managed SETs do not flush).

## MEDIUM
M1. The max_execution_time cache used None both for "server default" and "unknown": a SET cancelled before it was written left the old server limit in force while the cache read as default, so later deadline-free queries were killed with ER 3024. (PostgreSQL's twin was fixed under 91hka0 item 7.)
M2. commit() returned Ok after the server had already ended the transaction (an InnoDB deadlock rollback, 1213, or a DDL implicit commit); statements after that point autocommitted. (PostgreSQL's twin: 91hka0 item 4.)
M3. (OWNER) statement_timeout_override and max_result_rows survive pool return, so one borrower's settings govern the next borrower's queries. The PostgreSQL manager has the same gap; resetting per-checkout knobs changes pooled semantics for both clients.
M4. (OWNER, test-pinned) Prepared-statement TIME values come back as "D HH:MM:SS" ("0 01:00:00") and fractional seconds ignore the column's precision, unlike the text protocol. tests/conformance/mysql_stmt_prepare_execute.rs pins the current form ("-1 02:03:04", "0 10:20:30.000005").

## LOW
L1. An ERR packet sent instead of the greeting (1040 "Too many connections", 1129) was reported as a malformed handshake, losing the server's code. (Classifying 1040 as transient is an OWNER decision.)
L2. URL keys were case-sensitive and unknown keys ignored, so `sslMode=REQUIRED`, `ssl_mode=required` and `SSL-MODE=required` connected in plaintext. (Rejecting other TLS-intent keys such as `ssl` or `useSSL` is an OWNER decision.)
L3. (OWNER) connect_timeout=0 fails every connect and also sets the KILL QUERY bound to zero.
L4. (OWNER) The connection id (the KILL QUERY target) and the echoed charset come from the unauthenticated pre-TLS greeting; an on-path attacker could redirect KILLs or choose the charset. Fix options cost a round trip per TLS connect.
L5. The text protocol failed on column types the client does not know (MySQL 9 VECTOR, 242) with a binary payload; the binary protocol returns bytes.
L6. (91hka0 item 12, never landed) An ERR packet after some rows (KILL QUERY 1317, max_execution_time 3024) left an in-sync connection marked closed, so a healthy connection was discarded.

Judged SOUND: see the report (desync protection, KILL bounds, timeout reconciliation on stream and prepared paths, typed binary parameters (no PG-style reinterpretation), framing bounds, LOCAL INFILE and multi-results never enabled, authentication and TLS fail closed).

title: Pool audit: an idle checkout's detach skips the marginal wake (a waiter sleeps to the 30 s acquire timeout beside an idle resource); return_to_pool re-pools a resource marked broken; a resource returned after close() lingers
description:
Read-only audit of src/sync/{mutex,contended_mutex,barrier,once_cell,pool,waiter}.rs at origin/main 6ad7540cd (SapphireHill audit agent S1, 10-05). Each finding below was confirmed by re-reading the code.

No HIGH. Sound:
- Mutex handoff, cancel and poisoning; guard map/try_map.
- ContendedMutex lock-order tracking.
- WaiterChain id/ABA handling.
- Barrier generation, cancel and leader election.
- OnceCell (InitGuard resets on cancel, error or panic; no lost wakeup).
- Pool cancel paths, create-slot rollback and FIFO window.

## MEDIUM
M1. An idle checkout's detach skips the marginal wake, so a waiter can sleep until the 30 s acquire timeout beside an idle resource.
- Where (pool.rs at 6ad7540cd):
  - try_get_idle(Some(id)) (~2034-2050) pops an idle resource and adds one to `active`, but leaves the taker queued in state.waiters through its health check (~2405-2425).
  - detach_waiter (~2214) then removes it without the marginal wake that WaiterCleanup::drop does (~2330-2350).
- What goes wrong:
  - While the taker is still queued, `available` already counts its checkout. A waiter polling in that gap finds itself at index == available, outside the window, and parks.
  - The detach moves it to available-1, inside the window, and nothing wakes it.
  - The dispatcher handoff covers this only when the taker was return_wakers[0]. A taker that was eligible on its first WaitForNotification poll has no return entry.
- Trigger (max_size 2, health_check_on_acquire, deterministic through the pool clock and health-check hooks):
  1. X and Y hold both resources.
  2. A finds the pool full. Both return during A's first idle probe, so A's wait queues it at index 0 of an open window and it returns Ready with no return waker.
  3. A takes one idle resource.
  4. During A's health check, B polls and parks at index 1 (available == 1).
  5. A detaches. B is now at index 0 with an idle resource free, and receives no wake.
- Impact:
  - B waits for the next return or discard, or fails with PoolError::Timeout after acquire_timeout.
  - Without a health check the window is narrower (ActiveCheckoutGuard::new), but a multi-thread race still opens it.
- Fix (taken by SapphireHill):
  - detach_waiter returns the waker of the waiter its removal moves into the window, using the same rule as WaiterCleanup.
  - DetachedPoolWakers.retire wakes it outside the locks.

## LOW
L1. A resource returned after close() is not destroyed until some later pool call (pool.rs ~609-631, ~2724).
- The Return sits in the channel. c11v6v item 5 only drains returns already queued when close() runs.
- A pool kept for the life of the app holds the connection, counted as active.
- Fix: give PooledResource the pool's closed flag; when closed, send Discard and drop the resource locally. This is a structural change.

L2. PooledResource::return_to_pool re-pools a resource marked broken (pool.rs ~541-543).
- It calls return_inner unconditionally. The mark_broken contract says the resource "never re-enters the idle pool", and Drop and CheckedPooledResource already discard it.
- Fix (taken by SapphireHill): return_to_pool routes a broken resource through discard_inner.

L3. Mutex::is_locked() returns false while the lock is handed to a woken waiter that has not resumed yet, but try_lock() returns Err(Locked) (mutex.rs ~169-171). waiters() also leaves out that waiter.
- Fix: report `locked || granted_waiter.is_some()`, or document it.
- mutex.rs carries unsafe-ledger line locators up to line 1041, so any edit must be line-neutral.

L4. Docs.
- Pool::health_check (pool.rs ~297-315) is documented as "called before returning an idle resource", but nothing calls it.
- README ~1541 says Mutex "tracks contention"; only ContendedMutex does.
- README ~1546 labels once_cell.rs "OnceLock".
- PoolConfig's unwired knobs are tracked in y6naky item 4.
close_reason: done
