comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
Narrowing accepted after re-reading src/cx/cx.rs 5058-5083 (SapphireHill, 2026-09-12 03:3xZ).

Admission denials such as RegionAtCapacity are delivered through the task handle (with_admission_error_slot publishes JoinError::Cancelled with the admission error text), so the coordinator observes a join and the tally balances. My bead overstated that trigger. The synchronous Err paths that drop the closure or the built factory un-joined are:
- spawn_in_cancellation_dominant 4533-4542: no spawn gateway handle, or no pending-spawn counter for the scope (RuntimeUnavailable).
- spawn_via_gateway 4987-4993: runtime mask without SPAWN, or the gateway liveness guard already gone (RuntimeUnavailable).
- spawn_via_gateway 5082: gateway.enqueue_and_notify refusing the request after the factory (which owns the future and the guard) was built; the request is dropped un-admitted.
All of these are runtime-unavailable or shutdown-window conditions, so the managed-supervisor spin is realistic mainly while a runtime is going away, not during steady state. The mechanism (guard fires with no matching join; wait_exit self-wakes on every poll while other children run) is unchanged.

Pipeline: agreed, the error-path drain after the execution block does not run the tally-checking scan, so no spin there; map_reduce keeps its bounded self-wake during abort drain.

Suggested fix shape stands: count a synchronous failed spawn as an observed join in each Err arm, with a deterministic regression that plants a failing spawn and asserts the coordinator parks (no re-wake) while another child is still running.

title: Region deadlines never wake a parked task: enforcement is checkpoint-only on both runtimes (a region with a 50 ms deadline outlives it indefinitely)
description:
## Finding (lab/native differential harness probe PRB2b 3f4c8dafd, hz4)
A child region opened with a deadline budget (`ChildRegionSpec { budget: Some(Budget::new().with_timeout(now, 50 ms)), .. }`) does not wake a task that is parked inside it when the deadline passes. Neither runtime does:
- lab: the task stays parked. LabRuntimeTarget::block_on runs out its steps and panics "task did not complete".
- native current-thread: the run hangs (the harness's 60 s hang guard fired).
If the task checkpoints on its own (it sleeps 5 ms and calls checkpoint in a loop), both runtimes agree. All 12 runs cancel it with CancelKind::Deadline at its next checkpoint after 50 ms. So deadlines are enforced lazily, at checkpoints. A task parked in a cancel-aware wait (mpsc recv, lock, semaphore, barrier, notified) is never polled again, and never learns that the deadline passed.

## Why it matters
A region deadline reads like a bound on the region's work. Today it bounds only work that keeps polling. A region whose task waits on a channel outlives its deadline indefinitely, and so does anything that closes or joins that region. The README says, for example, that the SQLite wrappers "respect region deadlines". RuntimeBuilder::deadline_monitoring only warns.

## Decision (owner)
- (a) Make deadlines proactive: when a task with a finite budget deadline parks, arm a timer at the deadline (the timer wheel has O(1) generation cancel) that requests cancellation with CancelKind::Deadline and wakes the task. The cancel-aware primitives then return Cancelled as they do for abort.
- (b) Document deadlines as checkpoint-enforced, with the explicit consequence for parked waits. Point users to timeouts (Scope::timeout / time::timeout) for waits that must end.
Either way, the harness scenario region_deadline_cancels_a_parked_task (tests/kernel_semantics_differential.rs, currently #[ignore] with this bead's id) is the regression: un-ignore it for (a), or rewrite it for the documented behavior for (b).
close_reason: done

SapphireHill (rc_20260923) 2026-10-05: claiming. DECISION: option (a), deadlines are proactive.

Why (a):
- budget.rs documents a deadline as "Absolute time by which work must complete".
- The README says the SQLite wrappers "respect region deadlines".

Built in stack P (P1 8f400c6a8, not pushed; lanes running):

- When it fires, the context is cancelled with CancelKind::Deadline, exactly as a checkpoint past the deadline would, and its cancellation targets are woken.

Details:
- Nothing is armed without a deadline, without a timer driver, or for Time::MAX.
- The timer holds the context weakly, and the context's guard removes the timer when the context drops.
- An earlier cancellation keeps its reason.
- A deadline past the 7-day wheel horizon re-arms instead of cancelling early.

Regression tests:
- kernel_semantics_differential::region_deadline_cancels_a_parked_task, un-ignored;
- region_deadline_is_the_reason_a_parked_task_ends;
- cx::tests::budget_deadline_* (5).

title: sqlite: row streams pin the 4-thread global pool; Debug/is_open/close block the runtime thread

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
Evidence (SapphireHill fresh-eyes review, 2026-09-10, base bcb22504b; reviewer trace verified in code):

1. Row streams pin the process-wide SQLite blocking pool. All SQLite work shares one `BlockingPool::new(1, 4)` (src/database/sqlite.rs:115). A `query_stream` worker holds one of the four threads for the stream's whole lifetime and sleeps in a 1 ms loop while the consumer is not polling (~2873-2911). Four half-consumed streams waiting on client backpressure block every other SQLite operation in the process, including the dropped-transaction rollback cleanup that releases SQLite write locks. The `query_stream` docs mention the connection borrow but not the global thread pin. Fix shape: document the cap on `query_stream`, and either run streams on a separate pool or make the pool size configurable (additive).

2. `Debug for SqliteConnection` and `is_open()` lock `inner` (~2543-2556, ~4193-4196), which a pool worker holds for the whole statement or row stream; formatting or polling `is_open()` from an async task during a long query blocks the runtime thread until the statement ends. Fix shape: `try_lock` in `Debug`; document `is_open` as potentially blocking (v0.4.3 signature must stay).

3. `close()` holds `inner` and sleeps synchronously (50 ms + 100 ms retries) plus busy-handler waits while checkpointing (~4108-4140, ~4198-4243); called from an async task this blocks the runtime thread. Legacy shape, low priority.

title: [testing-golden-2] Freeze three-lane adaptive replay traces for seeded fairness paths
description:
The scheduler already asserts seeded replay determinism, but it does not freeze the actual replay artifacts. A policy or queue-order refactor could preserve `trace_a == trace_b` while still silently changing the fairness witness we review.

Evidence:
- src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs:8262-8320 defines replay_adaptive_cancel_flood_trace(seed) and currently only checks that the timed lane appears before the ready lane and that the fairness certificate holds.
- src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs:8323-8328 only compares two runs of the same seed; it never snapshots the dispatch trace itself.
- src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs:10150-10190 defines replay_adaptive_limit_trace(seed, epochs) and only asserts same-seed equality plus `distinct_limits >= 2`.
- Existing scheduler goldens cover state dumps (tests/three_lane_scheduler_state_dump_golden.rs and src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs:10417-10423), not replay traces or adaptive-limit sequences.

Why this matters:
These helpers are exactly the deterministic outputs we need when reviewing fairness-policy drift. Without a golden, reviewers only learn that a trace changed after reverse-engineering the failing invariant.

Concrete fixtures to freeze:
1. Seed 0xC0DE_CAFE_BEEF_0603 for replay_adaptive_cancel_flood_trace(), snapshot the full dispatch sequence plus the timed/ready insertion indices and adaptive limit used for the run.
2. Seed 0xC0DE_CAFE_BEEF_0001 with epochs=24 for replay_adaptive_limit_trace(), snapshot the exact limit vector and distinct-limit count.

Acceptance sketch:
- Add insta json snapshots for both replay helpers.
- Preserve the current invariant assertions; the golden should augment them, not replace them.
- Keep task IDs stable via TaskId::new_for_test and do not scrub ordering-sensitive fields.

title: plan rewrite: race-affecting rules bypass absolute cancel_safe==Safe gate
description: src/plan/rewrite.rs:818-833 (affects_race_loser_drain branch) + src/plan/analysis.rs:1267-1292 (rewrite_preserves_loser_drain). Non-race rules require cancel_safe(before)&&cancel_safe(after) (both CancelSafety::Safe). But the 3 race-affecting rules (RaceAssoc/RaceCommute/DedupRaceJoin) substitute a RELATIVE check: after.cancel<=before.cancel (Ord: Safe<MayOrphan<Orphan<Unknown) + leak_on_cancel set not growing. That admits a rewrite when BOTH sides are MayOrphan/Orphan/Unknown — exactly the states README.md:1028 + docs/plan_certified_rewrites.md:122-123 say are NOT proof of safety. ReachABLE: Race[Race[x,y],c] analyzes to MayOrphan; a RaceCommute/RaceAssoc whose after stays MayOrphan passes the relative gate but the documented cancel_safe(before) gate would reject it. No concrete runtime orphan is demonstrable from this module alone (analyzer keeps both sides equally pessimistic for current rules), but the gate is UNSOUND BY CONSTRUCTION and contradicts both the README invariant and its own design doc. FIX: in check_side_conditions' race branch additionally require checker.cancel_safe(after) (and ideally before); or add 'if !after_a.cancel.is_safe() { return false; }' near analysis.rs:1273. CAUTION: this makes the engine more conservative and may disable race rewrites on MayOrphan plans — verify against the rewrite-engine tests (a test asserting a race rewrite applies to a MayOrphan plan would break, which itself signals the relative behavior is baked-in). Also Finding 2 (MEDIUM): analysis.rs:319-340 BudgetEffect::is_not_worse_than omits max_deadline + parallelism, so a rewrite (notably DedupRaceJoin) can loosen the worst-case deadline / increase parallelism unchecked. The obligation/independence/structural gates ARE sound and fail-closed; only these two are gaps.

title: [PLAN-RT] Certified plan rewrites at runtime — wire the dormant e-graph optimizer into real combinators
description:
WHY: src/plan/ contains a complete, tested e-graph rewrite engine (hashcons + union-find, conservative/aggressive policies, obligation-safety and cancel-safety side-condition lattices, rewrite certificates, min-plus latency algebra) and src/combinator/laws.rs documents the algebraic laws — but recon confirmed apply_rewrites is never invoked outside tests. The optimizer is a parked alien artifact. Wiring it in gives asupersync a unique claim: combinator DAGs that are *provably* optimized (certificates included) without breaking cancel/drain/quiescence semantics.

CHILD TASKS: (1) opt-in plan capture — combinator builders (join_all/race/timeout/quorum/hedge trees) can emit a PlanDag describing their structure; (2) certified rewrite application — run the conservative rewrite policy over captured DAGs, verify side-conditions (obligation-safety, cancel-safety, deadline min-plus), execute the rewritten plan, and surface the RewriteCertificate through trace/observability; (3) differential equivalence testing — lab-based differential runs proving rewritten plans produce outcome-lattice-equivalent results and identical obligation resolution across seeds.

DISCIPLINE: conservative policy only by default; aggressive policy stays behind a feature flag with its own differential gate; any rewrite without a checkable certificate is rejected at runtime (fail closed to the unrewritten plan).

SUCCESS METRIC: a benchmark workload (nested race/join tree) shows measurable scheduling-overhead or latency improvement under rewrite with certificate, and the differential suite proves equivalence across >=1000 seeded lab runs.

title: [PLAN-RT] Opt-in plan capture — combinator trees emit PlanDag descriptions

WHY: the rewrite engine cannot optimize what it cannot see: combinators execute directly today with no DAG representation at runtime (PlanDag exists but nothing builds one from real code — recon confirmed apply_rewrites has zero non-test callers).

WHAT: (1) a PlanBuilder surface: plan::capture(|p| { p.race(p.join(a, b), p.timeout(d, c)) }) constructing a PlanDag whose leaves are real futures (type-erased slots keyed by node id), with combinator-builder sugar so the shapes mirror the direct API; (2) direct execution path for captured plans (no rewriting yet — that is I2): executing a captured plan must be semantically IDENTICAL to the equivalent direct combinator nesting (this equivalence is the bead's central proof obligation and the substrate for I3's differential testing); (3) capture is zero-cost-when-unused: no changes to the direct combinator paths; (4) scope: race/join/timeout/first_ok/quorum node kinds first (the law-sheet-covered set).

Determinism: interpreter scheduling identical to direct combinators (reuse their internals, do not reimplement).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Capture+execute for each node kind matches direct-combinator behavior on outcome, cancellation semantics, and obligation resolution (differential lab tests per kind — the I3 harness in miniature). 2. Loser-drain preserved through the interpreter (oracle). 3. Zero-overhead-when-unused: direct-path benches unchanged (baseline gate). 4. Captured-plan overhead measured + documented (interpreter tax, honestly stated). 5. Doctests on the builder. 6. Type-safety: root output typed end-to-end (no Any leaks to users).
notes: RELATION: I2 rewrites captured plans; I3 generalizes the differential harness. Design constraint recorded: interpreter REUSES combinator internals — a second execution engine would be a correctness disaster.

title: [PLAN-RT] Certified rewrite application — optimize captured plans, surface the certificate, fail closed
description:
WHY: this is the payoff: the e-graph rewriter (conservative policy, side-condition lattices for obligation-safety/cancel-safety, min-plus deadline reasoning, certificates) finally runs against real plans. Differentiator: no other runtime can say 'this combinator tree was restructured AND here is the machine-checkable certificate that the restructuring preserves your cancellation semantics'.

WHAT: (1) plan::capture_optimized(...): capture (I1) -> conservative rewrite pass (plan/rewrite.rs) -> side-condition verification (plan/analysis.rs lattices) -> execute the rewritten DAG; ANY verification failure = fail closed to the unrewritten plan with a logged reason (never a hard error — optimization is always optional); (2) RewriteCertificate surfaced: attached to the plan execution's trace events + queryable from the result (which rules fired, what the latency-algebra predicted, side-condition evidence) — feeding [INTROSPECT] J4 and test assertions; (3) aggressive policy stays feature-gated (plan-aggressive) with its own differential gate (I3 must pass at higher sample counts before it ever defaults); (4) at least two rewrites must demonstrate REAL wins to justify the machinery: candidates from laws.rs — race/join distributivity reducing redundant subtree execution, timeout-hoisting via min-plus (prove on benches, or close with documented negative result per the honesty discipline).
design: FILES: src/plan/rewrite.rs (entry wiring), src/plan/certificate.rs (surface), src/plan/execute.rs (rewritten-DAG path), trace event for certificates. The fail-closed ladder: capture -> rewrite -> verify -> (ok: execute rewritten | fail: log + execute original). Certificate schema versioned (it is now a public artifact).
acceptance_criteria: 1. End-to-end: a nested race/join fixture rewrites under conservative policy, executes, certificate appears in trace with fired-rule list (golden-tested schema). 2. Fail-closed: a side-condition-violating fixture (obligation-unsafe reorder) is REJECTED and runs unrewritten with the reason logged (the safety proof). 3. Bench evidence: >=2 rewrite rules show measurable improvement on representative fixtures (numbers committed) OR documented negative result. 4. Differential gate green (I3) before any default-on discussion. 5. Aggressive policy feature-gated with its gate documented. 6. Certificate docs + galaxy-brain card (what the side-condition lattice checks, with a worked example).

title: [PLAN-RT] Differential equivalence testing — rewritten vs baseline across seeds, outcomes, and obligations
description:

WHAT: a differential harness: (1) plan-fixture generator (seeded random plan shapes over the supported node kinds, with leaf futures of controlled behaviors: delays, errors, cancellations, obligation-holding leaves — the adversarial leaf set is the key design element); (2) equivalence relation precisely defined + asserted: final Outcome (severity-lattice equal), obligation resolution multiset equal, loser-drain events equivalent (Foata-class equality where event-level identity is too strict — reuse trace canonicalization), budget consumption within documented tolerance; (3) corpus scale: >=1000 generated plans x >=8 seeds each in the full lane (smaller fast lane for preflight); divergences auto-minimized (C4 integration) + crashpacked; (4) the harness IS the gate for I2's policies (conservative: always-on gate; aggressive: higher sample counts).

title: Messaging audit 2: a cancelled Kafka poll lets the next poll overwrite (lose) a record; Redis pooled UNSUBSCRIBE desync; Pub/Sub cancel drops events uncounted; NATS handshake unbounded; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of src/messaging at origin/main 81112c8f1 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-04; read from origin), deduplicated against asupersync-messaging-client-audit-k6pxks.

## HIGH
1. A cancelled Kafka poll() can make the next poll lose a record (kafka_consumer.rs ~1864, ~1946-2003; buffered_outcome field ~1071). Each poll slice runs on its own blocking thread holding broker_ops and writes its result into the single buffered_outcome slot, replacing it (~1960, ~1984, ~1991, ~1995). Poll #1 dropped while thread A is inside consumer.poll; poll #2 finds the slot empty and spawns B (waits on the lock); A stores R1; B fetches R2 and overwrites; poll #2 returns R2: R1 is never delivered and its position has advanced (auto-commit stores it): silent loss. Two concurrent poll(&self) calls overwrite the same way. Fix: after taking the lock, skip consumer.poll when the slot is already Some (or make it a queue).

## MEDIUM
2. NATS handshake has no time bound (nats.rs ~1878-1896 read_info, ~2229-2247 TLS, ~2082-2109 expect_ok; reconnect ~2120-2165): a server that accepts TCP but never sends INFO wedges try_reconnect forever (max_reconnect_attempts and backoff never trigger, queued commands never run). Initial connect too. A Cx deadline is not a workaround (the supervisor inherits the caller's budget). Fix: handshake timeout; NatsConfig has public fields, so a new field needs a builder or owner approval (as k6pxks item 8).
3. Pooled RedisClient::cmd allows UNSUBSCRIBE/PUNSUBSCRIBE/SUNSUBSCRIBE (redis.rs ~3391-3418, ~3929-3978): changes_reply_count refuses them only for Pipeline. On RESP2, cmd(["UNSUBSCRIBE","a","b"]) gets one reply per channel, one is read, the connection returns to the pool with the rest unread: the next borrower's GET receives ["unsubscribe","b",0] and every later command gets the previous reply. Fix: refuse changes_reply_count(args) in cmd_bytes.
4. A cancelled or timed-out Pub/Sub ping() or subscribe() discards buffered messages with no lag signal (redis.rs ~4621-4633, ~5170-5199, ~5148, ~5202-5215): PubSubControlGuard::drop clears pending_events without counting pubsub_dropped_events; reconnect copies the unchanged counters; no SubscriberLag. Fix: count cleared events as dropped (or keep them deliverable).

## LOW
5. JetStream counts a message dropped at max_ack_pending twice (jetstream.rs ~1884-1900, ~1702-1711, Drop ~1166-1179): increment_pending rolls back, then the dropped PENDING JsMessage decrements again: after k drops the limit admits k extra and the counter sticks at 0.
6. NATS INFO fields are read with the fixed pattern "key": (nats.rs ~579-619, ~1082-1103): "tls_required" : true (valid JSON with whitespace) reads as false, so the TLS upgrade is skipped and the password goes out in cleartext. Fix: read from the parsed Value.

## Partly fixed items of k6pxks
- 7: request()/request_with_headers() still fail on any -ERR, including keep-connection permission errors from an earlier publish (nats.rs ~2799-2803, ~2906-2909).
- 14: a cancel before the delivery report still returns Cancelled for a record librdkafka will deliver (kafka.rs ~378-382); module doc (~21-26) promises cancellation waits for pending acks.
- 4: only process() was fixed; a timed-out supervised request() or ping() still holds the supervisor.

## Checked and sound
Redis discard-on-cancel guards, next_event cancel safety, pipeline refusals, frame bounds, redirects, redaction, RESP3 push cap; NATS partial-write reconnect, SUB replay sids, UNSUB ordering, TLS floor, MSG/HMSG lengths, request inbox cleanup; JetStream ack subject, InFlightAck rollback, status replies, v2 ack layout; Kafka delivery-before-cancel ordering, transaction fencing, commit-resume bound.

title: [bug-hunt] net/happy_eyeballs: stagger_sleep + timeout_sleep use Sleep::with_time_getter (waker registration footgun)
description: src/net/happy_eyeballs.rs:323-324 use Sleep::with_time_getter for stagger_sleep and timeout_sleep. Per memory: 'Sleep::with_time_getter is a footgun: Skips waker registration. Use Sleep::new(deadline) instead.' The stagger/timeout sleeps don't register their own wakers, so the parent RaceConnections future relies on in-flight connect futures' completion to drive its re-poll cadence. Pathological cases: (1) all in-flight connects stuck on SYN timeout AND stagger elapsed (next address never started); (2) all started but none succeeded/failed AND overall_timeout passed (TimedOut never returned). Fix: replace both with Sleep::new(deadline). Second sighting (see audit_index Apr 3 batch 1qfd0.529).
close_reason: RaceConnections::{new,from_futures} now use Sleep::new(deadline) instead of Sleep::with_time_getter. Per Sleep::poll source, with_time_getter only schedules a wakeup if a timer driver is reachable (bound or ambient Cx); when neither exists the future stores the waker but never registers a timer — connect/timeout loop hangs forever. Sleep::new takes the same poll path but falls through to the background-waiter-thread fallback when no timer driver is present. time_getter field on RaceConnections preserved (still used by connect_one/start_next).

title: [EPIC-INFRA] OpenTelemetry Metrics Export
description:
## Overview

Implement OpenTelemetry metrics export for runtime observability, enabling integration with standard monitoring systems like Prometheus, Datadog, and Grafana.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Production systems need metrics for monitoring and alerting. Without standard metrics export, operators must build custom solutions.

**Why OpenTelemetry**: OTel is the emerging standard for observability. It supports multiple backends (Prometheus, OTLP, etc.) through a single API.

**Production Requirement**: Any runtime targeting production use needs metrics. This is table stakes for enterprise adoption.

## Metrics Categories

### Runtime Metrics
- `asupersync.tasks.active` - Currently running tasks (gauge)
- `asupersync.tasks.spawned` - Total tasks spawned (counter)
- `asupersync.tasks.completed` - Tasks completed by outcome (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.regions.active` - Currently open regions (gauge)
- `asupersync.regions.created` - Total regions created (counter)

### Timing Metrics
- `asupersync.task.duration` - Task execution time (histogram)
- `asupersync.region.lifetime` - Region open duration (histogram)
- `asupersync.scheduler.poll_time` - Time spent in poll (histogram)

### Cancellation Metrics
- `asupersync.cancellations` - Cancellation count by reason (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.drain_duration` - Time spent in drain phase (histogram)

### Budget Metrics
- `asupersync.deadline.remaining` - Time remaining at task start (histogram)
- `asupersync.poll_quota.usage` - Poll quota utilization (histogram)

### Resource Metrics
- `asupersync.obligations.active` - Undischarged obligations (gauge)
- `asupersync.obligations.undischarged` - Obligations dropped undischarged (counter)

## Integration Design

### Feature Flag
```toml
[features]
metrics = ["opentelemetry", "opentelemetry-prometheus"]
```

### Metrics Provider
```rust
pub trait MetricsProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn task_spawned(&self, region_id: RegionId);
    fn task_completed(&self, task_id: TaskId, outcome: &Outcome<()>, duration: Duration);
    fn region_created(&self, region_id: RegionId, parent: Option<RegionId>);
    fn region_closed(&self, region_id: RegionId, lifetime: Duration);
    fn cancellation(&self, region_id: RegionId, kind: CancelKind);
    // ... etc
}
```

### OpenTelemetry Implementation
```rust
pub struct OtelMetrics {
    tasks_active: ObservableGauge<u64>,
    tasks_spawned: Counter<u64>,
    task_duration: Histogram<f64>,
    // ...
}

impl MetricsProvider for OtelMetrics { ... }
```

### Integration
```rust
RuntimeBuilder::new()
    .metrics(OtelMetrics::new(meter_provider))
    .build()
```

## Prometheus Example

```
# HELP asupersync_tasks_active Currently running tasks
# TYPE asupersync_tasks_active gauge
asupersync_tasks_active 42

# HELP asupersync_tasks_completed_total Tasks completed
# TYPE asupersync_tasks_completed_total counter
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="ok"} 1000
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="err"} 50
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="cancelled"} 10
asupersync_tasks_completed_total{outcome="panicked"} 2

# HELP asupersync_task_duration_seconds Task execution duration
# TYPE asupersync_task_duration_seconds histogram
asupersync_task_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.001"} 500
asupersync_task_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.01"} 800
...
```

## Acceptance Criteria

1. MetricsProvider trait defined
2. OtelMetrics implementation
3. All metrics categories implemented
4. Feature-gated (no mandatory OTel dependency)
5. Prometheus exporter example
6. Grafana dashboard template
7. Documentation with setup guide

## Dependencies

- Optional opentelemetry dependency
- Uses runtime hooks for metrics collection

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #15 because while essential for production, metrics are a "nice to have" during development. Users can add metrics later once they move toward production.

title: polling 3.11's Linux wait makes 4 extra system calls per reactor turn (timerfd + notifier re-arm): measured defect for the polling KEEP decision (3u3tej.4)
description:
OWNER DECISION REQUESTED. The polling KEEP decision (asupersync-3u3tej.4, artifacts/polling_socket_platform_decision_v1.json) says it may be reopened when "a measured defect" justifies it, and that changing it needs owner review. This is that measured defect.

## What was measured
- Probe 8ccda6b2b: origin 0023804e6 source plus the zz_probe crate (default features, release). Never landed.
- strace -f -c, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive GET with a 5-byte body, asupersync's Http1Listener against hyper on tokio. Each side runs alone in its own traced process, client and server together.
- At 1 connection, asupersync makes about 18 system calls per request and hyper about 6. The full table is on kpmoy5.1.
- About 8 of the 18 are made inside polling 3.11's Poller::wait. Each reactor turn calls, besides epoll_wait:
  - timerfd_settime: polling arms its timerfd on every wait, even for a zero or whole-millisecond timeout;
  - epoll_ctl, re-arming the timerfd's oneshot registration;
  - read on the notifier eventfd, which returns EAGAIN unless a notify happened;
  - epoll_ctl, re-arming the notifier's oneshot registration.
  - Source: polling-3.11.0/src/epoll.rs, Poller::wait_deadline, which calls timerfd_settime and modify(timer_fd, Oneshot) before epoll::wait, then notifier.clear() and modify(notifier, Oneshot) after it, unconditionally.
  An HTTP/1 request costs 2 reactor turns at 1 connection, so 8 calls. mio makes 1 call per turn (epoll_wait with a millisecond timeout).
- This is inside the dependency. asupersync's own code cannot remove it without changing how polling is used.

## Why it matters
- It is the largest single source of the system-call gap behind the README's HTTP/1.1 row: asupersync is 1.6 to 2.0 times slower than hyper, both measured in the same process, on three hosts.
- It is paid on every reactor turn of every runtime, not only by HTTP.

## Options for the owner
1. Keep polling for registration, and on Linux wait on its epoll fd directly: epoll_wait with a rounded-up millisecond timeout, plus our own eventfd for wakes, registered level-triggered.
   - Cost: a direct rustix dependency with the event feature (rustix is already in Cargo.lock through polling); a Linux-only wait path; epoll.rs and its three sha pins re-pinned.
   - The timer wheel's resolution is already 1 ms (r75eky), so millisecond waits lose nothing.
2. Replace polling on Linux with an owned epoll reactor over rustix's safe API, keeping polling for kqueue and IOCP.
3. Keep polling unchanged, and record the per-turn cost as an accepted cost in the decision artifact and the README performance row.

## What would close this bead
- The owner's choice is recorded.
- For 1 or 2: an implementation with its own tests, an in-process A/B (asupersync before and after, same run) on tcp_rr and http1 rows, and the syscall count per request repeated.
- For 3: the accepted cost is written down where the decision lives.

title: Pool active accounting lacks rollback between commit and wrapper handoff
description: Pool acquisition increments active before a complete PooledResource wrapper exists. Idle checkout increments active when popping the resource, then performs waiter cleanup, callbacks, timing, metrics, and wrapper construction. Fresh creation commits creating into active, then performs get_now, metrics, and PooledResource construction. Any panic in these post-commit pre-handoff windows drops a bare R without a return message and permanently consumes capacity. Public with_time_getter gives a deterministic max_size=1 repro by returning once during try_get_idle or creation and panicking in PooledResource construction after active commits. Introduce an ActiveCheckoutGuard armed immediately when active increments and disarmed only after a complete wrapper exists; on unwind roll back active and acquisition accounting and wake the marginal waiter. Regress injected one-shot time-source panics for both fresh-create and idle-reuse paths, then assert accounting and replacement acquisition. Existing close-during-create and caller-panic beads do not cover post-commit handoff panic. Independently confirmed by source audit and direct second review on 2026-07-15.

title: Pool clear drops arbitrary values while holding storage mutex
description: src/util/pool.rs Pool::clear calls VecDeque::clear through a live MutexGuard, so every arbitrary T destructor runs under the non-reentrant storage mutex. A safe Rust value holding Weak<Pool<T>> can upgrade in Drop and call len, try_get, put, or clear, permanently deadlocking; slow destructors also convoy every pool user. RecyclingPool::clear delegates and inherits the bug. Public reachability is asupersync::util::Pool/RecyclingPool, though the current TaskTable use has no custom Drop or clear call. Fix by taking/replacing the whole queue under the lock, dropping the guard, then dropping the retired queue. Add deterministic Pool and RecyclingPool DropProbe regressions that prove storage.try_lock succeeds and public len can re-enter during destruction. Independently confirmed by two fresh-eye reviews 2026-07-15; no existing bead or clear test covers this occurrence.

title: Panicking pool resource destructor leaks active capacity on discard
description: PooledResource::discard_inner takes and destroys R before it sends PoolReturn::Discard, discharges the return obligation, or wakes pool waiters. title: [security] distributed/snapshot.rs: deserializer allocates a 4 GiB buffer for attacker-supplied metadata_len before bounds check — OOM-DoS via crafted snapshot frame
description:
src/distributed/snapshot.rs:319-321 — the snapshot deserializer reads a u32 metadata_len from untrusted input and IMMEDIATELY allocates a buffer of that size, with no bound check before allocation:

  let metadata_len = cursor.read_u32()?;
  let metadata = cursor.read_exact(metadata_len as usize)?.to_vec();

An attacker that can deliver a snapshot frame to the decoder (cross-runtime bridge, replay file, network peer) can supply `metadata_len = 0xFFFFFFFF` (~4 GiB). The deserializer attempts to allocate 4 GiB before discovering the body is short. On a memory-constrained host (containers, edge runtimes, browser-edition WASM) this is OOM-DoS or process-kill.

Comparison: the same file's task-list and children-list paths DO cap pre-allocation (lines 276-277). Metadata bypasses that defence.

Concrete repro: send a 32-byte frame consisting of valid header + task_count=0 + children_count=0 + `metadata_len = 0xFFFFFFFF` + 1 byte of metadata. Decoder OOMs.

Fix direction: introduce `MAX_METADATA_BYTES` (suggest 1 MiB) and add the same `if metadata_len > MAX_METADATA_BYTES { return Err(...) }` guard the task/children paths use. Reject before allocation; the read_exact failure path then becomes unreachable for the OOM shape.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting src/distributed/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Added MAX_METADATA_LEN=16MB cap + MetadataTooLarge error variant; bounds check happens BEFORE Vec allocation in RegionSnapshot::from_bytes so a crafted metadata_len cannot drive 4GB OOM

title: PostgreSQL client audit (r10): prepared binds reinterpret int/float values (silent corruption); a dropped failed transaction wedges the parameterized APIs; streams and COPY skip statement_timeout; stale cached plans; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of the PostgreSQL client (src/database/postgres.rs, postgres_tls.rs, mod.rs) at origin/main dd83aee26, re-checked unchanged at a936e25e1 (SapphireHill audit agent round 10, 10-07). Report: /data/tmp/rc_20260923/audit_r10_database.md. mysql.rs, sqlite.rs, pool.rs and transaction.rs were not audited in this round; the report's appendix keeps unverified leads for them.

## HIGH
H1. Prepared statements bind binary values without checking the parameter types the server inferred (prepare sends Parse with no type hints; query_prepared/execute_prepared check only the parameter count). A same-width mismatch is reinterpreted by the server and stored without an error: `execute_prepared(&s, &[&100i64])` for a `double precision` parameter stores 4.94e-322; an f64 bound to an int8 parameter stores its bit pattern. The query_params path sends the Rust type OIDs, so the same call there stores 100.0. Planned fix (fail-closed, narrow): refuse integer/float binary pairs before any write; NULLs pass. Wider type checks (int8 into timestamp/time/money, int4 into date/oid) stay an OWNER decision: some callers may bind PostgreSQL's binary representation on purpose.

## MEDIUM
M1. A PgTransaction dropped in a failed block (the common `?` return) wedges the parameterized APIs on direct (unpooled) reuse: execute_unchecked, query_params, execute_params, query_prepared and execute_prepared send the managed `SET statement_timeout` before the orphan ROLLBACK, the SET fails with 25P02 inside the aborted block, and every later call repeats it. A related case: tx.execute_params("ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp") inside the caller's own failed block is refused the same way.
M2. query_stream, query_stream_params and copy_in never reconcile statement_timeout, so they run under whatever the previous query left in the session (docs/deadline_propagation.md promises per-query reconciliation): a stream with no deadline after a 150 ms budgeted query is cancelled by the server at 150 ms (57014).
M3. (OWNER) Pool-return session isolation keys off command tags: set_config() (the RLS tenant idiom), LISTEN subscriptions and buffered notifications, temp tables, SQL PREPARE, DECLARE WITH HOLD and session advisory locks survive into the next tenant. Options: reset on checkout (CLOSE ALL; SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION DEFAULT; RESET ALL; UNLISTEN *; pg_advisory_unlock_all(); DISCARD TEMP; DISCARD SEQUENCES) or discard on detection.
M4. A cached prepared statement whose plan the server refuses after another session altered a table (0A000 "cached plan must not change result type") stays cached: prepare keeps returning it and every call fails until the connection is recycled.

## LOW
L1. PgRowStream::next silently skipped unknown backend messages: query_stream("COPY t FROM STDIN") waits forever after CopyInResponse, and COPY TO STDOUT drops all data and reports success. It also ignored CommandComplete tags, so a SET or DDL through a stream set no discard flag and left the prepared cache stale.
L2. A budget or override past INT_MAX ms (~24.8 days) is sent unclamped; the server refuses it (22023) and every query fails.
L3. (OWNER) Transparent idle reconnect drops advisory locks, temp tables and set_config values, and under ssl_mode=Prefer can reconnect in plaintext.
L4. PgTransaction::rollback with an already-cancelled Cx sends no ROLLBACK (the transaction and its locks stay open on an unpooled connection); with_pg_transaction was fixed under 91hka0 item 10, rollback itself was not.
L5. (OWNER, behaviour change) Duplicate column names resolve to the last column; libpq and tokio-postgres return the first.
L6. With bytea_output = 'escape', bytea values come back as the escaped text.
L7. connect_timeout=0 fails every connect at once; libpq reads 0 as "wait indefinitely".
L8. Hostile-server robustness: a non-ASCII SQLSTATE panics in is_constraint_violation / is_connection_error / is_transient / is_retryable (&c[..2]); i32::MIN interval fields panic in debug builds (months.abs()); ParameterStatus reports grow an unbounded map.
L9. SCRAM skips SASLprep, so some non-ASCII passwords fail authentication.

Also found: 91hka0 item 12 (its LOW batch) never landed although that bead is closed; its PostgreSQL parts still hold on origin (OIDs above 2^31 fail i32 parsing, MERGE reports 0 rows, CancelRequest re-resolves the host).

Judged SOUND: see the report (desync protection, cancellation and CancelRequest ordering, error resync, transaction obligation handling, prepared-statement generations, framing bounds, frontend encoding, SCRAM bounds and constant-time checks, TLS negotiation, budget math).

title: epoch_tracking: LocalEpochPin::pin missing SeqCst fence after announce (dormant EBR reclamation race)
description: Found by bug-hunt (SapphireHill 2026-06-29, sibling of aasraf epoch_gc finding). src/runtime/epoch_tracking.rs LocalEpochPin::pin() announces the pin (pinned_epoch.store(Release) ~:277, is_active.store(true, Release) ~:281) after the Acquire load of the global epoch (~:276) with NO fence(SeqCst) between the announce-store and the reader's subsequent shared-data access. SafePointDetector::compute_safe_point() (~:437-446) reads is_active/pinned_epoch with plain Acquire while the global epoch advances via fetch_add(AcqRel) (~:217). The announce-store<->scan-load is a StoreLoad pair with no total order -> a reclaimer can miss a just-pinning reader -> premature reclamation. This is exactly the fence crossbeam-epoch places after the pin announce. NOT reachable today: LocalEpochPin/SafePointDetector/GlobalEpochCounter are instantiated only in that module's own #[cfg(test)] and the deferred work is opaque closures, never wired to real pointer reclamation. Would bite only if this EBR is adopted for real reclamation. FIX: add fence(SeqCst) after the pin announce-store (mirror crossbeam-epoch).
close_reason: Fixed (SapphireHill, commit pending): added the crossbeam-epoch StoreLoad SeqCst fence PAIR. LocalEpochPin::pin now does fence(SeqCst) after announcing the pin (pinned_epoch/is_active stores); SafePointDetector::compute_safe_point does fence(SeqCst) before scanning thread_pins. Together they give the pin-announce store and the reclaimer scan-load a single total order, so the reclaimer cannot advance the global epoch and miss a just-pinned reader (premature reclamation). Dormant (EBR is test-only, not wired to real pointer reclamation) so no runtime test; memory-ordering fences are not meaningfully unit-testable on x86 (loom would be the tool). clippy/tests green.

title: [bug-hunt-deep-2] postgres deallocate retry path treats caller cancellation as backend failure
description:
Observed in `src/database/postgres.rs:4006-4012` and `src/database/postgres.rs:4062-4075`.

The prepared-statement cleanup path conflates caller cancellation with actual CLOSE/deallocate wire failure:

- `try_close_or_enqueue_deallocate()` treats `Outcome::Err(_) | Outcome::Cancelled(_) | Outcome::Panicked(_)` identically and always calls `enqueue_failed_deallocate(...)`.
- `flush_pending_deallocates()` does the same: on `Outcome::Cancelled(_)` it increments `consecutive_deallocate_failures`, may set `unhealthy = true`, and stops draining.

Why this is a real bug:
- `close_statement()` begins with a `cx.checkpoint()` short-circuit. If the caller is already cancelled before any bytes are written, the function returns `Outcome::Cancelled` without any server-side CLOSE attempt having failed.
- Counting that as a deallocate failure poisons a healthy connection: repeated user timeouts/cancellations on `prepare()` / query entry paths can trip `DEALLOCATE_FAILURE_UNHEALTHY_THRESHOLD` and force needless pool eviction.
- This also bloats the retry queue for purely local cancellation reasons, which is the wrong failure model: a cancelled maintenance pass should preserve the pending close, but it should not degrade transport-health accounting as if the server rejected CLOSE.

Invariant(s) to preserve:
- Real CLOSE transport/protocol failures must still mark the connection unhealthy after repeated occurrences.
- Cancel-correctness: cancellation may defer best-effort maintenance work, but should not fabricate backend-failure evidence.
- Prepared-statement leak containment: evicted names should remain queued for a later retry when appropriate.

Suggested fix:
1. Split maintenance outcomes into at least: success, actual close failure, and caller cancellation.
2. On cancellation before/without a proven CLOSE failure, requeue the statement name but do not increment `consecutive_deallocate_failures` and do not set `unhealthy`.
3. If cancellation occurred after the connection was already forced closed by `cancel_in_flight()`, rely on `inner.closed` / discard semantics rather than double-counting it as a deallocate health failure.
4. Add regressions for:
   - pre-cancelled `Cx` entering `try_close_or_enqueue_deallocate()`,
   - pre-cancelled `Cx` entering `flush_pending_deallocates()`,
   - proof that the pending name is preserved while `consecutive_deallocate_failures` and `unhealthy` remain unchanged.
close_reason: Fixed postgres deallocate retry path to distinguish caller cancellation from backend failure. Added enqueue_cancelled_deallocate() that preserves statement names without incrementing failure counters. Added comprehensive regression tests.

title: [bug-hunt] messaging/redis: Pipeline::exec aborts on first -ERR, dropping later responses + connection
description:
Severity: HIGH (semantic mismatch with how Redis actually works; quiet data-loss).

src/messaging/redis.rs:1389-1391 (`Pipeline::exec`):

    match resp {
        RespValue::Error(msg) => return Err(RedisError::Redis(msg)),
        other => out.push(other),
    }

When the FIRST RESP `-ERR ...` arrives in a pipelined response stream,
`exec` returns `Err` immediately and drops the rest of the response
stream. The `DiscardOnDropGuard` then closes the connection (per the
struct's own docstring at 1331-1334).

This is a fundamental misunderstanding of Redis pipelining. Pipelines
are NOT atomic. Redis processes each command independently and emits
one reply per command. `-ERR` for one command (e.g.
`LPUSH foo bar` against a STRING-typed key returns
`-ERR WRONGTYPE`) does NOT affect the others — the server already
processed them and their replies are sitting in the read buffer.

Net consequence: a caller pipelining
    [SET foo 1, LPUSH foo bar, GET foo]
on the same key:
  - SET succeeds.
  - LPUSH fails (WRONGTYPE).
  - GET succeeds and returns "1".

The current implementation:
  - returns `RedisError::Redis("WRONGTYPE")` for the whole pipeline,
  - drops the GET response on the floor,
  - closes the connection (forcing every pipeline retry to start with
    a fresh handshake),
  - gives the caller no way to learn which command in the batch
    failed.

Fix shape (any one):
  (a) Change return type to `Vec<Result<RespValue, RedisError>>` — one
      Result per pipelined command. Each command's error is visible
      next to its index. Connection is preserved. This is the
      redis-rs / fred shape.
  (b) Keep the current return type but represent per-command errors
      as `RespValue::Error(_)` in the output Vec rather than
      converting to `Err` — lower-impact API change, but loses the
      typed-error ergonomics on the calling side.
  (c) Add a sibling `exec_collect` that returns
      `Vec<Result<RespValue, RedisError>>` and deprecate `exec` as
      'Returns an err on the first error; for full per-command results
      use exec_collect'.

Other clauses verified SOUND in this pass:
  - Two-pass RESP parser (check_complete then decode_at) avoids
    O(N²) reallocation on partial buffers.
  - Bulk string null `$-1`, array null `\*-1`, negative-but-not-(-1)
    rejection, max_bulk_string_len / max_array_len / max_nesting_depth
    DoS guards all present.

title: atpd logs ANSI color escapes to pipes and files (breaks line-oriented log consumers)
description:
atpd's init_logging (src/bin/atpd.rs, tracing_subscriber::fmt::layer()) leaves ANSI at its default. It therefore writes color escape sequences even when stdout is a pipe or a file. A field renders as ESC[3mbind_addr ESC[0m ESC[2m= ESC[0m127.0.0.1:57849, which breaks line-oriented consumers: log files, journald, and scripts that parse the readiness lines. It turned tests/atp_cli_quic_loopback::atpd_quic_listener_accepts_atp_send_and_reports_diagnostics deterministically red. That test's parser is now ANSI-tolerant (FX2).

The CLI proper already follows the convention in src/cli/output.rs: color only on a terminal, and NO_COLOR disables it. Proposal: with_ansi(stdout is a terminal && NO_COLOR is unset) for atpd, and the same for any other binary that installs a fmt layer.

Compatibility: this changes the bytes atpd logs when piped, by removing the escapes. The log format is not a documented contract, and escapes in a pipe are only noise to a consumer. Still, it is a visible output change, so flag it in the release notes.
close_reason: Fixed in 3e62ee850: atpd colors its log only when stdout is a terminal and NO_COLOR is unset (CLI convention). title: [PROOF-ORCH] Shared-main clean-overlay proof orchestration

title: [IDEA-WIZARD][PROOF-TRAFFIC] Shared-main proof traffic control for RCH lanes
description:
## Background
Idea-wizard Phase 1 was grounded in AGENTS.md, README.md, live open/closed beads, and today's shared-main failure mode: focused proof lanes are routinely blocked by active project exclusions, heartbeat-fresh/progress-stale peer builds, peer-dirty compile failures, and drift between documented clean-overlay command shapes and the installed `rch exec` capabilities. Agents then park useful work without a deterministic, resumable proof receipt.

## Phase 2: 30 ideas winnowed to top 5
The strongest 5 ideas after considering robustness, reliability, performance, ergonomics, usefulness, accretiveness, and pragmatism were:
1. Proof Traffic Controller: a repo-local planner/receipt layer that tells agents whether to run, queue, park, or hand off a focused RCH lane.
2. Installed-RCH Capability Drift Gate: checked evidence that documented proof commands are actually supported by the installed RCH CLI, with fail-closed docs updates when they are not.
3. Reservation-Aware Clean Overlay Runner: a real command-generation path that overlays only owned, reserved paths when supported, or emits a deterministic blocker when not.
4. Proof Parking Lot: a machine-readable backlog of blocked validation commands with exact command, blocker, owner, retry condition, and Agent Mail handoff fields.
5. Stale-Build Ownership Policy: no peer-cancel by default, but owner-targeted notification and self-cancel guidance for heartbeat-fresh/progress-stale jobs.

## Phase 3: next 10 complementary ideas
6. Per-lane resource-envelope predictor for target dir, slots, timeout, and memory class.
7. Proof command linter that catches local Cargo fallback, missing CARGO_TARGET_DIR, and overbroad workspace sync before execution.
8. Deterministic target-dir allocator to avoid cross-agent cache corruption while preserving warm remote caches.
9. Agent Mail + br comment template generator for every proof outcome.
10. Live validation dashboard row that distinguishes not-run, refused, blocked, progress-stale, rerun-required, and green.
11. RCH queue fairness hints so tiny focused lanes do not starve behind broad proofs.
12. Clean-overlay poison-path fixture that proves excluded peer dirt cannot reach a build when the backend supports overlay.
13. Proof lane resume command that rehydrates the exact parked command once queue/owner conditions clear.
14. No-claim boundary checker that prevents stale or refused jobs from being cited as proof.
15. Cross-agent blocked-lane deduper so multiple agents hitting the same peer blocker converge on one handoff thread.

## Overlap audit
This does not duplicate the closed Validation Frontier v2 work or the existing clean-overlay proof orchestration contract. Those artifacts define proof semantics and documentation. This tree addresses the practical shared-main operations gap: capability drift, queue/admission policy, proof parking, owner notifications, and resumable agent handoffs under the current RCH/Agent Mail workflow. It should interoperate with `asupersync-agent-native-dx-zxqaqs`, `clean-overlay-proof-orchestration-contract`, and proof-status artifacts rather than replace them.

## Non-goals
- No branch/worktree/scratch-clone workflow.
- No local Cargo fallback.
- No permission to delete files or clean peer work.
- No claim that this makes RCH fleet capacity healthy; it only makes proof admission and parking honest.

## Success Criteria
Future agents can answer, with one deterministic command or artifact, whether a focused proof lane should run now, be queued, be parked with a retry condition, or be escalated to the owner of a peer blocker. Refused/stale runs produce machine-readable receipts and cannot be mistaken for green evidence.
notes: Phase 6 refinement pass 1 (structure): created as an additive, non-duplicate tree after overlap check against Validation Frontier v2, clean-overlay proof orchestration, Agent-DX, and current RCH/ATP blocker receipts. Scope is proof-traffic operations, not runtime behavior.

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A1] Installed RCH capability drift gate

## Why

## How

## Risks

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A2] Queue/admission decision receipt for focused proofs
description:
## What
Build a deterministic proof-admission receipt that consumes current RCH queue/status state plus a focused validation intent and returns one of: run-now, queue-wait, park-rerun-required, blocked-by-peer, blocked-by-capability-drift, or no-local-fallback-refused.

## Why
Today agents manually infer from `active_project_exclusion`, stale progress, worker health, and peer dirty state. The result is inconsistent handoffs and repeated duplicate attempts.

## How
Model the receipt as an artifact-friendly struct with exact fields: head commit, command intent, target dir, selected/owned paths, queue snapshot, active build summaries, refusal text, retry condition, and no-claim boundaries. Keep it read-only and non-mutating.

## Risks
Do not cancel peer builds or imply authority over RCH. The receipt only advises and records.

## Success Criteria
- Fixture tests cover empty queue, active project exclusion, heartbeat-fresh/progress-stale, unsupported overlay flags, and remote-required local fallback refusal.
- Receipt has deterministic JSON and Markdown operator report forms.
- Agent Mail/br comment templates can be generated directly from the receipt.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Decision taxonomy is exhaustive for run-now, queue-wait, park-rerun-required, blocked-by-peer, blocked-by-capability-drift, remote-required-refused, and report-only.
2. Unit fixtures cover empty queue, active project exclusion, worker-health refusal, heartbeat-fresh/progress-stale, peer-owned stale build, self-owned stale build, and unsupported overlay capability.
3. Markdown and JSON reports are deterministic and include head commit, command intent, target dir, selected paths, active build IDs, retry condition, and no-claim boundaries.
4. No decision path recommends cancelling peer builds, running local Cargo, creating branches/worktrees, or deleting files.
5. Report rendering includes Agent Mail and br-comment-ready bodies with structured fields.
notes: Phase 6 refinement pass 2 (decision sanity): acceptance now requires exhaustive classification and no-peer-cancel/no-local-fallback invariants.

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A3] Reservation-aware clean-overlay runner handshake
description:
## What
Connect the existing clean-overlay planner/command surfaces to real installed-RCH capability evidence and Agent Mail reservations, so an agent can request a focused proof over only owned paths and receive either an exact RCH command or a deterministic blocker.

## Why
The repo has clean-overlay documentation and command rendering, but current `rch exec --help` may not expose the advertised backend flags. This needs to fail closed instead of letting agents assume peer dirt was excluded.

## How
Validate selected paths against held reservations, consult the A1 capability artifact, and render either an admitted command or a blocker receipt. If overlay is unsupported, preserve the selected paths and retry condition but emit no Cargo invocation.

## Risks
Never upload or imply ownership of peer-dirty paths. Never use branches, worktrees, scratch clones, or file deletion as an overlay substitute.

## Success Criteria
- Selected reserved dirty path admits only when backend capability exists.
- Peer dirty paths are excluded and named in receipts.
- Unsupported backend capability emits `blocked-by-capability-drift` with no Cargo command.
- Tests include a poison peer path that would fail compilation if synced.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Selected dirty/untracked paths are admitted only when covered by active self reservations and installed-RCH overlay capability is supported.
2. Unsupported overlay capability emits a blocked-by-capability-drift receipt and no Cargo command.
3. Peer-dirty and unselected paths are excluded or fail closed; a poison fixture proves they cannot appear in an admitted command.
4. Deleted selected paths are refused; no file deletion or synthetic branch/worktree overlay is attempted.
5. Tests cover reservation matching, peer reservation conflict, report-only mode, admitted mode, and unsupported-backend mode with deterministic JSON/Markdown output.
notes: Phase 6 refinement pass 3 (dependency/test): acceptance now distinguishes reservation, backend-capability, and poison-path proof cases.

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A4] Proof parking lot and resumable retry manifest
description:
## What
Create a checked format for parked proof attempts: exact command intent, head commit, owned paths, reservation evidence, blocker classification, owner/handoff thread, retry predicate, and no-claim boundaries.

## Why
Agents now leave uncommitted work with prose-only status packets. A future agent should be able to resume the proof without reconstructing the command from chat history.

## How
Define a JSON schema/artifact and a small renderer for Markdown/Agent Mail/br comments. Integrate with the A2 receipt classifications. Parking a proof must be read-only with respect to code and must not mark the associated implementation bead complete.

## Risks
Avoid creating a second issue tracker. This is a proof-attempt ledger, not source of truth for task status; Beads remains the task tracker.

## Success Criteria
- Parked attempts include enough data to rerun exactly once conditions clear.
- Duplicate parked attempts against the same blocker can be grouped.
- Stale or refused attempts cannot be cited as green proof.
- Contract tests pin JSON schema, Markdown report, and no-claim boundaries.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Parked proof manifest schema includes head commit, command intent, exact RCH command or blocker marker, target dir, owned paths, reservation evidence, blocker class, blocker owner/thread if known, retry predicate, and no-claim boundaries.
2. Duplicate parked attempts with the same blocker key can be grouped without losing per-agent command details.
3. Resume renderer emits the exact command only when the retry predicate is satisfied; otherwise it emits a fresh blocker receipt.
4. Markdown/Agent Mail/br comment renderers are deterministic and include enough context for a future agent to continue without chat history.
5. Contract tests prove refused/stale/parked attempts cannot be interpreted as green proof.
notes: Phase 6 refinement pass 3 (resume quality): acceptance now requires duplicate grouping, retry predicates, and deterministic handoff text.

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A5] Agent-affordance e2e for blocked proof loops
description:
## What
Build an end-to-end scenario that simulates a fresh agent trying to validate a focused code slice while peer dirt, stale RCH progress, and reservation constraints are present.

## Why
The feature is only useful if it prevents real agent failure modes: duplicate attempts, accidental peer-file edits, local Cargo fallback, and false green claims.

## How
Use deterministic fixtures rather than live fleet assumptions. The scenario should show: owned path selected, peer poison path excluded or fail-closed, RCH unavailable/refused path parked, Agent Mail/br comment body rendered, and retry command preserved.

## Risks
Do not depend on actual live RCH worker health for the deterministic e2e. Live fleet evidence can be attached as an operator receipt but not as the correctness proof.

## Success Criteria
- E2E logs every decision with structured fields.
- Fails if a local Cargo fallback appears.
- Fails if peer dirt appears in an admitted overlay command.
- Produces a replayable artifact bundle with command, receipt, and handoff text.
acceptance_criteria:
1. E2E scenario uses deterministic fixtures for owned dirty path, peer poison path, missing overlay capability, active-project refusal, and progress-stale peer build.
2. Scenario emits structured logs for each decision: input command, selected paths, reservation state, queue snapshot, decision, rendered handoff, and no-claim boundary.
3. Test fails if any local Cargo fallback, branch/worktree/scratch-clone command, destructive command, or peer path appears in an admitted proof command.
4. Artifact bundle includes JSON receipt, Markdown report, Agent Mail body, br comment body, and replay/resume command.
5. Live RCH fleet state may be attached only as operator evidence; deterministic fixture proof is the correctness source.
notes: Phase 6 refinement pass 4 (e2e/logging): acceptance now requires full structured logs and replay artifacts.

title: [PROOF-TRAFFIC][A6] Docs, manifest, and final signoff for proof traffic control

## What
Close the proof-traffic-control program with README/AGENTS/docs integration, proof-lane manifest/status rows, final signoff artifact, and operator runbook language that is honest about scope.

## How
Document the decision taxonomy, no-claim boundaries, RCH-only policy, no-peer-cancel policy, reservation expectations, and examples for admitted, parked, and blocked proof attempts. Add a final contract test tying artifacts, docs, and manifest rows together.

## Risks
Do not claim broad workspace health, release readiness, live fleet availability, performance improvement, or permission to run local Cargo.

- README/AGENTS markers point at the operator runbook and final signoff artifact.

title: Protobuf wire limits: ProtoCodec encodes messages its decoder refuses (fixed 65,536-field and 4x work caps); der_min version/extension and critical BasicConstraints decisions
description:
From the read-only audit of src/grpc/protobuf_wire.rs, src/tls/der_min.rs, src/codec/{base64,hex}.rs and src/io/{owned_split,copy_session,copy_session/bidirectional}.rs on origin/main 07608dadb (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-03). It found no HIGH. base64, hex, owned_split, copy_session and bidirectional copy are sound. OWNER DECISIONS NEEDED, so this bead is not claimed.

MEDIUM (owner decision): ProtoCodec can encode messages it then refuses to decode. ProtobufWireLimits::for_message_size (protobuf_wire.rs:81-90) fixes max_fields at 65,536 and max_work at 4 x len whatever the byte ceiling. Decode charges one shared budget across the whole message tree. Encode through the derive counts one level per encoder, and each nested message is encoded with a fresh ProtobufWireLimits::default() (asupersync-macros/src/proto.rs:695-702).
- Batch{repeated Item items}, with Item{uint64 id; string name} and 22,000 items: about 220 KB, about 5% of 4 MiB. encode is Ok; decode is FieldCountExceeded (66,000 > 65,536). prost/tonic peers send and accept this.
- A payload nested k deep is charged k+1 times on decode. At 4 MiB, decode fails beyond about 3.36 MiB of nested payload, while encode succeeds.
- No API lifts the cap for a single level with more than 65,536 records.
- ProtoCodec::with_max_size(16 MiB) still encodes nested messages with the 4 MiB default.
Options: (a) aggregate encode-side accounting, so encode fails exactly where decode would; (b) derive the decode field cap from the byte ceiling. Either way, document the field and work caps in the ProstCodec migration table. Pinned: nested_descent_is_charged_against_the_shared_budget (protobuf.rs ~2520) pins aggregate decode accounting, which a fix should keep. (The OTLP side of the same limits is on the OTLP audit bead.)

LOW (owner decision; no production caller until A6): der_min accepts v1/v2 certificates carrying extensions or unique ids. The version is parsed into _version and discarded (der_min.rs:1137, 1163-1183), contrary to RFC 5280 §4.1.

LOW (owner decision, pinned by generated_fixture_profiles_document_intentional_strictness): the pinned-leaf profile rejects critical BasicConstraints as UnknownCritical. Let's Encrypt and OpenSSL default self-signed leaves mark it critical, so the exact-pin fallback would break once A6 wires it in.

description: Optimize RaptorQ hot loops by reusing buffers and eliminating per-iteration allocations while preserving deterministic behavior and RFC 6330 correctness. title: [fresh-eyes] http/h2/frame.rs: frame_length() panics on attacker-influenced encode payload >16MB
description:
src/http/h2/frame.rs:186-194 — frame_length() asserts len <= MAX_FRAME_SIZE (16777215 / 16M) and panics if exceeded:

  fn frame_length(len: usize) -> u32 {
      assert!(len <= MAX_FRAME_SIZE as usize, ...);
      ...
  }

Called from encode() on DataFrame, HeadersFrame, PushPromiseFrame, ContinuationFrame, GoAwayFrame, and Frame::Unknown. If any upstream caller passes a Bytes payload >16M into a single frame (e.g., a proxy echoing attacker-supplied request/response body without honoring peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, or a HEADERS+CONTINUATION chunker bug that produces a >16M block fragment), encode panics inside the connection task — defense-in-depth gap.

The encoder side is server-controlled, so the immediate risk is a server-bug-triggered panic; an attacker cannot directly inject the >16M payload via wire, but they can influence it (large echoed headers, large echoed body in proxy mode) so any chunker bug becomes a panic-on-attacker-input.

Fix options:
(A) Change frame_length to Result<u32, H2Error> returning H2Error::frame_size; propagate through encode() callers (BREAKING — encode signatures change).
(B) Downgrade assert! to debug_assert! + saturating clamp + log error in release. Current behavior in release: panic; with debug_assert: silently emit a length that disagrees with the bytes written — corrupts the wire. So (B) is worse than panic.
(C) Add upstream guards in each encode() impl to early-return Result with H2Error::frame_size. This requires changing each encode() to fn encode(&self, dst) -> Result<(), H2Error>, also breaking but smaller refactor surface than (A).

Recommended: (C) — keeps frame_length as the inner assert (truly unreachable per RFC 9113 §4.2 24-bit limit), but each encode() validates upstream and returns an error.

Audit: SapphireHill 2026-04-26 fresh-eyes-14d-diff via subagent a40c2136; verified live at lines 186-194 (frame_length) and call sites at 267, 342, 470, 718, 868, 999, 1110.

title: AsyncWriteExt single-attempt helpers reject legitimate zero progress
description:
src/io/ext/write_ext.rs routes both one-attempt Write and WriteVectored results through checked_write_progress, which converts Ok(0) with nonempty offered input into ErrorKind::WriteZero. title: [perf] runtime/scheduler/local_queue.rs: every push/pop/is_empty/len takes the same parking_lot::Mutex — defeats SPMC design intent
description: src/runtime/scheduler/local_queue.rs:69 inner = Arc<Mutex<SmallVec<[TaskId; 32]>>>. The doc string at line 62-65 advertises 'single-producer, multi-consumer' with LIFO push/pop owner + FIFO steal, but the implementation wraps everything in a parking_lot::Mutex. Every owner push (line 164), every owner pop (line 201), every is_empty (line 209), every len (line 218), and every steal (line 357) takes the SAME lock. The owner-vs-stealer contention is the canonical problem that lock-free deques (Chase-Lev, crossbeam-deque) were designed to solve. The current design loses to crossbeam by 5-20× under heavy stealing pressure (per published benchmarks). The backoff loop in three_lane.rs:2659 also calls fast_queue.is_empty() which contends on the same mutex. Mitigation: use crossbeam_deque::Worker / Stealer for the owner-stealer split. Severity HIGH for high-worker-count deployments where steal frequency dominates.
close_reason: Partial fix landed in 4a14e7844. cached_len: Arc<AtomicUsize> mirrors inner.queue.len() updated on every push/pop/steal/steal_batch under the existing mutex. is_empty() and len() (on both LocalQueue and Stealer) now do a lock-free Acquire load instead of taking the deque mutex. This eliminates the most-frequent contention point — the worker backoff loop calls is_empty() on every iteration and previously contended with stealers from other workers on the same lock. Power-of-Two-Choices stealer sampling is also now lock-free for length probes. NOT FULLY FIXED: push/pop/steal still take the parking_lot::Mutex<LocalQueueInner> for actual queue mutation. A true lock-free SPMC deque (Chase-Lev / crossbeam_deque-style) would eliminate ALL mutex acquisitions; that requires either a new dependency or ~300 lines of careful unsafe code. Bead remains open for that follow-up. Most contentious read path (is_empty in backoff loop) is fully mutex-free now.

title: Unsolicited CONTINUATION must be connection error per RFC 9113 §6.10
description: RFC 9113 §6.10: 'A CONTINUATION frame MUST be preceded by a HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE or CONTINUATION frame without the END_HEADERS flag set. A recipient that observes violation of this rule MUST respond with a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.' Currently src/http/h2/connection.rs:process_frame only enforces the case where we ARE expecting CONTINUATION but get something else — it does not enforce the inverse (CONTINUATION arrives unsolicited). When CONTINUATION arrives with continuation_stream_id == None, process_continuation either returns 'CONTINUATION for unknown stream' (stream-level via H2Error::protocol — wait that's connection... let me re-check) or stream.recv_continuation returns a STREAM-level ProtocolError. Both miss the MUST connection-level error mandate. Existing tests cover the inverse (SETTINGS/PING during expected CONTINUATION) but not unsolicited CONTINUATION.

title: fs/io audit: fs::File writes bytes twice when reads and writes interleave on one handle (copy_bidirectional, split); io-uring path ops and IoUringFile block the worker; LOWs
description:
Read-only audit of src/fs and the generic I/O helpers in src/io at origin/main 7f1ee49d4 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-04; read from origin).

## HIGH
1. fs::File writes the same bytes twice when reads and writes interleave on one handle (file.rs ~189-196 assumption, ~722-731, ~818-825, ~847, ~868-882; reachable via io/copy.rs ~951-969 copy_bidirectional and io/split.rs). The poll-trait state machine treats any call that does not match the pending Write as abandoning it: poll_read/poll_seek/poll_flush settles the live write, discards its byte count and starts its own op; the write's owner retries and the same bytes are submitted again. With a blocking pool: poll_write(b"hello") Pending, pool finishes the write; poll_read settles it (count discarded) and submits a read; poll_write(b"hello") retries and writes again: file contains hellohello. On tty/pty/FIFO the ReadAhead rewind seek fails with ESPIPE (copy errors, read bytes dropped) or the command is sent twice. Fix: a separate completed-write slot (chunk + result) that survives settlement by reads/seeks/flushes and is consumed by the next poll_write whose buffer starts_with that chunk. Test: deterministic with BlockingPool + FileCursorOperationProbe.

## MEDIUM
2. With the io-uring feature, path ops (rename, remove_file, symlink, create_dir, remove_dir; path_ops.rs ~278-306, ~378-385, ~714-734; dir.rs ~25-99) build a new IoUring per call and submit_and_wait on the async worker, contrary to the module docs ("true async"), with no fallback: EPERM (Docker seccomp, io_uring_disabled), ENOSYS (gVisor) or opcode EINVAL make them always fail; an interrupted wait can report "no completion received" for a rename that still commits. Fix: std calls via spawn_blocking_io, or a shared probed ring with fallback.
3. validate_safe_path rejects any `..` (path_ops.rs ~164-210, applied ~256-257, ~273-274, ~296, ~457, ~552): fs::write("../out"), remove_file("/a/b/../c"), rename, copy, write_atomic return InvalidInput while File::create, fs::read, remove_dir_all, hard_link, symlink accept the same paths; absolute paths are allowed everywhere, so it is no security boundary; undocumented; fs mirrors std::fs. Owner decision (relaxes a deliberate check).
4. IoUringFile does every read/write/fsync with a blocking submit_and_wait on the worker although its docs claim fully asynchronous I/O (uring.rs ~649-660, ~1119-1243); poll_flush does a durable fdatasync (~1246-1249), so copy() (flushes whenever the reader is Pending) and every BufWriter flush fsyncs on the worker.

## LOW
5. write_atomic fsyncs the parent directory on the async worker (path_ops.rs ~515-520, ~580-582, ~666-670).
6. read_line / LineReader leave part of an invalid-UTF-8 line in the caller's buffer (read_line.rs ~176-182, ~222-230); std/tokio restore it (the comment ~115-116 claims parity).
7. write_f32/write_f64 (+ _le) canonicalize -0.0 and NaN payloads (write_ext.rs ~25-45, ~232-290); read_f64 decodes raw bits, so -0.0 does not round-trip; tokio writes to_bits().
8. The poll path drops ReadAhead bytes before their rewind seek runs (file.rs ~868-882, ~968-981); on a socket/pipe the seek fails with ESPIPE and the next read skips them. The owned path restores them.
Minor: fs::BufReader::lines inherits a 64 KiB line cap (io/lines.rs ~24) not mentioned in the fs docs.

## Checked and sound
fs::File owned cursor ops, into_std settle-and-rewind, 128 KiB per-syscall cap, prefix-matching retry credit for abandoned writes; blocking pool cancellation; io and fs BufReader/BufWriter; copy family (flush, half-close, guards, sessions); read/write ext helpers; Lines, StreamReader, ReaderStream, Take, Chain, ReadBuf, split; ReadDir, DirEntry, OpenOptions, Metadata, Vfs; write_atomic temp files.

title: [protocol-state-machine] http/h2/stream.rs: recv_headers accepts trailing HEADERS without END_STREAM on Open / HalfClosedLocal — direction-agnostic state machine fails to reject server-side malformed trailers
description:
src/http/h2/stream.rs:388-429 — Stream::recv_headers accepts a HEADERS frame on stream state Open or HalfClosedLocal WITHOUT END_STREAM and silently leaves the state unchanged (lines 416-417, comment 'informational 1xx or trailing headers before DATA').

The accept-on-Open-without-end-stream branch is correct for clients receiving 1xx informational responses (RFC 9110 §15.2). But it is INCORRECT when the same code path is reached on a SERVER receiving HEADERS from a client: RFC 9113 §8.1 says trailers from the request side MUST carry END_STREAM. A client sending request trailers without END_STREAM is malformed and the server MUST respond with a stream error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

The current implementation cannot tell client from server because Stream is direction-agnostic. The pseudo-header validator in connection.rs::decode_headers (line 862+ via validate_h2_pseudo_headers) catches some malformed trailer shapes (presence of pseudo-headers in trailers is rejected) but does NOT reject the structural error of 'trailers without END_STREAM'. So a client that sends a trailer block consisting of legitimate response-style header names (none starting with ':') without END_STREAM passes both layers and the server processes it as if the request body continues.

Concrete trigger:
  Client -> Server: HEADERS (END_STREAM=false) ... DATA (END_STREAM=false) ... HEADERS (END_STREAM=false, no pseudo-headers, e.g. 'x-trailer: ok')
  Server's stream is on Open at the time of the second HEADERS.
  Stream::recv_headers hits line 416 -> state stays Open, headers_complete is set.
  decode_headers does NOT flag missing END_STREAM in trailers.
  The server now treats the connection as still expecting more DATA frames, but the client has already sent everything it intends to — head-of-line stall.

Fix direction:
  1. Thread  (or an explicit Direction enum) through Stream so recv_headers can apply RFC 9113 §8.1 trailers-MUST-have-END_STREAM specifically when the receiver is a server.
  2. Or: enforce the rule at decode_headers in connection.rs after determining client/server context — return a stream error with ProtocolError when the second HEADERS frame on a stream lacks END_STREAM in the server-receives-request direction.
  3. Add a regression test that drives a server connection with trailing HEADERS without END_STREAM and asserts the stream is reset with PROTOCOL_ERROR.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/http/h1/* + h2/* + h3_native.rs (2026-04-26).
close_reason: recv_headers now direction-aware via is_client param; server-side trailing HEADERS without END_STREAM rejected as stream PROTOCOL_ERROR; client-side 1xx informational path preserved; 3 regression tests

title: [fs/uring.rs] Audit io_uring AsyncRead/AsyncWrite invariants for completion attribution bugs
description:
AUDIT REQUIRED: Recent commits (c92b1754c, 6c8f78f4f) show complex io_uring completion attribution logic with critical invariants:

RISK SURFACES:
1. **Unknown CQE Attribution**: ignores_unknown_completion_before_{read,write,sync} - spurious completions could corrupt tracked operations
2. **Drop-drain behavior**: Pending operations during drop must complete or be properly cancelled
3. **User data tracking**: user_data collision could cause operation misattribution  
4. **Async boundary violations**: Some operations (set_len) must be sync boundaries

INVARIANTS TO VERIFY:
- Unknown CQEs never satisfy tracked operations (completion hijacking)
- Buffer corruption cannot occur via stray CQEs 
- Drop always drains pending ops (no leaked kernel state)
- Sync boundaries leave no pending operations
- User data namespacing prevents collision

AUDIT METHOD: Fresh-eyes code review of completion handling, attribution logic, and buffer management for race conditions and invariant violations.

RECENT CHANGES: Multiple commits added unknown completion tests - suggests prior issues or high-risk area requiring systematic audit.

Moved test constants to high-bit namespace (0xFF00...) to prevent collision with production user_data values. This eliminates risk of completion hijacking, operation misattribution, buffer corruption, and data loss.

title: RegionCommand::Close's cancel reason has a constant 1 s timestamp, so it outranks any real cancellation once the runtime is older than 1 s (remote_owned close reports the wrong reason; deterministic full-lib red)
description:
RegionCommand::Close cancels the region's remaining tasks with CancelReason::user("owned child region body finished") (src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs ~6883, src/lab/runtime.rs ~4195). CancelReason::user/new stamp a constant Time::from_nanos(1_000_000_000), and CancelReason::strengthen breaks a same-severity tie by the EARLIER timestamp. So once the runtime clock (the shared process epoch) is past 1 s, i.e. in practice always, this internal close reason outranks any real cancellation it races with: an explicit close/cancel of an owned remote invocation reports "owned child region body finished" (origin region 0:0, no task) instead of the caller's reason.

Observed: distributed::remote_owned::tests::owned_remote_close_keeps_its_report_with_an_already_cancelled_observer (e6537c737) fails in every full-lib run (2/2 on vmi1227854: 10-10 cb_lib, 10-11 fl_lib on main 5a03368e6, the only failure in 25671 tests) at tests.rs:561: reply.cancellation is the close reason at 1 s instead of the observer's reason at 23 s / 40 s. Filtered runs pass (hz4 80/0, bare origin) because the process is under 1 s old when the test runs, so the observer's timestamp is the earlier one.

Fix: stamp the close reason with the close time (three_lane: the drain_now the worker already captured for these commands; lab: the lab's virtual now), line-neutral above both files' line locators. Make the test deterministic by waiting until the runtime clock is past 2 s before the observer cancels, so the old code fails it in any run.
close_reason: done
