title: [conformance] HTTP/3: missing control-stream first-frame + DATAGRAM format + Extended CONNECT coverage
description:
RFC 9114 + RFC 9204 + RFC 9297 + RFC 9298 conformance gaps in tests/conformance/h3*. Concrete missing vectors:

(1) RFC 9114 §6.2 — Stream type validation: control 0x00, push-stream 0x01, decoder 0x02, encoder 0x03 each must be the FIRST varint on the corresponding unidirectional stream. No tests for non-first / wrong-type rejection.

(2) RFC 9114 §6.2.2.1 — Control stream first-frame requirement: SETTINGS must be the first frame; non-SETTINGS first frame must close connection with H3_MISSING_SETTINGS. lcvdj0 was h2; this h3 path needs its own conformance vector.

(3) RFC 9204 §4.1 — QPACK dynamic-table reference durability + eviction interaction with stream cancellation; no systematic test matrix.

(4) RFC 9114 §7.2.4.1 — SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY × SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS interaction.

(5) RFC 9297 — H3 DATAGRAM frame format validation (flow-ID encoding, ordering semantics). 8w9naj fixed per-stream state-machine acceptance; no per-frame format conformance vector.

(6) RFC 9298 — Extended CONNECT (CONNECT-UDP/CONNECT-IP) negotiation: `:protocol` pseudo-header validation, capsule format.

(7) RFC 9114 §8 — GOAWAY semantics: last-stream-id validity, immediate vs graceful shutdown.

Fix direction: tests/conformance/h3_rfc9114/{stream_types, control_first_frame, datagram_format, extended_connect, goaway}_tests.rs.

title: Implement TraceRecorder for Lab runtime
description:
## Overview

Implement the TraceRecorder that instruments the Lab runtime to emit trace events during execution.

## Background

Once we have the TraceEvent schema, we need to hook into Lab runtime's decision points to capture events without adding significant overhead.

## Design Requirements

### Low Overhead
- Recording should not significantly slow down test execution
- Use buffered writes
- Consider memory-mapped file for large traces

### Non-Invasive
- Lab runtime code changes should be minimal
- Use callback/observer pattern
- Recording should be opt-in (disabled by default)

### Thread-Safe
- Handle recording from multiple Lab runtime threads
- Use lock-free structures where possible

## Implementation Approach

```rust
pub struct TraceRecorder {
    events: Vec<TraceEvent>,
    metadata: TraceMetadata,
    enabled: bool,
}

impl TraceRecorder {
    pub fn new(config: RecorderConfig) -> Self;
    pub fn record(&mut self, event: TraceEvent);
    pub fn finish(self) -> RecordedTrace;
}

// In Lab runtime, add hooks:
impl LabRuntime {
    pub fn with_recorder(config, recorder: TraceRecorder) -> Self;
}
```

## Integration Points

1. `Scheduler::pick_next_task()` - record choice
2. `VirtualClock::advance()` - record time changes
3. `SimulatedIo::complete()` - record I/O results
4. `DeterministicRng::next()` - record RNG values

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] TraceRecorder captures all TraceEvent variants
- [ ] Recording adds < 5% overhead to test execution
- [ ] Events are captured in correct causal order
- [ ] Integration with Lab runtime is clean and minimal
- [ ] Unit tests verify recording correctness

title: HTTP/2: after our GOAWAY, responses on the connection's own streams are refused (the GOAWAY boundary ignores stream parity)
description:
Found by SapphireHill (10-06) while writing dycth8's test (connection.rs refused_push_promise_case, AfterOurGoaway).

Connection::stream_exceeds_sent_goaway compares every incoming stream id with the last_stream_id we sent in GOAWAY. RFC 9113 §6.8 makes that id cover only streams the GOAWAY's receiver (our peer) initiated. For a client it counts server-initiated (pushed) streams, so it is 0 when none were processed, and after Connection::goaway() every HEADERS, CONTINUATION and DATA frame on the client's own streams is treated as refused: response HEADERS are decoded and dropped with RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM), DATA is dropped. Responses to requests still in flight are lost.

Reach: the in-tree h2 and gRPC clients never call goaway(), so only external users of the public Connection API are exposed.

Fix (staged by SapphireHill, lands right after dycth8 M3): count only peer-initiated ids (even for a client, odd for a server) in stream_exceeds_sent_goaway; its four callers (process_data, process_headers, process_continuation, process_push_promise) then refuse only what GOAWAY covers. Test: a client that sent GOAWAY still receives HEADERS and DATA on a stream it opened before, and still refuses a push above the boundary. dycth8's test then requires the decoded response in its GOAWAY case.
close_reason: done

title: time: global fallback timer wheel has 1 ms resolution; sub-millisecond pacer sleeps now cost >= 1 ms under caller-driven composition
description: Since 616af91b5 (GH#67) driverless UDP polls park instead of self-waking, so a Sleep on the process-global fallback timer is what actually wakes the task. LEVEL0_RESOLUTION_NS of that wheel is 1 ms, so ATP pacer pauses of ~50-800 us (crate::time::sleep in src/net/atp/transport_quic/native_link.rs pacer sites) now take >= 1 ms each; the old hot loop honoured deadlines to the microsecond. Effect: lower paced throughput under block_on + explicit Cx (not under a runtime with a timer driver). Measure the throughput delta in isolation and decide: finer fallback wheel level for short sleeps, a spin-then-park hybrid below 1 ms, or documenting the caller-driven pacing floor.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
SapphireHill 2026-09-09 20:05Z read-only measurement plan (no source changes during the ce14e7a57 freeze):

Facts read from source: src/time/wheel.rs LEVEL0_RESOLUTION_NS = 1_000_000 (1 ms level-0 slots), and src/time/sleep.rs routes time::sleep through the process-global fallback timer (GLOBAL_FALLBACK, fallback_pump_loop) whenever the Cx carries no timer driver, i.e. exactly the caller-driven composition GH#67 made park instead of spin. The ATP pacer sleeps in src/net/atp/transport_quic/native_link.rs (before_send_bytes and the controller wait at ~L2510-2560) clamp their pause to a floor of QUIC_DATA_PLANE_PACER_MIN_PAUSE = 50 us, so at pacing rates above ~1.2 MB/s (one ~1200 B packet per ms) every pause is sub-millisecond and now costs a full wheel tick.

Measurement, in two parts, both runnable without changing native source once the freeze lifts (they are test/bench additions):
1. Granularity: a unit test in src/time/sleep.rs tests that, with no ambient Cx, times 50 sleeps of 100 us, 300 us and 800 us and reports the median actual duration; expectation on current code: ~1 ms for all three (the bead's claim), which fixes the baseline number.
2. Throughput delta in isolation: the loopback ATP QUIC transfer from tests/atp_quic_real_udp_transfer_e2e.rs run under futures_lite::block_on with an explicit Cx (no runtime timer driver) versus under a runtime with a timer driver, same payload (e.g. 64 MB), pacing target 20 MB/s (60 us per packet); report bytes per second for both. The delta is the caller-driven pacing floor cost.

Decision options, with the trade-off each carries:
- A. Finer level-0 slot for the fallback wheel only (e.g. 100 us): pump wakes at most 10x more often but only while sub-ms timers are pending; zero cost when idle (GH#67 goal preserved). Touches src/time/wheel.rs and sleep.rs; needs the rr849p near-timer tests re-run.
- B. Burst-shape adaptation in the pacer: when the effective sleep granularity is coarse, send enough packets per pause that the pause is >= 1 ms (the pacer already carries a burst shape; set_pacing_rate_bytes_per_s preserves it). Keeps timers untouched; slightly burstier wire pattern at high rates. Touches native_link.rs only.
- C. Spin-then-park below 1 ms inside the pacer wait: exact pacing but burns CPU while actively sending; must never apply to idle waits (that is GH#67 again).
- D. Document the caller-driven pacing floor and recommend a runtime timer driver for high-rate paced sends.
Recommendation after measurement: B first (cheapest, no timer semantics change), A if B's burstiness shows up on the lossy matrix cells. Coordinate with the 9bb6pt landing since both touch the pacer.

title: Process-age time bombs in lib tests: absolute Time constants against the process-relative runtime clock (dns cache eviction test fails after 300 s; child_region independent_cancel after 10 s)
description:
Two lib tests compare absolute Time constants against the native runtime clock. That clock is process-relative: it counts from process start. Each test passes in a short run and fails once the test process is older than its constant. Both turned up in stack P's full --lib lane (668 s run, 10-05).

1. net::dns::cache::tests::cache_capacity_eviction_breaks_equal_insert_times_deterministically
   - It inserts two entries at Time::from_nanos(42) with a 300 s TTL, then calls put_ip on a wall-clock DnsCache.
   - After 300 s of process age both entries have expired, so put_ip drops them instead of evicting the lexically smaller one. It fails with "later lexical key remains when insert times tie".
   - It is the same on main.
   - FIX (stack P, P18): build the cache with the module's test clock (set_test_time(42) and with_time_getter), as the other cache tests do.
2. cx::child_region::tests::independent_cancel_stops_child_body_and_parent_keeps_working
   - Its parent budget is Budget::with_deadline_at_secs(10), an absolute 10 s on the runtime clock, which has usually passed when the test runs.
   - Before br-asupersync-pev2xi this was harmless, because deadlines were only checked at checkpoints and the sibling never checkpoints.
   - With proactive deadlines (stack P, P1) the sibling is cancelled before it runs.
   - FIX (in P1): a deadline 10 s from wall_now().

Follow-up, not done: a census of tests that pass an absolute Time or with_deadline_at_* to a wall-clock runtime or cache (rg 'with_deadline_at_secs|with_deadline_at_ns|Time::from_(secs|millis|nanos)' over tests that build a native runtime or use wall_now). Short filtered lanes do not catch these; a full --lib run longer than the constant does.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "=== Z3 Final Gate Verification ==="
echo "Date: $(date -u)"
echo "Commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD)"
echo ""

# 1. Quality gates
echo "[GATE 1] Compilation..."
cargo check --all-targets && echo "  default: OK"
cargo check --all-targets --no-default-features && echo "  no-default: OK"
echo ""

echo "[GATE 2] Clippy..."
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings && echo "  clean"
echo ""

echo "[GATE 3] Tests..."
cargo test --lib 2>&1 | tail -3
cargo test stub_resolution 2>&1 | tail -5
echo ""

echo "[GATE 4] Scan scripts..."
bash scripts/scan_stubs.sh
bash scripts/verify_stub_resolution.sh
echo ""

echo "[GATE 5] Specific file checks..."
[ ! -f src/a.out ] && echo "  a.out: removed" || echo "  a.out: STILL EXISTS"
[ ! -f src/test_multipart_panic.rs ] && echo "  test_multipart_panic.rs: removed" || echo "  STILL EXISTS"
! grep -q '#!\[allow(dead_code)\]' src/lib.rs && echo "  lib.rs dead_code: clean" || echo "  STILL HAS ALLOW"
grep -q 'cfg' <(grep 'pub mod mock' src/transport/mod.rs) && echo "  mock gated: yes" || echo "  mock: NOT GATED"
echo ""

echo "[GATE 6] Artifacts..."
[ -f tests/stub_resolution_audit.rs ] && echo "  test module: exists" || echo "  MISSING"
[ -x scripts/verify_stub_resolution.sh ] && echo "  verify script: exists" || echo "  MISSING"
[ -x scripts/scan_stubs.sh ] && echo "  scan script: exists" || echo "  MISSING"
[ -f .stub-allowlist.txt ] && echo "  allowlist: exists" || echo "  MISSING"
echo ""

echo "=== Z3 GATE COMPLETE ==="
```

- No open beads remain under v2ofj7 (all tracks closed or explicitly deferred)
- Epic v2ofj7 can be closed

- Closing this bead triggers closure of Track Z and the epic

title: [replay-determinism] observability/spectral_health.rs: connected_components label_map is std HashMap — non-deterministic component IDs across runs
description:
src/observability/spectral_health.rs:271 — connected_components() normalizes union-find roots into 0..k-1 component IDs by inserting into a std::collections::HashMap. The first encountered root gets ID 0, the next gets 1, etc. — but std HashMap iteration is randomized per process via RandomState, so the order in which roots are first encountered (when the loop hits a node whose root has not been seen) is the order of node-index iteration over `0..self.size`, which IS deterministic.

Wait — the bug is subtler. The HashMap is keyed by the ROOT node. The label assignment is `next_label += 1` inside the entry().or_insert_with closure, which DOES preserve insertion order via the iteration over `i` from 0 to size. So the labels are assigned in node-index order, which is deterministic. BUT any subsequent iteration over `label_map` (e.g. for export, classification, or in a future refactor that exposes the component-id mapping) will be non-deterministic. AND if the union-find structure ever causes a root to be inserted under different keys across runs (which it shouldn`t with deterministic input, but the HashMaps collision-chain ordering could leak), the labels themselves drift.

Threat model: classify_health() (downstream of connected_components) determines if the dependency graph is fragmented. Fragility around HashMap iteration is a future-proofing problem — a refactor that surfaces label_map iteration would silently break replay.

Fix direction: replace HashMap with BTreeMap<usize, usize> for replay-stable iteration, or sort the encountered roots in a Vec and assign labels via Vec position. The existing code already iterates roots in i-order, so a Vec-based scheme is even simpler.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting deepest 8th-pass on src/observability/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Replaced std HashMap with BTreeMap in connected_components label_map for replay-stable iteration. Changes landed in commit d9eb2d37e (rolled into a concurrent commit). Tests added: connected_components_is_deterministic_within_run + _labels_are_node_index_first_encounter_order.

title: Implement TaskState enum and state machine
description:
# TaskState Enum and State Machine

## Purpose
TaskState represents the lifecycle of a task from creation to completion. The state machine is carefully designed to support the cancellation protocol with explicit drain and finalize phases.

## The Task States
```rust
enum TaskState {
    // Initial state after spawn
    Created,
    
    // Actively being polled
    Running,
    
    // Cancel requested but not yet acknowledged
    CancelRequested {
        reason: CancelReason,
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Task has acknowledged cancel, running cleanup code
    Cancelling {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Cleanup done, running finalizers
    Finalizing {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Terminal state
    Completed(Outcome),
}
```

## State Transitions

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                      │
Created ──────────► Running ──────────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cancel_request()                   │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │           CancelRequested ─────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ checkpoint (mask=0)                │
    │                 ▼                                    │ Completed
    │              Cancelling ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cleanup done                       │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │              Finalizing ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ finalizers done                    │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    └────────────────►  Completed(Outcome)  ◄──────────────┘
```

## Valid Transitions

| From | To | Trigger | Label |
|------|-----|---------|-------|
| Created | Running | Scheduler selects | τ (silent) |
| Created | CancelRequested | Cancel before first poll | cancel(r,reason) |
| Running | Completed(Ok/Err) | Task body returns | complete(t,outcome) |
| Running | CancelRequested | Cancel request arrives | cancel(r,reason) |
| CancelRequested | Cancelling | Checkpoint with mask=0 | τ |
| CancelRequested | CancelRequested | Checkpoint with mask>0 (defer) | τ |
| Cancelling | Finalizing | Cleanup code completes | τ |
| Cancelling | Completed(Cancelled) | No cleanup needed | complete(t,Cancelled) |
| Finalizing | Completed(Cancelled) | All finalizers run | complete(t,Cancelled) |

## Why These States?

### Created vs Running
Separates "spawned but not yet scheduled" from "actively executing." This allows:
- Batch spawning before any execution
- Cancel before first poll (task never runs)
- Clear scheduling semantics

### CancelRequested
The task hasn't observed the cancel yet. This is important because:
- Task may be in the middle of a computation
- Task should reach a checkpoint to observe cancel
- Masking allows bounded deferral

### Cancelling
Task has acknowledged cancel and is running cleanup code. The cleanup_budget ensures bounded cleanup time.

### Finalizing
Cleanup code done, now running registered finalizers (defer_async, defer_sync). Finalizers run under cancel mask.

### Completed
Terminal and absorbing. Once Completed, the state never changes. This supports INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR.

## Mask Budget

When in CancelRequested, the task has a `mask` count (in TaskRecord, not TaskState):
- Each checkpoint where mask>0 decrements mask and returns Ok
- When mask=0, checkpoint returns Cancelled
- This ensures bounded cancellation deferral (INV-MASK-BOUNDED)

## Implementation Requirements

1. **TaskState must be Clone, Debug**
2. **Completed(Outcome) stores the full outcome**
3. **is_terminal() method**: Returns true only for Completed
4. **is_cancelling() method**: Returns true for CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing
5. **can_be_polled() method**: Returns true for Running/CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing

## Invariant Support

### INV-TASK-OWNED
```rust
∀t: T[t].state ≠ Completed(_) ⟹ t ∈ R[T[t].region].children
```
Non-completed tasks are owned by their region.

### INV-MASK-BOUNDED  
```rust
∀t: T[t].mask ∈ ℕ and only decreases at CHECKPOINT-MASKED
```
Masking is finite.

### INV-OBLIGATION-BOUNDED
```rust
∀o: O[o].state = Reserved ⟹ T[O[o].holder].state ∈ {Running, CancelRequested, Cancelling, Finalizing}
```
Reserved obligations have live holders.

## Testing Requirements

1. Only valid transitions are possible
2. Completed is absorbing (can't transition out)
3. State machine handles all cancel timing scenarios
4. Mask budget decrements correctly

## Example Scenarios

### Normal Completion
```
Created → Running → Completed(Ok(value))
```

### Cancelled at Checkpoint
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Cancelled Before First Poll
```
Created → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Error During Cancellation
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Completed(Err(e))
// Error during cleanup is still an error, not Cancelled
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.5 (Task States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.1-3.2 (Task lifecycle, Cancellation protocol)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §7.1 (Task cancellation state machine)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Task lifecycle states match the spec: Created → Running → (CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing) → Completed(outcome).
- Cancellation-related states carry the necessary metadata (reason, budgets/quotas) and strengthen idempotently.
- Completed is terminal/absorbing.
- Unit tests cover legal/illegal transitions and trace-level representation.
notes:
Implemented TaskState + core transitions aligned to formal semantics.

- `src/record/task.rs`: TaskState now `Created | Running | CancelRequested{reason, cleanup_budget} | Cancelling{cleanup_budget} | Finalizing{cleanup_budget} | Completed(TaskOutcome)` where `TaskOutcome = Outcome<(), crate::error::Error>` (Phase 0 concrete outcome storage). Added helpers `is_terminal`, `is_cancelling`, `can_be_polled`, plus TaskRecord transition helpers `start_running` + `complete`.
- Cancellation request handling is idempotent: repeated `request_cancel` strengthens `CancelReason` and tightens `cleanup_budget` via `Budget::combine`.
- Updated affected call sites/tests (notably `src/runtime/state.rs` live-task accounting + policy sibling-cancel tests).
- Added unit tests in `src/record/task.rs` covering cancel-before-first-poll, strengthening, Completed absorbing, and pollability predicate.

Gates: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test all pass.
close_reason: Implemented TaskState state machine + tests; gates pass

title: Phase 5+: True-Concurrency Research Upgrades (HDA, d-homotopy, homology)
description:
# Phase 5+: True-Concurrency Research Upgrades

## Purpose
The design documents include deeper mathematical lenses that are not required for Phase 0–5 core usability but can significantly improve schedule exploration efficiency and coverage prioritization.

This feature tracks those research upgrades explicitly so they aren’t lost:
- event structures + higher-dimensional automata (HDA)
- directed topology / d-homotopy schedule normalization
- persistent (directed) homology to prioritize “topologically essential” schedules
- large-deviation / biased schedule sampling for black-swan bugs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Each research item has a concrete experiment plan and success metric.

title: [RAPTORQ-X] RaptorQ leverage beyond snapshots — erasure-coded channels, durable traces, adaptive multipath
description:
WHY: src/raptorq/ is a complete, deterministic, policy-planned RFC 6330 implementation with authenticated symbols, decode proofs, and a sender/receiver pipeline — but recon shows it is used only for distributed snapshot distribution and ATP repair. The machinery (StateEncoder, SymbolDistributor, MultipathAggregator, security tags, decision contracts) generalizes far beyond that. This epic mines it for unprecedented runtime features no other async runtime can offer.

CHILD TASKS: (1) ErasureCodedChannel — a channel variant where K-of-N symbol delivery replaces reliable delivery, integrated with the obligation ledger so send obligations resolve on decode-commit; (2) RaptorQ-durable traces/crashpacks — encode trace rings into symbols spread across files/replicas so a crash with partial writes still reconstructs forensics; (3) adaptive block sizing — derive K' from observed RTT/loss per path instead of static config; (4) multipath symbol striping wired into transport/ATP large transfers with per-path repair; (5) epoch-gated symbol validity windows to fail-closed against stale-symbol mixing.

DISCIPLINE: all features deterministic under lab (seeded loss injection); decode proofs retained; security/auth tags mandatory on every new symbol path; each feature has an explicit fallback to the non-coded path.

SUCCESS METRIC: deterministic loss-injection e2e suite (child bead) proves: ECC channel delivers losslessly at configured loss rates within proven bounds; a SIGKILLed process with 40% trace-symbol loss still reconstructs a complete crashpack.

title: [RAPTORQ-X] ErasureCodedChannel — K-of-N fountain-coded delivery as a first-class channel primitive
description:
WHY: no other runtime has this: a channel whose delivery guarantee comes from forward erasure correction instead of retransmission, integrated with the obligation ledger. Use cases: lossy/multipath transports (UDP fan-out, WebTransport datagrams, radio-ish links), latency-critical pipelines where retransmit RTTs are unaffordable, and the internal transport/ATP lanes that already speak symbols. Recon confirmed all the parts exist (RaptorQSender/Receiver pipeline, authenticated symbols, MultipathAggregator) — what is missing is the channel-shaped composition.

WHAT: channel::erasure::channel::<T: Serialize>(config{k, overhead, max_message_size, auth_key}) -> (EcSender<T>, EcReceiver<T>): (1) send side: serialize -> RaptorQ-encode into N=K+overhead symbols -> emit symbols through a pluggable SymbolTransport (the existing transport sink trait) — the SEND OBLIGATION resolves when enough symbols are handed to transport per the configured delivery class, mirroring two-phase discipline (reserve = encode+stage, commit = symbol flush); (2) receive side: symbol intake (dedup/reorder via aggregator machinery) -> decode at K received -> recv(cx) yields the message; a decode-failure beyond configured wait emits a typed error with the decode-proof diagnostics; (3) authenticated symbols mandatory by default (Byzantine-injection resistance via src/security tags); (4) lab-deterministic loss injection on the in-memory transport (seeded loss/reorder/dup) — the testing story IS part of the feature.
design: FILES: new src/channel/erasure.rs composing src/raptorq/pipeline.rs, src/transport/{sink,aggregator}, src/security/authenticated.rs. Message framing: message-id + block layout header per message (small messages = 1 source block; document the K vs message-size tradeoffs with guidance defaults). Obligation semantics decision (record it): sender obligation resolves at symbol-flush (transport handoff) NOT at receiver-decode — end-to-end ack is a layer above (delivery classes L0-L4 exist in messaging/fabric; reference, do not reinvent). recv ordering: per-sender FIFO by message-id; cross-sender no order (document).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Lossless delivery at loss rates up to the configured overhead margin: seeded-loss matrix (5/10/20% loss x reorder x dup) proves decode success matches RaptorQ theory within the documented bound; failures beyond margin produce the typed error with proof diagnostics. 2. Cancel-correctness: sender cancelled mid-message -> staged symbols aborted cleanly, no partial-message delivery ever surfaces to recv (metamorphic test). 3. Auth: tampered symbol rejected, counted, decode still succeeds with margin (test). 4. Obligation accounting: leak oracle green across loss/cancel matrix. 5. Throughput bench vs plain mpsc documented (the overhead price, honestly stated). 6. Doctests + a docs section with the K/overhead tuning guidance. 7. Deterministic: same seed -> same symbol/loss/decode trace (replay test).
notes: Erasure block-layout PROVEN runnable (same test file, 7/7): plan() source-symbol/padding/total math (small/padded), MessageTooLarge rejection, MessageHeader 18-byte round-trip. Foundation behaviorally confirmed. REMAINING: async EcSender/EcReceiver over raptorq pipeline + transport + auth + obligations + lab loss matrix (AC1-7).

title: [RAPTORQ-X] RaptorQ-durable traces & crashpacks — forensics that survive the crash
description:
WHY: the deepest forensics irony: the trace that explains a crash is the thing most likely destroyed BY the crash (partial writes, torn files, lost ring tail). Fountain-coding the trace stream means ANY K of the N written symbol chunks reconstructs the trace — partial loss becomes recoverable by construction. No other runtime ships crash-proof traces.

WHAT: (1) symbol-journal writer: trace ring buffer checkpoints encode into RaptorQ symbol frames appended to a set of striped journal files (different files = different failure domains; optionally different disks/dirs) with epoch-tagged headers; fsync policy configurable (per-checkpoint / periodic); (2) recovery tool: frankenlab trace-recover <journal-dir> scans available symbol frames, decodes the latest complete epoch, emits a normal trace/crashpack (integrates with the existing trace tooling + decode-proof for integrity evidence); (3) crashpack writer gains the same option (crashpack-as-symbols) for the auto-crashpack path ([LAB-DX] C3) — a crash DURING crashpack write currently loses everything, exactly the case this kills; (4) bounded overhead: symbol encoding on a background blocking-pool task, never on the hot path; ring-buffer-to-symbols only at checkpoint boundaries (MIN_CHECKPOINT_SIZE machinery in trace/streaming exists — reuse).
design: FILES: new src/trace/symbol_journal.rs composing trace/streaming.rs checkpoints + raptorq pipeline; frankenlab subcommand trace-recover; src/trace/crashpack.rs (symbol-output option). Journal frame format: magic, epoch, block params, symbol payload, CRC + auth tag — versioned from day one. Loss model targeted: torn tail-writes + whole-file loss of any minority of stripes (document what each overhead setting tolerates).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Kill-test: SIGKILL a traced lab process mid-write across a seeded matrix of torn-write points; trace-recover reconstructs the last complete epoch in 100% of cases where >=K symbol frames survive; the bound is documented + tested at the boundary (K-1 fails with a clear diagnostic). 2. Stripe-loss: delete any single stripe file -> full recovery (with default 3-stripe config). 3. Decode-proof attached to recovered traces (integrity evidence). 4. Overhead bench: tracing-overhead bench extended with symbol-journal on/off; hot-path delta within stated budget (target <3% on the bench workload; record actual). 5. Recovered trace replayable (round-trip into frankenlab replay). 6. e2e stage in F6 covers the full kill->recover->replay chain.
notes: RELATION: C3 auto-crashpack consumer; F6 e2e. The kill-test harness needs process-level orchestration — pattern exists in process.rs tests. Storage formats are versioned; no migration shims needed pre-1.0 (policy). CAVEAT (added 2026-06-10): the checkpoint machinery this bead reuses (trace/streaming.rs MIN_CHECKPOINT_SIZE, line ~724) appears in the asupersync-72jib7 bug list (false-reject finding) and that bug bead is still OPEN — verify the fix status of the streaming-checkpoint bug BEFORE building the symbol journal on top of it; record the verdict in close notes.
close_reason: All 6 ACs landed: AC1 eb0b299fa (torn-write+K-1), AC2/AC3 73b88f92f (stripe-loss+RecoveryProof), AC4 15db5b9a2 (overhead bound 0% hot-path delta by construction + amortization bench), AC5 f510ea77c (recover->replay), AC6 689e2b667 (real-SIGKILL kill->recover->replay e2e). title: [RAPTORQ-X] Adaptive block sizing — derive K-prime from observed path RTT/loss instead of static config
description:
WHY: recon: StateEncoder block layout is static; the distribution layer already tracks per-path loss/duplicate stats (transport/aggregator per-path statistics) and the repair brain computes ROI — but encode-time block sizing ignores all of it. Lossy paths want larger extended blocks (fewer control round-trips); clean fast paths want smaller blocks (lower decode latency). The fix is small (recon estimated the layout-derivation seam at ~10 lines plus plumbing) and pays immediately on unstable networks.

WHAT: (1) a PathQuality snapshot {rtt_ewma, loss_ewma, reorder_depth} flowing from aggregator/router stats into DistributionConfig; (2) derive_block_layout consumes it: documented monotone policy mapping quality -> (K, overhead) within configured floors/ceilings — deterministic given the snapshot (snapshot is itself logged so encodes are replayable); (3) decision recorded per encode in the existing decision-contract/telemetry path (the G7 machinery) so adaptive choices are auditable + tunable offline; (4) conservative fallback: quality-unknown -> current static defaults (never worse than today).
design: FILES: src/distributed/encoding.rs (derive_block_layout seam), src/distributed/distribution.rs (config plumb), src/transport/{aggregator,router}.rs (quality export), src/raptorq/decision_contract.rs (telemetry row). Policy table committed as data (const table or config) with the monotonicity property unit-tested (worse loss never decreases overhead). Galaxy-brain card: expected-completion-time model justifying the table breakpoints.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Lab matrix: {clean, 5%, 15% loss} x {low, high rtt} virtual paths -> adaptive layout beats static default on replica-ack completion time in the lossy cells and never regresses the clean cell (seeded, deterministic, numbers recorded). 2. Monotonicity property test on the policy table. 3. Telemetry row per adaptive decision (snapshot + chosen layout) asserted in tests; replay-deterministic. 4. Unknown-quality fallback test. 5. Docs: tuning guidance + the galaxy-brain card.
notes: AC2/AC3/AC4 PROVEN by a RUNNABLE focused integration test: tests/adaptive_block_layout_proof.rs (cargo test --test adaptive_block_layout_proof --features test-internals -> 5/5 PASS). Tests the EXISTING encoding.rs adaptive policy (derive_layout_decision + ADAPTIVE_BLOCK_LAYOUT_POLICY) through public StateEncoder API: AC4 unknown-quality->static fallback, AC3 adaptive telemetry carries the snapshot, AC2 repair symbols + multiplier monotone non-decreasing across loss 0..1000permille (the policy table's required property — VERIFIED monotone), lossy>=clean, determinism. This is the --test path that runs reliably (links lib WITHOUT cfg(test), avoids peer test-module WIP). REMAINING: AC1 lab loss x rtt completion-time matrix (needs lab harness) + AC5 docs/galaxy-brain card. NOTE: src/distributed/adaptive_layout.rs (shipped earlier this session) remains REDUNDANT vs encoding.rs — recommend consolidation/removal (needs file-deletion permission).

title: [RAPTORQ-X] Multipath symbol striping — spread symbols across paths with per-path repair
description:
WHY: MultipathAggregator handles intake (dedup/reorder/per-path stats) but recon found no SEND-side striping policy wired: large transfers (snapshots, ATP, F1 channels) should stripe symbols across available paths proportional to quality, and repair symbols should prefer the fastest-now path rather than re-sending on the original. Fountain codes make this trivially correct (any symbols work — path assignment is pure scheduling) which is exactly why it is our unfair advantage.

WHAT: (1) StripingPolicy on the send side: weighted round-robin over paths by PathQuality (F3's snapshot type), rebalancing each window; per-path inflight caps (queueing-theory informed defaults — coordinate with [CONTROL] H2 only as a note); (2) repair routing: repair requests (ATP repair coordinator) dispatch on argmax-quality path, decoupled from original assignment; (3) path failure mid-transfer: in-flight symbols on a dead path are simply re-scheduled on survivors (no retransmit protocol needed — encode more symbols if the loss budget demands; the fountain property doing real work); (4) per-path + aggregate telemetry surfaced (symbols sent/acked/lost per path, completion ETA).
design: FILES: src/transport/router.rs (striping policy on SymbolDispatcher), src/transport/aggregator.rs (consume), src/atp/repair_{coordinator,scheduler}.rs (repair routing), shared PathQuality from F3. Rebalance window + caps in config. Determinism: striping decisions pure functions of (snapshot, window-seq) for lab replay.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Lab multipath matrix: 3 virtual paths with asymmetric quality -> throughput beats single-best-path and naive equal-split (numbers recorded); path-death mid-transfer completes with zero protocol stall (the fountain headline — assert no retransmit round-trip in the trace). 2. Repair routing: degraded path's repairs observed on the fast path (trace assertion). 3. Inflight caps honored under pressure (telemetry assertion). 4. Determinism: seeded replay identical. 5. Telemetry fields documented + asserted. 6. Bench: striped vs single-path on the raptorq throughput bench harness, committed.
notes: DEPENDS on F3 (PathQuality type). RELATION: F1 channels plug in as transport users; ATP beads (existing ATP-D track) own disk-side concerns — this bead is network-side only, boundary documented.

title: [RAPTORQ-X] Epoch-gated symbol validity windows — fail-closed against stale-symbol mixing
description:
WHY: recon flagged the correctness hole class: long-delayed symbols from an earlier encode epoch arriving during a later one (same object identity, changed content — snapshot v2 decode poisoned by v1 symbols if ids collide, or wasteful if not). src/epoch.rs already provides monotone epochs with validity windows; symbols do not carry them.

WHAT: (1) extend symbol envelope with EpochRange {valid_from, valid_until} (versioned envelope change — coordinate with the wire-format-stability posture: pre-1.0, no compat shims, but version the header); (2) receiver/aggregator: out-of-window symbols rejected + counted (telemetry distinguishes stale vs foreign vs corrupt); (3) epoch transitions: distributor bumps epoch on re-encode of the same logical object; in-flight prior-epoch transfers either complete within their window or fail-closed with a typed error (never mix); (4) auth tags cover the epoch fields (no stripping attacks).
design: FILES: src/types/symbol envelope (recon: src/types/ symbol types), src/transport/aggregator.rs (gate), src/distributed/{distribution,encoding}.rs (epoch bump), src/security/authenticated.rs (tag coverage), src/epoch.rs (consume). Window semantics: closed-open [from, until); clock = logical epoch counter, NOT wall time (determinism).
acceptance_criteria: 1. Stale-mixing attack test: interleave v1+v2 symbols for one object id -> decode uses only in-window symbols, never mixes, types the failure when v2 lacks quorum (the poisoning scenario provably dead). 2. Auth-coverage test: epoch-field tamper rejected. 3. Window-expiry mid-transfer -> typed fail-closed error + clean obligation resolution. 4. Telemetry counters (stale/foreign/corrupt) asserted. 5. Envelope version bump documented; all symbol-path tests migrated. 6. Deterministic under lab.
notes: P3: correctness hardening whose triggering scenario needs long delays + re-encodes — real but not urgent until multipath/long-haul lanes (F4, DIST) are live. Sequence after F4. RELATION: G6 anti-entropy assumes epoch discipline.

title: raptorq DecodeProof::content_hash omits s/h/l (attestation collision)

title: RateLimit token refunds do not wake exhausted clones
description: RateLimit clones share one token bucket, but an exhausted clone registers only a deadline Sleep. When another clone drops an unused readiness reservation, or ReservedTokenGuard/ExistingReservationGuard refunds after inner Pending, Err, or panic, shared tokens can transition from zero to positive without waking the parked clone. It can therefore idle available capacity for the full configured period. Add a cancel-safe deduplicated shared waiter registry, atomically register while observing zero tokens, centralize refunds, detach and wake all waiters outside the mutex on zero-to-positive refunds, and retire per-handle registrations on acquisition/drop. Deterministic regression: A reserves the sole token, B parks at Time::ZERO with a counting/reentrant waker and a maximal period, drop A without advancing time, require a wake and immediate Ready on B. Independently confirmed by two read-only fresh-eye reviews 2026-07-15; existing dropping_clone test manually polls only after the drop, and the Sleep regression never exercises refunds.

title: [idea-wizard] RCH proof freshness broker for swarm agents
description:
Idea-wizard top-5 idea: make proof execution itself cancel-correct and operator-friendly. The current release work repeatedly hits fresh-heartbeat/stale-progress RCH builds, active-project exclusion, cold target directories, and ambiguous proof freshness. This bead designs and implements an explicit proof freshness broker so agents can queue, reuse, cancel, and cite RCH proofs without blocking each other or mistaking stale work for evidence.

Problem: proof lanes are currently coordinated by chat plus manual rch queue polling. That is fragile under many agents and one or more degraded workers. Agents need a deterministic receipt model that distinguishes fresh remote execution, stale heartbeat, canceled job, active-project exclusion, approved cache hit, zero-test filter, and local fallback refusal.

Required work:
1. Inventory existing proof_lane_manifest_v1, proof_status_snapshot_v1, RCH status fields, and Agent Mail coordination patterns.
2. Define a broker receipt schema with build id, command, git tree, dirty-tree caveats, worker id, heartbeat/progress timeline, local-fallback status, and proof claim scope.
3. Add deterministic tests that reject stale-progress receipts as proof and reject broad claims from narrow commands.
4. Add operator/agent runbook language for when to wait, when to cancel owned builds, and how not to cancel peer builds without handoff.
5. Keep this separate from the fourth-wave governor implementation; it is proof ergonomics, not runtime admission control.

Acceptance: a versioned artifact and contract tests exist; RCH-backed proof demonstrates the broker rejects stale or local-fallback evidence; Agent Mail closeout templates cite receipts precisely; no claim implies broad workspace health unless the manifest lane covers it.

title: [reality-check][conformance] Make live registry counts and dormant-suite disposition self-checking
description:
Fix the conformance-suite truth gap and make the registry self-checking.

Evidence from the reality check:
README.md says the live registry wires 61 `pub mod` suites. The live file `tests/conformance/mod.rs` currently has 63 active `pub mod` entries and 21 dormant/commented `// pub mod` entries. The dormant lanes include broader HTTP/1 siblings, `sqlite_prepared_statements`, `websocket_rfc6455`, old gRPC health/status/deadline paths, H3 settings, QUIC initial, trace event, UDP/Unix listener, and other bit-rotted modules. Some dormant modules have explicit comments explaining API drift. The README limitation language is directionally honest about partial coverage, but the specific count and proof posture are stale.

Scope:
Create a durable source-of-truth mechanism for conformance registry counts and dormant-suite disposition. Prefer a small test or script that reads `tests/conformance/mod.rs` and asserts the README/support matrix either matches the live count or avoids hardcoded counts entirely. Classify every dormant conformance suite as one of: rewire now, superseded by a named live suite, intentionally deferred with a bead, or obsolete but retained because file deletion is forbidden. Do not remove dormant files without explicit user permission.

Acceptance criteria:
- README no longer contains stale live-suite counts, or the count is generated/checked against `tests/conformance/mod.rs`.
- A machine-checkable artifact or test records active module count, dormant count, and each dormant suite's disposition.
- Every dormant suite has a clear owner bead or a documented supersession path.
- `rch exec -- cargo check --test conformance` passes or any unrelated blocker is captured exactly.
- If docs are changed, include a narrow doc truth test so future count drift is caught.

Non-goals:
Do not try to fix every dormant suite in this bead. This bead creates truthful registry governance and fans out implementation work. Broader WebSocket RFC6455 closure is handled separately by `asupersync-rckwsf`.
design:
Implementation design:
Create a small conformance-registry truth source that is derived from `tests/conformance/mod.rs` instead of copied by hand. The preferred shape is a checked manifest or test helper that classifies active `pub mod` suites and dormant `// pub mod` suites, then validates any README/support-matrix count or removes hardcoded counts entirely. Dormant suites should be classified as rewire-now, superseded, intentionally deferred with a bead, or obsolete-retained because file deletion is forbidden.

User-facing optimization:
A user should never see a stale suite count or infer that commented conformance modules are active. The docs should say what is live, what is dormant, and why, without forcing users to read the registry file.

Test and logging design:
Add unit coverage for the parser/classifier, including blank lines, commented modules, real modules, duplicate names, and malformed classification rows. Add an e2e/script proof that scans the live registry and docs, emits deterministic lines for active_count, dormant_count, each dormant disposition, doc_count_source, and verdict, and fails with the first mismatched module/count.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance criteria:
- Active and dormant conformance module counts are derived from the live registry or hardcoded public counts are removed.
- Every dormant suite has a disposition: rewire-now, superseded-by-live-suite, deferred-with-bead, or obsolete-retained-no-delete.
- Unit tests cover registry parsing, dormant classification, duplicate/malformed entries, and doc-count matching or count-removal behavior.
- An e2e/script proof logs bead_id, registry_path, active_count, dormant_count, every dormant suite disposition, docs_checked, verdict, and first_failure.
- README/support matrices cannot drift silently from `tests/conformance/mod.rs`.
- `rch exec -- cargo check --test conformance` passes or an unrelated blocker is captured exactly.

title: [reality-check] Close README/live-code release-readiness gaps
description:
Umbrella epic for closing the gap between the public project narrative and the live code/proof surface found in the 2026-05-04 reality check.

Background and evidence:
The audit read AGENTS.md and README.md end to end, then inspected Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, core runtime modules, tests/conformance/mod.rs, docs/integration.md, docs/WASM.md, formal/, the Cargo feature graphs, and the active Beads backlog. The core runtime is real and substantial: Cx/Scope, region-owned task spawning, task/region/obligation records, the three-lane scheduler, two-phase channels, LabRuntime, trace/DPOR/TLA export, HTTP/TLS/DB/RaptorQ/browser surfaces, and policy-gate workflows all exist. The remaining problem is not that the project is fake; it is that several README-visible claims are broader than the live implementation/proof posture.

Ground truth to preserve:
- Default production asupersync has no normal-edge Tokio dependency: `rch exec -- cargo tree -e normal -p asupersync -i tokio` printed `warning: nothing to print.`
- Full workspace/features graphs still show Tokio through documented compat/conformance/dev/test/OTel paths.
- `rch exec -- cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features test-internals` reached Cargo exit 0 with warnings.
- `rch exec -- cargo check --test conformance` reached Cargo exit 0 with warnings.
- tests/conformance/mod.rs has 63 live `pub mod` suites and 21 dormant/commented suites; README currently says 61 live suites.
- src/remote.rs is a real transport-agnostic protocol/state-machine module, but it explicitly does not embed a production network backend.
- Browser main-thread and dedicated-worker lanes are shipped; service/shared worker direct runtime and public browser-native messaging APIs are not.
- HTTP/3/QPACK, broader WebSocket RFC6455 conformance, Lean mechanization, placeholder conformance bins, and Phase 6 main-only enforcement all need closure work.

Execution contract:
Every child bead must reserve files before editing, work only on main, use `rch exec --` for Rust validation, avoid deleting files, and update docs only after source/test truth is verified. If a surface is intentionally deferred, close it truthfully with a support-matrix downgrade and a durable follow-up bead rather than pretending it shipped.

Done criteria:
This epic is closable only when every child gap bead is closed or deliberately superseded by a narrower bead, README/docs/support matrices agree with live source and proof artifacts, and the final signoff artifact enumerates each gap, commits, proof commands, and residual risks.
design:
Program design:
Treat this epic as a release-readiness correction program, not a one-patch cleanup. The optimal order is: first make the conformance registry self-checking, then close or bound each technical support lane, then reconcile public docs, then publish the final proof pack. This preserves the current strong core-runtime truth while preventing adapters, formal proofs, and browser/remote lanes from being overstated.

The user-facing optimization is to produce support classes that downstream adopters can trust without reading the source: shipped, guarded, preview, virtual/lab proof, substrate-only, deferred, or unsupported. Every child bead should either promote a lane with source plus proof, or make the limitation explicit with stable diagnostics and a follow-up bead. Do not collapse large protocol work into prose-only downgrades if the existing architecture is close enough to ship the feature correctly.

Testing strategy:
Every child bead must include local unit tests for its core invariant, plus at least one integration/e2e or script-level proof for user-visible behavior. E2E proof logs must be deterministic and grep-friendly, with bead id, scenario id, support class, command, artifact path, expected behavior, actual behavior, verdict, and first failure line.
acceptance_criteria:
Epic-level acceptance criteria:
- Every child bead records the live files, docs, support matrices, and proof artifacts it inspected before editing or closing.
- Every child bead preserves existing features unless live source proves a feature is unshipped and docs are explicitly narrowed with stable diagnostics or a linked owner bead.
- Every child bead includes unit tests for local invariants and at least one e2e/script/integration proof when users can observe the behavior.
- E2E/script proofs emit deterministic logs with bead_id, scenario_id, support_class, command, artifact_path, expected behavior, actual behavior, verdict, and first_failure line.
- README and support matrices do not broaden claims beyond source plus proof artifacts; closed tracker status alone is never enough evidence for public docs.
- asupersync-rckdoc runs only after technical beads settle source truth and must verify stale-closed technical beads against actual artifacts/commands.
- asupersync-rcksgn runs last and refuses closure unless every gap is implemented, truthfully downgraded, or explicitly deferred with a live bead and durable evidence.
- Final closeout records br and bv graph health, including exact degraded-tool output if graph checks cannot run, and records any DB-only/JSONL-flush-skipped bead operations as control-plane residual risk.

title: [reality-check][formal] Promote Lean/TLA coverage from scaffold to checked proof posture
description:
Promote the formal-methods story from scaffold/coverage artifacts to a checked mechanization posture, or narrow the README wording to match the live proof state.

Evidence from the reality check:
README says the runtime design is backed by small-step operational semantics and an accompanying Lean mechanization scaffold. formal/ contains TLA+ specs and TLC outputs, formal/lean/Asupersync.lean, lake files, theorem inventories, coverage matrices, proof-impact reports, and CI profile artifacts. The artifacts are meaningful, but the README limitations table still says Lean mechanization remains scaffold/in progress.

Scope:
Inspect formal/README.md, formal/impl_refinement_map.md, formal/lean/Asupersync.lean, formal/lean/coverage/*.json, and existing Lean-related tests. Define the exact promotion bar for Lean coverage: what theorem families are checked, what invariants are linked to runtime tests, what remains modeled only in TLA/lab tests, and what is still assumption-bound. Then implement the next closure step: either add checked Lean proofs/build wiring for the core invariants, or update docs and coverage artifacts so the partial state is impossible to misread as full mechanized verification.

Acceptance criteria:
- `lake build` or the repo's documented Lean check command is run and recorded if Lean files are touched.
- Coverage artifacts map at least structured concurrency, no orphan tasks, no obligation leaks, cancellation finalization, and no ambient authority to theorem/test evidence or explicit gaps.
- Any `sorry`, `admit`, assumption, or scaffold marker is inventoried with a bead or doc-bound explanation.
- Runtime-facing docs state the exact proof tier: TLA checked, Lean checked, coverage-planned, lab-oracle backed, or unproved.
- Add/update Rust tests that validate formal coverage artifacts if those artifacts change.

Non-goals:
Do not claim formal proof of the full runtime unless every advertised invariant has a checked artifact and a runtime refinement mapping.
design:
Implementation design:
Define proof tiers before changing claims: TLA checked, Lean checked, coverage-planned, lab-oracle backed, assumption-bound, or unproved. Map structured concurrency, no orphan tasks, no obligation leaks, cancellation finalization, no ambient authority, loser drain, and region close/quiescence to concrete formal artifacts, runtime refinement mappings, or explicit gaps. Promote Lean only where `lake build` proves the theorem family without `sorry`/`admit` leakage.

User-facing optimization:
Formal-methods language should let users distinguish real checked proof from scaffolding and coverage planning. The project should not sound less rigorous; it should be more precise about which invariant has which evidence.

Test and logging design:
Unit/Rust tests should validate any coverage artifact schema and ensure advertised invariant names match known proof/test evidence rows. Lean checks should be recorded if Lean files change. E2E/script proof should emit a proof coverage report with theorem family, artifact path, proof tier, assumptions, linked runtime tests, and first missing evidence row.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance criteria:
- Formal coverage maps structured concurrency, no orphan tasks, no obligation leaks, cancellation finalization, no ambient authority, loser drain, and region close/quiescence to theorem/test evidence or explicit gaps.
- Unit/Rust tests validate coverage artifact schema, invariant names, proof tiers, and missing-evidence behavior if artifacts change.
- `lake build` or the documented Lean check command is run and recorded if Lean files are touched.
- Every `sorry`, `admit`, assumption, scaffold marker, or coverage-planned row is inventoried with a bead or doc-bound explanation.
- E2E/proof script logs bead_id, invariant_id, proof_tier, artifact_path, linked_runtime_test, verdict, and first_failure.
- Runtime-facing docs state the exact proof tier and do not imply full mechanized proof unless every advertised invariant has checked evidence.

title: [reality-check][phase6] Make methodology gates match main-only workflow
description:
Align Phase 6 policy-gate enforcement with the repository's main-only, no-PR/no-branch workflow.

Evidence from the reality check:
README says Phase 6 methodology gates are live on pull_request events targeting main, with no advisory-only gates. `.github/workflows/methodology-gates.yml` is indeed PR-triggered and enforces baseline benchmarks, flamegraph, golden checksums, proof notes, and summary comments. AGENTS.md, however, forbids branches, worktrees, and pull-request workflows for this project; agents commit directly to main and mirror main to master. That makes a PR-only enforcement story incomplete for the actual workflow.

Scope:
Decide how Phase 6 gates should operate in a main-only repo. Options include adding push-on-main equivalents, adding a local `rch`-backed gate script agents can run before commit, moving PR-specific wording out of README, or creating an explicit exception that these GitHub gates are external/release-only while local agents use another proof pack. The chosen solution must not create branches or require pull requests.

Acceptance criteria:
- README Phase 6 text matches the actual enforcement mechanism for direct main commits.
- If push-on-main gates are added, they do not require PR-only variables and handle missing PR numbers without false failures.
- If local gates are added instead, document exact `rch exec --` commands and artifact locations.
- At least one test or shellcheck-style validation proves the workflow/script still parses after changes.
- The final signoff artifact records whether gates are PR-only, push-enforced, local-enforced, or intentionally release-only.

Non-goals:
Do not weaken the methodology. The closure should make enforcement real for the current workflow, not remove gates because PR assumptions are inconvenient.
design:
Implementation design:
Make Phase 6 enforcement fit the actual main-only workflow. Inspect the GitHub methodology gate workflow, local validation scripts, README claims, and AGENTS branch prohibitions. Choose an enforcement model that does not require feature branches or PRs: push-on-main gates, local `rch`-backed gate script, release-only gate language, or a documented hybrid. Preserve the gate substance: benchmarks, flamegraph/profiling evidence, golden checksums, proof notes, and summary artifacts.

User-facing optimization:
Agents and maintainers should know the exact command path that enforces methodology before or after direct main commits. Public docs should not tell users the project has live PR enforcement as the primary gate when the repo forbids PR workflows.

Test and logging design:
Unit/static tests should validate workflow/script parsing and missing-PR-variable behavior. E2E/script proof should run the gate in a local dry-run or parse-only mode and log every required artifact check with deterministic verdicts.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance criteria:
- README Phase 6 text matches actual enforcement for direct main commits.
- If push-on-main gates are added, workflow logic handles missing PR numbers and push event context without false failures.
- If local gates are added, docs name exact `rch exec --` commands and artifact locations.
- Unit/static tests cover workflow parsing, push-context behavior, required artifact detection, and missing optional artifacts.
- E2E/script proof logs bead_id, gate_mode, event_kind, command, checked_artifacts, missing_required_artifacts, verdict, and first_failure.
- Final signoff records whether gates are PR-only, push-enforced, local-enforced, hybrid, or intentionally release-only.

title: [reality-check][http3] Close or truthfully bound HTTP/3 full-QPACK parity
description:
Close the HTTP/3/QPACK support gap by either implementing full advertised behavior or narrowing docs to the verified static-only lane.

Evidence from the reality check:
README.md lists QUIC + HTTP/3 as feature-gated and active, but the limitations table says HTTP/3 is partial and QPACK is static-only: dynamic table and Huffman encoding are not supported. The codebase contains HTTP/3 and QPACK-related surfaces, but the public claim must not imply h3/quinn parity unless dynamic table/Huffman/QPACK stream behavior is implemented and tested.

Scope:
Inspect `src/http/h3_native.rs`, `src/http/h3/`, any QPACK/HPACK modules, `tests/conformance/h3_rfc9114.rs`, docs/tokio_quic_h3_* matrices, and README support tables. Decide from live code whether closure means implementing dynamic table/Huffman/QPACK stream support, adding a hard fail-closed static-only guard, or rewriting docs to say the static-only profile is the intended support boundary. Prefer implementation if the existing architecture is close; prefer truthful downgrade if full QPACK would be a large protocol project.

Acceptance criteria:
- A live test matrix names the exact HTTP/3/QPACK features supported: SETTINGS/control streams, DATAGRAM/Extended CONNECT if applicable, static table, dynamic table, Huffman, encoder/decoder streams, blocked streams, and error handling.
- If full QPACK is implemented, add RFC-backed encode/decode vectors and stateful dynamic-table tests.
- If full QPACK is deferred, README and docs/integration.md state static-only support prominently and link to a follow-up implementation bead.
- `rch exec -- cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features http3,test-internals` or the narrow current equivalent is run and recorded.
- Any conformance test changes also pass `rch exec -- cargo check --test conformance`.

Non-goals:
Do not pretend static-only QPACK is full HTTP/3 parity. Do not add new protocol dependencies that drag in Tokio to the core runtime graph.
design:
Implementation design:
Split the HTTP/3/QPACK decision into a proof-backed support matrix before editing protocol code. Inspect the native h3 and QPACK modules, current conformance tests, and docs. If the existing architecture can support full QPACK in a bounded slice, implement dynamic table, Huffman, encoder/decoder stream, blocked-stream, and error-state behavior with RFC vectors. If not, make the static-only profile explicit, fail closed for unsupported dynamic features, and create a follow-up implementation bead.

User-facing optimization:
Applications must not infer full HTTP/3 parity from feature-gated presence. The support class should be exact enough for a user to decide whether they can deploy with static-only QPACK, whether dynamic table/Huffman are supported, and what error they get when they use unsupported behavior.

Test and logging design:
Unit tests should cover static table, dynamic table state if implemented, Huffman vectors if implemented, unsupported dynamic/Huffman fail-closed paths, stream ordering, blocked-stream limits, SETTINGS/control stream handling, and protocol error mapping. E2E/script proof should run a named h3/QPACK matrix and emit per-feature support plus proof command results.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance criteria:
- A live support matrix names SETTINGS/control streams, static table, dynamic table, Huffman, encoder/decoder streams, blocked streams, DATAGRAM/Extended CONNECT if applicable, and error handling.
- Unit tests cover every supported QPACK feature and every intentionally unsupported fail-closed path.
- If full QPACK is implemented, RFC-backed encode/decode vectors and stateful dynamic-table tests pass.
- If full QPACK is deferred, README and docs/integration.md prominently state static-only support and link to a follow-up bead.
- E2E/script logs include bead_id, scenario_id, feature, support_class, command, artifact_path, verdict, and first_failure.
- Run `rch exec -- cargo check -p asupersync --lib --features http3,test-internals` or the current narrow equivalent, plus conformance checks if touched.

title: [reality-check][remote] Add transport-backed remote lifecycle proof or narrow support claims
description:
Turn the remote/distributed runtime story from transport-agnostic contract into a proven transport-backed lifecycle, or narrow the public wording so users do not infer production distributed execution is shipped.

Evidence from the reality check:
`src/remote.rs` is substantial: it defines RemoteCap, RemoteRuntime, RemoteTransport, spawn/ack/cancel/result/lease messages, idempotency, lease renewal/expiry, protocol state machines, trace events, and deterministic Phase-0 fallback. The module docs explicitly say the core crate does not embed a production network backend and that transport is injected through RemoteRuntime/RemoteTransport. README and docs/integration.md describe distributed runtime primitives and remote named computations, but the support posture needs a concrete lifecycle proof.

Scope:
Add the first end-to-end remote lifecycle proof using an existing transport substrate or a lab virtual RemoteTransport that exercises the same state machine as a real backend. The proof must include successful spawn, accepted ack, result delivery, cancellation before ack, cancellation while running, lease renewal, lease expiry, duplicate/idempotent spawn handling, transport send failure cleanup, and region-close/quiescence obligations. If a production transport is not appropriate yet, update docs so the support level is explicitly protocol/state-machine plus virtual harness, not production network execution.

Acceptance criteria:
- A live integration or lab test drives `spawn_remote` through RemoteRuntime/RemoteTransport rather than only unit-testing structs.
- The test asserts no orphan remote handles, no unresolved lease obligations, deterministic fallback behavior, idempotent duplicate handling, and trace event emission.
- Docs/integration.md clearly distinguishes protocol contract, virtual/lab proof, and production transport support.
- `rch exec -- cargo test -p asupersync remote --features test-internals -- --nocapture` or a narrower named remote test command passes.
- If a real transport adapter is added, it is capability-gated and does not introduce ambient authority or Tokio into the core graph.

Non-goals:
Do not ship closure serialization or arbitrary remote code execution. Remote computations must remain named/capability-gated per `src/remote.rs`.
design:
Implementation design:
Build the first transport-backed remote lifecycle proof at the `RemoteRuntime`/`RemoteTransport` seam, not below it. Prefer a deterministic lab/virtual transport that exercises the same protocol state machine as a future network backend, unless a production adapter already exists and can be used without ambient authority. The lifecycle should cover spawn, ack, result, cancel-before-ack, cancel-while-running, lease renewal, lease expiry, duplicate/idempotent spawn, send failure cleanup, trace events, and region-close quiescence.

User-facing optimization:
Remote support should read as a concrete support tier: protocol/state-machine plus virtual/lab proof, or production transport-backed execution. Users must not infer arbitrary remote code execution or an embedded production network backend from the docs.

Test and logging design:
Unit tests should cover idempotency keys, lease state transitions, cancellation states, failure cleanup, trace event generation, and obligation finalization. E2E/lab script should run deterministic named scenarios and log remote handle counts, lease obligations, trace events, transport events, expected state, actual state, and first failure.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance criteria:
- A live integration or lab test drives `spawn_remote` through `RemoteRuntime` and `RemoteTransport` rather than only testing structs.
- Unit tests cover idempotent duplicate handling, lease renewal/expiry, cancellation states, send failure cleanup, and no orphan handles/obligations.
- E2E/lab proof covers success, cancel-before-ack, cancel-while-running, duplicate spawn, lease expiry, send failure, and region-close/quiescence scenarios.
- E2E logs include bead_id, scenario_id, transport_kind, expected_state, actual_state, trace_event_count, obligation_count, verdict, and first_failure.
- Docs distinguish protocol contract, virtual/lab proof, and production transport support.
- Run `rch exec -- cargo test -p asupersync remote --features test-internals -- --nocapture` or a narrower named remote proof command.

Required gap rows:

- Broad WebSocket RFC6455 conformance.
- HTTP/3/QPACK support boundary.
- Remote transport-backed lifecycle proof.
- Browser service/shared worker and messaging support boundary.
- Lean/TLA formal proof posture.
- Optional metrics/fuzz Tokio dependency boundary.
- Placeholder/stub conformance and product surfaces.
- Phase 6 enforcement under main-only workflow.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every dependency of this bead is closed.
- The signoff artifact has a stable schema version and is checked by a Rust test or jq contract.

design:
Implementation design:
Create the final proof pack only after every dependency is closed. The artifact should be schema-versioned and durable enough for operators to audit the reality-check closure without replaying the whole session. It must enumerate every gap, closing bead, commit hash, touched files, proof commands, artifacts, support posture, residual risk, and any control-plane degradation encountered during planning or implementation.

User-facing optimization:
The signoff should make release-readiness legible: what became shipped, what became guarded/preview, what remains deferred, and which evidence proves each claim. It should refuse closure rather than hide unresolved gaps in prose.

Test and logging design:
Add a Rust or jq contract test that validates artifact schema, required gap rows, dependency closure, command result fields, support classes, and residual-risk fields. Add an e2e/signoff script that regenerates or verifies the proof pack and logs exact graph/proof health.

title: [reality-check][stubs] Classify and close placeholder conformance/product surfaces
description:
Eliminate misleading placeholder/stub surfaces that survived outside the existing stub-resolution ratchet.

Evidence from the reality check:
A targeted marker scan found real placeholder/TODO clusters in conformance and product-adjacent surfaces, including OTel conformance bins with TODO replacement notes, raptorq RFC6330 fixture maintenance placeholder output, HPACK differential placeholder results, and at least one gRPC streaming path returning `Status::unimplemented("feature not yet implemented")`. Many test mocks are legitimate harnesses; this bead is not a blanket ban on mocks. The issue is unclassified placeholder behavior that can be mistaken for shipped support.

Scope:
Run a fresh marker scan over src/, tests/, and conformance/ for TODO/FIXME/stub/placeholder/unimplemented markers. Classify each hit as legitimate test harness, documented deferred surface, product bug, obsolete scaffold retained because deletion is forbidden, or implementation task. title: [memory-ordering-cross-atomic] runtime/scheduler/worker.rs Parker: Release on notified does not pair with Acquire on waiting — lost wakeup window
description:
src/runtime/scheduler/worker.rs:860-940 — the Parker's `waiting` counter and `notified` flag lack proper cross-atomic synchronization.

  Line 860: park() does `waiting.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Release)`.
  Line 929: unpark() does `notified.compare_exchange(false -> true, Release, Relaxed)`.
  Line 940: unpark() does `waiting.load(Ordering::Acquire)`.

The Release on `notified` does NOT synchronize-with the Acquire on `waiting` — they are independent atomics. A Release on atomic A and an Acquire on atomic B do not establish happens-before; only an Acquire that pairs with a Release on the SAME atomic does.

Race window:
  T0 — park() increments `waiting` to 1 (Release).
  T1 — unpark() executes the CAS on `notified` (Release).
  T2 — unpark() reads `waiting` with Acquire and observes 0 (stale!) because the Release on `notified` did not flush the Release on `waiting`.
  T3 — unpark() takes the no-waiter branch and skips the mutex+condvar signal.
  T4 — park() goes to sleep on the condvar; the permit was published but no signal was sent — lost wakeup.

Concrete failure modes:
  (a) Worker thread misses runnable tasks and sleeps until park_timeout fires — 25ms latency spike.
  (b) Under load, finalizer tasks never get polled because the worker that should pick them up is parked.
  (c) Lab oracles that watch worker progress flake intermittently.

The scheduler's Relaxed loads in the backoff loop (worker.rs lines around 150 and 218) compound the problem: those loads provide no ordering, so the parker's Release-Acquire pairing is the entire happens-before edge — and that edge is broken.

Fix direction:
  1. Promote line 940 to `waiting.load(Ordering::SeqCst)` — SeqCst loads on independent atomics participate in a single total order.
  2. Or: use a single atomic that encodes both `waiting` and `notified` (pack into u64 with two halves) so the Release-Acquire pair is on the SAME atomic.
  3. Or: insert a SeqCst fence between the CAS and the load so the load can use plain Acquire.
  4. Add a Loom regression test (loom-tests feature) that drives concurrent park/unpark and asserts no lost wakeup.

Severity HIGH because (a) reachable from the production runtime hot path, (b) the failure mode is silent latency or hang (not a panic), and (c) the same issue is the textbook example of "Release/Acquire on different atomics doesn't pair".

Source: /reality-check on src/runtime/scheduler/* + src/runtime/state.rs deepest 10th-pass (2026-04-26).
close_reason: fixed via Dekker-style SeqCst fences; stress test added

description:
Read-only audit of src/runtime/reactor (epoll backend, token/interest layer) and how I/O types register with it, at origin/main 4ef260a14 (SapphireHill audit agent, 10-04). The epoll backend and the shared token/driver layer are SOUND; the defects are in how some I/O types use them. SapphireHill re-read MEDIUM 1 in the code.

## MEDIUM
1. 33 or more concurrent waiters cause a permanent wake cycle (CPU spin while idle): src/net/tcp/listener.rs 73-85, src/net/unix/listener.rs 57-67 and the waiter list in src/net/udp.rs 1748-1760 (used by UnixStream's &self ancillary methods, unix/stream.rs 480, 549). When the list already holds 32 wakers, register() removes the oldest and wakes it; with 33 tasks awaiting accept() on one listener the 33rd evicts task 1, task 1 re-polls, hits WouldBlock and evicts task 2, forever, each step also doing an epoll_ctl MOD and an eventfd write; after 64 rapid WouldBlocks the storm backoff (listener.rs 227, 256-265) adds a timer that wakes the whole list on every poll. Fix: per-future waiter identity (a dropped future removes its own entry) instead of evicting live waiters.

## LOW
2. Process pipes close their fd before removing it from epoll: ChildStdin/ChildStdout/ChildStderr (src/process.rs 3211-3214, 3371-3375, 3471-3475) declare inner before registration with no Drop impl, so the fd closes before IoRegistration::drop deregisters it; another thread can get the same fd number and register it, hitting epoll.rs 353-358 ("fd already registered"), and an unrelated socket's first I/O fails with AlreadyExists. Fix: declare registration first, as TcpStream/UdpSocket/Unix types do. (process.rs has unsafe-ledger line locators: keep the swap line-neutral.)
3. One panicking waker strands the rest of its batch: io_driver.rs 792-794 fires wakers in a plain loop after the one-shot registrations fired and the pending-interest record is cleared (466); wakers after a panicking one are dropped unwoken and their tasks hang. Fix: wake each under catch_unwind and re-raise after the loop.
4. A fallback-driver startup failure is cached for the life of the process (udp.rs 1533-1578, OnceLock<Option<...>> stores None on a transient create_reactor/thread-spawn failure), so driverless polls self-wake forever (the GH#67 hot loop). Fix: do not memoize the failure; retry with backoff.
5. Sharing one reactor between runtimes (Builder::with_reactor, builder.rs 3493, 5858) gives each runtime its own token table over the same epoll starting at the same tokens: colliding registrations fail AlreadyExists, and either leader can collect the other's one-shot events, find no token and drop them (owner hangs). Fix: reject a reactor already attached to a driver, or partition token ranges.

## Performance only
wait_for_connect (tcp/stream.rs 996) schedules a 1 ms self-wake even after a successful WRITABLE registration; every register/re-arm wakes the reactor (io_driver.rs 661, 940); waker collection dedups tokens with a linear scan (O(n^2) per turn).

## Checked and sound
One-shot epoll by default, syscall-then-MOD ordering (kernel re-checks readiness), no cached readiness; MOD and waker-slot update under the driver lock; union-of-directions arming for single-owner sockets, per-direction generation-tagged waiters for split halves; token generations reject stale tokens in both epoll bookkeeping and the token table; interest changes vs epoll_wait under one mutex with consistent lock order; ERR/HUP fold into both directions; ENOENT/changed file identity cleanup; EINTR retried; eventfd coalescing; shutdown with weak driver refs; TcpStream/UdpSocket/Unix types/listeners deregister before closing.
close_reason: done

title: README API reference drift: Cx::mask()->MaskGuard doesn't exist, OnceCell example doesn't compile, Pool per-thread caches gone, receive_once network-I/O nuance
description:
Discovered during the 2026-08-13 asupersync-mega-skill refresh + adversarial verification pass (SapphireHill). Grab-bag of README reference-section drift at HEAD 91c7da69f; every item verified against source. Individually small, but two sit in the most-copied tables ("Coming from tokio?", Core Types Reference).

1. README:699 — Core Types Reference shows `pub fn mask(&self) -> MaskGuard;  // Defer cancellation` on Cx. No public `Cx::mask()` and no public `MaskGuard` exist at HEAD; the live public mask surface is `Cx::masked<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> R` taking a synchronous closure (src/cx/cx.rs:2761-2764). The only MaskGuard-like type is the private AsyncMaskGuard in src/gen_server.rs:151. Fix the signature row to `masked`.

2. README:109 — "Coming from tokio?" OnceCell row shows `cell.get_or_init(async { ... }).await`, which does not compile: the signature is `get_or_init<F, Fut>(f: F) where F: FnOnce() -> Fut` (src/sync/once_cell.rs:385-388), so it must be `cell.get_or_init(|| async { ... }).await`. This is a copy-paste-broken example in the most-read migration table.

3. README:1017 — sync table row "Pool | src/sync/pool.rs | Object pool with per-thread caches". Pool has no per-thread caches at HEAD: the module is GenericPool/PoolConfig with obligation-based return semantics (PooledResource returns on drop or return_to_pool()); the only thread_local is cfg(test), and pool.rs:655-665 notes Send is auto-derived with no manual unsafe impl. Reword the row (e.g. "Object pool with obligation-tracked checkout/return").

4. README:1064 — e880xo REALITY paragraph: "`send_path`/`receive_once` refuse to run (before any network I/O)". Precisely true only for send_path (posture check before any socket work; contract test default_config_sender_fails_closed_before_any_network_io). receive_once accepts the TCP control connection first (src/net/atp/transport_rq/mod.rs:10062-10077) and rejects in receive_connection (:10127) — before any handshake, UDP, or data transfer, but after one accept(). Suggested wording: "send_path refuses before any network I/O; receive_once rejects the connection before any handshake or data transfer."

ACCEPTANCE:
- Four rows/sentences corrected; docs-only change, no runtime surface touched.
- Item 2's snippet compiles as written (ideally cover the corrected form with a doctest or point at an existing compiled example).
- Quick sweep for siblings: grep README for other signature-style rows in the Core Types section and spot-check each against src/cx/cx.rs before closing.
