Hello symbol_size must equal the receiver's own and be non-zero, max_block_size symbol-aligned and <= 32 MiB before adoption, manifest total within max_transfer_bytes, set_object_params failure fatal, datagram lengths checked. The one peer-sized allocation (source stream Vec::with_capacity(entry.size), 8466) is capped by max_transfer_bytes.
- transport_rq/adaptive.rs: SOUND (sender-side math, counters only).
- sdk/bonded.rs, udp/mod.rs: SOUND (no frame parsing).
- transport_rq/bonded.rs receiver: SOUND against unauthenticated donors (donor hello must match the descriptor; shared datagram parser, auth before insert, bounded retention 2K+64 per block). It builds decoders through new_udp_entry_decode_state, so it inherits the source_block_progress_for K check from the Hello-geometry fix, not the Hello/entry/budget refusals.
- MEDIUM-1, FIXED in this session's stack (R48): the bonded DONOR sized its work from a receiver NeedMore window: schedule_bonded_repair_continuation reserved Vec::with_capacity(end - start) (up to ~17 GiB of u32) and filled it, one emission and one encoder per ESI. The bonded control plane is plaintext JSON, so the receiver the donor connected to or anyone on the path could abort the donor with one frame. SapphireHill (rc_20260923) 2026-10-05: read-only audit round 9 (RaptorQ decode from untrusted input, origin 66d50abcc, re-checked at 3d43b3fe9 on 10-06; /data/tmp/rc_20260923/audit_r9_raptorq.md) found HIGH 2's pattern on the QUIC transport, which this bead's 10-03 census had called sound for allocations:
- transport_quic/mod.rs block_repair_requests_with_accounting (~6807) and quic_pending_decode_progress (~3902), driven once each per feedback round (from native_link.rs and from mod.rs ~10647/~10659), call pipeline.block_status(sbn) for every pending block. block_status runs block_rank_status (decoding.rs ~1370): the full (S+H+K')xL constraint matrix plus a dense elimination. With the adopted 32 MiB max_block_size and 1144-byte symbols, K' is about 29k: roughly 0.9 GB and 10^13 GF operations per call, twice per incomplete block per round, for up to max_feedback_rounds (1024). The atpd QUIC listener accepts unauthenticated clients (with_no_client_auth; transport auth leaves per-symbol HMAC off), so this is a CPU/memory amplification.
- Not a mechanical swap like 63934ff84: both sites use the rank. Repair requests are sized by status.rank_deficit (falling back to needed - received), and progress reports publish the rank. Proposed: use block_symbols_received while received < needed (the rank deficit then equals the count deficit except for dependent symbols); run the rank analysis only for blocks with received >= needed that are not decoded, cache it per block keyed on the received count so a feedback round without new symbols reuses it, and build only the S+H rows the rank needs. Optionally a receiver-side K cap below 32 MiB blocks. Needs ATP end-to-end receipts (repair-round counts and transfer times before/after) under the bench integrity rules, so I have not changed it.
- MEDIUM, new: one wrong-payload repair symbol with an in-range ESI wedges a block for good. A failed solve (CorruptDecodedOutput / inconsistent row -> MatrixInversionFailed -> Retry) restores the bad symbol (decoding.rs ~303-309, ~1264, ~1321), so every later arrival re-runs the same failing solve and a block that needs FEC never recovers. Availability only: SHA-256 + Merkle still refuse a bad commit. 604f81b64 fixed only the out-of-range-ESI variant. Fix: cap consecutive failed solves and evict repair symbols, or map corrupt/inconsistent outcomes to Failed instead of Retry-and-restore.

title: Unit and integration tests for Separation Logic specifications and proofs
description:
Comprehensive test suite for the Separation Logic proof infrastructure (specifications in bd-1xwvk.1, no-aliasing proof in bd-1xwvk.2, no-leak proof in bd-1xwvk.3).

BACKGROUND: While the formal proofs are verified by the proof tool (Creusot/Verus), we need a complementary runtime test suite that: (1) validates the proof assumptions hold in practice, (2) provides defense-in-depth with dynamic checking, (3) catches regressions when the implementation changes, and (4) verifies the proof tool integration with CI.

UNIT TESTS:
(1) Proof tool integration: verify cargo creusot (or verus) runs successfully on all annotated files and produces a verified result. This is a CI gate -- any proof regression fails the build.
(2) Ghost state consistency: add debug-mode runtime checks that mirror the ghost state in proofs. For each obligation lifecycle (create, transfer, release), verify the runtime ghost counter matches expected values.
(3) Specification coverage: for each formal specification in bd-1xwvk.1, write a runtime test that exercises the specified behavior and verifies the pre/post conditions hold dynamically.
(4) No-aliasing dynamic check: use a global debug-mode registry of outstanding permits. On create, insert. On transfer, move entry. On release, remove. At any point, assert each permit has exactly one owner. Test with 100 concurrent permit lifecycles.
(5) No-leak dynamic check: at region quiescence, assert the obligation counter for that region is zero. Test with 50 regions, each spawning 10 tasks with random obligations.
(6) Cancellation path coverage: verify Drop runs on all cancellation severities (Ok, Err, Cancelled, Panicked) and releases obligations correctly.
(7) Mutation testing: introduce known-bad mutations (clone a permit, skip release on one path) and verify either the proof tool rejects or the runtime check catches the violation.

INTEGRATION TESTS:
(8) Full obligation lifecycle under FrankenLab: run all obligation types through complete lifecycles with deterministic scheduling. Verify ghost counters are zero at completion.
(9) Cross-obligation interaction: test scenarios where multiple obligation types interact (SendPermit held while Lease is active), verify no cross-contamination.

PROPERTY-BASED TESTS (proptest):
(10) Random obligation lifecycle sequences: generate random create/transfer/release sequences, verify invariants (no aliasing, no leak) hold for all valid sequences.
(11) Random cancellation injection: generate random task trees with random cancel points, verify all obligations released after quiescence.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each test logs: test_name, proof_tool_used, verification_time_ms, ghost_counter_final, obligations_created, obligations_released, obligations_leaked (must be 0). On ghost counter mismatch: log full obligation lifecycle trace with create/transfer/release events. CI summary: proofs_verified, runtime_checks_passed, mutations_caught.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) All formal proofs verify successfully in CI. (2) Runtime ghost counter checks pass for 10000 random obligation lifecycles. (3) All mutation tests detect the injected bug (either proof tool or runtime check). (4) Zero obligation leaks across all cancellation scenarios. (5) Tests complete in under 5 minutes on CI.

title: Implement futurelock detector (lab/debug)
description:
# Futurelock Detector (lab/debug)

## Purpose
Detect and surface the design-rule violation:

> Never allow a primitive to stop being polled while holding an obligation without transferring it, aborting/nacking it, or escalating.

In practice this shows up as a *futurelock*: a task holds one or more unresolved obligations (permits/acks/leases/IoOps) but is no longer being polled (e.g. it awaited something that never wakes, or it was dropped/forgotten by a buggy primitive).

Phase 0 needs this in **lab/debug** mode so we can turn “subtle deadlocks/leaks” into deterministic test failures with actionable evidence.

## Spec Background
- Design Bible §8.6: “Futurelock detector”
- Operational Semantics §1.9 + §3.4: obligations are linear; leaks are semantic errors
- Key invariant: a region cannot close while obligations in the region remain `Reserved`

A futurelock is *strictly worse* than a normal leak:
- a leak is “task completed while holding obligation”
- a futurelock is “task *didn’t* complete, but is also no longer being polled, so it can’t resolve the obligation”

## Design (Plan-of-Record)
### Observable behavior
When enabled, the lab runtime MUST:
1. Detect tasks that hold ≥1 `Reserved` obligations and have not been polled for a bounded number of lab steps (configurable).
2. Emit a trace-visible event with enough context to debug.
3. Optionally fail-fast (panic) in lab mode when the threshold is exceeded.

### Data we need
- `last_polled_step: u64` per task (updated every time we poll the task).
- Ability to query “held obligations” per task (from the obligation registry).
- Global `step_counter: u64` in the lab runtime.

### Detection rule
On each lab step (or at least whenever the scheduler makes progress):
- For each task `t` that currently holds ≥1 `Reserved` obligation:
  - if `step_counter - last_polled_step(t) > futurelock_max_idle_steps` then `futurelock_detected(t, …)`.

We should explicitly ignore tasks that are already terminal.

### Trace model
Add a semantic trace event (names flexible):
- `TraceEvent::FuturelockDetected { task: TaskId, region: RegionId, idle_steps: u64, held: Vec<ObligationId>, kinds: Vec<ObligationKind> }`

Constraints:
- The trace event must be deterministic and stable.
- Do NOT allocate on the hot path in production; this is lab/debug functionality.

### Config knobs
Add lab config fields (names flexible):
- `futurelock_max_idle_steps: u64` (default: conservative but small, e.g. 10_000)
- `panic_on_futurelock: bool` (default: true in lab tests)

## Testing
### Unit tests
- Construct a tiny obligation registry state where a task holds a reserved obligation and has an old `last_polled_step`; assert detection triggers.

### E2E lab scenarios
- Scenario: task reserves a SendPermit and then awaits a future that never wakes; another task continues making progress so the lab runtime keeps stepping. Assert:
  - a FuturelockDetected trace event appears
  - (if enabled) the runtime panics with a message that includes task id + obligation ids

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deterministic detection in lab mode (same seed/config => same detection point and trace).
- Trace event contains enough context to debug (task, region, obligation ids/kinds, idle steps).
- Does not introduce stdout/stderr logging in core runtime (only trace + test harness output).
- Clear documentation in the issue text about what counts as a futurelock and what does not.
notes: Implemented futurelock detection in lab runtime (TraceEventKind::FuturelockDetected + TraceData::Futurelock) with config knobs + unit tests; still blocked in Beads by asupersync-1mm/asupersync-l6l/asupersync-jdg status.
close_reason: Implementation verified complete: FuturelockDetected trace event, TraceData::Futurelock, InvariantViolation::Futurelock, config knobs (futurelock_max_idle_steps, panic_on_futurelock), and detection logic all implemented in src/lab/runtime.rs. All dependencies satisfied.

title: [fuzz] fuzz/fuzz_targets/bytes_chain.rs:190-333 oversized-op panic checks construct fresh temp_chain instead of testing live chain
description:
bytes_chain.rs:190-200, 231-240, 258-267, 284-293, 329-333 — the "should panic on oversized op" branches construct a BRAND NEW `temp_chain = first_data.chain(second_data)` and assert THAT panics, instead of asserting the actual `chain` panics on the oversized op. Since temp_chain has the FULL original capacity (first_data.len() + second_data.len()) while the live chain has been advanced down to smaller remaining(), the two chains are NOT equivalent for the test in question.

Concrete divergence scenario:
  - first_data.len() = 100, second_data.len() = 100 → initial total 200
  - Several Advance{50} ops → chain.remaining() = 100, position = 100
  - Operation: CopyToSlice{dst_len=150} → can_copy = (150 <= 100) = false
  - Test branch line 231-240: creates `temp_chain = first_data.chain(second_data)` (FRESH, remaining=200)
  - temp_chain.copy_to_slice(&mut [0u8; 150]) → SUCCEEDS (200 >= 150)
  - panic::catch_unwind returns Ok (not Err)
  - assert!(result.is_err(), ...) FIRES (false negative — test reports panic-expected when none occurred)

Same pattern at every "underflow / oversized → expected panic" branch:
  - Advance oversized (190-200)
  - CopyToSlice underflow (231-240)
  - GetU8 underflow (258-267)
  - GetU16 underflow (284-293)
  - OversizedAdvance (329-333)

Effect: the panic-test branches are effectively dead — they assert behavior of a phantom temp_chain that has nothing to do with the live chain's state. Real underflow bugs in Buf::Chain (e.g., panic missing on a particular variant) would NOT be caught.

Suggested fix:
  Either (a) call the oversized op on the actual `chain` and catch_unwind that, OR
  (b) skip the panic-test branch entirely (the AssertEq invariants already ensure the chain's state matches shadow on the success path).

Option (a) requires care because catch_unwind on `chain` consumes/poisons it for subsequent ops — would need to either return early after the panic-test, or recreate chain after catching.

Option (b) is simpler — drop the panic-test arms entirely, document that the oversized-op behavior is tested elsewhere (e.g., dedicated unit tests in src/bytes/buf/chain.rs).

P2 because the test smells correct but isn't, masking real Buf::Chain panic-discipline regressions.

title: Three lib tests fail under fleet load (wall-clock races): blocking_pool mr_scaling_linearity, mysql dropped_result_set_query_keeps_connection_closed, consensus native_idle_udp_retry_ticks
description:
The cron watchdog's targeted-lib lane at fd8e9fe5b (10-11 04:30Z, 2.26 h on a loaded worker) failed 4 lib tests. One is pz66t0 (fixed in cda53c8fa). The other three are wall-clock races under fleet load; they passed in e8's later full-lib runs on 5a03368e6 and cda53c8fa:
- runtime::blocking_pool::comprehensive_metamorphic_tests::mr_scaling_linearity: tasks sleep 200 ms and are counted 50 ms after submission. A test thread descheduled for more than 200 ms counts pool1 after its first tasks finished: "base_in_flight=3, doubled_in_flight=8, ratio=2.67".
- database::mysql::tests::dropped_result_set_query_keeps_connection_closed: the scripted server waits 2 s for the client's cancellation ("wait for client cancellation: Timeout"), then closes. The client then reads EOF: "query unexpectedly completed before cancellation test point".
- distributed::consensus::authenticated::driver::retry::tests::native_idle_udp_retry_ticks_recover_loss_and_retire_owned_receives: a 5 s recovery deadline elapsed ("native UDP loss recovery deadline: Elapsed").
Each new red in a watchdog run is bisected serially with full-lib probes (about 2 h each), so one flaky red holds the watchdog for most of a day and can blame an innocent commit.
Fix (test-only):
- the scaling tasks hold their worker on a release flag until the measurement, which happens once both pools are saturated (same 1.5..=2.5 oracle);
- the mysql peer's bounds go to 30 s;
- the consensus recovery deadline goes to 30 s.
Controls inject the delay that load causes (250 ms before the scaling measurement, 2.5 s before the mysql release, one 6 s stall of the consensus poll). Origin must go red under them and the fix must stay green.

title: LoadShed: an idle overloaded handle keeps its ConcurrencyLimit FIFO wait again since 8ef1cd867 (1sxucf H1 regression)
description:
8ef1cd867 (tw9dg0) moved LoadShed's release of the inner readiness from poll_ready's Pending branch into call. That reintroduces 1sxucf H1 for an idle handle: an overloaded LoadShed handle that polls ready but never calls (for example a clone whose caller checks readiness and decides not to send) keeps its inner wait. Under ConcurrencyLimit that wait is a queued OwnedAcquireFuture on a strictly FIFO Semaphore ("a try-acquire would wait for capacity or an earlier FIFO waiter"), so once the active request finishes, every later acquirer is blocked behind a waiter nobody polls: other handles shed or hang until the idle one polls again or is dropped. readiness_tests::shed_idle_clone_cannot_keep_the_semaphore_queue_head does not catch it because it always calls the shed handle after polling it.

8ef1cd867 was made to satisfy load_shed_reuses_its_probe_waker_while_shedding_over_a_full_buffer (1sxucf M1), which asserts the overloaded task is queued in the Buffer and woken exactly once. Its guard is against waker growth (one waker per shed request); an overloaded LoadShed returns Ready immediately and needs no wake, so zero queued wakers satisfies M1's intent.

Fix: release the inner readiness again when the inner service is Pending (keep the call-time release, harmless), relax M1's assertion to "at most one wake" with the reason, and add a test where the shed handle polls ready, never calls, and another ConcurrencyLimit handle must still acquire after the active request ends.

title: [fuzz-gap] raptorq/proof.rs: DecodeProof::replay_and_verify has no fuzz target — adversarial ReceivedSymbol stream may panic or OOM during replay
description:
src/raptorq/proof.rs:80 — DecodeProof::replay_and_verify(symbols: &[ReceivedSymbol]) is the canonical witness-checker for a previously-recorded decode proof. The proof itself is content-addressed (content_hash at line 65), but the symbols slice is fully attacker-controlled at replay time: any party that holds the proof and a malicious symbol vector can drive the decoder along the witness path with arbitrary data lengths, ESI values, and source/repair flags.

Input space the fuzz target would need to cover (1 byte per dimension is enough to seed):
  - symbols.len() in [0, K + sysmax_overshoot] including duplicates
  - per-symbol: kind in {Source, Repair}; esi in [0, 2^24); data length 0..symbol_size*4; coefficient byte for repair: arbitrary
  - K (config) in [1, 56_403]; symbol_size in [1, 65_535]
  - DecodeConfig combinations: inactivation_strategy, max_inactivation_threshold, time budget

Concrete risks the target should catch:
  (a) panic on out-of-range ESI (esi >= L for source) — index out of bounds
  (b) panic on length mismatch between symbol.data.len() and config.symbol_size
  (c) panic on duplicate ESIs that contradict the recorded peeling/elimination trace
  (d) infinite loop / pathological CPU when the proof's recorded pivot order is replayed against an inconsistent symbol set
  (e) OOM when symbols.len() is huge

Existing raptorq_decoder* fuzz targets exercise the FORWARD decode path; replay_and_verify is the BACKWARD oracle path with different invariants. They are not equivalent.

Fuzz target shape:
  fuzz_target!(|input: (DecodeConfigSeed, Vec<SymbolSeed>, ProofSeed)| {
      let config = DecodeConfig::from_seed(input.0);
      let proof  = DecodeProof::from_seed(input.2, &config);
      let syms   = input.1.into_iter().map(SymbolSeed::into_received).collect::<Vec<_>>();
      let _ = proof.replay_and_verify(&syms);  // must NEVER panic
  });

Source: /testing-fuzzing on src/raptorq/* (2026-04-26).
close_reason: Fixed in b7d241d92: raptorq_proof_replay fuzz target feeds DecodeProof::replay_and_verify arbitrary (DecodeConfig, ReceivedSymbol[]) tuples; asserts no panic, only Result<(), ReplayError>. Bounded by MAX_K=32, MAX_SYMBOL_SIZE=256, MAX_SYMBOLS=64.

title: dispatch_unary_with_stream_enforcement leaks stream registration when future is cancelled mid-await (RST_STREAM)
description: src/grpc/server.rs:1080 dispatch_unary_with_stream_enforcement registers the stream in the connection's active_streams map at line 1094, awaits the inner handler at line 1111, then unconditionally calls registry.remove_stream() at line 1114. Problem: if the awaiting future is dropped before the handler completes — which is exactly what happens when the client RST_STREAMs the in-flight stream and the transport propagates the cancel by dropping the dispatch future — the cleanup line is never reached. The stream stays in active_streams indefinitely (until idle_timeout, often minutes). DoS scenario: an attacker opens max_concurrent_streams+1 streams in rapid succession and RSTs each one mid-handler; the server's registry fills with leaked entries; subsequent legitimate streams fail with Status::resource_exhausted until idle_timeout sweeps. There is no Drop guard. Fix: replace the post-await remove_stream() with an RAII guard that decrements the active_streams count in its Drop impl, so cleanup runs whether the future completes, returns early, or is cancelled. Add regression test: poll the future once (registers the stream), drop it without polling further, then assert the registry's active_stream_count for the connection is 0.

title: WASM WritableStream cancellation misattributes old write to new buffer
description: src/io/browser_stream.rs WasmWritableStreamSink::poll_write stores only (old_len, old_promise). If write A enqueues its JS chunk and returns Pending, its Rust future is dropped, then write B polls after A resolves, the sink returns Ok(len(A)) without inspecting or enqueueing B. BrowserWritableStream accounting and Write/WriteAll treat that stale count as B progress, causing silent data loss or impossible over-report. Fix: drain prior JS promises without crediting the current buffer; after writer.ready, enqueue/copy the current chunk, retain its promise for deferred error/flush/shutdown observation, and return buffered acceptance for the current length. Add deterministic wasm-bindgen controlled-promise regressions for equal and unequal lengths. Independently confirmed by two fresh-eyes audits 2026-07-15; unchanged since 4696bd446 and no existing bead/test covers the pending-promise cancellation path.

- Without a deterministic replay harness, these features will be hard to validate and easy to regress.
- This bead provides the proof substrate so topology-aware features do not become unverifiable host magic.

Candidate surfaces:
- tests/* scheduler/runtime determinism suites
- src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs
- src/runtime/builder.rs and config seams for explicit topology descriptors

Required design:
1. Define an explicit topology fixture format (cohorts, worker placement, local/remote latency classes).
2. Ensure lab/runtime tests can inject topology deterministically without ambient host inspection.
3. Add reusable assertions for locality preference, spill behavior, and starvation safety.
4. Keep the harness usable by both scheduler and blocking-pool topology beads.

Proof / validation:
- Golden or snapshot coverage for topology fixtures and outcome traces.
- Regression proving identical results across reruns of the same topology scenario.
- At least one reusable helper consumed by another topology bead.

Success criteria:
- Topology-aware runtime features have replay-safe proofs instead of hand-wavy benchmark-only evidence.
design: Ship a reusable topology fixture DSL plus trace-comparison helpers before locality-aware behavior beads land. The harness must model cohorts, worker placement, and local-vs-remote latency classes without ambient host inspection, and it must be easy for both scheduler and blocking-pool tests to share.

title: [protocol-state-machine] http/h2/connection.rs: process_settings applies remote_settings non-atomically — settings before the failing one stay applied when a later setting in the same frame fails
description:
src/http/h2/connection.rs:1018-1059 — process_settings iterates the SettingsFrame's settings and applies each one to remote_settings sequentially. If the apply call fails on setting N, all settings 0..N have already been written to self.remote_settings; the function then returns Err and the connection is torn down via GOAWAY.

  for setting in &frame.settings {
      // ... validation checks ...
      self.remote_settings.apply(*setting)?;   // <-- early return on first failure
      // ... per-setting handlers update derived state ...
  }

The connection ends up in a half-applied state for the brief window between the partial apply and the GOAWAY emit. Concrete observable consequences:

  (a) **Stream window-size desync.** Setting::InitialWindowSize is applied to self.streams via set_initial_window_size BEFORE the next setting fails. If the subsequent failing setting (e.g., a malformed MAX_FRAME_SIZE = 16383, below MIN_MAX_FRAME_SIZE) is what triggers the error, the streams have their initial windows resized but NO ACK is sent. Any DATA frame queued in the brief window before GOAWAY is dispatched will be sized against the new (partially applied) window — potentially over-sending against the OLD window the peer believes is in effect. RFC 7540 §6.9.2: 'In addition to changing the flow-control window for streams that are not yet active, a SETTINGS frame can alter the initial flow-control window size for streams with active flow-control windows... A change to SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE can cause the available space in a flow-control window to become negative.' The tolerance for a partial apply is implementation-defined; partial application means the local-side bookkeeping diverges from the peer's expectation.

  (b) **HPACK encoder table size leak.** Setting::HeaderTableSize updates self.hpack_encoder.set_max_table_size before the failing setting. The HPACK encoder uses the new size for subsequent encodes; if the connection stays open (e.g., because GOAWAY drains for a while), HEADERS encoded during the drain use the half-applied table size — and the peer may not have ACKed it.

  (c) **Test-suite snapshot instability.** Settings frames carrying both 'good' and 'bad' values are a fuzz-corpus shape. The current code emits non-deterministic crashpacks because the partial-apply state depends on the iteration order of frame.settings (which is the wire order, fine) but the EXTERNAL effects (streams + hpack + flow control) are observed by snapshot tests as a non-RFC-compliant intermediate state.

Fix direction:
  1. Validate ALL settings in the frame BEFORE applying any. Compute the deltas to a temporary RemoteSettings clone, then commit the clone in one shot if validation passes.
  2. Or: apply settings to a staged buffer, only flush to remote_settings (and call set_initial_window_size / set_max_table_size / etc.) once the whole frame validates.
  3. Add a regression test that sends a SETTINGS frame with a valid InitialWindowSize followed by an invalid MaxFrameSize and asserts that streams' initial_window_size is UNCHANGED post-error.

Source: /multi-pass-bug-hunting on src/http/h1/* + h2/* + h3_native.rs (2026-04-26).
close_reason: process_settings stages settings onto a clone for atomic apply; on validation failure remote_settings + streams + hpack are untouched; regression test drives [valid-IWS, invalid-MFS] and asserts no partial state leaks

title: [PERF] timer wheel register() hot path: 26.4ns/insert baseline; cache WheelLevel.range_ns + drop redundant current_time() re-read
description: MEASURED BASELINE (RCH cargo bench --bench timer_wheel --features criterion-benches, build on remote fleet, no fabrication): timer_wheel/insert/single = [25.864 ns 26.371 ns 26.999 ns]; timer_wheel/insert/level0_1ms = [29.654 ns 30.090 ns 30.714 ns]. The TimerWheel::register hot path (src/time/wheel.rs:489 register -> insert_validated:524 -> insert_entry:638) is already lean (no per-call heap alloc after warmup; Waker is moved not cloned). HOTSPOT (code-inferred; flamegraph infra is fleet-blocked so this is NOT a profiler-attributed breakdown): the dominant per-insert cost is the inherent data movement of self.active.insert(generation) (slab) + level.slots[slot].push(entry) into Vec<Vec<TimerEntry>> (TimerEntry ~40B incl. Waker). Two concrete, behavior-preserving MICRO-optimizations (each likely ~1-3ns, i.e. within criterion noise on a 26ns op — measure carefully before claiming a delta): (1) WheelLevel::range_ns() (wheel.rs:303) recomputes resolution_ns.saturating_mul(SLOTS_PER_LEVEL) on every call; its only caller is the insert scan loop (wheel.rs:658, up to 4x/insert). Cache it as a range_ns:u64 field set in WheelLevel::new() (wheel.rs:294). (2) insert_validated (wheel.rs:524) computes  then DISCARDS it (_current param) while insert_entry (wheel.rs:638) re-reads current_time() (field read + saturating_mul) — defeating the comment's stated 'avoids a redundant current_time() read'. insert_entry is shared by 4 advance/promotion callers (wheel.rs:781,799,812,934), so add a hot-path insert_entry_at(entry,current) variant for register and keep the self-computing one for the advance callers. STRUCTURAL alternative if the Vec-of-Vecs allocation becomes a real hotspot under high churn: the alloc-free src/time/intrusive_wheel.rs intrusive variant. Measured+filed by SapphireHill 2026-06-14.
notes: Implemented src/time/wheel.rs hot-path slice: WheelLevel caches range_ns at construction and register/try_register now use a current-aware insert_entry_at helper instead of discarding the precomputed current. Local rustfmt --edition 2024 --check src/time/wheel.rs and git diff --check passed. One scoped RCH cargo test was attempted exactly once: build 29887347701055610 (cargo test -p asupersync --lib --features test-internals time::wheel::tests -- --nocapture) failed before timer-wheel tests due concurrent peer-owned QUIC TLS edits adding QuicTlsError::ServerCertificateUnverified without all match arms in the synced tree; no retry per fleet discipline.
close_reason:
Optimization committed in 064a9ceee (WheelLevel.range_ns cached at construction; insert_validated/register use insert_entry_at(entry,current) instead of discarding the precomputed current + re-reading current_time()). Both micro-opts from the bead are in HEAD; src/time/wheel.rs clean.

AFTER-BENCH (controlled same-host criterion A/B, no fabrication): reverse-applied 064a9ceee -> bench --save-baseline before; restored HEAD -> bench --baseline before. CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/rch_target_asupersync_bench, --features test-internals,criterion-benches, filter timer_wheel/insert, via rch. This fleet host runs ~58ns/insert (vs the 26.4ns recorded baseline = ~2.2x slower/more-loaded host, which is exactly why a cross-run before/after vs 26.4ns would be meaningless and a same-host criterion A/B was used).

RESULT — No statistically significant change on any insert benchmark:
  level0_1ms: 58.5ns, change +0.76% [-6.5%, +8.4%] (p=0.84) — No change
  level1_1s:  59.2ns, change +2.75% [-4.5%, +10.7%] (p=0.47) — No change
  level2_1min:59.5ns, change +2.56% [-4.9%, +10.1%] (p=0.49) — No change
  level3_1h:  59.1ns, change +1.95% [-4.9%, +9.3%] (p=0.60) — No change
  overflow_48h:78.1ns, change +2.03% [-5.0%, +9.9%] (p=0.59) — No change
  (single scrolled off the captured tail; conclusion uniform.)

HONEST CONCLUSION: the micro-opt is below the criterion noise floor on the loaded shared fleet — exactly as the bead predicted ('each likely ~1-3ns, i.e. within criterion noise on a 26ns op'). NO measurable speedup, but also NO regression; the change is a strictly-fewer-instructions cleanup (removes a saturating_mul up to 4x/insert + a redundant current_time() read+mul) and is behavior-preserving (reverse/forward git-apply round-trips exactly; bench correctness ran). A measurable delta would require a quiet/dedicated host; not worth blocking a P3 on dedicated perf infra. Closing as implemented + measured. Did NOT fabricate a speedup. Bench correctness verified by SapphireHill 2026-06-14 per user direction (CobaltForge was the holder; coordinated via Agent Mail; no source edits beyond the transient local A/B which was fully restored to HEAD).

title: atp/quic: receiver rejects every RELATIVE destination path with 'No such file or directory' after the manifest (prepare_quic_destination_root walks the empty ancestor after create_dir_all); shipped in v0.4.10 and v0.4.11
close_reason: Landed bad26eba5: QUIC receiver accepts relative destinations (empty ancestor skipped after create_dir_all); RED unit+e2e NotFound on old code, GREEN units 241/0, e2e sweep 20/0/1, clippy + fmt clean

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
Found (SapphireHill, 2026-09-10T06:50Z) while running the 0gj4k3 encrypted bad/broken matrix: the very first cell (500K/bad/atp-quic-tls13, pre-9bb6pt binary) failed with the receiver dying right after the manifest — recv.time: "[atp-quic] receiver: manifest transfer=... total_bytes=512000" then "atp failed: io error: No such file or directory (os error 2)"; the sender then re-sent into the void until its 360 s proof timeout. The harness passes RELATIVE paths (artifacts/atp_bench_matrix/<run>/cells/.../recv), so every cell would have failed the same way; the run was stopped after one rep (artifacts/atp_bench_matrix/20260910T063223Z_0gj4k3_pre, results.jsonl 1 row, status=error) and its netns removed.

Reproduced on plain loopback, no netns, with both the pre-9bb6pt and the current-HEAD release binaries (atp 0.4.11): `atp recv recvdest/recv --listen 127.0.0.1:47002 --transport quic --once ...` fails identically; the same command with an absolute destination commits sha_ok=true. So it is the destination spelling, not the bench.

Root cause: src/net/atp/transport_quic/mod.rs prepare_quic_destination_root (introduced by f06cab3d4 on 2026-07-10, "wire metadata-preservation policy into the QUIC, TCP, and RQ transports"; present in v0.4.10 and v0.4.11). It walks `dest_dir.ancestors()` twice — before create_dir_all (tolerating NotFound) and after it (NotFound is an error there, deliberately: an ancestor that vanishes after the create is suspicious). For a relative path the ancestors() walk ends at the EMPTY path, which names no file, so symlink_metadata("") fails with ENOENT and the post-create pass returns it as the receive error. Every other ancestor walk in the three transports already filters the empty ancestor (`.filter(|path| !path.as_os_str().is_empty())` in quic_safe_base..., transport_tcp, or tolerates NotFound in the RQ/TCP pre-checks); this one did neither. Absolute paths end at "/" and were never affected, which is why the e2e suite (absolute tempdirs) and the July benches (older binaries) never saw it.

Fix (working tree): both loops skip the empty ancestor; no other behaviour change (a real vanished ancestor after the create still fails closed). Tests: unit prepare_quic_destination_root_accepts_a_relative_path (transport_quic_tests.rs; a tempdir created inside the package-local target/ so its path is relative to the test cwd) and the public-API reproducer real_udp_quic_transfer_accepts_a_relative_destination_directory (tests/atp_quic_real_udp_transfer_e2e.rs, send_path -> receive_on_endpoint over real UDP into a relative destination, asserting the commit, the bytes and no staging residue). RED = base HEAD + the two test files overlaid; GREEN adds mod.rs; then the full e2e sweep, transport_quic units, strict clippy, fmt. Escaped-defect notes: found by the in-repo bench harness, not a downstream report; no downstream canary exists for the CLI relative-destination path; the CLI (`atp recv <relative>`) is the same public sequence the e2e reproducer exercises one layer below (receive_on_endpoint), and the release-binary loopback repro above covers the CLI layer.

title: [perf] sync/mutex.rs: O(N) waiter scan in LockFuture::poll and cleanup_waiter
description: src/sync/mutex.rs:265 (cleanup_waiter) and :349 (poll re-register path) both do state.waiters.iter().position(|w| w.id == waiter_id) — linear scan over a VecDeque<Waiter> to find a waiter by its monotonic u64 id. Under contention with N concurrent waiters, every poll/cancel does O(N) scan; total work for N waiters becomes O(N²). The waker-update path (line 349) also does this scan every time a poll re-attempts (e.g., after spurious wake or waker change). Mitigation: maintain a parallel HashMap<u64, position-or-handle> alongside the VecDeque, OR use an intrusive linked-list slab keyed by id, OR replace the queue with parking_lot::WaiterQueue (purpose-built for this). Severity HIGH for high-contention async mutexes (per-task waker churn × N waiters).
close_reason: Fixed in f49630a8e: O(1) waiter cleanup via slab-backed intrusive doubly-linked list. WaiterChain replaces VecDeque<Waiter>; cleanup_waiter, poll's still-queued check, unlock, grant_next_waiter, and push_front (re-register-at-front for cancel-on-grant) are all O(1). FIFO contract preserved. waiter_id changed from monotonic u64 to slab index (usize); next_waiter_id counter removed.

title: [cap-boundary] cancel/symbol_cancel: ungated pub new_for_test allows cancel token forgery
description:
SymbolCancelToken::new_for_test (src/cancel/symbol_cancel.rs:499) is a PUBLIC function without cfg(test)/feature gating. Any consumer crate can call it to forge arbitrary cancel tokens with controlled token_id and object_id. This bypasses all cancel-protocol invariants and allows unsanitized code to fabricate tokens that cancel unrelated tasks.

ATTACK: Production crate depends on asupersync; malicious dep chains call SymbolCancelToken::new_for_test(attacker_token_id, victim_task_object_id) to poison the cancel graph.

FIX: Gate the function with #[cfg(any(test, feature="test-internals"))] to match the pattern already applied to Cx::for_testing* constructors (br-asupersync-2x6hbi).
close_reason: SymbolCancelToken::new_for_test now gated behind cfg(any(test, feature = test-internals)); production builds compile-fail on any reference; only existing caller is the in-file test module. Regression test pins the forgery shape and the gate's purpose.

title: Fuzz src/http/h2/hpack.rs block-start size update sequencing
description:
Target: `src/http/h2/hpack.rs`

Harness target: a dedicated HPACK decoder oracle for consecutive block-start table-size updates and stale dynamic-index rejection.

Concrete corpus seed:
- insert one dynamic entry via incremental indexing
- next header block begins with dynamic table size update `0`, then a second update back to `128`
- same block then attempts an indexed reference to the previously inserted dynamic entry

Oracle:
1. Consecutive dynamic table size updates are only accepted at block start.
2. The intermediate shrink to `0` is applied before the later grow.
3. A stale dynamic-table index is rejected after the eviction.
4. Decoder state remains usable for the next valid block after the rejection path.
close_reason: Added fuzz target hpack_block_start to verify HPACK dynamic table size update rules per RFC 7541.

title: transport_params validate(): is_forbidden_for_{client,server} are swapped/wrong -> server accepts client-forbidden params AND client rejects legitimate server params (RFC9000 18.2 fail-open + false-reject)
close_reason: FALSE POSITIVE (verified). validate(is_server) validates an endpoint's OWN OUTGOING params before the handshake (is_server = 'am I the server'), NOT received peer params — confirmed by test_forbidden_parameters (transport_params.rs:944-979): a client (validate(false)) with a server-only param FAILS; a server (validate(true)) is OK. The current is_forbidden_for_client (the 4 server-only params) + is_forbidden_for_server (false-for-all, a server may send every param) are CORRECT for that model, and the planned swap would have BROKEN the passing test + correct behavior. Landed a DOC-ONLY clarity fix (no behavior change) explaining the own-outgoing-params semantics + a 'do not fix this to true' note so the next audit doesn't repeat the misread. Separately noted (NOT a bug in current code): rejecting a PEER's forbidden params on receipt is a not-yet-wired future concern that would use inverted sets.

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text: Found during c5d0q fresh-eyes audit of transport_params.rs. validate(is_server) at line 431: line 448 'is_server && param.is_forbidden_for_server()' and line 451 '!is_server && param.is_forbidden_for_client()'. Per RFC 9000 18.2 these 4 params are SERVER-ONLY (a client MUST NOT send them): OriginalDestinationConnectionId, PreferredAddress, StatelessResetToken, RetrySourceConnectionId. Required net behavior: a SERVER validating the params it received from the client must REJECT those 4; a CLIENT validating the server's params must ACCEPT them. CURRENT CODE IS DOUBLY WRONG: is_forbidden_for_server (124-130) returns false for everything (both match arms -> false) so a server ACCEPTS the 4 forbidden params from a hostile client (fail-open). is_forbidden_for_client (113-122) returns true for those 4, so a CLIENT validating REJECTS a server's legitimate server-only params (false-reject, breaks real servers). FIX (swap-bodies): is_forbidden_for_server -> matches!(self, OriginalDestinationConnectionId|PreferredAddress|StatelessResetToken|RetrySourceConnectionId); is_forbidden_for_client -> false (RFC 9000 has no client-only params a server is forbidden to send). NOTE: existing validate() tests (transport_params.rs:886-1089, e.g. 978 validate(true).is_ok / 886 validate(false).is_err) pin the current behavior and MUST be reviewed/updated when fixing. LATENT today: decode()/validate() are exported but NOT yet wired into a live handshake (no production caller), and decode() does NOT auto-call validate() so range/forbidden checks only run if the integrator calls validate() — a second fail-open foot-gun (consider decode()->validate() or a must-validate marker type). Also (defense-in-depth): max_udp_payload_size (468) has a lower bound (>=1200) but no upper cap -> a consumer that casts it to u16/u32 or sizes a buffer on it could truncate/over-allocate; clamp to <=65527 here or document consumer must clamp. Filed under c5d0q audit; not landed (subtle RFC semantics + test updates in not-yet-wired code, build currently gated by peer transport_quic WIP).

## B1: 1da8da1a1 (ATP receiver journal: durable finalize of cancelled commits, file receiver recovery)
Sound:
- data and its directory are synced before each journal record;
- Finalizing precedes the commit, and resolve_finalizing checks identity, exact length and SHA-256 and syncs before Committed;
- every drop point leaves recoverable Finalizing or durable Committed, never Committed with missing data;
- a hostile journal stores no names, is bounded, and cannot panic;
- both files are flocked.
Findings:
- MEDIUM M1: file.rs ~302-322 (test ~1085). Appending Finalizing reserves no room for the Committed record. With the journal near max_snapshots, the application commit runs, Committed fails with StorageFull, and the pair is stuck for good; resolve_finalizing also fails StorageFull. Deterministic: max_snapshots 4 plus a one-epoch transfer, with each reconnect using a snapshot. The commit's own test asserts the stuck state. - LOW L1: file.rs ~528-552, tests/atp_receiver_journal.rs ~685. resolve_finalizing is documented as valid only for the built-in file sink, but the journal does not record the sink. ## B2: 6dd91ac7a (HTTP/2 liveness and admission on shared ports, src/http/auto.rs)
Sound:
- one private Http2Options applies the six Http2Listener builders, for both run and run_in;
- prior-knowledge and TLS ALPN-h2 share serve_h2_connection;
- defaults, clamping and behaviour at a limit match the dedicated listener;
- no new counters, so no leak or bypass;
- builder-only additions; HttpAutoListener postdates v0.4.3.
Findings:
- MEDIUM M1: auto.rs ~885-895 vs h2/listener.rs ~3563-3567, ~2649-2661. On TLS shared ports the write-progress counter sits above TLS, while the dedicated listener counts beneath it, so its deadline renews on every socket write. Each flush must drain rustls's ~64 KiB buffer within the timeout with no renewal, so a client slower than ~6.4 KiB/s at the 10 s default (or ~32 KiB/s at 2 s) is killed; the dedicated listener keeps it. The root cause predates the commit, but the commit makes the timeout configurable and claims parity. Fix: wrap the TcpStream in the byte counter before acceptor.accept and carry it through the handoff.
- LOW L1: tests/http_auto_listener.rs ~169-180, ~506-529. The keepalive test can flake: next_for discards stream-0 PINGs, so a response delayed 100 ms or more swallows PING #3.
- LOW L2: http2_write_progress_timeout has no test, and the new options are tested only via run, not run_in.
- LOW L3: grpc/server.rs ~1418-1437, ~1536-1560. A gRPC server's configured keepalive is still not applied on a shared port, so finding F7 is half closed. Translating it by hand is risky: gRPC treats timeout 0 as 20 s, but http2_keepalive turns 0 into 1 ms. Expose gRPC's mapping as a helper.

## B3: e6537c737 (region-owned remote invocation handles) and 4000c9fab (pre-TLS per-IP limits)
Sound:
- e6537c737: the owner task and the invocation region live in the caller's region. Drop, abort, close, parent close and owner panic all send a remote cancel and still wait for the result. The lease is released once, and the wait is bounded on the native runtime.
- 4000c9fab: the slot is taken before TLS and released exactly once by the connection guard on every path. Entries are pruned at zero, Some(0) refuses all, and the config struct has private fields.
Findings:
- MEDIUM (4000c9fab): remote.rs ~8338-8354, ~8768-8774. `asupersync remote serve` builds its config from TOML with no per-IP key, and unknown keys are rejected, so CLI deployments cannot enable the cap. Owner decision: a new TOML key, or a default.
- LOW: remote_owned.rs ~497-500. A close, abort or parent cancel landing between the owner's last checkpoint and its return gives a "cancelled" join error, losing the remote result and lease settlement (possibly a committed success). Nothing leaks, but the docs promise the report survives.
- LOW: remote_owned.rs ~572. run_remote whose polling task is aborted while its explicit Cx is not now waits until the configured timeout instead of stopping promptly.
- LOW: tests. The cancel and drop tests would pass without the owner's explicit child-region cancel. No test checks that the cancel reason reaches the remote side, and there is no owner-panic test.
- LOW: server/connection.rs ~259. IPv6 is keyed by full address, so rotating through a /64 evades the cap.
- LOW: each V3 operation uses its own connection, so the per-IP cap also limits an authenticated origin's concurrent operations. Refusals look like network errors and are reported together with global and drain refusals.

The dedicated `conformance/` crate has no region-close suite. `conformance/src/tests/runtime.rs` and `negative.rs` touch spawn semantics, but they never assert that region close waits for live children and finalizers before returning.

title: [SUB-EPIC] Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver
description:
# Sub-Epic: Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver

## Purpose

Define the platform-agnostic reactor interface and integrate it with the runtime's IoDriver. This is the foundation upon which all platform-specific reactors (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) are built.

## Background

The reactor abstraction already exists in stub form at `src/runtime/reactor/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub trait Reactor {
    fn register(&self, source: &dyn Source, interest: Interest) -> io::Result<Registration>;
    fn deregister(&self, registration: Registration) -> io::Result<()>;
    fn poll(&self, events: &mut Events, timeout: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<usize>;
    fn wake(&self) -> io::Result<()>;
}
```

We need to:
1. Finalize this trait design
2. Implement proper Registration/Token management
3. Integrate with IoDriver for waker coordination
4. Design the Source trait for I/O sources (sockets, pipes, etc.)

## Design Considerations

### Waker Efficiency
Phase 0 uses `wake_by_ref()` which causes immediate re-poll. Real reactor needs:
- Slab-based waker storage (like mio/tokio)
- Token → TaskId mapping for targeted wakeups
- Batch processing of ready events

### Cancel-Correctness for I/O
When a task is cancelled mid-I/O:
- Deregister interest immediately
- Any in-flight data may be lost (documented behavior)
- Registration cleanup must be atomic

### Two-Phase I/O Operations
For cancel-safety, consider:
```rust
// Reserve phase: register interest, get permit
let permit = stream.reserve_read(cx).await?;
// Commit phase: perform actual read
let bytes = permit.read(buf)?;  // Linear, must happen
```

This is optional for basic I/O but important for advanced patterns.

## Key Types to Define/Refine

1. **Registration** - Handle to registered I/O source
2. **Token** - Compact ID for mapping events to wakers
3. **Interest** - Bitflags for READABLE/WRITABLE/ERROR
4. **Source** - Trait for things that can be registered (sockets, pipes)
5. **Events** - Container for ready events from poll()

## Integration Points

- `RuntimeState`: Hold reactor instance
- `IoDriver`: Bridge between reactor events and task wakers
- `Cx`: Provide IoCap capability tier for I/O registration
- `Scheduler`: Wake tasks when their I/O is ready

## Deliverables

1. Finalized `Reactor` trait with complete documentation
2. `Source` trait for registerable I/O sources
3. `Registration`, `Token`, `Interest`, `Events` types
4. `IoDriver` implementation with slab-based waker storage
5. Runtime integration (reactor in RuntimeState)
6. Unit tests for token allocation/deallocation

title: Epic: Distributed Structured Concurrency (Phase 4)
description:
# Epic: Distributed Structured Concurrency (Phase 4)

## Overview

This epic extends Asupersync's structured concurrency guarantees to distributed systems. Tasks can span multiple machines while preserving the region ownership model, cancel-correctness, and quiescence guarantees.

## Background & Context

The Asupersync roadmap defines Phase 4 as distributed structured concurrency. This is the most ambitious phase, applying the runtime's formal semantics across network boundaries.

Key insight: **The same invariants that make local concurrency safe also make distributed systems reliable.**

- Region close = quiescence → Graceful distributed shutdown
- Cancellation protocol → Network-aware cancellation propagation
- Obligation tracking → Distributed transaction guarantees
- Two-phase effects → Saga/compensating transactions

## Challenges

Distributed systems introduce:
1. **Partial failure**: Some nodes fail while others continue
2. **Network partitions**: Nodes can't communicate temporarily
3. **Clock skew**: No global time, only happens-before
4. **At-most-once vs at-least-once**: Message delivery semantics

## Design Principles

1. **Remote regions are regions**: Same ownership model, same close semantics
2. **Leases for remote resources**: Time-bounded claims, renewable
3. **Idempotency tokens**: Safe retries for at-least-once delivery
4. **Saga pattern**: Compensating transactions for multi-step operations
5. **Logical clocks**: Lamport/vector clocks, not wall time

## Architecture

```
LocalRuntime ←→ RemoteProxy ←→ Network ←→ RemoteRuntime

RemoteSpawn:
  - Create task/actor on remote node
  - Returns RemoteHandle with lease
  
RemoteRegion:
  - Distributed region spanning multiple nodes
  - Close requires quiescence across all nodes
  
Lease:
  - Time-bounded claim on remote resource
  - Must renew before expiry or resource released
  
IdempotencyToken:
  - Unique ID for deduplication
  - Enables safe retry on failure
```

## Components

1. **RemoteSpawn**: Spawn tasks on remote nodes
2. **Lease Manager**: Track and renew resource leases
3. **Idempotency Registry**: Deduplicate retried operations
4. **Saga Executor**: Multi-step transactions with compensation
5. **Distributed Cancel**: Propagate cancellation across nodes
6. **Logical Clocks**: Happens-before ordering

## Success Criteria

- Tasks can spawn on remote nodes
- Remote regions close to quiescence
- Cancellation propagates across network
- Leases prevent orphaned resources
- Sagas provide transaction guarantees
- Lab runtime can simulate network conditions

## Dependencies

This epic BLOCKS on:
- bd-3t9g: Actor System (remote actors build on local actors)
- bd-1j64: Runtime Core Maturity (stable local runtime first)

## References

- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 4.3: Execution Tiers (Remote)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 6: Distributed Extensions
- Pat Helland: 'Life Beyond Distributed Transactions'

## Non-Goals (for Phase 4)

- Full consensus protocol implementation (use external like Raft)
- Persistent storage layer (integrate with existing DBs)
- Service mesh / network infrastructure

title: Mutex audit (10-09): lock_until reports the running task's cancellation as TimedOut (and can spin a retry loop); a panicking waker destructor poisons a just-acquired mutex
description:
Read-only audit of the async Mutex (src/sync/mutex.rs, mutex_cancel_tests.rs), focused on d7ba86cfe (cancellation wakes blocked acquisition; landed uncompiled 10-07) and its follow-ups 4d74ed03e, 2f6397d72, 80ff2a552, at origin 2094e0220 (SapphireHill rc_20260923 audit agent, 10-09; M1 re-verified by SapphireHill). No HIGH: the hand-off holds two invariants under the state lock (locked => no waiter holds a grant; unlocked and no grant => queue empty), so the lock is never granted to nobody or twice; cancel registration, repeated polls, poll after Ready, try_lock / is_locked, the boxed deadline Sleep and guard-drop wake were checked and are sound.

## MEDIUM
M1. lock_until treats the running task's cancellation as a timeout. poll_deadline_sleep (mutex.rs ~446) polls the deadline with the cancel-aware Sleep::poll, which returns Ready early when the ambient Cx::current() is cancelled (sleep.rs ~789-811, acknowledging that cancellation as a side effect); the mutex reads that as TimedOut(deadline). Sleep::poll_deadline (sleep.rs ~736, 2149fd860) exists for exactly this and app.rs / scope.rs / permit.rs / mysql.rs use it. It fires when the cx given to lock_until is not the running task's context (an explicit authority, or a parent cx captured into a child task): the waiter gets Err(TimedOut) about the full deadline early, while plain lock() ignores the same cancellation. A fresh lock_until polled twice in one poll (~560, then ~691) also defeats Sleep's one-trip guard, so each .await can finish TimedOut without yielding, and a loop retrying on TimedOut spins on a current_thread runtime where the holder can never run. Fix: poll_deadline at ~446.

## LOW
L2. A panicking waker destructor poisons the mutex right after a successful acquire (~517-523, from d7ba86cfe): on Ready(Ok(guard)) poll drops the cancel observer and the boxed Sleep, running user RawWaker destructors while the guard is held; a panic there drops the guard while panicking, and MutexGuard::drop poisons the mutex although no critical section ran. Fix: drop both helpers inside catch_unwind, release the result normally, then resume the panic.
L3. The "recheck after waker callbacks" step (~575) is untested: deleting it leaves all mutex_cancel_tests green (the race it guards is harmless; the commit message overstates it).

title: native QUIC never transmits CONNECTION_CLOSE on a local close (begin_close only enters Draining; sends are refused; no production frame construction)

comments.author: SapphireHill
comments.text:
Evidence (SapphireHill, 2026-09-10, while reviewing the lwoixd lifecycle patch; base db14f9ed7):

The native QUIC stack never transmits a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame for a locally initiated close.
- `NativeQuicConnection::begin_close` (src/net/quic_native/connection.rs:1449) calls `transport.start_draining_with_code`, which only sets `close_code` and enters `Draining` (src/net/quic_native/transport.rs); `close_immediately` sets `Closed`.
- `ensure_packet_send_state` refuses every packet send in `Draining | Closed` (connection.rs ~2110), and `drain_connection_frames_inner` (with lwoixd) returns no output for those states.
- No production code constructs `QuicFrame::ConnectionClose { .. }` under src/net/quic_native, src/net/quic_core or src/net/atp/transport_quic; the only constructions are in test modules. The peer therefore learns of our close only through its own idle timeout (or a later packet to a retired CID).

RFC 9000 s10.2: "An endpoint that wishes to communicate a fatal connection error MUST use a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame if it is able." s10.2.1: the closing endpoint SHOULD respond to incoming packets during the closing period by re-sending the close (rate-limited).

Fix shape: on `begin_close`/`close_immediately`, build one 1-RTT (or Initial/Handshake, matching the highest available key space) packet carrying `ConnectionClose { error_code, frame_type, reason }` before flipping the send gate, hand it to the managed endpoint's pending_outgoing as a terminal packet exempt from the terminal-output discard, keep the route for 3xPTO in a closing state that re-sends it on incoming packets, then reap. Coordinate with lwoixd (CopperOak) which owns the lifecycle deadlines.

title: [security-audit] Authentication bypass via crate-internal set_verified method
description:
src/security/authenticated.rs:91 exposes set_verified() as pub(crate), allowing any code within the asupersync crate to bypass authentication verification. An attacker who achieves code injection in any module can call AuthenticatedSymbol::set_verified(true) to mark unverified symbols as authenticated, bypassing HMAC-SHA256 verification entirely.

Attack Vector: AuthenticatedSymbol::from_parts(malicious_symbol, zero_tag).set_verified(true) → trusted symbol without cryptographic validation.

Fix: Change set_verified visibility to pub(super) or remove entirely, forcing verification through proper channels.
close_reason: done

title: [EPIC-TOKIO] Async Streams (tokio-stream equivalent)
description:
# Async Stream Infrastructure

## Overview
Stream trait and comprehensive combinators for async iteration with cancel-safety.

## Core Trait
```rust
pub trait Stream {
    type Item;
    fn poll_next(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>>;
}
```

## Combinator Categories

### 1. Transformation
- map, filter, filter_map
- flat_map, flatten
- then (async map)
- scan (stateful map)

### 2. Control Flow
- take, take_while
- skip, skip_while
- fuse
- peekable

### 3. Combination
- chain
- zip, zip_latest
- merge (non-deterministic)
- select_next_some

### 4. Buffering
- chunks, ready_chunks
- buffered, buffer_unordered

### 5. Timing
- throttle
- timeout (per-item)
- delay

### 6. Error Handling
- try_filter, try_filter_map
- try_fold, try_for_each
- catch_unwind

### 7. Collection
- collect
- fold, for_each
- next, try_next

## Channel Wrappers
- ReceiverStream (from mpsc)
- WatchStream (from watch)
- BroadcastStream (from broadcast)

## Cancel-Safety
All combinators respect cancellation at yield points.
Partial iteration is always safe.

## Lab Runtime
- Deterministic stream ordering
- Simulated delays
